Oṃ namaḥ śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥ | Śrītripurasundaryai namaḥ |

Oṃ! I perpetually bow down to that primordial Person, the God, upon whose pair of lotus feet the lotus-born Brahmā rests his heart and indeed creates the entire universe without flaw, while Viṣṇu protects it and Maheśa destroys it. 1.
Having beheld Lord Giriśa, Girijā, Gaṇeśa, Vāṇī, and the lords of sages, whose sprout-like feet are praised by them,
the *Jyāgamaka-vallī* is being composed by Yadunāthaśarman as a commentary upon the scripture.
Likewise.
Having examined the *Prapañcasārasiddhānta*, the *Śāradātilaka*, as well as the *Sārasamuccaya* together with its ancillary works; 1–3.
Having diligently provided the *Dīpikā*, as well as the *Laghudīpikā*,
the *Pūjāpradīpa*, and the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*.
The *Mantradarpaṇasiddhānta*, the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*,
the *Mantranetra*, the *Mantrārtha*, and the *Śrīrāmārcanacandrikā*.
The Mantramuktāvalī, Ratnāvalī, Jñānārṇava, and others; the Tantra of Sanatkumāra, the Nāradīya, and the Catuḥśatī. (1–6)
The Pūrṇayāga, the doctrine of Śomaśambhu, the Agastyasaṃhitā, and likewise the Vaiṣṇava Saṃhitā along with the Sāgara; || 1-7 ||
He [studied] with devotion the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Kapila, the venerable Saṃhitā of the Supreme Mantra,
and the Tantra of the venerable Bhuvaneśvarī, as well as the Siddhānta.
The ritual manual of Śrī Navadurgā, which consists of the Sanmohana;
likewise the Hayagrīvamata and the Vijñānabhārata. (1–9)
Having seen again and again the Śukla and the Mantrarāja,
as well as the Saṃhitā of all [the scriptures] and likewise the Piṅgalāmṛta.
And in the Vāmakeśvaratantra, the entire [teaching] of Rāmadīkṣita, the Siddhānta of Vijñāneśvara, and the essence of the Śrīsaṃhitās have been presented in sequence. (1–11)
The Vijñānalalitā, the Pāñcarātrī, and the Nārāyaṇī;
likewise the Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā, the Gārgyasaṃhitā, and the Bhairava.
[He composed] the Divyasārasvata, the Candrikā, the Kāmika, with devotion,
as well as the Homāvarottara and the Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha.
Likewise, he [revealed] the Vāyavī Saṃhitā, as well as the Brahma Saṃhitā,
the Kṛśānu Saṃhitā, and the Jāmalas originating from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others.
Likewise, the Yāmaloddhāra, the Matsyasūkta in due order, the dialogue between Pārvatī and Hara, and the Vārāhītantra—with great reverence. (1–15)
In the same manner, [he studied] the Yoginītantra sequentially in the Tripurārṇava, as well as the Īśānasaṃhitā and the Siddhānta of Viśvakarman. (1–16)
The *Tantra* of Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the *Saṃhitā* by Vaiśampāyana,
as well as the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi* and the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*.
The Kulārṇava, the Kulaśreṣṭha, and likewise the Haṃsapārāyaṇa;
various Purāṇas as well as the Smṛti scriptures and the Mahābhārata.
Having examined the treatises on astrology and the entire manual (paddhati) in its proper sequence, and having repeatedly consulted other compendia that exist; || 1-19 ||
Having extracted the essence of all [scriptures], the wise Lord of the Yadus has elaborated this manual of mantras, yantras, initiations, and so forth.

Having repeatedly contemplated the object of knowledge in accordance with wisdom, one attains that knowledge of the mantras residing in various tantras which is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (1.21)
Therefore, for their awakening, having deliberated with great effort, [the teachers] explain it concisely for the sake of knowledge of those of dull intellect. (1.22)
Nothing further is requested by me, the wise, with palms joined in supplication;
however, any deficiencies or excesses herein should be rectified by the magnanimous. (1.23)
2a) Likewise, I shall describe the defect pertaining to mortals who have been initiated;
knowing which, O best of beings, one should not perform initiation at all times.
In the Agastyasaṃhitā.
Let the wise hear the fault of those who, though possessing intelligence, have not been initiated:
for them, food is equal to excrement and water likewise equal to urine. (1.25)
If one performs a śrāddha for those who have not been initiated, or performs an initiation for one for whom a śrāddha has already been performed,
their ancestors, having taken [the offering], will fall into a most dreadful hell.
There is no doubt that [the fruits] fall [upon him], even as many as fourteen Indras,
provided he worships with thousands of ritual services while endowed with devotion.
Nevertheless, the gods do not accept the worship of one who is uninitiated;
since all ritual action is likewise [ineffective for him], therefore the uninitiated person is a *paśu* (a bound soul).
Therefore, having seen one who is uninitiated, one should not accomplish any rite;
for at the time of receiving initiation, the heap of sins is cast away. (1.29)
When that supreme [fire], joined with the state of Nirvana, goes forth, then it itself becomes the fulfillment of the rites for the gods and ancestors. (1.30)
Otherwise, whatever action is performed is like an oblation poured into ashes;
thus, the necessity of initiation in all stages of life is proclaimed.
Just as there is no protector on earth for a mantra that lacks its presiding deity,
so too for one devoid of initiation, there is no master either in this world or in the next.
Neither by austerities, nor by victories, nor by various fire-offerings, nor even by diverse means of practice,
does any ritual action ever attain success for one who is devoid of initiation.
The word "something" (kiṃcit) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
All recitation has initiation as its root; supreme austerity has initiation as its root.
Relying upon initiation, one may dwell in whichever stage of life (āśrama) one may be.
And one who dies without initiation shall go to the Raurava hell;
therefore, one should always diligently receive initiation from a Tantric master. (1.35)
But if a person, having seen the mantra during the eon, grasps it with arrogance,
no atonement whatsoever arises even after a thousand manvantaras.
It is certain that all those who have been initiated possess the qualification for this [practice].
Therefore, I shall first explain initiation in detail. (1.37)
And so it is said:
In the *Saṃhitā* [of the Mahābhārata], Vaiśampāyana addressed these words to Śaunaka:
"Because it bestows divine knowledge, and because it effects the destruction of sin... (1.38).
Therefore, that is declared as *dīkṣā* by the teachers who know the Tantras;
for as long as *dīkṣā*, which bestows the fruit of the goals of human existence, is not obtained. (1.39)
Initiation brings about all accomplishments and bestows all prosperity;
it grants radiant complexions and bestows beauty and physical vigor.
Delusion, paralysis, attraction, killing, and expulsion, as well as subjugation, poetic talent, and intellect endowed with the power of retention (dhāraṇā). 1-41.
It grants crossing over the ocean and coolness from fire; it brings victory in battle, as well as fearlessness in the forest, and likewise removes sorrow and suffering.
Without a doubt, she bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; this initiation accomplishes the impossible and makes even the non-divine divine.
Those from whom one receives the supreme initiation, which yields all desires upon this earth—they, being intent on the propitiation of the Guru, go to the highest abode. (1.44)
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Śrī-Āgamakalpalatā*.
2a) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple in the *Śrīmantramuktāvalī*.
The letter *ga* is declared to bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*), and the letter *ra* is the burner of sin.
The syllable *U* is said to be Viṣṇu; the supreme Guru is the essence of the triad.
Here, Gaṇeśa is joined with Agni and endowed with Viṣṇu. (2-2)
The mantra, consisting of two syllables, bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life;
and so it is stated in the Rudrayāmala:
Pure in his stainless nature, he was devoted to the practice of established conduct. || 2-3 ||
He should be a forest-dweller, a knower of the Vedas, free from anger, and learned in all the scriptures;
he should be full of faith, free from malice, pleasant-spoken, and of pleasing appearance.
Pure, well-attired, and youthful, he is devoted to the welfare of all beings; he is glorious, possessed of a steadfast mind, and capable of discerning between the auspicious and the inauspicious.
He should be wise, of cultivated intellect, tranquil, grateful, and affectionate toward his disciples;
capable of both restraint and favor, and devoted to patience and the sacred mantras.
One who knows the various kinds of delusion and is an abode of compassion for all beings—one endowed with such characteristics as these is a Guru, possessing the splendor of gravity. (2.7)
In the *Śrīśāradātilaka*:
"One who is pure by descent from both mother and father, pure in disposition, with senses subdued, who knows the essence of all Āgamas and understands the true meaning of all Śāstras. (2.8)
Devoted to helping others, intent upon recitation and worship, his word was never in vain; he was peaceful and had mastered the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas. || 2-9 ||
Following the path of yoga, he reached the heart of the deity;
capable of both withdrawal and retention, and self-controlled, he was the best of Brahmins. (2-10)
One who knows the secrets of the mantras, is a knower of mantras, and is the best among practitioners;
one who is noble, truthful in speech, and a householder—such a person is called a guru. (2-11)
Thus, endowed with such qualities, the Guru is approved by the Āgama; this is from the Devyāgama, the word of Śiva. (2-2)
Self-controlled, tranquil, of noble birth, humble, and wearing pure attire. || 2-12 ||
Pure in conduct, well-established, clean, dexterous, and wise;
devoted to the meditations of his stage of life and proficient in mantra and tantra. (2.13)
One who is capable of both punishing and favoring is designated as a guru;
and so it has been said in the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
Indeed, once the mantra has been received, it must always be kept secret by the practitioner.
A mantra that remains in the house of an enemy, or a mantra that is not recited regularly,
is a mantra devoid of consecration and bereft of the prescribed initiation.
Having abandoned it with every effort, it should be taken up again according to the prescribed rule. — *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa*
The initiation of a father is one thing, and the initiation of a forest-dweller is another. || 2.16 ||
And that initiation which belongs to one who is secluded is neither [merely] ritualistic nor bestowing [of results].
Thus it is stated in the Śrī Skanda Purāṇa.
O Maheśvarī, whatever mantra is to be accomplished, or an enemy who is to be subdued; || 2-17 ||
One should diligently abandon even a mantra obtained in a dream, as well as one received from a person of low caste or from a woman. (2-18)
One should avoid the initiation of a solitary ascetic or a father;
thus it is stated in the Vṛhad-matsya-sūkta.
One should not take up the mantra of one's father, nor likewise that of one's maternal grandfather. || 2-19 ||
Whether from a younger brother, a uterine sibling, or one who has taken the side of an enemy, or even through negligence or by command, one may likewise perform the initiation of the father. (2-20)
4a) Having then performed an expiation, one should undergo initiation once more;
[these include] the initiation of a father, the initiation of an ascetic, and the initiation of a forest-dweller. (2.21)
The initiation of those who do not belong to any stage of life (āśrama) is an initiation that destroys wealth;
thus it has been stated in the Śrī Nārāyaṇī Tantra.
One should not accept the mantra of one's father, nor that of one who has taken refuge in Śiva.
"Even if one should receive [the initiation] at some time, one must undergo consecration again.
From such statements, the meaning is that one should not receive the mantra from these [unqualified persons]. (2-23)
And so it is said:
If the mantra of the father (the Guru) lacks potency, it does not cause fault in the Śaiva or Śākta [traditions];
thus, the Kaulika mantra is the supreme initiation.
Because initiation is prohibited with respect to the *śakti-vidyā* in the *Yoginītantra*, there is no fault anywhere when an eclipse occurs at a great sacred site (*mahātīrtha*).
You have asked well, O Brahmin; I shall explain everything to you. (2.24)
This was previously told by Brahmā to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha;
and Vasiṣṭha himself imparted it to my father, his own excellent son.
O father, ocean of compassion, with a serene and clear heart,
you were gracious at the great sacred site of Kurukṣetra during the solar eclipse.
Thus, and so forth, in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā, from the words of Śrī Vyāsa addressed to Śaunaka.
The intention is that one may also receive the Viṣṇu-mantra from one's father. As for the expiation, it is the recitation of the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, since such is seen prescribed everywhere;
thus it is stated in the Yoginītantra.

A mantra that is devoid of power, as well as one belonging to a father or a maternal grandfather, or one obtained in a dream, or given by a woman, becomes pure only through formal consecration (saṃskāra). || 2-27 ||
And when a flask has been obtained in a dream, one should cause the life-force (prāṇa) of the Guru to enter it;
having written [the mantra] on a palm leaf with saffron, its reception is auspicious. (2.28)

Then one obtains the fruit; otherwise, it would be fruitless. However, in the absence of a true guru, or even when one exists, one should receive a single mantra from him. Regarding this, there is no restriction of time for a dream, because of the statement of Nārada: "In a dream, however, there is no restriction."
A preceptor who is to be avoided should be shunned by a practitioner desiring his own welfare.
In the *Vṛhanmatsyasūkta*:

One who is sonless, one whose sons have died, one afflicted with leprosy, as well as a dwarf, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who is dominated by women, and one with an extra limb. (2–30)
One who is deficient in limbs, deceitful, diseased, gluttonous, or excessively talkative—only he who is free from these defects is a guru approved by the learned. (2-31)
Now, the characteristics of the disciple of the best of scriptures are stated;
and so it is said in the Rudrayāmala:
The fault of anointing [the body] belongs to the queen, while the sin of the wife falls upon her own husband.
In the same way, a disciple certainly incurs the accumulated sins of the guru;
therefore, after careful deliberation, the characteristics of a disciple are now being stated with effort. (2.33)
And so it is stated in the Śāradātilaka:
The disciple should be of noble birth, pure in soul, devoted to the goals of human life, one who has studied the Vedas, skillful, and whose mind has driven far away the god of love. (2.34)
Always seeking the welfare of living beings, he is a believer and not an atheist;
devoted to his own duty with devotion, he is intent on the well-being of his father and mother. (2-35)
Devoted to serving the guru with the wealth of speech, mind, and body—one endowed with such qualities is a disciple, and no other. (2.36)
And so it is stated in the Yāmala:

The disciple, whose mind is purified by right knowledge and who is devoted to the goals of human life, having mastered the essential truth of the scriptures, is indeed always [the refuge] for those living beings. (2.37)
Free from the conduct of an atheist, he is a believer who has conquered his senses;
he is devoted to the excellent Dharma, pure, and intent on the welfare of his father and mother. (2.38)
Devoted to service and faithful to his guru, desirous of knowledge and endowed with faith,
he should be free from lust, anger, and other such passions, remaining intent upon the worship of the mantra.
Devoted to serving his teacher with the wealth of speech, mind, and body,
he desires to cross over the ocean of existence with his whole being, bringing an end to the suffering of worldly life.

A Brahmin seeking dharma and liberation, one seeking sensual pleasure, one free from longing, or a twice-born man who is desireless yet possesses wealth—what is his purpose for awakening and liberation? (2.41)

Toward the wives of one's mother's brothers and teachers, and likewise toward their sons, one should always perform worship with devotion, regarding them with the same mindset as one has toward the gods. (2.42)
Among these, one who is favored by fate avoids those who are to be shunned;
now I shall describe the characteristics of disciples who are to be avoided. (2.43)
The goad for the heretics.
They were free from impurity, yet wrathful; hypocritical, yet miserly;
wicked, yet impoverished; afflicted by disease, yet full of passion and craving for sensual enjoyments. (2-44)
Those seized by envy and malice, the deceitful, the harsh-spoken,
those who have acquired wealth through unjust means, and he who is devoted to the wives of others— (2.45).

Those who are enemies of the wise, those who are ignorant yet pride themselves on being learned, those whose vows have fallen away, those who are backbiters, and those who delight in cruelty—[these are to be avoided]. (2.46)
Those who eat excessively, those of cruel conduct, the wicked, and the censurable—these and others like them are the most sinful, the lowest of men. (2.47)
Those who are of such a nature should be abandoned; one should not admit them as disciples.
If they were admitted today, the deities would become vessels for their wrath.
Having been impoverished in this world and deprived of sons and wives, they become hell-beings at the end of the body and are reborn among the animals. (2.49)
5b) Those who, being enticed by base things, find peace in those censurable [pleasures], will perish entirely, like a field of rice infested by insects. (2.50)
And so it is stated in the Sārasaṃgraha:
One who is deceitful, cruel, and foolish; one who kisses [the image] while devoid of devotion; one who is excessively reckless, as well as one who is corrupt and a reviler of the deity. (2-51)
He who is free from these faults—namely, censuring his family, slandering others, and likewise being intent upon the wives of others—is a true disciple of Śaśin, esteemed by the learned. (2.52)
"One should not bestow [this knowledge] upon the disciples of others, even if they are devoted to service," as stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
One should never, even in thought, act in opposition to one's guru. (2.53)
I perpetually worship with the thought that you are Śiva; though your Guru resides in a distant village, I offer salutation to him with my mind. (2.54)
In the morning, one should remember the Guru—two-eyed, two-armed, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, peaceful—upon a white lotus on the head, preceded by his name. (2.55)
Oṃ. Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom the eye was opened for me, who was blinded by the darkness of ignorance, using the medicinal salve-stick of knowledge. (2.56)
One who worships Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others shall obtain fruitful results;
one obtains that same fruit by saluting the Guru every single day. (2.57)
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
when the Guru is satisfied, for him the three worlds are satisfied.
When Śiva is pleased, the guru is one's father; when the guru is pleased, there is no one else [to protect].
Whether ignorant or learned, the guru alone is indeed the deity. (2.59)
Whether situated on the wrong path or the right path, the Guru alone is the supreme refuge;
just as copper becomes gold through contact with the perfected elixir.
In the presence of the Guru alone, the disciple becomes one with Śiva;
the Guru alone is the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence, and the true refuge. (2.61)
6a) That fool who, while the guru is present, honors another seat, attains a miserable rebirth; that worship shall become fruitless. (2.62)
Having prostrated before the guru, if one subsequently acts contrary to his instruction out of delusion, one will likewise be cooked in hell for thousands of millions of aeons. (2.63)
Those most wicked men, the lowest of humanity, who disregard the command of their guru—for them there is no liberation whatsoever from the torments of hell. (2.64)
Those disciples who have constantly disregarded their gurus, whom they ought to honor, fall from prosperity—consisting of sons, friends, wives, and so forth—and enter into misfortune. (2.65)
Those who, out of delusion, revile their teacher and speak harshly to him, will indeed become pigs even throughout their future births. (2.66)
For those fools who are betrayers of their guru and constant evildoers, there is no doubt that they shall experience the consequences of both their good and evil deeds. (2-67)
For those who possess steadfast devotion toward their guru, liberation is held within their grasp;
[it is attained] through service, wealth, grain, clothing, and auspicious words. (2.68)

A steadfast person may indeed bring even a teacher under his control by means of a heart that acts according to its own will, provided he lacks devotion toward the teacher as well as such knowledge. (2.69)
Success does not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of eons;
therefore, devotion to the guru must always be practiced, even if the guru is possessed of faults. (2.70)
Or even if the Guru, who is Lord Sadāśiva, is joined with great sins;
and likewise in the Devyāgama:
The seat of the preceptor, as well as his vehicle, sandals, and small stool.
One should never step over the water used for bathing or the shadow [of the guru].
One should avoid performing worship separately in the presence of the guru and should refrain from intimacy. (2.72)
One should renounce before the Guru one's initiation, one's learning, and one's authority;
one should indeed contemplate with the intellect the oneness of the Guru, the mantra, and the deity. (2.73)
For the benefit of practitioners, a metaphorical representation of Brahman is fashioned, although consciousness is by nature an object of cognition, devoid of qualities, and bodiless. (2.74)
For where the Guru is satisfied, there the Lord of the World is satisfied;
when the God is angry, the Guru protects, but when the Guru is angry, no one can protect.
Relying upon the body of the guru, one abides with the deity of the mantra;
between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is superior. (2.76)
Therefore, one should always regard the teacher as even more venerable than one's father;
for that reason, the teacher must be honored with all effort through wealth and other means. (2.77)
By whose grace that supreme state, so difficult to attain on earth, is reached—having first worshipped the Guru with perfumes, garlands, and incense materials. (2.78)
Then, having covered his head with a cloth, he should receive the mantra;
likewise, ten [members] on the mother’s side and ten on the father-in-law’s side.
Fifty-one ancestors certainly go to heaven;
all the ancestors rejoice when the son is a witness to the meaning of the mantras. (2.80)
They obtain the enjoyments of heaven, and their residence in heaven is certain;
one should adopt the Vaiṣṇava [practice] within the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva within the Śaiva, and the Śākta within the Śākta. (2.81)
In the Kali age, [the path] is characterized by power (śakti) and is intended only for Brahmins and the other [twice-born castes];
there is no eligibility for a Śūdra in the Purāṇas which are of the nature of the Veda.
Knowledge of the *Manu* [tradition] should never be imparted to a Śūdra disciple, for there is no excellence in such a case;
if one were to do so out of greed for wealth, he would certainly not be fit for the mantra of Viṣṇu. (2.83)
A mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (Om) must never be given to a Śūdra under any circumstances;
likewise, one's own personal mantra, the guru’s mantra, and the mantra known as the *ajapa*. (2.84)
One should never give the *ātma-kaulika* mantra; rather, the mantra of Gopāla should be given, as well as that of Maheśa, at the feet [of the disciple]. (2.85)
Likewise, for the wife of Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and Maṇi—only one who has received initiation into these [deities] shall be authorized; otherwise, one becomes a partaker of sin. (2.86)
This has been stated in the Śrītantrarāja:
O beautiful one, for him by whom the vidyā written in a book is recited, success does not arise; rather, only loss occurs. (2.87)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Āgamakalpalatā. || 2 ||
For the sake of purifying his own inner self, the teacher should thoroughly purify his disciples;
a Brāhmaṇa becomes fit [for initiation] in one year, and a Kṣatriya in two years. (3-1)
A Vaiśya should always do so with three years, and a Śūdra with four; likewise, a disciple should act in this manner for the sake of attaining his own desired goal. (3-2)
In the beginning, by one who desires what is desired, the king must be served and known; "the guru" is the understood subject.
And likewise in the Gautamīya:
On an auspicious day, having performed his bath, he should bow down to Gaṇeśvara,
Sūrya, Śiva, Hari, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Kamalālayā.
Having bowed to his mother and father and embraced the brahmins,
he took auspicious fruits and flowers, filled with devotion.

For the attainment of the goals of human life, one should take refuge in a guru together with his disciples, having made a formal self-introduction that includes the lineages of one's father and mother. (3.5)
Having addressed him with the very title of "Guru," one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
then, rising before the Guru, one should stand with palms joined in *añjali*.
O great hero, deliberate upon this excellent mantra for my benefit;
afterwards, the preceptor should carefully deliberate upon these mantras as well. (3.7)
And thus:
One should practice the mantra in accordance with the white, red, and black aspects;
thus it is said.
One should not accept a mantra that lacks the syllable *jha*, nor likewise one that lacks the *kula*.
Because the investigation of the wheels (*cakras*) is necessary according to such statements, that [investigation] is first described:
"Next, for the sake of accomplishing the wheels, the investigation of the *vakṣyas* will be explained;
first is the *Kulākula* wheel, and the second is the one called *Makatha*. (3-9)
The third is called *jha-ṇa-dhana*, the fourth is designated as *varga*, the fifth is the *rāśicakra*, and the sixth is the *nakṣatracakra*. (3-10)
The seventh is the *gaṇacakra*; the eighth is known as the *akada*;
the ninth is the *mudita* circle; and the tenth is called the *nādikā*.
He states [the following] in sequence:
And so it is stated in the Śāradātilaka:
Since the *mātṛkā* has arisen from the five elements as its cause, therefore the phonemes consist of those elements, divided into groups of five each. (3.12)

And so it is stated in the Gandharva Tantra:
I shall declare the mantra known as Vakṣakana, which is perfected and bestows all accomplishments.
When receiving mantras, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should examine them in every respect;
the practitioner of mantra should write them out on a zodiacal chart (rāśicakra) and examine them in every respect, excluding the neuter vowels.
The wise one should write the letters in sequence from 'a' to 'kṣa';
just as the letters [of the Gāyatrī] are in the first square, so too [the letters of] the Gāyatrī [should be placed] in order. (3.84)

Having written them down, one should count and recite [the names] preceded by their initial syllables, [determining] the *siddha*, *sādhya*, and *susiddha* [categories] in their proper sequence again and again. (3.85)
If a mantra does not shine forth through investigation, how could it be otherwise?
Therefore, relying on the prohibitions, one should take up an excellent mantra. (3.86)
And furthermore:
The wise one should count the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' according to the sequence of the right-hand path, starting from Aries and ending with Pisces, in their proper order. (3.87)

Having recited from his own name down to the first syllable of the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should do so again and again in sequence, [identifying the syllables] as *siddha*, *sādhya*, and *susiddha*. (3.88)
Thus ends the wheel of the six mantras.
But this concerns the domain of cowherds.
This has been stated in the *Pāṣaṇḍāṅkuśa*.
I shall describe in brief the great wheel known as Uditā:
one should draw a six-cornered wheel with even lines, beautiful to behold. (3.89)
One should write the letters beginning with *na* and ending with *kṣa* in order starting from the east;
when [the moon] has risen, it is taught that there is equal prosperity, while in the second [watch], there is the destruction of wealth. (3.90)
In the third [house] one should know there is fortitude; in the fourth, relations and prosperity;
in the fifth, one will be of a doubting nature; and in the sixth, there is total destruction.
(Illustration 14b) One should count from the first letter of one's own name up to the first letter of the mantra.
Now, the *gaṇacakra*.
In the Yoginītantra.
The three [asterisms] preceding and following [Aśvinī], as well as Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī—these the wise call the human asterisms. (3.92)
Jyeṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Mūla, Dhaniṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Kṛttikā, Citrā, Maghā, and Viśākhā are the lunar mansions presided over by the Rākṣasa deities. (3.93)
Aśvinī, Revatī, Puṣya, Svātī, Hasta, Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśirā, and Śravaṇa—these indeed are the *tālaka* [asterisms]. (3.94)
This wheel is included within the circle of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-cakra*), for its purpose has already been fulfilled;
however, it is mentioned separately in accordance with the requirements of the assembly.
(Citram) thus ends the Gaṇacakra. Now follows the Nāḍīcakra.
And likewise in the Tantra:
If one's Guru, mantras, and deities reside within a single channel (nāḍī), one should predict the results in sequence as hatred, disease, and death. (3.95)
If two stars belong to different constellations (*rāśi*) yet are in conjunction (*nadamya*), those two shall obtain auspicious results there;
if they are in conjunction and belong to the same constellation, then it shall be auspicious—so the sages declare. (3.96)
And likewise, in the Jyotiṣa [treatise], there is a specific arrangement of the Sarpāka constellation.

15a) When the [ascendant] is at the beginning of Kṛttikā, there is madness; when it is at the end, there is the remainder [of the affliction]. When it is in the middle of those [asterisms], there is disease in the back.
Varāhamihira says that when [the ascendant] is divided by lines, there is marriage, but he does not say much regarding many sons.
Because this statement lacks a scriptural basis and pertains to the section on marriage, it is not included among the [twelve] types of sons.
Nevertheless, it has been written here in accordance with the tradition.
Thus concludes the wheel of the channels (*nāḍīcakra*).
First is the wheel of *Kula* and *Akula*, and the second is called *Nakathā*.
The third is called Debt and Wealth, and the fourth is designated as Group.

The fifth is the wheel of the zodiac signs (rāśicakra), the sixth is the wheel of the lunar mansions (nakṣatracakra); the seventh is the wheel of the groups (gaṇacakra), and the eighth is known as the kaḍema. || 3-98 ||
The ninth is the Mudita-cakra, and the tenth is the Nādikāṅkaṭā;
thus have the various types of cakras been described based on the teachings of diverse tantras. (3.99)
In the Vārāhī Tantra:
"The Tārā-cakra, the Rāśi-cakra, and likewise the Nāma-cakra—herein one should consider the most excellent mantras, and not any other cakra. (3-100)
Now, the refutation.

And so it is said in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "One should not examine the *siddha* and other [categories] for the eight-syllabled *haṃsa*, nor for the five-syllabled [mantra], nor for a neuter mantra. (3.101)
Through the division of mantra and vidyā, there are three types of mantra-lineages:
mantras are to be known as having male deities, while vidyās are traditionally said to have female deities. (3.102)

All mantras proclaimed [in this system] possess the nature of male, female, or neuter. Those ending with *hūṃ* or *phaṭ* are considered male; those ending with two [such syllables] are considered female. (3.103)
15b) Neuter [mantras] should end in *am*; they are divided into male, female, and neuter.
Mantras are of three kinds: for subjugation (*vaśya*), pacification (*śānti*), and malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
Having deliberated with certainty, the practitioner should select [a mantra] for the sake of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Without mantra, no accomplishment whatsoever arises for human beings. (3-104)
In the Yāmala:
Of the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha; of the Praṇava temple-mantra; and of both the condensed-syllable mantras and the joined-syllable mantras. || 3-105 ||
And so it has been said in the *Sārasaṃhitā*:
Likewise, in the case of the Ekārakūṭa and the Mālāmantra,
as well as for the *nityā* Haṃsa-mantras beginning with Siddha and so forth;
and likewise in the Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī.
Likewise, in the case of a single-syllable mantra, a peak (kūṭa) mantra, a garland mantra, or one consisting of three seed-syllables. || 3-106 ||
"Those [mantras] obtained in a dream, given by a woman, or given by a *siddha* and so forth;
mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are proclaimed as *mālāmantras*.
Thus it is stated in the *Śrīdevīpurāṇa*."
And in the Kārikā, in the Tārā, in the Kūllūkā, and in the Trikūṭaka. || 3-107 ||
Likewise, in the single-syllable *kūṭa* mantra, as well as in the five-syllabled *Śiva* mantra,
and in the six-syllabled and even the eight-syllabled mantra of that very Viṣṇu.
In the twelve-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu, in the seed-syllable of Rāmacandra,
in the Vaiṣṇava mantras, in the Bhairavī, and in the excellent mantra of Sundarī— 3.109.
And one should not examine the Siddhas and other [categories] regarding the Sarasvatī-mantra in the case of a young girl;
some scholars maintain this even for Vaiṣṇava mantras. (3.110)
In reality, however:
This is for the sake of supreme praise;
otherwise, by the power of evil views, there would be the attainment of such a mantra,
which would lead to the failure of propitiating the deity.
Then she shall explain the fruitful [practice] according to the sequence stated in the *Yāmala*.
By performing this sacrifice constantly, men shall obtain the fruit born of [eating] meat;
furthermore, one should prescribe that in the month of Vaiśākha, an auspicious initiation brings about abundant prosperity.
In Āśvina, it bestows death; in Kārttika, there is great prosperity; in Śrāvaṇa, there will be loss of jewels; and in Bhādrapada, it brings about the infliction of suffering.
In Āśvinī there shall be the accomplishment of jewels; in Kārttika, it bestows the accomplishment of knowledge;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, there is the attainment of happiness; and in Pauṣa, it destroys knowledge. (3.114)
In Māgha it increases intelligence; in Phālguna it brings everything under control;
in Caitra it indeed bestows suffering; one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa). (3.115)
But regarding the month of Caitra, it is according to what is stated in the Gautamītantra; and thus it is said:
Initiation may take place in the month of Madhu (Caitra) according to the statements of Yati and others; there is no prohibition against it occurring at other times.
I shall describe the time for initiation, which brings happiness to practitioners,
as stated in the Devīpurāṇa.
And in the autumn season and in the month of Vaiśākha, initiation bestows the most excellent fruit.
Initiation in the months of Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭha is declared to be middling;
in Āṣāḍha and the month of Māgha, it is proclaimed to be inferior.
It is censured in the months of Śrāvaṇa, Pauṣa, and Bhādrapada;
yet, even during these censured months, initiation is declared auspicious during an eclipse.
Nor [should it be done] regarding sense objects, nor during a dual conflict, nor at the time of the festival of Madana,
nor at the time of initiation rites, nor on the Aṣṭakā days, nor during the Pavitra rite, nor on the festival of the Guru.
The section on the festivals of the Guru.
In the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā.
In the sixth month, Bhādrapada, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
in Kārttika, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight; and on the third day of Mārgaśīrṣa.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the fourth days of Māgha, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, and the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra. (3.121)
In Vaiśākha there is indeed Akṣayā, and likewise Daśaharā in Jyeṣṭha;
the fifth day of the bright fortnight in Āṣāḍha, and the fifth day of the dark fortnight in Śrāvaṇa.
The wise call these the festivals of the Guru and the sacred sites (*tīrtha*).
In the *Śrīmantramuktāvalī* (3.123):
"The best of teachers should perform [the rite] during the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight."
In the bright fortnight there shall be complete prosperity, while in the dark fortnight it will be middling;
thus says the Rājamārtaṇḍa.
When Jupiter, the Sun, and Venus are pure [of unfavorable aspects], initiation brings about the destruction of enemies.
On an auspicious day and at an auspicious moment, initiation bestows sovereignty;
[as stated] in the Rudrayāmala.
In the bright fortnight, the auspicious initiation is performed; in the dark fortnight, it begins from the fifth day onwards.
The best of mantra-knowers should not perform the initiation for a vow when the moon has waned,
nor during the autumn season, on the Yugādi day, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
And for the propitiation of Durgā, one of clear intellect should undergo initiation; [as stated] in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa.
A wise person should always perform initiation during a solar or lunar transit, or during an eclipse.
There is nothing on earth equal to the time of a solar eclipse;
whatever action is performed during this [time] shall yield infinite fruit. (3.128)

Having reached the ninth lunar day (navamī) or the lunar day of purification (śodhana), one should perform it during a solar eclipse, at the time of a solar eclipse, and likewise during the sun's transit (saṃkramaṇa). || 3-129 ||
In this regard, the best of mantra-knowers should not perform the purification of the ascendant and other such factors; thus it is stated in the Vṛhad-matsya-sūkta.
Likewise, there is no certainty regarding the time for an eclipse or a sacred bathing place for an atheist. || 3-130 ||

On the occasion of the festival for cleaning the teeth, during the fierce consumption of the single kind of food by the holy ones, he who was performing the initiation with mantras purified [himself] from the food of the monthly initiation.
The festival known as Tantuparvan is celebrated on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha;
the Damana festival is proclaimed for the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.

The Guru did not observe the eclipse of the moon or sun at the disciple’s birth, nor the transit of the sun into Capricorn, nor the time of compassion, nor the initiation of the constellations and so forth. (3.133)
During the lunar eclipse, one should not perform the Sūrya or Śākta rites within the Viṣṇu-mantra;
or else, there is another excellent way to receive initiation.
When it is given by a Guru out of compassion to his disciples, then why indeed should anything such as the *lagna* (ascendant) or other astrological factors not be disregarded? (3-135)
On whichever day the Guru is satisfied, all the planets, all the lunar mansions, and the zodiac signs become auspicious and bring about every kind of welfare. (3-136)
For when the guru is satisfied, all the deities are satisfied;
whenever it is known [to be the right time], then initiation should be performed in accordance with the guru’s command.
In that [practice], there is no restriction regarding the syllable *na*, nor likewise any restriction regarding the location;
by means of devotion, one should satisfy the guru, and thus it will come to pass spontaneously. (3-138)
Now, the results of the lunar days (tithis):

I shall explain the results of the lunar days according to the sequence stated in the Yāmala. Initiation performed on the first lunar day (pratipad) is considered to cause the destruction of knowledge.
On the second day there is knowledge of existence; on the third, it shall be pure.
On the fourth, there will be loss of wealth; on the fifth, the increase of intelligence. (3.140)

On the sixth day, one obtains the bliss of the destruction of [ignorant] knowledge; on the seventh day, there is the loss of intellect; on the eighth day, there shall be the destruction of the mind; and on the ninth day, death occurs. (3-141)
On the tenth day there is royal happiness, and on the eleventh it shall be pure;
on the twelfth all success shall occur, but on the thirteenth there will be poverty. (3-142)
On the fourteenth day of the fortnight of animals, ending with the month of Kṛmimāsa, your success in dharma shall come; therefore, one should avoid teaching the lesson. (3.143)

During thunder at twilight, during an earthquake, and during the falling of meteors, the practitioner of mantra should avoid [the recitation] for three nights; he should also avoid those things prescribed by the Vedas [in such circumstances].
And likewise, in the Vaśiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
It should be performed on the twelfth day or even on the thirteenth;
as for the procedure prescribed for the thirteenth day, that likewise pertains to Viṣṇu.

Even on the twelfth day, the *Rāmārcanacandrikā* cites authoritative statements; furthermore, the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā* cites authoritative statements declaring that the thirteenth and the eighth days are praised as fulfilling all desires— thus, this [opposing view] should be considered.
I shall now describe the results for the hairs according to all the tantras:
two barleycorns [of hair] are to be removed for Jupiter, as well as for the Moon; the same should be done for Mercury and Venus.
On Sunday there will be wealth; on Monday, there will be peace through sesame seeds;
Mars destroys longevity, so one should avoid initiation on that day. (3-147)
Through Mercury one attains beauty, while through Saturn there is loss of fame.
I shall now briefly state the results of the lunar mansions as declared by Dakṣa.
Having performed the initiation right there, one shall obtain the fruit of both the existent and the non-existent;
and so it is said in the *Jñānamālā*:
One should perform the mantra-consecration (*mantrābhiṣeka*) under the asterisms of Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā, Hasta, Jyeṣṭhā, and the three Uttaras.
[Also] under Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three Uttaras. (3.149)
Puṣyā and Śatabhiṣak are likewise proclaimed for the initiatory rites and others; thus it is stated in the Yāmala.
Under Aśvinī one attains happiness; under Bharaṇī death is certain.
Under Kṛttikā one will be miserable; under Rohiṇī, one will be driven abroad;
under Mṛgaśiras, there is the attainment of happiness; under Ārdrā, there is the destruction of kinsmen. (3-151)
Furthermore, under Vaśa and Dhaniṣṭhā, there would be the destruction of one's enemies;
under Āśleṣā, death would occur; and under Maghā, there would be liberation from suffering. (3.152)
One attains beauty under Pūrvaphalgunī, of this there is no doubt;
and one attains knowledge under Uttaraphalgunī, of this there is no doubt. (3.153)
Knowledge is attained under Uttara-phalgunī, and one gains strength under Hasta;
under Citrā there shall be the perfection of knowledge, and bathing [under it] destroys enemies. (3.154)
In Viśākhā there will be happiness; Anurādhā bestows growth.
In Jyeṣṭhā there will be loss of sons; in Mūla there is the binding of fame. (3-155)
In the Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā constellations, there is the granting of fame for you;
in Śravaṇa one becomes miserable, and in Dhaniṣṭhā there is poverty. (3.156)
In Śatabhiṣaj there is growth; Pūrvabhadrā bestows happiness;
in Uttarabhadrā there is well-being; and in Revatī there is the increase of fame. (3.157)
I shall now proclaim the yoga of initiation as taught in the Rudrayāmala:
during the bright fortnight, it is auspicious; during the dark fortnight, it is favorable up to the tenth day.
Vyatipāta and Vaidhṛti are conducive to the bliss of initiation;
Śakutī and the like bestow auspiciousness, but one should carefully avoid Viṣṭi.
He states the definition of the Vyatīpāta yoga:
If, during the transit of the sun and moon through Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, or the beginning of Āśleṣā, there occurs a Vyatīpāta yoga, it is so designated. (3.160)
18b) If the constellation Āśleṣā, presided over by the Nāgas, is at the head of the first syllable, or if my mother is in Virgo, or if Mercury and Saturn are in Libra; (3.161)
When that seventh lunar day (Saptamī) falls on a Saturday with the Sun in Aquarius (Kumbha), it is equal to a solar eclipse; such a Vyatīpāta yoga is a destroyer of great sins.
I shall now declare the auspicious time for initiation as taught in the Rudrayāmala: during the zodiac signs of Taurus, Leo, Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces, and Aries. (3.163)
The Guru should always bestow initiation when the moon and stars are favorable;
for the Viṣṇu-mantra, a fixed (sthira) lagna is auspicious, while for the Śiva-mantra, a movable (cala) one is auspicious.
A lagna situated in a *viskambha* yoga is recommended for rites involving powerful mantras;
however, it is forbidden during certain months, with specific variations according to different sages. (3-165)

The sixth day of Bhādrapada, likewise the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, and the third day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa. (3.166)
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha,
and the thirteenth day— this is the reading.
In Vaiśākha there is indeed the Akṣaya [tithi], and in Jyeṣṭha the Daśaharā lunar day.

The fifth day of the bright fortnight in Āṣāḍha and the fifth day of the bright fortnight in Śrāvaṇa—these are the festivals of the gods; at these, the fruit of ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) is obtained.

And the mother’s death anniversary: the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, and the fifth day of Āṣāḍha known as Nāgapañcamī. (3.169)
The eleventh day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the eighth day of Bhādrapada conjoined with Rohiṇī,
and the highly meritorious Great Eighth (Mahāṣṭamī) of Āśvina are also granters of desired boons.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika, likewise the sixth and fourteenth days in the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, and the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in Māgha. (3.171)
19a) And the sixth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna— such is the determination of the time in the Yoginītantra.
At the solstices, during eclipses, and at the equinoxes of the moon and the sun.
O Goddess of the lords of the asuras, on the day of the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), on the anniversaries of the beginning of the yugas,
on all the Manvantara days, and likewise on occasions such as the Great Worship (mahāpūjā), || 3.173 ||

Furthermore, based on such scriptural statements as, "The fourth, the fifth, the fourteenth, and likewise the eighth—these lunar days (tithis) are declared to be auspicious," the [worship] on the fourteenth and eighth days pertains to Śakti;
whereas the worship on the fourth day pertains to Gaṇeśa, because each is prescribed in its respective Kalpa. (3-174)
Even during times that are censured, initiation is declared to be auspicious when performed during a solar eclipse;
there is nothing on earth equal to the time of a solar eclipse.
In that regard, if everything performed there were to yield infinite fruit—
whether at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) or likewise during a solar eclipse (sūryagrahaṇa)— (3.176)
In that regard, how could the ascendant and other factors not be considered?
And likewise in the case of a lunar eclipse as well.
The new moon day, Monday, Tuesday, and the fourteenth lunar day. (3.177)
In the Vārāhītantra: "The seventh lunar day on a Sunday is equal to hundreds of festival days (parvan) when the sun is present."
If Venus is increased by water or day and is situated before Jupiter and the others, [it brings prosperity]. || 3-178 ||
At that time, no fault exists during the signs of Aries, Taurus, and Leo;
I shall now describe the locations for initiation according to various tantras. (3.179)
In a cow-pen, in the house of a teacher, in a temple, and in a grove;
likewise in a sacred bathing place, in a garden, on a riverbank, and in one's own hermitage. (3.180)
But that which is performed near Dhātrī, on a mountain peak, in a cave, or at the Gaṅgā, all of that becomes multiplied by millions upon millions of times. || 3.181 ||
19b) Now I shall explain the food that grants all accomplishments to practitioners;
for it has been stated thus in the Śāradātilaka:
Edible food, sacrificial offerings, vegetables and the like, prescribed fruits, and milk. || 3.182 ||
Barley flour produced from barley is the food for these mantra-reciters;
thus it is stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
When the mantra-practitioner, having performed the initiation, observes a fast, || 3.183 ||
O Lord, he who is always angry has a curse fall upon his head;
therefore, one should not take food without having fasted, for such fasting would take away one's prosperity.
One should eat his food with sacrificial grain and vegetables. Thus ends the third chapter in the Āgamakalpalatā. 3.
Therefore, practitioners who desire accomplishment should diligently undergo initiation by relying on a true guru and following the path taught in the scriptures. (4.1)
In this context, the praise of the scripture is appended:
"Having performed the daily worship, one should prostrate like a staff before the Guru. (4.2)
Then one should pay homage to the Sun, as well as to one's mother and father;
thereafter, one should study the desired knowledge in the presence of the guru.
When the wise declare that one has understood the meaning of all the scriptures,
then, for the sake of conquering the world, one should thoroughly study the treatises on knowledge (jñānaśāstra).
There is no liberation without knowledge, nor indeed without devotion to knowledge;
and devotion arises through association with the devotees of the Blessed Lord. (4–5)
There are many treatises on knowledge; he will explain them in the mandala.
Whatever sciences are pleasing to one's mind, those very ones one should practice thoroughly. (4-6)
Many such modes have been taught by a single sage;
what does it matter whether they are true or not? For men do not possess the power to alter what is unreal.
20a) Therefore, a wise person, being disciplined, should diligently study the scripture of knowledge (āgama).
For all scriptures reside in the āgama, and all deities reside in the āgama. (4.8)
In the Āgama is all merit; in the Āgama, what is not obtained?
In the Āgama is all knowledge; all sciences are established therein. (4.9)
O Brahmin, that which is not found in the Āgama is not found anywhere else;
it has come from the mouth of Śiva and returned to the mouth of Girijā.
Therefore, the scripture is taught for the destruction of the three impurities;
[it explains] the origin of the body, the individual soul, and the play of karma through the power of *māyā*. (4.11)
Know that knowledge is obscured by it, which sets in motion the bondage of worldly existence;
Viṣṇu is the producer of the body, but through devotion to Him, one cuts that [obscuration] away.

For the sake of attaining knowledge of the yoga of devotion, one should study the scriptures with diligence; therefore, one should indeed perform initiation according to the path declared in the scriptures. (4.13)
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall describe the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā), since without it the fruit of all mantras cannot be attained. (4.14)
It is taught to be fourfold, according to the divisions beginning with Kriyāvatī: Kriyāvatī, Varṇamayī, Kalātmā, and Vedamayī. (4.15)
Among those, the initiation involving ritual action is not described here due to its great extent;
furthermore, there is that consisting of the Vedas, which is accessible through yoga and awakens the disciple. (4.16)
Now, the procedure for the initiation (dīkṣā) of Kalāvatī is described;
likewise, it is stated in the Śāradātilaka:
Having bathed according to the rules prescribed by the teacher and having performed the morning rites.
Having made himself silent for the sake of the sacrifice, he [entered] the sacrificial pavilion; then, upon a pure surface of the earth, free from husks and charcoal...
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should construct a beautiful pavilion with a width measured by five, seven, or nine cubits. (4.19)
Sixteen pillars, joined together with four situated in their center,
should be erected twelve cubits high on all sides.
They should be five cubits in measure, without holes, straight, and beautiful; the best of those skilled in the lute should strike that fifth note upon the earth with a sound.
That [mixture],
while being cooked, should be prepared with coconut leaves and bamboos equal to one-fifth part of those pillars;
then, at the doors, there should be arches (toraṇas) made from milk-bearing trees in due order.
Their height is recorded as being seven cubits each;
such is their gateway.
Its circumference is said to be ten finger-breadths in measure;
the measurement of the horizontal slabs should be half the size of the pillars.
The measurement of the horizontal plank should be such that it extends around both pillars; this is the distinction regarding the surrounding wood.
The remainder is that "half of that" is three and a half [yojanas].
One should imagine tridents in the middle archway, measuring one cubit,
and should fix banners in the cardinal directions that possess a radiance equal to that of the world-protectors.
And so it has been said in the Śāradā:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Lakṣa, Varuṇa, Pavana, Vidhu, Īśāna, the Lord of Mountains (Himavat), and beyond that, the Grandfather (Brahmā). || 4-25 ||
Yellow, red, white, and smoky; on the white [disk], both smoky and white; fair and ruddy—these are proclaimed in order according to their colors. (4.26)

Indra and the other [guardians of the directions] have faces that are, respectively, brownish-yellow, tawny, blue, dark, white, smoky, stainless, and pure white; this is according to their colors, as stated in the *Kramadīpikā*.
One should not decorate the pavilion with garlands of *darbha* grass and the like;
rather, at one-third of that [measurement], in the *kṣattra* [region], it should be raised to a height of eight *ratni*s.
Then, one should prepare a square altar-maṇḍala;
this has been stated in the Gautamīya:
The minister has the altar constructed as a square according to the prescribed rule.
The ground that is white like fine clay is proclaimed to be Brāhmī;
the Kṣatriyā is red clay, and the Vaiśyā is said to be yellow. (4.29)
Black soil with fissures is proclaimed to be of four kinds:
that of the Brāhmaṇa brings success in all aims, while that of the Kṣatriya is considered to bestow sovereignty.
O Sage, a Vaiśya woman brings wealth and grain, whereas a Śūdra woman is censured;
therefore, before the day of initiation, the wise man should have a pavilion constructed.
Those who know the tantras understand that a cubit (hasta) consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (pañgu-sāḍhya), measured from the middle joint of the right hand of the performer. (4.32)
The length of the middle [finger] is declared to be one *mātṛ-aṅgula*;
one *yava* [in length] is equal to one grain of rice, and eight [such grains] constitute one *aṅgula*.
The hand joined [to form the span] should not be too long; it should consist of twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The largest [span] is made with eight of those barley-corns (yavas), and the medium one with seven barley-corns.
O best of sages, the smallest [measure] is declared to be six [units], as is the *hasta*; he now describes the method for constructing the *sarvatobhadra* [mandala].
In a square divided into four compartments,
provided with diagonal lines, there shall be four corner-lines within each of the four compartments.
In such a way that there may be fish-like spaces between each pair,
the practitioner should cast two lines extending from east to west and two extending from south to north.
21b) One should drop four equal lines across those fish-shaped sections;
as before, one should drop the action-lines (karmasūtra) in the corner squares. 4-37.
One should lay down four threads upon those fish-shaped figures;
then, one should drop threads across those squares and fish.
As long as there are two jars, the mantra-practitioner should likewise cast the sacrificial oblations there according to the ritual procedure, even for fifty-six steps.
One should draw a lotus with excellent characteristics using thirty-six squares in the center;
the pedestal (pīṭha) should be formed by the outer row, and the pathways (vīthikā) by a pair of rows.
The practitioner of mantra, having fashioned the primary and secondary ornaments of the gateway according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures, should then draw a lotus.
Having abandoned one-twelfth part of the lotus-grid from the outside, the wise man should divide its center into three circles with equal proportions.

The first [layer] should consist of the pericarp and the eight directions; the second, of the filaments; the third, of the mechanical devices; and the tip of the petals should be made of pearls. (4.43)
The wise man, indifferent to external affairs, having placed moons all around the tips of his mane according to the prescribed rule, [proceeded]. (4.44)
Having drawn [the lines] at the junctions, one should drop the threads there;
and with the same measurement as that of the tips of the petals, one should draw a circle.
The wise one should draw the tips of the petals all around with the outer hand, using a thread whose two ends reach to the edge of that [central area]. (4.46)
One should arrange the *yagaṇa* at the inner bases as the mass of hair;
this is declared by the learned to be the common lotus design therein.
One should sweep out three square units at each corner of the pedestal for the purpose of the foot;
with the remaining squares, the wise one should fashion the limbs. 4.48.
When the *nivīthi* consecration has been performed, one should then clear the openings of the directions by means of two or four squares, according to the specific arrangement of the *mājaras*.
Then, there should be three squares and one square for the *śobhās* on both sides of the door;
the *upaśobhās* should consist of one square and three squares separated by an interval.
With the remaining six syllables, one should color the four corners;
with five colors, that beautiful hexagon should be made to shine.
Yellow powder should be made from turmeric; white, from dūrasambhava;
red, from safflower powder; and black, from burnt cow-dung.
The dark-colored lotus of the colors is said to consist of leaves such as those of the bilva;
these auspicious white lines have an extension of one finger-breadth each. (4-53)
The pericarp is yellow in color, the filaments are reddish,
the petals are white, and their joints are dark green.
The practitioner of mantra should conquer with vigor; the pericarp is yellowish-red, the filaments are reddish-yellow, and the petals are likewise reddish. (4-55)
The joints should be black, or they may be yellow, dark blue, or not colored at all. One should dye the limbs of the pedestal; the feet should be reddish with a radiant glow.
Upon its white walls and in its courtyards, one should draw kalpalatikās (wish-fulfilling creepers) provided with leaves and flowers. (4.57)
Variegated with various colors, they are enchanting to the sight of all;
the *tārā* beads are white in color, while those for beauty are said to be red.
The ornaments are yellow in color, and the hair is black;
three lines should be drawn on the outside, white, red, and white, respectively.
This mandala, known as Sarvatobhadra, is considered common to all;
having gone there, even a disciple, being pure and having previously fasted, [should enter].
Then he should make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana);
afterwards, the disciple, filled with devotion, should choose a preceptor there.
One should indeed honor Śakti with perfumes, garments, ornaments,
and decorations— with cattle, land, gold, clothing, and so forth, as well as with radiant earrings and other finery.
He should likewise deceive the teacher with other ornaments and wealth;
such a disciple, however, is auspicious if he worships the guru with devotion. (4.63)
One should avoid hypocrisy, egoism, and pride in the presence of the guru;
having prostrated with palms joined in reverence, one should please the guru before him. (4.64)

Therefore, O Blessed One, O Master who embodies the nature of the Supreme Self, O Most Compassionate One, please graciously bestow upon this person the initiation and consecration for the practice-mantra, preceded by the complete ritual means of attainment.
Having spoken thus, the humble disciple should remain for a long time to the right of the guru;
there, by the command of the guru, he should recite the Gāyatrī a thousand times.
In the sequence to be described hereafter, one should not abbreviate the supreme mantra; "of the guru," is the ellipsis.
Having consecrated the mantra ten times, I shall then commence the worship.
Having gone near the pavilion, he should wash his feet;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) properly according to the rules and having prepared the general offering of water (sāmānyārgha).
Having sprinkled the vessel with the Astra-mantra, one should fill it with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
having invoked the Tīrtha and cast in the perfumes and other offerings with the Praṇava.
One should display the *dhenumudrā*; this is declared to be the general *argha*.
Having sprinkled the door-mantras with water, one should perform the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*).
Above, one should worship Vighna, Malālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī;
then, on the southern branch, Vighna, and Kṣatraiśa from another [direction].
Then, on the two sides, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā with flowers and water;
at each door, one should worship the Weapon (astra) in this sequence.
Having touched a branch of the *pṛśniparṇī* plant, he should step over the threshold;
contracting his limbs from within, he should enter by the right side.
Immediately thereafter, the lords of the quarters, by means of their divine vision,
should dispel the divine obstacles and those moving through the atmosphere with the eight [mantras].
The wise practitioner should ward off obstacles with the three *pārigha* mantras on the ground,
using white mustard seeds and unbroken rice grains while maintaining the mental focus on the *nārāca* weapon.
May those beings who move about secretly and those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
Having recited this mantra at the end, one should scatter [the materials] within the pavilion;
one should worship Vāstu-īśa and Brahmā in the south-western direction.
With the water from the *argha* vessel containing the five *garvas*, one should sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion;
*vīkṣaṇa* (the act of gazing) is performed with the root mantra, while *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) is considered to be done with the *śara* mantra.

The wise consider that there is as great a difference between striking with deception and vomiting [impurity], and between fumigating with camphor, agallochum, and frankincense, as there is between those two. (4.77)
Having recited the mantra seven times over scattered offerings, he should scatter them there with an arrow;
likewise, the king [should scatter] sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, durvā grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken rice grains.
23b) Those designated as *vikirā* are the destroyers of the entire multitude of obstacles.
Having scattered the *vikirā* and other [offerings], the wise practitioner should perform the cleansing (*mārjana*). 4-79.
Having recited this mantra here, one should gather a handful of straight darbha grass and prepare a seat for the Vardhanī vessel in the northeastern direction.
The goddess Vadharṇī is declared to be the deity of the Vikirā offerings.
For his seat, the Vardhinī is in the northeast corner; its extent is described as "parivadanā," which is its well-known designation.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day and having satisfied the Brahmins,
one should draw one of the prescribed mandalas upon the altar.
The sage is Merupṛṣṭha, the metre is considered to be Pṛthivī, and the deity is said to be Kūrma; I meditate upon this with my vision fixed before me. (4.82)
Indeed, the application of the mantra for the seat is proclaimed as follows:
"O Goddess, you were held by Vṛścika in the world; you were held by Viṣṇu. (4.83)
"May you always support me; make the seat pure.
Reciting this mantra, one should sit upon the pedestal facing either east or north. (4.84)
The wise one should enter with the body straight, following the sequence beginning with the svastika posture;
the preceptor should place the articles of worship on the right side.
One should place a beautifully adorned vessel filled with well-scented water on the right side for the purpose of washing, and one should cause a vessel to be set down upon its back.
One should place auspicious islands illuminated with ghee all around, as well as a burning yak-tail whisk, a parasol, and a beautiful, circular cushion. (4.87)
24a) Having joined his palms in reverence and leaped up, and having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇeśāna on both the left and right sides, he should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
In the Yāmala:
Likewise, having joined the palms in *añjali*, one should worship the three Gurus on the left and Gaṇeśāna on the right, and then perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
In the Yāmala:
Likewise, having joined the palms in the *puṭāñjali* gesture, one should worship the three Gurus on the left and Gaṇeśāna on the right, while visualizing the Lord upon the crown of the head. (4.90)
Having performed the purification of the hands, one should then make three *tāla* gestures;
likewise, the preceptor should protect the directions and himself with the *ūrdhvordhva* mantra.
The radiance generated by that [mantra] shall provide protection on all sides;
thereafter, the instructor, with a steady mind, should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). || 4-92 ||
And so it has been said in the Sāradā:
The purification of the elements that constitute the body, through union with non-dual Brahman—this is considered the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). (4.93)
With a concentrated mind, one should unite the individual self with the supreme self through the Suṣumṇā channel, by means of the method joined with yoga and the *cinmantra*. (4.94)
With the *cinmantra*, that is, with the mantra "haṃsa."
One should contemplate the principles of all beings within their cause;
they are dissolved in the Supreme Self in the form of seeds, even when [the elements] are in reverse order. (4.95)
Then, one should dry up [the body] within the physical form by means of the wind through the seed-syllable of air (vāyubīja);
with the fire-seed-syllable (vahni-bīja), one should burn that entire body.
Then, separating the impurities neither with water nor with nectar,
he caused the body to be flooded from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
By means of the wind-seed, *yam*, and the fire-seed, *vam*—which is to say, the nectar-seed, *am*—the fire-seed becomes nectar.
Then, one should cause the principles (tattvas) dissolved in the self to reach their own respective places;
thereafter, O enjoyer, one should honor the Self within the heart as the Supreme Self.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other rites for Haṃsadeva according to Manu;
his essential nature (*svarūpa*) is "Haṃsadeva, haṃsa."
The knower of mantras should assign the seer, the meter, and the deity of the mantra.
Likewise, on one's own head, face, and heart, in that order;
as it is stated in the Vṛhad-matsya-sūkta:
The placement of the Ṛṣis is in the region of the head, while that of the Chandas is in the lotus of the mouth.
One should place the deity in the heart, the seed-syllable (bīja) in the secret region, the power (śakti) in the feet, and the peg (kīlaka) upon the entire body.
But the seer says:
He who, having known Maheśvara face-to-face through austerity,
accomplishes [his goal] with a purified soul— he is declared to be a true ṛṣi.
Because of its weightiness, it is proclaimed as the placement (nyāsa) upon the head;
because it covers all the principles of mantra (mantratattva), it is called the covering (chada). || 4-103 ||
Because it is imperishable and supreme, the Veda is said to reside in the mouth;
without a full knowledge of the seer and the meter, a mantra does not yield its fruit. (4.104)
"Failure occurs for those who do not know the application [of the mantra].
Thus, the necessity of the assignment (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth is established; this is the intended meaning. (4-105)
He states [the answer] by means of the seers and so forth.
In the *Mantracūḍāmaṇi*.
O Great Queen, listen to the names of the lay devotees (upāsakas) by which they themselves are known:
Manucandra, Kuvera, and after him, Manmatha. (4-106)
Lopāmudrā, Manu, Nadi, Śakra, and Skandhaśiva, as well as Krodhabhaṭṭālaka—these are proclaimed as the five. (4.107)
Dūrvāsas, Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, and Parāśara;
(25a) Aurva, Vahni, Yama, Nairṛta, and likewise Varuṇa. 4-108.
Vāyuviṣṇu, Svayaṃbhu, Bhairava, Gaṇapa, Aniruddha, Bharadvāja, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti; || 4-109 ||
Vaṭuka, Gaṇapa, Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Dhātrī, Śiva, Prasasta, and Unmattakulabhairava. (4-110)
Dhātrī, Dharitrī, Kṣatrapāla, Hanūmān, Dakṣa, Garuḍa, Śukadeva, Prahlāda, Rāma, and Rāvaṇa. (4.111)
Kaśyapa, Kausika, Jamadagni, Bhṛgu, Bṛhaspati, the best of the Yadus, Dattātreya, and Yudhiṣṭhira. (4.112)
Arjuna, Bhīmasena, Droṇācārya, Jayadratha, Duryodhana, as well as Kuntī, Sītā, and Rukmiṇī. || 4-113 ||
Satyabhāmā, Draupadī, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā;
Puṣpadanta, Mahābuddha, Vāṇakāla, and Maṇḍara. || 4-114 ||
Kailāsa, Ikṣusindhu, Udadhī, and likewise Himavat; and the great hero Yādava, along with the Kalpavṛkṣa and the Sādhaka.
"By the grace of Mahāvidyā, may each be endowed with their respective desires. Thus spoke Mahāvidyā.
And so it is stated in the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, and Bhuvaneśvarī. || 4-116 ||
Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and likewise the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī;
Vagalā, Siddhavidyā, Mātaṅgī, and she whose essence is Kamalā. (4.117)
O Great Goddess, these ten Mahāvidyās have been proclaimed;
having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) according to the rule with the root mantra. (4.118)
He states the definition of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The Compendium of the Essence of Tripurā.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the wind residing within the body; its extension and its restraint is called *prāṇāyāma*. Indeed, it is said to be of two kinds. (4.119)
That embryo is both with an embryo and without an embryo.
The mantra recitation with the inner core (*sagarbha*) becomes the "innermost core" (*nigarbhā*) through proper measure;
this was taught by the Jar-born One (*Kumbhaja*) in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*.
And [the rule applies] to the *mātrā* as well.
The time required to pierce each individual leaf in a cluster of lotus petals with the tip of a fine thread—that which expresses such a duration of time is called *kālavācaka*. (4.121)

They know that thirty lavas constitute a kalā, and a tuṭi is likewise [thirty kalās]; a kāṣṭhā should be known as having as many [tuṭis] as there are kalās, and a meṣaka consists of as many kāṣṭhās as there are [tuṭis]. (4.122)
The measure [of time] is said to be equal to ten snaps of one's own fingers;
it is the duration of time required for one's hand to reach one's own knee. (4.123)
The measure of the *paryāti* is equal to its own *asat*,
or else it is inferred from the *mātrā*.
The rotation of the hand placed upon the left knee should continue for as long as it takes. || 4-124 ||
That measure should be understood according to the time by the sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas, as stated in the Yāmala.
Then, being composed, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the Vāgbhava [syllable]. || 4-125 ||
Pressing the right nostril with the right thumb, the knower of mantras should gradually fill the air into the heart with sixteen measures (mātrās). (4.126)
Then, holding both nostrils with the thumb and the ring finger,
one should then retain the breath by means of four times the duration of inhalations (pūraka).
Likewise, holding the name "Anāmā" on the left and "Vāmā" on the right, one should perform the exhalation of the breath for thirty-two *mātrās*. (4.128)
Having placed one's own mind in the root-cakra, one should practice the retention of the vital breath (asūtsa);
then, by means of the path of exhalation, one should fill the prāṇa-vāyu.
Again, one should commence the retention (kumbhaka) for sixteen mātrās;
then, one should fill [the breath] through the path of exhalation (recana). || 4-130 ||
Furthermore, the practitioner of mantra, having restrained both nostrils, should perform the kumbhaka (retention) for sixty-four measures by means of sixteen measures.

Furthermore, the wise one should draw in the breath through the right [nostril] for thirty-two measures, and likewise draw in the breath through the left alone for sixteen measures in succession. (4.132)

Then, having pressed the two nostrils together, the wise practitioner should exhale the air through the right [nostril] with thirty-two measures, which are four times the measure of the inhalation (pūraka).
Holding the breath with the left hand while exhaling through the right is the first *prāṇāyāma*;
however, that [result] occurs through the repeated practice of *prāṇāyāma* over time. (4.134)
The procedure for breath control (prāṇāyāma) has been correctly explained by me with effort;
there are the inferior, the middling, and likewise the superior breath control.
If one practices the Dharma with inferior food, there is trembling; with middling food, one attains the siddhi of Khecarī; with superior food, one shall attain it—of this there is no doubt. (4-136)
By performing sixteen breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) constantly and daily, the wise man certainly destroys all the sins committed every day. (4.137)
The retention of the nostrils by means of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb—excluding the index and middle fingers—is to be understood as *prāṇāyāma*. (4.138)
There is no doubt that one destroys all sins through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform three breath controls every day with the root mantra. || 4.139 ||

Whether reciting or having recited [the mantra] with a desire for accomplishment, the practitioner should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *vidyā* and the *mātṛkā*, followed immediately by the placement of the mantra. (4.140)
One should assign [the mantras] to the fingers beginning with the thumb together with their respective seed-syllables;
and the seed-syllables are *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.
And thus.

The "sixfold birth" (jātiṣaṭka) is said to be joined with [the mantras] beginning with the heart (hṛd) and ending with the weapon (astra); one should perform the weapon-mantra at the palms of the hands, preceded by the three *tāra*s (oṃs).
Being composed, one should not direct [the breath] toward the directions with the *śoṭikā* [breaths];
then, the wise one, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the limb-mantras upon the heart and other [limbs], [should proceed]. (4.143)
First, "namas" for the heart; "vahnivallabhā" (svāhā) for the head;
"ṣaṭ" for the tuft (śikhā); and "huṃ" is declared for the armor (kavaca). || 4.144 ||
"Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; phaṭ to the weapon"—in this sequence, "svāhā" is the beloved of Agni (the fire-syllable).
Having recited the six-limbed mantras, one should apply them to the six limbs;
this applies when the six limbs have not been explicitly mentioned.
One should abandon the mantra of the eye in that [mantra] whose five limbs are the mind.
For a mantra that is deficient in its constituent parts, one should supply those parts by means of itself;
and by means of its own root-mantra (mūlamantra).
One should perform the various other nyāsas according to the procedure prescribed for each respective Kalpa.
The wise preceptor should sequentially fashion a throne within his own body by means of Dharma and the other [virtues], proceeding clockwise upon the pair of shoulders and the pair of thighs.
One should sequentially place Dharma, Jñāna, Vairājya, and Aiśvarya;
these, beginning with Dharma, are remembered as the feet, or alternatively, as the limbs of the pedestal.
One should visualize Adharma and the other [principles] on the face, the two sides, and the two sides of the navel;
Ananta is in the heart, and upon this lotus are the sun, moon, and fire.
27a) And on each of his own limbs, he should place [the syllables] preceded by the first letter of their respective names;
he should place the Sun, beginning with the letter *a*, and the Moon, beginning with the syllable *oṃ*.
One should place the fire element, beginning with the letter *sa*, conjoined with the circle of its digits (*kalā*);
then, having placed the three qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest, [one should proceed].
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are declared to be its divisions;
yet within this [nature], there are the Self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), and the supreme self (paramātman).
Having placed the three primordial seed-syllables preceded by the Śakti-bīja:
*Ā* / *Ātmane namaḥ*.
Aṃ, salutation to the inner self (antarātman).
Thus is the sequence of the ritual placement (nyāsa).
And also: "Homage to the self whose essence is the syllable Hrīḥ."
Having properly assigned the self whose nature is knowledge, one should then assign the mantra of the seat (pīṭha).
Thus, one should meditate upon the chosen deity on the seat consisting of the body;
having displayed the mudrās according to the rule, one should perform the ritual installation of the arghya offering.
Having sprinkled water upon the conch and the *mustā* root, one should place them to the left of the fire-mandala;
that is, within the triangular fire-mandala.
The wise one should establish the common vessel, which is praised by the *bindu*, with substances consisting of nectar.
From the moon situated on the head, the earth was [nourished] by its daughter, the waters consisting of that [moon],
by means of the root mantra.
One should fill [the vessel] with water, fragrant flowers, and other offerings according to the prescribed ritual.
One should meditate upon the support (ādhāra), fire (pāvaka), the conch (śaṅkha), the solar water (sūryatoya), and the moon (sudhākara);
at the end of these [meditations], the fires, sun, and moon dissolve into them respectively.
