Having touched it, one should apply the root mantra; then one should apply its limb-mantras.
Having performed worship with the heart-mantra, the king should cover it with both hands. (4.158)
The preceptor, regarding [the disciple] as a deity, should recite the vidyā according to the rule;
having protected him with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), he should envelop him with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Having performed the *dhenumudrā*, one should awaken [the offering] with its own mudrā;
then, having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel on the right, one should worship with these [mantras]. (4.160)
Having taken a small amount of water, one should add it to the water for sprinkling (prokṣaṇī).
To the north of the water for the guest-offering (argha), the water for washing the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be prepared.
The Guru should sprinkle himself, the sacrificial materials,
and the pavilion with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, using the mantra [prescribed] for each in due order.
Having touched [the disciple] during the placement of the root mantra, one should place the mantra of its limbs;
having worshipped thoroughly with the heart-mantra, the king should cover [him] with both hands. (4.163)
One should recite the mantra according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) within the bodies, and thereafter worship Dharma and the other [principles].
With perfumes and other offerings, using the mantras of the seats (pīṭha), one who is single-minded should again offer five handfuls of flowers to the deity of that city.
One should worship [the deity] sequentially on the head, the heart-center, the feet, and all the limbs,
without the offerings of food, incense, and other such services.
One should complete the remaining practice according to the method taught by the guru.
One should employ all of this with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel. (4.166)
Having sprinkled water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should worship it as before;
then the practitioner, with perfumes and other offerings, should properly worship that mandala.
Having filled the center of the pericarp with śāli rice and decorated it with rice grains on top,
the knower of mantras should place darbha grass blades across it.
One should place a *kūrca* (a bundle of grass) joined with unbroken rice grains upon their center;
beginning from the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), one should worship the seat (*pīṭha*) consisting of its respective mantra in detail.
Below, they are mounted upon tortoise-stones, possessing a radiance like that of the autumnal moon.
One should worship the Power of the Support (Ādhāraśakti), who bears two hexagons;
the meaning is that she stands upon the form of the Tortoise (Kūrma). 4.170ab.
One should visualize a dark-blue tortoise seated upon her head;
above it is Ananta, resembling a tortoise, who supports Brahmā and is cooled by the wind.
One should worship the Holder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), who bears the earth upon his head;
and there [one should worship] her who is dark as a tamāla tree and wears blue lotuses.
One should worship the Earth, girdled by the shimmering oceans;
upon her, an island made of jewels, and within that, a pavilion of gems.
One should worship the Kalpavṛkṣa (wish-fulfilling tree) therein, which grants the desired accomplishments of the practitioner;
below it, one should worship their pedestal, radiant with a mandala.
Thereafter, one should again worship upon that [seat] with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamaṇtra) and so forth;
[the deities] have the luster of red, dark-blue, yellow, and sapphire, filling the quarters.
When a bull has become a *sarī* (corpse), one should sacrifice it to the deities of the form of Bhara;
but when it has become a *bhūta* within human bodies, one should worship those [deities], yet not those who are unprecedented or of ill-omened lineage.
Then one should worship the lotuses in the corners beginning with the southeast and in the cardinal directions.
Having first worshipped the bulb of bliss (ānandakanda), immediately thereafter the stalk of consciousness (saṃvinnāla), and after that the lotus consisting of all the principles (sarvatattva).
Then the officiant should worship the primary principles (*prakṛti-tattva*) as the filaments consisting of transformations, and the pericarp enriched with the fifty seed-syllables.
One should worship her together with the Kalās, as well as Sūrya, Candra, and Pāvaka;
and with the three parts of the Praṇava, the qualities of Rajas, Sattva, and so forth.
One should unify the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self, as well as the Self of Knowledge, according to the rule, ending with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra). (4.180)

In the filaments of the *pīṭha-śakti*s and in the center, [one should place] a jar shining with gold and other materials, its interior cleansed by the *astra* [mantras], and [the deity] holding the *varada* and *abhaya* gestures. (4.181)
It is fumigated with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, possessing a beautiful form,
and its hollows are encircled by a triple-stranded thread.
By means of the sūtra concerning attachment to the objects of power.
Regarding Viṣṇu, the Tantrikas say it is with a white thread.

The practitioner of mantra, reciting the *tāra* (oṃ), should place water containing the nine gems, accompanied by *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), along with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (4.183)
The knower of the ritual procedure, having conceived the unity of the water-pot and the pedestal,
[should perform the rite] with fresh twigs from a milky tree or with leaves from a *palāśa* tree.
Or with waters from sacred fords, rendered fragrant with *vāka* flowers, incense, and blossoms,
one should worship the *mātṛkā* in reverse order according to the rules, identifying it non-differently with oneself.
In that same manner, one should recite the root mantra while mentally filling [the body] with the deity;
thus he spoke of the *pratiloma* (reverse) alphabet.
One should fill [the vessel] while reciting the root mantra consisting of the fifty syllables ending in the vowel *a*, beginning with *kṣa*, *ha*, *sa*, *ṣa*, *śa*, and *ya*.
When the conch is filled with the decoction, the eight fragrances grant one's desired objects.
Having stirred it, one should fill [the vessel] therein, having invoked all the *kalās*:
first the ten *kalās* of Fire, and then the twelve of the Twelve-fold Self.
One should pour into the jars the decoction situated in the conch, which consists of sixteen digits of the moon and fifty-five digits.
The threefold Tantra of the Eight Substances consists of Śakti, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; [the substances are] sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, colophony, saffron, and yellow pigment (rocanā). 4-189.
They know the eight fragrances (*gandhāṣṭaka*) to consist of *jatāmāṃsī*, *kapi* (camphor), and *śakta*.
"Theft" (*cora*) refers to *kuṇḍa*; alternatively, it refers to black *śaṭī*, musk (*kastūrī*), or red sandalwood (*raktacaṇḍana*).
29a) Sandalwood, agallochum, hrīverā, vīrā, kuṣṭha, saffron, and gorocanā—these are known as the eight [substances] for the month of birth.
Jatāmāṃsī, murā, and uśīra are known as the eight [substances] for Viṣṇu and the Gaṅgā. (4-191)
*Hrīvīrabhalhākuṣṭha* refers to *kuṭha*, *sevyaka*, and the root of *vīraṇa*.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, tamāla, water, saffron, kuśīta, and kuṣṭha— these they know as the eightfold fragrance of Śiva.
*Tamāla* is a specific type of tree, meaning *jalavallī*.
*Kuśīta* is red sandalwood; *kuṣṭha* is the same as *kuḍuma* (saffron). || 4-193 ||
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
This "eight-fragrance" (aṣṭagandha) mixture, consisting of rocanā, kapikā, kuṅkuma, nābhi, tvak, and candana, along with saurabha, is recommended for both the Śaiva and Śākta traditions.
Kapirakta-candana, kāśmīra, kuṅkuma, guḍatvak, dāru, and arcanī, combined with cora and kastūrī.
At the end of the syllables of Pāśāditya, there is again the non-principal word;
in sequence, here are the vital breaths (prāṇas), and likewise the individual soul (jīva) is situated here. (4.195)

One should further utter the word for the primary [organ], *mukhya*, after all the non-primary sense organs (*asarvendriya*), following the sequence of the words for speech, mind, eye, ear, nose, and breath. (4.196)
Having returned here afterwards, may you remain happily for a long time, O you two who are satisfied;
this is declared to be the salutation of the vital breath (prāṇa), which bestows life upon all living beings.
The syllable of the sun of the vital breath.
The three seed-syllables are Ā, HRĪḤ, and KRO.
The *ātman* is the *ātman-mantra*, namely *haṃsa*. By that [is meant]: *ā hrīḥ kroḥ haḥ saḥ ṭha dvayaṃ svāhā*.
By that [is meant]: *ā hrīḥ kroḥ haḥ saḥ amukhya prāṇā iha prāṇā ā hrīḥ kroḥ haṃ saḥ amukhya*.
The *jīva* remains here:
Ā HrīḤ KroḤ Ha Sa. [He] again [withdraws] all the sense-faculties.
O secondary speech, mind, sight, hearing, smell, and breath, having come here, may you remain happily for a long time;
svāhā!
There is no modification in the case of a non-primary vessel.
Behind him was the venerable Aśvarthapanasa,
tender with mango sprouts and bound with *indravallī* creepers, who was honored as if he were a celestial tree.
Indravallī (Cocculus cordifolius)
Aparājitā.
I shall place this cup containing unbroken grains and fruit upon the mouth of the jar;
for the cup is the Śālāva and the unbroken grain is that which was first [offered].
And one should duly place the fruit-bearing trees with the thought of their fruit;
then, one should wrap the water-pot with a pair of stainless cloths.

Having fashioned an image within this [mandala] using the root mantra, the practitioner of mantra should invoke and worship the deity of the mantra upon it, as if it were the shadow of the wish-fulfilling trees.
Having recited the root mantra, the wise one, with his mind fixed on the *suṣumnā*,
brings the light from its own place as it emerges through the aperture of the nose.

Having joined the Mātṛkā residing in the hand with the collection of the flowers of consciousness at the Bhoja [cakra], the wise one should invoke [the deity] into the image through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
One should always fashion the head of the deity well-proportioned;
at the time of worship, one should move the hand around the deity's vehicle.
One should perform the stabilization, the placement, and the immediate cessation;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual of totalization (sakalīkaraṇa) and the veiling (avaguṇṭhana).
Having performed the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), one should perform the supreme consecration (*paramikṛti*);
one should perform these in sequence with one's own mudrās, remaining concentrated in mind.
I shall now describe the mudrās for invocation and the other rites, as well as which mudrā is used for what purpose in their proper sequence. When these are performed, all the deities rejoice.
With flowers properly offered and with hands joined in *añjali* formed by the two digits (*kalā*), [the rite is accomplished]. (4.205)
This mudrā is declared by the best of masters to be the "invoking" (āvāhanī);
when turned face downwards, it is said to be used for the rite of "establishing" (sthāpana).
With the two fists joined together and the pair of index fingers extended, this mudrā is declared by the knowers of the three Vedas to be the Sannidhāna [mudrā]. (4.207)

That same [mudrā], with the thumb held inward and closed for restraint, constitutes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the body of the deity; this is the "entirely formed" (*sakalīkṛta*) rite. (4.208)
This is the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*: the form made with the left hand, with the index finger extended downward and facing down;
when this is rotated all around, it becomes the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā*.
Furthermore, when the ring fingers are joined face-to-face and likewise the middle fingers and index fingers are so placed, this is the Dhenu-mudrā, which bestows nectar. (4.210)
With the thumbs mutually entwined and the fingers slightly bent, this is declared by the wise to be the Mahāmudrā for the purpose of supreme union. (4.211)
That mudrā is employed by the deity in the ritual of yoga;
then the knower of mantras should perform the services beginning with the welcome. (4.212)
And so it has been said in the Bṛhanmatsyasūkta:
Various forms of worship have been described; among them, I take refuge in one:
the ten services (upacāra) in their proper sequence, beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the sacrificial altar (vedi).
The sixteen modes of service (ṣoḍaśopacāra) are stated in eight ways in the Śāradā-tantra.
Water for the feet, the respectful offering (argha), water for sipping, bathing, clothing, and ornaments;
likewise, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and garments. (4.214)
Betel, worship, hymn, libation, and prostration—these sixteen services he performed for his meal. (4.215)
And so it is said in the Jñānārṇava:
The noble one [is offered] a seat, water for the feet, water for sipping, and the honey-mixture; as well as garments and ornaments for the body. (4.216)
With perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and likewise water for the face—in this manner, O wise one, one should employ the sixteen services (upacāras). || 4.217 ||
The eighteen modes of service.
This has been stated in the Tripurārṇava:
A seat, a vehicle, a staff, water for the feet, and likewise water for sipping;
a bath, a garment, a sacred thread, and ornaments of every kind.
One should offer perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and libations; likewise, garlands, ointments, prostrations, and the ritual dismissal. (4.219)
The mantra-practitioner should perform the worship with the eighteen services (upacāras). Now, the thirty-six services:
This has been stated in the *Sundarīrahasyavṛtti*.
Likewise, by means of the seat, the fanning, and the rubbing and sprinkling with unguents. || 4-220 ||
Then [there are] the sweeping, the sprinkling with clarified butter, the bathing, and the invocation;
followed by the water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), the bath-water, and the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Furthermore, water for sipping, a garment, and a sacred thread; a saffron robe, perfumes, and flowers; as well as incense and a lamp. (4-222)
Betel leaves, food offerings, flower garlands, as well as ointments, fly-whisks, and fans. || 4.223 ||
Beholding the mirror, followed by prostration, singing, instrumental music, gifts, hymns of praise, fire-offerings, and circumambulation. (4.224)
The offering of a tooth-stick and then the dismissal of the deity;
these ritual services are to be known as the thirty-six [items] in the worship of the gods. (4.225)
31a) Now, the sixty-four offerings.
Placing [the image] upon a seat, anointing it with fragrant oil, entering the bathing hall,
and seating it upon the throne in the bathing pavilion.
Divine bathing water.
Anointment with fragrant unguents, bathing with camel-urine water, and the consecration by the waters of all sacred fords poured from golden jars.
The wiping with a washed cloth.
Wearing a lower garment and an upper garment of reddish-brown silk.
The entry into the plastered pavilion.
Seating upon a jeweled pedestal within a pavilion smeared with fragrant unguents.
Sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, musk, camphor, and gorocana— divine perfumes for anointing all the limbs;
and for the mass of hair, black agallochum incense, mallikā, mālatī, jasmine, and campaka flowers.
She entered the pavilion adorned with the ornaments of the mind— ketaka, lotus, punnāga, and pairs of kalhāra flowers blooming in all seasons—
and sat upon a jeweled throne; she wore a crown of fresh gems, a crescent moon as her parting line, vermilion as her forehead mark, and black collyrium as her jewel.

Various ornaments for the pair of hands, a necklace of emerald, a woven ornament, a wish-fulfilling jewel on the hand, a great breastplate, a pearl necklace, a single-string necklace, a *devacchandaka*, a *chadadmavīra*, four pairs of armlets, a row of bracelets, and a row of finger-rings.
Śrīmālikā wears a necklace, a jeweled crest-ornament, a thread-garland, the ornament called *śobhā*, anklets, jeweled foot-rings, and lotus-shaped finger-rings.

In one hand she holds a noose, in another an *ikṣu* bow, and in another a red lotus, a blue lotus, and a white water-lily; from her right shoulder she carries flower-arrows arising from a sprout of sugarcane.
The sandals, sitting upon one's own seat (31b), the single Amṛtāsana, the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), the camphor garden, the laughter of playful joy and exuberance,
the triple auspicious mark (maṅgalātrikā), the white parasol, the pair of fly-whisks, the mirror, the palm-leaf fan, and the fragrance.
One should offer flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
This has been stated in the Mānasollāsa:
The mantra practitioner should always recite the offerings with full awareness—
that is, by means of the words of awakening.
All ritual service mantras should be performed with "Tāra" at the beginning and ending with "namas."
And so it is.
Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, O Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, I offer water for the feet; obeisance, and so forth, until: obeisance.
All such [passages] are to be understood in this manner.
Thus is the water for the feet.
There is a longing for the subject of Śrīvidyā.
Others [attain] it through perfect awakening.
And so it has been said in the Jñānamālā:
I shall describe the procedure for the ritual service, or else [the procedure] after having provided a beautiful seat.
One should utter a greeting and inquiries after his welfare in the presence of the Guru; with a heart full of devotion, one should offer water for the feet at the lotus-feet of the Lord.
The meaning is "approved by the heart."
With these—*etacchayā*, *kadūrvāṅga*, and *viṣṇukrāntā*—it is said:
one should offer water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīyaka*) into the mouth with the *svadhā* mantra.
With nutmeg, cloves, and kakkola— so it is said by those who know the Tantras—
the mantra is *svadhā*.
The mantra is "vaṃ."
Then the preceptor should offer the *argha* upon the head with the *śiro-mantra*.
Fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice, *kuśa* grass, sesame, mustard seeds, and so forth—this is declared to be the *argha* for all the gods upon my head. (4.229)

32a) "Svāhā" means a mantra. With that very mantra, one should perform the respectful offering of water for sipping (ācamanīyaka). Then, with that same mantra ending in "svadhā," one should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka) into the lotus-face.
This mixture of clarified butter, curd, and honey has been declared by the wise. (4.230)
The auspicious mantra.
The mantra of self-power.
The meaning is that "vaṃ" is the mantra.
With that same mantra, one should perform the water for sipping;
with the mantra "te naivam," one should offer the *arghya* and then give the water for washing the feet.
This has been stated in the Kramadīpikā:
For it is heard in the scriptures that after offering a seat and uttering "Welcome," one should likewise offer the *argha*, *pādya*, and *ācamanīya* waters;
this is because the intention is that these are optional according to one's desire.
One should offer the three-fold *ācamanīya* (water for sipping).
As it is said regarding the *pūrṇā* sacrifice:
"Indeed, one should offer the *ācamanīya* three times into the lotus of the mouth with the word 'svadhā'. (4.231)
The wise one should offer a flower upon the crown with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*,
for the sacred tradition states that the offering of a flower is performed with *vauṣaṭ*.
The mantra is "vauṣaṭ namaḥ."
It is likewise stated in the *Sārasaṃhitā* regarding the offering of the *argha* and other oblations:
"One should offer [the mantras] in sequence as *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and *vauṣaṭ*. (4-232)
Having uttered the *ātman* mantra at the heart, one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the other articles;
one should perform the bath with scented water and clothe [the deity] in two garments. (4.233)

One should bestow the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) along with necklaces and other ornaments, using the letters of the *mātṛkā* recited according to the sequence of the sages' ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (4.234)
Having worshipped the deity with perfumes and other offerings, one should then worship the limbs and so forth,
as prescribed with perfumes, sandalwood, camphor, and black agallochum.
The two types of *kamala*, the *karavīra*, the two types of *kumuda*, the two types of *tulasī*, the two types of *jātī*, the two types of *ketakī*, and the *kalhāra* and *campaka* flowers. (4.236)
Kunda, mandāra, punnāga, pāṭala, nāgacaṃpaka, āragvadha, karṇikāra, pārvatī, and navamālikā. || 4-237 ||
The *saugaṇṭhika*, *sakoraṇṭa*, *palāśa*, *aśoka*, and *mallikā*; the *dantura*, *sarjaka*, *bilva*, *arjuna*, and *puṣpabilvaka*. (4.238)
Furthermore, the wise practitioner should take other fragrant flowers, even those consisting of mere blossoms, as prescribed by the teachers for the purpose of worship. (4.239)
The teacher should discard that which is dirty, touched by the ground, defiled by worms, hair, and the like, touched by a limb, smelled, or stale. (4.240)
"Touching with a limb" means touching with anything other than the hand; this is the remainder [of the sense].
One should not worship with buds, nor with those that have fallen, been broken, or even dried; nor with flowers or petals and leaves that are unfit for use.
With whatever flower, leaf, or petal,
having brought it from wherever it may be, or even one produced right there at the site [of the ritual].
One who desires prosperity and the preservation of life should not worship flowers from trees planted by others on ground that is not one's own. (4.243)
But for one who is not informed by them, his worship is fruitless;
and so it is said in the Jñānamālā:
Neither a flower, nor a leaf, nor a fruit should be offered with its face turned downward.
Setting aside the ritual of the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should offer [the offering] exactly as it arises;
likewise, it is stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa:
The food offering (naivedya) may be placed on the right, the left, in front, or behind. || 4.245 ||
One should offer the lamp to the right or in front, but not to the left;
likewise, the incense should be offered to the left or in front, but not to the new right.
33a) One should present perfume, flowers, and ornaments in front;
one should offer incense on the left—this is for the cult of Viṣṇu. However, in the case of the Śakti-cult, one should offer it on the right.
Whatever is suitable for images and the like, that same [quality] is present in the body when it has been bestowed by the lineage.
One should not place unsuitable food offerings, meals, and so forth before [the deity]; nor should one place a lamp upon a support—by doing such things, a person [incurs fault]. (4.248)
The entire earth, Sahā, together with him—these two things [endure]:
the blow from the master’s foot and likewise the heat of the lamp. (4-249)
Thus ends the Kālikā Purāṇa.
The preceptor should burn incense made of agallochum, śīla, kapūra, guggulu, sugar, honey, and sandalwood, mixed with clarified butter, while remaining in a low position.
Uśīra is the root of vīraṇa grass;
it is fragrant and contains camphor.
With clarified butter or with oil produced from sesame seeds.
Having placed them there, one should show lamps possessing a high fragrance,
along with sweet side-dishes and pure milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar.
One should offer it together with plantain fruit and clarified butter while reciting the mantra;
"upadaṃśa" refers to substances intended for chewing.
Modaka consists of coconut and similar substances.
In each of those instances, one should offer water, performing the ritual service in the prescribed manner.
Or one may worship the limbs ending with the world-protectors (lokapāla) as the objects of selection;
on the filaments, starting from the southeast corner, one should worship the heart-mantra and the others.
The weapons are to be placed in the eyes and the directions; the deities of the limbs are to be assigned.
Fire is said to be in the heart, and Śiva is declared to be in the nose and the southwest (nairṛta).
The letter *ṣa* in the northwest corner is declared to be the armor (*kavaca*); it is also [placed] in the directions starting from Śiva (the northeast).
Having worshipped the eye (*netra*) in the southeast, one should worship the directions starting from the east up to the west.
33b) He explains the manner of worship within the scope of one's capacity.
It is stated in the Śrī Navadurgākalpa:
One should perform the offering of flowers with the thumb and forefinger of the right hand;
one who desires their own success should not worship with only one hand. (4.256)
The right hand alone is fit for malevolent rites (abhicāra); the left alone is for enjoyment (bhoga). Through their union, it bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
The union of the thumb and the ring finger is the supreme essence of Śiva and Śakti;
the thumb is said to be Śiva, and the ring finger is called Śakti. (4.258)
Merely through contact with water, the substance becomes like nectar;
the two drops consisting of Śiva and Śakti become the ring. (4.259)

Therefore, that substance which has emerged from it is desired as the supreme nectar by the best of practitioners for the sake of accomplishing the mantras and eliminating defects such as being "cut" (chinnā). || 4-260 ||
One should practice the Yonimudrā according to the method of the teacher’s instruction,
as follows:
And in the foundation, at the location of the anus, there should be a four-petalled lotus.
Therein, one should contemplate the self-manifested (svāyaṃbhūva) liṅga as reddish-white;
therein it has three and a half coils.
One should contemplate Kuṇḍalinī, who has the form of a sleeping serpent.

By means of the syllable *huṃ*, having struck down the mental rod (*manodaṇḍa*), one raises [the breath] from the *mūlādhāra* and brings it to the *svādhiṣṭhāna* located at the root of the *liṅga*; then from the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, one brings it to the *maṇipūraka* cakra located at the navel; from the *maṇipūraka*, to the *anāhata* cakra located in the heart; and likewise from the *anāhata*, to the *viśuddha* located in the throat. It is exactly thus.

Having brought [the breath] from the pure space between the eyebrows to the *ājñācakra*, and having led it to the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasradalakamala*), one should contemplate its state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) with the light of Sadāśiva residing in that thousand-petaled lotus.

34a) Having brought Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is the root-mantra, from the station of Śiva’s command to the wheels [of the body], one should lead her from there through the sequence of the stations of Viśuddha, Anāhata, Maṇipūraka, and so forth, down to the Mūlādhāra.
Then, having meditated upon that mantra-deity within his heart and worshipped her with mental offerings, he should pay homage.
Thus is the Yonimudrā.
The wise practitioner, intent on practice, should perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
These ten purificatory rites of the mantra are said to bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*). (4.263)
First is birth, then life; thereafter is striking, and likewise life again;
then follows consecration, and from that, purification and nourishment. (4.264)
Satiating, inflaming, and protecting—these are the purificatory rites for mantras.
The extraction of mantras from the midst of the Mātṛkā is known as "birth" (janana). (4.265)

"Mātṛkā" refers to the fifty mother-letters; from among them, the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra) by taking [the required letters] from the midst of the mātṛkās is the "birth" (janana) of the mantra.
The wise one should recite the syllables of the mantra with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) interspersed between them;
those learned in mantra and tantra call this the "living" (*jīva*) mantra. (4.266)
"Interposed by the Praṇava."
The meaning is that one should recite the mantra by placing the *praṇava* after each individual syllable of the mantra to be given.
This is the life-force of the mantra.

Having written out the syllables of the mantra, one should strike each one with sandalwood water; that is declared to be the "striking" (tāḍana) of the mantra by means of the wind [vowel *i*]. (4-267)
Each individual syllable of the mantra should be offered with the wind [seed-syllable]; that is, with the seed-syllable *yam*, one should offer the consecrated sandalwood paste for each syllable.
Thus ends the striking with the mantra.
In the context of Gopāla, [this refers to] white sandalwood water;
34b) the Goddess [is worshipped] with water from red sandalwood, which is attached to the objects of the senses—this is the meaning.
One should write the mantra with *karavīra* flowers corresponding in number to the syllables of that mantra; by doing so, one would slay [the enemy], or at the end [of the rite], awaken him.
The meaning is that it should be engraved upon a copper plate.
In the word *yānta*, the *yakāra* of *ya* becomes *repha*.
And so it is said:
The syllable *raṃ* means the seed-syllable (*vīja*) of fire.
Thus is the awakening of the mantra.
The mantra-practitioner [should perform this] according to the number of the mantra, by means of the procedure taught in his own Tantra. (4.268)
One should consecrate [the disciple] with the mantra using *aśvattha* sprouts for the sake of purification, as stated in the *Svacchanda-tantra*.
In the case of Viṣṇu, it is with white sandalwood;
in the case of the Goddess, it is with red sandalwood—this is the meaning.
Having reflected upon the mantra with the mind, one should burn it away with the Jyotirmantra.
The mantra is the mother; this is the purification from the three impurities (mala).
As for the Jyoti-mantra: "Tāra, Vyoma, Agni, Manu-yuga, Daṇḍin"—this is considered the Jyoti-mantra. (4.270)
The syllable *tāra* is the *oṃkāra*.
The letter *ha* is space; the letter *ra* is fire.
Manu is Oṃkāra; Daṇḍin is [the letter] *da*.
With that, [he recites] "hrau" by means of the Jyoti-mantra.
By means of the mantra "Oṃ Hrau," the three impurities known as the māyīya, kārmaṇa, and śārīra are [purified].

The sprinkling of each [item] with water from *kuśa* grass over which the mantra has been recited is considered the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) of the mantra, performed according to the rule by means of that very mantra. (4.271)
By that mantra, by the mantra to be given.
This is for the nourishment of even this much.
The practitioner of mantras performs the great libation with water consecrated by mantra—
that is, with the root mantra.
And so it is said:
The practical application is as follows: having uttered the deity's mantra, one says, "I satiate the root mantra."
35a) The satiation of the mantra of the vow.
The union of Tāra, Māyā, and Ramā is said to be the illuminator of the mind.
Tāraḥ Oṃ.

*Māyā* is *hrīṃ*, and *ramā* is *śrī*. *Yoga* means connection; it means that these should be placed at the beginning of the mantra. Having first given the three seed-syllables—*oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*—one should recite [the mantra]; this is the meaning.
This is the illumination of the mantra. The concealment and the non-disclosure of the mantra being recited—these ten consecrations have been proclaimed and kept secret in all tantras. (4.273)
Having performed that according to tradition, the practitioner shall obtain his desire;
then, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) as prescribed in the scriptures, he should perform the purificatory rite for the disciple.

Then, having made that disciple— who has bathed and is composed— drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the *sudhā* mantra at its end, he should lead him to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having beheld that consciousness, which has been seen with divine vision, within the lotus of the heart, the Guru,
having united it with his own self, should perform the purification of the path (adhva-viśodhana).
It has been stated that there are three paths: the path of time, the path of the principles (tattva), and the path of the worlds (bhuvana);
and another triad consisting of the path of phonemes (varṇa), the path of words (pada), and the path of mantras. (4.277)
The five kalās, beginning with nivṛtti, are proclaimed as the path of kalā (kalādhvan).
The path of principles (tattvādhvan) is divided in many ways according to the different Śaiva Āgamas.
There are thirty-six Śiva-tattvas and thirty-two varṇa-tattvas; furthermore, there are twenty-four Maitra-tattvas within Prakṛti. (4.279)
The ten principles have been stated; seven belong to the nature of the Three-Footed One (Tripadātman). By means of these principles, one is liberated from Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva. (4.280)
Īśvara, together with Vidyā, indeed consists of these five purities:
Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, and Vidyā is further remembered [as the fifth]. (4.281)
Passion is a person; these are the [five] aggregates.
Not pure, and seven [factors] are pure.

The instructor [teaches] primordial nature (prakṛti), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), mind (manas), the five organs of perception, the five organs of action, the five subtle elements (tanmātra), the five gross elements (bhūta), and the [ten] faculties (daiśika). 4-282.
O best of sages, these are said to be seven or twenty-four according to their movements;
O most excellent of teachers, one should sever these six paths in their respective order.
One should contemplate the infant disciple as bearing the weight upon his feet, lotus-navel, heart, and head;
then, one should bind the eyes of the disciple with a cloth while reciting the mantra.
With the Netra-mantra and with the mantra ending in vauṣaṭ.
Taking that disciple by the hand, he should lead him from the *kuṇḍa* to the maṇḍala;
then, having filled his joined palms with flowers according to the ritual rule, [he should proceed]. (4.285)
Reciting the root mantra, one should cast [the offering] into the jar for the pleasure of the deity;
it should be placed upon the womb-cloth, situated at the junction of the two eyes.

Then, having further generated the consecrated [deity] through the sequence of the self-sacrifice (ātmayāga), the teacher should perform the respective placements (nyāsa) prescribed by the mantras upon the body of the disciple.
One should worship the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) residing in the water-pot with the five offerings (pañcopacāra).
Worship consisting of [the items] beginning with perfume (gandha) and ending with the food offering (naivedya) is the fivefold offering (pañcopacārikā).
O disciple, having consecrated [the disciple] in the maṇḍala, seat him in another place; O Brahmins, together with the five musical instruments, the wise one [should perform] with agallochum (agaru).
Having duly excavated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), he should place those celestial trees within its opening,
while mentally reciting the mantra *māṛḥkāṃ* and applying the vital seed (*śiśoṇiya*).
The knower of the Self should sprinkle himself with the waters consecrated by the root-mantra;
then, with the remaining water, the Guru should cause the disciple to sip it.
36a) Having risen and put on a clean garment, the disciple, having donned it...
Having sipped water and become restrained in speech, he should sit in the presence of the teacher.
When the deity has been transferred into his own disciple, the supreme teacher should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and should contemplate the identity of the two.
Since the five elements are the powers of the kalās of Nivṛtti, one should contemplate them within the body composed of the elements and cause the disciple to perceive them. (4.294)
The Nivṛtti-kalā, beginning from the feet, is established up to the knees; the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā pervades and remains from the knees up to the navel. (4.295)
From the navel up to the throat is the pervasion of Vidyā; beyond that, from the throat to the forehead, is the pervasion of Śānti, extending as far as its crest.
"Śāntyatītā is to be known as the *kalā*; the pervasion of the *kalās* has thus been declared.
Having performed this placement on the body of Śikhin, contemplate the deity with devotion. (4.297)

Having caused [the disciple] to hear the promise, "I shall give such-and-such a mantra," and when [the disciple] has not yet said, "Give it," [the teacher], preceded by the utterance of the *tāra* (oṃ), [should proceed]. (4.298)

Then he should impart the knowledge to that disciplined disciple preceded by the offering of water; having recited the *ṛṣi* and other [components] of the mantra, and having remembered the deity with his intellect. (4.299)
The guru, facing eastward, while the disciple stands facing the east, [should whisper it] three times into the right ear and likewise once into the left. (4.300)
This is the rule for Brahmins; however, for women and Śūdras, it is according to Vāmakeśvara.
Having caused [the text] to be recited on the fourth [day], you [should place] water again in the hand of the disciple.
"May this mantra yield equal fruit for both of us. "So be it," [the teacher] replied; and having accepted it, the disciple [said], "It shall be so. (4.302)
The preceptor, having commenced the rite of knowledge, should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
or else, with undistracted mind, he should recite the mantra eight times while offering clarified butter.
Perceiving through his intellect the identity of the Guru, the mantra, the deity, and his own name,
he should prostrate himself upon the ground like a staff before that Guru, who is of the very nature of the deity.
One should place his pair of lotus feet upon one's own head.
Now follows the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
And it is said in the Kramasaṃhitā:
A person who does not grasp the auspicious words of the Brahmins speaks in vain. (4.305)
Or even if one does not give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one will certainly go to hell along with one's kinsmen;
thus it is said.
He should present the sacrificial fee and a pair of garments to the preceptor.
And so forth, up to the necessity of performing the rite with the proper sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
He clarifies that very point with the words "at the end of initiation" (*dīkṣānte*).
Thus, it is said in the *Vṛhanmahāsūkta*: "At the conclusion of the initiation, they declare the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to consist of gold, cows, land, and ornaments."
One should offer everything—dwellings, vessels, clothing, food, livestock, gifts, and even the teachings, as well as one's own body, wealth, and life—to him. (4.307)
From that time forward, with no other thought, one should do what is pleasing to the guru;
whatever object is most dear to oneself, that one should offer to the guru. (4.308)
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru, who is Śiva himself manifest before one's eyes;
or one's entire possession, or half of that, or half of that again, according to his command.
If there were no transmigrating power, how could this [world] come to be?
And so it is said:
In the dialogue between Pārvatī and Hara.
One should give one's entire possession as the sacrificial fee, and one should also give a milch cow.
One should give land that provides a livelihood, which ensures the continuity of sons and grandsons;
likewise, it is stated in the *Pārijātasvara*:
"One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Guru, consisting of gold as prescribed. (4.311)
Otherwise, there would be no accomplishment at all; it would be unfit for the higher practice.
One should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests with a joyful mind, in its entirety. (4-312)
Without any stinginess regarding wealth, one should offer everything to the Guru alone;
the Guru himself shall consecrate the pavilion and the materials for the pavilion.

Or rather, what is the use of saying more here? Pārvatī would even sacrifice her own body for the sake of her guru when he is intent upon his purpose, for she always holds him as dear as her own life.
And thus:
In the *Smṛti* of Laghu-Hārīta:
"If a teacher should impart even a single syllable to a disciple, there is no wealth on earth that could repay him; by giving it, he becomes free from debt. (4.315)
One should also offer food, both solid and liquid, to the preceptor;
furthermore, one should provide the preceptor and the Brahmins with whatever delicious foods they desire.
One should provide various kinds of food for both the elderly and the children: namely, that which is chewed, eaten, sucked, licked, drunk, and masticated. (4.317)

Having first given [the offering] to the guru and immediately thereafter to the brahmins, one should afterwards gratify the brahmins with food and provide them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 4.318 ||
The Guru should recite the mantra a thousand times for the sake of protecting his own power;
the disciple, with a mind focused on nothing else, should strive with diligence to please the Guru. (4.319)
And so it is said:
In the Īśānasaṃhitā:
If, after having performed the initiation, the mantra-practitioner should observe a fast,
the deity will always be enraged and a curse will fall upon his head.
One who has not been formally accepted as a disciple, nor one belonging to our own lineage, should not take away [the offerings].
(37b) Alms-food, sacrificial oblations, vegetables and the like, prescribed fruits, and milk—these are the permitted items. (4-321)
Roots, sesame, and barley—these are the foods produced for mantra-practitioners;
therefore, O Śāṅkarī, one should eat food that is fit for sacrifice.
Because of the fear of enmity toward Viṣṇu’s mantra, or because of hearing of its bestowal, they maintain [the prohibition] out of desire;
for there is no contradiction with the eternal [rule].
As for the statement, "having smelled that which was used by the ancestors," this is the justification for the Veda; the underlying sense is that, in reality, it refers to something other than that.
This is declared to be the Kālāvatī-kṣā, which bestows all prosperity.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Āgamakalpa.
The fire-oblation (homa), however, is of three kinds, distinguished as obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya).
In all cases, the performance of the oblation is mandatory.
This has been stated in the Rudrayāmala:
"A mantra is never accomplished if it has not been recited, nor if it has not been offered in oblation;
for the purpose of worship is the protection of the form, through recitation and burnt offerings. (5-1) Thus [it is said].
Now, I shall describe the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) according to all the tantras;
since that very rite is to be accomplished within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), it is now being delineated. (5.2)
For Brahmins, it should be square; for kings, it is desired to be circular; for Vaiśyas, it has the appearance of a half-moon; and for Śūdras, it is prescribed to be [triangular].
For all [the deities], it should be square; however, some say it is three times as long.
This has been stated in the Sāgarasaṃhitā:
Thus, by following the traditional scriptures, fire is prepared by those seekers.
By those same finger-measures, let other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) also be prepared;
one should know that the form of the pit is the supreme body of primordial nature (prakṛti).
The head is declared to be in the east; the right and left arms are the [two] sides. The belly is said to be the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and the western part is the womb (yoni). 5–6.
The quadrangular pit is declared to bring about all accomplishments;
the quadrangular pit grants everything and is authoritative for all times.
O Great Goddess, by means of this fourfold hand-restraint, one accomplishes all ritual actions.
The Gautamīya.
Chariots and the like, as well as palanquins, rafts, and carts. || 5.8 ||
It must be constructed using the *mānāṅgula* (measurement finger); never by any other means.
Whatever measurements have been described, such as the *muṣṭi* (fist) and the *rātri* (night), [are to be understood in this context]. // 5.9 //
The duty of the sacrificer must be performed by him alone and never by anyone else;
this applies to the act of measurement that has been prescribed, as well as to that which has not been prescribed for the measurer.
This determination regarding the measurement of pride belongs only to the wise;
those who know the tantras understand a cubit to be enriched by twenty-four finger-breadths.
The measure of a standard finger (mānāṅgula) is declared to be equal to the length of the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand of the [architect] who performs the rite. (5.12)
Those who were in my presence.
One finger-breadth (aṅgula) consists of eight barley grains with their husks removed;
thus it is stated in the Sārasaṃgraha:
That which is one-eighth of a barleycorn (sasyāṅgula) is declared to be a *śo* (or *yo*). || 5-13 ||
A fifth part of that [measure] would be for sesame; a sixth part of a sesame seed would be for a māṣa.
For nīvāra grain, it would be that same fraction, or a sixth part of that, or even a lavā.
In all cases, the measurement should be taken from the middle finger; the measure of the middle joint of the middle finger constitutes one *aṅgula*. Twenty-four such *aṅgulas* make one *hasta*.

With hands joined that are not too long, measuring twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), the largest [measure] consists of eight of those barley-corns (yava), while the medium consists of seven barley-corns. (5.16)
O best of sages, the *kaniṣṭha* [measure] is declared to be six [units], as is the *hasta*;
likewise in the *Vasiṣṭha-pañcarātra*.
And in the Śāradā [script].
A pit measuring only one fist is prescribed for [the rite of] fifty [oblations].
With one hundred oblations, it becomes three spans in size; with one thousand, it becomes one cubit in size.
(From the *Śrībhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*).
If one intends to offer a thousand oblations, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) consisting of sixteen parts (kalās).
That [altar] should be ten thousand cubits for a two-hasta [fire-pit], and four cubits for a lakṣa-homa;
likewise, it is stated in the Jñānalalitā:
One hundred thousand [recitations] are required for six cubits, and one million for eight cubits.
"At ten cubits, indeed, at the limit of ten million, the calculation of cubits is established."
It is square, having four corners, and double [the size] starting from two cubits.
The measurement of each successive pit is proclaimed to be constructed by means of the diagonal cord of the preceding pit. (5.20)
Because it would follow that what was previously measured as two cubits, two fathoms, and so forth, would become four cubits.
And something else has been stated in the Yāmala:
In the case of ten thousand [repetitions], it is said to be two cubits; in the case of twenty thousand, four cubits; as is the width of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
At ten lakhs, however, it is remembered as being six cubits; at ten million, it is said to be one and a half cubits.
Or alternatively:
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit is prescribed for one hundred thousand recitations;
up to ten lakhs, one should increase it by half a cubit for each increment.
"A pit measuring ten cubits is prescribed for a *koṭi-homa* (ten million oblations).
Thus, the nature of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is described in the *Vasiṣṭha-pañcarātra*, verse 5.23.
The measurement of one cubit is declared for the four [sides];
the depth of the pit is held to be equal to the width of the fire-pit. (5.24)
Whatever form the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) have, such is the form of the girdle (mekhalā);
"quadrangular" means having four corners.

Regarding this, some maintain that in the fifth enclosure (mekhalā) there is only a single enclosure, while others prescribe all five enclosures or just three enclosures. This is stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
The knower of the tantras should fashion a fivefold girdle for every sacrificial pit.
Then there are three girdles, or else two, or even just one;
their width in finger-breadths (aṅgula) is respectively four, three, and two.
This has been stated in the Kriyāsāra:
In this context, it is stated that there is no break of even one finger-breadth in the primary girdle;
however, the break in the outer girdle is traditionally recorded as being five finger-breadths.
Beyond that, the cutting of the girdle (mekhalā) is measured at one and a half finger-breadths; then, in successive order,
two finger-breadths and four finger-breadths for the cutting of the second girdle, which is three finger-breadths wide.
Thus say some.
The three girdles of the sacrificial pits are measured respectively by one, two, and three finger-breadths.
The ladles should be known to measure two finger-breadths in width and length;
in a pit that is only as large as an oar, the sacrificial grass blades should be two finger-breadths long.
In a pit measuring one cubit, the dimensions are four, three, and two fingers;
in a pit of two cubits, by his command, they are six, ten, and eight fingers.
In a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) measuring four cubits, the innermost of the girdles (mekhalā) shall be eight, twenty-four, and sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) wide respectively;
the rim (nemi) surrounding it on all sides shall be one finger-breadth thick.
Mekhalā is like the girdle of a religious student (brahmacārin).
39b) They are like showers from a water-pot; they are soft and gentle.

And one should eat those [measures] starting from the lord of the sky (0) and the lord of the horses (7), excluding the neck-form of one finger; in height and width, they follow the sequence of four fingers and so forth.
Those contrary to this, even if mentioned in other tantras, are inconsistent with practice: the Vedas are four, and the fires are three.
What are the two eyes? The eyeballs.
Three, eight, and two yugas.
Eight, six, and four.
And likewise in the Kālottara:
Leaving one finger-breadth from the edge of the pit, the rule for the girdles (mekhalās) shall be established;
a wise person should increase them in sequence for a pit of one cubit.

The wise should know that the girdle (*mekhalā*) is ten cubits long in the middle, with its width varying according to the measurement of my fingers, and it should be cut [smooth] on all sides. (5.33)
He states that the procedure for a single pit (kuṇḍa) is to be performed in the western direction.
The Determination of the Great Gift.
In eating, in liberation, likewise in contentment, and similarly in the expulsion of digested food,
as well as always during fire-offerings and in rites for pacification, one should worship the single elephant of the direction of Varuṇa.
In the Sāradātilaka.
The source [of the girdle] is before the Hotṛ; it is above that, like an aśvattha leaf.

Among these, the one called Mekhalā is like an aśvattha leaf; by this [description], its base is four finger-breadths wide, and according to the stated sequence, its contracted width is one finger-breadth.
This has been stated in the Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā:
In the first enclosure, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be situated to the east of the officiating priest.
The account of Kuyādvīpa and that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possessing all characteristics [is as follows]:
the yoni is six aṅgulas long and four aṅgulas wide. (5.36)
In a wall measuring one cubit, the wise have declared the height [of the base] to be two finger-breadths;
its elevation here is indeed two finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width.
The yoni is declared to be one cubit for the Mukti [fire-pit];
likewise, in fire-pits of two cubits and so forth, one should increase the yoni proportionally.
"In the same way, one should increase the navel by the measure of one finger;
this is declared to be the yoni for sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) measuring one fist, one aratni, or one cubit."
It should be six or four finger-breadths in length and width, possessing a graceful curve;
one should make the tip of the yoni one finger-breadth wide and slightly downturned.

It is six finger-breadths long, four finger-breadths wide, and two finger-breadths high. Since the singular number is used here, this statement regarding its dimensions applies specifically to the case of a single *muṣṭi*-cubit.
In other sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), one should increase the width of the vulva (*yoni*) by one finger-breadth;
likewise, one should also increase the tip of the vulva by an increment of two barley-grains.
Thus [ends the section] concerning the objects such as the hands and so forth.
In this case, since there is no distinction [in the calculation], the truth is that there is no increase in the length, width, or inclination.
And so it is stated in the Yajñapārśva:
The place for the girdles (mekhalā) is prescribed as the base;
in the square [pedestal], there should be a stalk with a central aperture in the womb (yoni).
With a thick base and a fine tip, it should be charming with its two protruding ends;
one should fashion the outer girdle starting from the outermost part.
The term "saraṃdraka" is connected with both [the preceding and following words].
And Bhāskarācārya has said: "In the womb, there is a tube with a cavity."
Thus it is stated in the Rudrayāmala.
One should make the cavity of the *yoni* joined with that which is known as the *ājyagrāhin*;
starting from the base, there should be a stalk, and the middle of the *yoni* should have a perforation.
The best knower of the tantras should not place the yoni in the corner-pits (koṇakuṇḍa),
starting from the base of the girdles (mekhalā) at the site of the womb (raṃbha).
The meaning is: "or from the place where the vessel containing the invocation is situated."
Some say that *saraṃdhraka* is for the purpose of what is unseen (*adṛṣṭārthaka*). And so it is stated in the *Yāmala*:
And for the purpose of placing the enclosing sticks between the *nāla* and the *ukhala*. || 5-45 ||
"A wise man should likewise make an aperture on the second side of the mekhalā," according to the Śruti.
Thus, this statement does not indicate that the nose is devoid of nostrils.
But he states the circumference of the Nāla and Mekhalā [enclosures].
That is in the *Saṃyogapariśiṣṭa*.

The enclosing sticks (paridhis) should be of considerable length, straight, with their bark intact, unbroken at the tips, and there should be three of them, each placed toward one of the four directions. || 5.47 ||
Then, either according to the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or as prescribed for the Mānasa [rite], lines are struck:
first from west to east, and then another from south to north.

If one considers the other [wooden] enclosures (paridhi), it should be placed with its tip pointing north in the east; they should be without cracks or holes, and their tips and both sides should be smooth on all sides. (5-49)
From south to north, and from west to west.
With the top turned upward and the tip directed northward.
The essence of the three worlds.
