Śrī Āḥ on the forehead; Śrī Āḥ on the circumference of the face.
Śrī / i / in the right eye; Śrī / ī / in the left eye.
Śrī / u / on the right ear; Śrī / ṛ / on the right nostril.
Śrī Ṛ in the nose; Śrī Ḷ on the right cheek.
Śrī/Ḷī on the left cheek; Śrī/E on the lip.
Śrī Ai to the lower lip; Śrī O to the upper teeth.
Śrī/au/ to the lower teeth. Śrī/aṃ namaḥ to the head.
Śrī ĀḤ Ānamo Mukhe (on the face); Śrī Ka Dakṣavāhumūle (at the base of the right arm).
Śrī Kha at the elbow; Śrī Ga at the wrist.
Śrī Gha at the base of the finger; Śrī Ṅa at the tip of the finger.
Śrī at the base of the left upper arm; Śrī-chaṃ at the elbow.
Śrī Ja at the wrist-joint; Śrī Jha at the base of the fingers.
Śrī Ña at the tips of the fingers; Śrī Ṭa at the root of the right arm.
Śrī Ṭha at the knee; Śrī Ḍa at the ankle; Śrī Ḍha at the base of the toes.
Śrīṃ ṇaṃ at the tips of the fingers; Śrīṃ taṃ at the root of the left thigh.
Śrī Tha at the knees; Śrī Da at the ankles; Śrī Dha at the bases of the fingers.
Śrī/Na on the tip of the finger; Śrī/Pa on the right side.
Śrī Pha on the left side; Śrī Ba on the back.
Śrī Bha at the navel; Śrī Ma at the anus.
Śrī Ma, the essence of the skin, in the heart; Śrī Ra, the essence of the blood, at the base of the right upper arm.
Śrī-la-mā-aro-tma-ni-ka-ku-di; Śrī-va-me-dā-tma-ni-vā-bhu-mū-le.
48a) Śrī, Śa: These reside in the self, in the heart and so forth, and in the right hand.
Śrī, Ṣa, and Sa are in the self, the heart, and the left hand respectively.
Śrī, Sa, and Śukra are in the heart and so forth, up to the right foot.
Śrī Haṃ, obeisance to the life-force-soul in the heart and extending to the left foot.
Śrī Laṃ, obeisance! [I offer] into the individual self (jīvātman) [the elements] beginning with the heart and ending with the belly.
Śrī Kṣa. Homage to the Supreme Self in the heart and the other [limbs] up to the mouth.
Then one should perform the placement of the mantra (nyāsa).
Now, the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*):
with the two thumbs, [one should place] "Phaṭ! To the Weapon" on the backs of both palms.
Karanyāsa.
In this manner, beginning from the heart and ending with the crest-lock (śikhā), there are six [syllables].
Thus, with the base of the little finger [touching] the crest-lock, saying *kavacāya hūṃ*, one should place both hands crossed over the shoulders up to the chest; then, saying *netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*,
one should form the three eyes with the index, middle, and ring fingers.
Saying "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should strike three times upward with the palms and perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) with ten snaps of the fingers.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the seat of one's own body.
Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti. To Kūrma.
To Ananta; on the two earths.
To the ocean of nectar; to the island of jewels.
To the jeweled pavilion; to the jewel-encrusted altar.
Salutation to the Jewel Lion Throne; thus, [one should worship] in the heart.
Furthermore, one should again place [the syllables] on the two shoulders, the two thighs, the face, and the pair of sides, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
Oṃ, salutation to Dharma—thus [he places it] on the right shoulder.
Oṃ, homage to Jñānā on the left shoulder.
Oṃ, salutation to Vairāgya (Dispassion). [To be placed] at the navel.
Oṃ, for lack of sovereignty, on the right side.
Again, in the heart.
Oṃ, homage to Ānandakandā.
48b) Oṃ, homage to Saṃvinnārāyaṇa! Oṃ, homage to the one whose state consists of the essence of all reality!
Oṃ, to the petals consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti). Oṃ, to the filaments consisting of transformation (vikāra).
Oṃ, salutation to the pericarp beginning with the fifty seed-syllables.
Oṃ Ma. Homage to the fire mandala, whose self consists of ten kalās.
Oṃ aṃ, homage to the solar disc, whose self consists of twelve kalās.
Oṃ Ū. Homage to the lunar maṇḍala, whose essence consists of sixteen digits.
Oṃ saṃ, homage to Sattva. Oṃ raṃ, homage to Rajas.
Oṃ taṃ, obeisance to Tamasā. Oṃ Ā, obeisance to the Self (Ātman).
Oṃ A, obeisance to the inner self. Oṃ Paṃ, obeisance to the supreme self.
Oṃ Hrīḥ! Homage to the one whose nature is primordial wisdom.

Then, having recited the *pīṭha-mantra*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by saying "Obeisance to the seat of the principal deity" (*mukhadevatā-pīṭhāya namaḥ*). Having meditated upon the deity within the heart-lotus and worshipped her with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*),
one should display the mudrās, pay obeisance, and establish the vessel for the *arghya* offering.
As it is said, for example, in the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*:
They say the base should have three feet, or six feet, or four feet; otherwise, the goddess should be made upon a charming circular pedestal.
[The vessels] made of gold, silver, stone, tortoise shell, skull, water, or clay;
as well as those made of coconut, conch, and pearl-oyster shell. (5.108)
A wise person should fashion an alms-bowl from a tree grown of merit;
one should avoid that which is too thin, too thick, cracked, or broken. (5.109)
O Sage, [bowls] made of gold and silver bring about all accomplishments;
for rites of pacification, a stone vessel is used, and for rites of immobilization, one made of clay.
The coconut brings subjugation (*vaśya*) and the like; the tortoise-shell brings about the accomplishment of magical rites (*abhicāra*);
the conch bestows knowledge; and the pearl-oyster shell grants the power of learning (*vidyā*). (5.111)
49a) Skulls and bowls made of gourd are effective for yoga and bring about success;
rosary beads made from sacred trees remove all sins.
O Goddess of the gods, when the pretas have been addressed, one should prepare a single vessel;
the wise practitioner should place the vessels between himself and the deity. (5.113)
The vessel for the Guru is at the end of the jar; at its end is the vessel for enjoyment;
at its end is the vessel for the Śakti, and near that is the vessel for the Yoginīs.

At the end of that, the wise man should place the vessel for the heroes (vīrapātra) and the vessel for Bali nearby, as well as the vessels for water for the feet (pādya) and water for sipping (ācamanīya). 5-115.
Nine vessels are the best; seven vessels are middling.
Some who know the mantras say that five vessels are middling.
The minister of the lower [level] should not employ two vessels, nor likewise two pairs of vessels;
the minister who worships the deity should not cause even a single vessel to be used.
In the case of the five-bowl system.
The vessel of the Goddess, the vessel of the Guru, and the vessel of enjoyment—these three are recognized as vessels.
The vessel of worship and the vessel of power; such is the rule for the five vessels.
In five vessels.
The vessel for worship is to be known as that used for the gratification of the Yoginīs;
likewise, the vessels for water for the feet and for sipping are for the offering to the deities during the sacrifice.
Then follows the placement of the argha vessel.

Having drawn a triangular mandala to one's left, having placed a tripod upon it, and having sprinkled the conch with the mantra *astrāya phaṭ*, one should set it down upon that [tripod]. Filling it with pure water while reciting the root mantra, one should [visualize] the water as being composed of fire, sun, and moon, according to what was previously written: "maṃ to the fire-mandala."
Having fully worshipped.
Hrāḥ! Salutation to the heart. Hrīḥ! Salutation to the head. Svāhā!
49b) HRŪḤ! VAṢAṬ to the crest-lock. HRAIḤ! HUM to the armor.
Hrau! Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. Hu! Phaṭ to the weapon.
Having worshipped with the six-limbed mantras as well, and having covered it with both hands, [one should recite] the root mantra over that water.

Having recited the mantra as prescribed in the ritual manual, having protected it with the Astra-mantra and veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra, and having rendered it nectarine by means of the *vam* syllable and the Dhenu-mudrā, one should place perfume, flowers, and unbroken rice-grains (*akṣata*) therein.
In this manner, having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel to his right and taking a small amount of *argha* water,
he pours it into the *prokṣaṇī* water; then, with that water, he sprinkles the articles of worship and the five [offerings] of the sacrificial mantra.
In this manner, one should place the vessel for foot-water (pādyapātra) and the vessel for water for sipping (ācamanīyapātra) to the left of the vessel for the guest-offering (arghapātra).
Having thus established the *argha* offering, one should perform the installation of the vase (*ghaṭasthāpana*).
It is as follows:

First, having worshipped the maṇḍala with perfumes and other offerings, one should place rice grains in the center of the pericarp; upon that, spread kuśa grass, and on top of that, arrange a wide vessel containing unhusked rice. Upon that, one should place a jar that has been washed with the mantra *astrāya phaṭ* and filled with camphor and other substances.

Having well-sprinkled the blue lotus, which is most enchanting and wound with three-fold threads as prescribed, adorned with beginningless [sacred] ornaments, its neck decorated with flower garlands, accompanied by *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains,
and possessing nine jewel-petals, one should mutter the root mantra of the reverse-order alphabet (*vilomamātṛkā*).

Its interior filled with fragrant waters consisting of a decoction made from the bark of milk-exuding trees, combined with the eight prescribed perfumes; it is entwined by the creepers of Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, Nyagrodha, Āmrā, and Aparājitā, its opening covered with fresh sprouts, and a vessel of barley and fruit placed upon its mouth.

One should place the *oṃkāra*— wrapped in a pair of fine cloths and facing upward— upon the seat (*viṣṭara*) while reciting Vedic mantras beginning with "bhūr asi. Then, having touched the pitcher with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, one should perform the ritual installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) according to the mantra.
At the end of the syllables of Pāśāditya, there is the word *syodapuṣpam* again;
in sequence, here are the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*), and likewise the individual soul (*jīva*) is situated here. (5.120)

One should utter the word *amukhya* for all the sense organs (*indriya*), and then again the word *mukhya*; thereafter, one should utter the words *vāk*, *manas*, *nayana*, *śrotra*, *ghrāṇa*, and *prāṇa*. (5.121)
"Having come here afterwards, may they remain happily for a long time, Ṭha dvayam.
This is declared to be the life-mantra (prāṇamanu), which bestows life upon all living beings. (5-122)
Everywhere.
The essential point is that the word "Amukhya" (the non-principal) should be inserted at the end of the sequence "ā hrī krā ha saḥ. For example:

*Ā hrīḥ kroḥ haḥ saḥ*, [the vital breaths] of such-and-such deity, here are the vital breaths; *ā hrīḥ mi*, such-and-such deity, your life-force (*jīva*) is established here—thus first; likewise, *ā hrīḥ mi*, such-and-such deity, all your sense-faculties (*sarvendriyāṇi*), and so forth.
May the vital breaths come here and remain happily for a long time; svāhā!
Having thus performed the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).

Holding in the hollow of her hands, which were like a cluster of flowers reddened by the rays of the sun, the deity within her own heart, she brought the deity forth with the root mantra, visualized the form, and established it in the vessel; then performed the rites of *saṃsthāpana*, *saṃnidhāpana*, *saṃnirodhana*, *sakalīkaraṇa*, *avaguṇṭhana*, *amṛtīkaraṇa*, and *paramīkaraṇa*.
Having invoked the deity of the mudrā-ghaṭa, one should worship the seats (pīṭhas) within that jar.
Oṃ, salutation to the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti). Oṃ, salutation to the Tortoise (Kūrma).
Oṃ to Ananta. Oṃ to Pṛthivī.
Oṃ, to the ocean of nectar! Oṃ, to the island of jewels!
Oṃ, to the wish-fulfilling tree. Oṃ, to the jeweled pavilion.
Oṃ, to the jewel altar. Oṃ, homage to the great lion throne.
Having thus worshipped, taken a flower, and meditated upon the deity, one should place the flower in the jar and worship with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). It is as follows:
The sixteen services (upacāras), beginning with the seat, welcome, and the water offering (arghya), have been described previously.
This has been stated in the Mānasollāsa:
"The practitioner should give [the offering] with the vocative" means by means of the word of address, that is, the vocative case.
O such-and-such deity, I offer this seat; *namaḥ*.
Welcome; inquiries regarding your well-being. So it is.
I offer the respectful water (argha); svāhā!
Thus, one should place it upon the head.
"O illustrious deity [Name], this is for the feet," [saying] thus, [he offers water] at the feet.
In this manner, [one says] "O such-and-such deity, here is water for sipping" and pours it into the mouth.
In this manner, [he offers] the madhuparka into the lotus of the mouth.
In the same way, the water for sipping is likewise [offered] with "namaḥ," and the water for bathing is likewise [offered].
I prepare this garment; homage!
In this manner, I offer the sacred thread, in this manner the ornaments, and in this manner the perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps; homage!

Having brought the *naivedya* (food offering) before him, [sprinkle it] with the *argha* water while reciting *astrāya phaṭ* and performing the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) with *kāhum*, then transform it into nectar (*amṛtīkṛtya*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* while reciting *vam*. Having recited the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) eight times over it, offer it with: "O Śrī Amukadevatā, I present this *naivedya*; obeisance (*namaḥ*)," and then [recite]: "You are the spreading of the nectar, *svāhā*."
Having offered a mouthful of water, one should offer the five oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhutis*) beginning with the *praṇava* (Om), saying "to Prāṇa, Svāhā," and so forth, for her.
51a) To be meditated upon through acceptance: Oṃ amṛtavidhānam asvi svāhā.

Having thus again given the *apośāna* water, he should offer the five *prāṇa*-oblations beginning with the *praṇava*, saying "To Prāṇa, svāhā," and likewise offer the water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamanīya*) and the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*).
In this manner, one should worship with three handfuls of flowers.
In each of those places, one should offer water, and in the intervals between the services,
one should worship the heart-mantra and the others, beginning from the southeast corner among the filaments.
"Oṃ hrāḥ, homage to the heart," and so forth; likewise, "to the weapon, phaṭ" in the east and other directions—one should worship in the four quarters.
Then, having worshipped those very deities of the enclosure, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Pavana, Vidhū, Īśāna, the Lord of Serpents (Pannagādhīśa), and below and above, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha). || 5-124 ||
One should worship these according to the directions as previously described.
Then their weapons [were neutralized].
The wise know the sequence of these weapons to be: the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace, the spear, the discus, and the lotus. (5.125)
Having worshipped the weapons in sequence as well, one should perform the ten purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the mantra to be given:
first birth (*janana*), then life-giving (*jīvana*), thereafter striking (*tādana*), awakening (*bodhana*),
then consecration (*abhiṣeka*), purification (*vimalīkaraṇa*), and nourishment (*āpyāyana*).
Satisfying, kindling, and concealment—these are the ten purificatory rites for mantras.
The wise one should recite the syllables of the mantra by extracting them from the midst of the Mātṛkā and placing the Praṇava between them. (5.127)
Those proficient in mantra and tantra call this "living" (jīvana).
The meaning is that one should recite the mantra after placing the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the end of each syllable of the mantra, having inserted the *praṇava* between them.
This is the life-force of the mantra.
51b) Having written the syllables of the mantra, one should strike it with sandalwood water.

The striking [of the mantra] with the wind [seed-syllable] for each [syllable] is thus described. "For each" means that while reciting the wind-seed syllable (*vaṃ*) over each syllable of the mantra to be given, one should offer [the water] mixed with sandalwood water; this is the "striking" of the mantra.
Having written that mantra, the practitioner of mantras [should worship] with flowers born of the karavīra plant.
One should strike the newly acquired wealth at the end of each [verse] with a number equal to the syllables of that mantra;
this means on a copper plate or similar surface.
From the letter *ya* at the end, [one should place] *eṃ*, the letter *ra*, and likewise the lower [vowel], as the seed-syllable.
This is the awakening of the mantra.
The mantra-practitioner [should perform it] according to the procedure taught in his own [tantra], in accordance with the number of the mantra. (5.130)
One should consecrate the mantra upon an *aśvattha* sprout for the sake of purification,
as stated in the *Svatantra*.
The meaning is that [the offering] is with white sandalwood on the side of Viṣṇu, and with red sandalwood on the side of the Goddess.
Having intentionally reflected upon the mantra with the mind, one should burn it away with the Jyotirmantra.
The practitioner of mantra should purify the three impurities within the mantra by means of this "Light Mantra."
With the mantra "Oṃ Hrīḥ."
Oṃ Hrīḥ! The three impurities—consisting of the impurity of illusion (*māyika*) and that known as the impurity of action (*karma*)—are thus the three impurities.
The mind should perform the sprinkling of each [item] with water from kusa grass over which mantras have been recited. (5.132)
This nourishment is considered to be performed according to the rule by means of that mantra;
therefore, [the formula] "namas" is for the nourishment of this mantra.
The practitioner of mantra considers the libation performed with water consecrated by mantra to be the true libation.
It should be given with the mantra—that is, with the root mantra. And so it is said:
The application is as follows: having recited the root mantra, one says "tarpayāmi" (I satisfy).
This is the libation.

*Tārā*, *māyā*, and *ramā* constitute the "kindling of the mind" (*manodīpana*). *Tārā* is *oṃ*, *māyā* is *hrīḥ*, and *ramā* is *śrīḥ*. "Yoga" means connection; therefore, these should be placed at the beginning of the mantra to be given.
The meaning is that one should recite after having bestowed the three seed-syllables: *oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ*.
This is the illumination.
The concealment and not the disclosure of the mantra being recited. || 5-134 ||
These ten consecrations (saṃskāra) have been proclaimed in all tantras and kept secret;
by performing them according to the tradition, the mantra-practitioner shall obtain his desired goal. (5.135)
Then one should perform the fire oblation.
Likewise.

Seated facing the east, having performed the *svastivācana* (invocation of well-being) and recited "Sūryaḥ somo," and taking hold of *kuśa* grass and water, [he says]: "O Viṣṇu, today... [omitting] ...I, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and such-and-such name (*śarmā*), desiring the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life, [offer this] to the deity such-and-such, of the syllable-mantra..."

One should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "I shall perform the oblation (*homa*) one thousand and eight or one hundred times with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other materials, preceded by the [specific] syllables, for the sake of such-and-such deity who is a constituent part of the initiation rite (*dīkṣā-karma*)."
One should recite "yajjāgrataḥ. Then, first of all, I shall describe the square diagram (ḍaṃ) which pertains to all [ritual] authorities.
There, by means of a thousand oblations, a Linga the size of a man shines forth from its dissolution.
First, one should prepare that auspicious site for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
This has been stated in the Viṣṇusaṃhitā:
First, one who is skilled in the knowledge of sites should examine the ground; he should diligently clear away thorns and other such obstacles, or else have a man dig there. (5.136)
A man of human proportions.

First, having smeared the site of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with cow dung and established the general water-offering (sāmānyārgha), one should sprinkle it thoroughly with the water from that general offering and then perform a sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having fashioned a square measuring twenty-four finger-breadths, one should perform the eighteen purificatory rites.
52b) As it is said in the *Śāradā*:
Inspection is performed with the root mantra; sprinkling is considered to be done with the Śara mantra;
digging and uprooting are done with the Astra mantra; and filling is done with the Hṛdaya mantra. (5.137)

In the service [of the ritual], equalization is performed with the *samīkaraṇa* mantra; it is held that the armor is performed with the *varma* mantra; the pounding is done with the *heti* mantra; and the cleansing is done with the *carma* mantra. (5.138)
Immediately after that, one should perform the visualization of the form as an ointment;
then follows the drawing of the three lines, and finally, worship with the heart-mantra is prescribed. (5.139)
One should perform the vajrīkaraṇa rite with the Astra-mantra and strike the crossroads with auspicious kusa grass and that same armor-mantra, causing the [obstacles] to fall to the right. (5.140)
In the yoga, one should fashion the fire-pit with the consecrations as they have been set forth;
one should gaze upon that place with the root mantra and the mantra to be given.
Having sprinkled that place with "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should again strike it with darbha grass;
having sprinkled it with "Hum," one should strike it.
"Oṃ astrāya phaṭ"—with this, the excavation of the sacrificial pit is performed.
The excavation of the pit is desired to be as wide as the extent of the vessel.
With the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should remove the earth; with the mantra "Namaḥ," for the purpose of leveling it with other earth, one should fill the place from which the earth was removed.
With "astrāya," one should level that place;
with "huṃ," one should sprinkle it.
The firming of the sacrificial pit is performed with "phaṭ," or alternatively, the firming of the pit is performed with "astrāya phaṭ."
Alternatively, one should cleanse the site of the sacrificial pit with the mantra "Ahuṃ" and smear it with cow dung using the mantra "Vama."
Then, with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should visualize that wall as having the form of a digit (*kalā*).
With that mantra, one should encircle it with a middle girdle using either three red threads or three white threads;
this is the "making of the triple thread" (*trisūtrīkaraṇa*).
One should consecrate the sacrificial pit with "namaḥ," and one should contemplate the pit as being of the nature of a vajra with "astrāya phaṭ."
Thus is the vajrīkaraṇa.
With the mantra "namaḥ," one should fashion a square within the pit using kuśa grass.
The middle portion belongs to the Āvasathya fire, and the eastern portion belongs to the Sabhya fire.
In the west is the portion for the Āhavanīya fire.
On the following day, the Annāhārya [Śrāddha] is performed.
"The Gārhapatya fire is in the south"—thus is the making of the crossroads performed.
Thus say some.
In reality, however, that consists simply in the offering of four *kuśa* blades in the sequence of middle, east, south, and north of the *kaṇḍa*.

With the mantra *namaḥ*, one should spread out kuśa grass blades, twelve finger-breadths in length and consecrated with the root mantra, upon three seats in the north-western part of the girdle of the sacrificial pit for the purpose of installation.
And so it is stated in the Rāghavabhaṭa:
But for the purpose of spreading out the extensive [seat], it should be consecrated with the root mantra.
The axle-base (akṣapāṭa), however, is proclaimed to be twelve finger-breadths in measure. Thus ends the section on the axle-base.
Thus, one should perform the eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
Alternatively, one should unify those [elements] by means of the four [actions], beginning with gazing. || 5.143 ||
Just as the sacrificial pit [is prepared] afterwards with the root mantra.
One should sprinkle the sacrificial pit with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ."
In this manner, one should strike.
One should sprinkle with the syllable *hūm*.
Thus one should perform the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

If one is unable to prepare a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) of the size of a hand, perform the purificatory rites as far as possible, and then carry out the fire-oblation (*homa*).
The sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) as prescribed.
One should fashion it as a square, one cubit in length and very broad, with the thumb raised.
53b) This has been stated in the Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī:
Alternatively, the best of mantra-practitioners should prepare a sacrificial mound for the purpose of performing the fire oblation.
The cutting of the thumb-joint from the hand should be even and auspicious;
or, the cutting at the base of the four fingers [should be made] all around with sand.
Thus [it is said].
Then, having drawn three lines starting from the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and extending toward the east, one should place the arghya vessel;
to its south, one should place the praṇīta vessel and the prokṣaṇī vessel just as one does for the arghya vessel, and pour a small amount of arghya water into them.
Then, uttering the *praṇava*,
having thoroughly sprinkled the line with the *argha* water, one should worship in the sequence of the first line, which has its tips pointing eastward.
On the first line: Salutation to the illustrious Mukunda.
Second: To Īśānā.
Third: to Purandara;
on the northernmost line: obeisance to Brahmā;
second: to Vaivasvata; to Kūrma.
To Ananta; to Pṛthivī; to the Ocean of Nectar; to Ratnadvīpa; to the Kalpavṛkṣa, obeisance!
To Indu, the third line, obeisance!
Having thus worshipped, one should draw a triangle in the center of that, a hexagon above it, and a circle above that; then,
while uttering the syllable *Oṃ*, having sprinkled it with water from the *argha* vessel, one should worship the *pīṭhas* upon it, as follows:
Oṃ, salutation to the Supportive Power (Ādhāraśakti).
Oṃ, homage to the Tortoise; Oṃ, homage to Ananta; Oṃ, homage to the Earth;
thus, homage likewise to the filaments consisting of the [subtle] transformations and so forth.
Oṃ, salutation to the pericarp enriched with fifty seed-syllables.
Oṃ, to Dharma. Oṃ, to Jñāna.
Oṃ, to Vairāgya.
Oṃ, for sovereignty; Oṃ, for dharma;
Oṃ, for ignorance; Oṃ, for lack of dispassion;
Oṃ, for lack of mastery. Homage to the deity Amuka residing on the sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila).

Having thus worshipped the sacred seats (pīṭhas), one should worship Vāgīśvarī in their midst— she who has bathed after her menses and resembles a blue lotus— as she is united with Vāgīśvara, using the ritual offerings (upacāras).
For example:
Having invoked them with "O Vāgīśvarī, together with Vāgīśvara, come hither," [one offers] this water for the feet: Oṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara.
Having worshipped Vāgīśvarī with the *arghya*, water for the feet (*pādya*), and other offerings, [one says]: "Homage to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara."
Thus, with three handfuls of flowers;
and with "Oṃ Vāgīśvarī," as previously stated, one should pay homage.

Then, having placed fire— produced either from a fire-drill (*araṇi*) or from the hearth of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*)— into a bronze vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*) on his own right side, and taking a single piece of wood from it,
[he offers it] with: *oṃ dhruvādebhyaḥ svāhā*.
With this [verse], one should cast [it] into the southwest direction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, at the base of the fire, [sprinkle it] with the water for the *argha* offering while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ";
sprinkle the fire with the water for the *argha* offering using *darbha* grass while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ" and "Hūm"; and in that fire, offer oblations with the mantra "Rām jvālāgnaye namaḥ."

"Obeisance to the fire of the *nīva* and the *indu*. Thus, having contemplated the identity of the names of the *jāṭhara* (digestive) and *vaidavaka* (cosmic) fires, and having joined the consciousness of the purifier (*pāvaka*) therein with the syllable *ram*, one consecrates the fire with the *praṇava*. Then, with the syllable *vam* and the *dhenumudrā*, and with *amiti kṛtyāstrāya phaṭ*, [one performs the ritual].
Having protected the fire with the syllable *huṃ* and performed the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) rite, he should worship the fire with the root mantra of the fire.

Taking it up with both hands, he should lift it and circumambulate the pit three times clockwise while touching the ground with his knees and uttering the *praṇava*, [thus uniting] the fire from his own mouth with the fire in the pit.

With the consciousness of Paramaśiva as the individual soul (jīva), or with the consciousness "I am he" (so'ham) regarding the individual soul, one should deposit [the seed] into the womb of Vāgīśvarī.
Then, [the offering of] water for rinsing the mouth [is made] to Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara: "Namaḥ."

Having meditated upon the union of Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara, and having joined that consciousness to the central channel within the womb of Kāmeśvarī, one should cover the womb of the Goddess with *kuśa* grass; then, for the protection of the womb and for protection against obstacles,
one should place a *darbha* bracelet and display the Jvālinī mudrā.
He states the definition of the mudrās.
Having made the hands even at the wrist with the fingers pressed together, [one should perform the mudrā].
Having placed [the hands] at the middle of the forehead, one should insert the thumbs into their centers;
thereafter, one should ignite the fire with this Rudra-mantra, Jvālinī.
Then one should kindle the fire with the fire-mantra:
*cit piṅgala hana 2 daha 2 paca 2 sarvajñāpaya svāhā*.
Having thus kindled the fire, with palms joined in reverence, he says:
"Oṃ, I bow to Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all births, the seat of oblations;
who is golden-hued, stainless, well-kindled, and whose faces are turned in every direction."
With this [verse], one should worship the fire.
Then, one should place the seven tongues of fire, which are peaceful in nature, within one's own body.
In the genitals, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes, everywhere.
The mantras of the tongues of fire, consisting of the letters from *sa* to *ya* joined with *vaḥ* and *īśa*, have been proclaimed by the teachers as seven in number. (5.148)
One should place the anus-bulb, which pervades everything, everywhere.
Vahni is *repha* (the letter *r*), *iro* is the letter *y*, and *arghīśa* is the letter *u*;
by that [sequence], in reverse order,
*sa*, *ṣa*, *śa*, *va*, *la*, *ra*, and *ya* are joined with the *bindu*, that is, endowed with the nasal dot.
By that: syu, myu, śryu, vyu, lyu, tryu, yryu.
Thus is the mantra of the seven tongues of fire.
He states another variety of seed-syllables for the tongue.
It is stated in the Yāmala:

The two syllables *vi* and *le*, followed by *pha* and *vartti*, with *mau* placed after the sixth vowel (*ū*) and joined with the moon (*i*) and the bindu (*m*), are the seed-syllables of the tongues in their proper order. (5.149)

The last two groups are the *ca* and *cha* groups; *ya*, *la*, *va*, and *śa* constitute the *ya*-group (*yavarga*). *Śa*, *sa*, and *la* together constitute the *śa*-group (*śavarga*). The final two groups are those without the letter *ra* (*virepha*), meaning they are devoid of *ra*.
Thus: *ya*, *la*, *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*.
By that reverse order, those six are the bracelets (valayas).
The meaning is that it is joined with the "moon," which is the half-moon (ardhacandra), and further joined with the "drop" (indu), which is the anusvāra.
Śāradā spoke this supreme Mālatī.
The tongues are said to be of three kinds according to the distinction of qualities in their functions: Hiraṇyā, Gagaṇā, and Raktā; in the others, they are considered to be Kṛṣṇā and Prabhāvatī.
Vahurūpā is intensely red; Sāntvikī is engaged in yogic practices; Padmarāgā is golden; and the third, Varddhalohitā, is deep crimson.
Red, black, white, smoky, and dark-grey—
these are the girdles of fire prescribed for rites performed for desired ends.
O Viśvamūrti, those [flames] are said to be Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, Manojava, Lohitā, Kalālākhyā, Kālī, and Tāmasī. (5.153)
These seven are employed by evil ministers for cruel deeds;
their tongues, which possess auspicious seed, are equal in number to their respective names. (5.154)
One should first perform the placement (nyāsa) of the sattvic fires of auspicious seed-syllables within one's own body.
Homage to Hiraṇyā.
In the case of the linga.
Śrīyu / Homage to Gaganāyī. At the molasses.
Śrīṃ; salutation to Raktā. [On the] head.
Vṛyū / Homage to Kṛṣṇā // [In the] mouth.
Lryū / Homage to Suprabhā. [Located] in the nose.
Rryū / Homage to Vahurūpā. [To] the eyes.
Pryū / Salutation to Atiraktā; one should place [this] upon all the limbs.
Then Hiraṇyagargī, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā are the presiding deities of the seven tongues.
The immortals, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, nāgas, piśācas, and rākṣasas are said to be associated with the seven tongues.
The presiding deity.
The immortal god.
One should also perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the presiding deities within one's own body.
Oṃ, salutation to the gods. At the liṅga.
