Oṃ, to the Gandharvas, on the head.
Oṃ, to the yakṣas at the mouth.
Oṃ, to the Nāgas, at both nostrils.
Oṃ, to the piśācas, the two eyes.
Oṃ, homage to the Rākṣasas. One should perform the pervasive placement upon all limbs.
Then one should assign the limbs of the fire according to the ninefold path of the mouth:
"Sahasrārcis," "Svastipūrṇa," and again "Utiṣṭhapuruṣa. (5.155)
"Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara"—these are declared to be the six-limbed mantras in sequence, joined with the seed-syllables and the [mudrā] sounds. (5.156)
In that same manner, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the hands.
Oṃ sahasrārciṣe, homage to the two thumbs; [to be placed] on the two thumbs.
Oṃ svastipūrṇāya with the two index fingers;
likewise, oṃ uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya with the two middle fingers.
Oṃ, to Dhūmavyāpin, with the two ring fingers.
Oṃ, to the one with seven tongues, with the two little fingers.
Oṃ, to the wielder of the bow, to the weapon, phaṭ!
Salutation to the backs of both hands.
Then one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
In this manner, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs, beginning with the heart.
Thus, having struck the ten directions with three claps of the hands and the *chotikā* gesture, one should send forth fire upwards.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the formless.
Then the preceptor should assign the eight forms of Jātavedas:
[the head], the two shoulders, the two sides, the two knees, and again the two sides of the knees. (5.157)
In the placement performed while circumambulating from left to right, they are designated in their proper order as Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and Havyavāhana. (5.158)
Another is known as Aśvodaraja; furthermore, there is Vairśva, called Nara.
Kaumāratejas would be Viśvamukha, who is remembered as Devamukha. || 5-159 ||
Those which are the syllables *tāra-agni-ya* are the dancing forms of Fire.
Regarding "the syllables *tāra-agni-ya*": [this refers to the seed-syllables *oṃ*, *raṃ*, and *yaṃ*.]
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Jātavedas, and so forth.
Then, one should place [the mantras] upon one's own body.
Oṃ, homage to the fire-born Jātavedas.
On the crown of the head.
Oṃ, to Agni Saptajihva; [at] the right shoulder.
Oṃ, to Agni Havyavāhana; on the right side.
Oṃ, to Agni Aśvodaraja; [place this] on the right hip.
Oṃ, for Agni Vaiśvānara, [may he] protect me from drinking [the poison].
Oṃ, to Agni, the youthful splendor, on the left hip.
Oṃ, salutation to Agni Viśvamukha; [this is] the left side.
Oṃ, to Agni, whose mouth is the Vedas, on the left shoulder.
Then, having prepared a central seat.
Having worshipped with "Oṃ, salutation to the seat of fire," one should meditate upon the fire.
Just as if one were taking a flower.
Holding in his long arms the desired Śakti, the Svastika, and the Abhaya mudrā, he has the luster of a Japā flower.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god, adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, possessing three eyes, and having faces resembling the rising sun.
Having meditated thus, one should fashion the form with the root mantra.
Having offered a flower into the fire situated in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and contemplated [the deity] as having become one with it, [one should invoke him] with:
"Oṃ Vaiśvānara, come here; stay here. Having thus invoked him, [one offers]: "O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, red-eyed one, come here; accomplish all rites! Svāhā! Oṃ! Homage! (Namaḥ).
Furthermore, in this manner, [offer] the water of honor (arghya); homage!

In this manner, having offered water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), perfumes (*gandha*), flowers (*puṣpa*), incense (*dhūpa*), lamps (*dīpa*), and food offerings (*naivedya*), and having again given water for sipping and betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*), one should worship the Fire with three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) in the central triangle and the six corners.
And so it is said in the Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī: "Those with the luster of gold and heated gold are situated in the direction of the Trident-bearer."
Those of the color of beryl and gold are situated in the eastern direction.
Resembling a black-blue lotus, she is situated in the south-western direction;
possessing many forms, she stands from south to north as previously described.
Outside those six corners, in the eastern direction, is the auspicious Suprabhā;
Hiraṇyā is said to be in the south-east, Śāṅkarī in the south, and Bahurūpikā in the south-west. (5.162)
The one to the southeast is red on the left side, while Mātṛraktā is situated there;
Kanakārasanā is established in the middle of the sacrificial pit.
Hiraṇyakā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Dakṣā, Panasthitā, Suprabhā, Atirakṣā, and Vahurūpā—these are considered the [Mothers]. || 5.164 ||
One should worship the seven-tongued one.
Oṃ, homage to Pūrvahiraṇyā.
Oṃ, to Gaganā in the southeast; to Raktā in the southwest; to Kṛṣṇā in the west.
In the wind [element], there is Suprabhā.
In the northeast, to Vahurūpā.
In the center of the triangle: "Obeisance to Atiraktā.
Thus one should worship the deities residing in the filaments and the pericarp.
57a) As in the southeast, for the heart of Sahasrārcis;
in the southwest, svāhā to the head of Svastipūrṇa.
In the northwest, to Utiṣṭhapuruṣa, for the Śikhā, Vauṣaṭ;
in the northeast, to Dhūmavyāpin, for the Kavaca, Hum.
To Madhyasaptajihva, with two eyes, Vauṣaṭ!
[This is] the Gopāla-pakṣa. To Netra, with two eyes, Vauṣaṭ!
To the bow-wielder, the weapon, in the east, west, south, and north—phaṭ!
Then, on the eight petals.
The forms of the fire-gods (Vahni-mūrtis) in the east and other directions are to be worshipped.
To the eastern fire, Jātavedas.
In the southeast: Oṃ, likewise to Saptajihva.
To Havyavāhana in the south;
to Aśvodaraja in the southwest.
The western [direction] is for Vaiśvānara.
In the wind: to the splendor of youth.
Oṃ, to the one who faces all directions, the Northern One.
To Īśāna: Oṃ, salutation to Agni, the mouth of the Vedas.
Then, one should worship the world-protectors, Indra and the others, in the eight directions starting from the east in the sequence beginning with Indra, with the mantra "Oṃ."
Indra, Vahni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, as well as Vāyu, Kuvera, Īśāna, Ananta, and likewise Brahmā.
They should be worshipped in the directions starting with the east with flowers, incense, and sandalwood paste.
Their meditation.
Yellow, red, and likewise blue, dark, white, and smoky;
white, fair, as well as Śūdra, and likewise of red complexion. (5.165)
Their weapons.
One should worship the weapons in sequence: the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace, the trident, the discus, and likewise the lotus. (5.166)
The meditation on the missiles.
Oṃ! When they possess the luster of sapphire, silver, lapis lazuli, cloud-colored [sapphire], ruby, gold, emerald, and coral;
when their respective crowns are marked with their own [emblems] and their two hands are joined with their own weapons and the gesture of fearlessness—these are the Vajra-youths.
To Indra in the eastern direction, *namaḥ*.

Thus: *rāṃ* to Agni in the southeast; *yāṃ* to Yama in the south; *kṣāṃ* to Nirṛti in the southwest; *vāṃ* to Varuṇa in the west; *yāṃ* to Vāyu in the northwest; *śāṃ* to Kuvera in the north; *hāṃ* to Īśāna in the northeast;
*oṃ* to Brahmā above; and *hrīṃ* to Ananta below. *Namaḥ* (obeisance) to each.
Outside of that, one should worship their weapons as before: "Obeisance to Vajrāyudha."
In the southeast: *oṃ* to Śakti; in the south: *oṃ* to Daṇḍa; in the southwest:
*oṃ* to Svarga; in the west: *oṃ* to Pāśa; in the northwest: *oṃ* to Aṅkuśa; in the north: *oṃ* to Gadā; in the northeast: *oṃ*.
Homage to Śūlā.
Above: Oṃ, obeisance to Padmā.
Then, having worshipped with "Oṃ, obeisance to Cakrā" at the bottom, one should wrap [the cord] around the middle girdle in a clockwise direction.
On the middle girdle, one should spread twelve finger-breadths long *naga* blades of *kuśa* grass for the purpose of placing [the vessels] in the south, west, and north.
Upon that, one should place the enclosing sticks (paridhi) in detail, starting from the south as before.
In the *Cchandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"The enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) should be of many joints and straight."
There are three types of *satyavovraṇa* (true wounds): some have their tips shattered, while others extend in the four directions;
its measurement is said to correspond to each respective joint.
58a) Thereafter, one should prepare the sacrificial fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
For example:
Having placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles together with their openings facing downward into the fire and heated them three times, one should hold them in the left hand and,
using *kuśa* grass in the right hand, perform the tracing of the tips, middle, and bases of the two; then, having sprinkled them with water, one should place them upon the [ashes] three times.

Having poured the clarified butter (*ājya*) from the vessel for holding *ājya* (*ājyasthālī*) into the *ājya* [vessel], having washed it with the root mantra while reciting "Vīhma astrāya phaṭ," and having heated it over the fire, one should place it in the left hand, sprinkle it three times with water from the *argha* vessel using the right hand, heat it again over the fire, and place it facing oneself.
Having brought the clarified butter (ājya) and poured it into the vessel, one should gaze at the base of the butter with the mantra "astrāya phaṭ.

Having sprinkled the clarified butter with water while reciting "astrāya phaṭ," one should heat the ghee with darbha grass while reciting "hum," and then sprinkle it thoroughly with the water of purification (aghajala).

Having thus performed the four purificatory rites (saṃskāras), one should remove the embers from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), place them in the northwest corner, and establish the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī) with the mantra "Namaḥ."
This is the heating [of the body].
Then, having ignited a pair of darbha grass blades and cast them into the eye, one should throw the burnt residue into the fire with the mantra "Namaḥ".
This is the rite of purification.
Having rekindled it with a pair of *darbha* blades while reciting the mantra "hum," one should perform the *ghṛtanīrājana* (circumambulation with ghee) and cast them into the fire.
Thus ends the consecration by sprinkling.
Then, taking a handful of blazing kuśa grass while reciting the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," [he should proceed].
Having displayed blades of *darbha* grass ignited in clarified butter, one should cast them into the fire; this is the rite of illumination (*udyotana*).

Therefore, having brought coals that are fit for burning and placed them before oneself, one should cast those coals into the fire, sweep the place where the coals were, and then touch water-born [substances].

Then, with the hands extended and the thumbs and little fingers [joined], having separated the two strainers (*pavitra*) with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," he should pour the clarified butter forward while reciting the mantra.
One should place the purifier in another location.

Again, in that same manner and in the same way, having taken another strainer with clarified butter and reciting the mantra "Namaḥ," he should pour the clarified butter toward himself through that strainer and then cast the two strainers previously placed into the fire, saying, "This is the strainer."
Thus, by means of lifting up or lowering down, one should perform the external purification (*saṃskāra*). Six purifications have been proclaimed.
Then, a pair of *darbha* blades with a knot, measuring a span (*prādeśa*), [should be placed] in the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*).

Having placed clarified butter in the middle, one should contemplate the right side as the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) and the left side as the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa); [one should visualize] Iḍā on the left, Piṅgalā on the right, and Suṣumnā in the middle.
Having meditated, one should perform the fire offering (homa).
Then, reciting the mantra "Namaḥ," he takes ghee from the southern portion with the *sruva* ladle for the sake of the oblation.

One should offer oblation into the right eye of the Fire with the mantra "Oṃ agnaye svāhā," and one should pour the residue of the clarified butter (saṃpāta) into that very place on the southern side.
Saying "Punar namaḥ," he takes ghee from the left side and [offers it], saying: "To Soma, svāhā!"
Thus one should offer oblations into the left eye.
One should place the remaining clarified butter (saṃpāta) right there on the left side.
Again, taking ghee from the middle portion in this same manner, [one offers] "Svāhā to Agni and Soma."

Having thus offered oblations into the fire at the forehead and the eyes, one should pour the remaining clarified butter (saṃpāta) into the middle portion; however, in the tradition of the Gopāla school, one should not perform the offering at the forehead and the eyes.

One should indeed perform the Narasiṃha-rite again; then, taking clarified butter from the southern part and offering it into the mouth of the fire with "oṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā" (59a), one should cast [the remainder] into the southern part as previously described.
Thus is the opening of the mouth of Agni. With the word *svāhā*, one takes the clarified butter (*ājya*) from that portion;
there, one should place the remainder clinging to the *sruva* ladle.
And so it is said: "Having uttered the word *svā* and offered the oblation, having uttered the word *hā*, [one places] the remainder of the oblation."
The meaning is that one should place the ghee in that very same spot.
Then one should perform the Mahāvyāhṛti-homa.
Then, having placed a vessel filled with water to one's left, one should deposit the remainder of each oblation right there.
Oṃ bhūḥ svāhā.
Oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā.
Oṃ, O Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, bring [the offerings] here; O red-eyed one, may I accomplish all rites, svāhā!

Having thus offered three oblations with the *agnimantra*, one should place the water remaining from the oblation into the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*). Regarding the *svāhā* in the *homa*, he has stated: "tatā māha."
By Yajñapārśva.
Taking the sweet oblation in his right hand,
he should face the east and, with the other hand holding a lotus, offer it into the fire, O Wife.
Thus.
The wise one, with a mantra purified by the syllable Oṃ and ending with Svāhā,
should offer oblations at the conclusion of the word "Svāhā," while indeed meditating upon the deity of the mantra.
The "three sweets" (trimadhura) consist of ghee, honey, and sugar.
Thus it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Milk, honey, and ghee are known as the three sweets."
[He offers] with the mantra "vahnijāyā svāhā. Then, he should perform the sixteen purificatory rites (saṃskāra) beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna) for the fire.
As it is said in the Sāradātilaka:
One should perform the rites for the fire, beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna), in their proper sequence.

With eight oblations of clarified butter, each accompanied by the *praṇava* (Om), one should perform separately the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the male-impregnation (*puṃsavana*), and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*). (5.170)
Immediately following the birth-rite (jātakarman), the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa) is performed;
thereafter, the rite of going outside (upaniṣkramaṇa) and the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) are prescribed.
Following the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), there is further the Mahānāmnī and the Mahāvrata;
then the Upaniṣad, the ritual bath (snāna), the Godāna, and marriage, ending with death.
In auspicious rites, those ceremonies ending with marriage are prescribed;
in cruel deeds, they are declared to end with death, as in the rites involving the arrival of fire.
The Mahānāmnī is the holy life.
The *abhyeṣṭi* sacrifice is performed when [the sacrificer] has died.
It is as follows:
I perform the ritual conception for Agni; svāhā!
Thus one should offer eight oblations:
"Oṃ, I prepare the rite for the generation of a male for Agni, as before."
Oṃ, this very [rite] is the leading out from the birth-chamber for me; Oṃ, this is the birth-rite of Agni.
Oṃ, I perform the naming ceremony of Agni; svāhā!
At that time, O Agni, you are named so-and-so;
[the officiant] should assign names to each respective presiding deity of the maṇḍala.
Or alternatively:
O Agni, you are named Varada, or you are named Viśvarūpa; or one may utter another name.
The names of Agni should be understood according to the authorities written previously; they are not written here again due to the abundance of texts.
Having worshipped the fire with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings for the fire named so-and-so, and having offered *tāmbūla*, [one should proceed].
One should pay homage.
Then, one should offer eight oblations with the mantra: "Oṃ, I prepare the exit of the fire named so-and-so; svāhā! Thus one should sacrifice.
I perform the first feeding of solid food for the fire named so-and-so; svāhā!
Thus is the making into a heap.
In this way, the Upanayana and the Mahānāmnī [chants].

I ordain the Mahānāmnī vow, or the study of the Vedas; likewise, I ordain the Mahāvrata, the Upaniṣad vow, the Godāna, the Samāvartana, the marriage, and the establishment of the sacred fires—Oṃ Svāhā! (8)
60a) Having thus performed the sixteen purificatory rites for the fire, and having honored its two parents, one should employ it [for the ritual].
The two parents of that fire are Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara, just as they are.

Having worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings, saying "Obeisance to Vāgīśvarī," and having offered three handfuls of flowers while saying "Obeisance to Vāgīśvara," one should pay homage to Vāgīśvarī.
Then one should worship Vāgīśvara.

Again, having paid homage with "Oṃ A vaṃ," one should worship Vāgīśvarī together with Vāgīśvara; then, joined with the *saṃhāra-rudrī*, carrying [the deity] as far as the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should bring it into the nostrils and establish it within one's own heart.
This is according to the *Vaiśvānara-saṃhitā*.
One should establish Brahmā in the fire as the witness of the ritual for the sake of the *phara* rite.
Having established Brahmā to the south of that pit, one should worship him with water for the feet and other offerings.
Then one should offer five fuel-sticks, soaked with root-juice, tip-juice, and clarified butter.
Then, one should cast the five sacrificial substances (pañcamedha) mentioned with ghee into the fire.
Then, one should offer oblations with the single-syllable *hūṃ* mantra into the tongues of the fire, which are the embodiments of its limbs.
One should offer twelve oblations, beginning with "SRYŪ / Hiraṇyāyai namaḥ," etc., one by one, saying "Vauṣaṭ" to the seven tongues and the three eyes;
according to the Gopāla tradition, one says "Vauṣaṭ" to the seven tongues and the two eyes.
Oṃ, to Agni Jātavedas, the wielder of the bow.
Oṃ, to Havyavāhana; to Aśvodaraja;
to Vaiśvānaraja; to Kaumāratejas; to Viśvamukha; to Vedamukha, svāhā!

Then, having placed the *caṇa* in the left hand and taken the *sruk* with the right hand while reciting the mantra "Namaḥ," one should offer four oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *sruva* into the *sruc*, cover the *sruc* with the *sruva* turned face down, and stand up.
O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here; O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites—vauṣaṭ!
60b) Having thus offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra of Agni, one should offer ten oblations with the mantra of Śrī Mahāgaṇapati, both in its collective and its distributed forms.
For example: Oṃ svāhā.
Oṃ śrī svāhā. Oṃ śrī hrī svāhā.
Oṃ śrī hrī klī svāhā.
Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau svāhā.
Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau gaṃ svāhā.
Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau gaṇapataye varavarada svāhā.
Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau gaṃ, O bestower of boons, bestow boons upon all people, svāhā!
Thus, as previously stated.
Bring all people to peace for me; svāhā!

Having thus offered ten oblations into the fire, having meditated upon the deity and the *yantra* within the fire, having meditated upon the deity on the seat of the *bindu*, having contemplated the identity [of the deity] with the fire of the clarified butter (*ājya*), having visualized her as being of the nature of fire, and having fully worshipped her along with the sequence of worship and the retinue, having offered the *naivedya*, one should again offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*).
Having offered betel-leaf with the root mantra, and having worshipped with three handfuls of flowers while reciting "Obeisance to [Name] Devatā," one should prostrate.
Then, having contemplated the oneness of the fire and one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), one should offer twenty-five oblations into its mouth.
Likewise, while reciting the mantra, one should offer twenty-five oblations in this sequence, saying: "Svāhā! To such-and-such deity, this [oblation]."
This is the unification of the three.
Then, having contemplated the identity of the fire, the deity, and one's own self, one should offer eleven oblations with the root mantra;
this, however, is the "joining of the channels" (nāḍī-saṃdhāna).
The best of teachers should properly offer one oblation at a time with clarified butter for each of those principal limbs of the ritual sequences in their proper order. (5.174)
Of the principal limbs—that is, of the primary enclosures (āvṛtis).

61a) For whichever deity there is a specific number of subordinate deities (*āvaraṇadevatā*), one should offer one oblation (*āhuti*) for each of those subordinate deities at the root [of the mantra], directed toward them.
Regarding the division of the limbs (*aṅga*) of Agni, it is stated in the *Śrīsāradā*:
From barley comes wood; from that [wood], [fire].
From the ear comes smoke; here, the nose [is the path].
Where the eye has little heat, from where the pupil is, there is the head;
where the blazing flame is, that is the tongue for Jātavedas.
One should offer oblations into the mouth of the fire for all rites, O wise one;
if the offering is made into the ears, disease will result, and blindness of the eyes is declared [to follow]. (5.176)
There will be pain in the nose and a loss of wealth in the head.
Having performed the prescribed *homa*, one should offer one oblation each to Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, Śiva, Gopāla, and the others.
Then one should perform the Mahāvyāhṛti oblation:
*oṃ bhuḥ svāhā*, and so forth.

Regarding "four oblations": having worshipped the root deity with perfumes and other offerings, one should perform the prescribed fire-oblation (homa) with parched grain, clarified butter, and so forth.
He states the method for the fire offering (homa):
The offering of oblations, however, should be performed with the hand turned downwards.
This has been stated in the *Gavākṣaratantra*:
It should be performed with the hand of the mind, never with a mindless hand. || 5-177 ||
The cause for the destruction of the eye is relinquished by the sacrificer.
And so it is stated in the *Tripurātattvasāra*: "O Consumer of Oblations, the offering of the oblation is made into the hand of the one who holds the fire-stick (*cintre*). (5.178)
"There is no fruit of merit for the donor, and the officiant shall go to hell.
This is also stated in the Bhairavatantra.
The oblation is as if poured with an outstretched hand into the mouth of Vaiśvānara. || 5.179 ||
The one who performs the oblation perishes, for it is the cause of the destruction of the eyes.
In the fire-oblation (homa), three mudrās are prescribed: the deer, the goose, and the boar. (5.180)

The deer-mudrā is formed with the little fingers and index fingers; the swan-mudrā is formed with the little fingers released; and the sow-mudrā is formed with the hands joined—these are proclaimed as the *miti*-mudrās. (5.181)
The female deer is for the purpose of obtaining sons; the female swan bestows all fruits;
and the female pig is declared by the wise to be for all rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*). (5.182)

Having completed the primary fire-oblation (prakṛtahoma), the Guru, after having the disciple drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the rules, should lift the Arghya water-pot that was installed according to the ritual and sprinkle the child with water from the pitcher consecrated by the root mantra, while mentally reciting the Mātṛkā.
Let us two sprinkle the disciple with the remaining water.
Having risen, washed his limbs, and performed his ablutions, he put on his lower garment and a turban.
Then, while reciting the mantra "vauṣaṭ," he should bind the eyes of the disciple with a fine cloth.
Next, taking that disciple by the hand, he should lead him near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), remove the eye-binding, and cause him to sit upon a bed of kuśa grass to his left.
Then the guru should cause [the disciple] to hear the vow: "I shall give such-and-such a mantra."
Then the disciple should say, "Please give [it]. Thereupon, the Guru,
having performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* upon the disciple's body, having first covered the disciple's head with a cloth,
and having recollected the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] while regarding the disciple as the deity, should recite the three *praṇavas* into the disciple's right ear.
One should say.

The Guru should speak once into the left ear; having bestowed the mantra and taken hold of the disciple's head, he should say: "Whether this vidyā or this mantra, may it be the common nourisher for both you and me, and may it be the giver."
Thus, he should offer water into the hand of the disciplined disciple.
The disciples should say, "So be it. Then the disciple should contemplate the oneness of the name of the Guru, the mantra, and the deity.
62a) One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Or eight times.
And so it is stated in the *Vijñānasaṃhitā*:
Having observed the teacher's conduct and having abandoned [faults], one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Or else, with undistracted mind, one should recite the mantra eight times.
The Guru, for the sake of accomplishing his own power (*śakti*), should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight or one hundred times.

Then, having completed the recitation, the disciple should prostrate like a staff before the Guru, who is identical with the deity, and placing the pair of the Guru’s lotus feet upon his head, he should offer a hymn of praise.
Oṃ, homage to you, O Lord, Blessed One, Śiva in the form of the Guru.
To Him who has assumed various forms for the sake of accomplishing the descent of knowledge,
whose essential nature is Nārāyaṇa, and whose form is composed of Ramā.
Then, [salutation] to the Sun, who is the manifestation of all knowledge, whose form is the Veda, who is independent, whose body is cast down by his own feet, and whose essence is Śiva.
To the one who is dependent upon his devotees, who possesses a form for those destined for liberation,
who is discernment itself for the discerning, and who is investigation for the investigative.
For the illumination of illuminators, for the one whose form is knowledge for the wise—
by your grace, O God, I have accomplished all that was to be done in every respect.
"I am liberated from the great noose of death and I am Śiva.
Having recited this, one should bow again to the Guru.
Then, holding the disciple’s head with both hands, the teacher should cause him to rise.
"Just as you have arisen, so you are fully united; become one whose conduct and speech are perfect.
Having spoken thus, he should cause the disciple to rise and explain the mantras and the rules of conduct.
Then one should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor.
62b) This has been stated in the Brahma-saṃhitā:
That mortal who accepts the words of a Brahmin in vain,
or who does not give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at an auspicious occasion, certainly goes to hell.
At the conclusion of an initiation (dīkṣā), they say the sacrificial fee consists of gold, cows, land, and ornaments.
One should grant land that provides a livelihood and which shall follow one's sons and grandsons. || 5-189 ||
And likewise, in the Pārijātasvara:
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru, who is Śiva himself manifest before one's eyes;
for the sake of the Guru, the wise man should always be ready to sacrifice even his own body. (5.190)
If a teacher should awaken even a single syllable for a disciple, there is no wealth on earth that he could give which would equal the merit of that act; by such a gift, he becomes a Jhaṇī. (5.191)
Therefore, it was full in former times.
Oṃ, Agni, you are Mṛdunāman; to Agni Mṛdunāman, this water for the feet, obeisance.
Having thus worshipped with water for the feet and other offerings, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as follows:
The Agni Purāṇa.
With the mantra of Mūrdhānanda and with a continuous stream of the residual flow.
The gods generated Agni Vaiśvānara—the head of heaven, the navel of the earth, born of Truth—as the guest of men, the wise one praised by the Kapis and Guṅgus, the vessel that receives all. (5.192)
"One should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* while standing, never while seated"—this is the rule for the followers of the Yajurveda, as known from the *Ānandivetti*.
For the followers of the Sāmaveda, it is: "I offer the *pūrṇāhuti* for the sake of glory."
And so it is stated in the *Kṛṣṇānusaṃhitā*:
And having taken up the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles with their openings facing upward by means of the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, || 5.193 ||
Having stood and performed the *anābhisaṃskāra*, one should meditate upon the god Maheśvara,
leaving a space of five finger-breadths below with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.
One should hold [the vessel] with the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, leaving five finger-breadths outside,
according to the statement in the *Mahādānanirṇaya* composed by Vācaspatimiśra.
He states the Tantric view:
Having taken the *sruk* and *srūva* ladles as his two nostrils.
Oṃ, svāhā to the earth, to the wind, to the intermediate space, to the mind, and to the great!
Oṃ, svāhā to the divine Āditya, to the Moon, to the constellations, and to the Great One.
Having turned the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles face downwards, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.

Then, having worshipped the fire with water for the feet and other offerings, one should offer garments, coconuts, fruits, and so forth into the fire; thereafter, one should pay homage to the fire by reciting the previously mentioned verse: "sarvataḥ pāṇipādosi."
Longevity, health, sovereignty, fortitude, courage, strength, and fame. || 5.195 ||
Luster, splendor, cattle, seed, solar power, sovereignty, good fortune, success in action, and the prosperity of the eldest of the lineage—[these are attained]. (5.196)
I bow to Agni, the witness of all, who is free from desire, the one who knows all that is born, and the consumer of oblations—him who is like the sun illuminating everything. (5.197)
Having recited, "The one of golden color, stainless, well-perfected, and facing in all directions," one should pay homage.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should pray to the Fire with this [mantra] as follows: || 5.198 ||
Oṃ! O Brahman, may the splendor of the Brahman be born; may the Kshatriya be a king, a hero, skilled in archery, a piercer of targets, and a great chariot-warrior.

May a hero be born to this sacrificer—swift, a burner of enemies, a milch-cow of plenty, one who does not perish, a subduer of the seven cities, and one who is most desired by Viṣṇu. May he be the best of his peers and youthful.
Oṃ! May Parjanya rain according to our desire; may the plants bear fruit for us;
may there be security and prosperity for us.
Thus one should pray.
Then, one should visualize the host of deities dissolved into that limb.
Having honored the Blessed One with the words "Train yourself," one brings [the deity] back to one's own heart by means of the withdrawal mudrā;
then, with palms joined, the fire is dismissed.
Oṃ, go to sacrifice after sacrifice, go to the Lord of Sacrifice, go to your own source; svāhā!
This is your sacrifice, O lord of the sacrifice, accompanied by the hymn of praise; you, who possess all heroes, accept it—svāhā!
Having recited this, one should perform the dismissal of the fire.
Then one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin.
And likewise, there is a Smṛti text:

The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) that has been prescribed for the Brahmin should be given at the conclusion of the rite when he is being released; it should be greater than the full vessel (pūrṇapātra). || 5-199 ||
It is also heard in the scriptures that the causes are a pair of garments and a bronze vessel.
And thus, due to the distinction between the capable and the incapable, there are two cases;
for example, having brought a full vessel and taken sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and water, [one says]: "Viṣṇu..."

Oṃ. Today, in the month of [name], in the fortnight of [name], on the lunar day of [name], for the sake of the firm establishment of the fire-offering (*homakarma*) which is a constituent part of the initiation rite (*dīkṣākarma*) for the syllabic mantra of the deity [name] Śarmā, I give this full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) to the Brahman priest.
Having thus released the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should perform the dismissal of the Brahman priest with this [mantra].
Oṃ, arise, O Brahman! For you, O God, there is that great truth; may the Maruts come forward with their own gifts.
May Indra be the protector of the cattle.
Thus one should perform the release of the Brahma-thread.
Then, one should silently cast the kuśa grass used for spreading, soaked in ghee, into the fire.
Then, for the purpose of the *tilaka*, one should take ashes from the northeast corner of the *kuṇḍa* with the *sruva* ladle and place them in another vessel;
thus says Vasiṣṭha in the *Śāntidīpikā*.
Then, having brought ashes from the northeast with a sacrificial ladle or even with the hand, one should cause them to be bound upon the head, the throat, and the shoulders. (5.200)
64a) One should cause [the disciple] to recite the mantra according to the sequence and through yoga;
thereafter, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) and the formal recitation of the commitment (avadhāraṇa-vācana). || 5-201 ||
Now, regarding the sacrificial fee for the fire-oblation (*homa*), it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra*:
One should always give half of eleven *kaśikas* of gold to the guru during a thousand-fold oblation (*sahasra-homa*).
The [line] on the right side of her face is said by the sages to be of three kinds: half of a fifth part, two sixths, and one and a half [parts].
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
At the thousand-fold oblation, one should bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to what is being offered;
or half of that, or gold, according to the extent of one's wealth.
The option of "a niṣka or half of that" is based on one's capacity, not on personal whim, because [otherwise] there would be no engagement [with the rule].
The traditional teaching is that it means "unwavering."
And that [weight] consists of four *suvarṇas*. Five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *varṇa*.
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*.
The definitive conclusion of the treatise.
A *kṛṣṇala* is a gold *māṣaka*.
In the Viśvaprakāśa.
A *niṣka* is the source for [measuring] *akṣas* and ornaments; it consists of four *svarṇas*.
Eight *niṣkas* more [than that] is a *śata*; a *dīnāra* consists of one *karṣa* of gold. (5.203)
Thus it has been said.
Oṃ; eight *kalmāṣas* make one *nidrā*, and thirty *raktikas* are said to be a *niṣka*.
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given, followed by the dismissal of the planets and other deities;
then, having offered hot milk, one should say, "O Earth, may you become cool."
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he said, "May the performance of the fire-oblation be flawless."
Having gone near the jar at the site of the Guru’s sacrifice, he should sit down.
Then the disciple should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teacher.

Just as Viṣṇu, having taken sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and water, according to the previously mentioned procedure beginning with "Today, in such-and-such month," [recites] for the purpose of the initiation rite and consecration of the syllable-mantra: "This gold I give to you, the Guru, of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name; may the Guru say 'Svasti'."
May he blow.
Without stinginess regarding wealth, one should offer everything to the guru;
one should offer the pavilion and the materials for the pavilion to the guru.
Then the Guru, having worshipped the root deity within the jar with water for the feet and other offerings, having offered betel-leaf,
and having again offered water for sipping, should visualize the host of limb-deities as dissolved into its body,
and take up the remains of the offering (nirmālya).
One should worship upon the mandala with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to [Name] Devatā."
Then, one should remove this food offering (naivedya) whose essence has been consumed;
having given a small portion of it to the northeast direction, one should purify that spot.
Viṣvaksena is remembered as the one who consumes the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) on the arm of Viṣṇu; likewise, Caṇḍa Vivasvat is his splendor.
Caṇḍīśvarī is the Śakti, and Caṇḍeśa belongs to Śaṅkara. Lambodara is the one for Gaṇapati, and Amījyu is for the consumer of leavings (*ucchiṣṭabhojin*).
And so it is stated in the Āgamakalpadruma:

During the initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should worship [the deity] in the water-pot (*kumbha*), the yantra, and so forth, and perform worship every day. Then, having carefully lifted the pot and placed it in another location, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should say: "O [Name of the] Deity, may the rite of initiation for this mantra performed today be rendered flawless."
One should not consecrate the disciple with water from a jar.
For example:
May the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—consecrate you.
May Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, be for your victory.
The lord Agni, Ākhaṇḍala, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth, and likewise Śiva.
65a) Śeṣa is the companion of Brahmā; and those who are his [companions] are always the guardians of the directions (dikpālas):
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, Kṣamā, and Mati. (5.211)
Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapuḥ, Śānti, Stuti, and Kānti—may these mothers, the wives of Dharma, assembled here, consecrate you. (5.212)
May the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn,
as well as Rāhu and Ketu when propitiated, consecrate you with their blessings.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas;
the ṛṣis, munis, cows, and likewise the divine mothers. || 5.214 ||
The wives of the gods, the Daityas, the hosts of oceans, all weapons, all missiles, kings, and vehicles; 5.215.
The medicinal herbs, the jewels, the divisions of time, the rivers, the oceans, the clouds, the sacred fords, and the rain-giving clouds. (5.216)
May these [mantras] consecrate you for the accomplishment of all desires and goals.
The great Vāmadevya is the seer (ṛṣi), the Virāj is the meter (chandas), Indra is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is in rites of pacification (śāntika).
Oṃ! With what aid will he, the wonderful one, who is ever-increasing as our friend, come to us? By what means will the most powerful one be chosen?
Who among the exhilarating draughts is the true one that shall intoxicate you with the soma-juice?
Savitar bestows wealth upon the one who presses the juice for the sake of the firm and unyielding wood, acting as a friend to those who sing his praises.
A hundred [lives] for the sake of existence.
Oṃ! May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the all-knowing, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unbreakable, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us. 5-217.
Having thus sprinkled [the disciple] with water from the jar, one should perform the *vandanā* (salutation) with sacrificial ashes;
[this is done] after taking up the sacrificial ashes.
Oṃ kaśyapa, one should place the longevity of Kaśyapa on the forehead of the disciple;
"Jamadagni, [grant] the longevity," one should place it on the throat.
Oṃ *yad devānāṃ trāyuṣam*, [reciting this] on the two shoulders;
Oṃ *tat te astrutrāyuṣam*, [reciting this] he should place it on the heart.
Then one should offer a blessing.
Then the disciple, having prostrated before the guru like a staff, may live according to his ease.
The teacher, too, should go to whatever place [is appropriate].
One should give something to others who are distressed or destitute,
and one should feed a maiden.
And so it has been said in the Āgamakalpadruma:
Then, with a perfectly steady mind, one should practice the yoga-exercises;
by this, it is as if one had given a cow in gift at the Ganges for three hundred divine years.
Whatever fruit is obtained by constantly worshipping [the deity],
one attains that same fruit at Kurukṣetra, at the Yamunā, at Prayāga, and at Puruṣottama.
Whatever fruit is obtained by the gift of a thousand cows, one attains that very same merit here on earth, without a doubt. (5.220)
Whether complete or incomplete, whoever should offer it, or take away that which has been honored—be it leaves, flowers, and so forth, in great quantity, whether occasionally or constantly. (5.221)
What is the use of visiting sacred fords or of many other acts of giving that have been described?
One who is incapable of performing formal worship should instead give the means for worship.
He who is unable to give at all should perform worship;
it is sufficient to rescue one falling for a moment into the ocean of existence from the Lord. (5.223)
He who daily observes this ritual of worship shall attain incomparable prosperity in this world and reach the supreme state through the mantra. (5.224)
Regarding the verse previously written—"When the mantra-practitioner, having performed the initiation (dīkṣā), should observe a fast"—[it is said]:
"The giver and the receiver should not fast; fasting would destroy auspiciousness.
Therefore, O Daughter of Śaṅkara, one should eat food that is fit for sacrifice (haviṣya). (5.225)
Now follows the abbreviated initiation (saṃkṣepadīkṣā).
Having placed a new pitcher upon a *muhūrtta-sarvatobhadra* diagram,
it should be adorned with sweetmeats, perfumes, and flowers, and covered with a cloth.
Combined with all medicinal herbs, the nine gems, and the five salts,
along with *surāmaṃsī*, *vaca*, *kuṣṭha*, *śaileya*, and the two types of *rajanī*.
Śaṭī, caṇupaka, and musta are known as the group of all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhigaṇa).
[Also included are] mṛśniparṇī, śyāmalatā, tejapattra, and śatāvarī. (5.228)
Guḍūcī and sahadevā are known as the mahauṣadhi group. Surā, māṃsī, jaṭā, māṃsī, śaileya, and śailaja [are also included]. (5.229)
Two types of Rajani (turmeric), Haridra, Daruharidra, Prsniparni, Pippali, Sahadeva, and Dhṛtakumari.
But the nine gems are described in the Śāradā-tantra.
Kukta, māṇikya, vaiḍūrya, gomeda, anvakravikrama, padmarāga, and marakatanīra, respectively. (5.230)
Then, having performed the worship of the deities, one should offer oblations more than a hundred times;
the instruction "one should offer" refers to the capacity [of the practitioner].
Having made the disciple assume the *sūla* posture, one should cause him to sit near the altar according to the injunctions. || 5-231 ||
Having consecrated [the disciple] with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel as well as the water from the *śānti* jar,
one should sprinkle him with the root mantra recited one hundred and eight times.
Then, having accomplished it with the mantra, he should place his hand upon the head and give them the wings with the words, "May there be peace."
Then the disciple should worship the guru.

Alternatively, according to the procedure for another initiation (*dīkṣāntarakrama*), having worshipped the conch with *akṣata* grains, one should sprinkle it with water from that [conch] while reciting the root mantra eight times; then, having performed the *kekara* [gesture],
one should mutter [the mantra] eight times into the ear— this is the rule for the nature of oral instruction (*upadeśatva*).
He states another instruction:
At a sacred ford during an eclipse of the moon or sun, in a field of accomplishment, or in a temple of Śiva; || 5.233 ||
"Because it consists solely in the proclamation of the mantra, it is called 'instruction' (upadeśa).
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Mārga-kalpalatā* composed by the illustrious Yadunātha Cakravartin. 1.
66b) Now, the measure of the substances for the fire-oblation (homa) is stated here:
one karṣa of clarified butter is prescribed for the oblation, and milk is recorded as being one śukti in measure.
Two *śāstrīya* *tolas* constitute a *karṣa*, which is one-fourth of a *pala*.
A *pala* consists of four *suvarṇas*, and likewise, a *śukti* is half a *pala*. (6.2)
The five products of the cow have been described by those wise ones who possess knowledge;
honey and milk are declared to be equal to them, even in the measure of a single bean.
Milk-rice and *paramānna* should be the measure of an *akṣa*, which is two *tolakas*;
for that which has curd as its primary ingredient, it should be the measure of a handful.
Two *pala*s of flattened rice (*pṛthuka*) should be the measure; the roasted flour (*saktu*) is likewise declared to be that same amount.
Jaggery (*guḍa*) should be half a *parārddha* in measure, and sugar (*śarkarā*) is considered to be the same.
Half a mouthful (*grāsārddha*) is the measure for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*); this is recorded as the rule for the various directions.
The morsel of food should be equal in size to a peacock’s egg. One should likewise prepare single leaves and flowers, as well as cakes;
they know that plantains and oranges should be offered in great numbers.
The *mātuluṅga* is divided into four sections, and the *panasa* is made into twenty pieces.
The *mātuluṅga* is a citron, while the *niṃba* is a seed; the *panasa* is specifically the fruit of the *kaṇṭhakī*.
The wise know that the sacrificial posts (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the stakes (*ārakīla*) should not be cut.
The fruit of the bilva tree is divided into three parts, while the kapittha fruit is split in two;
however, in the homa of the uvāruka fruit, it is said that it should be divided into three parts.
The fruit of the uvāruka is the karkaṭī.
The fruits should be of various kinds and unbroken; the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be ten finger-breadths long.
Three blades of dūrvā grass are prescribed, and the guḍūcī should be four finger-breadths long.
There should be a handful of rice, or likewise mung beans or moṣa seeds; or there may be half that amount of rice, or vegetables measured by a handful. (6.10)
Wheat and red lotuses are measured by a closed fist;
sesame seeds are the size of a handful, and mustard seeds are of that same measure.

A *culaka* measure, a *kaṣa* measure, a *śukti* measure, twenty grains of salt and black pepper, and a quantity equal to a *pura* of *vadaras*—this is remembered as the equivalent amount of *rāmaṭha*.
*Pura* is *guggulu*; *rāmaṭha* is *hiṅgu*.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron. || 6-12 ||
The seeds of the partridge (tittiri) have been specified as the standard measures by the teachers;
however, another measure is declared in the Śāradātilaka. (6-13)
It has been stated regarding the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) that one should hold it attentively before the image;
for the oblation (homa), one karṣa of ghee is prescribed, and one śukti of milk is traditionally taught.
Eighty guñjās are measured as one śāstroktatolaka.
Those two together constitute one *karṣa*, which is stated in the scriptures to be two *tolakas*; this is called a *śukti*.
The five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) have been described by the sages as being equal in measure to that.
They are like mother-of-pearl.
That [mixture] is declared to be equal to honey, milk, and boiled rice, each in the measure of an *akṣa*.
An *akṣa* is the measure of a *vadbhiḍa* fruit; it should be consumed in a small vessel (*culuka*), for some say this is the measure of honey.
This would involve contact with a human being, or rather, it would be a liquid substance, according to the sacred scripture.
How then can [the nectar] come from a mere mouthful of honey or milk?
It is said: through the procedure involving a leaf of the *śvattha* tree, that which follows shall come to pass. (6.17)
In reality, however, that which is in the middle of the ladle is equal;
what contradiction is there in an offering made from a substance into a substance? (6.18)

The measure for curd should be one handful; parched rice should be measured by a single fist; flattened grains (pṛthuka) should be equal to that, and likewise, roasted barley flour (saktu) is said to be the same.
Sugar should be half a *pala* in measure, as declared by Arcchaka;
the portion for the sacrificial pap (*caru*) should be half a mouthful, and sugarcane is considered to have the same limit as the former.
67b) A mouthful equal to a peacock’s egg; half of that is equal to a peacock’s egg, which is equal to a peacock’s plumage.
One should arrange the leaves and flowers one by one, as well as the cakes;
likewise, the wise should know that the plantain fruits and oranges should be placed individually.

The *mātuluṅga* fruit is divided into four parts, and the *panasa* fruit into ten; the *mātuluṅga*, the *niṃba* fruit, and [the *panasa*] are each one [part]. Some here have recited "the *mātuluṅgas*" as a singular collective.
The wise know that coconuts are of eight kinds when split open.
Having divided them into three parts each, the sacrificial fuel sticks (samidhs) shall be ten finger-breadths long.
The fuel sticks should never be thicker than a thumb;
they must not be devoid of bark, nor infested by insects, nor split.

It should not be longer than a span (*prādeśa*), nor should it have more than two branches; "not more, not less" means it should be neither deficient nor excessive. "Not having branches" means it should be devoid of side-shoots.
Furthermore, one who is wise should know that fuel-sticks that are leafless lack potency for use in *homa* offerings.
Not devoid of vigor, not withered.
One who understands should offer fuel with its tip pointing eastward for the sake of prosperity.
Wood that is sapless, hollow, or rotten, or that has been split, shattered, burnt, crooked, or full of holes—such wood is not suitable for the purpose of a ritual fire. || 6.25 ||

Those that are long, thick, crooked, pleasing to the wise, yet cause the destruction of the success of one's actions; those that are hollow and full of pits—thus spoke the venerable Somaśambhu. (6.26)
The authoritative source regarding radishes and other such items [is the Veda].
One should offer three portions of roots and fruits according to their respective measures, as well as five *akṣa* seeds of food measured by the size of the temple, into the fire.
One should offer oblations according to another ritual procedure: for creepers, the measure is two finger-breadths; for bulbous roots, one-eighth part of that.
Three blades of dūrvā grass are prescribed, along with guḍūcī and caturaṅgula;
there should be a handful of rice, or even mung beans and black gram.
68a) Sesame seeds should be the size of a handful, and mustard seeds likewise;
some have stated that for oblations, mustard seeds should be half of half a *karṣa*. (6.30)
One *śukti* measure of salt and twenty black peppers;
some say that one *śukti* consists of half a *pala*, which is four *āṣakas*.
A *pura* is the size of a jujube fruit (*vadara*), and asafoetida (*rāmaṭha*) is considered to be equal to that. (6.31)
The vegetable dish should be four finger-breadths in measure, and likewise the *kṛsara*—
the mixture of sesame and rice— should be twelve joints in measure, that is, four finger-breadths.
Thus has the measurement of the *tilaka* been declared by those expert in mantra and tantra.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron—
each weighing as much as a tamarind seed— are prescribed by the wise.

The measurements for sandalwood and other substances as taught by Śrī Somaśambhu are as follows: these [other materials] should be the size of a pea, while guggulu should be like the stone of a jujube fruit.
Camphor, sandalwood, musk, and saffron—each [particle] the size of a chickpea—is what has been declared by others who are knowers of the Vedas. (6.35)
When the substance for the oblation is not specified, sesame and clarified butter are prescribed;
and when the substance for the collyrium is not specified, they know that clarified butter alone is the collyrium.

When no number is specified, it is one thousand; when no substance is specified, it is clarified butter (ghṛta); and regarding fuel-sticks (samidh) that are not specified, those made of Palāśa wood are traditionally prescribed.
But in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Tantra it is said: "Ghee, situated in the left horn [of the sacrificial ladle], is prescribed as the substance for oblations when no specific material is enjoined. (6.38)
All this has been prescribed according to the path seen in the Smṛtis;
the oblation of parched grains and so forth is not ordained to be performed with the hand, including the fingers.

The oblation of nearby flowers, fruits, and so forth should be performed with the deer-mudrā; thus has the substance for each substance been declared for those who are experts in the mantras and tantras. (6.40)
One should join one's own secret parts to the thumb of the Mīlinī;
the remaining fingers should be extended—this is declared to be the Mṛga-mudrā. (6.41)
In this context, the authority as stated in the treatises is now set forth:
five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those [māṣas] make one *suvarṇa*.
Four suvarṇas make one pala; a niṣka is one hundred and eight [māṣas]. Some say that a niṣka is an akṣa, while others say a niṣka is a pala, or even half a pala.
Two guñjās shall be one silver māṣa; ten dharaṇas shall be one pala;
and thirty-two palas constitute a prastha, as declared by the Self-born One himself.
Four *prasthas* make one *āḍhaka*, and four *āḍhakas* make one *droṇa*.
That same measure constitutes a heap (*rāśimāna*), which consists of sixteen such *vārī* measures.
Twenty [tolas] make a *kuṃbha*, ten of those make a *vāha*, and three times three *tarkārīs* are declared by the scriptures to be a *bhāra* in due order.
However, two thousand [palas] are correctly declared to be the load that may be carried for profit. || 6-46 ||
Some do not desire a necklace weighing more than a tenth part of a *bhāra*.
A *muṣṭi* should be the measure of one *palā*, and two *palas* would constitute a *prasṛti*. (6.47)
Eight handfuls (muṣṭi) make one kuñca; eight kuñcas make one puṣkala;
and four puṣkalas, in that sequence, make one āḍhaka.

Thus, eight such [units] are called a *puṣkala*; a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) is said to be [the same]. A *kumbha* is declared to be sixty-four *palas*, and four *prasthas* [make one *āḍhaka*]. || 6.49 ||
There would be the consequence of two [fingers], and that pair would be the *prasava*; that pair is the *kula*, the *vaṃ*, the *vighna*, the *prastha*, and the *pātra* in sequence. (6.50)

Likewise, some say that five *guñjās* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those make one *kaṣa*. Furthermore, an *āḍhaka*, a *śiva*, an *athadreṇa*, and a *khārī* are [measures of capacity]; some maintain this. (6.51)
"Viṣṇu has stated here that twelve māṣas indeed constitute one akṣa;
this is a technical definition in the Vedic tradition, yet it is highly esteemed among the worldly sciences. (6.52)

Therefore, those who know the scriptures maintain that worldly things such as a handful of grain, a cowrie shell, or a water-pot should be accepted [as valid] in the same way as a mother-of-pearl shell [mistaken for silver]. (6.53)
The preceptor, having attained perfection, should meditate on Vaiśvānara as standing during the offerings of flowers;
as reclining during the offerings of clarified butter; and as seated during all other matters. (6.54)
One should offer oblations into the center of this fire for all rites, O wise one;
[otherwise], in the case of an ear-oblation, disease would arise, and blindness of the eyes is declared [to follow]. (6.55)
If [the smoke] reaches the nose, there is mental distress; if it reaches the head, there is loss of wealth.
Wherever the smoke enters the stomach, from that point the ear is affected; wherever it reaches the nostrils, from that point the nose is affected.
Where the eye is a small flame, from which the charcoal [proceeds] is the head;
where the blazing flame is, that is the tongue of the Fire-god (Jātavedas).
Of Jātavedas, the fire.
Resembling gold, vermilion, the morning sun, saffron, and honey—
such is the auspicious color of Suvarṇaretas as it is proclaimed.
The sound of a water-jar being struck by the hand of a potter, or the roar of a great elephant, brings good fortune;
likewise, fragrances resembling those of the nāga, caṇpaka, punnāṭa, pāṭalā, and yūthikā flowers are auspicious.
"Experts in the Tantras state that the auspicious fragrance of fire is like that of a lotus, a blue water-lily, a garland, ghee, and guggulu resin. (6.60)
Cocks with crests as bright as umbrellas that turn to the right while crowing bestow auspiciousness upon the sacrificer, and especially upon his kingdom. (6.61)
Smoke that is as white as jasmine or a conch shell is declared to bring auspiciousness from fire;
black smoke, with the color of a black path, would destroy the sacrificer.
When Kṛṣṇa has departed, [there is] the state of fire.
A sound resembling the cry of a crow quickly destroys one's white kingdom;
O Fire, a sound similar to the bray of a donkey brings about total destruction.
If the sacrificial fire is foul-smelling like the Ganges, it brings suffering to the sacrificer.
If its flames are severed, obscured, or crestless, it causes death and the total loss of wealth.
In the bright fortnight, one should know that the smoke is like the color of a pigeon;
it brings about loss for the Raghu dynasty and for cattle after a long time.
When such defects have arisen among the disciples,
the preceptor should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra as an act of atonement.
Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Āgamakalpalatā. || 6 ||
I shall now describe the general worship that bestows accomplishment upon practitioners of mantra;
having risen at dawn during the hour of Brahmā, the wise one [should proceed].
In the lotus situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), adorned with a thousand petals,
one should meditate upon the venerable Guru, who is the Supreme Self (paramātman), his hands graced by the gesture of exposition (vyākhyā-mudrā).
One should meditate upon [the deity] who has two eyes, two arms, and is joyful, bestowing all perfections.
Having meditated thus, [one should bathe him] with the stream of nectar remembered from his feet.
Having washed his own body and steadied his mind,
he should meditate, according to the rules, upon his chosen deity within the lotus of his own heart.
One should contemplate one's own body as pervaded by a mass of that light;
having prostrated and taken up the fire [mantra], preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.
Recalling the meaning of the mantra, one should go to the stūpa according to the path prescribed in the [relevant] Śākhā;
having bathed, one should then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth with one's own mantra.
Having meditated upon one's chosen deity, one should invoke the sacred water (tīrtha) using the goad mudrā (aṅkuśamudrā) with the mantra: "O Gaṅgā and Yamunā... and so forth. (7–7)
Having rendered that sacred water (tīrtha) immortal with the seed-syllable *vaṃ* and the mudrā known as the Cow (*dhenusaṃjñā*), one should protect it with the arrow [mantra] itself.
Having meditated upon the form of the deity in that water,
the wise man should immerse himself three times in the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) flowing from its feet, while mentally reciting the mantra.
Having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* bath again, preceded by the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and other rites,
one should then recite the root mantra twenty-eight times.
One should satisfy [the deity] for that many repetitions with the mantra to be spoken;
then, one should consecrate [the disciple] on the head in the same manner with the water-pot mudrā.
Having recited the Gāyatrī of that deity as well as the Pakti, [he should recite]: "Oṃ, the radiant Sūrya Āditya; may there be offerings for the Sun. (7-12)

Having offered the *argha* with the root mantra, and having sipped water (*ācamana*) ten times while reciting the mantra over the water, one should bow to the lords of the directions and then proceed to the temple of the deity.
The consecration with nectar is performed by means of the seed-syllable *vaṃ*.
Since bathing is of many kinds, in this context "immersion" refers to the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite, which pertains to those other than Śūdras.
Now, as for the libation (tarpaṇa):
First, one should satisfy Acyuta there once with each of the *santarpaṇa-pīṭha-mantras*.
Having invoked [the deity], one should worship with all those offerings prescribed in the tantra;
then, having formed the dhenumudrā and prepared the materials for the libation (tarpaṇa) with water.
With the thought "this is he," offer libations with palms joined as if holding a golden cup;
then, once again, satisfy the retinue members individually, each according to their own ritual procedure.
One should join the word "tarpayāmi" (I satisfy) at the end of the mantras, followed by one's own names;
then again [the word] in the accusative case for those [names], and thus complete the remaining worship.
Thus, at the beginning of the ritual application.
And the Gāyatrī verses should also be meditated upon accordingly.
The mantra "ghṛṇiḥ sūryaḥ," however, pertains exclusively to the twice-born, because that mantra belongs to the Vedic domain.

Then, one desiring prosperity should indeed perform the worship of the doors and other parts;

As it is stated in the *Pūrṇapaddhati*:
"Likewise, the Gaṅgā and Yamunā [are placed] on the branches extending to the right and left," so say some here.
O Sage, the union with the left side of the Lord of the Vine (Gaṇeśa) and with Gaurī is likewise [taught] for the two sides of the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa).
"In the same way, Dhātṛ and the others [should be understood]," so they say.
That is not so.
Because there is no consistency between the words and their meaning.
It has been stated [that this is so] also because of the contradiction with the words.

Because there is an absence of a means of valid cognition for that.

some say that Nanda and others occupy the pairs [of gates], while Kuvera and the others each occupy one.
Furthermore, the Kaśmīrīs now say that the removal of obstacles takes place outside.
71b) Because there is no purpose for its utterance externally;

since the removal of internal obstacles occurs through the removal of external obstacles, that [utterance] is solely for the sake of purifying the interior of the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*), which is an established reality.
And so, "or in the interval" is the direction [for further consideration].
Touching a branch slightly with his left hand, the Guru should touch the lintel.

Immediately thereafter, the Lord of Teachers, by gazing down with divine vision, [perceives it]. (7.31)

One should dispel divine obstacles with the *astra* mantra, those moving in the atmosphere with the *abhicāra* mantras, and terrestrial obstacles with three slaps of the heel; thus one should ward off all obstacles.

With the root-mantra while gazing upward with divine vision, the mantra is "phaṭ" for that which is devoid of the *astra* [mantra]; the meaning is "with that together with the *abhi*. Then, from the sky-dwellers—that is, those born in the intermediate space—the Guru [should offer] white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, and flowers with the thought that they are the *nārāca-astra*.
"But those beings who depart," thus [it is said].
Having recited this mantra for the weapon (*astra*), one should encircle the interior of the pavilion.
Regarding the strikes with the heels of the feet, he says:
Then, having struck the left foot upon the ground three times, he should proceed from there.
Then one should perform three claps of the hands, binding the directions from above downwards,
repeatedly with three snapping sounds in a clockwise sequence.
Thus [it is said].
This has been stated in the *Sundarīrahasyavṛtti*:
And in the *Āgamakalpadruma*:
"One should worship Vāsava and Īśa in the southwest direction, as well as Brahmā;

He describes the method for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya):
In the treatises on Smṛti.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with kuśa grass—

Half a part of cow urine, three parts of dung, three parts of milk, two parts of curd, one part of ghee, and one part of water boiled with *kuśa* grass. (7.37)
Taking cow's urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with the *gaṃdhadvārā* mantra, milk with the *āpyāyasva* mantra, and curd with the *dadhi krāvṇa* mantra. (7.38)
One should purify with the mantra "tejo'si" using ghee, and for the deity, with water from a kuśa blade;

Likewise.

likewise, [he is] Mahākāla with sharp fangs.

Scattering the scattered [obstacles] there with arrows over which mantras have been repeatedly recited.
Royal sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken grains—

Having placed one of the prescribed seats— consisting of an antelope skin over kuśa grass—

Having worshipped the deities there, beginning with Ādhāra and ending with Pṛthivī—Meru is considered the back, the Ṛṣi, and the *Sutara* is held to be the metre of the Earth. (7.49)

One should remember the deity known as Kūrma, preceded by the sages; reciting the mantra, "O Earth, by you the worlds are supported," the wise practitioner, with body straight, should sit upon the seat facing either east or north,
following the sequence beginning with the Svastika posture.

The sequence beginning with the svastika and so forth should be understood in detail; [one should be] seated in the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana), observing silence, and [using] well-perfumed water and offerings—thus one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūta-śuddhi).
Otherwise, worship performed without devotion will yield contrary results.
Thus, because of the scriptural statement regarding the censure of not performing that [rite],
and because of the phrase "the recitation and so forth of all mantras," as well as the case of the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, it is likewise [required].
As it has been stated in the *Kramadīpikā*:
And because of the statement, "Thus it is said: 'the placement (nyāsa) has been performed,'" those two [mudrās] are necessary for worship, since they bestow the state of divinity upon them.
Thus it is stated in the *Kramadīpikā*:

Having bathed, wearing clean, washed, and dry garments, with hands, feet, and face washed, having sipped water for purification (ācamana), his hands marked with pure sacred threads (pavitra), resplendent with a white umbrella and a fly-whisk, facing the eastern direction, he assumes a very firm posture such as the lotus (padmāsana) or the cross-legged (svastika).
Residing there, one should salute one's own gurus and the Lord of the Gaṇas with joined palms.
Having joined his palms in reverence and bowed to the Guru and Gaṇeśāna on his left and right sides, he should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
The salutation follows the very order of the recitation.
Some [place] Guru on the left, Gaṇeśa on the right, Durgā in front, and Kṣatrapati behind;
by this [method], some [also include] Durgā and Kṣatrapāla.
Likewise, having joined his palms in the *puṭāñjali* gesture, he should perform obeisance to the three Gurus in the world on the left,
to Gaṇeśāna on the right, and to the Lord (Īśvara) upon his head.
Thus says the Kalpataru.

One should cast [the offerings] to the north with the flower-mantra and the *nārāca* mudrā.

Then, having purified the hands with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and smeared them with ashes from a fire-pit containing much wood,

One should perform three claps (tritāla), rising higher and higher, accompanied by the weapon-mantra.
Then, with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should perform three *tāla*-claps, rising higher and higher;
by that, one should effect protection everywhere against the splendor thus generated.
Because of this statement.
Hutāśāla means a rampart of fire.
Then:

With a concentrated mind, one should join the individual self to the Supreme Self by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*, according to the method joined with yoga and by means of the consciousness-mantra (*cinmantra*).

By means of that [nature], through the state of being one's own self for all beings, one plays by transgressing [duality] within the Supreme Self; this is the *cinmantra*, the mantra "I am He" (*so'ham*).
According to the *Pūjāpradīpa*, the invocation is performed with this mantra of the Lord Haṃsa, namely the mantra "Haṃsa."
The accomplishment of the mantra does not truly consist merely in the thought "I am that";
rather, one should join [the self] with the Supreme Self by means of the consciousness-mantra (cinmantra), even if applied in reverse order.
Thus says the sacred scripture (śruti).
Since there is no contradiction in both being mantras, the principles (tattvas) are either twenty-five or twenty-four.

(73b) The senses consist of the five organs of cognition and the five organs of action, making ten.
The cessation of the ten faculties and their objects is the end-maker.
The intellect (manas), the growth [of ego] (buddhi), the I-maker (ahaṃkāra), and the mind (citta) are proclaimed by others.

Earth, water, fire, air, and ether; smell, taste, form, touch, and sound; the olfactory, gustatory, visual, tactile, and auditory organs;

Having contemplated that the twenty-five principles are dissolved therein in the form of seeds.
Then the mantra-practitioner should emit smoke from the mouth of Iḍā, together with the seed-syllable *Tivīja* and the vowel *Ra*,
which causes the drying up of all previously mentioned worlds.
With that expanded body, he should cause his own form to emerge from the city called Asakala-viśoka by way of the path of the wind toward the sun; then,

Likewise, for the Mātṛkā-mantra, Brahmā is declared to be the Ṛṣi and Gāyatrī is said to be the Chandas; such are the five limbs (pañcāṅga) of that mantra. Regarding the instruction "one should abandon the mantra," it refers to the following.
For a mantra that is deficient in its constituent parts, one should supply those very parts oneself.
And the [six] classes of mantras: *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.

the fifth vowel is the short *u*. The meaning is that the letter *ha* is joined with that [vowel] and provided with the nasal bindu (*viṃdu*). Thus, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) becomes *huṃ*. Likewise...
"To the armor" (kavacāya), as before.
The Armor Mantra (Kavacamantra).

According to the statement in the *Kramadīpikā*, "Sadauṣaṭ for the crest, hum for the armor, and sthitam [for the eye]," otherwise there would be a violation of the meter (*chando-bhaṅga*) therein; therefore, in the *Tvaritā* mantra, it is stated as "dīrghaṃ tanucchadam" (the long body-armor).

And likewise, it is logically consistent that both [mantras] attain the status of armor-mantras (*kavaca-mantra*); thus, where there are three eyes, it is appropriate to say "to the three eyes" (*netratrayāya*), whereas where there are two eyes, one says "by the two eyes" (*netrābhyām*).

For one who lacks limbs or for whom the mantras for the missing limbs have not been stated, there is no basis here for using the root mantra alone in the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa), as there is no authoritative evidence for a practice such as "salutation to the two thumbs" and so forth.

Its meaning is as follows:

As follows:

For example:
Her face was adorned with the fifty letters of the alphabet, her chest was broad, she wore a radiant crescent moon upon her bound crown, and her breasts were full and high.
Taking refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who possesses the luster of lightning, who has three eyes, and whose lotus-like hands always hold a mudrā, a rosary, and a water-pot, O Brahmins.

The forehead, the face, the circle of the eyes, the ears, the nose, and the two cheeks. || 7.59 ||
On the lips, teeth, head, face, arms, sides, fingertips, on both flanks, on the back, at the navel, in the belly, and on the shoulders of the heart. (7.60)
One should place the letters of the Mātṛkā in sequence upon the shoulders, the heart, the pair of hands and feet, and the belly and face.
According to the opinion of some, there is a placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables *aṃ* and so forth upon the heart and other parts, as well as upon the shoulders and other locations.

Herein, the placement [of the letters] is performed: for the simple vowels, by the sequence of emanation; for those accompanied by the *visarga*, by the sequence of maintenance; and for those accompanied by the *bindu*, by the sequence of reabsorption.
There is a specific distinction regarding the placement [of mantras] at the beginning of the maintenance [rite] and so forth.
This has been stated in the Śāradātilaka:

Having meditated upon the Goddess according to the rule as being endowed with the emission (*sarga*) and the object of creation (*sṛjya*), one should place [the seed-syllables] within the *sarga-bindu* by means of the path of persistence (*sthiti*). (7.63)
And so it is stated in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā:
75b) Or like the pure, nectar-like moon [attained] by means of the auspicious path.
Next, one should place the moon upon the forehead; then, by reciting the letter *la*, one should cause that which consists of all the vowels to descend.
Furthermore, by reciting the letter *ya*, one should cause that entire body, which is like a flood of nectar, to flow forth from the mouth and other [limbs].
The meaning is that *ṭha* is the moon-seed syllable (*candrabīja*) for *ṭapana*; [it is drawn] from this moon on the forehead.
By the recitation of *paropakāra* from the mantra *laparajapāllapālaka*,
and by the recitation of the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*), namely *vaṃ*,
one should fashion a body with ashes of Vasiṣṭha, which is to be cast down as a stream of nectar.
The lamp.
Thus.
Then, one should dry the body with the wind through the wind-bīja;
thereafter, one should completely burn that entire body with the fire-bīja.
One should separate the impurities with the nectar-like water of the *mṛta-mantra*,
and having brought it forth, one should flood the body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
Once the body has become pure and capable of propitiating the deities,
one should then cause the principles (tattvas) residing within the self to return to their own respective locations.
One should bring the self into the lotus of the heart of the Supreme Self;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites with the mantra of the divine Haṃsa.
The nyāsa and other rites are as stated in its own tantra; the Haṃsadeva mantra is "haṃsaḥ."
And it is said in the Sārasamuccaya:
Then, having joined the life-force (jīva) with the difficult-to-attain subtle channel, one should [place it] within the lotus situated in Śiva.
May the Lord, preceded by the swan [Garuda] and accompanied by the crescent moon, bestow upon me that wisdom which has been fashioned by the Goddess Māyā.

Thus [it is said].
The wise one should know the seers and the other [components] previously mentioned, joined with the syllables of the *agasa*.

Bow down to the Mistress of Colors, who bears the crescent moon upon her head, who possesses the luster of a red lotus, and who is bent by the weight of her breasts.

And other types [of conduct] have not been written down here due to fear of excessive length.

The Gautamiya school.

Now follows the daily worship of all the deities in brief.
This has been stated in the Yāmala:
First, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the *ṛṣi* and other [limbs]; after that, the purification of the hands;

The *tuṣṭi* [mudrā] consists of the thumbs placed downward; the *śikhā* is formed by the fingers of both hands; the *varma* [mudrā] occurs when the arms are extended and the thumbs and index fingers are joined;
and the *astra* [mudrā] arises when the two index fingers are raised from the thumbs.

The mudrās distributed in all directions have been described; therein, when the two eyes are formed by the index and middle fingers, and the ring finger becomes the third eye, it is correctly described as the six-limbed mudrā (ṣaḍaṅgamudrā).
The meditation mudrā (dhyānamudrā) consists of the index fingers [joined]; it is also designated as Vāsudeva.
When the little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined, it is otherwise [known as Saṅkarṣaṇa].

The meaning is that, being placed upon a conch shell, she receives the name Satīgārī.

One should bind the left thumb with the right fist;
then, having made the fist turned upward, one should extend the thumb.

The two little fingers are bound together, as are the two index fingers and the two ring fingers. (8.14)
Placing the tips of the two thumbs beneath the long middle fingers which are joined together at their upper ends with the ring fingers, this is declared to be the *yonimudrā*.

For it is stated in the words: "The mudrās are declared for the invocation by the most excellent of masters."

with both fists turned upward, it is considered Sanmukhīkaraṇī. (8.19)
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs upon the limbs of the deity constitutes the act of sakalīkaraṇa (the process of making [the deity] complete).
And so it is said:

The left hand forms a fist with the index finger extended and pointing downward.

with the thumbs interlaced and the other fingers extended. (8.22)
This great seal (mahāmudrā) is joy (muditā) for the wise in the act of supreme transformation;
therefore, employ me as the seal in the rite of gladdening the deity.
The right hand is placed downward with the fingers extended in the *vara-mudrā*;

The ring finger, index, and middle fingers; likewise, those same four with the little finger added;

With the left hand facing downward and the right hand upward, one should join the fingers of one hand with the fingers of the other and then release them. (8.28)

I shall now describe the *mudrās* taught for the mantras of the secondary offerings (*upacāra*). (8.29)
One should extend both hands employed for the rite of inciting enmity;

In arranging the seat for the deity, one should display the lotus mudrā;
