The two hands in the svastika-mudrā are proclaimed as the mudrā of Dīrgha;
those same two hands, when extended, are proclaimed as the mudrā for the pādya offering.
The *deśinī* [finger] with the base thumb [extended], while the right little finger is extended and the middle finger remains bent, is proclaimed as the *asti-sromudrā* on the left side. (8.34)
The thumb and index finger joined together, while the other three fingers are extended—that is the *madhuparka* mudrā; one should visualize the water-pot (*kalaśa*) in the hand with this.
Having formed a fist during the bath with the middle finger and thumb joined together, while the other three fingers are extended—this mudrā is proclaimed as the *vaśyakī*. (8.36)

With the little finger and the thumb joined at their bases and the other three fingers extended, this is called the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread) mudrā by those who have mastered the mantras. (8.37)
The Madhuparka is considered the Samuttānā mudrā, adorned with ornaments;
the fist with the ring finger extended is proclaimed as the Gandha mudrā.
The middle finger raised with the thumb extended while facing downward is known as the Puṣpa-mudrā; it increases prosperity when used for the offering of flowers. (8.39)
With the thumb and index finger joined and the other three fingers contracted, this mudrā for the offering of incense brings satisfaction to the gods. (8.40)
The *pauṣpikī* mudrā, when turned upward with the tips of the five fingers joined and raised with the face directed upwards, is proclaimed as the *deva* mudrā. (8.41)
This mudrā, bound in three ways, is proclaimed for the food offering (naivedya);
the middle, ring, and thumb fingers have their tips joined together and are turned downwards.
When the other fingers are extended, it is proclaimed as the *gomukhī*;
when the index finger is released, it is known as the *sūcīmudrā*, the mudrā of liberation.

If one performs the protection mudrā as taught in the Śaiva tradition for the purpose of guarding all sides, one should join the two hands back-to-back and rotate them with the fingers interlaced. (8.44)
This is declared to be the *chotikā*; one should display this salutation by placing the four fingers between the ring finger and the thumb. (8.45)
Having formed a hollowed cup and released the two thumbs joined together, this is the Kumbha mudrā; it is considered the Hṛllekhā-kacchapī for one who possesses vision.
Extending the right hand, one should gradually contract the fingers starting from the little finger; this is considered the Dīrgha-mudrā according to the tradition.
Having placed the hands with their backs against each other and interlaced the fingers, and having formed this [mudrā], one should turn away and bow; this is the mudrā for asking for forgiveness.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Āgamakalpatoyā*.
I shall now proclaim the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) which bestows accomplishment upon those who recite mantras;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes a sovereign over all accomplishments.
For a mantra that is perfected through preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) is indeed the giver of fruit.
What is the use of fire-offerings (*homa*), what is the use of recitation (*japa*), and what is the use of the extensive ritual placements (*nyāsa*) of the mantra? (9.2)
If there were no preliminary rite for secret mantras, [they would be ineffective];
for the preliminary rite is said to be the primary life-force of mantras. (9.3)
Just as an embodied being devoid of life is bereft of all activity,
so indeed is a mantra proclaimed that is devoid of *puraścaraṇa*.

Therefore, having first performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), the best of practitioners should then carry out the ritual application (prayoga), which is difficult for all other practitioners to attain.
Having received the vidyā from a true guru, one should perform the puraścaryā;
and so it is stated in the Tārārahasyavṛtti:
Having received the mantra from the presence of the guru, he should be devoted solely to service for the guru. (9.6)
Having understood the mantra of the ear, the heart, the eye, and the vital breaths according to their true nature,

The Praṇava is proclaimed as the ear of mantras, and the letter *repha* is declared to be their mouth;
the vowels are to be known immediately thereafter by those who know the mantras as their two eyes.
And those additional syllables are proclaimed as the heart;

Recitation, fire-offerings, libations, consecrations, and the feeding of Brahmins.

Wherever the number of recitations, oblations, and so forth is not specified, there the number shall be eight thousand.
This has been stated in the Vārāha Tantra:
For those [mantras] for which no number has been stated by the wise regarding recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa), [the following applies].
The number for their recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) shall be eight thousand;

And in that Vedic scripture (nigama) wherein the rule for the number of mantras is prescribed... [9-11]
In that regard, the number of mantras increases everywhere according to the sequence of the ages:

In the Dvāpara age, the number is tripled, and in the Kali age, the number is quadrupled. This has been stated in the *Pūrṇāparādha-tantra*:
If no specific number is mentioned, one should drink ten [mouthfuls] at a time, either one hundred and eight times or one thousand times.
He states the places for recitation:
This has been stated in the Yoginīhṛdaya:
A meritorious field, the bank of a river, a cave, a mountain peak, a sacred ford, a region near the confluence of rivers, and a purifying forest—[these are places for practice]. (9.14)

The root of the *aśvattha* and *lakṣmaṇā* trees, the water from within a cow-pen, a temple, a family lineage, the ocean, and one's own home. (9.16)
The presence of gurus, a place of one-pointed concentration, as well as a cremation ground and so forth—each of these has been demonstrated in the various ritual manuals (kalpas). (9.17)
Having relied upon the lamp-site, one should perform auspicious rites;
having made the ground square, one should draw a diagram of nine squares.
One should write the seven syllables in order in the compartments starting from the east;
then, one should write the pairs of vowels in sequence in the northeast.
Wherever the interval between the *kṣatra* and *akṣa* lines begins from the cardinal directions and so forth, one should know that to be the *mūrava*; two cubits are situated on both sides of it.
The *koṣṭha* and the *kukṣi* are both said to be two [units] each; the tail is declared to be situated at the end.
By this sequence, one should divide even that which stands in the middle for the practitioner. (9-21)
If it is on the chest, one attains success; if held in the hand, one has a short life;
if seated in the belly, one is established therein; if on the feet, one shall experience suffering. (9.22)

This is declared to be the Kūrma-cakra, which brings about the accomplishment of mantras.

And for those who are unknown and for those without a dwelling, one should assign a name there in the group of seven.

then, one should write the root mantra in the center.

This has been stated in the Vīra-tantra:
On the eighth day and on both fortnights of the fourteenth day—
especially during the dark fortnight— one should accomplish the heroic practice (vīrasādhana).
O beautiful goddess, when half a watch— that is, three hours— of the night has passed,
[one should look for] either a corpse or a funeral pyre.
Having led [them] according to their pleasure.

and likewise in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:

[one should honor] one's own guru, the circle of brothers, or also Brahmins of excellent vows. (9.33)

This has been stated in the Yāmala:

He is indeed one of great daring, possessing great strength and prowess;

With the root mantra ending in the syllable *phaṭ*.

For example:

One should offer the bali-oblation with this [mantra]. As follows:
Oṃ hūṃ! O Lord of the Cremation Ground, take this food together with the bones, hūṃ! Take this great offering, take it, drink it; ward off obstacles and grant me accomplishment, svāhā!
Then, having worshipped Pūrvabhairava in the south with "Oṃ hūṃ, O Bhairava, terrifying lord of the cremation ground, [accept] this [offering] as before."

Accept this offering, O Mother; grant the supreme goal to be accomplished.
Oṃ hūṃ, Lord of Beings, Sovereign of the Cremation Ground!
This is the mantra.
Oṃ hūṃ; at the end of the word, those lords of all the gaṇas are in the position of the sovereign.
Having placed them upon the summit of the cremation ground, one should draw them up together as before. (9.47)

O beautiful one, having offered the bali-oblation to Tārā and the others, and having performed a sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using these mantras, one should then draw [the mandala] upon yellow cloth.
Then, on either birch bark or a banyan leaf, one should place the mantra of the seat (*pīṭha*).
Having spread that seat there, one should then assume the bound hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*).
O Goddess of the gods, one should perform protection in the directions with the *virāṇa* [mantra].
The meaning of this is as follows:
Having written the respective *pīṭha-mantras* prescribed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*) upon yellow cloth or other materials,
and having spread a seat such as a tiger skin over that, one should perform protection in the four directions using the *vidyā-virāndana-mantra* while seated in the *vīrāsana* posture.
Now, the mantra for bowing to the heroes:
Huḥ huḥ hrīḥ hrīḥ! O Kālī of terrible fangs, O fierce leader, rend, rend; strike, strike; destroy this great obstacle, destroy it! Svāhā phaṭ!
One should cast a clod of earth consecrated with this mantra in the ten directions.

If, however, the practitioner becomes overwhelmed by fear, then he must be protected by all his friends; thereafter, having completed the entire network of ritual procedures such as the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) as prescribed in the respective *kalpas*, and having worshipped the chosen deity and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he should meditate upon the chosen deity and recite the mantra.
But it is volition.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "I, [name], of [gotra] [gotra], [name] [śarman], desiring the perfection of such-and-such mantra, shall perform the recitation (*japa*) of that mantra [number] times," one should then recite it.
For a mantra with one syllable, one should perform a thousand recitations;
for a two-syllable mantra, fifty thousand; and for three-syllable mantras, eight thousand.
Beyond this, however, there are eight thousand and eight mantras;
that is to say, the number eight thousand and eight. (9.52)
If it is possible to bind his ears and eyes with a cloth,
then nothing at all will be seen until midnight.
One should scatter mustard seeds in all directions with the mantra known as Jayadurgā:
*oṃ durge 2 rakṣiṇi svāhā*.
Oṃ, you are sesame, having Soma as your deity. Thus [it is said].

Then, having caused [the deity] to swear an oath of truth, one should choose the most excellent boon;
having offered an oblation at the beginning of the recitation, one should offer an oblation at the end of the recitation as well.
And so it has been said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer an oblation (bali) to the deity according to the prescribed rule,
having taken either buffalo or goat meat, or even the best available.

Furthermore, say: "Give me a horse, give me an elephant, and whatever else you have;

The Śavamānīya rite should be performed; one should not take the nectar (amṛta) according to one's own will.
At the time of the first watch of the night, they should go there together.

Thus, one should draw a triangular wheel on the sole of his foot;

Having brought the lips together like a hollow vessel, with a steady mind and steady senses,

There is no fear for one who possesses power; should fear arise, one should speak thus:

"But on another day I shall give [it]; tell me your own name.
Having been addressed thus, he, being consecrated with devotion, recited [the mantra] again, free from fear. (9.90)
If he speaks sweetly again, one should certainly not speak with such restraint;

having cleansed the wheel of the feet, one should cast the materials of worship into the water.

in the morning, having performed the daily rites, one should drink water with bilva leaves.

having uttered the root mantra ending with "svāhā," and at the conclusion of the libation (tarpaṇa), the word "namaḥ. || 9-100 ||
By this rite, the best of teachers should satisfy the deity.
And so it is stated in the Mūlamālā:
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Lord, tell me the procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*), which is my most profound secret;
for by its performance, all desires are indeed fulfilled. (9–101)
The illustrious Lord said:

Having received initiation from a true guru on an auspicious day at nightfall, one who is a devotee of Viṣṇu is declared to be a Vaiṣṇava Ārāma; those initiated into the Śaiva path are called Madhyama.
He who is indeed initiated by this [initiation] is the supreme guru;
whether at the sacred sites of Śakti, at the Gaṅgā, at a river, or on a mountain peak.
And on a pure spot, O Goddess, one should perform sacrifice while accomplishing the Vidyā,
in a field of Śakti such as Kāmarūpa and others.
Staying there, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, becoming manifest in the very form of the Goddess.
Then this vidyā, which brings the three worlds under one's control, arises;
it was practiced for fourteen thousand [births] while serving the lotus feet of Hari.

95a) Therefore, O Goddess of the gods, that man who is devoted to her worship [attains this] through body, mind, and speech, by means of [offerings such as] hundreds of gold pieces and so forth. || 9.106 ||
Having satisfied the guru with supreme devotion, one should take recourse to initiation;
then, resorting to the previously mentioned place, one should undertake recitation and worship. (9-107)
One should recite [the mantra] beginning at dawn until midday.

Having departed during the first watch, until the end of the third watch.

That which is oily, that which has stood overnight, that which is devoid of oil, that which is infested with insects or causes suffering to them, as well as sour gruel, radish, wood-apple, karaja, and garlic— [these should not be eaten].
Lentils, kidney beans, mung beans, frogs, and the like;
betel nut, vessels of bell-metal, and eating during the day—[these should be avoided]. (9.113)

and the little finger is for attraction—these are auspicious for the practice of recitation.
One should perform the recitation with the thumb together with the other fingers;
an action performed without the thumb shall be fruitless. (9.256)
One seeking liberation should perform twenty-five [recitations], twenty-seven for nourishment,
thirty for wealth, and fifteen for malevolent rites.
Then, having bowed to the *kullukā* and performed the worship of the garland,
one should take it up with the right hand, O Lord, and not touch it with the left.
One should contemplate the *kullukā* at the regions of the navel, the heart, and the head.
A rosary made of crystal, rudrākṣa, putrajīva, indrākṣa, padmākṣa, pearl, coral, gold, kośa, or conch shell brings happiness to those who seek it. (9.259)
For the Goddess, there would be delight with ornaments made of coral, gold, crystal, or pearls;
for Śiva, there is pleasure with those fashioned from rudrākṣa beads or those made of crystal. (9.260)

A rosary of Rudrākṣa beads, or one made of Kuśa grass, or even of lotus seeds or pearls, is always highly praised as being pleasing to Viṣṇu; indeed, such a Rudrākṣa rosary is eternally auspicious. (9.261)
Tripurā should especially be fashioned from coral;
alternatively, her garland should especially be made from conch-shell gems. (9.262)
It is praised for all rites when performed with one hundred and eight seed-syllables;
it is likewise proclaimed that it may be performed with even fifty.
Or even with fifty-five [syllables] for rites such as killing and expulsion;
it is declared to be threefold: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic. (9.264)
The first garland is considered *sāttvika*, the second is regarded as *rājasa*, and the third is declared to be *tāmasa*; one should employ it for rites such as killing (*māraṇa*). (9.265)
A garland fashioned from white [flowers] is recommended for the rite of liberation;
a garland fashioned from black [flowers] is employed for rites such as killing. (9-266)
A garland made of silk threads is always pleasing to the Goddess;
a garland for Vaiṣṇavī may be made of cotton or even of silk threads. (9.267)
A garland for the Sun-god is proclaimed to be made either of wool or of bark;
for other deities as well, it may be fashioned according to one's preference.
On the twelfth lunar day, which belongs to Viṣṇu, a garland should be fashioned by those observing a fast, who are knowers of mantras, using the Viśvamantra during the daytime portion. || 9-269 ||
The *tulā* (weighing) of the *śaktis* should also be performed according to the prescribed rule at night,
on the eighth, the ninth, and likewise on the fourteenth lunar day.
O Goddess of the gods, on the thirteenth lunar day, one should also perform [the rite] for Śiva;
one should recite the mantra while wearing a garland that is half-round and consisting of both thick and thin beads.
It should be in the shape of a serpent, for it bestows auspiciousness in all ritual actions;
indeed, in every respect, there should be a *meru* bead on both sides of the rosaries.

One should never touch [the ground]; if one has touched it, however, one should perform the circumambulation again. Or one may do so on the joints of the hand; this rule is prescribed for all cases. || 9.273 ||
One should recite over the three joints of the ring finger starting from the base of the little finger;
two [joints] of the middle finger are the *meru*, and likewise three [joints] of the thumb. (9.274)
The practitioner of mantra should never touch [another] while constantly engaged in the rite of recitation;
the practitioner should recite according to his capacity, whether it be a thousand or ten thousand times.
Or having recited it one hundred and eight times, at the conclusion of the recitation, one should place [the rosary] upon one's head:
"Oṃ! You, O garland, are the giver of pleasure and the giver of auspiciousness to all the gods;
O blessed one, always grant me prosperity, fame, and valor. (9.276)
One should employ [the mantra] specifically for seizing, establishing, and worshiping. Now follows the procedure for recitation (japa).
Thus it is said in the Kapila-pañcarātra:
Now, the time for awakening from sleep and for the recitation of mantras is being described.

Mantras are to be understood as having the nature of fire and moon, being either fierce or gentle; they are said to be predominantly fiery for rites [of subjugation] and lunar for [peaceful] ones. (9.278)
The mantras belonging to Agni are those of the Anuṣṭubh meter, while those belonging to Soma consist mostly of syllables of nectar;
the fire-mantras awaken when the vital breath is in the right nostril.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) abides in this [central] portion, they attain gentle awakening;
when the vital breath has entered both channels, they attain total awakening.
All awakened ministers always bestow their fruit;
or rather:
The union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths is the meeting of Śiva and Śakti. || 9-281 ||
The time of awakening is to be known [as the waking state], and the time of sleep follows from that for one *pala*.
When the vital air flows through the left channel, that is the movement of the long vowels. (9-282)
When the wind is in the south, it is joined with the short [vowels];
when the wind is situated in both, it consists of the other two pairs.
Having encapsulated them with the mantra, one should emit [the letters] together with the bindu;
then again, together with the visarga, one should recite only the letter *kṣa*. (9.284)
If one recites [the mantra] in this manner when it is most desired and has awakened, it bestows swift accomplishment.
Thus ends the section on the time for awakening from sleep.
103b) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the recitation of the mantra according to its true nature. || 9-285 ||
First, however, the practitioner with a restrained mind should meditate upon the *kullukā*, which bestows the accomplishment of the mantra, in the regions of the navel, heart, and head. (9.286)
Just as with meditative absorption (dhyāna).
The goddess is seated upon a lotus that is both red and non-red, adorned with red ornaments, wearing red garments,
and more slender than a lotus fiber.
She is intent upon the sovereignty of desire, adorned with three enclosures,
resembling seven suns, radiant, and possessing a mandala with the form of the sun.
Having reflected thus, one who has conquered the senses, seated upon his seat, should perform the recitation.
Having first meditated on the *kullukā*, and having recited [the *kullukā*] one hundred and eight times,
he should again recite the root mantra.
The mantra for the *kullukā* is as follows:
"Oṃ vāhuṃ namaḥ paścāt"—this mantra consists of four syllables. || 9-289 ||
Oṃ hūṃ namaḥ.
Then, having bowed to the *kullukā* and performed the root worship (*mūlā-pūjā*), one should take hold of it with the right hand, O Lord, and touch it with the left. (9.290)
Recitation (japa) is to be known as threefold: vocal, whispered, and mental. It should be neither too loud nor indistinct, and neither too fast nor too slow. (9.291)
One should recite the mantra without distraction, with a single-pointed mind and in meditative absorption;
whatever the practitioner utters, it should be accompanied by clear sounds and vowels. (9.292)
One should recite the mantra slowly; this vocal recitation is the sacrifice of japa.
One should recite the mantra slowly, moving the lips only slightly. (9.293)

That which can be heard by someone nearby is known as *upāṃśu* (whispered) when accompanied by recitation (*japa*), wherein the mind perceives the sequence of syllables whose nature is supreme and unsurpassed. (9.294)

The mental recitation (mānasa-japa) is said to be the practice of contemplating the meaning of the words; that which is performed loudly or in a whisper shall be a thousand times more effective. (9.295)
It is taught that the mental [recitation] is a thousandfold more effective than even that;
one should meditate on the mantra with the mind, without moving the tongue or the lips. (9-296)
One should not shake the head or neck, nor should one show one's teeth;
for by the non-disturbance of syllables, the hosts of Siddhas and Vidyādharas [are pleased]. (9.297)
Since they carry [the mantra] away openly, one should therefore always keep it secret;
seated on a [proper] seat, one should recite the mantras correctly with a restrained mind.
Having offered salutation to that which is dissolved in the *bindu*, one should apply it to the path of *nāda*;
for when it is dissolved in the path of *nāda*, the mind goes nowhere else. (9.299)
"Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Gāyatrī and other mantras;
by this alone, whatever accumulation of great sins (mahāpātaka) there may be, shall be purified. (9.300)
"By reciting [the name] even once, one does not go to the destruction of merit or fall into sin."
I shall describe the stringing of the garland, which is concealed in all the tantras.

Having performed the daily rites regularly, the knower of mantras, regarding these aforementioned [objects], should diligently bring the dice under his control according to his desire and according to his will. (9.302)
They should be uniform in appearance, neither too thick nor too thin, free from defects such as insects, and indeed new rather than worn out. (9.303)
Having washed each of those separately with the five products of the cow—
cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass— (9.304)
One who knows all mantras for all rites should understand the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in their proper order: milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar.
One who accomplishes all rites should understand the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then, O best of the twice-born, [one should know] that which is fashioned by a virtuous woman and is free from knots.
Having tripled the three-stranded thread and washed it as before,
[one should use] white, black, and likewise red for the rites of pacification, subjugation, and malevolent sorcery respectively.
One should cause the Brahmins to prepare a thread of cotton or even a silk thread, placed upon nine *aśvattha* leaves arranged in the shape of a lotus. (9.308)
One who possesses the luster of camphor should wash the thread and the gems and place them within the vessel of recollection;
then, one should project the *tāra*, the *śakti*, and the *mātṛkā* onto both the thread and the gems.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one should worship with clarified butter and offer oblations according to one's capacity;
if one is unable to perform the rite of fire-offering (homa), one should perform double the number of recitations (japa).
Then, taking each jewel one by one, he should indeed join them to the thread;
he should join mouth to mouth and tail to tail.
It should be made resembling a cow's tail, or else auspiciously in the form of a serpent;
one of the same kind as that should be placed in front by means of the *marut* mantra.
One should cause a *brahmagranthi* to be placed within each individual bead;
having thus fashioned the rosary, one should then perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*).
One should have it washed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) by virtuous people while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra, as follows:
Oṃ, I praise Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! In existence, in non-existence, in that which transcends existence, favor me; salutations to Bhavodbhava.
One should rub [the image] with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and so forth, while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to the beloved; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Kāla;
salutation to Kalavikaraṇa; salutation to Vikaraṇa; salutation to Balapramathana; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana; salutation to Manonmana.
One should fumigate it with the Aghora mantra and smear it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
Oṃ! To those who are not terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible;
to all you who are everything, everywhere—to you in your forms as Rudra, obeisance! (9.315)
Oṃ. We know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us toward that.
One should mutter [the mantra] five hundred times, and for each [deity], one hundred times each:
*Oṃ īśāna sarvavidyānām īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ brahmādhipatiḥ brahmaṇo 'dhipatiḥ brahmāṇi vāme 'stra sadāśivom*.
One should not even mention Sumeru as the fifth; therefore, one should recite it with the mantra.
Having thus consecrated the rosary, he should then place it upon his vital breath;
having done so, the wise one should perform recitation over the rosary using the Mātṛkā.
From the various divisions of the *mātṛkā* mantras, all mantras were born;
therefore, the recitation of all mantras should be performed with this [mātṛkā] as a garland. (9.318)
Having worshipped the Guru, one should receive [the rosary] from his hand for the sake of attaining all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*).
Some say that by reciting the *Gāyatrī*, one should tie a knot in the rosary while reciting the mantra. (9.319)
For such a method of stringing [the beads] has not been described anywhere in the scriptures of mantra;
one who is impure should not touch it, nor should one allow it to fall from the hand.
One should move the rosary located on the thumb from the tip of the middle finger;
one should not touch it with the index finger—this is the sequence of counting that bestows liberation.
The wise man should mutter the two dark syllables (Kṛṣṇa) with the middle finger during eating and liberation;
and he should mutter them with the thumb and ring finger during the highest rite.
Through the joining of the index finger and the thumb during recitation, one performs the rites of inciting hatred and expulsion;
through the joining of the little finger and the thumb during recitation, one performs the rite of killing.
Having worshipped that rosary at the time of recitation, one should conceal it;
the wise man should reveal the guru, but never reveal the mantra.
One should not show the rosary or the mudrā even to one’s guru.
When [the practice] is accomplished, there appear spirits, rākṣasas, vetālas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas.
Therefore, the wise person should recite [the mantra] secretly; for it destroys [obstacles] openly.
When the thread has worn out, one should string it again and recite it a hundred times.
"O Lord, I wish to hear the procedure for the consecration according to the truth.
Śrī-Īśvara said:
"First, one should worship the artisan with garments, perfumes, and ointments. (9.327)
One should draw forth the garland situated within the universe, which has the nature of gold,
according to the sequence, according to the reality, and as it was previously declared.
That garland should be without gaps and free from impurities and broken grains;
the wise practitioner should fashion it so that it possesses the appropriate number of knots.
One should not perform the *pañcagavya* rite for a person of the [brahminical] class; one should administer it for three days.
Furthermore, on the fourth day, one should wash the thread with the mantras of the *astra*.
One should string together threads of uniform color with the heart-mantra,
using the mantra "Namaḥ."
The supreme practitioner should also string it with qualities such as gold and so forth. || 9-331 ||
Then one should apply the Brahma-knot or even the Naga-noose; one should bind it with the Kavaca-mantra during the practice of the Sandhya.
For the armor [armour], with the mantra "huṃ mi."
Then, at the very end of all [the threads], the best of practitioners should tie a knot upon Mount Meru, provided with two threads, by means of the conjunction with the *praṇava*.
Having thus brought [the deity] forth, O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Having drawn a maṇḍala upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the sequence of the rules for the respective divisions.
Having worshipped the chosen deity in due order according to the rules,
one should first perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and then recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
One should perform oblations with a tenth part of that [number], offering whatever is dear to whichever deity;
thereafter, the wise one should place that rosary in the center of the mandala.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should then perform the placement of the root-mantra (mūlamantra);
the weapon-mantra is the mantra "phaṭ".
Having assigned those limbs [to the respective parts of the body], one should contemplate the form of the deity.
Having attained the form of non-duality, one should then fashion a garland consisting of that very essence;
thereafter, the supreme practitioner should indeed offer the bali-oblation according to the rule.
Having thus established the deity of one's choice within the garland, the mantra-practitioner should worship the preceptor and the artisan according to the prescribed ritual. (9.339)
One should not recite another mantra there if one desires the Supreme Self. Thus ends the ritual procedure for the consecration of the rosary.
Now, the general rules for the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
While accomplishing the mantra, one should worship the deity at the three junctions of the day.
One should recite the mantra alone at either two sessions or one session;
at the end of the recitation there should be worship, or at the end of the worship one should recite the mantra.
Because of this statement.
The necessity of worship.
The goddess should be visualized within the mind, and the ritual action should be stabilized in the heart.
One should then perform the drinking of food and other acts with water that has been consecrated by mantras. (9.342)
One should constantly perform the occasional rites and associate with virtuous people;
one should bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with pure myrobalan (amalaka) alone.
Just as in the ritual of *puraścaryā*, one should perform a bath for the sake of purification using clarified butter, curd, milk, or sesame paste. (9.344)
If one is able, one should bathe at the three sessions; if unable, likewise twice or once.
For one who does not bathe, there is no fruit, nor for one who does not offer libations to the ancestors.
Other rites performed for the sake of desire, as well as association with the wicked; speaking with women, Śūdras, outcasts, dogs, or atheists—these are [prohibited]. (9.346)
One should avoid speaking untruths and crooked speech;
one should renounce bathing with hot water and eating food that has not been offered. (9.347)
Always wearing clean garments, he should sleep upon a bed of *kuśa* grass;
every day he should wash his bed and lie down alone, free from fear. (9.348)
One should avoid reciting [mantras] at night if it contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, consisting of food, clothing, and so forth. (9.349)
By the mere satisfaction of the guru, all success will certainly be attained;
those who know the truth have said that everything has its root in the guru. (9.350)
Even if one resides in the same village, one should always go and pay homage to the guru;
for the guru alone is the Supreme Brahman, therefore one should worship him first.
One should eat various kinds of sweet foods together with one's kinsmen;
thereafter—
One should begin at the time of dawn and recite until midday.
In such cases, there is no restriction that [the rite] must end by midday.
Furthermore, this indicates only the limit.

Otherwise, if there were a fixed rule [regarding the number of recitations], one might fail to complete the vow on the day of completion because the count of recitations would fall short; such is the intended meaning.
Having withdrawn the mind from sense objects, with the intellect focused on the meaning of the mantra,
one should recite it neither too quickly nor too slowly, like a string of pearls.
Japa is the repetition of syllables, which may be mental, whispered, or vocal;
it consists of mentally contemplating the sequence of syllables composed of phonemes, vowels, and words. (9.354)
Mental recitation (*japa*) is said to be performed with the mind directed toward the goal;
one should move the tongue and lips slightly while the mind is fixed on the deity. (9.355)
That which is barely audible is known as *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation;
that which one utters the mantra with speech is known as *vācaka* (spoken) recitation. || 9.356 ||

Whispered recitation is proclaimed to be a hundred thousand times more meritorious than vocal recitation; mental recitation is praised as being ten million times more meritorious than whispered recitation. (9.357)

Having first performed the recitation (japa) in this manner, one should worship the form of radiant energy (tejas) with kuśa grass, flowers, and water for the arghya offering in the right hand of the deity.
107a) One should offer the recitation (*japa*) into the left hand, which is the sphere of power (*śakti*).
And so it is said:
Having thus performed the recitation (japa) first, [one should worship] with perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and water with kuśa grass.
The wise one should offer the recitation (japa) into the left hand of the Goddess, according to the statement:
"One should perform the recitation day after day, neither deficient nor excessive. (9.360)
If, however, one should act out of negligence, one will not obtain the desired fruit;
therefore, the practitioner of mantra should perform oblations every day as a tenth part of the recitations.
O Sage, one should perform libations and ritual ablutions with a tenth part of that [number]; every day, one should feed Brahmins to pacify any deficiency or excess. (9.362)
Alternatively, one may perform more oblations for every embodied form;
however, this applies when one is unable to perform the *haum* and other [mantras].
Whichever limb may suffer a breakage, the number of recitations for that [limb] shall be doubled.
In the absence of a fire sacrifice (homa), recitation (japa) should be performed, at a number four times that of the sacrifice;
and so it is stated in the Gautamīya:
And the quality of the twice-born Kṣatriyas is remembered as being equal in number [to that of the Vaiśyas]. || 9.364 ||
For Vaiśyas, the number is eight; this is the rule for their women. And whatever caste a Śūdra has taken as his support, he should observe the rule pertaining to that caste.
This statement refers specifically to the Vaiṣṇava domain.
And so it is stated in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"For Brahmins who are attached to other [rites], the recitation (*japa*) is double the measure of the fire-oblation (*homa*);
for the other castes, however, it is accompanied by triple and further multiples. (9.366)
Thus, this applies in all cases.
By this [argument], it is not the case that a Śūdra also has the entitlement to perform the *homa*.
Through the recitation of the *praṇava*, through burnt offerings (*homa*), through the worship of the *sāligrāma* stone,
and through approaching a Brahmin woman, a Śūdra shall become like a creeping vine.
The entitlement to perform the *homa* belongs only to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
however, a Śūdra should perform double the number of recitations (*japa*) as a substitute for the *homa*.
And likewise in the Nāradapañcarātra:
The rule for the fire-oblation (homa) has been declared for only the three [upper] castes;
however, a Śūdra desiring that same fruit should perform twice as much recitation (japa) as the oblation.
And so says the Smṛti:
For a Śūdra who lacks the sacred mantras, however, a Brāhmaṇa is taken [as officiant] by means of the mantra;
according to this statement.
The fire sacrifice, however, must be performed through the gateways of Brahman.
Otherwise, there would be no means of determination.
Otherwise, it would follow that even a Śūdra has the entitlement to perform the Soma sacrifice.
And thus there is this statement:
This refers to the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa.
And thus, women also possess the qualification for performing the fire-oblation (homa).
And thus:
The maiden offers parched grain mixed with the three sweets into the sacrificial fire.

Because of the statement, "By this rite, a maiden obtains her desired husband," which pertains to the section on marriage (*vivāha-prakaraṇa*), and because it prescribes only the act of gazing [at the groom]—just as in the case of the sacrificer's wife—the offering (*homa*) for women must also be performed through the agency of a Brahmin; such is the meaning of the statement, "But for these castes... (*eṣāṃ tu varṇānām*).
Regarding the phrase "applicable to all castes," some maintain that by this [statement], even a *śūdra* possesses the qualification for performing the *homa*.
That is trivial, because the meaning of this statement has not been understood.
Why? Because this statement is intended as a prescription for the *sūdra*-offering (*sūdra-homa*).
Furthermore, regarding the *sūdra* and other such cases, the use of the plural form in "the other lines" (*itarekhām*) is appropriate; therefore, [that objection is invalid].
This is the rule applicable to all castes.

If it is argued that because of the statement "the practitioner [should perform] daily at the end of the recitation," and since the practitioner is mentioned as such, even a Śūdra would possess the status of a mantra-practitioner (*māntrika*), and thus the qualification for the *homa* would follow—[we reply:

no, because of the specific scriptural injunction, "Let women and Śūdras not study," which applies specifically to the application of Vedic knowledge (*vidyā*). It is only in the case of the application of mantra-knowledge (*mantra-vidyā*) that such a qualification is permitted.
Nor should it be said that there is a contradiction in the section concerning the architect (sthapati),
because the injunction brings about the substratum.
The non-establishment of the installation of the fire-altar.
Because of the strength of the statement: "The Brahmin is taken hold of by means of the mantra for this Śūdra."
Nor should it be said that [the meaning] is restricted by the context.
Because there is no general sublation [of the rule],
and because there is no exclusion of Śūdras and others, this [rule] applies to all subjects according to the principle of the "performance of worldly acts" (*laukikādikaraṇanyāya*).
And as for that statement, "For Śūdras, it is a two-cornered pit," that is not so.
For a Śūdra, there is no possibility [of performing the rite] because the direct bestowal of the gift must have a Brāhmaṇa as its agent. Nor is it the case that...
"An alternative procedure (anukalpa) is prescribed for the twice-born who possess the capacity for liberation.

Based on this statement from the Smṛti, it must be explained how there can be a prescription for an alternative method of fire-oblation (homa) for one who possesses the capacity for liberation, since eligibility for an alternative procedure belongs only to one who lacks that capacity.
Because there is no secondary alternative for a Śūdra.
Because the performance of the *homa* and other rites is carried out by means of a Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, some maintain that for women and Śūdras, the injunction for the fire-oblation (homa) is to be performed through a Brāhmaṇa.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the hearing of specific fruits is mentioned in connection with *puraścaraṇa* and other such rites, they must be performed for the sake of desired results (*kāmya*); if so, how can ascetics (*yati*) be included in this?
Likewise, it is stated in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā:
The wise know the renunciation of optional rites to be renunciation (nyāsa).
Because of this statement.

Because they lack the qualification for rites performed with desire (*kāmyakarman*), they do not possess the qualification for *puraścaraṇa*. Thus, *puraścaraṇa* consists of five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) as a rule;

however, for ascetics (*yatis*), there is qualification only for the *puraścaraṇa* consisting of mere recitation (*kevalajapa*). The meaning is that [their qualification] is not distinguished [by other requirements].
In reality, however, they have the authority to recite [the mantra] because it is a means for the destruction of their sins.
108b) Because there is an absence of an awakener [of knowledge], one engages in recitation and so forth with the desire for liberation;
and one engages in hearing the Vedānta, breath control (prāṇāyāma), and so forth—this constitutes the pair [of causes] consisting of that awakening scripture.
But when sacrifice is impossible for all of them, there is a twofold recitation.
And so it is stated in the Yoginīhṛdaya:
Or, with undistracted mind, one may recite the mantra twice as many times for the sake of the fire sacrifice.
One should not recite mantras while wearing a single garment, nor when clothed in many garments;
likewise, one should not do so upon seeing or hearing the speech of outcasts or those of the lowest castes.

Upon the obstruction of sneezing while walking, or when one yawns, one should recite a mantra; likewise, having sipped water (ācamana) upon reaching that [spot], one should perform a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma) consisting of six limbs.
Having performed the recitation correctly, one should perform the remaining rites, or else gaze upon the sun and so forth;
by the word "and so forth," fire and a Brāhmaṇa are included.
In this way, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall accomplish all desired objects.
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner:
during an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, one should first remain pure and have observed the fast.
Standing in a river flowing toward the ocean with water reaching up to his navel,
he should recite the mantra with one-pointed mind from the time of touch until liberation.
In the absence of a river.
Or else, having bathed in sacred water and being pure, having first observed a fast,
one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind from the beginning of the eclipse until its release.
Having seen [the deity] and bathed, one should perform the recitation with a firm resolve until liberation is attained.

By thus reciting, the perfection of the mantra will surely come to pass; of this there is no doubt. However, if a person abandons the recitation due to a lack of faith or through obstruction, [the result is lost]. (9.377)
"One who commits an offense against the deity becomes a betrayer of the ancestors and falls into hell"—
this statement from the *Sanatkumārasaṃhitā* is intended to prohibit the performance of *śrāddha* rites that fall within the midst of an already commenced great *puraścaraṇa*.
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.
With a concentrated mind, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa.
Alternatively, one should perform the auxiliary rites of the fire-oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that [number].
Indeed, in this world, the worship of the five ancillaries is intended as the *puraścaraṇa*.

According to this statement, the supreme five-limbed [rite] consists of: *puraścaraṇa*, recitation (*japa*), fire-offering (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and feeding the Brahmins (*brahmaṇabhojana*).
But in the case of devouring and so forth:
Based on the force of the syntactic unity of such passages as "beginning from sunrise until the next sunrise," the term *puraścaraṇa* is understood to denote recitation (*japa*) alone.
If it is asked, "How is there the contingency of [the need for] oblations and so forth?"
Until then, at the conclusion of the eclipse, a pure man should perform duties superior even to a sacrifice.
Because of this statement.
Nor [is it so] because the *puraścaraṇa* indicates five constituent parts (*pañcāṅga*).
Or else, it must be stated that everything would possess the capacity to convey [the meaning];
in this case, there would be the consequence of the loss of the distinctness of the words at the end of the compound.

The procedure for *grahaṇa* (eclipse) and *puraścaraṇa* is intended to demonstrate their equality with the primary rite; it is not meant to imply that one lacks the qualification for liberation if these two are performed as mere five-limbed rites (*pañcāṅga*). Therefore, if those two are not performed, one has the qualification through a *puraścaraṇa* consisting solely of the limb of recitation (*japa*).
The doctrine established by all people.
Or else, one attains supreme perfection through the heroic practice (*vīrasādhana*) in a cremation ground.

Having gathered the previously mentioned substances and seated oneself in the cremation ground, one should perform all the ritual placements (nyāsa) and so forth, as before, for the sake of protection.
One should worship around the seat, starting from the west, then from the north, then from the northeast, and then from the east.
One should offer oblations of black gram rice (*māṣa-bhakta*) to the one named Kārabhairava, known as Mahābhairava, and to the two Bhairavas, Vaṭu and Bhairava. (9.381)
Then, one should worship the deity before oneself with the fivefold offering;
thereafter, with eyes closed, one should meditate upon the god and recite the mantra.
If there is danger from a strung bow, one should bind the eyes and ears with a cloth;
or, if there is danger from the discharge of missiles, one should maintain composure regarding the eyes or the ears.
Then, if nothing whatsoever is obtained until the end of midnight—
Having offered the arghya water to Jayadurgā, one should not scatter mustard seeds at all.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ Durge Durge Rakṣaṇī Svāhā.
Having lifted up the right foot and then gone seven steps, || 9-384 ||
Having worshipped the deity there as well, one should mutter the excellent mantra;
one should continue to mutter it fearlessly until success is attained by the person.
Then, having caused him to swear an oath of truth, one should request the supreme boon:
"If the god grants it, whether it be a multitude of men or even a single man... (9.386)
"But on another day I shall give [it]"; having accepted this, he should go to his own home.
On the following day, as before, he should give human figures made of flour. (9.387)
The best of practitioners should arrange everything else as before;
alternatively, the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) is desired in another manner.
Regarding the eclipse, it is of either the moon or the sun; as for the location, it is in a river flowing toward the ocean, and so forth, as previously stated.
Or one should recite the mantra twice as many times; the remainder should be performed as before.
At its conclusion, for the sake of attaining perfection in the mantra, one should worship and honor the Guru.
From that, the accomplishment of the mantra will arise and the deity will be pleased;
or else, one should propitiate the Guru, who is the very form of the deity, with devotion. (9.390)
Even one who is devoid of the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) will undoubtedly achieve success in the mantra;
now I shall describe the ritual application (prayoga) of the rite of preliminary practice.

On the previous day, having eaten a single meal free from meat, on the following day one should go to a river or similar body of water, perform bathing and other rites, emerge from the water, put on two washed garments, and, having sipped water (ācamana), [resolve]: "For the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa* of the mantra of the syllables of the venerable deity [Name],..."
"I have taken this ground; may this mantra be accomplished.

Having spoken thus, one should go as desired from the village or the city to a distance of one *krośa* or two *krośas* toward rivers, mountains, and so forth, and select a site suitable for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*).

Taking eleven or six stakes made from milky trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) measuring one *vitasti* in length, and having consecrated each one individually with the Weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) either eleven or six times, and having worshipped the Weapon [mantra] within them, he should worship the Guardian of the Field (*kṣetrapāla*) in the center of the seized field and offer him an oblation (*bali*) of black gram and cooked rice.
As for the mantra of Kṣetrapāla: the Brāhma-ṛṣi is the seer, Gāyatrī is the meter, Kṣetrapāla is the deity, and the application is for the purpose of protecting the preliminary ritual (puraścaraṇa).

Having thus performed the *karanyāsa* and *aṅganyāsa*, and having worshipped the *pīṭha-śaktis*— namely Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavīkaraṇī, Balapramathanī, Sarvabhūtadamanī, and Manonmanī— within the *pīṭha* starting from the east and so forth, as well as in the center.
"Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One; salutation to the one who is the self of all qualities and endowed with power, the vehicle, the protector, and the essence of the yoga-seat.
Having thus worshipped the seat, one should meditate.
For example:
With hair standing erect like a mountain of blue collyrium,
possessing round and fierce eyes, he held a skull and a trident in his hands.
I bow down to the God whose garment is the sky, whose ornaments are lofty, whose fangs are most formidable, and whose wondrous body pervades the field.
Having meditated thus.
One should worship with incense and other offerings, reciting: "Oṃ kṣī kṣaḥ, obeisance to Kṣattrapāla."
One should worship the limbs upon the filaments.

One should not worship [the deity] on leaves, nor when the wind or fire is present, nor during the time of the *kalā* (sixteenth digit of the moon), nor at the sound of a bell, nor during great anger, nor when there is flesh, nor when the eyes are tawny, nor when the hair stands erect.
One should worship Indra and the others outside of that, as well as their weapons.

Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should offer a large ball of black gram rice (*māṣabhakta*) along with side dishes into that skull-bowl (*karaka-pātra*), saying: "Salutation to Trapālā together with his retinue. This offering of black gram rice is called *vṛhatpiṇḍa*.
Then one should offer an oblation in the eight directions with this [mantra].
Those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce places;
the Mothers of foremost form, and those who are the lords of the hosts.

"Likewise, others who have become obstacles and who dwell in the cardinal and intermediate directions—may they all, with delighted minds, accept this offering out of affection. Thus one should offer the bali-oblation in the eight directions.
Then, having taken possession of the field, one should go to its eastern boundary and, proceeding in order starting from the east, drive stakes into the eight directions with the following [mantra].
And those who create obstacles here, whether dwelling in heaven, on earth, or in the intermediate space; || 9-394 ||
And whatever others have become obstacles to the success of my mantra, I have driven that host far away and pinned them down with stakes. (9.395)
Reciting, "May you all depart; may there be success for me without obstacle," he should plant the stakes in the eight directions.
Then, upon those stakes, starting from the east in due order, he should invoke Indra and the other deities with their respective names and mantras, using clarified butter as the offering.

Having worshipped him, one should offer an oblation of black gram and rice with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Indra," and so forth, offering the black gram and rice oblations in the sequence starting from the east.
On the third day prior to the commencement of the practice (*puvāla*), having eaten *haviṣyānna* once,

and having bathed on the following morning, one should perform the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of ten thousand recitations (*ayuta*) of the *Gāyatrī* mantra for the sake of destroying the sins known and unknown that obstruct the attainment of the mantra; thereafter, [one may proceed with] the meal.
Having satisfied the Brahmins with gifts such as clothing and ornaments, having honored the Guru with many garments and decorations,
and having made him well-pleased, one should receive his permission; on that day, eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should sleep at night upon a bed of Kuśa grass.
Then, in the absence of the guru, one should receive the guru’s command through the mind alone.

Then, having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, performed his morning duties, bathed, and completed his daily rites, he should go to the door of the hut, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), bow to the guardians of the directions, and facing east, take up sesame seeds, *kuśa* grass, and water, [reciting]: "Oṃ, today... and so forth, [followed by] "I, of such-and-such lineage, the illustrious..."

O [Name] Śarman, for the sake of the deity [Name], desiring the perfection (*siddhi*) of this syllable-mantra (*akṣaramantra*), beginning from today, whatever number of recitations (*japa*) have been performed of this [specific] mantra, one-tenth of that [number] is the *homam* (fire-oblation) using that mantra as the instrument; one-tenth of that is the libation (*tarpaṇa*) using that mantra as the instrument; and one-tenth of that libation is the [final] offering.
I shall perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) consisting of feeding Brahmins to the extent of one-tenth of the number of mantra-recitations performed during the consecration ceremony.

According to some, the specific distinction is that for every ten recitations (*japa*), there is no fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), or ritual purification (*mārjana*); instead, there is the additional practice of meditating upon the deity in place of feeding a Brāhmaṇa.

Where the specific number for the fire-oblation and so forth is explicitly stated, it shall be performed exactly as specified; however, where no specific number is mentioned, the number shall be eight thousand.
And so it has been said in the Vārāhītantra:
For those [mantras] for which no number has been prescribed by the wise regarding recitation (japa) and burnt offering (homa), [the following applies].
One should count eight thousand of these for the recitation and the fire-oblation;
one should offer eight thousand oblations during the performance of the *lakṣayāga*—so reads the text on the northern petal.
111b) This has been stated in the *Pūrṇāpaddhati*:
When no specific number is mentioned for recitations and the like, one hundred or one thousand and eight [repetitions] are prescribed.
With palms joined in reverence.

For this particular mother [mantra], the Ṛṣi is so-and-so, the Chandas is so-and-so, the Devatā is so-and-so, the Bīja is so-and-so, and the Śakti is so-and-so; its application is in the recitation for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
Thus, one should perform [the rite] with kuśa grass, unbroken rice, and water immediately after the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).

Then, having prepared the general *arghya* near the hut and worshipped the deity of the door, he enters the house; having sprinkled the interior with the *arghya* water, he spreads out a seat of red woolen cloth (*raktakaṃvala*) and sits upon it,
[visualizing] the presence of Śiva, or of Agni, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, or the Guru.

Having arranged the proximity of a lamp and placed four full water-jars in the fire-corners of the pedestal, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Sarasvatī, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla within them in sequence; then, having worshipped the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) according to the prescribed method, [one proceeds] until the end of the fire-oblation (homa).
Having completed the ritual action, one should offer the bali-oblation.
Namely, having recited "those who are fierce and perform fierce deeds," one should offer the bali-oblation to the eight directions and then present the bali-oblation to the spirits (bhūta).
As follows:
The beings who dwell upon the earth, having received the offering duly presented according to the ritual, [are satisfied].
May all attain contentment and forgive me for these [faults]; salutations to them!

Then, having completed the worship, having smelled the flower and placed it upon the heart, having propitiated the deity with mental offerings, having performed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs, and having performed three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
one should recite [the mantra] according to one's capacity.
Having understood the ear, mouth, heart, and eyes of the mantra, one should recite it.
This has been stated in the Viśuddheśvaratantra:
The Praṇava is the ear of the mantra, and the letter *repha* is proclaimed to be its mouth;
the vowels are to be known as its two eyes by those who know the mantra immediately thereafter. (9.398)
Furthermore, those syllables that are in excess are proclaimed to be the heart.
[The author] now states the place for recitation:
A field of merit, the bank of a river, a cave, and the summit of a mountain.
Sacred sites, the confluence of rivers, a forest of *pavana* trees, secluded gardens, the foot of a *bilva* tree, and the slope of a mountain. (9.400)
A grove of Tulasī, a cow-pen, a temple of Śiva devoid of bulls, the roots of an Aśvattha or Āmalakī tree, a cow-shed, and the midst of water [are auspicious]. (9.401)
A temple of the deities, one’s own family, the ocean as one’s natural home, the presence of spiritual teachers, and likewise a place for single-pointed concentration of the mind. (9.402)
And one should recite this in the morning, beginning with the Kāma-bīja "Kaṃ."
Page 112 is missing.
113a) Having also placed the *śrībīja*, one should recite the mantra for the sake of accomplishment.
*Hṛllekhā* is *hrīḥ*; the *kāmabīja* is *klīṃ*.
The seed-syllable of Śrī is Śrīṃ.
Having placed the three seed-syllables *hrīḥ*, *klīḥ*, and *śrīḥ* at the beginning of the mantra, one should recite it.
Or, when encapsulated by the *tāra* mantra, even a wicked mantra becomes effective.
"Tāra" is "praṇava," according to the Saṃhitā.
Now follows the abandonment of hostile mantras.
Having become pure and composed, on an auspicious day, the preeminent instructor should undertake the ritual for the sake of destroying all suffering without exception. (9.404)
First, having established the ritual jar (kumbha) in the temple according to the sequence of the initiation rite,
the wise one should place it within the mandala and fill it with auspicious waters.
Having invoked the deity there by reciting the mantra in reverse order,
and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and withdrawn the eight-limbed enclosure, one should perform worship.

In this manner, having offered oblations with clarified butter even from a cow, the twice-born practitioner of mantra should worship the deity of the mantra along with its covering, using the mantra in reverse order. (9.407)
Then, one should offer oblations (bali) to the deities with unhusked grains as prescribed,
both in the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions, according to the sequences of mantras that will be described.
Come, O Indra, sovereign of the gods, lord of Śacī, you of a hundred sacrifices!
Salutations to you; accept from me this offering of flowers, incense, and the like.
O Lord of splendors, O best of fire-givers, come indeed! Accept these flowers, incense, and other offerings, well-honored as this oblation.
O you who are equal to the Aitareya king and possess a luster like that of crushed collyrium, accept this offering given by me; being well-pleased, be a granter of boons.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the Rakṣasas, Nirṛti; you have come here.
Accept this offering, worship, and other gifts presented by me with devotion.
Come, O Guardian of the Western Quarter, obeisance to you, Lord of the Waters!
Accepting this worship offered with devotion, may you find satisfaction. (9.413)
O Wind, Lord of Life, come here with your retinue;
accept with respect this offering duly presented by me.
"O Kuvera and Tārakādhīśa, best of gods, come here;
being pleased by flowers, incense, and other offerings, become granters of boons to me. (9.415)
O Lord, refuge of all sciences, O Sovereign! You alone, when worshipped with flowers, incense, and other offerings, become pleased for the sake of prosperity.
O Brahmā, Lord of all beings, please accept this worship;
may you turn back all my obstacles—salutations to you! (9.417)
Come, O bestower of boons, O Viṣṇu, leader of the universe;
worshipped with supreme devotion, may you be the giver of happiness to me. (9.418)
Then, one should worship the deity of the mantra along with its retinue using flowers, lamps, and other offerings, employing the mantra in reverse order.
Then the wise one, having considered what is favorable along with me, Valabuddhi, should pray to the worshiped deity of the mantra. (9.420b)
O Lord, since this vessel has been honored and you have assumed the form of a mantra,
by that means, completely dispel the agitation of my mind.
May my evil be destroyed and may eternal welfare increase evermore;
therefore, let there be auspiciousness for me through your supreme devotion alone.
Having thus made this prayer to the Lord of Mantras, one should write the mantra in reverse order upon a leaf and worship it with *āmalaka*, camphor, and sandalwood.
Having placed it upon the water-pot (kalaśa) endowed with supreme devotion,
the wise man should thereafter bind that leaf to his own head.
One should bathe with the auspicious waters contained in the consecrated pitcher, which consist of mantras;
then, being self-restrained, one should fill the pitcher again with other water.
Having placed the mantra-leaf in the middle of that, one should then worship it;
one should cast that pitcher into a riverbank, a sacred ford, or a body of water.
Beyond that, having consulted with the Brahmins, he should feed them according to his capacity;
for even a malevolent mantra, when merely contemplated, does not bear fruit unless it is established in its proper place.

For the practitioner who has performed the ritual procedures in this manner, in due order, the pliancy of the mind certainly arises; there is no doubt. Through that sequence, one becomes intensely accomplished and proceeds through one's own lineage in succession.
Thus ends the procedure for abandoning the *āri* mantras.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Āgamakalpalatā*, composed by the illustrious Yadunāthacakravartin.
Salutations to Śrī Rāma!
I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra according to all the tantras, by the recitation of which all practitioners shall obtain their desired fruit. (10.1)
In this regard, first of all, I shall set forth the mantra of Śrī Raghunātha, which accomplishes all human goals, beginning with dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
And so it is said in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
"I salute Vināyaka, the best of the Raghus, whose hands are intent upon exposition, and who is surrounded by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva. (10.2)
To Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa, his preceptor and son of Satyavatī—
the sage established in meditative absorption, tranquil, and possessing the radiant splendor of the sun— (10.3).
Having prostrated with the eight limbs of his body, Śaunaka questioned that treasure of asceticism who was seated on the highly meritorious bank of the Gaṅgā.
Śrī Śaunaka said:
O lady, make your face gracious; make my mind joyful.
By your grace, many great mantras have been performed by me.
With eyes filled with the essence of compassion, I beheld the Self, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, the eternal Brahman—thus I have come to know it. (10.6)
I wish to hear the mantra of Viṣṇu, who possesses immeasurable splendor and has descended as the soul of Rāma, together with its ancillary rites and the method of worship. (10.7)
Tell me, O Blessed One, everything if I am worthy to hear it, concerning that by which the world is afflicted with misfortune and poverty. (10.8)
By means of which a man may obtain incomparable good fortune, the arising of great sovereignty, knowledge of the scriptures, poetic talent, and omniscience. (10.9)
Śrī Vyāsa said:
Well asked by you, O Brahmin;
I shall relate it all to you—just as it was previously told by Brahmā to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha also bestowed the Manu upon my father, his own grandson;
my father was pure, compassionate, and possessed of a devoted heart. (10–11)
On the highly meritorious occasion at Kurukṣetra, he gave [it] as a gift.
And by me this mantra has been accomplished through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth;
previously, O messenger, this king of mantras was not spoken by me to anyone.
Thus, having been transmitted from one to another, listen with devotion to this mantra from me;
O Sage, this king of mantras must not be given by you to one who is unworthy.
And you must protect with effort this secret which bestows prosperity and renown;
[do not give it] to one who is lazy, impure, afflicted, or possessed of hypocrisy and greed. (10.14)
One who is impoverished, diseased, angry, lustful, craving for enjoyments, seized by envy and malice, deceitful, and harsh of speech; || 10-15 ||
One who has acquired wealth through unjust means, who is always devoted to the wives of others,
who is an eternal enemy of the learned, who is ignorant yet considers himself a scholar— (10.16)

One who has fallen from his vows, who follows a wicked livelihood, who is a slanderer, evil-minded, gluttonous, cruel in conduct, and a preeminent person of wicked soul—[should not be honored]. (10.17)
One should designate as a disciple one who is free from these defects;
for if one were to accept someone possessing such a defect, it would affect even the preceptor. (10.18)
Just as the fault of a minister reaches the king, and the fault of a wife reaches the husband, so too does a fault committed by a disciple certainly reach the teacher. (10.19)
Therefore, a teacher should always accept a disciple only after examining him, [specifically one] who is devoted to serving the teacher in body, mind, and speech. (10.20)
He was of a non-stealing disposition, possessed of faith, always making effort toward liberation,
constantly devoted to celibacy, firm in the vow of truth, and stainless.
One whose heart is steadfast, pure, and free from deceit, who is devoid of arrogance, devoted to helping others, and free from longing for the sake of another. (10.22)
One should bestow the mantra upon such a disciple who brings complete satisfaction to the Guru with his heart, wealth, and body, and not otherwise.
If one should speak otherwise regarding him, the deity would become a giver of a curse.
O Mādhava, whatever devotion one has for another, such [devotion] should be shown toward one's own guru. 10.24b–25a.
He states the extraction of the mantra:
Having extracted this splendor— which ends with the letter *ma*, is joined with the bindu, and is adorned by Nārāyaṇa— one should then again [extract] that same [splendor] devoid of the bindu.

The letter *m* ending in *mānta* (the letter *ma*) is "water-maker" (*toyakāra*). In that [letter], the letter *ta* is the *repha* (the letter *ra*). The *bindu* is the *anusvāra*; that joined with it is Nārāyaṇa, the letter *a*.
That joined with *te* is *narām*. Again, that is the single-syllable seed-mantra (*ekākṣarabīja*) without the *bindu*.
Furthermore, that is *itirām*; one should remove the *bindu* from this seed-mantra.
And so it is said:
It becomes "rā," and likewise it becomes "rāṃ rā."
One should extract the letter *mā* joined with the vowel *ā*; "the letter *bhā* joined with the vowel *ā*" refers to the letter *ma* joined with *ā*. (10-26)

"Ākārasaṃyuktaṃ te namā iti bhavati māntāntati muddharediti": that which ends with the letter *m* (i.e., *namaḥ*) should be extracted as "te namā. Thus, one should provide "namā" for that which ends with the letter *y*. And so it is said:
Oṃ rāṃ, obeisance to Rāma.
Thus is the mantra.
This six-syllabled mantra bestows all sovereignty, generates all good fortune, and brings all the worlds under one's control. (10.27)
O Sage, it bestows knowledge and accomplishment upon men and carries out great commands;
Brahmā is said to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra, and its meter (chanda) is Gāyatrī. (10.28)
The Vaiṣṇava abode known as Rāma is proclaimed to be the deity;
one should know the first syllable as the seed (bīja), the power (śakti), and likewise the salutation (nati).
The heart mantra is not proclaimed in the pair of fire-seeds (RAUṂ),
nor is the head mantra likewise stated in the fourth.
The wise know that very mantra joined with the vowel *ra* (rasa) as Śivā;
joined with the vowel *ri* (ravi), they know it to be the armor (*kavaca*). || 10-31 ||
The mantra for the eyes is fourteen [syllables] joined with the visarga;
these aforementioned mantras for the limbs and fingers are to be applied on the two joints.
Having placed [the syllables] on those two palms, one should place them upon the heart and other limbs;
or else, one should perform the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅga) using the individual letters of the root mantra.
The knower of mantras should perform the placement of the syllables (akṣaranyāsa) of the root mantra in the following locations:
the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), between the eyebrows, the heart, the arms, and the secret place. (10.34)
Having placed [the mind] upon the two feet, O Sage, one should cultivate meditative absorption;
one should cultivate devotion within the foundation (ādhāra), which consists of the bliss of awakening and one's own true nature.
O best of sages, one should thus conceive of the visualization of the support (ādhāra) as being like the rising sun and consisting of its radiance. (10.36)
Then, from that [state], there arose a form consisting of consciousness in the shape of a crest of flame—
resembling ten million flashes of lightning and yet as cool as ten million moons.
Having opened the mouth of the *suṣumṇā* through this instruction, one should lead [the breath] upward by way of the path of Brahman to the lunar orb at the *dvādaśānta*. (10.38)
With the intellect, one should [conceive] that nectar of immortality according to the procedure for prāyaścitta;
then, it is enveloped by streams of pure nectar flowing forth from it.
One should contemplate one's own body and the entire universe as having become one—
devoid of phenomenal elaboration, formless, faultless, and stainless.
O best of sages, one should meditate upon the Self as the emptiness of emptiness, supreme, devoid of both existence and non-existence, and consisting of indivisible bliss. 10.41
The practitioner of mantra should contemplate the identity of himself with the deity, the guru, and the mother;
reflecting thus, he should recite the mantra every day. (10.42)
Having enjoyed all worldly enjoyments and reached the end [of his life], he shall go to the supreme state;
or else, having withdrawn that splendor into the lotus of his heart.
One should meditate upon the Name, which consists of light, the sole witness of all worlds,
and Hari, who brings about the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe.
Meditation is served by the lords of gods, asuras, and sages, as well as by hosts of yogis,
just as follows.
Oṃ, [I salute Him] who has four arms and who holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
Having thus meditated upon [the deity] adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, gems, and earrings, one should recite the mantra six thousand times day after day.
O Sage, having become the Lord of the Splendor of Speech and having become a poet, he went to the foot of the Kalpa tree and reached a golden pavilion within a year.
In the midst of that was a divine and supreme celestial chariot named Puṣpaka;
in its center was a lion-throne adorned with various sounds.
In its center is an eight-petaled lotus resembling the rising sun; O great sage, Śrī Rāma is seated within it, equal in extent to that [lotus].
Holding the seal of perfect knowledge (samyak-jñāna-mudrā) in his right hand, he displays the gesture of victory (jaya-prakāśana) with his left knee and the other [hand] upon his head. (10.50)
The Lord who is the beloved of Jānakī, possessing a splendor like that of a blue sapphire,
the God devoted to the forest retreat, the two-armed joy of the Raghus.
He was surrounded by sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva,
with Sītā, who resembled gold, seated on his left side.
To those who worship her, she eternally grants their desires; she holds a red lotus in her hand, and at her western side stands Lakṣmaṇa, holding a parasol for the gods and immortals.
On his two sides are Bharata and Śatrughna, both holding palm-leaf fans;
having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra, for such a person becomes a vessel for the goal of knowledge.
O Sage, for wise practitioners who recite this mantra through the yoga of recitation, mastery of the scriptures and poetic skill arise within six months. (10.55)
A mantra yields its fruit even without the performance of *puraścaraṇa* rites;
having thus accomplished the mantra of Rāghava, the Supreme Person. (10.56)
115b) There, one should perform worship externally upon the Vaiṣṇava seat (pīṭha) that has been described.
This is stated in the Gautamīya:
Worship is said to be fivefold; hear now their various divisions from me.
Approaching, taking up [the materials], union, and likewise private recitation—these five modes of worship I shall now describe in sequence. (10.58)
In that context, "approaching" (abhigamana) consists of cleansing the deity's place, smearing it with unguents, and removing the faded floral offerings. (10.59)
Upādāna is the gathering of names, perfumes, flowers, and so forth; likewise, yoga is the contemplation of one's own deity as being identical with the Self.

Svādhyāya consists of the recitation of mantras, meditative contemplation, worship, and the chanting of japa; it also includes the recitation of sūktas, hymns, and the like, as well as the communal chanting of the names of Hari. (10.61)
The practice of the scriptures concerning reality and so forth is proclaimed as *svādhyāya* (self-study);
thus is the worship of one's own deity according to its true meaning. (10.62)
Thus, O lady of excellent vows, five types have been described to you:
Sārṣṭi, Sāyujya, Sāmīpya, and Sālokya, in that order. (10.63)
Now, the Great Yantra in the form of the descendant of Raghu is described;
it bestows good fortune, brings about subjugation, and is supreme in destroying enemies.

This mantra-yoga is declared to be a yantra consisting of mantra that bestows long life and health upon men and wards off the fevers caused by the planets; for the deity is of the very nature of the mantra. (10.65)
Long ago, it was proclaimed by the Blessed One in the tantra called Sammohana:
"Just as there is a distinction between the body and the self, so too is there a distinction between the mantra and the deity. (10.66)
Therefore, having written the great mantra upon the pedestal, one should worship there;
for without a yantra, the worship does not please the deity. (10.67)
Next, I shall describe the form of the yantra as shown by my own guru:
having first drawn a hexagon, one should draw a circle in front of it. (10.68)
Having thus drawn an outer eight-petaled lotus and below it the terrestrial mandala— a beautiful, distinct, and radiant mandala— (10.69).
Having written this great mantra upon this yantra, one should worship it there;
within the hexagon, one should write the seed-syllable containing the name of the person to be acted upon and the ritual purpose. (10.70)
One should surround that seed with the Manmatha seed;
then, one should surround that Manmatha with the letters of the mind (manas) which are not distinct [from it].
One should again encircle all of that with the ten-syllable mantra;
furthermore, one should assign the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) to the six corners beginning with the southeast.
One should write "Oṃ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ" on the sides of the hexagon;
then the seed-syllable *Ī* at the tips of the corners, and the vowels in sequence upon the filaments. (10.73)
Then, the knower of the seven mantras should place the garland of mind-syllables upon the eight petals starting from the east, numbering them according to the count of logic (six).
One should draw the remaining five colors on the eighth petal; one should encircle all of that in a circular form with the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*.

O Sage, one should subsequently write two seed-syllables within the earth-palace (bhūgṛha), as well as in the cardinal and intermediate directions: the great seed-syllable of Nārasiṃha and that of Vārāha, in due order.
Having invoked the son of Indrāṇī into this yantra, worship him—the one with a gracious countenance, the peaceful one, the bestower of benefits in this world and the next. (10.77)
Having extracted the fifth *prapañca* in reverse order and ending with *cara*,
joined with the *śānti* and the *bindu*, it is declared to be the *kāmabīja*.
