Having first uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), then the word "Jānakī," and again "to the beloved" (*vallabhāya*), one should extract the mantra ending with *svāhā*. (10.79)
This ten-syllable mantra bestows all accomplishments;
having first uttered the word "Oṃ namaḥ," one then says the word "Bhagavate. (10.80)
Having uttered the first word, "To the Joy of the Raghus," the best of mantra-knowers should then extract the fourth word, "To the Destroyer of Rākṣasas and Poison."
To her whose face has a sweet and gentle smile, one should say the word "valāya" for Amitatejas, and likewise say "rāmāya" thereafter. 10-82.
Having addressed Viṣṇu with the word "pada," one should extract the mantra ending with "namaḥ.
This is declared to be the mental garland-mantra (mālāmantra) consisting of forty-seven syllables.
O Sage, the letter *e* born from the letters *kṣa* and *ra*, adorned with the *bindu*, is the great mantra of Nārasiṃha, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree for those who recite it. (10.84)
The letter *ha* joined with the fifth vowel and adorned with the *bindu*;
the letter *ha* joined with the sixth vowel and adorned with the *bindu*. (10.85)
The seed-syllable of Varāha is said to bestow fortune, wealth, and the earth;
its subterranean abode should be square and adorned with eight vajras. (10.86)
Having drawn this yantra on a golden or silver plate, or having properly drawn it on birch bark and formed it into a ball, one should wear it. (10.87)
A sonless man obtains a son, and one without wealth shall attain riches; what need is there for much speaking here? It bestows all perfections upon men. (10.88)
This yantra is of great merit; by wearing it, one is cleansed of sins.
Having invoked Rāma into this yantra, one should worship him in due order.
One should worship Maṇḍūka and the others ending with Pṛthivī in sequence upon the pericarp;
one should worship Agni and the others on the legs of the pedestal, and the four beginning with Dharma.
One should worship all the [deities] starting from the east in their proper sequence;
likewise, one should then fully worship Ananta and the lotus in the pericarp.
It is enriched by the three mandalas of the sun, fire, and moon, distinguished by the color white;
it consists of the three qualities beginning with sattva, and from that, the fourfold self.
From the cognition of the self as distinct from the self and the supreme self, and by means of the self, there arise for you the [stages] Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and the fifth, Yogā. (10.93)
One should install Prahvī, Satyā, Tathā, Īśānā, Anugrahā, and the ninth, Parā,
in sequence upon the eight petals starting from the east and on the pericarp.

Then, the knower of mantras should worship in the pericarp with the fourth [syllable] joined with *namaḥ*, using each of their own respective names, and subsequently with the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*).
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then say the word "namaḥ";
having addressed the word "bhagavate," one should then say the word "viṣṇave."
And [one should offer] to the Self of all beings, and also to Vāsudeva;
thereafter, [one should say]: "Salutation to the one who is the union of all selves, the essence of the Yoga-pīṭha."
If one should again offer a handful of flowers in the center with this mantra, having thus worshipped the pedestal, one should invoke the deity and worship him. (10.98)
Having performed the ritual services beginning with the water of honor (argha) and ending with the lamp and incense,
one should then request permission from the Lord of Gods and worship his retinue.
In the centers of the six preceding triangles, one should worship the six [limbs] beginning with the Heart in sequence;
then, one should worship Sītā seated on his left side with that mantra.
Having first uttered the seed-syllable of Śrī, one should extract the word *sītā* followed by the wife of Vahni; this mantra is a wish-fulfilling tree for those who worship it. (10.101)
Janaka is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be its metre (chanda).
The deity is the one named Sītā, the sustainer of the world, who is Śrī, whose nature is the entire universe. (10.102)
In front of the deity, on the left and right sides, [one should place] arrows;
then, upon an eight-petaled lotus, [one should place] Hanumān and the reciter (vācaka).
In front of the God sits the learned one holding a book;
on the eastern petal is Sugrīva, on the fire-petal (southeast) is Agni, and on the southern petal is Maruta.
And Vibhīṣaṇa in the southwestern petal, Lakṣmaṇa in the western petal, Agada in the northwestern petal, and Śatrughna in the northern petal. (10.105)
In the northeast, one should worship Jambavanta as the second in the enclosure;
one should perform the bath and worship with their respective names, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Sṛṣṭi, Jayanta-vijaya, Surāṣṭra, Rāṣṭravardhana, Akopa, Dharmapāla, and Sumantra is considered the eighth.
Thus, one should worship the eight ministers in the third enclosure;
one should worship the guardians of the directions, beginning with Ananta, in the ten directions in due order.
The ten [directions], beginning with Indra and ending with Ananta.
By high-souled sages such as Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva,
and by others such as Nala and Nīla, who were divine beings in human form.
The Lord of Gods was seated with his retinue, each announcing their own name, while being attended by sages such as Nārada and others.
Thus, having propitiated the joy of the Raghus along with his retinue with divine perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and unbroken grains of rice; 10.111.
Having worshipped with devotion according to the prescribed rules, he should offer the food oblation (naivedya);
having displayed all the royal services of honor, the great sage [should proceed].
Having praised [the deity] correctly, the practitioner, endowed with devotion, should prostrate;
thereafter, he should withdraw the deity, together with the retinue, into his own heart.
O best of sages, the identity of the self and the deity is to be contemplated;
having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should then conclude the ritual worship.
Acting thus every day, one will certainly have fulfilled all that is to be done;
the wise person should move about, constantly perceiving the Self as Rāma. (10.115)
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the rule for the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa):
one should subsist on alms, or eat sacrificial food fit for oblation, or consume rice-milk, vegetables, and barley-gruel.
When the Lord faces westward, in a temple of Śiva that is utterly empty,
on the bank of a river flowing to the ocean, in a cow-pen, or in the presence of cows, O Sage.

At the root of an Aśvattha or Bilva tree, on the bank of the Indus, at a reservoir of water, on a mountain peak, or in an eighth sacred place, the practitioner of mantra should perform the recitation.

One should recite the mantra one million six hundred thousand times (ṣaṭlakṣa) and perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that. "One million six hundred thousand" (tarkalakṣa) means six hundred thousand.
With the fruits, flowers, and leaves of the vitva tree, combined with the three sweets (trimadhu).
One should perform a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth [of the recitation]; then it will become perfected.
When the mantra has been thus perfected through the preliminary rites and other means, one should accomplish the ritual actions.
A person should offer oblations with *jāti* flowers mixed with sandalwood water for the subjugation of kings;
with lotuses for the subjugation of kings; and with grains for the attainment of wealth.
Indirā-Lakṣmī.
By performing a fire sacrifice with *durvā* grass, the practitioner shall become long-lived and free from disease.
By offering red lotuses, the practitioner of mantra obtains his desired wealth;
those desiring intelligence should offer palāśa flowers.
A wise person who drinks water consecrated with that mantra becomes a poet within a year;
by eating food consecrated with that mantra, one shall attain great health.
One should not offer oblations with the three kinds of honey or with milk-rice;
rather, one should perform them with *asadṛśa* (the "unlike") ghee, for by means of this knowledge, one becomes a master of the world.
But he who thus worships with devotion the Lord Rāghava, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and attended by Sītā, through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth— he,
having enjoyed all pleasures, shall attain that supreme state at the end. (10.125)
Enough with this dispute; he is superhuman, the slayer of the king of the rākṣasas in the form of Rāma.
Having abandoned his serpent-couch, Nārāyaṇa himself has descended to the surface of the earth.
Thus ends the Śrī Rāma-Ṣaḍakṣara-kalpa.
Now follows the extraction of the yantra.
Within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by a square, there is a hexagon;
in its center is the seed-syllable *rā*.
"In the center, make such-and-such [person] my glory."
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) together with the seed-syllable *klīm*,
one should encircle it with the seed-syllable of Manmatha within the six corners.
rā, rī, ru, rai, rau, raḥ.
Having thus written the six limbs.
Hrīḥ—thus for Koṇakapolā.
Having written "huḥ," the seed-syllable of Varāha, at the tips of the corners, one should write the sixteen vowels beginning with 'a' in pairs upon the filaments.
Then:
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the joy of the Raghus, the slayer of demons, the bestower of poison-remedy, whose face is radiant with a sweet smile;
salutations to Rāma, the Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor and strength.
Thus, having written six letters for each of the forty-seven syllables on the eight petals of the lotus, one should write five letters outside the lotus.
Having encircled it with the ten syllables "oṃ jānakīvallabhāya svāhā," one should then encircle it with the letters from 'ka' to 'kṣa'.

Then, one should write the *narasiṃha* seed-syllable "kṣauṃ" in the directions starting from the east of the square; the *varāha* seed-syllable "huṃ" in the corners starting from the southeast; and the eight *vajras* with the syllable "īṃ" in the eight directions of the earth-pavilion (*bhūgṛha*).
Thus ends this dhāraṇayantra of the illustrious Raghunātha;
and likewise in the Śāradātilaka:

The six-syllabled mantra for Rāma, beginning with *yam* and ending with *namaḥ*, preceded by the infinite seat (*anantāsanāya*) and the moon-seed (*sendu*), is declared to grant all desires to those who worship it. (10.127)
This is its meaning:

The letter *a* is Ananta; *ra* is Agni; likewise, *ra* joined with the letter *a* and joined with the Moon—the Moon being the *anusvāra*—becomes *rā*. Thus, having extracted the seed-syllable *carā*, one forms *rāṃ rāmāya namaḥ*.
Thus one should extract [the mantra].
And so it is said:
"Rāṃ rāmāya nāma"—this is the six-syllable mantra.
For this six-syllable mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrī Rāmacandra is the deity (devatā),
and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desired goals such as wealth.
RĀM, salutation to the heart.
Rī! Svāhā to the head!
RŪ / to the crest-lock, VAUṢAṬ.
RAI / to the armor, HŪM. RAU / to the two eyes, VAUṢAṬ.
*Raḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Thus is the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
After the ritual placement on the hands and limbs, follows the ritual placement of the syllables of the mantra.
RĀM at the aperture of Brahmā; RĀ between the eyebrows; MĀ in the heart; YĀ in the navel; NA in the generative organ; MA in the two feet.
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Yogā, Prasvī, and Satyā.
These are the sovereign powers of grace, the yellow energies.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, the self of all beings, Vāsudeva;
homage to the one whose self is the lotus-throne of the union with the self of all.
Thus ends the mantra of the seat (pīṭhamantra).

Oṃ! [I salute] Rāghava, who possesses a splendor like that of a dark rain cloud, who perpetually sits in the heroic posture (vīrāsana), who holds in one hand the mudrā consisting of primordial wisdom, while his other lotus-hand rests upon his knee;
and [I salute] Sītā, who stands by his side, holding a lotus in her hand and resembling a flash of lightning.
Beholding Him whose limbs are radiant with various ornaments such as crowns and armlets, I worship Him. || 10-128 ||
Thus concludes the section on meditation.
In the side [section] of the offering to the obstructions.
With the mantra "Śrīṃ sītāyai svāhā," [he offers] to Sītā.
In front, on the left and right sides, are Śārdūla and Rāma; outside of that, on the filaments (kesara) in the corners starting from the southeast, are the Heart, Head, Crest, and Armor mantras.
In front is the Eye, and in the cardinal directions is the Weapon mantra; [these are placed] on the petals of the deity’s lotus, beginning from the front petal and proceeding clockwise.
Hanumān, Sugrīva, Bharata, Vibhīṣaṇa, Lakṣmaṇa, Aṅgada, Śatrughna, and Jāmbavān.

On the tips of the petals starting from the front, [one should worship] Sṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Surāṣṭra, Rāṣṭravardhana, Akopa, Dharmapāla, and Sumantra; outside of that, the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Outside of that, one should worship those weapons as well.
Herein is the visualization of Hanumān and others.
One should worship Hanumān, who holds a book and recites [the scriptures], positioned at the front;
and Bharata and Śatrughna, who hold chowries, at the two sides. (10.129)
One should worship Lakṣmaṇa in the west with two hands holding a palm-leaf fan;
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform the ten-part oblation with auspicious lotuses.
One should offer oblations into the consecrated fire and also feed the Brahmins.
Thus ends the *Śrī Rāmacandra Pūjā-paddhati*.
Salutation to Śrī Rāma.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
Oṃ! O Blessed One, Lord of all gods, God of gods, salutations be unto you. (10.131)
O Lord, I have related everything to you regarding the specific mantra of Rāma;
the armor known as Trailokyamohana, which was previously indicated.
"Tell me, O Mahādeva, that secret which is dear to you.
Īśvara said:
"Listen, O Queen of the Gods; I shall speak of the most wonderful armor (kavaca)."
This is the secret protection, the hidden essence, the embodiment of the manifestation of the Brahma-mantra.

Oṃ. Of this Śrī Rāma-kavaca, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrī Rāmacandra is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is in the recitation for the attainment of the four aims of human life.
Oṃ! May the Praṇava, whose form is the Tāraka Brahman, protect my head.
The seat of Ananta, accompanied by the moon, is the single-syllable name "Rā";
"Oṃ Rāṃ Rāmāya Namaḥ" is the six-syllabled mantra that bestows both enjoyment and liberation. May Rāma, known as the two-syllabled name, protect my forehead and the pair of eyes. (10.135)
May *klīṃ*, the single-syllable mantra that deludes, protect my pair of ears;
may *klīṃ rāmāya namaḥ* protect my face. || 10.136 ||
Oṃ rāṃ rāmacandrāya svāhā—this eight-syllable mantra is for my two arms. "Śrīrāmāya namaḥ" is for the shoulders, as is "yastu kharāntakaḥ. (10.137)
"Śrī rāmacandrāya rakṣoghnāya namaḥ"—this twelve-syllable mantra [protects].
May He who is born of the Raghu dynasty protect my heart forever.
"Hrīḥ rāmacandrāya namaḥ"—may this protect the pair of my thighs.
"Śrīrāmabhadrāya svāhā"—this is the eight-syllable mantra for the navel. || 10.138 ||
Hlī! May he who ends with the two ṭha-syllables (ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ), the destroyer of the lord of Rākṣasas, who is constantly intent on Sītā and is the husband of Rāmabhadra, protect me forever. || 10.139 ||
May the eight-syllable mantra, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with "Rāmabhadra," protect my knees at all times—he who is the destroyer of the race of Rākṣasas. (10.140)
The eight-syllable mantra beginning with *praṇava* (om) and ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā), dedicated to Rāmabhadra and the destroyer of the race of demons, may it always protect my knees. (10.141)

The eight-syllable mantra, beginning with the Praṇava for Rāmabhadra and ending with the Dviṭha (Svāhā), may its pair of feet always protect you, bestowing the glory of sovereignty upon men. || 10.142 ||
"Hrīṃ! Salutations to the Lord of Sītā—may he always protect me from the east. Huṃ! To the Beloved of Jānakī—may the Lord always protect me from the south. (10.143)
"Klī! To Jānakīnātha"—with this, may he always protect me in the west; "Śrī! Obeisance to Raghunātha"—with this, may he protect my head in the northern direction. || 10.144 ||

One should utter "Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One," followed by the vocative case ending for the fourth [case], and address the Joy of the Raghus as the slayer of Rākṣasas who is coming to bestow poison; one should then pronounce the sweet [words] and so forth. (10.145)
To Prasannavadana, then to Amitatejas;
after that, to Bala, then to Rāma, and immediately thereafter to Viṣṇu. || 10.146 ||
This garland-mantra (mālāmantra), beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, has been proclaimed;
may he who is born of the Raghu lineage protect [you] always in the royal station.
Thus, O Goddess, I have related to you this armor (kavaca) named *Trailokyamaṅgala*, which embodies the entire flood of mantras and is of the nature of Brahman.
Whoever recites this at dawn shall obtain his desired fruit;
and the best of practitioners who recites this armor-mantra at the time of worship— || 10-149 ||
One certainly becomes increased in fame, fortune, beauty, intelligence, and longevity;
this is the armor (kavaca) consisting of the mantra of Rāma, which is Brahman itself, as proclaimed from the mouth of the Holy One.

Having worshipped the Guru according to the prescribed rule, he should then recite the armor-mantra (kavaca) either twice or once, as is appropriate; he too shall become the best among the meritorious.
Having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rules, one should perform the *puraścaryā* ritual;
having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should perform the fire-oblation (*havana*) and other rites consisting of one-tenth of that number.
Then, having perfected his armor, he shall accomplish all tasks;
through the performance of *puraścaryā* according to the prescribed rules, the mastery of the mantra will be attained for him. (10.153)
In whose mouth the speech consisting of prose and verse flows,
in his mouth dwells Sarasvatī, and Lakṣmī resides permanently in his home.
Having offered eight handfuls of flowers while reciting the root mantra just once,
one obtains the fruit of worship performed for even thousands of years.
If one writes [this] on birch bark and wears it placed in gold—
either around the neck or on the right arm— he shall make the world act like his servant.
He truly agitates the three worlds and becomes the conqueror of the three worlds;
having reached his body, even those weapons such as the Brahmāstra and others [become ineffective].
For indeed, garlands and flowers alone are the givers of happiness;
may prosperity dwell in your home and Sarasvatī reside in your mouth.
If one recites the Rāma-mantra without knowing this armor (kavaca),
then even if it has been recited seven hundred thousand times, that mantra will not grant success.
He shall suffer a wound from a weapon and shall meet his death before long.
Thus ends the armor (kavaca) named Trailokyamohana of Śrī Rāma, in the venerable Brahmayāmala Tantra, within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
The son of Śrī said:
Oṃ. Once, Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord were seated comfortably together. (10.160)
With their arms and hearts joined to one another, they were intent on protecting the world;
he, the supreme among the supreme, was served by Indra and the other guardians of the world.
Then Pārvatī inquired about the supreme dharmas.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, protector of the worlds, Great Lord of all the realms! (10.162)
Through your grace, I have learned the unsurpassed Dharmaśāstra;
I have heard the expiation for sins in their entirety and without exception. (10.163)
"You ought to speak of the expiation for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this great secret, more secret than the secret. (10.164)
Having prostrated before the Lord of the Gaṇas, who was seated in a secluded place, he [related] the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vighneśa that destroys all sins.
Sanatkumāra asked for the definitive determination of all dharmas.
Sanatkumāra said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, destroyer of all obstacles! (10.166)
"O Lord, you ought to tell me the atonement for the killing of Brahmins;
apart from you, there is no one in the three worlds who can speak of this dharma."
"Therefore, O Gaṇapati, grant me your abundant grace.
Śrī Vināyaka said: "O Brahmin, you have asked well; this is for the benefit of all the worlds. (10.168)
"O sinless one, you have reminded me of a deed I committed long ago.
In the past, I was born in the form of an elephant, as massive as a mountain. (10.169)
Having obtained the mantra from the tree, I began the slaughter of sages;
then, indeed, many hosts of sages were slain by me through force.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the Brahmins on all sides;
at that time, I was surrounded on every side by a thousand killings.
Seeing me unconscious and like one dead, O grandfather,
my lord [Bali] propitiated Rāma, the Lord of the worlds who dwells in the hearts of all.
He directly beheld the Lord, the joy of the Raghus, who acts for my welfare;
then the Blessed Śrī Rāma spoke to my father.
The Blessed Lord, whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, said: "I am pleased, O Mahādeva; what do you request from me, O Lord?"
"I shall grant whatever is desired, even that which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O Lord, this son of mine is possessed by the sin of killing a Brahmin. (10.175)
"O Lord of Gods, make me free from sin if you have compassion for me. Having spoken thus, I was then looked upon by him with compassion.
At that very moment, having regained consciousness and being nourished by stainless knowledge, I praised him with many prose and verse passages and bowed down before him. (10.177)
Then the Lord Rāma, whose resolve is ever true, spoke to me.
Śrī Rāma said:
"I shall tell you the expiation for a thousand killings of Brahmins."
"By reciting the thousand names, one is liberated from all sins";
thus Rāma gave his own secret *nāmasahasraka*.
It is the means for accomplishing all desired goals, such as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
therefore, by its mere acceptance, I am indeed at that very moment freed from sin.
Then, O best of sages, I shall be worthy of worship by all the gods;
and you too, by studying this [work] of the high-souled Rāghava, [shall attain that same status]. || 10.181 ||
"O Great-minded One, you have proclaimed the Thousand Names throughout the worlds.
Sanatkumāra said:
"I am blessed, I am favored, I have achieved my purpose, O Lord of the Gaṇas! (10.182)
"By your grace, I shall recite the Thousand Names of Rāma.
Śrī Mahādeva said: Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, and having circumambulated and prostrated before him... (10.183)
O fair-faced one, by constantly reciting this hymn from that time forward,
my son Vināyaka attained supreme perfection.
"Free from both merit and demerit, he shall attain sovereignty over the hosts.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear that which grants all desires. (10.185)
"Recite the thousand names of Rāma with devotion.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"Now, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the thousand names of Rāma."
And listen with a one-pointed mind to this great hymn, more secret than the secret.

Of this mantra of the *Śrīrāmasahasranāmamālā*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śrī Mahādeva, the meter (*chandas*) is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity (*devatā*) is Śrī Rāma, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). [This is recited] for the purpose of pleasing Śrī Rāma,
for the attainment of the fourfold aims of human life (*caturvidhapuruṣārtha*), and for the fulfillment of all desires.
The application (viniyoga) for the recitation of the Śrī Rāma Sahasranāma Stavarāja.
Then one should meditate upon Dhyāna, whose nature is Brahman, consisting of supreme nectar, served by the lords of the gods,
attended by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, wearing forest attire, and possessing the luster of a full-blown blue lotus.

[He meditated upon] the Lord of the Universe, whose form is the universe, who removes the fear of worldly existence, who shines with the brilliance of ten million suns, the descendant of Kakutstha, the Lord of Kosala, the burner of the weeds of impurity, holding the curved bow in his hand. (10.187)
Oṃ! The lotus-eyed, glorious Śrī Rāma, the bull among the Raghus;
Rāmabhadra, of virtuous conduct, the lord of kings, the husband of Jānakī. (10.188)
Foremost in the assembly, most excellent, the bestower of boons, the Supreme Lord;
Janārdana, who has conquered all enemies, whose sole purpose is the welfare of others. || 10.189 ||

The beloved and self-controlled friend of Viśvāmitra, the conqueror of enemies, the scorcher of his foes, the omniscient one, the progenitor of all the gods and others, the worthy refuge, and the crusher of Vālin.
He is to be distinguished by the enjoyment of knowledge, eloquent, devoted to truth, and pure;
he is accessible through wisdom, firm in intellect, a destroyer of the wicked, and majestic.
Resplendent, self-possessed, heroic, having conquered anger, the crusher of enemies;
possessing universal form, large-eyed, the Lord, the Sovereign, the steadfast one.
The Lord, the glorious wielder of the sword, O Kausalyā, is the one of noble birth; he is broad-shouldered and large-chested, the supreme abider, the ultimate refuge. || 10.193 ||
He is devoted to truth, faithful to his promises, the teacher, and supremely righteous;
he knows the worlds, is worshipped by the worlds, is the soul of the worlds, the creator of the worlds, and the Lord.
The Lord is beginningless and worthy of service; he has conquered death and is the best of the Raghus.
Rāma is compassionate, skillful, all-knowing, and the purifier of all. (10.195)
Hari is the source of the Brahman, the wise protector, beloved by all the gods;
he is beautiful, clad in yellow garments, the ancient author of the Sūtras.
The gentle great seer, wielder of the bow, all-pervading, and skilled in all things;
the poet, the bestower of boons upon Sugrīva, and the giver of that which exceeds all merit. || 10-197 ||

The fortunate one who has conquered the sixfold group of enemies, the most magnanimous destroyer of afflictions, possessed of excellent fame, the primordial person, the beloved, and the source of the scriptures composed by those who have performed meritorious deeds. (10.198)
Stainless, four-armed, invincible in all dwellings,
speaking with a smile, self-restrained, mindful, heroic, and powerful.
Dignified and self-controlled, dark as a rain cloud, skilled in all weapons, he is the abode of the yoga of the supreme self; he is the proud elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa. (10.200)
He consists of all holy fords, he is the hero, the bestower of the fruit of all sacrifices;
he is the embodiment of sacrifice, the Lord of sacrifice, and is devoid of old age and death.
The teacher of the castes and stages of life, the religious student, the conqueror of enemies, the Supreme Person, the installer of the Śiva-liṅga, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest. (10.202)
He who has become the means of valid knowledge, who is difficult to comprehend, who is full, the conqueror of the cities of others,
whose vision is infinite, who is bliss, the science of archery, and the wielder of the bow.
The mine of virtues, the most excellent quality, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
he of the great body who is to be saluted, the architect of the universe, the learned one.
He whose self is disciplined, who is free from passion, the ascetic, the lord of men, whose nature is entirely auspicious, the Lord of all, the bestower of all desires. || 10.205 ||
The imperishable Person, the Witness, Keśava, the Supreme Person;
the Overseer of the World, the Great-bodied One, the bestower of boons upon Vibhīṣaṇa. || 10-206 ||
The embodiment of bliss, light, the Lord Hanumān, the imperishable, the radiant, the victorious, the enjoyer, the speaker of truth, and the one of vast learning. || 10-207 ||
The giver of happiness, the cause, the agent, the liberator from the bonds of existence;
the crest-jewel of the gods, the leader, the friend of Brahman, and the increaser of Brahman.
Rāma is the savior from saṃsāra, the one who effects liberation from all suffering;
he is the most learned, the destroyer of the universe, the sustainer of the universe, and the creator of the universe.
Eternal, of constant auspiciousness, the destroyer of Sītā’s grief;
the descendant of Kakutstha, the lotus-eyed one, who removes the fear of Viśvāmitra.
Rāma, the crusher of Mārīca, skilled in the slaying of Virādha, the destroyer of evil dreams, the delightful one, the wearer of the diadem, and the lord of the thirty gods. || 10-211 ||
Possessing a great bow and a massive body, he is formidable and of terrifying prowess;
he is the embodiment of reality, the knower of reality, the speaker of reality, and one of excellent valor.
The self of all beings, the creator of beings, the lord, the knower of time, the highly skillful one;
beyond Viṣṇu, the multitude of virtues, stainless, and free from strife.
Svabhāvabhadra, Śatrughna, Keśava, Sthāṇu, Īśvara, Bhūtādi, Śambhu, Āditya, Sthaviṣṭha, Śvāśata, and Dhruva. || 10-214 ||
Wearing armor, earrings, and a discus, bearing a sword, he is beloved by his devotees;
he is deathless, free from birth, the conqueror of all, and the range of all.
He is the unsurpassed, immeasurable self, the source of all, an ocean of virtues;
he is equanimous, of an equanimous nature, impartial, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Invincible, the self of all beings, Viṣvaksena, of great asceticism; the overseer of the worlds, long-armed, immortal, and the foremost knower of the Vedas. || 10.217 ||
The patient one, the one of good destiny, the teacher, the source of the universe, the one of great splendor; the sleepless, the powerful, the tall, Upendra, Vāmana, and Bali. (10.218)
Madhubhedī, Vidhātṛ, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Haṃsa, Marīci, Govinda, Ratnagarbha, and Mahādyuti. || 10-219 ||
Vyāsa, Vācaspati, the all-seeing, the father, the destroyer of the Asuras, the beloved of Jānakī, the worshipful, the manifest, the increaser of love. || 10-220 ||
He is the source of existence, beyond the senses, the object of knowledge, the one who can be described,
the lord as bright as gold, the intoxicator, the mind-stirrer, the light, the one whose form is the universe, and the stainless one.
The leader of the Nārāyaṇas, the virtuous one who increases the joy of Jaṭāyu,
the multiform Lord of the World, the Master who acts for the welfare of the gods' cause.
He who has conquered anger and subdued the enemy, the bestower of sovereignty upon the lord of monkeys,
the giver of wealth, the one with beautiful arms, the possessor of manifold illusions, and the one who brings joy to those to be transformed.
He is the fierce-rayed sun, one whose resolve is perfected, and one who is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge;
he is the remover of disease through Agada, a knower of mantras, and one whose meditation consists of mantra.
The son of Sumitrā, who is affectionate, pre-eminent, and who assumes both manifest and unmanifest forms;
the illustrious Vasiṣṭha, the leader of the community, who is well-disposed toward his kin and speaks kindly.
Incomparable, virtuous, and steadfast, he was skilled with the bow;
the eldest, endowed with all virtues, powerful, and the slayer of Tāḍakā.
Vaikuṇṭha, the life-breath of all living beings, the tortoise, the lord of Kamalā, the upholder of Govardhana, the one in the form of a fish, and the ocean of compassion.
The shatterer of Kumbhakarna, surrounded by cowherds and cowherdesses,
the master of illusions who induces sleep, the all-pervading one, and the remover of the strength of Rāvaṇa.

Then, having saluted Pināka, the one whose banner is Garuḍa—who is intoxicated with the True, who is beloved by the three worlds, who fills the worlds, and who is the elder brother of Bharata—was honored. || 10-229 ||
The illustrious Lord, the refuge of the virtuous, the witness of the world, the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa;
he who possesses the speed of thought, whose form is mind, the perfect one, the bull among men. || 10-230 ||
The best of the Yadus, the lord of the Yadus, the abode of all beings, possessed of great prowess; the sustainer of splendor, the unagitated one, the fourfold manifestation, the great treasure.

He who crushes the arrows of the senses, he who is worthy of worship, he who is peaceful, he who is honored by Bharata; whose nature is profound like the ocean of sound, whose limbs are delicate, and who is ever awake. || 10.232 ||
He travels through the worlds, reclining on the serpent Śeṣa; he dwells in the ocean of milk, his abode is the sky;
he is the light of the self, whose essence is never diminished, the Lord of the gods, and the thousand-footed one.
Parjanya, Kumuda, Vāsas, Kamalalocana;
Śrīvatsavakṣas, Śrīvāsa, Vīrahā, and Alakṣmaṇāgraja. (10.234)
Delighting the world, the crusher of the world's enemies, dear to his servants, the eternal one, the cloud-like dark-hued destroyer of the demon Tama. (10.235)
Bearing divine weapons, glorious, immeasurable, and having conquered his senses; venerable to the gods on earth, the beloved of Janaka, and the great-grandfather. || 10-236 ||
The most excellent, characterized by goodness, truth, true to his promise, Trivikrama, observer of noble vows, easily accessible, subtle, soundless, bestower of happiness, and wise. || 10-237 ||
Dāmodara, Ucyuta, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Vāmana, the Lord of Mathurā, the son of Devakī, the descendant of Śūra, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and the crusher of Kaiṭabha. || 10-238 ||
He is the shatterer of the seven palm trees, the increaser of the lineage of his friends;
he is the embodiment of Time, the soul of Time, Time itself, the bestower of auspiciousness, and the Kali age.
He is the year, the season, the fortnight, the year, the day, and the auspicious path;
he is the one to be praised, the solitary, the untainted, the praise itself, the all-pervading, and the undisturbed. (10.240)
Without beginning or end, worshipped by all the worlds, free from affliction;
the essence of taste, the knower of taste, full of flavor, and the soul of the ocean of the world.
The bull among the Raghus is the one who has transcended all suffering, the venerable heap, the supreme object of experience, the remainder, the distinct, and the one free from defilement.
The best of castes, the essence of caste, the excellence of caste, the lord of the qualities of caste;
the witness of all, the most excellent of qualities, the bestower of boons upon gods and asuras.
The god of gods, the divine sage, saluted by gods and asuras,
consisting of all the gods, with the bow Kṛśāṅga in his hand, he is unsurpassed.
He is the growth of the mind, the ego, primordial nature, and the Supreme Person;
he is the just one, the unjust, and the leader; he is the glorious one, the path of policy, the wearer of the serpent-king, and the eternal.

The Lord of Lakṣmī, the Sustainer of the World, the Consort of the Queen of Gods, the Destroyer of Vālin, the Foe of Bāṇa, the Destroyer, the Sacrificer, the Supreme, and the Best of Sages. || 10.246 ||
The leader of the gods, intent on meditation upon Śiva, supreme, the highest, the singer of the Sāman hymns, beloved, heroic, of meritorious fame, and of beautiful eyes. || 10.247 ||
The meritorious one, the one exceeding in merit, the ancient one, the full one, the one who fills, the sun;
he with matted hair, the fire that scatters the darkness of impurity. || 10.248 ||
Manifest yet characterized by the unmanifest, he is the ten-faced lion among elephants;
the storehouse of digits, whose form is the digit itself, he is the increaser of the joy of Kamalā.

The conqueror of enemies through recitation is complete; he is dark-hued, the destroyer of worldly existence, the one who desires to adorn [all], the immovable, the radiant, and exalted by his prowess.
Swift, the lord of sound, the object of sound, the delighter, the light, soundless, the person, the illusory, the gross, the subtle, and the distinct. (10.251)
He is self-born and yet unborn, the seven-tongued one with a thousand feet;
he is the portion of nectar, the great embryo, whose longing for sense objects has ceased. || 10.252 ||

The Sage, who knows the three times, the witness, who has abandoned all states of existence, the creator, the most eternal, the blissful, the compassionate, and the supreme among victors—may he be victorious. (10.253)
He is the possessor of power, the devourer of power, the Lord; he bears the mace and holds the discus;
he is effortless and free from conceptual construction; he is the form of consciousness, transcending all fear.
He has a hundred faces and a thousand eyes; he possesses a hundred forms and a dense radiance.
He reclines upon the lotus of the heart, and is both solid and fluid.
Sūrya, the lord of the planets, the glorious one, the capable destroyer of misfortune;
the subduer of unrighteousness and enemies, invoked by many and praised by many. (10.256)
Brahmagarbha, Vṛhadgarbha, Dharmadhenu, Dharāgama,
Hiraṇyagarbha, Jyotiṣmat, Sulalāṭa, and Suvikrama.
The glorious one who delights in the worship of Śiva, who acts for the pleasure of Bhavānī and is self-controlled;
he is Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Rāma, Kapardin, and Nīlalohita. (10.258)
Rudra, Paśupati, Sthāṇu, Viśāmitra, Dvijeśvara, Mātāmaha, Mātariśvan, Viriñca, and Viṣṭaraśravas. || 10-259 ||
Akṣobhya, the fierce one among all beings, whose valor is truth;
Vālakhilya, the great aeon, the wish-fulfilling tree, and the lord of the arts.
The summer heat, the cloud that rains, Śakra who destroys the enemy forces;
the divine crusher of Kavaṃdha, Kaṃvugrīva, the beloved of Śiva. || 10-261 ||
The wind was pleasant, perfectly formed, fragrant, and cool in nature; it was a guest that had not been sought out, yet it was heroic, all-subduing, and a destroyer of evil. || 10.262 ||
Vasuśravas, Kavyavāha, Pratapna, Viśvabhojana, Roma, Nīlotpalaśyāma, Jñānaskandha, and Mahādyuti. (10.263)
He whose feet are pure; the enemy of sin; the city of jewels; he who moves through the sky; the deliverer; the destroyer of evil deeds; the invincible; the unbearable; the source of fear.
He is the one whose body is nectar, the possessor of dharma, the mine of compassion for dharma;
he is Bhaga, Vivasvat, the primordial teacher of yoga, and Bṛhaspati.
He of noble fame, the energetic one, whose nature is speech and who consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
he who wears a garland of stars, whose hair is the sky, who is self-established, and who has the six as his support.
He is the group consisting of the four aims of life, the one who possesses the fruit of those groups, the treasure of the three powers,
the womb containing all treasures, the guileless one, the lordless one, and the crusher of deceit.
Śrīvallabha, Śivārambha, Śānta, Bhadrasamañjasa, Bhūśaya, Bhūtakṛt, Bhūti, Bhūṣaṇa, and Bhūtavāhana. || 10-268 ||
Bodyless, yet abiding in the body of the elements; knowing the [proper] time, he is exceedingly skillful;
moving among the conduct of others, he is solitary and an ocean of sacred learning. || 10-269 ||
Naturally auspicious, impartial, and the destroyer of the fear of saṃsāra;
he is to be known through the Vedas, the protector of the sky, and the lord of the seven excellent sages. || 10.270 ||

The lord of the gods, the instrument, the doer of deeds, the one who strikes with a plow, the one born from water, the object of meditation, the foremost among the fierce, the lord of the earth, volition, and the lord of the night. (10.271)
The teacher of the ultimate truth, the rain-cloud, the pure one, affectionate toward those who take refuge in him;
Viṣṇu, the victorious, the all-pervading, the sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, and the protector of sacrifice.
The Lord Viṣṇu, the devourer, the soul of the moving world, the creator of light; Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, the body, the goal, and the cause of all causes. (10.273)
Kāvya is the creator, Vāsudeva is the one whose parts alone remain, and he is praised by many;
Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, is the primordial creator and the Boar.
Nārāyaṇa, Nara, Haṃsa, Viṣvaksena, Janārdana,
the creator of the universe, the great sacrifice, the luminous one, and Puruṣottama.
Vaikuṇṭha, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Kṛṣṇa, he who is worshipped by the Sun and the gods;
Narasiṃha, the most terrifying, whose fangs are the discus and whose weapons are his claws.

The primordial god, the creator of the world, the lord of yogis, he whose banner bears Garuḍa; Govinda, the lord of the rays, the protector, the lord of forms, the sovereign of the universe. || 10-277 ||
Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Dhātṛ, Dāmodara, Prabhu, Trivikrama, Trilokeśa, Brahmeśa, and Prītivardhana. || 10-278 ||

The subduer of the wicked-minded Vāmana, the lord of cowherds, the beloved of the cowherds, the one dear to devotion, the infallible, the truthful, the one of true fame, fortitude, and memory. || 10-279 ||
Compassionate, mercy itself, the expander [of wisdom], the destroyer of sin, the increaser of peace;
the renunciant, the knower of the truth of the scriptures, whose banner is Mount Mandara. || 10.280 ||
He whose abode is the jujube tree; he who is tranquil; the ascetic; the one who has descended; the Lord;
the dwelling place of all beings; the dweller in the cave; the abode of Śrī; the husband of Śrī. || 10.281 ||
He who dwells in austerity, the abode of joy, the abode of truth, the eternal;
the Supreme Person, the lotus-like, the meritorious, the lotus-eyed Maheśvara. || 10-282 ||
He is the one of perfect form, the knower of the Purāṇas, the giver of merit, and the increaser of merit;
he holds the conch, the discus, and the mace upon his limbs, and wields the plow, the pestle, and the halberd.
Wearing a crown, earrings, necklaces, a girdle, armor, and bearing a banner;
a warrior, a conqueror, possessed of great heroism, the slayer of enemies, and the scorcher of foes.

The Teacher, the maker of well-being, the scripture, the one who brings peace, the benefactor, the Son, the charioteer of the virtuous, the Lord, the lover of the Sāma Veda, and the Equanimous One. || 10.285 ||
He is variegated, impetuous, powerful, complete in limb, and prosperous;
he is the giver of heaven, the giver of desires, the giver of fortune, the giver of beauty, and the bestower of splendor.
The lotus-eyed one is the giver of liberation; he who has made his abode in the ocean of milk is the lord of all worlds, the performer of what is dear, and the destroyer of calamities.
Vaikuṇṭha, the lotus-eyed one, saluted by all the gods;
the all-pervading Lord of the world, the great sovereign of all realms.
The God who effects creation, preservation, and dissolution; who brings happiness to all gods; who is imperishable, eternal, and infinite; and who is devoid of decay or increase. (10.289)
Untainted, devoid of qualities, subtle, changeless, and stainless,
it is liberated from all limiting adjuncts and established as pure existence alone.
The Supreme Self is changeless, all-pervading, eternal, and ancient;
it is powerful, stainless, omnipresent, eternally satisfied, and independent. || 10-291 ||

Dark-complexioned, youthful, with red eyes and a radiant face, he was moderate in speech; his arms reached down to his knees, his countenance was handsome, and he possessed the shoulders and great arms of a lion. || 10.292 ||
Possessed of strength, endowed with virtues, blazing with his own splendor,
the Lord Time is the soul of time and the one who sets the wheel of time in motion.
The supreme light is Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Supreme Self;
he is the enjoyer of the universe, the consumer of the universe, and the perpetual protector of the universe. || 10-294 ||
The Lord of the Universe, whose form is the universe, the soul of the universe, the creator of the universe;
the friend of all beings, peaceful, and unshakable among all beings.
He is the Lord of all lords, the All, who is affectionate toward those who take refuge in Him;
He is omnipresent, the Lord of all beings, and dwells within the hearts of all beings.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme dispeller of the inner darkness;
he is Hari, the Lord of the Prajāpatis, the creator who is without beginning or end.
Narasiṃha, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Self of all, the creator of all,
the protector of the moving and the stationary world, the leader, the eternal,
the beloved, the sustainer, the ordainer, and the Lord and Master of all.
Viṣṇu, the thousand-headed, the soul of all, the all-seeing, and the imperishable.
The ancient Puruṣa, the creator, thousand-eyed and thousand-footed—
He is the reality, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, the eternal Vāsudeva.
The Supreme Self, the supreme light, the supreme Brahman, higher than the highest;
the infallible Puruṣa, Kṛṣṇa, the eternal, auspicious Lord. || 10.301 ||
He is eternal, omnipresent, immovable, Rudra, the witness, and Prajāpati;
he is Hiraṇyagarbha, Savitṛ, the creator of the worlds, the enjoyer of the worlds, and the all-pervading Lord.
The Blessed One, the Lord of the Śrībhūḥ, the Sovereign, is denoted by the syllable *a*;
he is the Lord of all worlds, the Consort of Śrī, the Omniscient, and the one whose face is turned in every direction. (10.303)
The Lord is virtuous, easily accessible, omniscient, and omnipotent;
His desires are eternally fulfilled, and He is naturally friendly and blissful. (10.304)
The ocean of nectar for the world, the refuge of all embodied beings, is the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the master, the lord, and the sovereign of the worlds. (10.305)
The Lord of Śrī, the refuge of all beings, the bestower of the desires of those who have sought his protection;
the infinite Rāma, Lord of Śrī, who bears all qualities yet is beyond qualities, the Great One.
"O Hare Rāma, Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma, Hare Hare!
O Madhusūdana, let my speech always utter this very [name]. (10-307)
These and other names have been enumerated;
each single name of Rāma destroys all sins.
It bestows the fruit of the thousand names, grants all sovereign powers,
provides all perfections for men, and yields the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
All this has been declared from the mantra as the most auspicious of all;
whoever should read or even hear it shall attain the state of Brahman.
For those who have committed great sins, that [sin] remains in their hands only so long as the roar of the lion that is the name of Rāma is not heard. (10.311)

The slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, the violator of the Guru’s bed, the killer of one who has sought refuge, and the betrayer of a trusted friend—[these are the great sinners]. (10.312)
Even those who have killed their mother, their father, or committed an abortion, as well as those who have slain a hero—
all of them are purified by reciting the Thousand Names of Rāma.
Even thousands of millions upon millions of accumulated sins perish at that very moment by reciting the Thousand Names.
Having recited [the mantra] daily in the presence of Rāma for the duration of a year,
one becomes stainless and happy, and thereafter shall attain liberation.
Thus ends the complete Thousand Names of Śrī Rāma, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the glorious Liṅga Purāṇa.

Svāhā to the beloved of the cowherd women.

Agnisundarī svāhā.
Now begins the ritual procedure for worship.
In the morning, one should meditate upon the Guru— two-eyed, two-armed, peaceful, and holding the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness— upon a white lotus on the head, preceded by his name.

Regarding the phrase "blind with the darkness of ignorance": one meditates upon the threefold light as having become one—the Supreme Self (Paramātman) in the form of the sun within the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, the individual self (Jīvātman) in the form of fire in the heart, and Kuṇḍalinī in the form of the moon at the Mūlādhāra; by that light, the body of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda), is revealed.

Having reflected in his heart that [the Lord] has manifested, and having contemplated that the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa— who pervades the millions of Brahmāṇḍas beyond even the parārdhas— resides right there within that body.
The Lord of Brahmāṇḍa is the master of millions upon millions of world-systems;
be gracious, O Supreme Bliss, I bow down to you, Mādhava.
127a) Having thus bowed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa with speech, mind, and body, one should prostrate; then, from the *mūlādhāra-cakra*,

which is the station of the earth, red in color, possessing four petals endowed with four rays of light, there resides Kuṇḍalinī— fierce like the sun, cool like the moon, and brilliant like lightning— from the *mūlādhāra*.
Two finger-breadths above the base of the perineum and two finger-breadths below the penis, the Svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra is located;

it is one finger-breadth in circumference, the seat of fire, endowed with the six letters va, bha, ma, ya, ra, and la, and possesses six petals. Above the Svādhiṣṭhāna, at the navel, is [the Maṇipūra-cakra].
In the maṇipūraka-cakra, there is the water-element, beginning with the jewel.
The ten-petaled lotus of Maṇipūraka, endowed with the ten syllables ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, and pha,
is located in the heart above [the navel]. The Anāhata-cakra, the seat of Vāyu and the locus of deep sleep, consists of the syllables ka, kha, ga, gha, and ṅa, followed by ca, cha, ja, and jha.

The Viśuddha-cakra, located at the throat above the Anāhata-padmam, consists of twelve petals joined with the twelve syllables *ña, ṭa, ṭha, ḍva, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha, kṣa; it is the locus of dreams and the locus of space.
The [Ājñā-cakra] consists of sixteen petals joined with the sixteen vowels: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ.
Above the Viśuddha-cakra, in the middle of the eyebrows, one should contemplate the Ājñā-cakra as the place of waking and the locus of space,
consisting of two petals joined with the letters Ha and Kṣa.
Then, having pierced the six chakras known as Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā, Kuṇḍalinī reached the lunar orb situated in the thousand-petaled lotus;
having drunk the nectar of the lunar orb, she returned again to the Ājñā.
One should contemplate that Kuṇḍalinī has reached the Mūlādhāra after piercing through the Viśuddha, Anāhata, Maṇipūra, and Svādhiṣṭhāna centers.
Then, having risen, one should discharge feces, urine, and so forth, and cleanse the hands, feet, and other limbs.
Having cleaned his teeth and sipped water according to the rules, he should perform his bath in a body of water, or with water drawn out [from it].
From the solar mandala by means of the goad mudrā.
Oṃ, O Gaṅgā and Yamunā, O Godāvarī and Sarasvatī, O Kāverī and Narmadā, O Sindhu—be present here in these waters! (10.409)
Having thus invoked the *tīrtha* with this mantra, one should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) eight times over the water. One should then meditate upon Hari within that water.
Thereafter, one should offer the water upon one's own head three times using the *kuṃbha-mudrā*.
Then, having cleansed his body and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should offer libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.

Then, having rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, one should invoke Śrī Kṛṣṇa from the solar orb with "O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, come, come! Having recited the root mantra and offered libations while saying "I satisfy Śrī Kṛṣṇa," and having chanted the Gāyatrī,
one should offer the *argha* water to the Sun.
Then, having emerged from the water, put on two washed garments, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should wash his hands and feet.

With his right hand marked by the *pavitra* mudrā, and bearing a white vertical *tilaka* on the middle joint of the ring finger, he should sip water again. Taking water in his right hand, he should place it in his left hand while reciting the mantra "Namaḥ."
One should sprinkle one's own head with drops of water from the joints of the fingers of the left hand, using the mantra "svāhā."
Then, *strāya phaṭ*.
Taking water with the right hand from the left hand, one should pour it down.
One should do this four times. Then, taking water in the right hand with the mantra "namaḥ" and smelling it with the left nostril.
Thinking that some water has entered within the nostril through the right breath, one should contemplate this and expel it downward.

Having recited the Śrī Kṛṣṇa Gāyatrī—“Oṃ, let us know the Beloved of the Gopīs; let us meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Kṛṣṇa impel us”—one should offer this arghya with the following mantra to Śrī Kṛṣṇa residing within the solar orb: “Arghyaṃ namaḥ.”
Thus, one should offer the arghya with water to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus concludes the mantra-sandhyā.

Likewise, having sat at the door of the worship pavilion and worshipped the deities of the door with scents and other offerings, saying "Obeisance to the deities of the door," one should enter the interior of the house and say:
