One should worship with the mantra: "Oṃ, homage to Vāstupuruṣa."
In front of that, having spread a seat of *kuśa* grass, and upon it a tiger skin or a deer skin, and over that a cloth, and having sprinkled it, with palms joined in reverence:
"The *ṛṣi* is Merupṛṣṭha, the *chandas* is Sutala, the deity is Kūrma; this is the application (*viniyoga*) for sitting upon the seat."
Having recited thus.
O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
Therefore, support me as well, O Goddess, and make this seat pure.
Thus, one should empower the earth with the mantra of the earth.

Then, having worshipped the seat with the mantra "Obeisance to the one whose seat is the lotus of the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti)," one should sit upon it after assuming a posture such as the svastika-āsana. One should place one's own articles of worship on the right side.
A beautiful water-pot, filled with *vusa* grass, should be held in the left hand by the married women.
One should place the vessel on the back of the two hands, which have been washed and rubbed together;
one should also arrange it in close proximity to a burning lamp. || 10-412 ||
One should always place flowers upon the head of the deity;
during the time of worship, one should move the hand around the deity.
Salutation to the Gurus on the left cheek;
salutation to Gaṇeśa on the right cheek;
salutation to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the center.
Thus, having prostrated.
Having recited "asurāntakacakrāya svāhā | astrāya phaṭ," one should cleanse both hands— the palms and the backs— and perform three *tāla* claps in successive upward order.
Having offered [the oblation] with the Nārāca-mudrā and performed the binding of the ten directions with crystal-like [mantras], [recite]: "Protect, protect the three worlds, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!"
Having enveloped oneself with water while reciting this mantra, one should contemplate a rampart of fire in the four directions.
Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) as follows:

Having placed his hands palms-upward upon his own lap, he should contemplate the individual soul (jīvātman), which resides in the heart in the form of a lamp-flame, as being merged with the Supreme Self (paramātman) situated in the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, together with the Kuṇḍalinī located at the Mūlādhāra, while reciting the mantra "So 'ham."
One should contemplate the region of the earth as being square from the feet to the knees, marked with a wheel, joined with the syllable *laṃ*, and yellow in color. (10.414)
One should meditate upon the region of water as being white in color, marked with a lotus, resembling the crescent moon from the knees up to the navel, and endowed with its seed-syllable. 10.415.
From the navel up to the throat, the mandala of fire is triangular, reddish in color, marked with a svastika, and joined with its own seed-syllable. (10.416)

One should contemplate the mandala of air as being black, extending from the throat to the space between the eyebrows; it is hexagonal, joined with six dots, and [marked] with the seed-syllable. (10.417)

One should meditate upon the space of the sky as being from the center of the brows to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), circular, marked with a banner, smoke-colored, and joined with its own seed-syllable.
Laṃ is the seed-syllable of earth, vaṃ is the seed-syllable of water, raṃ is the seed-syllable of fire, yaṃ is the seed-syllable of air, and haṃ is the seed-syllable of space.
Having meditated thus, one should then dissolve those elements:
earth into water, both of them into fire, and fire into air.
Having thus dissolved space into space, and then that [space] into primordial nature (prakṛti),
one should dissolve that power of illusion (māyāśakti) in the form of the lower Brahman into the Supreme Self.
Thus, having dissolved the entire manifold of the body and so forth— which has been accumulated through beginningless existence— into the Supreme Self in the form of the Puruṣa.
He has the murder of a Brahmin as his head, the theft of gold as his two arms,
the drinking of liquor associated with his heart, and the violation of the Guru's bed as his two hips.
That pair of associated words was a sin against the limbs and sub-limbs, with its hair consisting of minor offenses and its beard and eyes red. (10.423)
One should visualize a black figure holding a sword and shield in the left side of the abdomen.

That is the mouth of the *iḍā*. Reciting the wind-seed syllable "yaṃ," which is smoke-colored, sixteen times while filling the body with air through the left nostril, one should perform this by reciting it sixty-four times.

Having dried up the body, one should exhale the breath through the right nostril while reciting "Yam" thirty-two times. Then, with the seed-syllable of fire, "Ram," which is bound by the ruddy wind and has been recited sixteen times, [one should proceed].

Having filled the body with air through the right nostril while reciting [the mantra] sixty-four times, one should perform kumbhaka (retention), contemplating that the body has been reduced to ashes; then, while reciting "ram" thirty-two times, one should exhale the air along with the ashes through the left nostril.

Then, reciting the syllable *ṭhaṃ*— the white seed-syllable of the Moon (*candrabīja*), which is by nature feminine (*prakṛtyātmaka*)— sixteen times through the left nostril while it is masculine (*puruṣātmaka*), one should lead it to the Moon on the forehead.

Then, while reciting "Vam" sixty-four times, one should cause a shower of nectar consisting of those syllables to fall from the moon at the forehead; by means of that, making the entire body fit for the worship of the deity, one should recite "Lam" thirty-two times and exhale the air through the right nostril.
One should again cause the body, which is the pure supreme self, to arise.

Māyā, whose essence is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), is the Mother (Mātṛkā) and the supreme primordial nature (Prakṛti). From the unborn Mother of the world was born Ākāśa; from Ākāśa came Space (Nabhas), and from Space came Wind (Anila). || 10.425 ||
From the wind arose fire; from fire, water; and from that, earth.
Having returned to its own state among the elements, it attained a body whose form was light.
One should contemplate that what has arisen here is fit for the propitiation of the deity;
within this body resides this Supreme Self, omniscient and omnipotent. (10.427)
Having the form of all deities, consisting of all mantras, and auspicious, he dwells within the body in the form of the self through his own nature as the vital principle (jīva). || 10-428 ||
Thus has the primary purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) been described here through visualization;
then, having placed the hand upon the heart—
Ā Hrīḥ Kroḥ Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Ha Sa—thus my vital breaths are here as vital breaths. (12)
My life-breath remains here.
Thus: O all my sense organs—speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths—come here and remain happily for a long time; svāhā!
Thus one should practice the seed-syllable.
Then, one should place [the mantras] in sequence upon the head, face, eyes, ears, nostrils, cheeks, lips, the two rows of teeth, and the head and mouth together.
And the wise [should place] the letters beginning with *ya* in the joints of the arms and feet, on the tips of the fingers, on the left side, on the two backs, the navel, and the belly;
and those ending with *va* in the heart, the two armpits, the two shoulders, the roots of the two hands,
the two feet, the belly, and the mouth.
First, let him perform the placement upon the heart daily, according to this [method], for the sake of attaining mastery over the body.

Oṃ. The Brahman-sage is [the source], the Gāyatrī is the metre, Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the deity, the consonants are the seeds, and the vowels are the powers; this is the application in the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
(129a) Then, having meditated upon the Goddess of Speech with the fifty letters and so forth, one should pay obeisance.
Then, having completed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa beginning with "Aṃ, salutations to the Brahma-randhra," one should perform the Keśava-kīrti-nyāsa as follows:
I bow to Viṣṇu, who possesses the radiance of a hundred rising suns, who is as pure as molten gold, who is attended on both sides by the Daughter of the Ocean and the Mother of the Universe,
who wears various garments shimmering with diverse jewels, and whose ornaments are radiant with manifold gems.
Salutation to the one who holds the lotus, the Kaumodakī mace, and the discus in his hands;
salutation to Aṅkeśa for glory;
Āṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa for splendor.
Oṃ, obeisance to Mādhava for the constellation Puṣyā; ī, obeisance to Govinda for the constellation Puṣyā;
Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu for the constellation Vṛttī.
Oṃ, salutation to Madhusūdana for peace;
Ṛ, salutation to Trivikrama for action;
Ṛ, salutation to Vāmana for compassion.
Ḷ: Homage to Śrīdhara and to Medhā.
Ḹ: Homage to Hṛṣīkeśa and to Harṣa. E: Homage to Padmanābha and to Śraddhā.
Ai! Salutation to Dāmodara and Yajñā.
O! Salutation to Vāsudeva and Lakṣmī. Au! Salutation to Saṃkarṣaṇa and Sarasvatī.
a/ Homage to Pradyumna, to Prīti;
aḥ homage to Aniruddha, to Rati;
kaṃ homage to the wielder of the discus (Cakrin), to Jayā.
Khaṃ, salutation to Gadī Durgā; Gaṃ, salutation to Śārṅgī Prabhā; Ghaṃ, salutation to Khaḍgī Satyā.
Ṅaṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkhinī and Caṇḍā; caṃ, obeisance to Halinī and Vāṇī; chaṃ, obeisance to Musulinī and Vilāsinī.
Jaṃ, salutation to the wielder of the trident, to Vijayā; jhaṃ, salutation to the wielder of the noose, to Virajā; ñaṃ, salutation to the wielder of the goad, to Viśvā.
Ṭaṃ, obeisance to Mukunda and Vinodā; ṭhaṃ, obeisance to Nandaja and Sunandā; ḍaṃ, obeisance to Nandin and Smṛti.
Ḍhaṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa, to Ṛddhi; Ṇaṃ, salutation to the Conqueror of Naraka, to Samṛddhi; Taṃ, salutation to Hara, to Śuddhi.
Thaṃ, salutation to Kṛṣṇa, the awakened one.
Daṃ, salutation to Satya, the enjoyer.
Dhaṃ, salutation to Sāttvata, the truth.
Naṃ, salutation to Sāra and Kṣamā; Paṃ, salutation to Śūra and Ramā;
Phaṃ, salutation to Janārdana and Umā.
Baṃ, salutation to Baṃdhudhara and Kledinī; Bhaṃ, salutation to Viśvamūrti and Klinnā;
Maṃ, salutation to Vaikuṇṭha and Vasudā.
Salutation to the skin-self, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), and to Vasudhā; 129b) salutation to the blood-self, Balarāma, and to Parā;
salutation to the flesh-self, Kṛṣṇa (Balānuja), and to Parāyaṇā.
Vaṃ, salutation to the self of marrow, to Valāyā, to Sūkṣmā. Śaṃ, salutation to the self of bone, to Vṛṣaghnā, to Saṃdhyā.
Ṣaṃ, salutation to the self of marrow, to Vṛṣa, to Prajñā.
Saṃ, salutation to Haṃsa, whose essence is semen, to Prabhā; haṃ, salutation to Varāha, whose essence is breath, to Niśā;
laṃ, salutation to Vimalā, whose essence is power, to Moghā.
"KṢAṂ! Salutation to Narasiṃha, whose nature is wrath, who is like lightning!"—
thus one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in the locations of the Mātṛkā,
if one desires prosperity (*śrī*).
One should perform the placement [of mantras] as follows: "Obeisance to the glory of Śrī-Aṅkeśava," and so forth.
Now follows the placement of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*):
"Maṃ, obeisance to the supreme self, the essence of the individual soul (*jīva-tattva*)."

"Paṃ, obeisance to the Supreme; naṃ, obeisance to the Self of the principle (tattva). These three [syllables] are for the heart. "Naṃ, obeisance to the Supreme; obeisance to the Self of the principle of sound."
Thus on the head. "Dhaṃ, salutation to the supreme one whose self is the principle of touch," thus on the mouth.
"Daṃ, salutation to the one whose nature is the supreme reality; salutation.
Thus, at the heart.
*Thaṃ*, obeisance to the Supreme, the essence of the principle of taste; *namaḥ* to the Liṅga.
*Taṃ*, obeisance to the Supreme, the essence of the principle of smell; *namaḥ* to the two feet. *Ṇaṃ*, obeisance to the Supreme, the essence of the principle of hearing; *namaḥ* to the two ears.
"Ḍhaṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the self-nature of the principle of skin"—thus [one should worship] on the skin and all the limbs.
Ḍaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, salutation to the essence of the principle of sight (dṛk-tattva) in the two eyes;

Ṭhaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, salutation to the essence of the principle of the tongue (jihvā-tattva) in the tongue; Ṭaṃ, salutation to the supreme one, salutation to the essence of the principle of the nose (nāsā-tattva) in the nose.

Ñaṃ, obeisance to the supreme one, the essence of speech; obeisance to the mouth. Ṛṃ, obeisance to the supreme one, the essence of the hands; [obeisance] to the two hands. Jaṃ, obeisance to the supreme one, the essence of the feet; obeisance to the two feet.

Chaṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the self-nature of the principle of the anus, at the anus. Caṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the self-nature of the principle of the generative organ, at the generative organ.

Ṅaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self whose essence is the element of space, on the head; Ghaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self whose essence is the element of air, on the mouth; Gaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self whose essence is the element of fire, on the heart.
*Khaṃ*, salutation to the supreme one; *namaḥ* to the essence of the water-tattva, salutation to the two ears.
*Gaṃ*, salutation to the supreme one; *namaḥ* to the essence of the heart-lotus-tattva, salutation to the heart.
*Haṃ*, salutation to the supreme one; *namaḥ* to the essence of the solar orb pervaded by the twelve digits (kalās), salutation.
*Saṃ*, obeisance to the Supreme, the essence of the lunar disc pervaded by sixteen digits; obeisance! *Vaṃ*, obeisance to the Supreme, the essence of the fiery disc pervaded by ten digits; obeisance!
One should place these three in ascending order, one above the other.
*Ṣaṃ*, obeisance to the supreme Vāsudeva, the self of the *parameṣṭhi-tattva*; obeisance to the head.
*Yaṃ*, obeisance to the supreme Nārāyaṇa, the self of the *puruṣa-tattva*; obeisance to the mouth.
*Laṃ*, obeisance to the supreme Pradyumna, the self of the *viśva-tattva*; obeisance to the heart.
*Raṃ*, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the *nivṛtti-tattva*, salutation to Aniruddha—at the *liṅga*.
*Laṃ*, salutation to the supreme one, the self of all *tattvas*, salutation to Nārāyaṇa—at the two feet.
*Kṣauṃ*, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the *kāma-tattva*, salutation to Nṛsiṃha—at all the limbs.
Thus ends the placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa).
Thus instructed, he certainly becomes authorized for the recitation and other rites of all Vaiṣṇava mantras.
Then, having recited the Kāmabīja sixteen times, one should exhale the breath through the right nostril.
Having recited the Kāmabīja thirty-two times, one should inhale the breath through the left nostril.
Having recited the Kāmabīja sixty-four times while holding both nostrils, one should perform the *kumbhaka* (retention).
...thus [one should recite]. This is one breath control (prāṇāyāma). In this manner, one should perform three breath controls.
Now follows the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭha-nyāsa).
In one's own heart: obeisance to Ādhāraśakti.
Salutation to Prakṛti. Salutation to Kamaṭha.
Salutation to Śeṣa. Salutation to Kṣamā.
Salutation to the Ocean of Milk. Salutation to Śvetadvīpa.
Salutation to the great pavilion, radiant with jewels.
In the east: Salutation to Mandāra. In the south:
Homage to Santānakāya in the west.
Homage to Parijātā. In the north.
Homage to the Kalpavṛkṣa (Wish-fulfilling Tree). [In the center.]
Salutation to Haricandana. [On the right shoulder.]
Homage to Dharma. [To be placed] on the left shoulder.
Salutation to Jñāna; [this is] on the root of the right thigh.
Salutation to Vairāgya (Dispassion); [this is] at the base of the left thigh.
Homage to Aiśvarya; [this is] on the face.
Homage to Adharma. [At] the waist.
Salutation to Ajñāna. On the right side.
Salutation to Avairāgya (Non-detachment). [On] the left side.
Homage to Anaiśvarya.
Again, [the mantra] "Obeisance to the one remaining in the heart."
Salutation to the one born from the lotus.
Aṃ, obeisance to the solar disc, whose self consists of ten digits; Ūṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc, whose self consists of sixteen digits;
Maṃ, obeisance to the fiery disc, whose self consists of ten digits.
In successive order from above:
*saṃ* salutation to Sattva;
*raṃ* salutation to Rajas.
Salutation to that Tamas;
salutation to Āṃ, the Self (Ātman);
salutation to Aṃ, the Inner Self (Antarātman).
Paṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Self. Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Self of Knowledge. Āṃ, obeisance to Vimalā.
Ī: Homage to Utkaṣiṇī.
Ūṃ, homage to Jñānā;
E, to Kriyā; Ai, to Yogā;
O, homage to Prati.
Having worshipped [the goddesses] beginning with Satyā and ending with Īśānā on the eight petals of the heart-lotus, one should worship [the central deity] in the pericarp (karṇikā).
AḤ, salutation to Anugrahā;
[this is] upon the pericarp.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Viṣṇu, the self of all beings, Vāsudeva;
salutation to the self who is the lotus-throne of the yoga of union with the self of all.
Thus one should perform the placement (nyāsa).
Then, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), one should recite:

"The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra is Nārada; the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Virāṭ; the deity presiding over Prakṛti and Durgā is Kṛṣṇa; *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*); and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of the four aims of human life."
The meaning is that *prakṛti* is the fundamental cause.
Then, "Salutation to the Sage who grants boons," [at] the head.
"Salutation to the Virāṭ meter," thus [he places it] on the face.
"Salutation to the deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the auspiciousness of all the worlds."
Thus one should place [the mantra] in the heart.
Having joined the palms in *añjali*, one should recite: "Salutation to Durgā, the presiding deity; *adhiṣṭhātṛ-devatāyai namaḥ*."
Then, the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga).
To the one with the wheel, svāhā!
"Hṛdayāya namaḥ" on the two thumbs; "Sucakrāya śikhāyai vauṣaṭ."
Thus, on the crest-lock.
Svāhā to the wheel for protecting the three worlds!
Hūṃ to the armor!
Thus on all limbs.
*Asurāntakacakrāya svāhā | Astrāya phaṭ* | Thus [for] the palms and backs of the hands.
Having raised it higher and higher by three *tāla*s, one should perform the binding of the ten directions with snapping sounds.
Now, the ten limbs:
Gaṃ, salutation to the heart;
Pīṃ, salutation to the head.
Jaṃ, homage to the crest-lock;
Naṃ, homage to all limbs.
Vaṃ, salutation to the two hands.
Laṃ, obeisance to the right side;
Bhāṃ, obeisance to the left side.
Yaṃ is at the hips.
Svāṃ on the back.
Hāṃ, salutation to the head.

Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) of the root mantra— enclosed by the *praṇava* (oṃ)— both internally and externally on the hands and on the sides, Kṛṣṇa, who consists of the supreme light that is most excellent of all, is [meditated upon]; next, the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) is taught for the purpose of his ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
Now, regarding creation.
Oṃ; thus [one places it] on the first joint of the thumb of the right hand.
Thus ends the second section.
Oṃ, salutations in the third section.
Thus.
Oṃ pīṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus on the three joints of the index finger;
oṃ bhā oṃ namaḥ—thus on the three joints of the middle finger.
Oṃ na; Oṃ namaḥ on the three joints of the ring finger. Oṃ va; Oṃ namaḥ on the three joints of the little finger.
Oṃ lla/ Oṃ namaḥ—thus on the three joints of the little finger.
Oṃ lla/ Oṃ namaḥ—thus on the three joints of the little finger.
131a) Oṃ bhāḥ; oṃ namaḥ—thus for the ring finger.
Oṃ naṃ oṃ namaḥ for the middle finger;
Oṃ svāṃ oṃ namaḥ on the three joints of the index finger.
Oṃ hāṃ oṃ, homage to the three joints of the thumb.
Thus [ends the section] on creation.
Then he stood still.
Oṃ ga; Oṃ namaḥ—thus [one places it] on the right thumb of the index finger.
Oṃ pī. Oṃ, homage! [Touch] the right index finger with the right thumb.
Oṃ jaṃ oṃ; homage to you, O Na-madhyamā.
"Oṃ naṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, [one should touch] the right ring finger;
"oṃ vaṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, the little finger;
"oṃ laṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, the left index finger and the left thumb.
Oṃ bhāṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus [one should touch] the index finger with the thumb of the left hand; oṃ yaṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus [one should touch] the middle finger;
oṃ svāṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus [one should touch] the ring finger.
"Oṃ hāṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this [mantra], it is placed on the little finger; such is the established rule.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of reabsorption (saṃhāra).
"Oṃ gaṃ oṃ namaḥ"—thus on the left thumb.
"Oṃ pīṃ oṃ namaḥ"—thus with the left thumb on the left index finger.
Oṃ jaṃ oṃ namaḥ; with this, [one should place it] on the middle finger.
"Oṃ naṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, [he should worship] in the navel.
Oṃ vaṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus on the little finger [of the left hand].
Oṃ laṃ oṃ namaḥ—with the right thumb, [place it] on the right little finger.
"Oṃ bhāṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, [he should touch] the ring finger;
"Oṃ yaṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, the middle finger.
"Oṃ svāṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, [place it] on the left index finger.
"Oṃ hāṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, [place it] on the right thumb with the right index finger.
This is the *saṃhāranyāsa* (dissolution-assignment).
Furthermore, creation and maintenance are to be performed.
Oṃ gaṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus [one should touch] the right thumb with the right index finger.
Oṃ pīṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus with the right thumb on the right index finger;
oṃ jaṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus with that [thumb] on the middle finger;
oṃ naṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus with that [thumb] on the ring finger.
"Oṃ vaṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, [it is placed] on the little finger.
Saying "Oṃ laṃ oṃ namaḥ," he [should touch] the left little finger with his left thumb.
Oṃ bhāṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus [is the mantra] for her name.
Oṃ yaṃ oṃ namaḥ; with this [mantra], [one should worship] on the middle finger.
"Oṃ svāṃ oṃ namaḥ"—with this, [one performs] the *tarjanī* (threatening) gesture.
Oṃ hāṃ oṃ namaḥ—thus [one should touch] the right thumb with the index finger; this is for the sake of emanation (sṛṣṭi).
In this way, it should also be performed while remaining stationary.
This ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed in five ways.
Furthermore, the placement of the ten limbs (daśāṅga-nyāsa) should be performed according to the sequence of their positions on the fingers.
Oṃ go! Homage to the thumb of the right hand.
Pīṃ, salutation to the right index finger;
jaṃ, salutation to the middle finger.
Homage to Nāmikā.
Vaṃ; salutation to Kaniṣṭhā.
Laṃ, homage to Vāmāṅguṣṭhā.
Bhāṃ, homage to the index finger;
Yaṃ, homage to the middle finger;
Svāṃ, homage to the ring finger.
Hāṃ, obeisance to the little finger.
Then: Svāhā to the wheel of speech.
Salutation to the two thumbs; svāhā to the Discus of Victory.
With the two index fingers.
To the one with the excellent wheel, svāhā to the two middle fingers;
to the wheel that protects the three worlds, svāhā to the two ring fingers.
"Obeisance to the wheel that destroys the asuras, svāhā!

Obeisance to the two little fingers"—thus one should also place the five limbs, beginning with the thumbs, while reciting the mantra either in its measured form or with the letters of the alphabet (mātṛkā) joined with the bindu. Furthermore, [one should perform this] without distinction.
Due to the distinction between the paths of withdrawal and emanation, there are ten principles (tattvas) which partake of the phonemes of the mantra.
Having recited the root mantra, one should place the fifty letters in their respective locations of the Mātṛkā according to the sequence beginning with *aṃ hā svā yabhā llava na japogo* and so forth.
Next is the placement of the reality of the mantra (*mantratattvanyāsa*).
*Go*—salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the essence of the earth element at the feet.
*Oṃ pīṃ*—salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the essence of the water element at the generative organ.
"Jaṃ namaḥ parāya pāvakatattvātmane namaḥ" [is] in the heart;
"naṃ namaḥ parāya anilatattvātmane namaḥ" [is] in the mouth;
"vaṃ namaḥ parāya ākāśatattvātmane na" [is] on the head.

Llaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self, obeisance to the essence of the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva). Bhāṃ, obeisance to the supreme self, obeisance to the essence of the principle of the great one (mahat-tattva).
Thus, these two are in the heart.

Yaṃ, salutation; namaḥ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the principle of primordial nature (prakṛti-tattva). Svāṃ, salutation; namaḥ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the principle of the person (puruṣa-tattva). Yaṃ, salutation; hāṃ, salutation to the supreme one, the self of the supreme principle (para-tattva).
Thus, these three are present throughout the entire body.
Thus is the withdrawal.
Now, the creation.
Hāṃ! Salutation to the Supreme, whose essence is the Tattva.
SVAṂ, obeisance to the supreme one; obeisance to the self whose essence is the principle of Puruṣa. YAṂ, obeisance to the supreme one; obeisance to the self whose essence is the principle of Prakṛti.
[To be recited] over the entire body.
Bhāṃ, salutation to the supreme one; salutation to the self of the principle of Mahat.
Laṃ, obeisance to the supreme; obeisance to the self of the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva). Thus, these two [syllables] are at the heart.
"Vaṃ, obeisance; as a synonym for the self of the principle of space (ākāśatattva), obeisance"—thus [one should offer salutation] to the head.
"Naṃ, salutation to the supreme one, salutation to the self whose essence is the wind-principle," [this is recited] in the mouth.
That which is salutation to the Supreme, to the Self whose essence is purification; salutation to the Heart.
Pīṃ, obeisance to the supreme one; obeisance to the self whose essence is the water-tattva, located in the generative organ.
Go! Salutation to the supreme, salutation to the self of the earth-element in the feet.
Thus ends the account of creation.
One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) three times with both hands, beginning from the hair and ending at the feet, reciting the root mantra encased by the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
132a) Now follows the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa) according to the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
In that regard, emanation is as follows:
With "Goṃ Namaḥ," [he should touch] the head with the middle finger.
Saying "Piṃ Namaḥ," [one should touch] the two eyes with the middle and index fingers.
That which is [placed] on the two ears with the fingers excluding the thumbs;
Saying "naṃ namaḥ," [one should touch] the two nostrils with the thumb and ring finger.
Saying "vaṃ namaḥ," [one should touch] the mouth with all the fingers.
"Namaḥ" with the thumb and forefinger at the heart.
With "Bhāṃ Namaḥ," [one should touch] the navel with the thumb and middle finger.
When [the word] "namaḥ" is used, [the fingers] excluding the thumb are placed upon the linga.
With the mantra "svāṃ namaḥ," one should touch the two knees with all fingers except the thumbs.
"Hāṃ Namaḥ" with all the fingers on both feet.
"Go nāma" is on the head of the middle [finger].
With "Pīṃ Namaḥ," [one should touch] the two eyes with the index and middle fingers.
That which is [placed] on both ears with fingers excluding the thumb.
Naṃ namaḥ to the two nostrils with the thumb and ring finger.
Vaṃ; salutation with all the fingers to the mouth.
Such is the established position.
Now follows the dissolution.
Hāṃ! Salutation with all the fingers to both feet.
One should touch one's own two knees with the [remaining] fingers, excluding the thumbs, while reciting "namaḥ."
That which is with the [fingers] excluding the thumb is for the liṅga.
Bhāṃ namaḥ to the thumbs and middle fingers at the navel.
Llaṃ namaḥ to the thumb and index finger at the heart.
Vaṃ; salutation with all the fingers to the mouth.
Naṃ namaḥ to the two nostrils with the thumb and ring finger.
That which is called *namaḥ* [is performed] with the fingers excluding the thumbs on both ears.
Pīṃ, salutation to the two eyes with the index and middle fingers.
Saying "Go," one should perform the salutation with the middle finger upon the head.
Furthermore, creation and maintenance must be performed.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the cage of manifestations (vibhūtipañjara).
The word "go" (cow) is used in the sense of a substratum.
The *pīṭha* is Liṅga and the *upapīṭha* is Janābha.
Not in the heart.
Or on the throat.
In the mouth.
Bhā on the right shoulder.
On his left shoulder.
Svā on the right thigh.
Alas, O lady with beautiful thighs! (1)
Goṃ in the throat.
Pī at the navel.
That which is in the womb.
Not in the heart.
And on the right hand.
Or on the left breast.
Bhā is on the right side.
Or on the left side.
O you who are well-established in the loins!
Alas, O you of shapely hips! (2)
On the head of the cow.
And also in the mouth.
Ja is in the right eye.
Nor in the left eye.
Or on the right ear.
Or [the letter] *lla* on the left ear.
O Bhā, you are the skillful one.
Or you who are dwarfed.
Svā on the right cheek.
Or [the letter] on the left cheek (3).
Go to the right arm of Dakṣa.
Pī on the elbows.
At the wrist-joint.
Not at Aṅgulimāla.
Or like [the reflection] on the tip of a finger.
In the root of the left arm.
Alas, my elbows!
To Yamani-bandha.
Obeisance at the base of your fingers.
Alas, on the tip of a finger! (4)
Go to the root of the right thigh.
[The hands] should be placed upon the knees.
Ja is at the ankle.
Not at the base of the fingers.
Alas, on the tip of a finger!
Above the head (5).
Go forth!
Also in the southeast corner.
That which is in the south.
Not in the southwest corner.
Or in the west.
Or else, in the northwest corner.
The vowel *bhā* follows.
He who is in the northeast corner.
Svā is between Īśāna and the East.
Alas! Between the southwest and the west. (6)
On the entire surface of the earth.
And yellow on the right arm.
That which is on the left arm.
Nor on the thighs or the calves.
Or on the left thigh.
On the head.
Bhā is in the right eye.
Or that which is in the left eye.
Svā in the mouth.
Alas, upon my throat! (7)
Go to Dakṣa’s eye.
Ja is in the heart.
Not in the stomach.
Or [it is] at the mūlādhāra.
In the case of the linga.
The syllable *bhā* is at the right knee.
Or on the left knee.
Svā at the tip of the right foot.
Alas! At the tip of your left foot! (8)
Go to the right ear.
Or again, [the syllable] *pī* in the left ear.
That which is on the right cheek.
Not on the left cheek.
Or on the right shoulder.
On the left shoulder.
Bhā is on the right breast.
Or that which is on your left breast.
Svā is on the right side.
Alas! On your left side! (9)
On the upper part of the right thigh, at the hip.
Ja on the right thigh.
Nor on the left thigh.
Or on the right knee.
Or on the left knee.
Bhā is on the right calf.
Ya on the left calf.
Svā on the right foot.
Alas, on your left foot! (10)
Thus has been described the cage of manifestations, which bestows all happiness, wealth, virtue, and liberation;
it is the delighter of the minds of excellent young women, the lotus feet of Hari, and the increaser of devotion.
One should cause this "Mantra-body-cage" to manifest;
it is proclaimed as the destroyer of afflictions, malefic planets, and poisons, and the bestower of fame, prosperity, beauty, splendor, and nourishment.
Oṃ aṃ keśavāya dhātre namaḥ—thus on the forehead.
Naṃ āṃ nārāyaṇāya aryamaṇe namaḥ—thus on the belly. Mo iṃ mādhavāya mitrāya namaḥ—thus on the heart.
Bhaṃ īṃ, obeisance to Govinda, to Varuṇa; [this is] at the pit of the throat.
To Gaṇḍa, to Viṣṇu, to Aṃśu, obeisance! On the right side: Vaṃ ūṃ, to Madhusūdana, to Bhaga, obeisance!
At the base of the right arm.
Taṃ aiṃ, salutation to Trivikrama Vivasvat; on the right throat:
vāṃ aiṃ, salutation to Vāmana Indra.
On the left side.
"Suṃ oṃ śrīdharāya pūrṇa namaḥ" at the base of the left arm.
"Daṃ oṃ, obeisance to Hṛṣīkeśa Parjanya"— thus on the left throat.
"Vāṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Tvaṣṭṛ, the lotus-navelled one," on the back;
"Yaṃ Aḥ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the belly-bound one (Dāmodara)."
133a) Kakudi.
"Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva; salutation to the head"—thus is the placement of the five limbs (*pañcāṅgali-nyāsa*) with palms joined.
"To the Discus, Svāhā;
salutation to the heart"—in this sequence and so forth, one should again perform the placement of the five limbs.
The fingers, with the thumbs straight, form mudrās at the heart and the head.
The fist with the thumbs tucked underneath is for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); the fingers of the two hands joined together are for Brahmā;

the sound produced by the two thumbs and index fingers raised upward from the pair of arms is for Nārāyaṇa; and when they are interlaced crosswise, these are said to be the *mudrās*. If the middle finger is on the right, it is known as the *saṃjñikā*.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣi and the other [limbs].
Salutation to the venerable sage Nārada, and so forth.
Then, having assumed the *karakacchapikā* posture and holding a flower, one should meditate upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
whose splendor is equal to a fresh blue lotus born from a mass of clouds shattered by the jewels of Indra’s bow.

With hair that was very glossy, dark blue, thick, and curled; with a crest like the beautiful peacock feathers of the blue-throated Śiva, adorned with a net-like pattern; beautifully fashioned with a fresh tree from the Saradruma grove cherished by the Rolamba bees; wearing an ear-ornament of a blooming, newly opened blue lotus; with a forehead radiant with a shimmering lock of hair swaying over it, and with cheeks glowing like the face of a makara, and a high, lovely nose. (2) 10-11ab.
Her lower lip is more beautiful than vermilion, and her shoulders are illuminated by the radiance of her gentle smile, which is like the Sindhu, Kunda, and Mandara flowers.

His conch-throat was beautiful and radiant, adorned with clusters of wild sprouts and flowers arranged like necklaces; his shoulders were embellished by spreading garlands of *santānaka* blossoms, frequented by intoxicated, wandering bees;
and the vault of heaven, resplendent with his thick thighs shining like rows of pearl necklaces, was illuminated by the light of the Kaustubha gem. || 10 ||
He was beautifully marked with the auspicious *śrīvatsa* sign; his arms were elevated, long, thick, rounded, and well-formed;
his belly was concave and his navel was noble and deep; he possessed a line of auspicious body hair like a swarm of female bees;
and he was adorned with armlets, bracelets, wave-patterned necklaces, girdles, and anklets set with various jewels.
His slender body was suffused with the glow of divine unguents, and the curve of his hips was draped with yellow garments.
With beautiful thighs and knees, his form was pleasing and well-proportioned; with his lovely, high, and prominent heels, he surpassed the beauty of the tortoise.
His beautiful lotus-feet shine with rows of nails gleaming like rubies and with finger-nails adorned with jewels;
they are lovely with the soles of his reddish hands and feet marked by the fish, goad, flagstaff, barley-corn, lotus, and thunderbolt.
(7) Whose bodily beauty has surpassed the splendor of the body of the Mind-born God (Kāmadeva), having utterly conquered it with the totality of the essence of loveliness;
(8) Whose flute-holes are filled by his lotus-like mouth, and who, with fingers moving upon them,
produces divine melodies that eternally melt the continuous succession of all living beings, becoming an infinite ocean of nectar for the wise.

One should meditate thus: at the *mūlādhāra* is Kuṇḍalinī in the form of the moon; in the center of the heart-lotus is the individual soul (*jīva*) in the form of fire; and in the head is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in the form of the sun. By means of these splendors, the dark-complexioned form [of Kṛṣṇa] is manifested.
Or else: Oṃ! [I salute Him] who is as beautiful as a full-blown blue lotus, whose face is like the moon, who wears a peacock feather as an ornament, and who is beloved.
He who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the magnificent Kaustubha gem, clad in yellow garments and most beautiful.

I worship Govinda, whose body is honored by the lotus-eyes of the gopīs, who is surrounded by hosts of cows and cowherds, who is intent on playing his melodious flute, and whose limbs are adorned with divine ornaments.
Or one should meditate thus.
Then, having meditated "I am Kṛṣṇa," one should worship Him with mental offerings such as arghya and so forth;
thereafter, one should place the arghya vessel.
For example:
Having fashioned a mandala with water, one should place a tripod upon it [reciting]: "Svāhā to the discus that destroys the Asuras!"
Having washed the conch with "Astrāya phaṭ," one should place it upon a tripod;
there, in that conch, [one offers] "Ā cakrāya svāhā."
Salutation to the heart.
Thus one should scatter perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice.
Then, reciting the Vimalamātṛkā, one should fill the conch with pure water;
and for the tripod, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala consisting of ten kalās."
Aṃ, obeisance to the solar disc, whose self consists of twelve kalās.
Thus is the conch.
One should worship the water with: "Oṃ, salutation to the lunar disc, whose self consists of sixteen digits.
Then: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in this water!"
Thus, from the solar disc, one should invoke the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) into that water by means of the hook-gesture (aṅkuśamudrā).
In that water, one should also invoke Śrī Kṛṣṇa from the lotus of one's own heart. One should meditate on Gaṅgā in the conch-water to the left, Sarasvatī in the center, and Yamunā to the right.
Over that water, one should display the Gālinī mudrā while reciting: "To the excellent wheel, to the crest-lock, vauṣaṭ!"
134a) One should gaze at that water with "vauṣaṭ.

Then, one should veil [the water] with both index fingers while reciting: "To the wheel for the protection of the three worlds, svāhā; to the armor, huṃ. One should contemplate that water as being the very nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then: Svāhā to the Ācakrā; homage to the heart.
Svāhā to the moving wheel; vauṣaṭ to the head and the crest-lock.
*Trailokyarakṣaṇacakrāya svāhā kavacāya hūṃ*.
Having placed [the mantra] into that water: *Asurāntakacakrāya svāhā*.
Phaṭ to the weapon!
Having thus performed three claps of the hands, one should perform the binding of the directions with ten snaps of the fingers;
while touching that water, one should recite the root mantra eight times.
Then, one should consecrate it with nectar using the Dhenu-mudrā.
Having placed a little water in another vessel, one should set it down in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Therefore, having taken a little water and recited the root mantra three times, one should sprinkle oneself and the ritual implements for worship.
Then one should worship the Guru on the crown of the head and Gaṇapati at the mūlādhāra.

Then, one should meditate upon the threefold light— the *kuṇḍalinī* in the form of light at the *mūlādhāra*, the individual soul (*jīva*) in the form of light in the heart, and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in the form of light between the eyebrows— as having become unified from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra* through the recitation of the *Kāma-bīja*, appearing as a mass of bliss like a flash of lightning.
By that splendor, [I offer] to my own heart-lotus, svāhā to the heart-mantra (ācakrāya svāhā hṛdayāya).
For the head that has spread out.
To the beautiful wheel, the crest-lock, vauṣaṭ!
Svāhā to the wheel for the protection of the three worlds!
Hūṃ, for the armor.
Svāhā to the wheel of flames; vauṣaṭ to the two eyes.
Svāhā to the discus that ends the asuras; Phaṭ to the weapon!

Thus, having meditated upon the manifestation of the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, complete in all its limbs through the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantra), and having contemplated the identity between one’s own body and the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [one should perform] within that body— which is non-different from the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the rites beginning with the *vibhūti-pañjara* and ending with the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*).
Having performed the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa) in the prescribed order, one should worship.

One should worship the Lord, whose body is non-different from the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, with the ten services consisting of: a seat, welcome, water for the hands, water for the feet, water for sipping, the honey-mixture, water for sipping again, bathing materials, garments, and ornaments.
Furthermore, beginning from the location for the placement of the *vibhūti* with palms joined (*añjali-nyāsa*) up to the location for the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*),
one should worship one's own body with the mantras of those two placements, extending as far as those respective locations of placement.
Furthermore, in the self-perception, one should worship the flute at the heart, the forest garland above the breast, and the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha gem.
If one is unable to do so here, one should perform the worship with the mantra of the *vibhūtipañjara-nyāsa*.
However, one should worship the seats and ornaments in the sequence beginning with the placement of the *pīṭha* (sacred seat) and so forth;
if one is unable even for this, one should worship with six *añjali* gestures.
Then, having recited the root mantra, one should smear all the limbs with sandalwood paste.
Then, from the tip of the flame of the lamp, one should apply twelve long *tilaka* marks with the ring finger (*nāmikā*) at twelve locations:
with "Oṃ aṃ Keśava, obeisance to Dhātṛ" on the forehead; with "Naṃ āṃ Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to Aryaman" on the left [side].
Moṃ Iṃ, to Mādhava, the Friend, in the heart.
Bhaṃ īṃ, to Govinda and Varuṇa, at the pit of the throat.
To Gaṇḍa Viṣṇu Aṃśu, on the right side.
Vaṃ ūṃ, to Madhusudana Bhaga, at the base of the right arm.
To him, the three-striding Vivasvat, on the right throat.
VĀM AIṂ, for Vāmana and Indra; on the left side.
Suṃ Oṃ, to Śrīdhara, at the root of the left upper arm.
Daṃ Oṃ, to Hṛṣīkeśa, to Parjanya; [this is] on the left neck.
Vām-aṃ to Padmanābha; Tvaṣṭṛ on the back.
Aṃ Aḥ, salutation to Dāmodara Viṣṇu on the hump.
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Vāsudeva; salutation—thus [one should recite] on the head.

Then, having filled the hollow of one's hands with white *tulasī* leaves mixed with white sandalwood paste, and having recited the mantra at the base [of the plant], one should offer it, saying: "Obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; this handful of *tulasī* leaves is offered."
Thus, one should place it near the right foot.

With red *tulasī* leaves mixed with red sandalwood paste, according to the previously established procedure, one should offer a handful (*añjali*) of *tulasī* leaves at the left foot, saying: "Obeisance (*namaḥ*)."
Then, having filled his joined palms with white sandalwood mixed with white sandalwood flowers,
he should offer a handful of white karavīra flowers smeared with white sandalwood paste to the chest, saying "Namaḥ," as before.
Then, having filled his joined palms with white and red lotuses smeared with white and red sandalwood paste,
and having recited the root mantra, he should place the joined palms of white and red lotuses upon his head, saying: "Obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇā."

Thus, having filled his joined palms with various kinds of flowers smeared with the two types of sandalwood paste, he should apply them to all limbs [of the deity] while reciting: "Obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇā, this handful of flowers.
In the same manner, he should offer incense and a lamp.
Then, with the mind, one should satisfy Śrī Kṛṣṇa with nectars flowing from the lunar orb situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Then, having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he should offer betel-leaf with camphor.
Then, having gratified Śrī Kṛṣṇa with dance, song, and instrumental music, one should take water and, with the *brahmārpaṇa* mantra, offer oneself and the act of worship into one's own hand.
135a) Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Oṃ, let us know Kāmadeva; let us meditate upon the one with the flower-bow; may he impel us.

Having thus recited the *kāmagāyatrī*, one should offer the recitation with devotion; then, while contemplating the true nature of the mantra's meaning—the state of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—one should recite the root mantra ten times.
Having again performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should offer the recitation (*japa*) into the right hand of the Blessed One with [the words] beginning with "* * * ti * * ?tyādi*."
Furthermore, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) once more.
Having recited the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) one hundred and eight times, encased by the syllable *oṃ*, one should practice yoga.
As for the yoga:

In the Mūlādhāra, within the triangle and the four-petalled lotus presided over by the four syllables va, śa, ṣa, and sa, is the seed-syllable *klīṃ*, resembling a bandhūka flower and marked with a bindu pervaded by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. Above that is the syllable *aiṃ*.
Therein is Kuṇḍalinī, in the form of a sleeping serpent, situated with three and a half coils, [awakened] by the syllable *huṃ*.

Having struck with the mental rod (manodaṇḍa), one should lead [the breath] through the sequential piercing of the six chakras— Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and the thousand-petaled lotus located in the head— and there,
by means of the stream of nectar dripping from the lunar orb situated therein, which is red in color and composed of the essence of the maṇḍala, [one should reach] the end.
Having thoroughly satiated Kuṇḍalinī and meditated for a long time upon oneself in the form of the deity to be visualized while reciting the mantra,
[one should lead] Padma through the piercing sequence of the Ājñā, Viśuddha, Anāhata, Maṇipūraka, Svādhiṣṭhāna, and Mūlādhāra [cakras].
One should lead that [consciousness] to the place situated in the mūlādhāra.
Thus is the yoga.
Violating the teacher's bed, drinking [intoxicants], killing a twice-born, and the theft of gold are sinful acts.
Everything becomes disagreeable when one's conduct is like that of a new bridegroom.

Thus, having arisen from the yoga and performed *prāṇāyāma* again, one should offer the recitation of the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) with the mantra beginning "O most secret of secrets" (*guhyātiguhyā*) into the right hand of the Blessed One.
Then, one should perform worship upon the external seat.
Worship of Hari should be performed in this manner using a śāligrāma, a mind-machine, a mandala, an image, and so forth; however, it should not be performed upon the bare ground alone.
Now follows the extraction of the yantra.

First, having fashioned a hexagon, above it an eight-petalled lotus, and outside that a square abode provided with four doors and adorned with eight tridents in the eight directions; then, in the center of the pericarp of the hexagon, [one should place] the Kāma-bīja, saying: "Grant me the accomplishment of my desired goal."
Having written it, one should encircle it with ten syllables.
135b) In the four corners, beginning with the southeast (āgneya).
One should write the seed-syllable of Śrī in the four directions starting from the east, and likewise the seed-syllable of Māyā.
On the pericarp and externally on the six angles, one should write the six syllables: *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya namaḥ*.
Having divided the three syllables of the *kāmagāyatrī* mantra into three parts, one should write them in the middle of each pair of filaments.
Having divided the six syllables of the *kāmadevamālāmantra* into six parts, one should write them on each petal.
Having drawn the circle on the ground, one should write the seed-syllable *śrīṃ* and the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* in pairs, two by two, in the eight directions beginning with the east.
And the *kāmagāyatrī*.
"Kāmadevāya vidmahe," and so forth, is the garland mantra (*mālāmantra*) of Kāmadeva.

Klīṃ! Salutations to Kāmadeva, who is dear to all people, who deludes all people; blaze, blaze, burn brightly, burn brightly; bring the hearts of all people under my control, bring them under my control! Svāhā!
One should worship in that yantra.
Salutation to the foundational power, to Prakṛti.
To the Tortoise.
To Śeṣa.
For the sake of forbearance.
To the ocean.
To Śvetadvīpa.
Homage to the Pavilion Blazing with Jewels.
In the east, obeisance to Mandāra.
To Santānaka in the south, homage!
Salutation to Pārijāta in the west.
In the north, obeisance to the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
In the center, "Homage to Haricandana."
Homage to the Jewel Lion Throne.
In the southeast corner of the lion throne:

"Homage to Dharma in the form of a bull, red in color, who is the foot of the pedestal. In the southwest corner: [Homage to Dharma in the form of a bull, red in color, who is the foot of the pedestal].
For the sake of knowledge, [homage] to the one in the form of a lion, of dark complexion, as before.
In the northwest corner.
"To him who is for the sake of dispassion, who has the form of a man, who is the five jewels, and who is yellow in color"—as before.
In the northeast corner, for the pedestal-foot in the form of an elephant, sapphire-colored, for the sake of sovereignty, obeisance!
On the eastern side of the lion throne.
Salutation to Ardharmāya, whose limbs rest upon a seat.
On the right side.
For ignorance, as before.
In the western part.
And [it is taught] as "for the sake of non-enmity."
In the northern part.
Homage to Anaiśvaryā, who resides on the pedestal.
Again, in the middle.
Salutation to Śeṣa.
Homage to the Unborn One.
Aṃ, salutation to the solar disc, whose nature consists of twelve kalās.
Ūṃ, salutation to the lunar orb, whose essence consists of sixteen digits.
136a) Maṃ, obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten digits.
Saṃ, obeisance to sattva.
Raṃ, obeisance to Rajas. Taṃ, obeisance to Tamas.
White is Sattva, red is Rajas, and dark is Tamas.
Āṃ, salutation to the Self. Aṃ, salutation to the Inner Self.
Salutation to the Supreme Self.
Hrīṃ, salutation to the Self of Knowledge.
Then, on the eastern petal of the lotus.
Āṃ, obeisance to Vimalā; [this is] on the southeastern petal.
Īṃ, obeisance to Utkarṣiṇī.
On the southern petal.
Oṃ, salutation to Jñānā.
On the petal of Nairṛta.
Aiṃ, salutation to Kriyā.
On the western petal.
Aiṃ, salutation to Yoga.
In the petal of the northwest.
Oṃ, homage to Prasvī.
On the northern petal.
Oṃ, salutation to Satyā.
On the petal of Īśāna.
Aṃ, obeisance to Īśānā.
In the middle.
Aḥ, salutation to Anugrahā.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, the self of all beings, Vāsudeva; homage to the one whose self is the lotus-throne of the yoga of union with the Self of All.
Then, in the center: *śrīkṛṣṇāya namaḥ*.
Having thus offered a handful of flowers to the image.
Śiva in the northeast.
In the south-eastern direction, Gaṇeśa.
In the southwest, Sūrya.
One should worship Durgā in the northwest,
just as [one worships] in the northeast.

Oṃ! One should constantly meditate upon Maheśa, who resembles a mountain of silver, who has the beautiful moon as his crest-jewel, whose limbs are radiant with jeweled ornaments, who holds an axe, a nectar-pot, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who is gracious.

Seated upon a lotus, praised on all sides by hosts of immortals, wearing a tiger skin, the primordial source of the universe, the seed of the universe, the remover of all fears, five-faced and three-eyed—[I praise him]. (10.439)
Having meditated thus, one should perform the external worship.
In the south-eastern direction.
Having the luster of vermilion, three eyes, and a broad belly, he holds with his lotus-like hands a tusk, a noose, a goad, and a desirable citron fruit that delights the many bees.

Worship Gaṇapati, whose crown shines like the crescent moon, whose face is like that of an elephant, whose cheeks bear the marks of the *dāna* ichor, who utters a roar like a lordly elephant, and who is clothed in red garments and smeared with red unguents.
Thus, as before,
in the southwest.

I worship the Sun, who sits upon a red lotus throne, the singular ocean of all virtues, the sovereign of all worlds, holding two lotuses, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons in his lotus-like hands.
Wearing a beautiful crown with a ruby crest and possessing three eyes.
In the northwestern direction.
Oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ, homage to Durgā.
The meditation on this [is as follows].
Seated upon a lion, crowned with the moon, resembling emerald in hue, she holds a conch, a discus, a bow, and an arrow in her four arms; adorned with three eyes,
she is graced by armlets, necklaces, and a tinkling girdle with jingling anklets.
May you, adorned with earrings shimmering with jewels, become the remover of miserable rebirths from difficult states of existence.
Having thus meditated upon Mahiṣamardinī, one should worship her with clarified butter.

Then, having taken a handful of flowers from the *karakacchapikā* vessel and meditating upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is composed of light, within the lotus of one's own heart, one should recite the root mantra. Then,
[the mantra] flows from the lotus of one's own heart through the path of the *suṣumṇā*, out through the nostrils, consisting of the phonemes of the *mātṛkā*.

Thinking, "Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is consciousness, has arrived within this handful of flowers," one should invoke Him with: "O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, come here, come here! Stay here, stay here! Be present here, be present here! Be firmly established here, be firmly established here! Svāhā to the moon! (Ācandrāya svāhā).
Salutation to the heart; to the all-pervading wheel, salutation to the head.
To the beautiful wheel, the crest-lock, vauṣaṭ!
Hūṃ! To the armor that is the wheel for protecting the three worlds.
To the wheel of flames, vauṣaṭ to the two eyes;
to the wheel that is the end of the asuras, svāhā!
Phaṭ to the weapon!
Thus, having struck three times upward with the *tāla* gesture, one should perform the sealing of the directions with ten snaps of the fingers.
Saying "Hūṃ," one should conceal [the area] with the two index fingers; saying "Vaṃ," one should transform it into nectar by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* and then make it supreme.
In all cases, one should display one's own *mudrā*.
Then I shall display the marks of the flute, the forest garland, the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha jewel, and the Bilva fruit.

A seat, a welcome, water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), further water for sipping, bathing materials, garments, and ornaments. || 10.443 ||
The wise one should sequentially arrange the sixteen services: perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and likewise prostration. (10.444)
Regarding this, he states the distinction:
With perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
Taking water mixed with *durvā* grass, [one offers] the *arghya* to Śrī Kṛṣṇa with the utterance "svadhā."
Thus, one should place it upon the head of the deity.

Taking water mixed with *śyāmāka*, *dūrvā*, lotus, and *aparājitā*, and reciting the root mantra, one should offer it to the lotus feet with the formula: "This is the *pādya* for Śrī Kṛṣṇa; obeisance.
Then, taking water mixed with nutmeg (*jātī*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), and *kakkola*, as before, [one should offer] this *ācamanīya* for Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
One should offer [the water] with "namaḥ" into the lotus of the mouth.
Having placed clarified butter, curd, and honey in a bronze vessel and covered it with another bronze vessel,
one offers the madhuparka into the lotus of the mouth with "namaḥ."
This water for rinsing the mouth is offered; salutations!
One should bathe with fragrant water.
Then, the cloth for wiping the body.
Then, a pair of garments to be worn.
The sacred thread, necklaces, and other ornaments.
Anointing with musk, saffron, and gorocanā.
Sandalwood, agallochum, drīvera, aṣṭa, saffron, and sevyaka.
Jaṭāmāṃsī, māṃsī, and mura are known as the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu.
Hrīṃ: Varā, balā, kuṣṭha, kuṭha, savyaka, the root of vīraṇa, murā, and māṃsī.
One should offer various kinds of flowers and incense prepared from guggulu, agallochum, daśīra, sugar, honey, sandalwood, and clarified butter.
One should offer a ghee lamp within a casing filled with camphor.
Sweet side-dishes, pure milk-rice, and sugar with honey.
One should offer together with plantain fruit that which is fit for consumption with clarified butter (*sājya*).
*Upadaṃśa* refers to substances to be chewed, such as pieces of sugarcane and the like; *pāyasa* is a preparation of milk.
One should offer curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, sugar, and milk with the letter 'śa' [in its name].
This is the procedure for the offering of food (naivedya).
A wise person should prepare an offering for Śrī Hari using a vessel made of gold, silver, bell-metal, copper, or even clay, or one made from the wood of the Palāśa tree. (10.445)
Having brought the food offering (naivedya) before him, [recite] "Astrāya Phaṭ."

Having thus protected [the offering] with the *cakramudrā*, having sprinkled it with water while reciting "Yam," one should dry up the defects of the food offering (*naivedya*). Having touched it with the hand while reciting the fire-seed-syllable "Ram," one should burn away the defects. Having performed the rite with the wind-seed-syllable "Yam," one should contemplate it as being filled with the essence of nectar by reciting the nectar-seed-syllable "Vam. Then, by means of the root mantra, one should transform it into the nature of nectar.

Having reflected, touched [the water], and recited the root mantra eight times, one should visualize it as being filled with nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā*, and worship it for the sake of the food offering (*naivedya*) with the words, "Salutation to fragrance and flowers."
Salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having worshipped with sandalwood paste and flowers, one should contemplate that the splendor issuing from the mouth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa has entered the food offering (naivedya).
Reciting the root mantra, one should say: "This food offering is for Śrī Kṛṣṇa; salutation."
Thus, one should offer water for the food offering (naivedya).
Taking that food offering with both hands, one should offer it while saying: "I offer this to the Blessed One; may Hari accept this oblation," and then perform the *arghya* rite.
With the left hand, one should display the *grāsamudrā*, which resembles a full-blown blue lotus.

Having offered water into the mouth of the deity with the mantra, "Thou art the under-layer of nectar, svāhā," and touching the thumb, the little finger, and the ring finger of the right hand, [one offers] with the mantra, "To Prāṇa, svāhā."
Likewise, touching the middle finger with the thumb for *apāna*;
similarly, touching the ring finger with the thumb for *samāna*.
In this manner, touching the index finger, middle finger, and ring finger with the thumb.
To the inspired utterance, svāhā!
Thus, with all the fingers: svāhā to vyāna.
Thus one should say.
Thus, the five mudrās of prāṇa and the others have been declared.

Reciting the mantra, "Ṭhaṃ Voṃ Namaḥ Parāya Paramātmane Niruddhāya Naivedyaṃ Kalpayāmi Namaḥ," one should display the *naivedya-mudrā*, which consists of touching the two ring fingers with the two thumbs.
Having offered water into the mouth of the deity with the mantra "amṛtāpidhānam asi svāhā," and having again offered water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīya), one should offer betel-leaf with camphor.
It is desired that [the offering] be made first to the deity between the object of attainment (sādhya) and the means of attainment (sādhana).
To the east of the deity.
Salutation to Dāma.
On the right.
Salutation to Sudāmā.
In the west.
Homage to Vasudāmā;
[this is] in the north.
Salutation to Kiṅkinī.
In the southeast corner of the deity's [mandala].
To the revolving heart, svāhā; homage to the heart!
In the southwest corner.
To the one who has spread out the wheel.
On the head.
In the northwest corner.
To Sucakrā, the crest-lock.
In the northeast.

"Hūṃ! To the armor, the wheel for protecting the three worlds, hūṃ! "Phaṭ! To the weapon, the wheel that destroys the asuras in the four directions beginning with the east, phaṭ! Thus one should worship the five limbs.
To Rukmiṇī, salutation on the eastern petal of the Lord.
On the petal in the southeast.
To Satyabhāmā.
On the southern petal.
To Agnijitī on the southwestern petal;
to Sunandā on the western petal.
To Mitravindā.
On the petal of Vāyu:
to Lakṣmaṇā.
On the northern petal.
To Jāmbavatī.
On the petal of Īśāna: salutation to Suśīlā.
Thus, one should worship with [the mantra] beginning with the *praṇava*.
There, at the tips of the petals in the east and other directions.
Oṃ, obeisance to Vasudeva.
Oṃ, obeisance to Devakī. Oṃ, obeisance to Nanda.
Oṃ, homage to Yaśodā.
Oṃ, homage to Valabhadra.
Oṃ, homage to Subhadrā. Oṃ, homage to the cowherds.
Oṃ, salutation to the Gopīs.
Then, one should worship outside the petals in the sequence starting from the east: first, in the east.
"Salutation to Mandāra"—thus [he recites] in the four directions as previously described.
In the center: "Salutation to Haricandana."
Then, in the square of the deity:
in the east, *oṃ indrāya namaḥ*.
In the southeast corner.
Oṃ, homage to Agni;
in the south:
Oṃ, homage to Yama.
In the southwest.
Oṃ, to Nairṛta, in the west.
Oṃ, to Varuṇa.
In the northwest corner.
138a) Oṃ, homage to Vāyu.
In the north.
Oṃ, homage to Kuvera;
in the northeast: Oṃ, homage to Īśāna.
Between Indra and Īśāna.
Oṃ, homage to Brahmā.
Between the south-west and the west:
Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta.
Furthermore, one should worship near that [deity] again, following the sequence starting from the east.
Oṃ, homage to Vakrā.
Oṃ, to Śakti.
Oṃ, to Daṇḍa.
Oṃ, to the miserable one!
Oṃ, to the noose.
Oṃ, to the goad!
Oṃ, to the mace!
Oṃ, to the trident.
Oṃ, to the Lotus.
Oṃ, to the wheel.
Oṃ, to Śaṅkha.
In the center: Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; obeisance to Vāsudeva.
Oṃ, to Nārāyaṇa.
Oṃ, to the son of Devakī.
Oṃ, salutation to the best of the Yadus.
Oṃ, salutation to Vārṇeya.
Oṃ, homage to the one who removes the burden of the asuras.
"Oṃ, obeisance to the establisher of the Dharma.
Having thus worshipped, one should again worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa with the arghya and other offerings.
In that regard, there is a specific procedure for the incense:
having worshipped the bell with a flower while reciting "Oṃ, obeisance to the bell," one should ring the bell with the left hand.
Holding incense with the right hand, one should contemplate.

Thus, holding a lamp with the right hand, one should show it to the Lord from the eyes down to the feet; then, having uttered the root mantra, saying "I satisfy Śrī Kṛṣṇa," one should offer libations of water into the mouth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa three times.
Then, one should offer fragrant water for drinking.
Then, having offered a mouthful of water into the mouth of the deity with the mantra, "Thou art the lid for the dead, svāhā," [one offers] a tooth-stick for the purpose of cleaning the teeth.
One should offer camphor powder for the purpose of cleansing the hands and water for sipping (ācamana).
Thereafter, one should present anointing unguent mixed with camphor, betel leaf, and flowers.
One should contemplate that the splendor which issued from the mouth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa has entered one's own mouth once again.

Then, having fanned [the deity] with a chowrie and shown him a mirror, and having gratified the Lord with dance, song, and instrumental music, he performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). Having recited the root mantra one thousand and eight times—or one hundred times—and again performing three breath-restraints, he said: "O you, the protector of the most secret of secrets, accept that which has been performed by us."
"O Lord Janārdana, may there be success for me through your grace. Having said this,
he should offer the *japa* into the right hand of the deity with the water from the *argha* vessel.
Then, having praised Him with the verse beginning "navīnanīradaśyāmam" (dark as a fresh rain-cloud) and having circumambulated Him,
one should perform a prostration like a staff— the eight-limbed salutation— with the chest,
the head, the gaze, the mind, and likewise with speech.
Prostration with the two feet, the two hands, and the two knees is declared to be the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) salutation.
Now.
Prostrations with the two feet, the two hands, and the head are known as the five-limbed (pañcāṅga) salutations.
Those with eight limbs are declared the best, while those with five limbs are recorded as middling.
One should never perform a prostration while keeping the deity behind one's back;
then, having sat down and taken a mouthful of water, [one should proceed].
Therefore, prior to that, from the authority over the functions of the body,

may whatever has been thought by the mind, spoken by speech, or performed by action— with the hands, feet, belly, and genitals— whether in the states of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep, all of that become an offering unto Brahman.
Svāhā!
I offer myself and everything belonging to me to Hari.
With the mantra "Oṃ tat sat," one should offer oneself at the lotus feet of the Deity.
Then, having taken the remains of the offerings with the *saṃhāramudrā* (withdrawal gesture),...

Having said, "O Lord, you have been worshipped; please accept [this]," and having smelled [the flower], one should bring the effulgent Śrī Kṛṣṇa from the nostril into one's own heart and discard the *nirmālya* on the ground.
Then, taking another *nirmālya*, one should say: "Salutations to Viṣvaksena."
One should cast [the remains] toward the northeast.
Taking the remainder of the food offering (*naivedya*), one should cast it toward the northeast, saying: "This remains of the food offering (*ucchiṣṭanaivedya*) is for Viṣvaksena; obeisance."
Having placed the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) upon one's head, and having consumed the water from the feet (*caraṇodaka*) and the food offering (*naivedya*), one should drink them,
contemplate oneself as being of the very nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and remain at ease.
In the ritual procedure for the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*), one should separately recite forty thousand times the excellent ten-syllable mantra.
Gradually:
if it consists of eighteen syllables, the number is said to be twenty thousand.
Now follows the sequential order.

Then, first of all: breath control (prāṇāyāma), the ritual placement of the body as a cage of deities (mūrtipañjara-nyāsa), the ritual placement on the hands (kara-nyāsa), and the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa).
The ritual placement of the sages and others (ṛṣyādinyāsa); the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa); and meditation (dhyāna).
The display of mudrās;
the placement of the argha vessel.
Following the sequence of the *mūrttipañjara*, one applies twelve *tilakas* at the twelve locations;
thereafter, one performs the offering of six handfuls of water upon one's own body.
Then follows breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Then follows the recitation of the Kāmagāyatrī.
One should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, one should recite the Kāma-bīja, encased by the Praṇava (Oṃ), one hundred and eight times. Following that, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The offering of the recitation into the right hand of the deity; [the salutation] to the Guru at the crown of the head.
139a) One should pay homage to Gaṇeśa at the mūlādhāra.
Thus ends the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), concluding with "then the yoga."
Then, the external worship is as follows.
One should offer a single handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) above the deity.
One should worship Śiva in the northeast (*aiśānī*), Gaṇeśa in the southeast (*āgneyī*), Sūrya in the southwest (*naiṛtī*), and Durgā in the northwest (*vāyavī*).
Then, having meditated once more, one should invoke the deity into the image;
this is the worship with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra-pūjā).
One should worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa with the Kṛṣṇāṣṭaka hymn.
To the deity, one should offer three handfuls of flowers.
Three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The recitation of the root mantra.
Having again performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should offer the recitation (japa) into the right hand of the deity.
Then, one should perform a circumambulation.
The prostration with the body.
The recitation of the hymn.
The offering of incense.
The extinguishing of the lamp.
The offering of oneself.
The bringing of the deities to the heart by means of the saṃhāramudrā.
The worship of Viṣvaksena, the wearing of the remains of the offering (nirmālya), and the consumption of the food offering (naivedya).
Thus is the sequential order.
Thus ends the *Śrīgopālapūjāpaddhati*.
Now follows the Gopālaka-kaṣava (The Armor of the Cowherd).
He spoke first:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, O Lord, please out of compassion tell me that armor which has been revealed, known as the 'Auspiciousness of the Three Worlds'."
The venerable Sanatkumāra said: Listen, O best of Brahmins, I shall proclaim this most wonderful armor (kavaca), which was formerly told out of compassion by Nārāyaṇa to Brahmā.
Brahmā has told this to me; out of great affection, I shall speak it to you—this most secret reality, which is the embodiment of the flood of Brahmā-mantras.
By retaining and reciting which, Brahmā certainly expands the creation;
by retaining and reciting which, Mahālakṣmī pervades the three worlds. (10.450)
Śambhu, the knower of all principles, is the destroyer who wards off the Pāṭhānas;
Durgā, the mother of the three worlds, [is the slayer] of the great Asuras such as Mahiṣa.
I did not slay him because he was arrogant toward the boon, but rather because of his recitation and retention [of this mantra].
In this way, Indra and all the others shall attain complete sovereignty.
One should reveal [this] to a disciple who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and a spiritual practitioner;
by giving it to a rogue or the disciple of another, one shall meet with death. (10.453)
The Prajāpati [Brahmā] is the seer of this armor of Trailokyamaṅgala;
the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Nārāyaṇa himself. (10.454)
The application [of this mantra] is proclaimed for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa:
"Oṃ, may the Praṇava protect my head, and may there be salutation to Nārāyaṇa. (10.455)
The syllable *bāṃ* with two eyes (*ba*) protects; the eight-syllabled mantra bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
*klīṃ* with two eyes (*kḷ*) protects; the single-syllabled mantra (*e*) deludes all. (10.456)
Klīṃ! To Kṛṣṇa, [I offer] my nose always; to Govinda, my tongue;
to Gopījanavallabha, my feet—svāhā! May there be victory for me! 10-457.
May the eighteen-syllable mantra protect the throat; may the ten-syllable mantra protect [the face];
and may the phrase "gopījanavallabhāya svāhā" protect the two arms.
*klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ*—salutation to the dark-limbed one; this is the ten-syllable mantra for the shoulders.
*klīṃ* Kṛṣṇa *klīṃ*—the means of the hands; *klīṃ*—this indeed is the life-force of Kṛṣṇa. (10.459)
The heart is *śrībhuvaneśī* (*klīṃ*); may my breasts belong to Kṛṣṇa. May the pair of my flanks always belong to Gopāla, with the wife of Agni (*svāhā*). (10.460)

Klīṃ; may the most excellent mantra protect the two sides for Kṛṣṇa at all times. May the mantra consisting of Kṛṣṇa and Govinda, joined with the word "ḍe" and preceded by "smara," provide protection. (10.461)
May the eight-syllable mantra protect the navel; may "Kṛṣṇe" protect the heart, and "Vidvat" the throat.
May "Klīṃ Kṛṣṇakaṃ Kālaṃ Klīṃ" protect the back, and "Kṛṣṇāya Dviṭhāntakaḥ" protect the head. || 10-462 ||
May the Śrī-hrīṃ-klīṃ-kṛṣṇaṭha-dvaya mantra always protect the hips; may the seven-syllable mantra protect the thighs, and the thirteen-syllable mantra likewise. (10.463)

The mantra beginning with *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *klīṃ*, followed by the words *gopījanavallabha*, then *mama bhāryāṃ svāhā* for the anus, and ending with *klīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ*, consists of ten syllables. (10.464)
May Hrīḥ, Śrīḥ, and Klīḥ always protect the knees; may the ten-syllable mantra protect [them]. May the thirteen-syllable mantra, bearing the discus and other weapons, protect the shanks. (10.465)
The eighteen-syllable mantra beginning with *hrīḥ* and *śrīḥ*, consisting of twenty syllables—may the powerful leader of Dvārakā always protect all my limbs. (10.466)
"Obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, who is beyond that;
may this twelve-syllable mantra beginning with 'Tārā' always protect me in the east. (10.467)
Śrī klī hrī; the ten-syllable mantra is klī hrī śrī—the sixteen-syllable [mantra].
May Viṣṇu, bearing the mace and other weapons, protect me from the direction of Agni. (10.468)
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ! May the ten-syllable mantra always protect me on the right.
Tārā! Homage to the Blessed One, the beloved of Rucibhaṇī! (10.469)
"SVĀHĀ"—this sixteen-syllable mantra shall protect me in the southwestern direction (Nairṛtī).
"KLĪṂ HRṢIKE PADAṂ ŚĀYA NAMO MĀṂ VARUṆEVA TU. (10.470)
The mantra consisting of eighteen syllables ending with "Kāma" (namely *namaḥ kāmadevāya*) should always protect me in the northwest;
the mantra of two syllables (*dviṭha*) is *śrīkāmāya sakṛṣṇāya govindāya*.
May Viṣṇu, whose essence consists of twelve syllables, always protect me in the north:
Vāgbhava (AIM), Kāmakṛṣṇāya, Hrīḥ, and thereafter Govindāya. (10.472)
And "Śrīgopījanavallabhāya svāhā"—
this twenty-two-syllable mantra shall always protect me in the northeast.
I bow to that son of Devakī, the unswerving King of Dance, who performs divine dance in the midst of the hoods of Kīlīya.
The twenty-two-syllable mantra also protects me from all sides:
"We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon the one with flower-arrows; may Anaṅga impel us. May *ṣā* protect me from above.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have described to you that which embodies the multitude of Brahma-mantras.
The armor named Trailokyamaṅgala, which has the nature of Brahman,
was heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa by the lords headed by Brahmā and Īśa.
Out of affection for you, I have told this; it must not be spoken to anyone.
Then, having prostrated before the Guru according to the rules, one should recite the armor (*kavaca*).
Whether once or thrice, according to his knowledge, that teacher is likewise entirely free from delusion regarding all mantras; of this there is no doubt. (10.478)

The traditional rule for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is one hundred and eight repetitions; having performed the fire-oblations and other rites with a tenth part of that number, one will certainly accomplish that goal. (10.479)
If one should indeed become oneself the all-pervading Lord whose armor is perfected,
then for him there shall be the accomplishment of mantra through the performance of *puraścaryā* according to the prescribed rules.
Then Lakṣmī and Vāṇī shall dwell there, constantly rousing emulation;
O Lord, one should recite this eightfold handful of flowers at the root of the deity just once.
If one writes [this] on birch bark, places it in a pill, and wears it within gold, one shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand years of worship. (10.482)
Whether on your neck or on your right arm, he too is Viṣṇu, without a doubt;
[it is equal to] thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
Even those great gifts and the circumambulation of the earth do not equal even a sixteenth part of that which results from reciting [this] just once.
By the grace of the armor-mantra, a man shall become liberated while living;
he truly agitates the three worlds and becomes a conqueror of the three worlds. (10.485)
If one worships Puruṣottama without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca),
then even if the mantra is recited a hundred lakhs of times, it will not grant success.
Thus ends the armor-rite named Trailokyamaṅgala in the venerable Sanatkumārasaṃhitā.
Now follows the Thousand Names of Gopāla.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, Gaurī questioned Śaṅkara:
"You are the Lord of the entire universe, the agent of creation and destruction. (10.487)
"You alone are worshipped by the worlds, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods;
O Lord of Gods, whose hymn of praise do you, Maheśvara, constantly recite? (10.488)
"O Śaṅkara, this which has been told produces wonder within me.
Therefore, O Lord of my life, O highly wise one, O Śaṅkara, cut through my doubt. (10.489)
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O Pārvatī, you are blessed and you have performed meritorious deeds, since you ask for this secret among secrets, O lady of beautiful countenance, who are as dear to me as my own life. (10.490)
O Great Goddess, because of your feminine nature, you ask this again;
it must be concealed, concealed, concealed with great effort. (5) 10-491
If it is disclosed, there will be failure; therefore, one should guard it with effort.
This is the supreme secret that bestows the goals of human existence. (10.492)
Merely by being remembered, it bestows a flood of wealth, jewels, rubies, horses, garlands, elephants, and so forth, and grants great liberation. (7) 10-493
I shall explain that to you; listen with focused attention, my dear.
That stainless God, Janārdana, whose nature is consciousness—(8) 10-494.
In order to enable men to cross the ocean of saṃsāra forever, he remains pervading the three worlds in the form of the glorious Gaṅgā’s current. (10.495)
Then those who are greatly deluded in the world and devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu do not attain certainty, thinking again that Hari is Nārāyaṇa. (10-496)
Stainless and formless, out of a desire to please his devotees, he manifested the form of Gopāla for the sake of sporting in Vṛndāvana. (10.497)

The Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, who was raised by the eminent cowherd Nanda, and his mother Yaśodā, who is the personification of the Earth and the bestower of joy; (13) || 10-499 ||
O Queen of the Gods, requested by Brahmā and even by the gods, the Lord, cherished by the two [parents], was born from Devakī through Vasudeva. (14) 10-500.
Born from the earth and protected by Muralīvada Recikā, he took counsel with her and was then born upon the surface of the earth. (15) || 10-501 ||
I meditate upon this eternal, worshipful light—the dark yet radiant splendor that is the very essence and all-in-all of saṃsāra. (16) 10-502
O Śivā, one who has been distressed by the splendor of a fair-complexioned person should worship the splendor of a dark-complexioned one;

O Maheśvarī, one who kills a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a stealer of gold, and the fifth who associates with such persons—by these defects one becomes defiled through the piercing of the vital energy (tejas). (10.504)
From that, the light known as the form of Rādhā-Mādhava arose;

Therefore, O Goddess of gods, in the Kali age, only a few rare Vaiṣṇavas who have received it from Nārada know this; it must be guarded with great effort.
