Of this *Śrīgopālasahasranāmastotra*, Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śrīgopāla is the deity (*devatā*), Kāma is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Māyā is the power (*śakti*), and Candra is the peg (*kīlaka*).
Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining the state of being a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra during the recitation of the *Śrīgopālasahasranāma*.
Now, meditation.

Vāmana, who became Vāmanī; the vomiter, born from vomiting;
the delighter of Yaśodā; the agent; the bestower of liberation from the Yamalārjuna trees. (49) || 10-535 ||
Ulūkhali, Mahāmāna, Dhāmavad-dhāhayīśami, the Lord Keśava who acts in accordance with his devotees and who bears the plow. (50) 10-536

the lotus-hued, the lotus-eyed, and he who is ever-devoted to the face of Kamalā. (54) 10-540 ||

The slayer of Tāraka, the brother of Surabhi, the agitator of Mārīca, the beloved of Viśvāmitra, the self-controlled, Rāma, the lotus-eyed one. (56) || 10-542 ||

Candrāvalī’s husband, the shore, Kaṃsa’s slayer, the killer of Kaṃsa, Mādhava, the destroyer of Madhu, the wine, the wife of Mādhava, and the all-pervading Lord. (58) 10-544 ||
Wading through the mud of the Muñjāṭavī forest, the son of Nidhara [resided] there;

Likewise, the region of Tālavana, the grove of Bhāṇḍīra, Tṛṇāvarta who acted with compassion, and the husband of Vṛṣabhānu’s daughter; (60) 10-546.
Equal to the very life-breath of Rādhā, a bee at the lotus-face of Rādhā, the divine astrologer who delights the gopīs, and one worshipped with the lotus of his playful pastimes. (61) 10-547
A multitude of play-lotuses, the delighter of the cowherd girls' affection, the dyer, the stage for the art of coloring, the one who colors, and the great tree of the theater. (62) 10-548

Bhramarā, Kuntalī, Kuntī, Sutarakṣī, Mahāmakhī, Yamunā, Varadātā, and Kaśyapasya-varapradā. (67) || 10-553 ||

Phalguna, the friend of Phālguna, the slayer of Virādha, the lord of Rukmiṇī’s life, and the one who brings joy to Satyabhāmā. (69) 10-555 ||
The tree of the eon, the great tree, the forest-fire tree, the one of great fruit;
the goad, the bull among men, the radiant one, the illuminator, the bewilderer, the tawny one. (70) 10-556 ||
He is straightforward, eternal, heroic, a scion of the Yadu lineage, and identical with Śiva;

Śūra, Sūrya, Mṛkaṇḍa, Bhāskara, Viśvapūjita, Ravi, Tama, Mahāvahni, Vāḍava, and Vaḍavānala. (73) 10-559.
The destroyer of the pride of the Daityas, Garuḍa, the elder brother of Garuḍa;
the Lord of the Gopīs, the Great Lord, the Lord of Vṛndā, the adversary. (74) || 10-560 ||
He is the fivefold form of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), the creepers and shrubs, and the Lord of Cattle (*gopati*);
likewise, he is the forms of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Vetravatī. (75) 10.561
The Kāverī, Narmadā, Vāpī, Gaṇḍakī, Sarayū, and Araja;
he is the essence of the Rājasa, Sāttvika, and all limbs, and he whose eyes are everywhere.
Śiva is composed of joy, composed of nectar, and the beloved of the Yoginīs;
he is the Awakened One, the best among the wise, Viṣṇu, the Victorious One, and the Lord of Śacī. (77) 10-563 ||
The flute, the bearer of the flute, the world, the destroyer of the delusion of the beholder, Kharava, Orava, Vala, Vālā, [and] Valāhaka.
Śiva-Rudra, Nala, Nīla, the one who takes recourse in the tail, the plow, and the goad;
the mercury, the purifier, the swan, the one mounted upon a swan, the Lord of the World. (79) 10-565
The deluder, the deluding one, the illusory power, the great illusionist, the great-faced;
the poison, the bull-leader, time, and the subduer of Kālī. (80) 10-566 ||
Bubja is the bestower of fortune, a hero who brings about the destruction of washermen;
Komala is the king of the western quarter, born of water and a bearer of water. (81) 10-567
The destroyer of all sins, the supreme lord, the grandfather;
the wielder of the sword, the doer of compassion, the beautiful lover of Rādhā. (82) || 10-568 ||
Dvādaśa, Araṇya-sambhogin, Śeṣanāga-vanālaya, Kāma, Śyāma, Sukha, Śīda, Prīha, Prīda, and Patikṛtī. (83) || 10-569 ||
Hari, Hara, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme among Men, the Beloved of Arrows, the Protector of the Cowherds, the Stealer of the Heart, the Doer, and the Savior from Saṃsāra. (84) || 10-570 ||
The primordial god, the non-god, the teacher of Gaurī, the one without refuge;
the virtuous one, the ordainer of virtue, the sustainer, the protector, and the one devoted to the cruel. (85) 10-571
Rālaṃvī, Hayagrīva, Vānarāri, Vanāśraya, Vana, Vanīvalādhyakṣa, Mahāvadha, and Mahāmuni. (86) || 10-572 ||
He is the worshipful Śyāmantaka gem, the wise one who destroys obstacles;
he is Govardhana, who is to be magnified, and he who is dear to Vardhanī and Vardhana. (10.573)
The one who causes prosperity, the prosperer, the one who prospers, the one who brings prosperity, the one who is dear with happiness;
the one who causes prosperity, the prosperer, the one who prospers, the one who brings prosperity, the one who is dear with happiness. || 10-574 ||
The builder, the elder, the aged, the one dear to the elderly and the infirm;

It is one's own welfare, auspicious, propitious, bringing prosperity, bringing well-being, and virtuous;

Kṛṣṇa is the lover, eternally black, the doer of what is dear to all;
he is Nanda, the joyful one, the great sound, the destroyer of pride, and the subduer of the arrogant. (10.580)
Kilī, milī, hilī, gilī, golī, golo, golālayo, gulī, guragulī, mārakī, sākhī, vaṭaḥ, pi*vakaḥ, and kṛtī. (10.581)
The slayer of Mlecchas, the destroyer of Time, Yaśodā, and Yaśas; Acyuta, Keśava, Viṣṇu, Hari, Satya, and Janārdana. (10.582)
The swan, Nārāyaṇa, the indigo-blue one, the absorbed one, devoted to his devotees;
Rāma, the beloved of Jānakī, the cessation [of suffering], the destroyer of the world. (10.583)
He of a thousand rays, of great radiance, of heroic luster, the great ocean;
the sea, the deep, the shoreless, that which has both near and far shores, the lord of rivers. (10.584)
He is the bringer of joy to Gokula, the fulfiller of his vows, one who delights in his wife, one who delights in compassion, one who delights in great joy, and the wielder of the bow. (10.585)
Parvata, Parvatākāra, Gaya, Geya, Dvijapriya, Kaṃvala, and then Rāma, the promulgator of the Rāmāyaṇa. (10.586)
He is the sky, the heavens, and the day; he is the one to be seen, the future, and the bringer of fear.
(100) Accompanied by Pārvatī and fortune, he is a brother, Lakṣmī, and full of splendor. (10-587)
He is playful, daring, and proud of all things, with eyes full of arrogance;
he is Murāri, the knower of the ways of the world, the giver of life, and the ender of life.
Yama, the enemy of Yama, the one who is restrained, the one who restrains, and the ordainer of restraint;
Vaṃśulī, Pāṃśulī, Pāḍu, Pāḍura, and the beloved of Arjuna. (10.589)
Līlīta, Candrikāmālin, Mālin, Mālāmbujaśraya, the great Yakṣa named Ambuja, Dakṣa, Cintāmaṇi, and Prabhu. (10.590)
Maṇi, Dinamaṇi, Kedāra, and Vadarīśraya;
(4) Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, who delights in the Badarī forest. || 10.591 ||
He is the destroyer of the enemy of delusion, the ocean of the *svadhā* offering, and the rising moon;
he is the moon, the sun, Śiva, the wielder of the trident, the wielder of the discus, and the bearer of the mace. (10.592)
The creator of prosperity, the lord of prosperity, the giver of prosperity, the god of prosperity, the beloved of Devakī.
(6) || The Thousand Names (1000). ||
Thus, the thousand names of the Lord of Śrī Rādhikā have been proclaimed. || 10-593 ||
Through its recollection, there is the destruction of heaps of sins and the eradication of death;
it brings delight to the Vaiṣṇavas and destroys great poverty. (10.594)
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, likewise sexual intercourse with another's wife,

A Vaiṣṇava who is devoted to Viṣṇu, even if afflicted by great poverty, should recite this one hundred and eight times at night on the full moon day of Kārttika. (10–597)
Clad in yellow garments, the wise one, having worshipped the book with fragrant flowers, sandalwood paste, and indeed with food offerings and the like, (11) || 10-598 ||
Marked by meditation on Rādhā, steadfast, and adorned with a forest garland, O Goddess, one should recite the Thousand Names one hundred and eight times. (10-599)
On the day of the new moon during the transition [of the sun] in both the bright and dark fortnights of Caitra, one should strive to fall [into the fire];
in an instant, one may delude the three worlds. (10-600)
Endowed with a garland of *tulasī*, the Vaiṣṇava is intent upon devotion (14).
On Sundays, Fridays, the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), and on the day of the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*)—10.601.
Having honored a Brahmin and fed him according to the prescribed rite, one should recite the Thousand Names; from that, success is born.
Whoever constantly recites this Vaiṣṇava [text] during the deep of night, Lakṣmī, even if she has gone to another region, will surely return; of this there is no doubt. (10.603)
And in the three worlds, the great goddesses, infatuated by desire for Sundarī, come of their own accord in their bewilderment and worship her as a Vaiṣṇavī. (10.604)
The sick shall be freed from disease, and the bound shall be released from bondage;
the pregnant woman shall give birth to a son, and the maiden shall find a virtuous husband. (10.605)
Even a king comes under one's control, let alone an ordinary human being, O beloved, through hearing, reciting, or worshipping the Thousand Names. (10.606) 144a)
By retaining [this knowledge], the devotee of Viṣṇu attains everything; there is no doubt in this matter.
[There are sacred sites] at Vaṃśīvaṭa, at Anyavaṭa, and likewise at Pippalakī. (10.607)
A Vaiṣṇava who recites this daily in the presence of the image of Gopāla at Kadambapītapata attains the abode of Hari. (10.608)
It was not told by Kṛṣṇa to Rādhikā, nor was it previously told to me, O Śivā;
it was told by me to Nārada, yet it was not revealed by me to Nārada. (10.609)
O Varāha, I have told you this which is very difficult to obtain;
it must be guarded with effort and never revealed under any circumstances. (10.610)
It must never be given to one who is deceitful, nor to a sinner, and especially not to one who is addicted to sensual pleasures;
it must never be given, it must never be given, it must never be given. (10.611)
It should be given to one who is peaceful, free from disciples, and devoted to Viṣṇu;
it is equivalent to the gift of a cow, the Brahma-sacrifice, and likewise a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices. (10.612)
By reciting this, O Tree, one obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices;
it effects delusion, paralysis, as well as killing, expulsion, and so forth. (10.613)
Whatever a Vaiṣṇava desires in his heart, he certainly attains it;
provided that on Ekādaśī, having bathed with fragrant substances and oils, he observes the vow. (10.614)
Having given food, a brahmin, as well as a sacrificial fee, gold, and ornaments, that man who performs the undertaking thereafter obtains everything. (10.615)
Whoever recites [this] a hundred or a thousand times before a Vaiṣṇava shall obtain everything through the grace of the Śrī Vṛndāvana-cakra. (10.616)
O Goddess, in that house where this book remains worshipped, there shall be no famine, nor scarcity, nor affliction, nor fear anywhere. (10.617)
Snakes, spirits, yakṣas, and the like are brought under control; of this there is no doubt.
O Great Goddess, Śrī Gopāla likewise shall dwell in his house. (10.618)
"In that house where the Thousand Names remain worshipped," (33) thus ends the *Śrīgopālasahasranāma* within the *Śrīsammohanatantra*, in the dialogue between Pārvatī and Hara.
Now, the hymn to Gopāla is written.
Oṃ, [I meditate upon Him] who is dark like a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like blue lotuses. || 10-619 ||
I bow to Kṛṣṇa, the delight of Vṛndāvana, who assumes the form of a cowherd, his dark curly hair bound with shimmering peacock feathers. (10.620)
Adorned with a forest garland entwined with kadamba flowers, his swaying golden earrings brushed against the contours of his cheeks. (10.621)
His chest was illuminated by a necklace of large pearls, and his body was radiant with a golden crown and exquisite golden armlets. (10.622)
The mass of his garments was stirred by the gentle agitation of a light breeze, while the sweet sounds of the flute were placed within his lovely lips. (10.623)
The two lips of the cowherd girl repeatedly delude the mind—those lips which are like bees to the honey of the face of the Bhoja princess. (10.624)
He agitated their minds with his smiling side-long glances, as they stood close together, their bodies blossoming with youth. (10.625)
It was variegated, surrounded by cowherd women adorned with exquisite ornaments, and eager for the pleasure of sporting in the waters of the Kālindī, which resembled crushed collyrium. (10.626)

In one place he was training the cowherd boys, and in another he was calling out to the herd of cows, while the cool breeze from its contact with the waters of the Yamunā caused them to tremble. (8) (10.627)
Where in Vṛndāvana does he dwell, seated upon a jeweled throne nestled against a mountain of gems, beneath the shade of a kadamba tree? (10-628)
Seated in the midst of wish-fulfilling trees within a golden pavilion, the quarters of the sky were made fragrant by the scent of spring blossoms. (10-629)
He was situated on the beautiful Govardhana mountain, eager for the pleasure of the rasa dance, with the palm of his left hand placed beneath the parasol of the excellent mountain. (10-630)
It was thick with pearls released by Indra, who had been shattered, and it resounded with the sounds of "huṃ" uttered amidst the great joy of flute-playing. (12) 10.631
He was constantly gazed upon by the cowherd boys, who were joyful and looking up at him, singing only of Kṛṣṇa, and remaining under his sovereign control. (10.632)
It was graced by cowherds with staffs and nooses raised in their hands, and by the foremost of sages, such as Nārada, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. (10.633)
That supreme being who is being praised with speech exceedingly tender with joy—whatever human being should contemplate this god and praise him with devotion; || 10.634 ||
Satisfied by him at the three junctions of the day, he grants the desired boon:
one becomes a favorite of the king and dear to all people. (10.635)
One attains unshakable prosperity and certainly becomes eloquent.
Thus ends the *Gopālastava* in the *Gautamītantra*.
Now, the twelvefold purification of the Vaiṣṇavas is described here.
Approaching the house, as well as following after Hara with devotion, performing circumambulation, and again the cleansing of his feet; || 10.637 ||

Furthermore, the cleansing of the feet for the sake of worshipping with leaves and flowers, and the devoutly lifting up of leaves and flowers for the sake of worship—Hara [is pleased by these]. (10.638)
Among all purifications of the hands, this purification is preeminent:
it is the chanting of that [Name] and the chanting of its qualities as well. (10.639)
Through devotion to the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the purification of speech is desired;
likewise, the listening to his stories and the witnessing of his festivals [are required]. (10.640)
The complete purification of the three eyes of Śrī is now correctly described here:
the wearing of the water from the feet (pādodaka), the remains of the offerings (nirmālya), and even the wearing of flowers.

O ascetic, it is said that for one who has prostrated before Hari, there is the purification of the head, as well as the smelling of fragrant flowers and the like that have been offered to Him. 10-642.
Purification is prescribed for the tongue and also for the nose;
therein, flowers and the like are offered to the pair of feet of Kṛṣṇa. (10.643)
That alone is the purifier in the world, for it indeed cleanses everything;
one should fashion the form of a mace on the forehead and likewise the bearer of a bow upon the head.

And having [visualized] the Nandaka sword in the center of the heart and the conch and discus on the two arms, if a Brahmin marked with the conch and discus dies even in a cremation ground, [he attains liberation]. (10.645)

O Gautama, the destiny that has been proclaimed for one engaged in [such practice] is the destiny for him—namely, Candana—as it is heard as a censure regarding the branding with heated seals and so forth. (10.646)
And so it has been said in the Bṛhannāradīya Purāṇa:
Concerning the Brāhmaṇa.
But that man whose body is marked with signs such as heated conch shells and other emblems shall experience every form of torment as a caṇḍāla for ten million births.
Furthermore, that twice-born man whose body is marked with signs such as the heated conch and other emblems goes to the Raurava hell for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
No one whatsoever should dwell where the body of one marked with the wheel-signs remains;
if such a great sinner should stay, he would become the equivalent of a thousand killers of Brahmins.
Having seen one with a slender body marked by the wheel-sign, one should look at the sun and recite the Vedic verses;
one should also recite the Puruṣasūkta, otherwise one shall go to the Raurava hell.
The body of a Brahmin should be known as the refuge of all the gods;
O King, if that [body] is tormented, what can I say? Homage to the Great One! (10.651)

O King, one whose body is marked with the wheel or even marked with the sectarian sign (liṅga) should be understood as ineligible for the performance of rites prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis. (10.652)

When the prescribed materials are available, one should perform worship through mental resolve by means of the ten offerings, beginning with the five types of perfumes and so forth, along with the five starting with water for the feet. || 10.653 ||
Keśava will protect him who bears on his head the remains of the garland worn by Keśava, who does not eat without first having offered [the food] to Him. (10.654)
In the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara.
One should worship all the gods; one should not worship a god alone. Having performed the worship of the gods with faith, one will certainly attain that world. || 10-655 ||
If flowers are not available, one should offer even leaves;
if fruits are not available, one should offer even grasses, shrubs, and medicinal herbs. (10.656)
If herbs are not available, one should offer water alone;
in the absence of even water, the deity becomes fully worshipped through one's intention and devotion. (10.657)
If one does not perform dance and song before Keśava on the day of Hari, has he not been consumed by fire, or has he gone to the bottom of the netherworld? (10.658)

Thus are the thirty-two offenses: riding in vehicles, or on sandals, or on foot, within the house of the Blessed One; or sitting during festivals of the gods; or failing to prostrate oneself before him. (10.659)
Nor should one perform the salutation of the Blessed One and so forth while impure from food remnants, nor offer a prostration with only one hand, nor circumambulate in front [of the deity]. (10.660)
Stretching out one's feet in front [of others], likewise assuming the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka), lying down, eating, and speaking falsely; || 10-661 ||
Speaking loudly, mutual chatter, obstructions, and quarrels;
as well as punishment and favor, and harsh speech toward women. (10.662)
Covering oneself with a blanket, censuring others, praising others, speaking indecently, and the emission of downward wind (flatus). || 10-663 ||
When possible, there is the figurative practice of consuming what has not been offered;
likewise, there is the non-offering of fruits and other items produced at that particular time. (10.664)
The assignment of Vasiṣṭha’s gift and whatever condiment there was, as well as the clarification of the seat, the censure of the virtuous, and the praise of the virtuous. || 10.665 ||
Disrespect toward the guru, reciting one's own praises, and likewise reviling the deity—
these, along with others, are proclaimed as the thirty-two offenses against Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the tenth [chapter] in the Āgamakalpalatā.
Now follow the mantras of Śrī Viṣṇu.

The word "Tāra" (Om), followed by "Namaḥ," and then the letters "Bhū" and "Ya" joined with "Na" and "R," along with "Dīrgha" (Ū) and "Sama" (A)—this mantra, consisting of its own syllables, is declared to be "Pavano-nāya. (11.1)

The syllable *tāram* is *oṃ*; *namaḥ* is its essential form (*svarūpa*). The letters *na*, *ra*, *u*, *na*, and *ka*, joined with the long vowel (*dīrgha*), combined with the letter *ā*, thus become *nārā*. The letter *ya* is *pavana*; thus, *nāya* is its essential form. Accordingly: *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya*.
Thus, this is the eight-syllable mantra.
O virtuous one, for this mantra, Nārāyaṇa is the sage (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Śrī Viṣṇu is the deity (devatā),
and its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
In this regard, the Śāradā states that the six limbs are assigned using six syllables, while the remaining two syllables are merely to be placed on the belly and the back.
Oṃ, homage to the heart.
To the head, svāhā!
To the crest-lock, Vauṣaṭ!
HŪM for the armor of the [deities] named.
RĀṂ, to the two eyes, VAUṢAṬ.
Yaḥ astrāya phaṭ!
Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other limbs, one should place [the mantra] on the navel, the belly, and the back.
Then, having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the *kirīṭa-mantra*, one should meditate. The *kirīṭa-mantra* is as follows:
Oṃ, homage to the one who possesses a crown, armlets, necklaces, makara-earrings, and the discus, conch, mace, and lotus in his hands; who is clad in yellow garments;
whose chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa; whose two hands shine with the fire and the self-luminous light accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi;
and who possesses the splendor of a thousand suns.
Thus, one should perform the pervasive sprinkling with the *kīrīta* mantra.
Oṃ! Today [I meditate upon] Him who shines like ten million suns, who incessantly bears the conch, mace, lotus, and discus, whose two sides are graced by Indirā and Vasumatī,
who wears a crown, armlets, necklaces, and earrings, who is clothed in yellow garments, who is illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and who sustains the universe.
"I worship Him who has a beautiful chest, the Śrīvatsa mark, and auspicious signs.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the worship.
The conch and discus are in the lower right and left hands;
the lotus is in the upper right hand, situated above the [lower] pair.
Beginning with the upper right hand, there is the arrangement of the four—conch, discus, mace, and lotus—in sequence.
In the six corners, Keśava, Madhusūdana, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Dāmodara, Vāmana, and Pradyumna— the six Mūrtis— are to be worshipped.
Thus, beginning from the left upper hand, they are in order Viṣṇu, Mādhava, Niruddha, Puruṣottama, Adhokṣaja, and Janārdana.
Beginning from the lower left hand, there are Govinda, Trivikrama, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Nṛsiṃha, and Acyuta;
beginning from the lower right hand, there are Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, Padmanābha, Upendra, Hari, and Kṛṣṇamūrti.

In the offering to the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*), the Heart, Head, Crest, and Armor mantras are placed in the corners starting from the southeast of the pericarp (*karṇikā*); the Eye mantra is in front, and the Weapon mantra is in the cardinal directions. Then follow Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Yogā, Prahvī, Satyā, and likewise Īśānā; Anugrahā is considered the ninth.
Thus end the powers of the seats (pīṭhaśaktis).
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Viṣṇu, the self of all beings, Vāsudeva; salutation to the self who is the essence of the yoga-pīṭha of the union with the self of all.
Thus is the pīṭha-mantra.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite this mantra sixteen hundred thousand times (one hundred and sixty lakṣas). A "vikāra-lakṣa" consists of sixteen lakṣas.
The syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) is proclaimed as "to the Heart," and "to the Blessed One Vāsudeva" is declared to be the primary twelve-syllabled mantra of Viṣṇu:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*.
Thus is the twelve-syllable mantra.
The seer is Prajāpati, the meter is proclaimed to be Gāyatrī, and the deity of this mantra is declared by the wise to be Vāsudeva. (11.2)
Oṃ, homage to the heart.
Homage to the head; Svāhā!
To the Blessed One, Śikhā, Vauṣaṭ!
Hūṃ, for Vāsudeva, the armor.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva; to the weapon, phaṭ!
Thus ends the section on the mantra of the limbs.
The powers of the seats (pīṭha-śaktayaḥ) and the mantras of the seats are also as before.
Oṃ: Viṣṇu, resembling ten million autumnal moons, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, residing upon a white lotus, enchanting the world with his splendor.

I bow to Him who is praised by the lords of sages, whose armlets, necklaces, and earrings are fastened, whose hair radiates from His great crown, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and wears the noble Kaustubha gem.
Thus concludes the section on meditative absorption.
Here, at the beginning, the four [emblems] starting with the conch shell are to be assigned in a clockwise sequence, beginning from the right hand; this is the worship mandala.
First an eight-petaled lotus, and then a twelve-petaled lotus;
having been initiated and having conquered his senses, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the syllables.
One should offer that thousand-fold oblation with sesame seeds saturated with clarified butter.
Now follows the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa mantra: the pair of *hṛllekhā* seed-syllables, followed again by the pair of *ramā* seed-syllables. (11.5)

This mantra, beginning with the *praṇava* and consisting of fourteen syllables, is declared to be for Vāsudeva within the heart; it is the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (*surapādapa*). By means of that—11-6. 11-tena.
Oṃ hrīḥ hrīḥ śrīḥ śrīḥ. For the mantra of Lakṣmīvāsudeva, everything except the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras) and the visualization (dhyāna) is the same as for the twelve-syllable mantra.
The limb-mantras, however, are as follows:
Oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ, homage to the heart.
Oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ, svāhā to the head.
Oṃ lakṣmī, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Oṃ, to Vāsudeva, for the armor, hūṃ.
Oṃ, homage to the weapon; phaṭ!

Oṃ! His body resembles lightning and the moon; having attained oneness through the power of affection between the Lotus-born and Vaikuṇṭha, he is adorned with a profusion of ornaments shining with jewels.
He holds a mirror made of pure knowledge, a jeweled pitcher, a lotus, and a mace.
May He, who bears the conch and the discus, bestow upon you eternal prosperity in every direction. || 11-7 ||
The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
then he should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with a thousand blooming lotuses mixed with the three sweets.
An oblation performed with milk-rice bestows the power to subjugate Lakṣmī;
by offering sesame seeds smeared with honey, one shall accomplish all undertakings. || 11-9 ||
Now follows the mantra for vomiting curd.

*Tāra* (Oṃ), then *hṛt* (Namaḥ), then *vaiṣṇave*, followed by *taḥ* for the Lord of the Gods (*sureśvara*), then *mahābalāya*, and finally the pair *ṭha* (Svāhā). This is the eighteen-syllable mantra. || 11-10 ||
As for the mantra, it is as follows:
Oṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods, the one of great power; svāhā!
Of this mantra.
The seer is R̥ṣiṛindu, the metre is Virāṭ, and the deity is Dadhivāmana;
the application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the attainment of desired powers, prosperity, and success. || 11-11 ||
Oṃ, homage to the heart.
Homage to the head; svāhā!
To Viṣṇu, for the crest-lock, vauṣaṭ!
Hūṃ, for the armor of the Lord of the Gods.
To Mahābala, vauṣaṭ from the two eyes.
Svāhā! To the weapon, Phaṭ!
This is the limb-mantra.
The powers of the seats (pīṭhaśaktayaḥ) are as before.
Meditative absorption.
Oṃ, we worship Him who is fair as a pearl, adorned with ornaments of fresh jewels, seated upon the moon,
holding in His lotus-like hands a golden pitcher filled with pure water and an uplifted golden cup.
One should visualize a golden goblet in the right hand.
The offering to the obstructions.
In the filaments of the corners starting from the southeast, one should place the Heart, Head, Crest, and Armor mantras; the Eye in front, and the Weapon in the cardinal directions.
One should recite the mantra three million times with offerings soaked in ghee and local grains.
One should offer oblations of milk-rice or curd-rice according to the prescribed rule.
A hundred thousand for each quality makes three hundred thousand.
Now, the Hayagrīva mantra:
having uttered the word "udgirat" (emit), preceded by the syllable *praṇava* and the word *udgītha*.
At the end of "sarvavāgīśvari," one should utter "īśvarī. || 11-14 ||
Having meditated upon the essence of all the Vedas, one should utter everything at the end of the steps;
one should awaken the second [tattva], the water, according to the method beginning with the mantra, the hand, and the star.
As in the case of a mantra.
Oṃ! Utter forth, O Praṇava-Udgītha, Lord of all masters of speech! You who consist of all the gods, contemplated by me, awaken everything, awaken! 11-16.

For the Astra-mantra: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Hayagrīva is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desired goals such as mastery of speech (vāgīśvaryādi).
Oṃ, homage to the heart.
Oṃ, O you who utter the Praṇava-udgītha, svāhā to the head.
O Lord of all lords of speech, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
"Sarvadeva mayā cintya kavacā huṃ;
sarvabodhaya bodhaya astrāya phaṭ.
Thus is the mantra for the five limbs (pañcāṅgamantra).
Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*).
The powers of the seat (*pīṭhaśakti*) are as before.
And the seat-mantra is also as previously described.

Oṃ! We worship the pair [of deities] whose faces are like the autumnal moon, who are adorned with necklaces of pearls, whose two arms hold a discus and a conch, and whose two hands rest upon their knees. [They are located] in the spokes starting from the southeast corner.
The heart, head, crest, armor, and first the eye, and finally the weapon in the cardinal directions.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, the Vaiṣṇava should offer oblations into the fire ten thousand times with *kuṇṭa* flowers soaked in honey.
One should worship Hayagrīva upon the eight-syllable seat (pīṭha);
having conceived the form by means of the seed-syllable (bīja), one should worship the seed-syllable upon the head as prescribed.

The seed-syllable *hasūṃ*— described as having the *vipad* (the letter *ha*), the *bhṛgu* (the letter *sa*), the *marghīśa* (the letter *ū*), and the *indu* (the crescent moon)— is proclaimed as the mantra for the visualization of the Form (*mūrtikalpanamantra*).
Now follows the Varāha-mantra.
Then one should utter "Namo bhagavate varāhapadāya. (11-20)

After that, for the sake of form (*rūpa*), [one should utter] *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ*, *syāte*, and *taye*. Then, at the end of the word, [say] *me* and *padānte*, followed by *jyante* and *pradadāpaya*. This mantra, ending with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*, i.e., *svāhā*), consists of thirty-three syllables. || 11-21 ||
As for the mantra, it is as follows:
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One in the form of the Boar, Lord of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; grant me, indeed, the sovereignty over the earth, svāhā!
Thus is the mantra.

The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is Bhārgava, the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, the deity (devatā) is Ādivarāha, and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desired goals such as sovereignty over the earth.
Homage to Ekadaṃṣṭra, the heart;
svāhā to Vyomālka, the head;
vauṣaṭ to Tejodhipati, the crest-lock.
HŪṂ to the armor of Viśvarūpa;
PHAṬ to the weapon of Mahādaṃṣṭra.
Thus is the mantra for the five limbs.
The powers of the seats (pīṭhaśaktayaḥ) and the mantra of the seats (pīṭhamantraḥ) are as before. Thus [it is said].
Now, the meditation:

Oṃ! From the feet to the knees, [the body] resembles fresh gold; from the region of the navel downwards, it has the luster of pearls; from the region of the throat upwards, it resembles the rising sun; and from the head, it has a blue radiance.

I praise the primordial Boar, who holds in his hands a chariot wheel and a discus, a sword and a shield, a mace, a spear, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and the earth; he whose tusks gleam with splendor.

The discus is the chariot-wheel and the conch is the *dara*. One should mutter this mantra one hundred thousand times; with lotuses smeared with honey, one should perform oblations amounting to a tenth part of that number, and then worship Viṣṇu upon the pedestal.
Above the two hands, a wheel and two conchs are to be visualized during the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjā) within the spokes in the corners beginning with the southeast.
And so forth, as before.
Now, the mantra of Dharaṇī:
the heart-mantra for the Blessed Lady Dharaṇī should follow immediately after that.
Dharaṇi, anta, dhara, dvaṃdva, dviṭha, toya, and that which exceeds Dhruva (the twenty-fourth). || 11-24 ||
As for the mantra: ||
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady, O Upholder of the Earth, svāhā!
Thus is the mantra.
"Dviṭhaḥ svāhā" and "dhruvaḥ praṇavaḥ"—
this heart-mantra is said to consist of nineteen syllables.
The sage is said to be Varāha, and Nivṛt is declared to be the metre. || 11-25 ||
The deity of all beings is considered to be Prakṛti, the Earth;
it is declared that [the mantra] consists of three [parts] as the heart and four [parts] as the head.
The *śikhā* is prescribed with three [syllables], the *kavaca* is considered to consist of five;
the *netra* is declared to be formed by two, and the *astra* likewise by two.
One who knows the ritual procedure should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the mantras of the individual syllables.
148a) Thus is meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Oṃ! We worship the Earth Goddess, who is dark-complexioned, adorned with garments of various colors and jewel ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne, with full and swelling breasts;
she holds in her hands a divine lotus, a cluster of fresh rice stalks, and a parrot.

The mantra practitioner, well-composed, should recite this mantra four hundred thousand times,
and offer forty thousand oblations of pure palāśa flowers.
By this rite, one should utter "Hūhū"; thus Manu shall certainly become perfected.
This is the Śrī Viṣṇu mantra.
Victory to Śrī Kṛṣṇa! Victory to Kṛṣṇa! Victory, victory to Kṛṣṇa! May there be auspiciousness.
Salutations to Śrī Śiva.
Now follows the Śrī Śiva mantra:
Oṃ namaḥ śivāya.
It consists of the letter *sa*, joined with the end of truth (*satya*), and is adorned at its head by the bindu. || 11-82 ||
The mantra named Prāsāda is proclaimed as the bestower of all perfections for those who worship it;
it consists of the letter *au* ending in *satya* (the letter *s*), followed by the letter *ha*, joined with the *bindu*, which is the *anusvāra*.
The mantra becomes joined with that: *hauṃ*.
I shall now describe the procedure for its worship, which grants success in all undertakings.
That is to say:
Furthermore, during the Brāhma-muhūrta, one should meditate on the Guru upon one's own head:
in the morning, the Guru is white, with two eyes and two arms, situated upon the head. (11.84)
One should meditate upon [the deity] who is peaceful, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, preceded by its name.

Having thus visualized and worshipped with mental offerings, one should consecrate oneself within one's own heart in that form, according to the verse beginning: "For me, who am blind with the darkness of ignorance... and so forth.
Having reflected upon the necessary purpose, one may go outside.
Thus concludes the morning ritual.
Then, at midday, having gone to a river or similar body of water for the purpose of bathing, one should bathe according to the prescribed rite and perform the mantra-bath.
152a) As follows:

First, having performed *prāṇāyāma* and having performed the ritual assignment of limbs (*kalāṅganyāsa*), one should draw a five-pointed wheel in the water and [invite the deity] from the solar orb by means of the *aṅkuśamudrā*.

Having invoked the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) with the mantra "O Gaṅgā and Yamunā," and having recited the root mantra eight times while meditating upon [the water] as the form of Śiva, one should offer seven handfuls of water upon one's own head using the *kumbha-mudrā*.
Then, after immersing oneself three times, rising, and performing *ācamana*, one should immerse again and perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having risen from the water, put on washed garments, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should offer water three times at the crown of the head with the root mantra.
Then, having offered libations three times with the mantra "Sadāśiva urvārāmī," and having recited the Gāyatrī, one should offer the arghya to the Sun and chant the Śiva-Gāyatrī as much as possible.
Just as with the yāyatrī.
Oṃ. May we know Sadāśiva; may we meditate upon the Three-eyed One; may Śiva inspire us.

Having thus recited the Gāyatrī, having taken water in a copper vessel and placed a red flower therein, and holding it with both hands, [one should offer it] to the Sun, the embodiment of Śiva’s splendor, who possesses the power of illumination: "Oṃ, obeisance to this flood of light."
Having thus offered the *argha* and having paid homage—or having smelled [the flower]—one should depart.

Then, having gone to the door of the worship hall and washed his hands and feet, he should worship the deities of the door with the words: "Obeisance to the deities of the door. Having thus worshipped the door-deities and entered the interior of the house, he should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) while reciting: "May those beings who move away... and so forth.
Merupṛṣṭha is the Ṛṣi, Sutala is the Chandas, Kūrma is the Devatā; this is the application (viniyoga) for the yoga of the seat (āsana).
Having recited: "O Earth, the world is supported by you."
Having prepared the seat with "Obeisance to the Support-Power, the Lotus-Seated One," and having sat upon the seat,
[one should place] "Obeisance to the Gurus" on the left and "Obeisance to Gaṇapati" on the right.
In the center, "Salutation to Sadāśiva.
Then, "To the weapon, Phaṭ!
Having thus cleansed both hands with sandalwood paste and flowers, one should perform the triple clapping of the hands (tālatraya) and effect the binding of the directions (digbandhana).

Then one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). With the mantra "So'haṃ," having projected the individual soul (jīva)— in the form of the flame of a lamp— from the heart into the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, one should contemplate the body as dried up by means of the seed-syllable of air, "Yaṃ," and [then] by "Raṃ."

Having burned the body with the fire seed-syllable (*vahnivīja*), having dispersed the ashes with the wind seed-syllable (*vāyuvīja*) while reciting "ayam," and having brought down a rain of nectar with the moon seed-syllable (*candravīja*) while reciting "ṭham," one should generate a body by means of that [nectar] and solidify it with the earth seed-syllable (*pṛthivīvīja*) while reciting "lam"; then one should contemplate oneself in that form.
Then, one should cause the living self (jīvātman) to enter into the heart.
Now follows the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
Brahmā is the seer, Gāyatrī is the meter, Sarasvatī is the deity; this is the application for the ritual placement of the Mātṛkās.
a. *namaḥ* on the forehead;
ā. *namaḥ* on the perimeter of the mouth; iṃ. *namaḥ* on the right eye.
Ī: Homage to the left eye. U: Homage to the right ear.
Ū: To the left ear.
Ṛ: on the right nostril; Ṝ: salutations on the left nostril;
Ḷ: salutations on the right cheek.
Ḷ: Salutation to the left cheek;
E: to the upper lip; Ai: to the lower lip.
Oṃ! Homage to the upper tooth. Auṃ! Homage to the lower tooth. Aṃ! Homage to the head.
Aḥ, homage to the mouth;
Ka, homage to the root of the right arm;
Khaṃ, homage to the elbow.
Gaṃ, homage to the wrist! Ghaṃ, homage to the base of the fingers! Ṅaṃ, homage to the tips of the fingers!
Caṃ at the base of the left upper arm; cchaṃ, obeisance to the elbow;
jaṃ, obeisance to the wrist.
Jhaṃ, homage to the base of the fingers. Ñaṃ, homage to the tips of the fingers. Ṭaṃ, homage to the base of the right thigh.
Ṭhaṃ, homage to the knees; Ḍaṃ, homage to the ankles; Ḍhaṃ, homage to the bases of the toes.
ṆAṂ, salutation to the tip of the finger; TAṂ, salutation to the root of the left thigh;
THAṂ, salutation to the knee.
Daṃ, salutation to the ankles;
dhaṃ, to the bases of the toes;
naṃ, salutation to the tips of the toes.
Paṃ, homage to the right side;
Phaṃ, homage to the left side;
Vaṃ, homage to the back.
*Bhaṃ*, obeisance to the navel;
*maṃ*, obeisance to the abdomen;
*yaṃ*, obeisance to the skin-self in the heart.
*Raṃ* namaḥ to the self of blood at the base of the right arm;
*laṃ* namaḥ to the self of flesh on the crown of the head;
*vaṃ* namaḥ to the self of fat from the heart down to the left foot.
Laṃ, obeisance to the individual self (jīvātman) at the heart and so forth, and in the abdomen. Kṣaṃ, obeisance to the supreme self (paramātman) at the heart and so forth, and in the mouth.
Then follows the meditation (dhyāna).

Oṃ! [I bow to her] whose face, arms, and middle of the chest are adorned with the fifty letters of the alphabet; who wears a radiant crown bound with a crescent moon; whose full and lofty breasts are pressed together;
and who holds in her lotus-like hands the ritual gestures (mudrās), a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and the [scriptural] knowledge.
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who possesses three eyes and bears a pure radiance. || 11-85 ||
Now follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the root-mantra’s seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*devatā*), and so forth.
For the single-syllable *Prāsāda* mantra, Vāmadeva is the seer, the *Paṅkti* is the meter, Sadāśiva is the deity,
and its application (*viniyoga*) is for my attainment of the four aims of human life.
On the head, salutation to Vāmadeva, the seer (ṛṣi).
In the mouth, salutation to Paṅkti, the meter (chandas).
In the heart, salutation to Sadāśiva, the deity (devatā).
Now, regarding breath control (prāṇāyāma):
filling [the lungs] sixteen times with the root mantra;
holding the breath (kuṃbhaka) sixty-four times.
Exhalation is through the right nostril;
filling is through the left nostril; retention is through both; and exhalation is through the right nostril.
Thus three times.
Now follows the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Hā! Homage to the heart. Hī! Svāhā to the head. Hū! Vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
HAIḤ / HŪM for the armor;
HAUḤ for all the limbs; VAUṢAṬ for the three eyes.
HAḤ ASTRĀYA PHAṬ!
Having thus struck three times upward with the *tāla* gesture, one should bind the directions with ten snaps of the fingers (*cchoṭikā*).
Now follows the ritual placement on the limbs (karanyāsa).

Hauṃ! To Īśāna, salutation to the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭha) on the thumbs. Haiṃ! To Tatpuruṣa, salutation to the two index fingers (tarjanī). Hūṃ! To Aghora, salutation to the two middle fingers (madhyamā).
Hī! Salutation to Vāmadeva with the two ring fingers; [salutation] on the two ring fingers.
Haṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta with the two little fingers;
Hāḥ, salutation to Īśāna, the upper face,
with the thumb on the head.
Oṃ haḥ, homage to Tatpuruṣa;
[place] at the mouth with the index finger.
Oṃ huṃ, homage to Aghora; [place] at the center of the heart.
Oṃ hi; *namaḥ* to Vāmadeva with the ring finger at the secret place. Oṃ haṃ; *namaḥ* to Sadyojāta with the little finger at the feet.
Thus is the ritual placement of the forms (*mūrttinyāsa*).
Ai Klī Vlū Strī Saḥ, salutation to the Heart, which is omniscient;
[place this] in the heart. Thus.
To Amṛtatejolinī Brahmaśiras, obeisance!
To the head, svāhā!
Thus.
To the one with blazing crests, to the primordial awakening, to the crest: *vauṣaṭ*!
[This is] for the crest.
Likewise, to the wielder of the vajra, to the one with the vajra in hand.
Homage to the independent one; *hūṃ* for the armor on all limbs.
*Oṃ sauḥ dhauḥ hauḥ*, homage with *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes of unimpaired power.
Netra-traya ślāḥ / Paśu huṃ phaṭ astrāya phaṭ. Then, one should perform the three *tāla* gestures and the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) as before.
Now, the placement of the vajras (vajranyāsa):
"Iśāna, lord of all sciences; salutation to Śaśinī" on the upper face.
"Iśvara, lord of all beings; salutation to Aṅgadā" on the eastern face.
Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmādhipati, the supreme lord of Brahmā, the bestower of desired boons in the Brahman state; [obeisance] to the right face.
Oṃ, may there be auspiciousness; obeisance to Marīci;
[obeisance] to the northern face.
Oṃ sadāśivoṃ, [to] Śumālinī;
in the western face. Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the four faces.
Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa;
[this is] for Peace (Śānti), salutation to the eastern face.
Oṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva.
To Vidyā, at the western face:
Oṃ Tanno Rudraḥ, for Pratiṣṭhā,
at the southern face.
Oṃ pracodayāt, obeisance to Nivṛtti; facing north. Oṃ aghorebhyaḥ, obeisance to Umā; at the heart. Oṃ atha ghorebhyaḥ, obeisance to Mahā; at the neck.

Oṃ, salutation to Ghorakṣamā on the right shoulder; Oṃ, salutation to Nidrā, who is more terrible than the terrible, on the left shoulder; Oṃ, salutation to Sarvavyādhī, who is [terrible] in every respect, at the navel.
Oṃ, to all those in the dance, to Ve, in the belly;
Oṃ, salutation to you, Kṣudhā, on the back;
Oṃ, salutation to those of Rudra-form, Bhṛṣā, on the chest.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to Rujā at the secret place.
Oṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭha; salutation to Dakṣā at the back. Oṃ, salutation to Rudra; salutation to Ratī at the right thigh.
Oṃ, to Kāla and Pāśinī, on the left thigh; Oṃ, to Kalavikaraṇa and Kāmā, on the right knee;
Oṃ, to Saṃyaminī and Valikriyā, on the left knee.
Oṃ, salutation to Valavikaraṇā for Vṛddhi on the right calf. Oṃ, salutation to Valisthirā for Pramathana and Rātri on the left calf.
Oṃ, salutation to Sarvabhūtaramaṇā for Bhrāminī on the right hip.
Oṃ, salutation to Unmanā; salutation to Mohinī on the left hip. Oṃ, salutation to Unmanā; [salutation] to Jarā on the left side.
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutation to Siddhi on the right foot.
Oṃ, salutation indeed to Sadyojāta on the left foot during the rite of growth; Oṃ, salutation to Dyuti on the right breast;
Oṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī on the left breast during the rite of prosperity.
Oṃ, salutation to Medhā in the beginningless existence; [place this] on the nose.
Oṃ, "be devoted to me," salutation to Prajā; [place this] on the head. Oṃ, salutation to Bhavaprabhā at the base of the right arm.
Oṃ, for Udbhava and Svadhā, on the root of the left arm. This is the placement of the thirty-eight kalās.
The thirty-eight kalās have been declared as being in addition to the five Brahma-padas.
"Exceeding the five Brahma-words" means that it is preceded by the five *praṇavas*:
*ai*, *klī*, *vlū*, *strī*,
and *sa*.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa).
Namely as follows:
Oṃ dharmārya, homage to the right shoulder;
Oṃ jñānāya, to the left shoulder;
Oṃ vairāgyāya, to the left thigh.
Oṃ, to Adharma, on the left side;
Oṃ, to Avairāgya, at the navel;
Oṃ, to Anaiśvarya, on the right side.
Oṃ, homage to Ananta at the heart;
homage to the lotus;
aṃ, homage to the solar disc consisting of twelve kalās.
Oṃ, homage to the lunar mandala, whose self is the sixteen digits.
Oṃ maṃ, homage to the fire mandala, whose self is the ten digits.
Oṃ saṃ, homage to sattva.
Oṃ raṃ, salutation to Rajas.
Oṃ taṃ, salutation to Tamas. Oṃ āṃ, salutation to Ātman.
Oṃ Aḥ, salutation to the inner self (antarātman).
Oṃ Paṃ, salutation to the supreme self (paramātman).
Oṃ Hrīḥ, salutation to the self of knowledge (jñānātman).
Having thus performed the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanayāsa*), one should meditate on the Lord within the heart:
"Oṃ! The Lord is adorned with five faces of pearl, yellow, cloud, pearl, and *japā* [flower] colors;
he possesses three eyes, wears a crown of Indra, and has the brilliance of ten million full moons."

One should meditate upon [the deity] who holds a trident, a hammer, a sword, a vajra, a serpent-king, a bell, a goad, and a noose that removes fear; he is immeasurable and radiant with his ornaments. || 11-86 ||
Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with mental offerings and paid obeisance, one should place an *arghya* vessel for the purpose of external worship.
As follows:
Having drawn a triangular mandala on one's left and placed a tripod upon it,
one should worship it with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-mandala consisting of ten kalās," and then place the vessel upon that tripod.
Having worshipped the vessel with the mantra, "Aṃ, obeisance to the solar disc consisting of twelve kalās," and having filled it with pure water while reciting the root mantra;
and having worshipped [the water] as before with "Ḍaṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc," and having recited the root mantra eight times.

Having meditated upon the six limbs [of the vessel] and rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, one should perform the binding with three *tālas* and ten finger-snaps while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ. Then, one should contemplate that *arghya* as being of the nature of the deity, and sprinkle the water and the articles of worship.

Then, with the root mantra, one should offer handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) upon all the limbs, beginning with the head. Thereafter, having fashioned the yantra together with the pedestal (*pīṭha*), the five compartments, the petals, the lotus, and the ground according to the prescribed method,
and having placed it before oneself, one should commence the worship (*pūjā*).
Upon an eight-petaled lotus.

a/ Homage to the Power of the Foundation (Ādhāraśakti). Likewise: homage to Primordial Nature (Prakṛti), to the Tortoise (Kūrma), to Ananta, to the Earth (Pṛthivī), and to the Island of Jewels (Ratnadvīpa).
To the jeweled pavilion; to the wish-fulfilling tree; to the jewel-encrusted pedestal.
Homage to Dharma; homage to Jñāna; homage to Vairāgya.
Homage to Aiśvarya.
In the four corners beginning with the southeast and in the four directions:
Homage to Adharma.
Salutation to ignorance.
Salutation to lack of dispassion. Salutation to lack of sovereignty.
Again, in the center: *Padmāya* (To the Lotus), *Ānandakandāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the Root of Bliss),
*Saṃ vijñānāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Consciousness).
Homage to the lotus that has all that as its self. Homage to the petals composed of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Homage to the filaments composed of transformation (*vikāra*).
Aṃ, for the solar mandala, as before;
oṃ, for the lunar mandala;
and likewise ma, for the fire mandala.
Saṃ for the being; raṃ for taste; taṃ for darkness.
aṃ to the individual self; āṃ to the inner self; paṃ to the supreme self.
*Hrīṃ*. Homage to the one whose nature is wisdom (*jñānātman*).

Then, having meditated [on the deity] as white or yellow and so forth, having brought [the deity] in through the nostril or by means of a handful of flowers, having established [the deity] upon the seat as described, and having performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), [one worships] with external water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings.
One should worship.
In the southeast:
*namas* to Mṛtyu. In the northeast: *namas*.
To Īśāna;
to the East; obeisance to Tatpuruṣa.
To Aghora in the south;
to Saumya in the north.
To Vāmadeva,
in the western corner;
to Sadyojāta.
Aṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti; Āṃ, salutation to Supratiṣṭhā;
I, salutation to Vidyā.

U: Salutation to Indrā.

E: Homage to Sukṣmāmṛtā.
Ai: Homage to Jñānā.
oṃ / Homage to Amṛtā. auṃ / Homage to Āpyāyanī. aṃ / Homage to Vyāpinī.
Aḥ, salutation to her whose form is space.
Again.
Aṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Ā, obeisance to Puṣā. I, obeisance to Sūkṣma.
Ī: Salutation to Trimūrti. U: Salutation to Amareśvara. Ū: Salutation to Arghaśa.
Ṛ: Homage to Bhārabhūteśa. Ṝ: Homage to Atithīśa.

oṃ | Homage to Sadyojāta.

Aḥ, homage to Mahāsena. On all sides: homage to Umā.
Salutation to Kātyāyanī.
Salutation to Gaurī.
Salutation to Kālī.
Salutation to Hemavatī.
Salutation to Īśvarā.
Salutation to Śivā.
Salutation to Śarvāṇī;
salutation to Sarvamaṅgalā;
salutation to Apūrṇā.
Salutation to Pārvatī.
Salutation to Durgā.
Salutation to Mṛḍānī.
Salutation to Caṇḍikā.
Salutation to Ambikā.
[One should worship] Indra and the others in the square.
Outside of that, having recited the Vajra-mantra and others as much as one is able, and having offered the recitation with the mantra beginning "guhyātiguhyatara...
and having praised and bowed, one should bring the floral remains (nirmālya) to the heart by means of the withdrawal mudrā (saṃhāramudrā) and dwell at ease.
Thus ends the manual for the worship of Śiva. Now follows the armor of Śiva (Śivakavaca).
Oṃ, homage to Śiva!
Oṃ! Having paid homage to Mahādeva, the Lord who pervades the universe, I shall describe the path consisting of Śiva, which provides protection for all human beings. (11.87)
Seated in a clean place upon a properly prepared seat, with senses conquered and vital breaths controlled, one should contemplate the creation and dissolution [of all things]. (11.88)
One should meditate upon Maheśa, who is seated within the lotus of the heart, who pervades the space of the sky with his own radiance,
who has conquered the senses, who is subtle, infinite, and primordial, and who consists of supreme bliss.
(3) Having shaken off the bonds of all karma through meditation, one whose mind is long immersed in consciousness and bliss—
One should perform protection with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) for those who are concentrated in the placement of the six syllables (*ṣaḍakṣaranyāsa*). (4) || 11-90 ||

May the God who is the soul of all deities protect me, who have fallen into the deep well of *saṃsāra*. May that divine name, the root of all mantras, shake off today everything impure residing within my heart.
May He whose form is the universe, who consists of light and bliss, and who is the conscious self, protect me everywhere.
May that one Lord, subtler than the subtle and possessed of great power, protect you from all of worldly existence. (6) || 11-92 ||
May Giriśa, who in his eighth form sustains the universe as the very essence of earth, protect me on the ground;
may he who revives men through the essence of water protect me from aquatic dangers.
(7) May he who, at the end of the kalpa, having consumed all worlds, dances with manifold playfulness, [protect me].
Or indeed, by means of the fire of the Mādana-mantra, one is liberated from all fear of wind and other elements, as well as from every sin. (8) || 11-94 ||

Blazing with lightning and the luster of gold, always holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness along with an axe in his hands, four-faced, three-eyed, and possessing that same form as the [central] deity, may he stationed in the eastern direction protect me without ceasing. (11-95)
Holding an axe, a spear, a goad, a noose, a trident, a drum, a rosary, and a mass of fire;
four-faced, blue-complexioned, and three-eyed—may Aghora protect the southern direction. (10) 11-96.

May Sadyojāta, who is as white as jasmine, a conch, a shell, or crystal; who is marked by the Vedas, a rosary, a bracelet, and the gesture of fearlessness; and whose splendor is like that of four faces, protect me from the west.
(11-97) [May he] whose hands hold a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and a drum, and whose complexion is like the filaments of a lotus...
May Trilocana, the beautiful four-faced one, and Vāsudeva protect me in the northern direction. (12) || 11-98 ||
Holding in his hands the Vedas, the thunderbolt, the goad, the noose, the crescent moon, the skull, the drum, the eye, and the trident;
white in luster, consisting of five faces and ten arms, with Īśāna as his head, he is the supreme light.
(13) May the Sun pervade my Vyāna breath; may the Moon-crested Lord pervade my forehead; may the Lord of the Eye pervade my forehead.
May Viśvanātha, who stole the eyes of Bhaga, protect my nose along with my wife from the calamity of the eye. (14)

May Śrutigītakirti protect my ears; may Kapālī always protect my cheeks; may Pañcavaktra always protect my face; may Dhūrjaṭi always protect my tongue. (15) May Nīlakaṇṭha protect my throat, and may Pinākapāṇi protect both my hands.
May Dharmabāhu protect my root; may the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice protect my chest. May Girīndradhanvan protect my belly; may the ender of Madana protect my waist.
May Heraṃbha protect my navel; may that Lord Dhūrjaṭi protect my hips.
May Kuveramitra protect my two thighs; may Jagadīśvara shield my two knees;
may Puṅgavaketu protect the pair of my shanks; and may he whose feet are worshipped by Murāri protect my feet. (18)
May Maheśvara protect me during the first watch of the day; may Vāmadeva protect me during the middle watch;
may Tryambaka protect me during the third watch; and may the Bull-bannered Lord protect me during the final watch of the day. (11.105)
May the moon-crested Lord protect me at the beginning of the night; may the bearer of the Gaṅgā protect me at midnight;
may the Lord of Gaurī protect me at the end of the night; and may the Conqueror of Death protect me at dawn. (11.106)
May Śaṅkara protect me while I am at home; may Sthāṇu always protect me when I am outside;
may the Lord of Beings protect me in the space between those two; and may Sadāśiva protect me on all sides. (21) || 11-107 ||

May the sole Lord of the universe protect me while standing; may the Lord of the Pramathas protect me while walking; may He who is known through the Vedāntas protect me while seated; and may the imperishable Śiva protect me while lying down. (22) May Nīlarudra protect me on the paths, and may the enemy of Tripura protect me in mountain fastnesses and other difficult terrains.
May the hunter Mṛgavyādha, who possesses noble power, protect you from the great dangers of dwelling in the forest and traveling abroad. (11.109)

May Vīrabhadra protect [us] from great fear—he whose fierce laughter causes the cosmic egg and the sky to tremble during the violent onset of the terrible jaws at the end of the eon, and who dwells amidst the ocean-like army of his formidable enemies. (24) 11-110.
O Mṛḍa, with the edge of your terrible axe, may you sever the hundred akṣauhiṇīs of murderous assailants—terrifying with their thousands of eyes, their rows of elephants, and their chariots. (25)

May the trident of the Destroyer of Tripura, blazing with flames like the fire of universal dissolution, slay the Dasyus; may the Pināka bow, the cloud of the universe, terrify the lions, tigers, bears, deer, and other beasts. [May it destroy] bad dreams, ill omens, difficult paths, mental distress, famine, and misfortunes. (26) 11.
[May it destroy] evil dreams, ill omens, difficult paths, mental distress, famine, and calamities.
May the Lord of the worlds destroy for me unbearable ill-repute, calamities, curses, the fear of poison, mental anguish, and diseases. (11.113)

Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Sadāśiva, who consists of all principles, who is remote from all principles, the sole creator of all worlds, the sole destroyer of all worlds, the secret of all the Vedas, and the sole bestower of boons upon all the worlds.

To the destroyer of all afflictions and misfortunes; to the bestower of fearlessness upon the entire world; to the one whose crest is the moon; to the one whose own abode is eternal; to the one free from disease; to the one free from distress; to the partless; to the one without dwelling;
to the one without food; to the one beyond phenomenal expansion; to the one free from dualities; to the one without attachment; to the one devoid of qualities.

Victory, victory to you, O Mahārudra, incarnation of Bhava, Mahābhairava, Kālabhairava, Kalpāntabhairava! You who are without attributes or manifestation, without support, eternally pure, perfect, consciousness-bliss, infinite, non-dual, supremely peaceful light, whose form is splendor and who consists of splendor.

O Bhairava of the end of the aeon! O Kapālabhairava! You who bear a garland of skulls, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a sword, a shield, a noose, a goad, a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), a trident, a bow, an arrow, a scimitar, a mace, a spear, a javelin, a slingshot, a club, a mallet, a lance, an iron bar, a bhuśuṇḍi, a śataghni, and a discus as weapons.

O thousand-faced one with terrifying hands, O you whose fierce and formidable loud laughter with bared fangs has split open the circle of the Brahmāṇḍa; O destroyer of the circle of the lords of serpents, O conqueror of Death, O ender of Antaka, O destroyer of Tripura, O ender of Kāma, O three-eyed one, O Lord of the Universe, O you whose vehicle is the bull, O ornament of the universe!

O you of universal form, O six-fold poison, O you whose face is everywhere, protect me on all sides! Blaze, blaze! Destroy the fear of great death and untimely death! || 2 || Destroy, destroy the Raurava hell! Expel, expel the enemies!
Tear asunder with the trident! Split with the axe! Crush with the *khaṭvāṅga* staff! Pound with the pestle!
Crush, crush! Terrify the *rakṣasas*, terrify them! Put to flight the *bhūtas*, put them to flight!

Strike terror into the hosts of *kuṣmāṇḍas*, *vetālas*, and *mārīs*, and into the hosts of *brahmarākṣasas*! Grant me fearlessness, grant it twice! Comfort me who am full of trust, comfort me twice! Gladden me who am afflicted by suffering, gladden me twice!
Ward off, ward off the affliction of hunger and thirst! Lift me up, lift me up from the fear of hell! Cover me, cover me with the armor of Śiva! Oṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva; salutation to you!
Ṛṣabha said: Thus has this supreme armor of Śiva been proclaimed by me;
it is the secret of all embodied beings that pacifies every affliction. (11.114)
Because a mortal would wear this supreme armor of Śiva, no fear whatsoever shall arise for him, by the grace of Śambhu. (11.115)
Whether one's life is exhausted, death has arrived, or one is even struck down by a great disease,
at the end of the body one attains liberation through the power of Śivavarman.
One attains immediate happiness and gains long life;
it pacifies all poverty and increases all auspiciousness. (11.117)
He who wears this armor of Śiva is honored even by the gods;
he is liberated from the multitude of great sins as well as the minor offenses.
"At the end of the body, one attains liberation through the power of the Śiva-armor.
Thus, O Ṛṣabha, the Śiva-kavaca has been proclaimed; it is complete.
Now begins the Thousand Names of Śiva.
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva! The sages said: "O son, how indeed was [the world] created by the God of gods, Maheśvara? (11.119)
"You ought to tell how Viṣṇu obtained the Sudarśana discus.
The son said:
"A most terrible conflict arose between the gods and the lords of the asuras. (11-120)
A great battle for the destruction of all beings took place;
those gods [assailed him] with spears, maces, and straight-knotted arrows.
Being shattered by the spears and overwhelmed by fear,
the defeated gods then fled toward Hari, the Lord of the gods.
With their minds overwhelmed by grief,
they bowed down to the Lord of the Gods at the place where the Blessed One, Hari, the Lord of the gods, was staying.
Having prostrated, he spoke these words to the gods who stood before him. Hari said:
"O sons of gods, why indeed are you here, deprived of your ornaments and finery?"
"O you of excellent vows, having assembled here in great distress, you ought to speak.
Having heard those words of his, the supreme gods became so.
Having prostrated, they reported what had occurred to the god Viṣṇu:
"O Blessed One, O God, O Lord of Gods, O Janārdana who reclines upon Śeṣa! (11.126)
Afflicted by the Dānavas, we have all come to you ourselves for refuge;
O God, Lord of Gods, O Supreme Person, you alone are our goal.
You alone are the Supreme Self; you are the father of the worlds as well.
You here are the slayer, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the giver, and Janārdana.
Therefore, O crusher of the Dānavas,
you ought to slay the Dānavas and the Daityas with Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Raudra, and Yāmya weapons that are most terrible.
And by those belonging to Kubera, those of the Moon, those of Nirṛti, and the firm ones of Varuṇa;
likewise by those of Vāyu, the Yakṣas, those of Īśāna, and the auspicious ones of Vāsuki.
O lotus-eyed one, even by the formidable lords of serpents—by the Kaṃpanas, Jṛmbhanas, and the Dṛḍhas—they were invincible due to the boon they had obtained. (11.131)
Your supreme discus, born from the solar orb,
was blunted by Dadhīca, the son of Cyavana, O Teacher of the World.
The staff and the Śārṅga bow—all have become fruitless;
they were fashioned long ago by the Enemy of Tripura to destroy Jālandhara. (11.133)
That terrible and sharp wheel of yours is capable of slaying those who bow before you;
therefore, he must be slain by it, even if he were protected by hundreds of other weapons.
Then, having heard their words,
the lotus-eyed Hari himself, the wielder of the discus, spoke to those whose mouths were the masters of speech.
Viṣṇu said: "O, O God Mahādeva, having now obtained the eternal Lord of All,
I shall accomplish everything for the inhabitants of heaven."
The gods, having obtained from him a sharp discus fashioned by Tripurāri to slay Jālandhara, used it to destroy the palaces of the lords of the gods.
"O Daityas, all those wicked ones with faces like kinsmen— the six hundred and fifty Asuras— I shall utterly destroy them along with their wealth in a mere instant."
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to the foremost of the gods, he worshipped Śaṅkara after duly installing the linga upon the auspicious peak of Himavat.
Resembling Mount Meru and fashioned by Viśvakarman,
Janārdana had it established after being installed by the Rudra named Tvarita.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings that supreme form shaped like a flame,
and having then worshipped Rudra and bowed before the fire, they were satisfied.
And one should offer oblations to Maheśāna, beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "Namaḥ," by means of the Thousand Names of the God, according to their sequence and with true devotion.
And with a lotus for each name, he worshipped Śaṅkara; and in the fire, he honored the God with oblations of fuel and other offerings accompanied by His names and meditations.

The Lord, having been offered oblations according to the ritual ending with *svāhā* ten thousand times for each [deity], was satisfied; and they, beginning with Bhava, praised Śambhu, the Lord of existence.

For this *Śrīśivasahasranāmastotra* mantra, Viṣṇu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Blessed Lord Śiva is the deity (*devatā*), and the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chanda*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining the aforementioned fruits and for the propitiation of Śrī Śiva, whether in recitation or in fire-oblation (*homa*).
Bhava, Śiva, Hara, Rudra, Puṣkara, Padmarocana, Agrakoṇya, Sadācāra, Śarva, Śambhu, and Maheśvara. || 11-145 ||
The Lord, the Immovable One, the Ruler, the Thousand-eyed, the Thousand-footed;
the Most Excellent, the Giver of Boons, the Worthy of Veneration, the Beneficent, the Supreme Sovereign.
Gaṅgādhara, wielder of the trident, whose sole purpose is the welfare of others,
the omniscient one, the god of all gods, who bears the mountain as his bow and wears matted locks.
Candrapīḍa, Candramauli, the wise one, Vidyāmaheśvara, the essence of the Vedānta, Kapālī, and Nīlalohita. || 11-148 ||
He is fit for meditation, discernible, the husband of Gaurī, the Lord of the Gaṇas;
he possesses eight forms, is the universal form, and is the means for attaining the three aims of life and heaven.
He is accessible through knowledge, possessed of firm wisdom, the god of gods, the three-eyed one;
he is Vāmadeva, the Great God, the skillful, the sovereign lord, and the ancient.
He is the one of universal form, the one with diverse eyes, the one praised by the lords of speech,
the one who accords with all means of valid cognition, the bull-bannered, and the one whose vehicle is the bull.
The Lord who wields the Pināka bow and the Khaṭvāṅga staff, whose attire is variegated, the ancient one, the captivating,
the great renouncer, the steadfast, born from the body of Brahmā, with matted hair.
The death of Death, clad in an animal hide, the fortunate one whose essence is the *praṇava*,
mounted upon a serpent, with beautiful eyes, wearing *durvā* grass, and the chastiser of Smara.
Armed with a firm weapon, the preceptor of Skanda, devoted to the Supreme Lord;
without beginning, middle, or end, the Lord of the Mountain, the kinsman of the mountain.
The friend of Kubera, Śrīkaṇṭha, the most excellent among the best of the world’s castes,
the common deity, the wielder of the bow, the blue-throated one, and the bearer of the battle-axe.
Viśālākṣa, Mṛgendra, Asya, Suratha, Sūryatāpana, Dharmadhāman, Kṣamākṣetra, Bhagavān, and likewise Bhagahṛt.
The fierce one, the lord of creatures, dear to Tākṣya, the beloved, the sweet-spoken, the giver, the compassionate, the skillful, the one with matted hair, and the crusher of desire. || 11-157 ||
The creator of the world, the lord of beings, the great medicine for great karma;
the northern one, the lord of rays, the protector, accessible through knowledge, the ancient one.
Nīti, Sunīti, Śuddhātman, Soma, Somarata, Sukhī, Somapa, Mṛtapa, Saumya, Mahārīti, and Mahādyuti. || 11-159 ||
Ajātaśatru beheld the venerable bearer of oblations,
the eternal creator of the worlds, the author of the Vedas, and the author of the Sūtras.
The great seer, the teacher Kapila, who illuminates all splendors;
the wielder of the Pināka bow, the god upon earth, the bestower of well-being and the giver of prosperity. || 11-161 ||
The sustainer, the creator of light, the all, the omniscient, the one whose range is everywhere;
the creator of Brahman, the creator of the universe, the emanation, the lover of the *karṇikāra* flower, and the pure one.
Śākha, Viśākha, Gośākha, Śiva, Anekakratu, Sama, Gaṅgāplavodaka, Bhavya, Puṣkala, Sthapati, and Sthira. (11.163)

158a) He who has conquered his self, whose self is disciplined, the charioteer of the manifestation of beings; he who loves ashes, who sleeps on ashes, the lover of Kāma, and the one who has mastered the sacred scriptures. || 11-164 ||
Endowed with equanimity, his self withdrawn, united with Dharma, he is Sadāśiva;
four-faced and four-armed, the abode of all, he is difficult to approach.
Difficult to traverse, difficult to attain, and difficult of access, he is skilled in all weapons;
he is the abode of the yoga of the supreme self, the excellent thread, and the increaser of the thread.
The Lord of the World, Janārdana, whose limbs are auspicious, who is the essence of yoga,
the purifier by means of ash, Meru, the vigorous one, and the one of pure form.
Hiraṇyaretas, Taraṇi, Marīci, Himālaya, Mahāhrada, and Mahāgarbha; she who is praised by the multitude of Siddhas and Apsarases.
Clad in a tiger skin, the serpent-like one, the great being, the great treasure;
the Lord of Nectar, whose body is nectar, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.

He was a knower of the twenty-five principles, one who had fully realized both the higher and the lower; he was easily accessible, firm in his vows, heroic, and the singular treasury of all that is expressed in speech.
He is the teacher of the castes and stages of life, the conqueror of enemies, and the scorcher of foes;
he knows the self, is compassionate, tireless, possessed of wisdom, and is both powerful and weak.
He is the embodiment of valid cognition, difficult to comprehend, possessing the form of Garuḍa, and having Vāyu as his vehicle;
he is the wielder of the bow, a treasury of the qualities of the science of archery, and the protector of the Śāka tree.
O Ānanda, Anantadṛṣṭi, who had subdued those who were difficult to subdue with his staff,
paid homage to the Great Teacher, who was an expert in all crafts.

One whose self is disciplined through freedom from passion, an ascetic who carries living beings, disguised in the garb of a madman, one who has conquered desire and is beloved by the people. || 11-174 ||
He is of auspicious nature, the cosmic eon, the lord of all worlds and progeny; he is the ascetic, the deliverer, the wise, the primordial matter, the source of manifestation, and the imperishable.

With his form concealed from the world-protectors, his eyes like the lotus at the beginning of the eon, he knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures; he is the restraint and the refuge of all restraints.
He is Rāhu, Sūrya, Śani, and Ketu; he is the cessation [of suffering] and possesses the luster of coral.
He is the Supreme Brahman accessible through devotion, the one who leads [beings] by bestowing the protection of his hand upon the deer.
The mountain-dweller, the one who rests upon the mountain, the peaceful one, the Supreme Self, the Lord of the universe,
the support of all actions, the auspicious one, and the one enveloped in auspiciousness.
He is the great ascetic, long-standing in austerity, the most ancient, the firm, the day,
the year, attainment, the standard of measure, and the supreme austerity.
The mantra that brings about the year, the means of realization, the all-seeing one;
the unborn, the Lord of All, the perfected one, possessed of great seed and great power.
Mahādeva is fit for yogis; he is the perfected one, the source of all, the giver of fire, the Vasu, the one whose mind is wealth, the Truth, and the nectar that removes all sins. || 11-181 ||
He is the immortal, the eternal, the peaceful, the one with a lute in his hand, the majestic,
the bearer of the water-pot, the archer, the sage who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
The one who rescues, the provider of enjoyment, the enjoyer, the leader of the world, the bearer of the burden;
he whose senses have ceased, the great illusion, existing in all states, the crossroads.

The yogin of time, the great sound, the one of great enthusiasm, the one of great strength, the one of great intelligence, the one of great heroism, the wanderer among beings, the destroyer of cities. || 11-184 ||
Night-walker, ghost-roamer, possessor of great power, of great luster, beloved of the Daityas, ever devoted to dance, illuminator, and burner of enemies. || 11-185 ||
The aged one, the mantra of six syllables, born from the essence of the six true measures;
the creator of the ages and the cycles of the ages, the profound one who has the bull as his vehicle.
He is the beloved, the distinguished, the most excellent among the disciplined, the Śarabha, the bow for the locusts,
the ocean, the foundation, and the knower of the time of victory and defeat.
Established [in his power], the golden-armored Hari, who knows the means of proof, has liberated the hosts of gods; he is the knower of all sciences and the refuge of the wise.
He who has the form of a child, the destroyer of the demon Bala, who is profound with his transformations, Guha;
he who is the instrument, the cause, and the agent, the liberator from all bonds. || 11-189 ||

He is resolve, steadfastness, the giver of station, and the conqueror of the world; he is the drum-sound, the graceful one, the universe, existence itself, and that which is established within the self.
Vīreśvara, Vīrabhadra, Vīrāsana, Vidhi, Virāṭ, Vīracūḍāmaṇi, Vettā, Tīvrānanda, and Nadīdhara. || 11-191 ||
The bearer of consciousness, marked with the trident, Śipiviṣṭa, the refuge of Śiva;
the Vālakhilyas, the great ascetic, the one of fierce rays, the support of strength, and the sky-goer.
Abhirāma, Suranya, Subrahmaṇya, Sudhāmarāṭ, Madyavān, Kauśika, Gomān, Virāma, and Sarvaśāsana. || 11-193 ||
With an eye on his forehead and tawny hair, he sustains the entire wheel of saṃsāra;
standing amidst the unfailing rod of punishment, he possesses the splendor of gold and the luster of Brahman.

The supreme noble one, the one who has reached the highest state, the restrainer, the wrathful tiger; he who is to be worshipped by the radiant and excellent lord, the master of speech, the protector of the day.
Ravi, Virocana, Skanda, Śāstra, Yama the son of Vaivasvata, Mukti, Unnakakīrti, Śāntarāga, and Purañjaya. || 11.196 ||
The lord of Kailāsa, the enemy of Kāvya, the one with the sun as his eye,
the most learned, the fearless, and the destroyer of the universe was warded off.
He is eternally fixed in auspiciousness, whose merit is found in hearing and chanting his name;
he is difficult to approach, the endurer of all, the object of meditation, and the destroyer of evil dreams.
The deliverer, the destroyer of evil deeds, the remover of sorrow...

(159a) the protector of all, the taker of all, the hero of his own valor, he of radiant armlets; the progenitor, the source of the birth of beings and so forth, the one possessed of joy, the one possessed of policy, and the one who leads by right conduct. (11.200)
Vasiṣṭha, Kaśipu, Bhānu, Bhīma, and Bhīmaparākrama;
Praṇava, Satpathācāra, Mahākāya, and Mahādhanu. || 11-201 ||
The lord of birth is Mahādeva, who has mastered auspicious conduct;
his soul is the discernment between reality and unreality, and he is adorned with the ashes of the desire for wealth.
The bull, the hater of Brahmins, the one who transcends birth, death, and old age;
the sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, the sacrificer, the limb of sacrifice, and the one of unfailing prowess.
Mahendra, Durbhara, Senī, Yajñānta, Yajñavāhana, Pañcabrahmasamutpatti, Viśveśa, and Vimalodaya. || 11-204 ||
Born of himself, eternal, the sustainer of the world of thirty-six principles,
the beloved of Gāyatrī, lofty, dwelling on Mount Vindhya, and the maker of light.
The infant, the one who has crossed over, he who possesses a great army, the slayer of the enemies of the gods,
the destroyer of unfailing misfortune, the deliverer from death, and the one free from all feverish affliction.
The remover of disease, he who is the light, supported by divine light;
tawny, reddish-brown, with a beard, having the scriptures as his eyes, and the triple Veda as his body.
The aggregate of knowledge (jñānaskandha), the great conscious one, the arising, the deluge;
Bhaga, Vivasvat, Āditya, and the teacher of Yoga, Bṛhaspati. || 11-208 ||
Of noble fame, diligent, a yoginī, and one who has transcended both existence and non-existence.
The sky is garlanded with constellations; its support is the self-abiding [cakra] located in the anus.
It has pure hands, is the enemy of evil, and its movement of mind is at Maṇipūra.
Seated upon a lotus, white, a hawk, Vṛṣākapi;
fierce, with a fierce abode, black, the capable destroyer of misfortune. || 11-210 ||
He who is the enemy of unrighteousness, who is invincible, who is invoked by many, and who is ancient;
he who contains the Veda within him, who possesses a vast womb, who is the bridge of Dharma, and the source of wealth. (11.211)
The Sugata who desires the welfare of the world, the Youthful One, the source of all that is wholesome;
he is golden-hued, radiant, and possesses a navel like the path of the earth.
