Viśvāmitra was the superintendent of health regulations, the lord of the twice-born, the light of Brahman, of perfectly pure soul, the supreme great light. || 11.213 ||
Mātāmaha, Mātariśvan, Nāgahāra, Pinākadhṛt, Pulyastya, Pulaha, Agastya, Jaṃbūkarṇa, and Parāśara. (11.214)
Viriñci, who knows the stainless dharma; Viṣṭaraśravas;
Ātmabhū; Niruddha; and Atri, the embodiment of supreme knowledge.
Of great renown, the crest-jewel of the world, whose valor is truth;
like a serpent, a great aeon, and the bearer of the arts of the wish-fulfilling tree.
He who adorns himself, he whose gait is unshakable, Viṣṇu, he of supreme prowess,
he whose movement is swift and intense, the purifier, and he whose charioteer is the fire.
Asaṃśliṣṭa, Tithi, Māthīva, Pāpanāśana, Vasuśravas, Kavyavāha, Pratapta, and Viśvabhojana. || 11-218 ||
The one to be recited is the son of Anūnapāt, who has red horses, who subdues old age and disease;
may he, whose horses are spotted, who is of beautiful aspect and a slayer of darkness, protect us.
The conqueror of enemy cities was like a cloud that dispels the heat of summer;
he was a pleasant breeze, most agreeable to the touch, fragrant, and possessed of the nature of the moon.
Vasanta, Mādhava, Grīṣma, Nabhas, Vījavāhana, Āṅgiras, Guru, Rātri, Vimala, and Viśvavāhana. || 11-221 ||
The Purifier, the Conqueror of Cities, the Wielder of the Discus, the Knower of the Three Vedas, the One whose Vehicle is the Mountain;
he is the mind, the intellect, the ego, the Knower of the Field, and the Protector of the Field. || 11-222 ||
Jamadagni, the ocean, the fruition, the creator of all; the lower, the higher, the knower, Jyeṣṭhā, and the abode of the supreme good.
The one who has consumed the mountains with fire, the enemy of the Dānavas, the subduer of foes;

he who possesses the four Vedas and the four states of being, the clever one, the beloved of the clever; he who is the traditional scripture and the eternal tradition, the deity of sacred fords, and the abode of Śiva.
He who possesses many forms, great forms, and beautiful forms, the illuminator of light;
he who is the logic that carries one across fear, accessible through reason, and free from passion.
The Lord of the Gods, the destroyer of all scriptures, has a thousand heads;
he is shaven-headed, deformed, and disfigured, yet he is a staff-bearer who possesses the highest quality of self-restraint.
Lord of wealth, tawny-eyed, blue-necked, free from ailment, thousand-armed, the all-pervading part, the refuge, and the sustainer of all worlds.
Padmasena, Padmagarbha, Viśvagarbha, Vicakṣaṇa, Parāvarajña, Vīreśa, Sumukha, and Sumahāsvana. || 11-229 ||
The god who is the teacher of gods and asuras, honored by gods and asuras;
the great minister of gods and asuras, the great refuge of gods and asuras. || 11-230 ||
The god of gods, the divine seer, the bestower of boons upon gods and asuras;
the lord of gods and asuras, the god who is the great sovereign of gods and asuras. || 11-231 ||
He who is conceivable through the sphere of all the gods, born from the self of the deity;
he is the Lord to be praised, the tiger among gods, the lion of the gods, and the maker of day.

The most excellent and supreme among those carrying quivers, the beloved of Śikhaṇḍin and Pārvatī, he who holds the thunderbolt in hand, the restrainer of himself, and the slayer of Narasiṃha. || 11.233 ||
He is the observer of celibacy, the wanderer of the world, the practitioner of dharma, and the lord of wealth;
he is Nandin, the Lord of Nandins, the naked one, the bearer of the vow of nakedness, and the pure one.
The overseer of the marks, the overseer of the gods, the overseer of the ages, the bringer of the ages;
he who has gone to heaven, heaven itself, the sound, and whose voice consists of the sounds of the Vedas.
The overseer of seeds, the creator of seeds, the maker of wealth, the increaser of dharma;
the deceptive, the deceptive one, the great deceptive one, the supreme lord of all beings. || 11-236 ||
Tīṣya, whose abode is the cremation ground, Ketu of incomparable form,
possessing supramundane and vivid vision, Tāmavaka, adorned with serpents.
Viṣṇu, the enemy of Andhakāsura, who severed his head; he whose qualities shine forth from the absence of defects, and who shattered the teeth of Dakṣa’s enemies.
Dhūrjaṭi, the one with the broken axe, the manifest, the unmanifest, the sinless;
the support of all supports, the pale-bodied, the compassionate, the supreme man. (11.239)
Pūrṇa, Purayitṛ, Puṇya, Sukumāra, Sulocana, Sāmagānapriya, Krūra, Puṇyakīrti, and Anāmaya. || 11-240 ||
He who is as swift as thought, the founder of a school, the one with matted hair, the lord of life, the ender of life, the infinite one, whose seed is wealth, and the bestower of wealth. || 11-241 ||

The one who leads to the good state, the one honored by the virtuous, the one who is attached, the dark-throated, the bearer of the arts, the one beyond the mind, the great time, the source of true prosperity, and the one whose stride is truth. || 11-242 ||
The Teacher who revives the moon, the Lord of the gods hidden from the world, the kinsman of the world, the Protector of the world, the grateful one, adorned with fame. || 11-243 ||
He is beyond the states of woe, the best among all upholders of the scriptures;
he is composed of splendor, the bearer of radiance, and the foremost leader of the hosts of lords of the world.
He of pure smiles, serene in soul, difficult to conquer, impossible to transcend;
the embodiment of light yet formless, the Lord of the world, the Sovereign of the waters.
He who possesses a beautiful lute and a great body, who is free from sorrow and the destroyer of grief;
the soul of the three worlds, the lord of the three worlds, the source of the pure, the impure, and that which is beyond both.
He was manifest in his characteristics yet unmanifest, both manifest and unmanifest, O Lord of the People;
he possessed excellent conduct and supreme qualities, and was more enchanting than the god of love himself.
He is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Prajāpati; he is the swan, the one whose gait is like that of a swan, and Yama; he is the Piercer, the Ordainer, the Creator, the Destroyer, and the Four-faced One.
Dwelling on the peak of Kailāsa, he is the abode of all and the refuge of the virtuous;
he is Hiraṇyagarbha, the progenitor, the Puruṣa, the first-born, and the Father.
The abode of beings, the lord of beings, the bestower of being, the sovereign of the world; the true yogi, the knower of yoga, the Brahman, and the beloved of the Brahmins. || 11-250 ||
Beloved by the gods, lord of the gods, knower of the gods, thinker of the gods;
with uneven eyes, with playful eyes, the increaser of prosperity. || 11-251 ||
He is the fleshless one, free from egoism, devoid of delusion, and free from affliction;
he is the destroyer of pride, the subduer of arrogance, the haughty one, and the transformer of all seasons.
He who has seven tongues and a thousand rays, who is gentle and naturally upright;
the lord of the past, future, and present, the source of all, and the destroyer of delusion. (11.253)
A great treasury of both profit and loss, he is a master of accomplishing the tasks of others; free from thorns, he brings joy to all, being sincere and a crusher of deceit. (11.254)
Possessing courage, he was a hero of truth; his fame was established by his arrival [at the battlefield];
he seized trembling planets [or: he captured the trembling elephants]; he was one whose soul was not shaken, performing deeds with singular focus.
The southern wind is exceedingly pleased, fair-faced, subtle, longing,
the bearer of the burden of mountain upon mountain, and the manifest increaser of affection.
Unconquered, the endurer of all, the burner of all, the vehicle of all; the immortal, the one trusted by the entire universe, the pure-formed, the upholder of glory. || 11-257 ||

He whose tusks are like boar’s, who exists for the sake of the elders, the leader of the Vala-demons, the illuminator of the Vedas, the one who intoxicates with the Vedas, and the sole creator of the burden of dharma. 11-258.

He who is like Śrīvallabha, whose undertakings are peaceful, auspicious, and consistent; who rests upon the earth, who bestows prosperity, who is prosperity itself, whose ornament is the earth, and whose vehicle is the elements.
Abiding in the body that is not a body, he knows the proper time; he is skilled in the ritual arts and ordinances.
He is firm in his vows of truth, a great renouncer, whose power is will, and who is the supreme refuge.
Bestower of the power to act for the sake of others, an ocean of pure learning, tireless, perceiving virtues, and one whose heart is stainless and free from blemish. (11.261)
Suprabha, residing in the midst of Vardhamāna, Śatrughna, the scorcher of enemies,
Śikhaṇḍī, the crest-jewel, the wielder of the trident, and the charioteer of the essence of worldly existence.
He is deathless, the all-conqueror, a lion, a mass of splendor, and a great jewel;
he is the immeasurable self in the incalculable, heroic, and skilled in action.
The physician, the protector of physicians, the lord of all inferior sages;
unsurpassed, invincible, sweet, and pleasant to behold. || 11-264 ||
The Lord of the gods, the refuge, the Word, the goal of the virtuous for the Brahman that is Sound; the devourer of Time, the maker of the kalās, with Vāsuki made into his bracelet. || 11-265 ||

He is the lord of the earth, the sustainer of the great, stainless and free from fetters; he is the jewel of heaven, the sun, the one to be honored, the bestower of perfection, and the means for accomplishing all goals.
He has become a perfected artisan, broad-chested and long-armed;
he is the singular light, free from affliction, and beloved by Nara and Nārāyaṇa.

Untainted, whose nature is free from conceptual proliferation, the destroyer of both agitation and its absence; You are the one to be praised, dear to those who praise, the embodiment of the sky of hymns, and untroubled.

He whose feet and so forth are irreproachable, who is a vast mass of knowledge, whose intellect reaches the end of existence, who is not mean, who destroys the mean, and who is eternally beautiful. (11.269)
The foremost among those worthy of meditation, the Lord of the Earth, the Destroyer, the Lord of the Night;
the supreme seer of ultimate reality, who is compassionate toward those who take refuge in him;
the knower of the essence and the non-essence, the knower of the rivers, the support for all sentient beings.
Thus, she gratified the bull-bannered god with these one thousand names.
The Lord bathed the All-pervading One and worshipped Him with lotuses;
then Maheśvara examined those lotuses for their fruits.
We shall protect that single lotus of the Lord of Beings;
there, Hari is the flower of the heart—what indeed should he contemplate? (11.273)
Having realized this, he plucked out his own eye— the support for all sentient beings— and with devotion, he honored the Teacher of the World with that jewel.
Then, having seen Hari there in such a state,
the omnipresent Lord Hara quickly descended from that scorching solar orb.
Resembling ten million suns, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
the god is encircled by garlands of flames, possessing sharp fangs and a terrifying appearance.
Holding a trident, a banner, a mace, a discus, a conch,
and a noose in his hands, he grants boons with both hands and wears a tiger skin as an upper garment.
Having thus seen him then, adorned with the ashes of worldly existence,
Janārdana quickly bowed again to the God of gods.
Seeing that the three-eyed god had abandoned him along with Indra and the other deities,
the abode of Brahmā trembled and the earth shook.
That splendor of Śambhu then burned for a hundred yojanas at its edge, both below and above, while cries of "Alas! Alas! arose at that time.
Then Mahādeva Śaṅkara, looking at Viṣṇu who stood with palms joined in reverence, spoke as if smiling out of affection.
O Janārdana, I have now understood this task of the gods;
I give to you this beautiful discus named Sudarśana.
O you of excellent vows, that form which was seen by you—terrifying to all the world—has been manifested for the sake of [our] welfare; indeed, it is for the benefit of all beings.
O Viṣṇu, the cessation of the excessive clamor of battle is the painful instruction for the gods;
for those who have attained peace, the weapon of the scripture is peace itself for the ascetics.
Meditate upon my own imperishable form, which is unappeased by the gods, as it wages war to destroy the power of a formidable enemy. (11.285)

O Janārdana, you who destroy the enemies of the gods, it is indeed not the time for patience or for performing other duties, but rather the time has arrived for fighting in order to save our lives. 11.286.
O destroyer of enemies, when this multitude of people is weak in both the future and the past, and when there is unrighteousness that is not timely and is ignoble. (11.287)
Thus addressed, she gave him a discus with a radiance equal to ten thousand suns;
furthermore, by her power, an eye appeared that resembled a lotus.
Furthermore, through his power, an eye emerged that resembled a lotus;
from that time onwards, those of excellent vows called it *padmākṣa*. (11.289)
He touched him with his two auspicious hands and said:
"I am the giver of boons; O best of boon-seekers, choose a boon as you desire."
"O Puruṣottama, you have indeed been made by me through devotion.
Having been addressed thus by the God of Gods, he prostrated before the God of Gods. || 11-291 ||
O Mahādeva, may there be devotion toward you; be gracious and grant this supreme boon: that for your devotees, no afflictions whatsoever shall ever arise. (11.292)
Having heard those words of his, the compassionate Lord Bhava was moved even further;
the God touched him and granted him a boon according to his desire.
And Mahādeva spoke thus to the Supreme Self, the Infallible One:
"I am his devotee, his kinsman, and indeed worthy of worship by both gods and asuras. (11.294)
O best of gods, by my grace there will be no doubt that you shall become fair-eyed, just as Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, was indeed reviled. (11.295)
O Kṛṣṇa of noble vows, at that time the divine Haimavatī shall become my mother, father, and capable guardian, O Lord of the Gods.
At the direct command of Brahmā, your sister shall bestow upon you that divine and auspicious goddess, the daughter of Himavat, who is endowed with perfect beauty.
"O Śaṅkara, from that time forward, you shall be my kinsman and worthy of worship among the gods; and [you shall regard] me with a divine disposition. (11.298)
"And you are worshipped here by me, who am well-disposed toward you as a friend.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Rudra, Nīlalohita, bestowed [the boon].
Then the blessed Janārdana, in the presence of the gods,
approached Brahmā, the best of the deities, together with the sages.
O Lotus-born One, this divine and beautiful hymn has been spoken by me;
whoever recites it, or hears it, or causes the best of the twice-born to hear it— || 11-301 ||
One shall obtain the fruit of gold given every month;
indeed, the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices accrues to that person.
One should bathe Rudra with ghee and other substances using auspicious jars placed upon a vessel,
while reciting this Thousand Names with faith toward Īśvara, the Auspicious One.
He too, having obtained the fruit of a thousand sacrifices, becomes worthy of worship by the lords of the gods; indeed, Rudra becomes pleased with him.
Then Janārdana, born from the lotus, spoke thus to him;
all the gods, having paid homage to the one who is worshipped, departed after bowing to the Lord.
O sinless ones, the twice-born should worship with the thousand names of Śiva;
by reciting the thousand names, one attains the supreme goal.
Thus ends the King of Thousand-Name Hymns (*Sahasranāmastavarāja*), known as the Greatly Powerful One, upon obtaining the glorious Sudarśana-cakra.
Homage to the glorious Śiva.
Oṃ. Brahman is one, without a second; all is truth, truth—here there is nothing else whatsoever.
Rudra is one, he did not stand with a second; therefore, I take refuge in You, the Great Lord, as the One. (11-307)
O Śambhu, you alone are indeed the creator of all; though one, you possess forms that bring about various desired ends.
Just as the sun, though single, appears as many to those on different paths, so too do you appear manifold—therefore, O Lord, I take refuge in you who are distinct from all else.
(2) A snake in a rope, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and water in a mirage called a "deer-thirst" are perceived by men before them.
Just as duality ceases when that in which the manifold world resides is known, I take refuge in that Great Lord.
(3) You are coolness and you are the burner; you are the heat in fire and the cold in the moon; you are negligence.
O Śambhu, since the ghee was consumed by the fire within the midst of the flowers, I therefore take refuge in you. (4)
I perceive sound though you are without ears; indeed, you smell though you are without a nose; you come from afar though you are without feet;
you see with your chest though you are without eyes; and you know tastes though you are without a tongue—who can truly know you? To you I take refuge. (5)
If you do not know him who is the Lord himself, nor Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor the Creator of all;
if neither the lords of yogins nor the gods headed by Indra know him—then, O Bhakta, may you attain him who is beyond darkness.
If you do not know him who is the Lord himself, nor Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor the Creator of all; [then, O Bhakta, may you attain him who is beyond darkness].
Neither the lords of yogis nor the chief gods are your devotees; therefore, I take refuge in you, who possess the nature of the Veda.

(7) Without lineage, without birth, without name, without form, without character, and without age—even being such as this, you are the Lord of the three worlds; you fulfill all desires, so one should worship you. (8)
"From you everything comes, for you are indeed all, O enemy of Smara; you are the Lord of Gaurī, and you alone are the tranquil one who is not naked.
You are the aged, you are the youth, and you are the child; what then is that which you are not? I am not that reality.
Having praised him thus, the Brahmin fell prostrate on the ground like a staff, bowing with joy.
Then the most venerable among all the elders spoke to that best of Brahmins: "Choose a boon! (10) || 11-316 ||
Then, having risen with a joyful heart, that virtuous man, a disciple of the sage, replied: "O Lord, what is unknown to you, the omniscient one? (11.317)
O Blessed One, you are the inner self of all, the All, and the bestower of everything; O Lord, command whatever is appointed for me, who am devoted to the service of the Daityas.
Having heard these words of that Viśvānara, the pure one of pure vows, the child then spoke with a pure smile: (11.319).
Vāla said:
This meritorious hymn, the *Abhilāṣāṣṭaka*, which has been recited by me, grants all desires when recited three times a day for one year in the presence of Śiva. (11.320)
The recitation of this hymn bestows sons, grandsons, and wealth;
it brings about all peace and destroys all enemies. (11.321)
It brings about the attainment of heaven and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having risen at dawn and bathed, one should worship the Śambhu-liṅga.
Chanting this hymn for a year, one who is childless shall obtain a son,
provided he observes special vows during the months of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha.
Whoever should recite this at the time of bathing shall obtain the entire fruit [of the vow],
by the grace of me, the Imperishable, during the month of Kārttika.
This *Abhilāṣāṣṭaka* should not be given to just anyone; it must be guarded with great effort by one who has produced a highly venerable offspring. (11.325)
Whether by a woman or even by a man, this hymn, when recited for one year with the observance of the rules in the presence of the Liṅga, bestows sons; there is no doubt in this matter. (11.326)
Having spoken thus, Bāla vanished, and that Brahmin also went home.
Thus ends the Śrī Vastotra.
Now, in the Padma Purāṇa, the characteristics and the greatness of the rudrākṣa [beads]. (11.327)
The man who wears rudrākṣas with devotion on his crest-lock, his hands, his neck, and also his ears, shall attain the world of Śiva. (11.328)
It is traditionally taught that for the wearing of Rudrākṣas, they should be without holes and self-perforated;
by means of a rosary of twenty-seven Rudrākṣas worn upon the body, [one attains the desired fruit].
Whatever merit a man performs becomes ten-millionfold if he gives a rudrākṣa to the twice-born while facing the earth. (11.330)
His son shall become Rudra, and Rudra bestows his own station upon him;
even if a dog dies while a rudrākṣa remains on its body.
Even he goes to the state of Rudra; how much more so, O Guha, a human being!
Śiva himself, when manifested with a single face, removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
If those two are recited in a low voice without being pierced [by other sounds], it creates a paralysis of fire;
the "Two-faced" (Dvivaktra) mantra of Hara-Gaurī effects the destruction of sins such as the slaughter of a cow.
The three-faced fire shall destroy the heap of sins accumulated over three births;
the four-faced one himself, Brahmā, removes even the sin of killing a human being.
The five-faced Kālāgni removes the sin of approaching those who should not be approached and eating forbidden food; the six-faced Guha himself removes the sin of foeticide. (11.335)
Ananta, however, has seven faces; he is golden and always removes the afflictions of yoga.
Vimāya has a square face and is the destroyer of all falsehoods. || 11-336 ||
Bhairava has a human face and bestows union with Śiva;
Viṣṇu is remembered as having ten faces and being the destroyer of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
Rudra with eleven faces bestows the fruits of various sacrifices;
from twelve [faces] arises the Sun, who bestows the fruit of all rituals.
Kāma has thirteen faces and bestows the fruits of all desires;
Śrīkaṇṭha has fourteen faces, and another is the upholder of the lineage.
A wise man should wear a nine-faced rudrākṣa on his left arm,
and he should wear a fourteen-faced one on his crest-lock.
Then, for the consecration of the rudrākṣa, one should employ the five-syllable mantra;
furthermore, one should apply the single mantra beginning with "Oṃ Tryambaka" in each respective instance.
At the time of bathing, one should employ the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
just as with the five-syllable mantra.
Homage to Śiva.
The Tryambaka mantra is as follows:
Oṃ, we worship the three-eyed one, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity. || 11-342 ||
Like a cucumber from its stalk, may she be released from death into immortality.
Oṃ hāḥ! Aghore!
Oṃ hauḥ! Ghore hre, O most terrible one!
Oṃ au/ hrī/ [be present] everywhere on every limb!
Homage to you, O form of Rudra, hrī/!
Even with a very brief mantra, O best of the twice-born, [the merit of wearing] a rudrākṣa [is attained]. (11.343)
One should perform the consecration according to the rules; thereby one obtains superior fruit.
Then, endowed with devotion, one should wear [the image] with its own respective mantra. (11.344)
In that regard, the mantra follows in sequence:
Oṃ oṃ bhṛśaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ oṃ namaḥ | Oṃ hrīḥ namaḥ |
Oṃ hraḥ, homage! [4] Oṃ hrūḥ, homage! [5] Oṃ oṃ huḥ hruḥ, homage! [6]
Oṃ saḥ hra/ namaḥ [7]. Oṃ ha/ namaḥ [8]. Oṃ hrī/ namaḥ [9].
Oṃ śrī/ Namaḥ [10].
Oṃ hu/ Namaḥ [11]. Oṃ kṣā/ kṣau/ Namaḥ [12].
Oṃ, salutations, salutations.
Thus ends the "Glorification of the Rudrākṣa" in the Padma Purāṇa.
Now, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Kārttikeya said: One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen, and fourteen Vasus. (11.345)
Among these faces, who is the deity here, O Śaṅkara?
Tell me truly that which is the secret, even more secret than the secrets of them.
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Six-faced one, to the truth according to each face in due order.
May the single-faced Śiva himself destroy the sin of killing a Brahmin. (11.347)
A two-faced [liṅga] certainly grants the attainment of a cow to the god and goddess;
a three-faced one is the manifest fire that removes the sin of killing a relative. (11.348)
Brahmā himself, with four faces, removes the sin of killing a human being;
Rudra himself, with five faces, [removes it] by means of the fire of time (kālāgni).
By wearing [the image of] the six-faced Kārttikeya on the right arm, one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. (11.350)

O Mahāsena, by [worshipping] the seven-faced one, one is liberated from the sins of violating the guru’s bed and so forth, as well as from the serpent named Ananta; of this there is no doubt. (11.351)
The eight-faced Mahāsena is the god Vināyaka himself;
yet such a one might even touch the wife of his guru with the back of his belly or hand. (11.352)
Indeed, such evils and even the most heinous sins are entirely destroyed;
his obstacles perish, and being liberated, he attains the supreme goal.
Indeed, all these qualities belong to Aṣṭavaktra through its wearing;
one becomes Navavaktra Bhairava by wearing it on the left arm. (11.354)
Kapila is declared to be the bestower of liberation; its power shall be equal to my own.
Even he who commits thousands of millions of crores of murders of Brahmins [is purified by it].
All that is quickly consumed by the wearing of the nine faces;
O Mahāsena, the ten-faced one is the god Janārdana himself. (11.356)
Planets, piśācas and other spirits, vetālas, brahmarākṣasas, and serpents are all destroyed by the wearing of the ten-faced [mantra]. (11.357)
An eleven-faced Rudrākṣa is known as the eleventh Rudra;
listen now to the merit of one who constantly wears it on the crest-lock. || 11-358 ||
Whatever fruit is obtained from a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, and a hundred thousand gifts of gold properly bestowed; [that fruit is attained here]. (11.359)
One attains that fruit by wearing eleven Rudrākṣas;
one should wear twelve Rudrākṣas on the face and in the region of the neck.
The one who is to be pierced (Ādabhya), established in the twelve suns, is eternally satisfied.
Therein, he states the mantras in sequence:
Oṃ Aiḥ [1].
Oṃ śrī.
[2] Oṃ bra dhryu.
[3] Oṃ jī hūṃ hrāḥ. [4]
oṃ hrīḥ [5] oṃ hrīḥ [6] oṃ hrāḥ [7]
Oṃ bru ra [8] Oṃ hrā [9] Oṃ hrī [10]
oṃ hrīḥ hraḥ [11] oṃ kṣrauḥ strīḥ [12] oṃ uḥ māḥ ṭhaḥ [13]
Oṃ, salutations, salutations.
Thus ends the *Rudrākṣamāhātmya* as spoken in the glorious *Skandapurāṇa*.
164a) Now follows the definition of great knowledge (mahāvidyā).
This has been stated in the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
Kālītārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, and Bhuvaneśvarī. || 11-361 ||
Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and likewise the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī;
Vagalā, Siddhividyā, Mātaṅgī, and she whose essence is Kamalā. (11.362)
O Great Goddess, these ten Mahāvidyās have been proclaimed;
thus it is stated in the Bhūtabharavī Tantra.
Then Nṛsiṃha, Hayagrīva, Bhairava, and Caraṇāyudha.
Kṣetrapāla, Mahākāla, the Yakṣas and the Yakṣiṇīs, Trijaṭā, Ekajaṭā, Tārā, Grāhikā, and Nīlasarasvatī. (11.364)
Śavarī, Tripurā, Vālā, Mahogrā, Kālasundarī, Brahmatārā, Caṇḍālī, Śyāmā, and Karṇapiśācinī. (11.365)
Mātaṅgī, Dhanadā, Kālī, Tuṣṇī, Phalapradā, Śavarī, Aritā, Caṇḍālī, and Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālī [are the goddesses] in the Kali age. (11.366)
In this [practice], there is no requirement for perfected beings (siddhas) and the like, nor is there any consideration of constellations and so forth;
there is no need for wealth presided over by the *kalās*, nor any defect such as the absence of a spiritual friend (*mitra*). (11.367)

Whether it be the science of accomplishment (*siddhividyā*) or the great science (*mahāvidyā*), there is no exertion whatsoever that is difficult to achieve through this pair, O Great Goddess; how could it be otherwise? (11.368)
In former times, Ekākṣī Mahāvidyā was devoid of seed-syllables;
Bhuvaneśī is three-syllabled—these are proclaimed as the Mahāvidyās. || 11.369 ||
In ancient times, the great lore Bhuvaneśī was propitiated by the king of the gods,
and even by Vajra she was completely enchanted.
The single-syllable [mantra] is devoid of seed-syllables; the supreme Vāgbhava is not radiant.
That Vidyā known as Kāmarāja was pierced by you, the wielder of the bow. (11.371)
Māyā is established solely as the form of Śiva and solely as the form of Śakti; she is Vidyā, Tārā, whose nature is that of the Moon. (11.372)
"Bhairavī is indeed the great vidyā, the bestower of great prosperity," thus it is said in the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
But surely, why should one abandon the Vaiṣṇava and other systems to exert effort in the Śākta? For by those very [other systems], enjoyment and liberation are attained;
what is the use of this? Likewise, it is said that one who possesses knowledge according to the Vedas enters into darkness along with the ignorant.
Thus it should be said by me that cyclic existence is of the nature of suffering; and so it has been stated by the Teachers:
In the Śāmbhava Sūtra.
Indeed, one should take joy in this: "This is what must be done by me; this is what must not be done."
Thus, indeed, the cause of this [world] is called Niyati (Destiny).
Therefore, this supreme Vidyā is established;
so too is the Anuṣṭubh Śruti.
The wise who know the reality of ignorance consider that [the state] beginning with the word "Brahman" has the individual soul as its locus. (11.374)

In this way, the individual soul (*jīva*), when severed from ignorance (*avidyā*), becomes the bestower of liberation; at the state of liberation, it is Brahman—that is to say, it is of the very nature of Brahman.
These are authoritative words:
"Where there is worldly enjoyment, there is no liberation; where there is liberation, there is no enjoyment.
But for one who has taken refuge at the pair of lotus feet of Śiva, both enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of his hand. Thus it is said.
The summary.
He speaks of the extraction of the mantra as being "in the hand."
And likewise, in the Bhūtabhairava:
Krodhīśa, seated upon a ground of blood and adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī, joined with Rudraḍākinī—this is remembered as the Speech situated in the Bindu. (11.375)

Krodhīśa is the letter *ka*; Kṣataja is the letter *ra*. That joined with Dhūmrabharavī, which is said to be the letter *ī*, and Rudraḍākinī, which is the bindu (*m*), joined with that—therefore, *krī* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
And likewise, in the Kālītantra:
The syllable of desire (KĀM) situated in fire (R), together with Indirā (I), Nāda, and the Bindu—this is known as the King of Mantras, difficult for those of sinful minds to attain. (11.375)

The syllable of desire is the letter *ka*; it is situated in fire—fire being the letter *ra*—joined with *Idirā*, which is the letter *ī*; joined above that with *Nāda*, then with *Candra*, and likewise joined with *Bindu*, thus the single-syllabled Vidyā becomes *cakrī*.
One should place the three *kāmas* situated in fire (*vahni*) and endowed with *rati* and *bindu*;
likewise, one should form a pair of *yugas*, followed by a pair of *lajjās*. (11.376)
One should utter the seed-syllables as before, ending with "Kālike" in the south;
at the end, one should give "Vahnivadhū"—this is proclaimed as the Queen of Vidyās.

The three *kāmas* are the three *ka*s; *vahni* is the letter *ra*; *rati* is the vowel *ī*. Joined with that is the *bindu*, the *anusvāra*. Joined with that is the pair of *kūrca*s, namely *hūṃ hūṃ*, which is the pair of *bījas*. The pair of *lajjā*s is *hrīṃ hrīṃ*, which is the pair. To the right is the form "Kālike. The preceding *bījas* are the *bījas* mentioned previously.
One should utter it.
And thus the mantra says:
*krī* *krī* *krī* *hū* *hū* *hrī* *hrī* | *dakṣiṇe kālike* *krī* *krī* *krī* *hū* *hū* *hrī* *hrī* *svāhā* ||
Thus ends the twenty-two-syllable mantra.
I shall proclaim the jewel of knowledge; having heard it, wear it as an ornament upon your ear:
the two *māyās*, the pair of *kur*s, ending with *maindra*, and the three *madanas*. (11.378)

One should extract the seven seed-syllables by means of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), beginning with the word *kālike* on the right, joined with the *māyā*, the *bindu*, and *viśvara*. (11.379)
The wise practitioner should perform the entire worship of the mantra of Kālikā, beginning with the twenty-one syllables starting with *Tārā*, in the same manner as the previously mentioned mantras.
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
The first letter of the class [ka], joined with fire [ra] and endowed with the pleasure-point [anusvāra];
then triple it, followed by a pair of *kūrca* [ha] and likewise a pair of *lajjā* [śa]. (11.381)
To the south is the seed-syllable of Kālikā as before; then again, joined with two *ṭha*s, the wise know this to be the mantra. (11.382)
In this [practice], there is no requirement for the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and the like, nor is there any defect regarding mantras and so forth;
there is no great expenditure of wealth, nor anything that causes physical exhaustion. (11.383)

The first of the consonant groups (*varga*) is *ka*; *vahni* is *ra*, joined with that [is *kra*]; *mati* is *ī*, thus [the seed-syllable] is *krī*. It is tripled, meaning three times. *Kūrca* is *hūṃ*; likewise, from its extraction in the hymn of praise, *lajjā* is *hrī*. Thus, as before, there are three seed-syllables.
The meaning is that, by the very same sequence as before, there are two *svāhā*s for the words; thus [it is].
*Krī krī krī hū hū hrī hrī dakṣiṇe kālike krī krī krī hū hū svāhā*. This is the mantra.
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times according to the rule, remaining pure during the day.
And likewise, being very pure, one should recite it one hundred thousand times at night.
And so it is stated in the Kālīkalpa:
*Namaḥ pāśāṅkuśau dveṭhā phaṭ svāhā kālikālike*—this fifteen-syllable mantra of Kālī has a long vowel at the end of the *tuccha* (the letter *u*). (11.385)
As for the mantra, it is as follows:
Namaḥ ā krā phaṭ ṭhaḥ pa svāhā kālikālike hūm.
Thus is the fifteen-syllable mantra.
HŪM, with a long final syllable and a short vowel.
In the Matsyasūkta:
Then the seed-syllable of *lajjā* (hrīḥ), followed by *krodha* ending in *phaṭ*, becomes the six-syllabled [mantra].
*Krodha* is *hūṃ*; thus, the mantra is *hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
Now follows the ritual for the worship, the method of adoration, of Śyāmasundarī, the Dark Beauty.
It is as follows:
Having arisen during the *brahma-muhūrta* and discarded the night-garment, one should put on two washed cloths, perform *ācamana*,
and meditate upon the Guru within the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrārakamala*) on one's own head.
Of what nature is he?
In the morning, [one should meditate on] the Guru with two eyes and two arms upon a white lotus on the head.
One should meditate upon him as peaceful, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, preceded by his name.
Having thus visualized him and worshipped him with mental offerings, one should pay homage with this [verse]:

Then, for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable *klīṃ*, representing the nature of desire (*kāma*), within the triangle of the *mūlādhāra*. It has the color of the rising sun and is adorned with the three qualities (*guṇas*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Above that, one should meditate on the power (*śakti*) of Kuṇḍalinī, shaped like a sleeping serpent, situated within three and a half coils, [awakened] by the syllable *hūṃ*.

Having performed the mental discipline (*manodaṇḍa*) and having raised [the vital energy] from the *mūlādhāra*, one pierces the six chakras known as *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūraka*, *anāhata*, and *viśuddhi*, and leads it to the thousand-petaled lotus at the head which faces downward; there, by means of the stream of nectar dripping from the lunar orb situated therein—

Having bathed Kuṇḍalinī, who extends as far as the Maṇipūraka, and having meditated for a long time upon the Self in that form, one should lead her back again through the sequence of Ājñā, Viśuddhi, and so forth, down to the Mūlādhāra.

Then, having gone out from the house and relieved himself of excrement and urine, he should enter [the ritual space] after performing the purification rites (śauca) and sipping water (ācamana), cleaning his teeth, and going to a river or similar body of water; there, having performed the bath according to the procedure prescribed in his own Vedic branch (śākhā), he should perform the mantra-bath (mantra-snāna).

Having recited the root mantra (*mūla*) three times and sipped water, having consecrated the water with the root mantra, protected it with "Astrāya Phaṭ," and turned it into nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*) while uttering "Vam," one should offer three handfuls of water upon one's own head using the vase-seal (*kalaśamudrā*) while reciting the root mantra and saying, "I consecrate such-and-such deity. This is the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*).

Having performed the salutation and the libations to the gods and ancestors, and having offered libations three times while reciting the root mantra and saying, "I satisfy such-and-such deity," and having muttered the Gāyatrī, one should recite the root mantra and offer the *arghya* water to the deity residing within the solar orb; thereafter—

Having meditated upon the chosen deity within the solar disc, [one should say] "O Blessed One, O Goddess [Name], O Auspicious One," and having brought the goddess into one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should recite the solar mantra, offer the solar *argha* oblation, and then, remaining silent, approach the door of the worship hall, wash one's hands and feet, and perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*).
One should perform the general offering (sāmānyārgha). Having washed the vessel with the weapon mantra (astramantra) and filled it with "Namaḥ," and having offered perfume, flowers, and so forth,
one should invoke the sacred water (tīrtha) with the tīrtha-mantra and display the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā) with the syllable Om (praṇava).

Then, having sprinkled the door with the *astra* mantra and worshipped it with "Oṃ, obeisance to the deities of the door (*dvāradevatābhyaḥ*"), one should dispel terrestrial obstacles by striking the ground three times with the left foot using the *astra* mantra, and dispel atmospheric obstacles with the *astra* and other mantras.

Having recited "May the divine obstacles, gathered by the root mantra and [perceived] through divine vision, depart," and having scattered the *vikā* flowers, he should enter the pavilion from the south, stepping first with his right foot and placing his left foot forward;
then, having worshipped Brahmā, the Vāstupuruṣa, in the southwest (nairṛtyā) with the mantra "Obeisance to Brahmā, the Vāstupuruṣa," he should prepare the seat.

166a) Having spread *kuśa* grass on a red seat such as a woolen blanket (*kambala*) and so forth, one should worship and meditate [upon it] with the mantra: *hsauḥ sadāśivamahāpretapadmāsanāya namaḥ*.
Regarding the seat, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Merupṛṣṭha, as previously stated.

Having prostrated with the words "O Earth, you... and then sprinkled [the ground] with arghya water, and having worshipped Sadāśiva-mahāpreta with "Hsauḥ," one should sit upon it facing either east or north, assuming either the padmāsana or the svastikāsana posture.

Then, one should offer salutation to the Gurus on the left with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Gurus," to Gaṇeśa on the right with "Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa," and in the center, one should pay homage to the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) with "Oṃ, obeisance to the chosen deity."
One should place the vessels for the conch-water, the foot-bath, and the water for rinsing the mouth to one's left.
Having set out all the materials for worship, such as perfumes and flowers, on the right, one should place a vessel behind for the purpose of washing the hands.
Then, having purified both hands with scents and flowers while reciting *tato hṛḥ astrāya phaṭ*,

and having performed three upward claps (*tāla*) while reciting *hraḥ astrāya phaṭ*, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), the two enclosures (*prākāra*), and the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). As follows:

Placing his hands palms-upward on his own lap and restraining the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he should lead the individual self (*jīvātman*)— shaped like the flame of a lamp— from the heart through the path of the *suṣumnā*, together with the *kuṇḍalinī* residing at the *mūlādhāra*,
piercing the six chakras beginning with the *mūlādhāra*, up to the thousand-petaled lotus situated at the head.

Having united [the self] with the light of the Supreme Self within the pericarp by means of the mantra "I am That" (so'ham), [one should contemplate] that which consists of earth, water, fire, air, and ether; smell, taste, form, touch, and sound; the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears;
speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; and excretion, grasping, movement, procreation, and enjoyment.

Having contemplated the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) there in the form of seeds, one should visualize the Person of Sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) situated in the left side of the belly, black as collyrium and radiant;
he has the murder of a Brahmin for his head, and the theft of gold for his two arms. (11.387)
The drinking of liquor is joined with the heart; violating the Guru’s bed is the two hips;
association with such persons is the pair of feet; and the minor sins are the limbs and sub-limbs. (11.388)
One should visualize the cruel one, whose body hair stands on end due to secondary sins, with red beard and eyes, bearing a sword and shield, upon the left side of the belly.

Having reflected thus, and having meditated upon the seed-syllable *Yaṃ*, smoke-colored, as being this left nostril, one should recite it while filling the entire body with the wind [emanating] from that seed-syllable for sixteen *mātrās*. Then, by means of that same wind,
one should expel the entire body along with the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) through the nostril for sixty-four *mātrās*.
One should exhale the breath.
Then, having visualized the fire seed-syllable (*raṃ*) of an immeasurable red color within the right nostril,
one should fill the breath with sixteen *mātrās* while reciting [the mantra], hold both nostrils, and perform the *kuṃbhaka* (retention).
Having burned that very seed-syllable together with the personification of all bodily sins by means of sixty-four measures (*mātrā*),
one should exhale the wind through the left nostril along with the ashes and the seed-syllable by means of thirty-two measures, as before.

Then, having meditated on the lunar seed-syllable *vaṃ*, white in color, in the left nostril, one should fill the wind with sixteen measures while reciting it and lead it to the moon at the forehead (*lalāṭa*).
From that moon, while reciting the watery seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should perform retention (*kuṃbhaka*) for sixty-four measures.
Having caused a rain of nectar— the rain consisting of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*—
to fall, one should generate [the deity] endowed with the entire body, faces, armor, and feet; then, the yellow-colored seed-syllable of earth (*laṃ*).
Exhaling the breath through the right nostril thirty-two times with the proper measure,
one should contemplate the entire body as having become firm.
Then, having brought the individual soul (*jīvātman*) into the heart-lotus by means of the mantra *haṃsa*, one should [use] that very same mantra.
One should also lead Kuṇḍalī back to her own place.

Having caused the principles (tattvas) such as earth and the rest to reach their respective locations, one should expand oneself through the differentiation of the deities; this is the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Now, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.

The venerable Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), the venerable Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā), the syllables *dga?* and *rāva* are the seed-syllables (vīja), the vowels are the power (śakti); that which is [the alphabet] is the application (viniyoga) in the placement of the Mātṛkās. Salutation to the seer Brahmā upon the head.
Homage to Gāyatrī, the meter, in the mouth;
homage to Svarasvatī, the deity, in the heart;
homage to the seed-syllables *ha* and *la*, in the feet.
In the secret [place], salutation to the vowels and the Śaktis.
167a) Aṃ ka kha ga gha ṅa, salutation to the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyām). I ca cha ja jha ña, svāhā to the two index fingers (tarjanībhyām).
Uṃ ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa Ūṃ, to the two middle fingers, Vauṣaṭ! Eṃ ta tha da dha na AIṃ, to the two ring fingers, to the armor (kavaca), Hūṃ!
Oṃ pa pha ba bha ma AUṃ, to the two little fingers, Vauṣaṭ!
Aṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha la kṣa a; to the palms and backs of the hands, for clothing, phaṭ!
A ka kha ga gha ṅa ā; to the heart, namaḥ! I ca cha ja jha ña ī; to the head, svāhā!
u ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ū—vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā).
e ta tha da dha na ai—hūṃ to the armor (kavaca).
o pa pha ba bha ma au—vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (netratraya).
A Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Ha La Kṣa Aḥ Astrāya Phaṭ.
Thus, having performed three upward claps as before, one should bind the directions starting from the east.
Then one should meditate.

Oṃ! To her whose face, arms, feet, and eyes are fashioned from the distinctions of the fifty letters; who possesses radiant matted hair adorned with a digit of the moon and wears a crescent moon on her head;
who holds a rosary, a water-pot, a lotus, and displays the gesture of granting boons in her hands; and who is three-eyed and seated upon a lotus.
I bow to that Bhāratī, who is pure, whose speech is flawless, and who bears the weight of the breasts of the Goddess of Speech. || 11-390 ||
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*). Likewise: *Aṃ* namas on the forehead;
*Āṃ* on the circumference of the face.

Having thus completed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* letters during the preliminary rites, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting one’s own mantra, the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*. Next is the placement of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [limbs].

Just as one places the hand upon the heart, for this mantra: Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), *ṛṣṇik* is the meter (*chanda*), *hrīḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hūṃ* is the power (*śakti*), *krīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*), Aniruddha-Sarasvatī is the deity (*devatā*), and it is employed (*viniyoga*) for the sake of attaining sovereignty over all actions.
On the head: *Namaḥ* to Bhairava, the seer (*ṛṣi*). In the mouth: *Namaḥ* to the *uṣṇik* meter (*chandaḥ*). At the feet: *Namaḥ* to the seed-syllable *hrīḥ*.
HŪṂ, salutation to Śakti. Now follows the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa).
Homage to the power of the support (ādhāra-śakti). Homage to Pratyeti.
At the mouth, homage to the Uṣṇih meter.
At the two feet: *Hrīḥ* to the seed-syllable, *namaḥ*;
*namaḥ* to the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*);
*namaḥ* to the garden of the thighs (*ūrudhyāna*).
Salutation to the golden altar.
Salutation to the cremation ground.
Salutation to the Śivas in the four directions.
Thus, in the heart.
To Dharma on the right shoulder;
to Jñāna on the left shoulder;
to Vairāgya on the hip of the garment.
To Dakṣa on the right thigh; to Aiśvaryā on the face; to Adharma on the left side; to Ajñāna.
To the absence of dispassion;
on the right side, to the absence of sovereignty;
to the central jeweled lion-throne, obeisance.
Salutation to the bulb of bliss (Ānandakanda). Salutation to the stalk of consciousness (Saṃvinnāla). Salutation to the lotus-seat consisting of all principles (Sarvatattvātmakapadma).
Salutation to the pericarp consisting of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Salutation to the filaments consisting of transformation (*vikāra*).
Salutation to the pericarp preceded by the seed-syllables of the fifty letters.
Aṃ, obeisance to the solar disc, whose self consists of twelve kalās. Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc, whose self consists of sixteen kalās.
Maṃ, obeisance to the fiery disc, whose self consists of ten kalās.
Saṃ, salutation to the Being;
raṃ, salutation to Passion;
aṃ, salutation to the Inner Self.
Paṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Self. Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Self of Knowledge.
Obeisance to the wheel of fifteen spokes.
In the eight petals and filaments of the heart-lotus, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise: [one offers] to Icchā, Kriyā,
Kāminī, and Kāmadā.
To Rati, to Ratipriyā, to Ānandā, salutation! In the center:
to Manonmanī, salutation!
"Hsauḥ! Salutation to Sadāśiva, seated upon the lotus-throne of the great corpse.
Thus one should worship. This is the seat-consecration (pīṭhanyāsa).
Then one should place the argha vessel.
Having placed a tripod upon the fire-mandala to the left, one should worship the fire-mandala there as before.
Having thus worshipped it, one should quickly wash the conch, place it upon that [tripod], and [pronounce] *aṃ*.

Having worshipped the solar disc in the water as before, one should invoke the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) located within the solar disc by means of the *aṅkuśa* mudrā while uttering "Krom," and then transform it into nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the *dhenu* mudrā while uttering "Vam. Then, having recited the root mantra eight times:

Having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with "Hrīḥ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth, having displayed the conch mudrā, having veiled [the vessel] with "Hūṃ," having covered it with the fish mudrā, and having secured it with the seal of confinement,
one should pour a little water from the sprinkling vessel into the water and, reciting the root mantra, [sprinkle] with that same water.
With those [mantras], one should sprinkle oneself and the ritual implements for worship.
Then, having performed the *aṅganyāsa* with "Oṃ Kāṃ" and so forth, one should meditate as follows:

One should meditate upon the divine Kālikā of the South, whose face is like the syllable Oṃ, who is formidable, with disheveled hair and four arms, and adorned with a garland of severed heads. || 11-391 ||

She holds in her upper left lotus-hand a sword with a freshly severed head, and in her lower left hand she displays the gesture of granting boons; in her upper right hand she shows the gesture of fearlessness, and in her lower right hand she displays the gesture of granting boons.
She is dark-complexioned like a great cloud,
likewise naked, with a garland of severed heads hanging from her neck, and smeared with blood from her throat.
Terrifying with a pair of human corpses serving as her ear-ornaments,
she had formidable fangs, a gaping mouth, and full, elevated breasts.
She wore a girdle fashioned from the joined hands of corpses, her face was laughing,
and her mouth quivered as streams of blood flowed from both corners of her lips.
She has a terrible roar and is exceedingly fierce; she dwells in the abode of the cremation ground, is jagged-toothed, extends to the south, and has loose, long, and disheveled hair.
O Lord, she is situated upon the heart in the form of a Śava, surrounded on the four sides by Śivās of terrible appearance. (11.397)

Having thus reflected upon Kālī, who dwells in the cremation ground, who is distressed by the reversal of her passion along with Mahākāla, yet whose face is serene and whose lotus-like countenance is smiling— (11.398)
Alternatively, the *Phetkāriṇītantra* describes the meditation as follows:
Having visualized her as wearing a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) of *nāgas*, with the crescent moon as her remaining ornament,
endowed with matted locks (*jaṭā*), and situated near Mahākāla— (11.399).
Having reflected thus, the practitioner should worship with jewel-flowers.
Having meditated in this way and propitiated the heart-mantra with the prescribed offerings, one should display the mudrā.
Then, visualizing oneself in the form of the Goddess, one should extract the yantra.
And likewise, in the Kālītantra:
Having first inscribed a triangle, one should then inscribe another triangle outside of it.
Then, having first drawn [the ground], one should duly draw a lotus possessing all its characteristic marks;
likewise, it is stated in another tantra:
Having first inscribed a triangle, one should then inscribe another triangle outside of it.
Then the practitioner of mantra should indeed scratch out three excellent triangles;
having drawn a circle according to the rule, he should draw a lotus endowed with its proper characteristics.
And so it is said in another Tantra:
"One should place a triangle, then again a pair [of triangles], and then another triangle;
and there, a hexagon—and in its center, one should establish Śivā. (11.403)
In that regard, [it is said] in the Kaumudī:
One should first draw a triangle, and then another triangle;
one should place a nine-cornered figure there, and in its center, one should establish Śivā.
Having thus fashioned the fifteen-cornered [mandala], one should perform the worship of the *pīṭha* as prescribed:
having worshipped in the center from Ādhāraśakti up to "Salutation to Śivā," one should then worship in the four corners beginning with the southeast.
Having worshipped up to "Obeisance to Dharma" and "To me,
[the power] of sovereignty," one should worship in the directions starting from the east, beginning with "Obeisance to Adharma," and so on, up to the end of the *pīṭha* mantra.
One should worship in the directions starting from the east, beginning with "Obeisance to Adharma," and so on, up to the end of the *pīṭha*.

Having performed the *aṅganyāsa* with the syllable "Hrāṃ," and having meditated [on the deity] according to the verses beginning with "karāmalakavadanām" and so forth, one should bring [the deity] with a handful of flowers, install it in the center of the *yantra*, and perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*.
As follows:
Ā hrīḥ kroḥ ya ra la va sa ṣa śa ho hā saḥ—the vital breaths of the Goddess are here as her vital breaths. (169a) Thus, Ā and so forth:
the life-force of the Goddess is established here.
Thus, "Ām" and so forth: (13) O gods, all sense-faculties, mind, eye, ear, nose, and breath, come here and remain happily for a long time; svāhā!

Then, having recited the root mantra, having invoked [the deity] with "O [Name], come here, stay here," having established [the deity] with the *saṃsthāpana-mudrā*, having brought [the deity] into proximity with the *sannidhāna-mudrā*, having caused [the deity] to be fully present with the *sannirodhana-mudrā*, and having restrained [the deity] with "Hūṃ," one should make [the offering] nectarine by means of the *dhenu-mudrā* with the mantra "Avatara avatara."

Having performed the consecration (*paramīkaraṇa*) with the *paramīkaraṇa-mudrā*, one should effect the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) of the deity’s six limbs with the six-limb mantras, beginning with "hrāḥ, to the heart, namaḥ," and so forth. Then follows the presentation of offerings, beginning with the seat (*āsana*).
Having recited the root mantra with the sixteen services beginning with "The seat is worthy; welcome, O Noble One," [one says]: "O Kālikā, may this seat be accepted."
Having recited the root mantra.
Welcome, Kālīka!
Having recited the root mantra as the *pravara*, [say]: "Obeisance! This is the *arghya* for Kālī, *svadhā*. Likewise, this is the *pādya*, obeisance.
Likewise, this is the *ācamanīya*, obeisance. [Recite] the root mantra.
"Kālike, this is the honey-mixture (madhuparka); svadhā.
Again, having offered water for sipping (ācamanīya) while reciting "vaṃ" followed by the root mantra, at the end he should offer the bath and other services.
Then, having offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra, he should worship the feet.
In the first trilateral.
Salutation to Kālī.
Salutation to Kalyālī.
Salutation to Kullyā.
In the second [petal], one should meditate on Ugrā; in the third, Dīptā; in the fourth, Nīlāvalī;

and in the fifth, Mātrāmudrānityā. All of them are dark blue in color, wearing garlands of severed heads, and one should meditate on them holding a threatening gesture (tarjanī) in their right and left hands.

Outside of that, one should visualize Vāhrmī, Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, Aparājitā, Vārāhī, and Nārasiṃhī, each in their previously described forms. In the central pericarp, one should visualize the Goddess in her aforementioned form, as well as Mahākāla.

Then, taking the *arghya* vessel, one should offer the *arghya* with the previously mentioned mantra. Thereafter, with the root mantra, one should offer three handfuls of flowers along with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should present the food offering (*naivedya*) with the root mantra according to one's capacity.
Then, O dear one, follows the worship, as previously described: in the fifteen corners, [one offers] *oṃ kālyai namaḥ* and *oṃ kapālinyai namaḥ*.
Oṃ, salutation to Kulyā.
In this manner, one should worship the deities installed in the other triangles in their proper sequence.
Outside of that, one should worship the group of Mothers according to the order of installation.
Then, having placed flowers, sandalwood paste, and so forth upon the head of the Goddess with the root mantra, [one should recite it] one thousand or one hundred and eight times.

Or one should recite the mantra ten times. Again, having placed flowers and sandalwood upon the head of the Goddess, one should dismiss her with the dismissal-mudrā; this is the summary. Now, as for the rites for specific desires (*kāmya*).
Wearing serpent-sacrificial threads and having the crescent moon as their crest-ornament,
they contemplated Mahākāla, who was free from old age and situated nearby.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, who possesses the pair of *kūrca* and *lajjā* as her seed-syllables (*bīja*), one should worship her with red flowers.
Pierced by the arrows of desire, shameless and agitated, women abandon their respective husbands—who are as if gods themselves—and embrace others. (11.407)
At the end [of the mantra] is Dakṣiṇakālī, together with the deity;
at the end of "Dakṣiṇakālī," the word "dva" (twice) is to be understood as the remainder;
and also at the beginning of the letter *ca*.
One [should visualize her] as red with a trident in her hand, and the other as bearing a trident.

Having visualized [the deity] situated at the tip of Mahākāla, one who recites [the mantra] while worshipping with yellow flowers—one by one—at the beginning and likewise at the end, [attains success]. (11.409)

In this way, there shall be attraction of both the stationary and the moving, even those dwelling in the depths of the netherworld; what need is there to mention those situated on the surface of the earth? (11.410)
All that comes to fruition, just as Mahākāla has said:
the three seeds beginning with Śakurca are each [to be understood] individually. (11.411)
Having meditated upon Kapilā, who has two arms and three eyes, holding a skull in her middle right hand—
and indeed [meditating] on everything else, and finally on the two alone— 11.412.
Having thus recited the mantra, one should worship with black flowers;
by that, the ritual performed for the sake of subduing will become effective.

With eyes wide open, she causes [the enemy] to be eradicated; with eyes squinting, she causes him to faint; with eyes cast askance, she causes him to flee; and with rolling eyes, she causes him to go mad. (11.414)
When agitated, it causes trembling; when falling, it causes destruction;
when bent, it causes contraction; when fully developed, it causes expansion; or, like an enemy, it creates opposition. (11.415)
Whatever state of being one is born into, one should also recollect that state of being;
in all these cases, the mind should be focused solely on the state of being. (11.416)
In this matter called "joining," sexual union is considered appropriate at all times;
one who has bathed, put on fresh garments, and performed his duties may engage in it. (11.417)
If one dreams of a mountain at night, or of lying down, or of being engaged in sexual intercourse,
or alternatively, of having disheveled hair— all these portend the accomplishment of all goals.

Stambhana (paralysis), mohana (delusion), and likewise vaśīkaraṇa (subjugation)—if a man, upon seeing another's wife naked, recites [the mantra] joined with the *prajāpati* [seed-syllable], [he attains these powers]. (11.419)
Indeed, he may be one who has reached the further shore of all sciences among all the gods;
by the mere sight of him, the opponent is considered to be rendered lusterless. (11.420)
His speech shall be entirely composed of both prose and verse;
then, with disheveled hair, the man should consume sacrificial food (haviṣya).

One should recite the mantra ten thousand times, O God; this is considered the standard for each [deity]. Having recited it one hundred and eight times, one should carefully address the face [of the deity]. (11.422)
He who makes his face radiant with pearls shall be endowed with wealth, grain, and sons;
he will become the most excellent among those devoted to all branches of knowledge—of this there is no doubt.
Having approached her during her fertile period, a man should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times;
even if he has no desire for it, his speech shall become composed of prose and verse.
The speech of one who has increased their zeal becomes impassioned;
thus, for the sake of liberation from great sin, one should practice the sevenfold "surata. (170b) 11-425.
Likewise, for the sake of acquiring wealth, one may approach another woman;
if there is contact with one who is distressed, then one should carefully discharge the semen. (11.426)
Then, having cast it aside for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals,
one should go to a cremation ground with disheveled hair and naked.
One should recite it ten thousand times for the accomplishment of all desired aims;
at that very place, the best of mantra-knowers should recite it in the morning.
One who is free from passion for ten thousand years, fearless,
and devoted to the Supreme, attains the highest perfection, which is very difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Attraction, piercing, binding, and summoning, as well as paralyzing, deluding, terrifying, and likewise causing diminution. (11.430)
Having attained eloquence, wealth, many sons, and likewise a wife with many sons, as well as being beloved by all. || 11-431 ||
One indeed attains the state of moving through the sky and even divinity;
one is neither a wanderer nor a non-wanderer, neither subject to death nor subject to fear.
There is no lack of affection among men in human existence, nor any downfall of speech or body;
or else, the twenty-four siddhis may arise eternally. (11.433)
Having worshipped the deity Vāgīśvara in the cremation grounds with a thousand sacred blades of grass smeared with the blood from one's own body, one shall attain identity with her.
Having worshipped the Goddess a thousand times with a vessel filled with water, and having worshipped her in cremation grounds, one attains all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 11-435 ||
One shall become wealthy, powerful, eloquent, righteous, and prosperous; one shall be happy, with no doubt regarding the recipient of the gift, just as Mahākāla has said. (11.436)
If one worships a woman in a cremation ground a thousand times as the seed-mantra—
she who has tawny eyes, is smeared with red sandalwood, and is adorned with red flowers— [11.437]
Having first honored you with flowers, one should then meditate upon Caṇḍikā;
thereafter, having gone [to battle], one shall obtain sovereignty, provided she does not flee. (11.438)
Furthermore, while lying in a cremation ground with his bow strung, he should recite the mantra repeatedly; thus he shall become the bestower of all accomplishments. (11.439)
Indeed, by means of the blood of a ram, a buffalo, and fresh blood, or by the blood of a mouse and a cat, eloquence arises for him. (11.440)
Likewise with four [fingers], and similarly with one's own body;
in sexual intercourse there are nine [faults], and also in the washing of the female organ.
He becomes wealthy, and every accomplishment arises for him;
in speech he is like Brahmā, and in wealth he is a lord of riches. (11.442)
By his command this king [is empowered], yet he is not Manobhava in form;
for he is indeed Pavana by strength, the accomplisher of all principles.
One should always offer meat that has been properly prepared and cooked, along with the bones, as a continuous stream;
namely, the meat of deer, goat, sheep, and buffalo.
Everything, including the bones, should be given, as well as the hair;
it should include the nails, the hair of the body, and the hair of the head. || 11-445 ||
One should offer it in a cremation ground, and it shall become the bestower of all accomplishments;
having offered a hundred excellent leaves joined with the menses of a woman. (11.446)
Then, O excellent one, one should recite the mantra for each [deity] and subsequently offer it into the fire;
by doing so for ten million ages, one becomes honored with sacrificial fees.
All accomplishments shall come to be.
All accomplishments shall arise for him who becomes a master of speech;
there is nothing whatsoever on earth that is difficult for him to obtain. (11.448)
Having fashioned the form of the womb (yoni) as a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one span (vitasti),
and likewise having made it one cubit (hasta) in width, he should then proceed accordingly.
In that case, the ritual for the installation of the fire should indeed be performed according to the *tantra*;
one should first offer the *āhuti* to the god Maśrakāla.
One should worship me with meat, clarified butter, blood, and fat;
especially with black flowers accompanied by clarified butter and goat’s blood.
In this manner, one should offer oblations with meat and other substances in the cremation ground;
having bathed, wearing white garments, pure, and with a restrained mind. (11.452)
This should indeed be performed during the day for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals;
however, at night, one should remain naked with disheveled hair even while engaged in sexual intercourse. (11-453)
For all the twice-born, two kinds [of conduct] are prescribed here;
and for all the Śūdras, there is the great vow (mahāvrata) by day and by night.

The most excellent of practitioners should diligently offer oblations first to Mahākāla and afterwards to the Goddess with great care, dividing [the offerings] threefold by means of the mantras and other elements. (11.455)
Meat, blood, sesame, hair, nails, cooked rice, milk-rice, and clarified butter—one should offer these with great care for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims. (11.456)
Having performed it according to this ritual procedure, they attain the supreme accomplishment;
whatever they pray for therein, they obtain it constantly.
By constantly offering oblations, one who is ever-vigilant attains the state of a deity, the state of a Dānava, as well as the status of a Siddha or a Cāraṇa. || 11.458 ||
Thus, enough of this elaboration.
Now follows the Thousand Names of Kālī.
At that very time, however, Bhṛgu, Rāma, Pārvatī,
and all the sons of Kārttikeya [beheld] their father in an instant.
Having heard those words of Reṇukā, which destroy even the most terrible sins,
Bhṛgu performed the *japa* of the supreme mantra for Rāma, who was like Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
Skanda, taking up an exceedingly beautiful axe—
the very one intended for his father’s curse— wandered upon the surface of the earth.
Then he went to Kailāsa together with Rāma’s axe;
seeing him as an excellent practitioner, Śiva spoke these words: 462.
"For what purpose have you come? Tell me the truth.
Having heard those words of his, [he replied] with eyes throbbing in anger.
They related the entire ritual for honoring their father’s curse;
at that time, it was a destroyer of the very jaws of Death for the sake of dispelling mental anxiety.
Sadāśiva bestowed upon him that extensive knowledge, Bhṛgūrāmāyaṇa,
and he related the auspicious armor-mantra (kavaca) which brings about the end of the Kṣatriyas.
172a) When he truly recited the Thousand Names— that Thousand Names which had been proclaimed by himself in the past at the beginning of the eon— 11-466.
Śaṅkara related all of that to Rāma,
[instructing him] to propitiate Dakṣiṇakālī along with the axe of Rāma.
At the end of my father's grief, the Goddess made me queenless;
thrice seven times, being enraged, she made the earth devoid of kṣatriyas.
He made a dark-colored image with five wheels; then, with a heart full of devotion, he offered blood.
Thereafter, with blood and flesh, he truly propitiated Kālī.
Then the goddess, the destroyer of the Dānavas, becomes satisfied.
Śiva said:
"This great mantra has been declared; it is the most excellent of all mantras. (11.470)
Having approached you, who are endowed with supreme devotion and have acted according to the prescribed rule, I have attained this highest state of sovereignty. (11.471)
He performed the worship of the Goddess out of a desire to conquer the three worlds.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O God, O Supreme Lord, if you were pleased with me previously, then [grant this]... (11.472)
O Lord, by the grace of the Supreme Goddess, please tell me the secret [of this] without worship,
without fire-offerings, without ritual placement, and without oblations.
Without perfume, without flowers, without the rite that is eternally manifest, and without breath control, there is no meditation that purifies the elements. (11.474)
"Without recitation and without giving, how does she become pleased?
Śrī Śiva said:
"O wise one born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, you have asked an excellent question. (11.475)
"You alone, who are most devoted to your devotees, shall accomplish it—the Goddess who slays millions of Dānavas and who delights in blood through her play. (11.476)
He always offered praise to her who was dear to him, fierce, and devoted to passion and curiosity; she whose heart was ever-giving and whose mind was entirely attached [to him].
She who delights in the flesh of the lotus, the supreme consort of Viṣṇu,
who dwells in the cremation ground, and who celebrates the great festival of death for the hosts of departed spirits.
O Yoginī, you who possess the splendor of yoga and are the sovereign of yoginīs, abiding here in my heart— you who are named Ugrakālikā, it behoves you to grant me your grace.
Her hymn of praise, which brings great merit, was revealed by Kālī herself;
I shall relate it to you—having heard it, indeed, you should retain it with care. (11.480)
This should be kept secret with great effort and recited as that which is higher than the highest;
by reciting it even once, those who are overwhelmed by all obstacles [are liberated]. (11.481)
They perish on all sides like moths in a blazing fire;
at midnight, one should be naked, with hair disheveled, and accompanied by a naked Śakti.
One should meditate upon Kālī in the mind; that which was not cherished by Mahākāla, one should recite the Thousand-Name hymn, the means for liberation. (11.483)
The gracious Kālikā took pity upon him as her own son,
just as Brahmā was formerly moved by the worship of Brahmā with ambrosial flowers.
Just as she is pleased by that, so too does Sadākālī always remain pleased.

Of this hymn to Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā, Mahākālabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Śmaśānakālikā is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of recitation for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Lady Kālikā!
Śmaśānakālikā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī. || 11-485 ||
Guhyakālī, Mahākālī, Kuru-kulyā, Virodhinī, Kālikā, Kālarātri, and Mahākālanitambinī. (11.486)
She is named Kālabhairavī, the illuminator of the family dharma;
she is the bestower of desires, the passionate one, the desirable one, whose nature is most lovely.
Kākinī, whose eyes are greedy for the essence of musk, who moves within the lord of the groves, whose every limb is composed of the letter 'ka', and who is beautiful with desire. (11.488)
Kāmāntā, Kāmarūpā, Kāmadhenu, Kalāvatī, Kāntā, Kālasvarūpā, Kāmākhyā, and Kāmapālinī. || 11-489 ||
She is of noble birth, possessed of a noble lineage, the destroyer of misfortune and evil destinies;
she is Kaumārī, born of a noble family, dark-complexioned, with a dark body, and a slender waist.
Kṛśāṅgī, Kuśalāṅgī, Klī, Kālī, Kamalā, Kalā, Karālāsthā, Karālī, Kulakāntā, and Parājitā. (11.491)
Ugra, Cogratarā, Dīptā, Vipracittā, Manā, Nīlā, Ghanā, Meghanādā, Mahāmudrā, Amitā, and Mitā. (11.492)
Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Bhadrā, Subhadrā, Bhaktavatsalā, Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Vārāhī, and Nārasiṃhikā. || 11-493 ||
She possesses vajra-limbs, she who acts with the vajra, she who wears human skulls and destroys the wicked;
she is garlanded with a row of human heads, adorned with dripping blood. (11.494)
Anointed with red sandalwood, her head crimson with vermilion,
she is of terrible form, with fearsome fangs, and most exceedingly fierce in combat.
Mahādaṃṣṭrā, Mahāmāyā, Sundarī, Yugadanturā, Sulocanā, Virūpākṣī, Viśālā, and Trilocanā. || 11-496 ||
Śāradenduprasannā shall be radiant, her lotus-like eyes throbbing with passion; Aṭṭahāsī shall be gracious, her lotus-like eyes throbbing with passion.
Laughing with a loud laugh, her face serene, she speaks like Smara;
her lotus-face is bright and white, and she is sweet-spoken.
She has a face like a clear lotus, a white countenance, and speaks pleasantly; she has deep-set eyes, is of noble lineage, great, and speaks much. (11.499)
Sumati, Kumati, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍātiveginī, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍi, Carcikā, and Caṇḍaveginī. || 11-500 ||
Well-adorned, with loose hair, long-haired, and possessing great tresses;
using the bodies of *pretas* as her earrings, and having the hands of *pretas* as her beautiful girdle. (11.501)
She whose seat is the departed, who is dear to the departed, and by whom the realm of the dead was created;
she dwells in the cremation ground, is meritorious, the bestower of merit, and the ornament of the lineage. (11.502)
She is the abode of merit, the embodiment of merit, she whose fame is meritorious, and the illustrious one;
she is the purified, the purifier, the supreme, the transcendent, and adorned with merit.
She whose name is merit, the remover of fear, the giver of boons, the protector of the sword;
she who holds a human skull in her hand, who wields a weapon, Chinnamastā, with a severed sword.
Entirely dark-complexioned, with breasts that are high and cause intense burning,
naked, making a terrible sound, she is drenched by the river Tārakā.
Ghorarāvā, Śivāsaṅgī, Visaṅgī, Madanāturā, Mahāpramatā, Pramadā, Svadhā, and Sindhunivāsinī.
Exceedingly intoxicated, she performs all manner of actions;
fond of song, delighting in instrumental music, the preta is devoted to dancing.
Four-armed, ten-armed, and likewise eighteen-armed;
O Kātyāyanī, Mother of the World, Sovereign Goddess of the Universe. (11.508)
O support of the world, O mother of the world, O bringer of joy to the world, O you who consist of the life-force of the world, O daughter of Himavat, O Great Illusion, we bow to you! (11.509)
She whose limbs are adorned with serpent-sacrifices, the female serpent, the giver of serpents;
the daughter of the Nāgas, the daughter of the gods, the Gandhārī, and the sovereign of the Kinnarīs.
Moharātri, Mahārātri, Vāruṇī, Bhāsvarīsvarī, Vidyādharī, Vasumatī, Yakṣiṇī, Yoginī, and Jarā. (11.511)
She is the protectress, the ḍākinī, composed of the Vedas, adorned by the Vedas;
she is the great knowledge of the Śruti and Smṛti, the ancient secret knowledge.
Cintyā, Acintyā, Svadhā, Svāhā, Nidrā, Tandrā, Pārvatī, Arpaṇā, Niścalā, Lolā, Sarvavidyā, and Tapasvinī. (11.513)
Gaṅgā, Kāśī, Śacī, Sītā, Satī, Satyaparāyaṇā, Gīti, Svanīti, Svaruci, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, and Kṣamā. || 11.514 ||
Vāṇī, Vuddhi, Mahālakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Līlā, Sarasvatī, Srotasvatī, Sāratī, Mātaṅgī, Vijayā, and Jayā. (11.515)
The bound river consisting of all things, Tārā who dwells in the void;
Śraddhā who possesses waves, Medhā, the Ḍākinī of many forms. || 11-516 ||
Sunandā, Nandinī, she whose form is worthy of praise; Rakinī, Ṭaṅkinī, Citrā, Vicitrā, and she adorned with wonderful ornaments.
Padmā, Padmālayā, Padmamukhī, Padmavibhūṣaṇā;
Hākinī, Śākinī, Śāntā, Rākinī, and Rudhirapriyā. (11.518)
O Bhavānī, O Rudrāṇī, O Svaḍānī, O crusher of enemies!
O Upendrāṇī, O Maheśānī, O Jyotsnā, you who are the very form of the moon! || 11-519 ||
She is the essence of the sun, the wife of Rudra, the fierce woman, primordial nature, and the male;
she is power, liberation, the intellect of liberation, and the devoted wife of liberation.
The sovereign of all, the mother of all, Śarvāṇī, the beloved of Hara;
she is omniscient, the bestower of perfection, perfected, auspicious, and the remover of fear.
She is the creator, the destroyer, and the protector; she is the night, the nameless, and compassion.
She dwells in darkness, yet is established in the quality of darkness (tamas); she is steadfast, firm, and devoted to austerity.
Cāṅgāṅgī, Cañcalā, Lolajihvā, Cārucaritriṇī, Upā, Upāvatī, Lajjā, Vilajjā, Hrī, and Irejomukhī. (11.523)
Sarasvatī is established in righteousness, most excellent, and a speaker of refined words; she is most venerable as the destroyer of the enraged, distinguished, and supremely compassionate. (11.524)
She is formidable, terrifying, and fearsome with her roar;
she shines forth as the Sovereign of Speech, the Fortune who carries away the sacrifice, and she is beloved by the Yajus.
She whose abode is the power of the Ṛg and Sāman, whose voice is like that of a passionate elephant,
who has a dark throat, whose neck is curved, and who is devoted to the Veṇā river.
Vaśinī, Vaiṣṇavī, Svachā, Dharitrī, Jagadeśvarī, Madhumatī, Kuṇḍalinī, Ṛddhi, Siddhi, and Śuci are remembered [as the powers]. (11.527)
Raṃbhā, Arvaśī, Rati, Āmā, Rohiṇī, Evati, Maghā, Śaṅkhinī, Cakriṇī, Hṛṣṭā, Gādini, and likewise Padminī. (11.528)
Śūlinī, Parighāstrā, Pāśinī, Śārṅgapālinī, Pinākadhāriṇī, Dhūmrā, and Śarabhīṣaṇamālinī. || 11-529 ||
Rathinī, Samarapritā, Veginī, Raṇapañcalā, Jadinī, Vajrinī, Nīlā, Bhavānī, Buddhi, and Caṇḍikā. (11.530)
Beloved by Vali, greatly worshipful, she who is accompanied by the lord of the Daityas in his full splendor;
she who destroys the earth along with its essence, the self-controlled one, whose teeth are red.
174b) She is red, with limbs stained by blood, holding a skull-cup in her hand;
she is fond of the red, delights in flesh, and has a mind deeply attached to it. (11.532)
She wears matted hair and is shaven-headed; she is adorned with a garland of skulls and sacred ash.
She has a corpse for her seat and dwells within the cremation pyre; she is the consort who rides upon a buffalo and a bull.
Vyāghratvagā, Varācīnī, Veriṇī, Siṃhavāhinī, Vāmadevī, Mahādevī, Gaurī, and Sarvajñabhāvinī. (11.534)
We worship the young woman from Valikā, the old woman, the mother of the aged, she who is afflicted by decay,
the fair-browed playful woman, and the Brahmanī who speaks of Brahman.
Svapnāvatī, Citralekhā, Lopāmudrā, Svarēśvarī, Amōghā, Rūḍhatī, Tīkṣṇā, Bhōgavatī, and Rāgiṇī. (11.536)
She is the Mandākinī who destroys pride, the flame that brings an end to the primary sounds;
