she bestows the mind, she is the measurer, she is worthy of honor, she is to be revered, and she is exalted by passion.
Madirā is fat with intoxication; Medhronmādā is impure; Mādhyā is negligent;
Sumedhyā possesses manifold virtues and is the most excellent among all the best in the world. (11.538)

She is the giver of victory, the swift one, the victorious, the glory of victory, and she who is resplendent with triumph; she is the bestower of auspiciousness, the giver of happiness, the truth, and she who always causes total upheaval.
Śivādūtī, Bhītimatī, Vibhūtibhūṣaṇānanā, Kaumārī, Kulajā, Kuntī, Kulastrā, and Kulapālikā. (11.540)
She is the glory of the Karmiras, an auspicious ornament, beloved by the Lord of Beings;
she is praised as possessing the six qualities yet free from all attributes, the ultimate goal, and firmly established in the Absolute.

Dhaniṣṭhā, the giver of wealth, the one rich in grain, the earth, the radiant one; the expansive, the venerable, the most excellent among the great, she who is beyond qualities yet consists of the three qualities. || 11-542 ||
The king and his subjects possess great wisdom; they are characterized by the six qualities and the absence of qualities.
They are of noble lineage, free from desire, liberated from desire, yet living according to their desires.
She is the artistry of Kāmadeva, delightful to Rāma, and the dancer of Śiva;
she is the wish-fulfilling gem, the desire-granting creeper, ever-awake, and compassionate toward the distressed. (11.544)
Kārttikī, Kṛtikā, Kṛtyā, Ayodhyā, Viṣabhāsamā, Sumantrā, Mantriṇī, Pūrṇā, Hlādinī, and Kleśanāśinī. (11.545)
Kṛṣṇā, the mother of the three worlds, is fleshless and has the form of Time (Kāla);
her belly is as vast as a lake, and she wears a garland of withered flesh and bones.
O Goddess who pervades the three worlds, you are descending— sweet, heart-pleasing,
manifesting as many forms both manifest and unmanifest, the Śarabhī who roars with a terrifying sound.
Kṣemaṃkarī, Śaṃkarī, and Sarvasamohakāriṇī;
Ūrddhatejasvinī, Klinnā, and likewise Mahātejasvinī. || 11-548 ||
She who bestows non-duality is to be worshipped by the auspicious as Sarvamaṅgalā;
she is the maker of all things dear, the object of enjoyment, the supporter, and the consumer of flesh.
She is the terrifying one, the remover of sin, the stainless one, and the benefactress; she is hope and thirst, the digit of the moon, the young maiden, and she who possesses the speed of the wind.
Resembling a thousand suns, with a radiance equal to ten million moons,
she stands in the center of a circle of fire, established as the support of all beings.
She who possesses all modes of conduct, she who is like all the celestial maidens, the deity, the daughter of Dakṣa, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, Durgā, the Savior.
Victorious is Kuhu, who is Varuṇā, whose form is Brahman, consisting of sacrifice, worship, fearlessness, prosperity, and true fame; she is the source of beauty and possesses a pleasing form. 11-553.
The wise one, the mother of the Vedas, the glorious, the observer of celibacy;
the giver of success, the giver of intellect, the intellect itself, enriched with all things, and the bestower of everything. (11.554)

She whose form is unfathomable, who is to be meditated upon, who dwells in the *mūlādhāra*, she is the Command (*ājñā*), Wisdom (*prajñā*), the one of fulfilled mind, the Moon-faced One, and the Kaulinī. (11.555)
She is the one who has taken the veil, whose navel is deep, who is true to her promise, firm in her vows,
skilled in the science of government, proficient in the three Vedas, and beautiful in the three ways.
Jvalinī, Jñāninī, Śailatanayā, Vindhyavāsinī, Pratyakṣā, Khecarā, Dhairyā, Turīyā, Vimalā, and Tulā. (11.557)
Pragalbhā, Āṣārūṇī, Chāyā, Vaśinī, Visphuliṅginī, Bhukti, Siddhi, Sadāprāpti, Prakāmyā, Mahimā, and Aṇimā. (11.558)
The accomplishment of desires, mastery, sovereignty, and dwelling in the upper realms;
likewise, lightness—O Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Bhuvaneśvarī! (11-559)
Manoharā, Vitā, Divyā, Devadārā, Manoramā, Piṅgalā, Kapilā, Jihvā, Rasajñā, and Rasikā—she is [all these]. (11.560)
Suṣumṇā, Oḍā, Yogavatī, Gāndhārī, Narakāntakā, Pañcālī, Rukmiṇī, Rādhā, Rādhya, and Bhīmādhikārikā. (11.561)
Amṛtā, Tulasī, Vṛndā, Kaiṭabhī, Kapaṭeśvarī, Ugracaṇḍeśvarī, Vīrajananī, and Virasundarī. (11.562)
Ugratārāyaṇī, Dakṣā, Devakī, Devamāninī, Nirañjanā, Citā, Krodhinī, and Kuladīpikā—the Goddess. (11.563)
Kulavāgīśvarī, Jvālā, Mātṛkā, Drāviṇī, Dravā, Yogīśvarī, Mahābhrāmarī, and Vidurūpiṇī. || 11-564 ||
Dūtī, Prāṇeśvarī, Guptā, Vahutvā, Bhramarī, Prabhā, Kubjikā, Jñāninī, Jyeṣṭhā, Bhusuṇḍī, and Prakaṭākṛti. || 11-565 ||
Drāviṇī, Gopinī, Māyā, Kāmavījeśvarī, Priyā, Śākambharī, Kokanadā, Musulā, Svāhā, and Tilottamā. (11.566)
These are Amīyā, Vikramā, Krūrā, Saṃviccholā, Trivikramā, Svasti, Havyavahā, Prīti, Uṣmā, Dhūmā, and Viraṅgadā. (11.567)
Tapiṇī, Tāpinī, Viśvā, Bhogadā, Bhogadhāriṇī, Trikhaṇḍā, Vodhinī, Vaśyā, and Sakalā, who is the embodiment of sound. || 11-568 ||
The Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is the form of the seed-syllable, the sovereign one who takes the form of yoga;
she is Anaṅgamadanā, Anaṅgā, Rekhānaṅgā, and Kuleśvarī. (11.569)
Anaṅgamālinī, Kāmeśvarī, Savārthasādhakā; she who consists of all mantras, whose form is the deluder, and whose nature is the bodiless one (Anaṅga). || 11-570 ||
Vajreśvarī is the reciter who brings about the destruction of all dualities;
she is the youthful mistress of the six-limbed yoga, joined with Jvālā and Sumālinī.

She who possesses evil intent, evil conduct, and is difficult to conquer; she whose form is formidable, whose end is difficult to reach, who removes misdeeds, who is supreme, and who is hard to transcend. (11.572)
Haṃśeśvarī resides in the triangle;
she is compassionate toward her devotees, eternally dwelling in the triangle, and is colored by the supreme nectar. || 11-573 ||
She is the Great Sovereign of the Universe, the White One, Bhīruṇḍā, and Kulasundarī;
she is Tvaritā, endowed with devotion, subject to devotion, and eternal.
O Goddess consisting of the bliss of devotees, O source of fearlessness to Your devotees, abode of all beauty, endowed with all auspicious fortune! (11.575)
The maiden who is the source of all enjoyment, who bestows all happiness, who delights in worship, and who grants liberation from the state of a preta. || 11-576 ||
The maiden is blissful through devotion; the maiden is the bearer of form;
the maiden is pleased with her worshiper; the maiden is dear to the spirits of the departed.
Kumārī, Sevakā, Saṃvā, Kumārisevakālayā, Ānandabhairavī, Bhālabhairavī, and Vaṭubhairavī. (11.578)
Śmaśānabhairavī, Kālabhairavī, Purabhairavī, Mahābhairavapatnī, and Paramānandabhairavī. (11.579)
Surānandabhairavī and Unmadānandabhairavī, as well as Sukaulabhairavī and Jñānānandasubhairavī. || 11-580 ||
She who causes great terror, possessing an exceedingly intense and swift impetus;
she is Tripurā, the Supreme Sovereign, the Beautiful One, the Adornment of the Cities.
Tripuraśā is the fifteenth, Puravāsinī is the fifth,
Mahāsaptadaśī is likewise [the seventh], and Ṣoḍaśī is Tripureśvarī.
She is Mahākuśasvarūpā and likewise Mahācakreśvarī;
she is Navacakreśvarī, Cakreśvarī, and Tripuramālinī.
The sovereign queen of the kings of kings, the steadfast Mahātripurasundarī;
she who is radiant with a flood of vermilion, the illustrious Tripurasundarī. (11.584)
Beautiful in all her limbs, she wears garments and upper cloths that are both red and not red;
she bears barley, barley-gruel, vermilion, and red sandalwood.
She has hair as dark and pure as a yak-tail whisk or a water-lily bud;
she is enriched with diamonds, pearls, and rubies, and is radiant with a crown and diadem. (11.586)
Adorned with red earrings, quivering and fierce, she is enchanting;
she is described as the jar of Kuleśvara, with her nose released and reddened.
Her breast-regions were enriched with necklaces of pearls, coral, and rubies;
she was adorned with sun-stones, moonstones, and radiant gems as ornaments for her neck.
The seed-syllable is radiant with the full moon; the row of teeth is most excellent. She who casts side-glances curved like the crescent moon rains down the fulfillment of desires.
Her chest was like the frontal globes of an elephant, her eyes were as beautiful as a net of lotuses,
and she captivated the mind with the swan-like song of her ears, which were as lovely as the feathers of the peacock, the enemy of Manojashanku.
O illuminator of the four directions, radiant as the lotus-bearing Gaṅgā, shimmering with various jewels and adorned with a pure golden girdle! || 11.591 ||
Her hands do not bear bracelets fashioned from the tusks of the king of serpents;
her limbs are adorned with rings and various small bells.
Clad in garments of fine silk, adorned with the tinkling sound of small bells,
and anointed with the liquid essence of camphor, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
The earth, variegated with jewels, though turbid, stands upon the surface of the netherworld;
it is an island of gems where radiant jewel-lions dwell.
She is the piercer of the six chakras, whose nature is supreme bliss,
and she dwells within the lunar mandala at the end of the thousand-petaled lotus.
O you who sport as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, delighting in various pleasures and amusements;
O you who are served by Hari, Viṣṇu, Viriñca, the Moon, and the lords of the planets.
The source of the self, the source of the world, the source of Brahman, born of no source;
she whose form is the *bhaga*, who abides in the *bhaga*, the threefold sister, seated upon the *bhaga*.
She whose essence is the *bhaga*, who is the support of the *bhaga*, she who possesses form, she who is garlanded with *bhagas*;
she who pervades the *liṅga*, she who is fond of the *liṅga*, she who dwells in the *liṅga*.
She who dwells in the *liṅga*, she who possesses the *liṅga*, she whose form is the *liṅga*, she who is beautiful as the *liṅga*;
she who is established in the *liṅga*, she who is the possessor of the *liṅga*, she who is dear to the *liṅga*, [she is for] those who do not desire the *liṅga*. (11.599)
Śivā, Śaivī, Rudrāṇī, Śivī, and Śivanādinī; Mātaṅgī, Tramarī, Mātā, and Mālavānatamālinī. || 11-600 ||
The Ḍākinī and the Yoginī, likewise honored by yogis;
Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Bhrāmarī, and she whose form is Śiva. (11.601)
Alaṃsvadhā, Vegavatī, Krodharūpā, Sumekhalā, Gāndhārī, Gajajihvā, Indrā, and Śubhaṃkarī. || 11-602 ||
Piṅgalā, Brahmadūtī, Suṣumnā, and Gandhinī;
Liṅgasthā, Liṅgeśī, and likewise Tripurābhairavī. (11.603)
Pārvatī is established in the Liṅga, she is the conduct of the Liṅga, as well as the song of the Liṅga;
she is the garland of the Liṅga, born of the Liṅga, and the Liṅga of the Liṅga.
Bhagavatī, Kauśikī, Premā, Priyaṃvadā, Gṛddheśā, Śivarūpā, Cakreśī, and she who bears the form of the wheel (Cakrarūpadhṛk). || 11-605 ||
The song of the *liṅga* is great joy; the song of the *bhaga* is delight in intoxication. The name of the *liṅga* is eternal bliss; the name of the *bhaga* is eternal passion. (11.606)
She whose ornaments are garlands of *liṅgas* around her neck, whose name is *bhaga*, who delights in her consort, and who is adorned with garlands of *liṅgas* and garlands of *bhagas*. (11.607)

Delighting in the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga, having the nature of the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga; neither delighting in the bhaga and liṅga, yet having the nature of the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga. (11.608)
Delighted by the worship of the bhaga and liṅga, you whose essence is the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga;
delighted by the worship of the bhaga and liṅga, O you whose very nature is the bhaga and liṅga! (11.609)
She is the very nature of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, and she brings about the bliss of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*. She is self-existent, fond of flowers, and is herself worshipped with flowers.
Her life-breath is the self-arisen flower; she has arisen from the self-arisen flower.
Without bathing in the self-arisen flower, she is offered as a flower to the self-arisen one.
The Self-Existent One is fashioned from flowers; the Self-Existent One bears flowers.
(177b) The Self-Existent One has flowers as her tilaka mark; the Self-Existent One is adorned with flowers. 11-612 ||
The Self-born One is devoted to flowers; the Self-born One is the gatherer of blossoms;
the Self-born One is the sacrifice of flowers; the Self-born One is the essence of flowers.
The Self-Existent One, whose abode is flowers; the Self-Existent One, who is fond of blossoms;
the Self-Existent One, who wears flowers; she whose mind is intoxicated with longing. (11.614)
The Self-born One, whose embodied form is moist with waves of joy from flowers;
the Self-born One, the support of flowers; the Self-born One, the abode of flowers. || 11-615 ||
Svayaṃbhū, abode of flowers; Svayaṃbhū, dweller in flowers;
Svayaṃbhū, affectionate with flowers; Svayaṃbhū, one who delights in flowers. || 11-616 ||
Svayambhū, Puṣpahārā, Svayambhū, Puṣpamālikā, Svayambhū, Kusumanyā, and Svayambhū, Kusumaprabhā. || 11-617 ||
Svayaṃbhū is the knowledge of flowers, Svayaṃbhū is the vow of flowers;
Svayaṃbhū is the meditation on flowers, Svayaṃbhū is the enjoyer of flowers.

The self-existent one who causes the blossoming of flowers, the self-existent one who rains down flowers, the self-existent one who possesses the fragrance of flowers, and the self-existent one who inhales the scent of flowers. (11.619)
The self-arisen one is the worshiper and wisdom; the self-arisen one is the source of the Hotṛ priest.

The Self-Arisen One who wields a blood-stained sword; she who is contemplated with devotion by the Self-Arisen One; she who devours the worshiper of the Self-Arisen One; she who is dear to the worshiper of the Self-Arisen One. (11.621)
The Self-Existent One is the support of speech; the Self-Existent One is the maker of the river.
The Self-Existent One is the giver of all wealth; the Self-Existent One is the giver of sons.
The self-arisen one is the giver of peace, the self-arisen one is the enemy;
she is the preta born from all lineages, arising at all times.
Always delighted by *kuṇḍa* flowers, always finding pleasure in *golaka* flowers;
the *kuṇḍa-gola* spirits arise from *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, and their very nature consists of *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*.
The Self-born, the auspicious supporter, the purifier of the world, O Purifier! Fame, the mistress of control, the one named Śuk-sundarī...
[bestower of happiness, bestower of liberation, liberation, O illuminator of the gift of liberation].
She is the support of semen, her form is semen, and she dwells in the ocean of semen. She is the abode of semen,
the enjoyment of semen, the worship of semen, and her constant delight.
She is worshipped by Śukra, she performs oblations for Śukra, she is well-pleased, and she is affectionate toward Śukra.
She is the utterance of semen, the maker of semen, the giver of sons to those who worship Śukra;
she resides in Śukra, possesses the seed, is encapsulated by semen, and is beautiful with semen.
She who has bathed in semen, whose body is semen, who is satisfied by semen, she who possesses semen;
she who is the great semen, born from semen, and who bestows a rain of semen. (11.629)
She is designated as Śukrā, she whose food is semen, and who is devoid of the cavity of semen;
she brings about the bliss of semen, she is Śukrā, and she eternally bestows bliss. || 11-630 ||
She is the festival of semen, ever pure, full, and delightful with semen;
she is the very essence of all who worship semen, and the destroyer of those who revile it.
She whose essence is semen, who is like a conch of semen, who draws forth semen;
she is Śāradā, the life-breath of the practitioner, her mind attached to the practitioner.

The compassion that brings joy and satisfaction to practitioners, that destroys the suffering of practitioners, that is the very essence of the supreme practitioner, and that brings about the end of [the cycle for] practitioners. 11-633.
She is the knowledge of the Self, the knowledge of Brahman, and the consort of the Supreme Brahman;
she resides on the three peaks, possesses five peaks, and is the embodiment of all peaks.
She consists of all phonemes, she is the phoneme itself, and she is the one who provides the rosary for recitation.
The Thousand Names (Sahasranāma) in One Thousand Verses.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Thus ends the thousand names of the illustrious Kālikā, as spoken by Śakti.
More secret than the secret, it destroys great sins within a month;
[it should be practiced] at the time of worship, at midnight, and during both twilights.
That best of practitioners who recites it, or who causes it to be recited, or hears it, or even causes it to be heard, shall attain the status of a lord of the Gaṇas. (11.637)
Whether with faith or even without faith, whatever man recites this, he, liberated from all sins, goes to the state of Kālikā. || 11-638 ||
By reciting the *Durgā-durgarati* [mantra], one shall become a favorite at the side of the Goddess;
even a barren woman, or one who bears only female offspring, or a woman whose children die, shall be transformed.
Having heard this hymn, one obtains long-lived sons;
whatever desire one may wish for, one attains it by reciting this unsurpassed hymn.
By virtue of the boon and grace of the Goddess, he constantly obtains that very [state]:
the Self-born One, fragrant with white flowers and endowed with blossoms.

With barley, roasted grain, vermilion, and red sandalwood combined with fish, meat, and other offerings—terrible [in their potency]—along with honey, clarified butter, and milk-rice (pāyasa). || 11-642 ||

With devotion, with offerings consecrated by mantras, together with the means of liberation, with the five types of service, with food offerings, and with oblations of blood from the sacrificial animal; || 11-643 ||
Having worshipped the Great Goddess with delightful lamps and incense, and having recited the great mantra and hymn, one should chant [the prayer] endowed with devotion. || 11-644 ||
Firm-minded, with hair disheveled and naked as the directions, mounted upon a corpse or seated within it, he has come to his dwelling in the cremation ground. (11.645)
Whether he has gone to an empty dwelling or is lying on his bed, one who is intent upon Śiva shall become known as "Kālikāputra. || 11-646 ||
The best among all possessors of knowledge, a lord of new wealth in matters of riches,
possessing strength equal to the wind in this world, he is invincible and a crusher of enemies.
Having cast off all distress and endowed with every accomplishment,
I remember the God of Love as he is being embraced by the goddess Madhumatī herself.
Maheśa is the lord of yogins, placed at the forefront of all sentient beings;
he is Kāminī, the wind, and the one who draws forth from all the Mārīs.
One born under Jalasūryendu-vāyu is a pillar of support, a favorite of the king, illustrious, respectful in conduct, wise, fond of meat, and possesses a voice like that of the cuckoo. (11-650)
Possessing many sons, a lord of elephants and horses, righteous and accomplished, he shall be long-lived like Mārkaṇḍeya, free from old age and grey hair. || 11-651 ||
Even one who possesses a thousand years of life would be endowed with fresh youth;
tell me more of that supreme [merit] of yours as you recite it.

There is nothing in this world difficult to obtain that has been conceived by the mind—not even the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, or sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife. (11.653)
By the grace of this hymn, every man shall indeed attain delight;
even one who beholds the vulva of a menstruating woman shall [attain it] by reciting the great mantra of Kālī.
Having praised with this hymn, what is there that practitioners cannot accomplish? Even one intent on stealing another's wife, having recited the mantra, should recite this hymn.
One who knows the essence becomes as wealthy as Kuvera and like unto Madana;
having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and having invoked the *yoni*, he becomes a knower of the essence.
By studying this [text] in conjunction [with the ritual], one becomes a master of all sciences (*sarvavidyāśvara*).
A man, standing in the *mithuna* position, naked, with disheveled hair, and smeared with ashes; (657)
Having recited the mantra and offered praise to Mahākālī, one becomes a *khecarī* (sky-walker) after a long time;
provided that there is no contact with the wise, then [one should practice] with semen through diligent effort.
Having recited [the mantra] first, they are then to be muttered for the sake of all accomplishments;
at the time of the emission of semen, one should be devoted to muttering and worship. (11.659)
Having praised Śmaśānakālikā with eloquence amidst the splendor of all the gods,
he gazed upon and contemplated that supreme woman who was naked.
Having recited and praised Mahākālī, one becomes a sky-walker after a long time;
likewise, having recited the mantra and praised the blessed Śivā during sexual unions [one attains the same].
A human being who has completely abandoned all sins becomes like the moon;
[this applies] on the new moon, the full moon, the solar transits (saṃkrānti), and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
On the ninth day, a Monday, the excellent practitioner should recite the hymn;
or at midnight on a Tuesday new moon, the man should go to a crossroads. (11-663)
Having offered an oblation of meat, cooked rice, fresh milk, fish, and blood,
and having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should recite the Thousand Names.
One who is devoted to the worship of Kālī will quickly attain the Sudarśana [discus], which is served by gods and gandharvas, by whatever means possible. (11.665)
One may paralyze all the worlds, delude even a king,
attract divine maidens, and bring even a lion under one's control.
It may win over all the worlds, it may even delude a king;
it may attract the daughters of the gods and one might even choose Keśava as a husband.
One who possesses the scripture may kill all enemies through hatred and cause their eradication by means of the blood of a man, a cat, a buffalo, a goat, and a mouse. (11.668)
With bones and flesh, honey, nectar, milk-rice, water for washing the womb, and the nectar of the female and male organs; 11-669.
At the conclusion of the recitation for the worship of Śakra, the practitioner, devoted to bhakti, fully satisfies Kālī and praises her with the divine Thousand Names.
O Kālikā, do not [be like] him who is devoted to censuring others, seeking to harm others, and intent on slandering others, even though she is beneficial to all. 11-671.

To one who is addicted to play, dependent on others, fallen, and a practitioner [of forbidden things]; to one who is hostile to Śiva, wicked, harmful, and evil-minded—[to these, [the mantra] should not be given]. (11.672)
To one devoid of devotion to Hari, to one intent on other things, to one who neglects worship and recitation, and to one who reviles the wives of others; || 11-673 ||

One who shows the divine vision to those who have not been initiated would become a destroyer of Śiva; [however, it may be shown] to one of noble birth, one of great aspiration, and one who is devoted to Durgā. (11.674)
To the devotee of Viṣṇu, the pure one, the practitioner of mantra who is devoted to Bhava,
whose form is non-dual bliss, and who delights in what has been offered— 11.675.
By her command, one should offer this hymn to Mahākālī for the sake of the practitioner;
she is Maheśvarī, who is non-different from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. (11-676)
There is no doubt that great light is produced here through the accumulation of loving-kindness;
he who is capable of devotion to Śiva is indeed the best among Vaiṣṇavas. (11.677)
He who worships and praises Kālī while maintaining the contemplation of me is honored;
the Goddess, filled with divine bliss, is delighted by his devotion, as she herself is devoted to her devotees. (11.678)
He alone is fortunate for whose sake Maheśa’s mind is so intent; having desired him, he would utter this very praise of yours. (11.679)
Completely freed from all diseases, he becomes like the god of love;
one should wear this true discus, attached to the body.
Having properly drawn [the image] according to the rules, that virtuous man himself becomes the very body of Kālikā;
he should then diligently consume everything offered by the Goddess.
Having assumed divine bodies, they shall become the attendants at the side of the Goddess;
seeing one who disparages the food offering, the hosts of yoginīs dance.
Arising from the drinking of blood, she is intent upon flesh, bones, and marrow;
therefore, having seen and praised her, a human being should offer [these] to the Goddess. (11.683)
With body, mind, and speech, the man who contemplates himself as the self of Kālikā becomes averse to all diseases. (11.684)

Having meditated upon the Guru who is like Śiva, he himself is indeed Sadāśiva. This hymn, which truly abides in the dissolution of [all things], was written by Bhavānī for those who know the ritual rules;
it is marked with yellow orpiment, red saffron, camphor, vermilion, and liquid honey.
There is no fear of thieves or enemies, no anxiety regarding water, nor any dread of fire;
there is no suspicion even of portents. Fortune herself dwells there, unwavering.
A person devoted to the lotus feet of Kālī should recite this hymn, which yields infinite merit;
at the conclusion of the ritual worship with excellent offerings, one should likewise utter the two syllables "Ṭha" twice.
Having thus worshipped with a flower, one should not worship with black [flowers] here; by means of this, there would be the act of killing for whomever the rite is performed. (11-686)
The tawny-eyed one causes eradication; the squinting one causes terror;
the open-mouthed one causes flight; the reeling one causes madness. (11.687)
She agitates the pure, she fans the wind, and she flows continuously; she restrains the fearful, she controls the restrained, and she awakens those who have not yet awakened. (11.688)
Whatever state of being one gives birth to, one should also recollect that very state;
in all these cases, one should practice the contemplation of the mere state of being.
In this regard, the doctrine known as "opening" (uddhāṭana) is everywhere accepted;
it serves both for the acquisition of wealth and for the seduction of another's wife. (11.690)
Having gone to a cremation ground, with hair disheveled and naked,
one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims.
Having mounted that very *preta*, the most excellent of men, being self-controlled, fearless, and devoted to no other, should recite the mantra ten thousand times. (11.692)
One attains the supreme accomplishment, which is very difficult even for the gods to obtain;
[powers such as] attraction, subjugation, binding, eradication, and so forth. (11.693)
Paralysis, delusion, terror, and likewise emaciation;
eloquence, wealth, and indeed the possession of many sons. (11.694)
Indeed, one attains the power of moving through the sky and even divinity; there is neither old age nor disease, neither death nor fear. (11.695)
There is neither delight among human beings nor the falling of speech;
or rather, it is the most excellent among the twenty-four attainments (siddhis) that may arise. (11-696)
Now begins the section on the days of the week (*vāra*).
In that Maṇḍeya where right conduct exists, there are views praised as Dharma;
by means of that, people become successful, attaining either heaven or even liberation.
No delusion should be entertained therein; for success (*siddhi*) is lost and ruin arises. [The state of] pure consciousness... || 11-698 ||
If [the mantra] should consist of one hundred eighty-one or one hundred eighty-two [syllables], success will arise; it bestows the group of [eight] powers.
Furthermore, success occurs at that very moment; there is no wonder greater than this. (11.699)
Filled with wonder, the deluded beings go to their dissolution;
likewise for the virtuous wife, the censure of the virtuous, and the theft of wealth.
A wise person should always avoid anger toward women and physical violence;
indeed, the entire world consists of women, and one should become like them oneself. (11.701)
With a restrained mind, one should contemplate that whatever is to be drunk, chewed, eaten, tasted, or enjoyed as a home and comfort—all of it is the form of the Youthful Goddess. (11.702)
Upon seeing that young woman of noble family, one should pay homage with a concentrated mind;
therein, one should perform a mental worship of them.
Whether she be a young girl intoxicated with youth, an old woman, or likewise a beautiful one;
whether she be despicable or a great devotee—having paid homage to her as the Goddess Vibhāvarī... || 11-704 ||
One should worship with a devotional mind a maiden who is red, white, or black in complexion, youthful, slender-waisted, and captivating, established in the prime of youth.
One should not practice laughter, derision, crookedness, or anything unpleasant; otherwise, it will create an obstacle to success. (11.706)
Women are the three gods, women are the three vital breaths, and women alone are the ornament;
one should always remain associated with women, for this is the rule.
There is no restriction regarding the day; there is no restriction on remaining seated or other such postures at any time.
There is no restriction on the time for recitation, nor for worship and the like, nor even for the offerings. (11.708)
In the practice of the great mantra of the *Svecchā-niyama-da-stotra*, there is no restriction regarding clothing, food, place, body, touch, and so forth, nor regarding water. (11.709)
One should not perform purification there; rather, the mind should move in a state free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).
One should worship with fragrant flowers—white and red—and with fruits.
With auspicious flowers such as vitva, maruvaka, and others—excluding tulasī—no unrighteousness exists here; rather, great merit shall accrue.
"One who acts according to his own will, whose mind is wicked, and who is unrestrained—such a person shall not practice [this path].

However, one who is devoted to right conduct, illustrious, dedicated to recitation (*japa*) and worship (*pūjā*), shall become an adept (*sādhaka*) who is the refuge of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *animā*. (11.712)
Thus ends the section on Śyā.
Thus ends the eleventh [third] chapter in the *Āgamakalpalatā* composed by the illustrious Yadunātha. Now follows the mantra of Nīlasarasvatī.
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
Seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, adorned with the crescent moon, the Daughter of the Mountain questioned him as he sat upon his chest. (12.1)
Now, O omniscient Lord, what knowledge did those sages obtain by which they were able to produce the *Tayodhana* and composed the *Bhārata* and other works? (12.2)
Having heard these words, the Supreme Lord smiled and, embracing his beloved, spoke while honoring her, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! (12.3).
Listen, O virtuous lady, to this Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) which destroys ignorance and wealth—
the [knowledge] by which great pride and tears are removed in the pursuit of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation.
The poets of pure intellect did not consider anything superior to this;
by the mere knowledge of the mantra and through its recitation, one may attain omniscience.
By merely placing [the mantra] upon the tongue, even a fool becomes a skilled poet.
A practitioner of mantra should place the mantra on the tongues of fetuses for three days with honey;
if a learned man recites it, he will not become a fool.
Alternatively, O Bālaka, having cut that channel on the tongue with honey and clarified butter as before,
the mantra-practitioner should write the root mantra with a golden needle, or else with white dūrvā grass on the palate.
By uttering speech, one becomes eloquent; by [the ritual] arising from hair, one becomes a poet.

Whether on the upper lip or the lower lip, according to the sequence previously written, within the interval of cutting the channel with a golden rod, a feather, or a bowstring, [it is applied] to the child's tongue.
One should write the mantra with white *dūrvā* grass upon his cheek; by thus beginning the recitation of the words,
the meaning is that one becomes a swift poet.
In the hymn of Mātaṅga.
The father’s brother should write the mantra, or else the mother’s brother. || 12-7 ||
Either the father himself should write the mantra, and never anyone else there.
Regarding the extraction of the mantra (*mantroddhāra*), the *Matsyasūkta* states:
Virūpākṣa said:
Now I shall proclaim the divisions of Tāriṇī, who bestows all accomplishments.
By the mere realization of these, the practitioner becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Therefore, for the sake of the true meaning of this tradition, I shall first describe the root of all sciences:
having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā (M), one should join it with the letter *ḍa* conjoined with fire (*ra*).
The second supreme seed-syllable is joined with Māyā, Indu, and Īśvara.
The *māyā* is the sound *nāda*, and the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*; joined with that, it becomes three.
Then follows the second seed-syllable, *kūrcabīja*, which is the syllable *kaṭ*.
After that is the mantra for complete accomplishment (*sampūrṇasiddhi*), consisting of the five rays and the *praṇava*.
This is the meaning; by that [process], the vowels *a*, *u*, *m*, along with *nāda* and *bindu*, reside there in the *Cūḍāmaṇi*.

Having extracted the unsurpassed, having extracted the supreme Māyottara, and having extracted the highest among the Māyottara-mata, that which is joined with the fivefold [elements] is proclaimed as the Five Rays (Pañcaraśmi). || 12-11 ||
The meaning is "the unsurpassed *a*-kāra.

"Beyond *māyā*" means that *māyā* is the vowel *ī*, and what follows it is *u*; with the fifth *pa*, which is *ma*, the meaning is *oṃ*. Devoid of the *tārā-astra*, the three-syllable Mahānīla-Sarasvatī is thus formed.
Some tantric practitioners declare that this is the *kullukā*. || 12-12 ||
Tārā and the others are five-colored; she is the glorious Nīlasarasvatī, composed of all languages, pure, and saluted by all the Āmnāyas.
When Śrīvijayā is the Vidyā, then Śrī is Sarvatomukhī;
indeed, when Mahāvidyā is present, Māyā and the others grant all desired objects. (12.14)
The great Vāśupā, beginning with Vāgbhava, is the all-pervading mother;
she has arrived through the sequence, being most auspicious, the source of birth, and the singular alternative.
The seed-syllable of Māyā, the seed-syllable of Vadhū, the seed-syllable of Kūrca, and likewise Phaṭ. (12–15)
This five-syllabled vidyā reveals the five elements;
the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū), the middle seed-syllable, and likewise the syllable *ḍaṃ* as a solitary *ḍa*-sound—
thus it was spoken by the venerable Teacher.

In the sixteen-fold result of the middle [syllable], the pure, solitary letter *U* is the "piercer" (*vidroṣa*). Here, within the middle seed-syllable, the secret nectar-seed-syllable *AVIṂ* has not been extracted because of its extreme secrecy;
therefore, it should be understood by the perfected ones (*siddhas*) that the middle seed-syllable is accompanied by the moon (*sacandra*).
Regarding this, he states the reason:
In the Tārārṇava:
"And Ugrā, propitiated by Vasiṣṭha, is the reality for the swift attainment of results. (12.16)
"O illustrious lady, this knowledge was given by Anasta, who is not easily destroyed, to Suniśāya, who was exceedingly cruel; from that time forth, it has remained with you like a bride. (12.17)
This lore is fruitful for all branches of knowledge; it is victorious for those who desire victory;
it is the science that destroys poison and bestows immortality.
Merely by knowing the mantra, one becomes victorious on earth;
[these are] Tārā, Ugrā, Mahogrā, Vajrakālī, and Sarasvatī. (12.19)
Kāmeśvarī and Bhadrakālī— these eight are remembered as the Tāriṇīs in the Phatkāriṇī Tantra.
He states the extraction of the mantra of Nīlasarasvatī: "Having first placed the letter 'sa' together with 'ra', adorned with the fourth vowel. (12.20)
One should then provide the syllable *traṃ*, mounted upon the letter *ra*, throbbing and radiant, and endowed with the lunar drop (*induvindu*); thus the mantra is fully perfected.
"First" refers to the letter *ha* together with its following [elements]: the fourth vowel *ī*, the *bindu*, and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).

The *bindu* here is the *anusvāra*. Thus, *hrīḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). "The first letter of the group" means the letter *ka* joined with the *anusvāra*; by the fourth vowel, namely *ī*, it becomes the seed-syllable *trīṃ*.
185a) "Dīrgha" means joined with the Lord of Argha; the Lord of Argha is the vowel *ū*, and that which is joined with it is the syllable *hū*.
Thus, *hūṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). With that, [the mantra] is *hrīṃ trīṃ hūṃ*; this is the mantra of Nīlasārasvata.
Saṭham va phaḍ anta thyet.
This is the Ekajaṭā mantra.
Beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *phaṭ*.
The Tārā mantra.
For this very reason, it has been stated:
This three-syllabled great mantra, ending with the syllable *phaṭ*, resides in the heart.
Endowed with five rays of light, it is the destroyer of wealth in the case of ignorance; thus, "ha ka" [is said].
Because there is a distinction of mantras through the designation of the syllable *phaṭ* at the beginning following the three syllables, it is called "Upakampa."
Or else, ending with *phaṭ*, it destroys ignorance; "endowed with five rays" means, for the sake of the yellow [color], the *praṇava* (Oṃ) which possesses five rays.
And it is stated in the *Śrīkrama-tantracūḍāmaṇi*:
Just as a young bride, out of modesty, makes a sound when her beloved commits an offense.
In that very same way, this Great Vidyā never dwells within the sphere of the Kula;
this Great Vidyā, Jaṭā, who bears the pair of Yugas, resides at the end of the weapons.
If she is endowed with the faces of the gods and so forth, Tārā is the one who delivers the world.
Because of shame (*hrī*), the seed-syllable *hrīḥ* is mentioned; the word *vadhū* refers to the female seed-syllable. Just as she commits an offense, so she manifests anger by that [syllable].
*Hrīḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) according to the *Metrodghoṣa*.
Thus, the letter *sa* is also obtained through the seed-syllable of the bride (*vadhū*).
This has been stated in the *Matsyasūkta*:
The seed-syllable was deficient in the letter *sa*; when it was uttered by Vasiṣṭha, the sage’s nose was struck off by the gods, a most terrible event.
From that time forward, this vidyā has not been fruitful for anyone.
The seed-syllable of Śakti is to be joined above the other seed-syllable at the end of the recitation. (12-24)

From that point onward, this vidyā is like a bride, adorned with the Tārā-kalpa; it possesses a pair of modesties (lajjā), the seed-syllable of the bride, followed by the long vowel at the end and the covering (chada). 12-25.
The supreme mantra of Sarasvatī is proclaimed to consist of four syllables:
the mantra is *hrīḥ hrīḥ strīḥ hūḥ*.
Lajjā means modesty (hrī). Vadhū-bīja refers to a woman, because it denotes her;
by that [word].
*Hrīḥ*, *Srīḥ*, *Hūḥ*.
These are the mantras. Ending with *phaṭ*, they are five-syllabled. Likewise.
The seed-syllables of Tārā, Śakti, and Vadhū, which possess long and slender wings.
The seven-syllable mantra of Agnivadhū consists of the weapon syllable at the end:
*oṃ hrīḥ strīḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the seven-syllable mantra.
It is thus proclaimed in the mantra scriptures by the long Varman.
The seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū) is encircled by another syllable consisting of the letters *sau* and *guṇa*.
It is said to be tripled by the syllable *guṇa-śakṣa*.
Thus, it becomes a mantra of three syllables. By that [mantra].

*hūḥ strī hūḥ*—this is the mantra. *Tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), *śakti* (*hrīḥ*), the seed-syllable of the bride (*strī*), the long *tanuchada* (*hūṃ*), and *agnivadhū svāhā*. By that: *oṃ hrīḥ strī hūḥ phaṭ svāhā*—this is the mantra.
Now, through the diligent effort of the Mother of the World, Ugratāriṇī, || 12-28 ||

I shall now proclaim the procedure for worship which bestows success upon practitioners of mantra. Having arisen at the Brahma-muhūrta as previously described, and having recollected [the verse] beginning with "prātaḥ śirasi," one should worship the Goddess with mental offerings and then meditate upon Her.

Just as the *kulakuṇḍalinī*, having reached the path by means of the sequence of piercing the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*), is led to the Supreme Śiva; having meditated upon their unity and worshipped with a mind of realization, she [the power] extends from the root center to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), as slender as a lotus fiber.
She is manifest as the root mantra itself, whose very nature is nectar and bliss.
One should contemplate one's own body as pervaded by a mass of that light;
having visualized oneself as the infinite [deity], one should go outside.
Having gone outside and completed the morning duties, one should go to a river or other location for the purpose of bathing.
Having bathed with the aforementioned treasure-water (nidhi), put on clean garments, and sipped water for purification (ācamana), one should recite:
"We know the glorious Rūpatārā; we meditate upon Nīlasarasvatī; may Tārā inspire us.
(186a) Having arrived at the worship pavilion (pūjā-maṇḍapa), one should perform the worship.
Having consecrated the water with: *oṃ vajrodake hūḥ phaṭ svāhā*;
having washed the hands and feet with: *oṃ hrīḥ svāhā*;
[one recites]: *oṃ hrīḥ viśuddhadharma sarvapāpāni śamala tārā pracodayāt*.
"May the remaining conceptual constructions be led away, led away, svāhā"—with this, the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*).
"Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi sarvavaśaṃkari hūṃ phaṭ"—with this, the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandhana*).
"Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"—with this, the purification of the ground through the sprinkling of water (*jalābhiṣeka*).
Reciting *oṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, one should scatter grains and dispel the three kinds of obstacles with the *nārāca* mudrā. Then,
having consecrated the ground with *oṃ pavitraṃ vajrabhūme hūṃ phaṭ*, one recites *oṃ āḥ surekhe vajrarekhe*.
Having worshipped the mantra-lamp with *hūṃ phaṭ*,
and having worshipped the seat with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lotus-Seated One, the Power of Support (*ādhāraśakti*)," one should sit down after assuming the *svastika* or other [meditation] postures.
"Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa rakṣa māṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"—with this, one should tie a knot at the end of the garment.
"Oṃ aḥ phaṭ svāhā"—with this, the flowers are consecrated; then, upon a seat made of gold or other materials, [one should place them].

Having written the yantra with red sandalwood, saffron, and so forth— a square with four gates containing an eight-petaled lotus within a hexagon— using the mantra *oṃ āḥ surekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ*, one should place *māyā* on the eastern petal of the lotus.
Hrīḥ in the south, strī in the north, phe in the west, phaṭ in the center, and hūṃ; having thus inscribed them.
One should place the apparatus upon the foremost seat.
Then follows the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*):
placing both hands in the *uttamā* position at one's own ears.

With the mantra *so'ham*, having joined the individual soul (*jīvātman*) from the heart and the *kuṇḍalinī* through the sequence of piercing the six chakras into the Self residing within the pericarp of the thousand-petalled lotus, one should meditate on the red-colored seed-syllable *māyā* at the navel; [the body] is then consumed by the fire arising therefrom together with the primordial Person (*puruṣa*).
Having meditated on the seed-syllable of the *vicintya* weapon, which is yellow in color, one should contemplate it in the heart;
having dispelled the bodily dust and ashes with the wind arising from that, one should contemplate a white-colored syllable *hūṃ* on the forehead;
having contemplated the entire body drenched by the nectar-essence arising from that, one perceives oneself as stainless.
One should contemplate [the deity] as consisting of the deities. Thus.
With the mantra "haṃsa," one should establish the individual soul (jīvātman) in the heart and the Kulakuṇḍalinī in the Mūlādhāra.
Next is the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkā-nyāsa).
After performing the *ṛṣi*-assignment (*ṛṣinyāsa*) and so forth, and having performed the syllable-assignment (*varṇanyāsa*), one should meditate upon the Mātṛkā.
Then follows the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*):
having recited "Hūṃ" four times, one should fill the air with "I U Pā" while holding the nostrils, [and then recite] "Hūṃ."

Having recited [the mantra] sixteen times and performed the breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) in the central channel, one should exhale the air through the right nostril with [the mantra] recited eight times.
One should perform this triad in the same manner.
Akṣobhya is the ṛṣi, Bṛhatī is the metre,
the glorious Ekaṭā is the deity, the syllable *hūṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*),
the syllable *phaṭ* is the power (*śakti*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of poetic skill, scholarship, and so forth.
Akṣobhya, the Ṛṣi, is honored on the head;
the Vṛhatī, the Chandas, is honored on the mouth;
Ekajaṭā, the Devatā, is honored on the heart.
Now, the ritual placement of the hand-limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*) for the *Mātṛkā*: HROḤ! To her whose form is the totality of speech, *namaḥ* to both thumbs on the two thumbs.
HRĪḤ! To her whose form is indivisible speech, *svāhā* to both index fingers on the two index fingers.
HŪḤ! To her whose form is the speech of Brahmā, svāhā with the two middle fingers.
HRAIḤ! To her whose form is the speech of Viṣṇu, svāhā with the two ring fingers. HŪḤ! HRAUḤ! To her whose form is the speech of Rudra, svāhā with the two little fingers.
HRAḤ SARVAVĀGRŪPIṆYAI KARATALAṢṬAPṚṢṬĀBHYĀM PHAṬ | HRĀḤ AKHILAVĀGRŪPIṆYAI HṚDAYĀYA NAMAḤ | And so forth, as in the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
With both hands crossed over the shoulders and extending down to the thighs:
*Hrauḥ*. To the three eyes, whose form is the speech of Rudra: *Vauṣaṭ*.
[This is performed] upon the three eyes with the index, middle, and ring fingers.
"HRAḤ SARVAVĀGRŪPIṆYAI ASTRĀYA PHAṬ. Having said this, one should perform the triple *tāla* strike above and the binding of the directions as before.
He now states the visualization (*dhyāna*).
Having visualized a red lotus arising from the syllable *ĀṂ* within the all-pervading water,

and having meditated upon a blue lotus above that arising from the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should contemplate the seed-syllable *Mātṛkā*— which possesses the luster of indigo juice— arising above that, and then meditate upon the Goddess above her.
For example:

Oṃ! She whose feet rest upon the head of the elephant, who possesses a fierce and loud laugh from her heart, who holds a blue lotus, a skull-cup, and a chopper in her hands, and who is born from the seed-syllable HŪṂ.
Dwarfed in stature, with a vast blue mass of matted hair and fierce roars,
Ugratārā herself, having placed her hand upon a skull, destroys the three worlds.
"Pratpāliṭā" means that she has performed the two circumambulations, clockwise and counter-clockwise;
"arpitā" means that her right foot and left foot have been placed upon the two feet of Śiva at his heart, and she stands encompassing them—
such is the meaning.

And he has his left foot placed upon the corpse, facing that [corpse], as indicated by the crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) therein; for there is no other indicator here. By this, his state of being mounted on a corpse is expressed. "Ghora" means terrifying; the "rava" is the sound of loud laughter (aṭṭahāsa).

The meaning of "yasyāḥ" (of whom) is as follows: "khaḍga" refers to one who holds a sword and a skull-bowl respectively in her two right hands, from top to bottom, and in her two left hands, from bottom to top; this is the meaning of "yasyāḥ" with respect to those hands.
In her right upper hand she holds a sword, sounding like a hero;
below that, she displays a hand making the gesture of granting boons, adorned with a small knife and a skull-cup.

According to the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, she holds in her left upper lotus-hand a blooming and enchanting blue lotus with a red stalk, and in the lotus-hand below that [another object]. Regarding the term *hūṃkāra*: it means a flaying-knife (*kartṛkā*) produced from the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, which has arisen upon that [lotus].

The meaning is that the sounds are born of the gods. "Kharvā" means short; "īśanilā" means dark-complexioned; "visālā" refers to the mass or collection of matted locks (*jaṭājūṭa*). Alternatively, "kharvā" may be a separate word [meaning] "with serpents.
She is adorned with Takṣaka and other snakes as ornaments and with special cords as a girdle (*mekhalā*). Everything else is easily understood.
It was not stated after having performed [the rite].
Now, the meditation on Ekajaṭā:
she is short, with a loud, boisterous laugh, blue like a fresh rain-cloud, pot-bellied, and clad in a tiger skin.
Her hips are broad and her full breasts are high;

she has three round, red eyes, a flickering tongue, and a face made terrifying by her fangs. Her single matted lock is tawny and fierce, while long garlands of blue lotuses hang from both sides; her mass of matted hair is bound with a very dark blue serpent.
On her forehead is a white bone-plate joined with five skull-caps;
she has earrings made of the Takṣaka nāga, which resemble the Japā flower; she wears a necklace made of the exceedingly brilliant white nāga;
and she has a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of the Kauśika nāga, dark like a blade of dūrvā grass.

Four-armed; above that, her right hand—with its fist adorned by a piece of raw red flesh—is joined to the top of a sword fixed in her mass of matted hair (jaṭājūṭa); her upper left hand holds a slightly blossoming, graceful red lotus belonging to a celestial red nāga; below that...
Her hands are adorned with a southern seed-syllable and a skull-cup;
her lower hands are decorated with a skull-bowl as white as the first-born of the three worlds;
she is of smoky hue, adorned with armlets made of golden-colored snakes and earrings.

She was mounted upon a corpse of white complexion; with the intent of intense restraint, her right foot was drawn up against the heart of the corpse, while her left foot, extended like a fly-whisk, rested upon both feet of the corpse.
Her waist-belt is made of snakes resembling sacrificial pits; her anklets are made of slightly red snakes;
she wears a garland of fifty human heads with their hair tied together, dripping with the fresh blood of a recently slain elephant, hanging from her lotus feet.
In the Moḍa [country], there is a woman with a blazing forehead-ornament, standing in the middle, wearing a garment over a piece of island-skin,
adorned with all ornaments, her head decorated with *akṣoṭi* fruit, and her face turned toward the west.
Now, the meditation on Śrī Nīlasarasvatī.
Oṃ, she who stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, the terrible one, adorned with a garland of severed heads. || 12-32 ||
She was short, with a protruding belly, and terrifying; she wore a tiger skin as her garment and was endowed with fresh youth, adorned with the five mudrās.
Four-armed, with a lolling tongue, most terrifying, and bestowing boons;
she holds a sword and a chisel in her right and left hands respectively.

One should meditate on her as being joined with a garland of skulls, endowed with a left hand [holding a skull-cup], possessing a single tawny and fierce matted lock, and adorned with a crown and breast-ornaments.
She has two arms on the left and two arms on the right,
endowed with a pair of left hands;
on her forehead, she is joined with five skulls together with a white band of bone.
The venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya also said: "One should contemplate her as wearing a garland of bones, a formidable skull, and five [marks] on her forehead. [Furthermore:
"A face that is handsome, square, round, or like that of a cow."
The five mudrās are proclaimed and celebrated as being known as the yonimudrā.
Adorned at the crown with Akṣobhya.

Akṣobhya is at the crown of the head; the author of the commentary is Śivadīkṣā, who is like a digit of the moon that destroys poetic ignorance; his body is [described as] "Candrāvataṃsā" because it is employed in all meditations.
Alternatively, Akṣobhya is in the form of the serpent Vāsuki.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*.
In Akṣobhya, one who possesses a divine form assumes the form of a *nāga*.

Therefore, having meditated upon the deity— whether as a *nāga* form on the head of the Guru or according to the specific division of the mantra— as appropriate, and having visualized oneself in the form of the goddess, one should worship her with the various ritual offerings (*anusopacāra*).
Having placed a flower upon one's own head, one should display the *yonimudrā*.
Then, for the purpose of external worship, one should place a conch shell;
that is, having drawn a triangular and quadrangular mandala on one's left, one should place a vessel with its support (*sādhāra*) there.
Having placed [the vessel] with "To the fire-mandala" as before, and likewise with "Aṃ,
to the sun-mandala," one should worship the vessel while reciting the root mantra.
Having filled it with pure water.
Oṃ, having worshipped the lunar mandala with "to Soma" as before,
one should place perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth into that water.
Hrām, salutation to the heart, whose form is the entirety of speech; Hrā, svāhā to the head, whose form is indivisible speech;
Hrū, vauṣaṭ to the tuft, whose form is the speech of Brahman.
Hrauṃ, to the armor (kavaca) of the one whose form is the speech of Viṣṇu, Hūṃ! Hrauṃ, to the three eyes (netratraya) of the one whose form is the speech of Rudra, Vauṣaṭ!
Hraḥ, to the weapon (astra) of the one whose form is all speech, Phaṭ! Having thus performed the three claps (tālatraya) as before, [one performs] the binding of the directions (digbandhana).
One should perform [the rite]:
having placed the six limbs in the directions of Agni, Śa, Sura, Vāyu, and in the center, one should recite the root mantra ten times.

Reciting "Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune caiva... and so forth, while using the *kuśa* grass and the *mudrā*, one should invoke the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) from the solar orb, contemplate the water as consisting of mantra, and sprinkle that water upon the self and the ritual implements three times. One should perform the sprinkling with that water.
Now follows the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhapūjā).
On the left, *namaḥ* to the Gurus;
on the right, *namaḥ* to Gaṇeśa;
in the center, *namaḥ* to the illustrious Ekajaṭā.
To the cremation ground;
to the wish-fulfilling tree;
to the jewel throne.
Oṃ, to the various ornaments!
Oṃ, to the sages!
Oṃ, to the gods!
Oṃ, homage to the female spirits (śivās) who delight in blood, flesh, and bones!
[189a] In the four directions: in the east, [homage to those] with corpses; in the south, [homage to those] with corpses...
To the *muṇḍas* in the west;
to the *citgāras* in the north; to the *asthis* [in the east]. Then, on the eight petals: in the east...
Oṃ, to Lakṣmī, in the south;
Oṃ, to Sarasvatī, in the west;
Oṃ, to Rati, in the north.
Oṃ, obeisance to Prīti; in the southeast. Oṃ, obeisance to Kīrti; in the southwest.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śānti; in the northwest.
Oṃ, obeisance to Puṣpā; in the northeast (īśāna). Oṃ, obeisance to Tuṣṭi.
Having thus worshipped each subsequent one in turn: Hsau! Obeisance to Sadāśiva, seated upon the lotus-throne of the great corpse (mahāpreta).
Thus one should worship in the center.
Then, having meditated upon the Goddess within a handful of flowers, one should invoke the form by means of the root mantra while performing the ritual visualization (saṃkalpa).
One should then perform meditation once again.
Having meditated in this way with the words beginning "pratyālīḍha," one should invoke from the heart the root mantra— consisting of radiant energy,
the nature of pure gnosis and consciousness, and full of bliss— through the left nostril or the mouth, into the manifested form.
O Goddess of gods, easily accessible through devotion, accompanied by your retinue:
as long as I worship you, remain steadfast here. O glorious Ekajaṭā, come here, stay here, stay here; be present here, be present here.

Having thus invoked [the deity] with the words "sva 2" while restraining [the breath] with the thumb and fist, one should then perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) upon the limbs of the Goddess:
Ā / Hrīḥ / Kroḥ / Svāhā.
Having thus established the vital breaths and uttered the root mantra:
"O glorious Ekajaṭī, accept this vajra-flower!
Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!"
"Obeisance, [this is] the water for the feet.
With these words, one should offer it to the lotus-feet.
"Obeisance, [this is] the respectful offering (argha). [With these words, one should offer it] to the head.
He sips water for rinsing the mouth;
"This scent, obeisance!
This flower, obeisance!"
This is the incense; obeisance!
This is the lamp; obeisance!
Having sprinkled the food offering with water, having stirred it with the two index fingers, and having consecrated it as nectar with the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Having recited the root mantra: *śrīmadekajaṭe vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha svāhā*.
189b) This is the food offering (*naivedya*); *namaḥ*.
I present it to the Blessed Lady, O Goddess who knows the body, may you enjoy it.
Having thus announced [the offering] and given the betel, one should offer three handfuls of flowers with the mantra: "O Śrīmad-Ekajaṭā, accept this vajra-flower, svāhā!
Then, having meditated upon the Sun in the north-western direction, one should worship him.
In the southwest:
the sage is named Gaṇaka, the metre is Gāyatrī, the deity is Agnighna; the application is for the attainment of the fruit seen upon seeing [the deity].
On the head:
*namaḥ* to the Gaṇaka-Ṛṣi; on the mouth: to the Nivṛt-chandas.
In the heart, for the sake of removing obstacles, [one says] "Salutation to the Deity.
*Gā*, *gī*, *gū*, *gai*, *gau*, *gaḥ*.
These are the mantras for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs.
Then, having meditated, one should worship.
Having meditated on Mahādeva in the southeast,
one should worship Gopāla in the northeast.
Thus it is said in the Tārākalpa:
"Having worshipped Gaṇapati in the east, and likewise Vaṭuka in the south, one should worship Kṣetrapāla in the west, and Yoginī in the north. (12.37)
Thus is the sequence born of Vāyu.
In the southeast:
"Salutation to the Heart, whose form is the entirety of speech. In the northeast:
"O you of unbroken austerity," svāhā to the head; in the southwest.
"O you who observe the vow of celibacy," vauṣaṭ to the tuft of hair; in the northwest.
"To the one whose form is the essence of Viṣṇu's austerity," huṃ to the armor.
In the center: *O Rudravāginī, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ*.
In the four directions starting from the east—in the east, south, west, and north:
*To the one whose form is all speech, to the weapon, phaṭ*.
Salutation to the gurus of the divine lineage (divyaugha). Salutation to the gurus of the accomplished lineage (siddhaugha).
Salutation to the gurus of the human lineage (mānavaugha).
Upon the head of the Goddess:
Akṣobhya-vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha svāhā. Then, on the eight petals starting from the east: in the east—
*Bhaivaurocanapuṣpaṃ praticcha huṃ phaṭ svāhā* | [Offer] in the south:
*śaṃkhapāṇḍuravajrapuṣpaṃ* as before. In the west: *padmanābhavajrapuṣpaṃ*. In the north: [as before].
190a) Oṃ, Amitābhavajrapuṣpaṃ, in the southeast; Oṃ, Nāmakavajrapuṣpaṃ, in the southwest;
Oṃ, Māmakavajrapuṣpaṃ, in the northwest.
Oṃ, white vajra-flower; on the petal of Īśāna.
Oṃ tāre, accept the vajra-flower, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā; at the eastern gate. Oṃ, homage to Padmāntaka; at the southern gate.
Oṃ yaṃ, to Yamāntaka; at the western gate. Oṃ viṃ, homage to Vighnāntaka; at the northern gate.
Oṃ naṃ, homage to Narāntaka.

Having thus worshipped and drawn a triangular, circular, and square mandala on the left, having honored it with flowers using the root mantra, and having placed there the sacrificial materials along with the vessel for the *bali* offering, he should touch them with his thumb and ring finger.

Oṃ, to Ekajaṭā, the great sovereign of yakṣas, accept this offered bali; cause it to be accepted! Grant me all peace! Kuru kuru! Draw forth the spells of others! Truṭa truṭa truṭa! Cut, cut! Hrīḥ! Svāhā!
Having thus given the bali and placed the rosary upon oneself, one should recite the root mantra as many times as possible; at the conclusion of the recitation—

Having praised the mantra "guhyātiguhyā" and so forth with a small amount of water while reciting the *japa* with the left hand of the Goddess, having again offered water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should withdraw [the deity] into one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāramudrā* as consisting of radiant energy; then, having meditated on the form of the mantra and placed the *nirmālya* upon one's head:
Having accepted the food offering (*naivedya*), one may enjoy oneself as is pleasant.
Thus ends the ritual manual for the worship of Śrī Tārā Ekajaṭā. Now follows the armor (*kavaca*) of Ugratārā.
Now I shall declare the armor (kavaca) of Ugratārā for the sake of all attainments.
Śrī Bhairavī said: "O Lord, the worship of Tārā and likewise all the vidyās have been heard."
Now I wish to hear the armor-mantra, which is the embodiment of sacred formulas.
The Enchanter of the Three Worlds (Trailokyamohana), which wards off all calamities—O Lord, you previously indicated its name; out of compassion for me, reveal it! (12.39)
Śrī Bhairava said:
O beloved of my life, when this Vidyā has been worshipped here by gods and dānavas,
listen now to the supreme armor (kavaca) named Trailokyamohana.
O Goddess, it consists of all vidyās, it emits the honey of all mantras;
it provides all protection and bestows the vidyā of all siddhis. (12.41)
Since even Vātsyāyana became omniscient by wearing and reciting it, and since the Lord Īśvara became the master who conquers the three worlds by wearing and reciting it. (12.42)
Even Kuvera, the lord of wealth, as well as Indra, the lord of cows and the earth, are truly the sovereigns of all directions because of their recitation and retention [of this]. (12.43)
O virtuous one, endowed with all sovereignty, one shall attain every accomplishment;
by whose grace, O Goddess of the gods, I am the lord of the Bhairavas. (12.44)
The lord of wrath, most terrifying, the renowned master among the gods, should bestow this upon his own disciples, but not upon the disciples of others. (12.45)
Even by giving it to unworthy sons, one may meet with death.
Furthermore, Śiva is the seer (ṛṣi) of the armor-mantra (kavaca) known as Trailokyamohana.
Chanda, Virāṭ, Devatā, Agra, and Tārā are proclaimed; they are celebrated for the four aims of life, for knowledge, and for victories. (12.47)
Oṃ hrīḥ strīḥ—may this protect my head; hūṃ phaṭ—may it protect my forehead; may Tārā, consisting of five and a half syllables, protect the pair of my eyes. (12.48)
Oṃ hrīḥ strīḥ huḥ, may Śrute protect [me] from sin; and Namaḥ protects the nose.
May Tārā protect the face, she who is terrifying with her severed head. (12.49)
Hrīḥ strīḥ hūḥ phaṭ! May she who is Maheśvarī protect the throat and the tongue. Hrīḥ strīḥ hūḥ! May Nīlasarasvatī protect the pair of cheeks. (12.50)
O you whose form is the single syllable *Tārā*, may you surely protect my two shoulders; O you whose form is the single seed-syllable *Hūṃ*, may you always protect my throat.
May *ai hrī strī hū phaṭ* protect my two arms;
may *śrī hrī strī hū* and *śrī* protect the two breasts of me, Tārā. (12.52)
191a) Hrīḥ hrīḥ strīḥ hūḥ phaṭ! May Māyātārā protect my heart! Oṃ hūḥ hrīḥ strīḥ hūḥ phaṭ! May Tārā always protect my back! 12-53.
May *klī*, *hrī*, *strī*, *hū*, and *phaṭ* protect the two sides, O you whose form is desire (*kāmasvarūpiṇī*).
May *oṃ hrī hū hū namaḥ*, the great six-syllabled mantra, protect the belly.
Ai Sauḥ Oṃ Ai Klī Phaṭ Svāhā—may this protect the region of the hips at all times;
this eight-syllabled Great Vidyā is the manifest form of Brahman itself. (12.55)
KHA HŪ HAU OṂ AI ŚRĪ HRĪ SĀ—this seven-syllabled root mantra, whose very nature is Ugratārā, always protects the secret place. (12.56)

Oṃ hrīḥ hāḥ hūḥ, homage to Tārā; then the phrase "sakalapadaṃ," followed by "dustaraṃ tārayadaṃ," then two *praṇavas* (oṃ), and "svāhā"—this is the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*); one should always protect the knees with it.
Ai so oṃ ai hrīḥ phaṭ svāhā; this is the mantra of Jaṅghapānu Parātmikā. || 12-57 ||
Oṃ hrīḥ strīḥ hūṃ ca phaṭ; Tārā, beginning with haṃsa, is this nine-syllable [mantra].
May the Great Goddess Mahogratārā protect my feet forever. (12.58)
Ai, Hrī, Śrī, Hsau, Sau, Sau, and Vedavadavāgvādinī; these are the three Kāma-bījas, which constitute the essential nature of Nīlasarasvatī.
Ai! Ai! Ai! Kati kati kle! Rī Svāhā! And Pārvatī! May Tārā, composed of these thirty-four syllables, protect my entire body.
Indrā (I), Vāmākṣī (Ā), Pṛthvī (L), Sarasvatī (E), and Analapriyā (Ra).
May the ten-syllable root mantra protect [the practitioner] from the kūrca-mantra and other such obstacles above.
Then Tāra, Māyā-vadhū, Kūrcakālī, and Kāmakalā; then Ugratārā, Maga, Kāma, Parā-lakṣmī, Śivā, and Aṅkuśa. (12.61)
O God, that Tārā has now been described by me as the Great Sixteenfold (Mahāṣoḍasī);
she is to be grasped according to the rules, for she does not lead one onto the path of death.
This great secret knowledge, which was at the beginning of the *Yāmalas*,
has now been told to you by me, O beloved, as it has come down through the lineage of the Kavis.
Thus, O Goddess, has been told to you this supreme armor, more secret than the secret, named Trailokyamohana, which is the very embodiment of mantra. (12.64)
O auspicious one, consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, it is purely of the nature of Brahman; and that armor, consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, begins with the word "sanmukha. (12.65)
If one recites the Kavaca mantra three times or more in the midst of the Guru,
like a fire, then at that very moment one becomes Jñānabhairava.
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall uplift ten million members of his lineage;
he shall be a guru, authorized in all sciences, in recitations, and other such rites.
One hundred and eight recitations of this [mantra] is recorded as the rule for the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*).
Having chanted it one hundred and eight times, one becomes a lord of the earth. (12.68)
The hero who wanders through the three worlds shall become like Gaṇanātha,
and his speech, consisting of prose and verse, shall flow like the current of the Gaṅgā.
Having offered eight handfuls of flowers, one should recite [the hymn] just once at the root;
one shall obtain the fruit of five thousand years of worship.
If one writes this on birch bark and wears it as a pill—on the right arm if one is a man, and likewise on the left arm if one is a woman; (71)
The woman shall possess many sons, and the man shall possess excellent sons;
having attained all perfections, he shall wander like Bhairava.
Having reached the Udgātṛ, even those weapons, such as the Brahma-missile and others, become garlands and flowers that grant happiness. (12.73)
In his home, the Goddess Lakṣmī shall surely dwell for a long time upon the tip of his tongue;
yet that base man who worships Tārā without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca) [attains nothing].
He will certainly have a very short lifespan and be foolish; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Śrītārākavaca in the Tārākalpa, from the dialogue between Śrī Bhairava and Bhairavī. May it be auspicious!
Now follows the Thousand Names of Tārā (Tārāsahasranāma).
Oṃ! On the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, the god Maheśvara is worshipped.
"O Bhavānī, O bestower of boons, [speak] out of affection for the secret.
The Illustrious Goddess said: O Īśāna, O omniscient one, how does one obtain the supreme Śakti? (12.76)
"O Radiant One, out of grace toward the practitioner, please tell me that [method]—the illustrious Śaṅkara said:
without worship, without meditation, without recitation, and without an offering. (12.77)
Listen as I declare to you those auspicious kalpas that one attains;
I shall describe them specifically, for they number a thousand tāras.
Listen, O Goddess, with constant devotion to that which is the supreme benefit for devotees:
the fruit that is obtained without ritual worship and without recitation. (12.79)
O Goddess, I shall describe its entire fruit; listen with devotion.

For this hymn (*stotra*) which is the very essence of the lineage of devotion to the venerable Goddess Tārā, Śiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Bṛhatī meter (*chandaḥ*), and the venerable Ugratārā Ekajaṭā Nīlasarasvatī is the deity (*devatā*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining all desires.
Oṃ, Tārarā, O Great One of the Three Times, O Night of Destruction, O Skull-Bearer! || 12-80 ||
Kālikā, the bestower of desires, Māyā, Mahāmāyā, and Mahotsavā;
she who delights in great giving, adorned with sacrifices and the festivals of sacrifice.
Like the moon, with a face as radiant as the sun, she has beautiful eyes and lovely vision;
she is three-eyed, with lotus-like eyes of noble lineage, and is utterly captivating.
Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Jyotsnā, Cārukeśī, Sulocanā, Vārāhī, Vārūṇī, Vidyā, Mahāvidyā, and Maheśvarī. (12.83)
O you whose form is the Great Sacrifice, why are Gaurī with tawny breasts and tawny hair, and Caṃpakavarṇā with slender limbs, worshipped? 12-84.
She is the embodiment of all bliss, the supreme one who bestows all bliss;
she is the sage who is free from all affliction and the savior from all perils.
Her body consists of eternal bliss; she is Bhadrānīlasarasvatī, Gāyatrī, and Sucarī, devoted to the supreme Kaula vow.
She whose joints are gold, whose womb is the earth, whose womb is the universe, who is possessed of glory;
she who is adorned with excellent ornaments by the Goddess whose vehicle is the snow-mountain.
O Mother of the World, Sustainer of the World, Benefactress of the worlds!
You are the power of Indra, of Soma, of Yama, of Varuṇa, and likewise of Vāyu.
The Āgneyī, the Nairṛtī, the Aiśānī, and the Antakāṃvikā—these are the *vidyās* of Sumeru and Hara, which are beneficial to all. (12.89)
She with the tremulous tongue and lotus-like eyes, adorned with a severed head and a goat;
she who is the great totality of all bliss, whose very nature is universal bliss. (12.90)
Fortitude, intelligence, as well as Lakṣmī, faith, the one who leads the hosts of serpents,
Rukmiṇī, Jānakī, Durgā, Satyā, Satyavatī, and Rati.
Kāmākṣī, Kṣudānantā, Nārasiṃhā, Sarasvatī, Mahādeva, Ratā, Caṇḍī, and Caṇḍaduryāvaḍinī. || 12-92 ||
Dīrghakeśī, Sukeśī, Sukeśī, Piṅgakeśī, Mahākacā, Bhavānī, Bhavapatnī, Bhavabhītiharā, and Sacī.
Paurandarī, Viṣṇujayā, Māheśvarī, and the supreme Parā—
she is the eternal mother of them all, worshipped daily, and the destroyer of the Daityas who obstruct the path.
O Maheśānī, you are of terrible form, the passionate one, and of excellent complexion;
you are the Great Vidyā, the Great Māyā, the Great Cloud, and the Great Festival.
Virūpā, Viśvarūpā, Mṛḍānī, and the beloved of Mṛḍa;
she who resembles ten million moons and possesses a splendor equal to a hundred suns.
The daughter of Jahnu, Manojñā, Pārvatī, the beloved of Hara, Kāmarūpā, Maheśānī, and Nityā—she is indeed the destroyer of the ego. 12-97.
The wife of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, as well as the beloved of Śaṅkara,
Kāśapī, Kamalā, and Kṛtsnā— all of them having eyes as long as lotus petals.
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull, her face resembling the full moon;
she is adorned with garlands of jasmine, the blessed maiden, as is the Himālaya mountain.
Śraparṇā, whose eyes are like lotus petals, who wears a serpent as a sacred thread, who holds a great conch, the beloved, the passionate one, the daughter who travels by vehicle. || 12-100 ||
O Śambhu, she is Brāhmaṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Jayā, Gaṅgā, and Janeśvarī;
she is Bhāgīrathī, Manas, Buddhi, and eternally composed of bliss. (12.101)
The beloved of Hari, the daughter of the mountain, the wife of Hara, the performer of austerities;
the goddess who removes great diseases and destroys both gods and demons.
O bestower of great fearlessness, O terrible one, O destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha!
You hold a discus, a sword, and a lotus in your hands, and you carry a book in your hand. 12.103
Cāmuṇḍā, Capalā, Tuṅgā, Bhadrā, Ityānvikṛntinī,
Śānti, Nidrā, Koṭinidrā, and Reṇukā.
Kaumārī, Kulatā, Kuntī, those devoted to the Kaula-vow, Vanadurgā, Vanācārā, Draupatī, and Drupadātmajā. || 12-105 ||
Glorious and bringing glory, the giver of self-control and the bestower of fame;
you are the creation and the sustenance, the one who does not age, and the destroyer of Sumbha’s life-force.
Padminī, Vasudhā, Pṛthvī, Rohirohinī, Vindhavāsinī;
Śivā, Śakti, Mahāśakti, Śaṅkarī, Śakti, Durlabhā. (12.107)

O Daitya, she is the destroyer of life, the giver, the heir, the one who honors the self, and the beloved; she is the intellect that brings peace and security, devoted to the excellence of the celestial mansion. 12.108
Śrīvidyā, Bhairavī, the auspicious one, Bhāratī, the destroyer of fear;
Tāpasī, the savior, the sharp one, the destroyer of the fierce Daityas. || 12-109 ||
The giver, devoted to giving, the giver, Durgā, the daughter of the demon; Suramā, the best of goddesses, the eldest, the mistress of life, she who is established.
She is the destroyer of darkness, the dispeller of gloom, devoted to her vows with a restrained soul;
she is the illuminator, the radiant one, who illumines all the worlds.
O wise one, of great prowess, you are the female swan who carries across the union;
you exist as the life-breath of all living beings, the captivator, and the destroyer of the Daityas.
She has a moon-like face, is most formidable, and is adorned with beautiful hair;
she is charming, auspicious for the month of Mādhava, blessed, worthy of honor, and possessed of great virtues.
Jyeṣṭhā, Śreṣṭhā, Maghā, Puṣpā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Pūrvaphalgunī;
she is the slayer of the enemy of red-seeded beings and the destroyer of red-seeded beings.
O destroyer of Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and Ari; O slayer, O annihilator of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa! O wielder of the sword, O reaper, O excellent cutter, O stainless one who carries the lineage! (12.115)
She is the stainless one, the sun-like one, the formidable one, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
she is Kālindī, Yamunā, Vṛndā, the youthful one, and likewise Vālikā.
Kauśalyā, Kaumudī, Mātrī, Rūdhatī, and also Arundhatī; the consort of Purāri (Śiva), Pūrṇā, Pūrṇakarmā, and Yaśaśvinī. || 12-117 ||
With a face like the full moon and a radiance equal to the crescent moon,
Revatī was a beautiful woman adorned with various and wonderful ornaments.
She who abides in virtue, possessed of true knowledge, glorious and renowned;
born from the flower of the hand, her origin is from the flower of a man.
Her offspring were a garland of human flowers, adorned with ornaments of human flowers;
their life-force was equal to human flowers, and they were as eager for human flowers. || 12-120 ||
She whose nature is the flower of man, who is adorned with flowers and earrings, who is endowed with the virtues of the flower of man, and who is beautified by the flower of man. || 12-121 ||
She who delights in human flowers, who is joyful while situated in the midst of the circle of pretas, who is the lamp for the Kula scriptures, and who causes the Kula path to flourish. || 12-122 ||
Śmaśānabhairavī, Kālabhairavī, the beloved of Bhairava; Bhairavī, whose life-breath is Bhairava, she who increases the bliss of Bhairava. || 12-123 ||
Guṇānandabhairavī, Bhairavīpurabhairavī, Māyābhairavī, Śaumyābhairavī, and Lokabhairavī. || 12-124 ||
And Vidyā, Bhairavī—thus Bhairavī is imperishable by virtue;
Padmā, Padmavatī, Kṛtsnā, Tuṣṭā, Puṣṭā, and likewise Urvaśī. (12.125)
Vajriṇī and Vajrahastā, likewise Nārāyaṇī and Śivā;
Śaṅkhinī and Śaṅkhahastā, and she who bears a knife and a skull-bowl.
Devāṅganā, Devakṛtyā, Puromajā, Śaṅkhinī, Sukhadātrī, and Sarvasaukhyavivardhinī. || 12-127 ||
She is virtuous and endowed with virtue, subtle and the source of subtlety, the bestower of boons;
she is speech, the giver of boons through her boon, and the stainless giver of knowledge to the wise.
Ugratārā, Yaśodākṣī, Pādavī, Vanavāsinī, Ugrakālī, Mahākālī, Bhadrakālī, and Dakṣiṇā. (12.129)
Born from the lineage of Bhṛgu, she is the daughter of Bhṛgu and the beloved of Bhṛgu;
she wields the trident, holds a spear in her hand, and is borne by a magnificent peacock.
Delighting in human flesh, she is red, holding a blood-stained skull-cup in her hand;
she is the beloved of the foremost of red asuras, a charming consort of the leaders of the gods.
Parānandā, Parājyeṣṭhā, served by the hosts of Yoginīs;
Ardhajāmbavatī, Satyā, Satyabhāmā, and Nagātmajā.
Raudrā, Raudrasvatā, Raudrā, the destroyer of the fierce Daityas; Kaumārī, Kauśikī, Vidyā, the destroyer of the Kāla Daitya. || 12-133 ||
She is the wife of Saṃbhu, the state of Saṃbhu, the consort of Saṃbhu, and Mahodarī;
she is the wife of Śiva, she whose sound is auspicious, the consort of Śiva, and the wielder of the trident.
The wife of Hara, the destroyer, likewise Ambikā, the consort of Hara; Madanākā, Kāntā, and the beloved of the ender of Madana.
Girijā, the daughter of the mountain, and the beloved of Giriśa;
she who is both being and non-being, the created, the purifier, and the protector of all.
Invisible and of unmanifest form, she moves within the sun;
she is the infallible, the fallen, the meritorious, the giver of life, and the sovereign of the Vasus.
Arisen from the hand-vessel (apāṇidhi), she is established as the Sustainer (Dhāriṇī);
the Supreme Goddess is the Source (Udbhavā), the Unshakable (Akṣobhanī), the Unshakeable (Akṣobhā), and the Womb of Glory (Śrīgarbhā).
She is the performer of deeds, the one with a nourished body, the performer of deeds, the lotus-eyed one; she is the refuge, the lotus-born Lakṣmī, the beloved, and the increaser of stainless bliss.
Another is Udīcībhūṣaṇā, another is Sureśvarī, the leader of the divine host;
then Kalpinī, Kalpalatā, and Sumatānandavardhanī. || 12-140 ||
In Śrīmatī is Śaktirākāntā, and Bhairavī is Śaśirā;
there is Sammohabhairavī, Puṣṭibhairavī, and Puṣṭibhairavī. (12–141)
She is Bhairavī of creation and sustenance, and Bhairavī of sustenance;
she is the one who dwells in the abode of Puṇḍarīkākṣa and the beloved of Puṇḍarīkākṣa.
Āvandasundarī, Vīrasundarī, Vitasundarī,
Guṇānandasundarī, Kālasundarī, and Purandarī.
Māyā-sundarī, Śaumya-sundarī, Loka-sundarī, Vidyā-sundarī, Nīti-sundarī, and Guṇa-sundarī. || 12-144 ||
Delighting in jasmine garlands and adorned with jasmine garlands,
she is beautified by the filaments of the sun-like blossoms of fresh campaka flowers.
Resembling the Javā flower, adorned with the Javā flower;
she is the refuge of virtues, possessed of virtues, and beautiful through the weight of her virtues.
Resembling the lord of stars (the moon), adorned with two *ṭaṅka* marks,
she is Kumudvatī, Kumudanī, Kumudā, and Kumudākarā.
Resplendent with the hue of kausumbha flowers, her head adorned with saffron-colored garlands,
