O Goddess, you stand at the foot of a tree, yet you are also situated upon the branches of that tree.
On the tree, she is Medā, Tilā, and Yā, dwelling in the middle of the tree;
she is a woman of virtuous character and intellect, beautified by form and youth.
The Self-Existent One is like a flower; the Self-Existent One is the bearer of flowers;
the Self-Existent One is foremost among those with lotus-lakes of flowers; she is always possessed of meditative concentration.
She who loves semen, who delights in semen, who is intent upon the production of semen;
she who has leaves, whose leaves are excellent, who is well-winged, who is leafless, and who destroys evil.
Endowed with the fragrance of wine, she bears the scent of wine;
she is the refuge of all and the bearer of the lineage that brings joy through all virtues.
One whose life-force is like a woman’s flower, who is eager for a woman’s flower, who is likewise a woman’s flower, or a woman devoted to flowers—this is the path. (12.153)
She has four arms, ten arms, and likewise eighteen arms;
she also has two arms and six arms, and is resplendent upon a lotus.
Kauveri, Kairavīkullyā, Kurukullā, Kapālinī, Viparitakadalī, Jaṅghā, Raṃbhā, and Nāvāmavallabhā. (12-155)
She is the night-stalker of great form, possessing a radiance equal to the moon of night;
she is the one with flowing streams, the one who possesses those streams, and she is the destroyer of all fame.
She consists of the support of all; she is everything; she is the perpetual increaser of all bliss;
she is the sovereign of all cakras; she is all; and she is eternally composed of all mantras.
O Prāṇa, you have a thousand paths; O beloved, you have a thousand eyes.
You have a thousand heads, beautiful teeth, and you are the speaker of all things.

She who abides in the sixty-fold wheel, bestowing the fruits of the six classes [of beings], residing in the center of the thirty-six lotuses, situated within the midst of the thirty-six petals. (12.159)
She whose abode is the letter *ha*, adorned with the syllable *ha*,
the Savior (*Tāriṇī*) who delivers [beings], she who is beautified by pearls and diamonds.
She is devoid of the three-fold variety and yet adorned by the one who possesses the three-fold variety;
she is like a digit of the *kadaṃba* tree and is satisfied by the *kaulinī* lineage. (12.161)
She delighted in *ketakī* flowers, was adorned with *ketakī*, and possessed a luster equal to that of camphor, incense, sandalwood, and the lord of the digits (the moon). || 12.162 ||
A bedstead and a pair of wagtails; eyes and ornaments of birds; in the Kali age, a beloved woman and the god of death; and longing for the kadamba flower. (12.163)
Moving with the gait of a rutting elephant, she proceeds like a lordly elephant; as difficult to perceive as a firefly, she is as flickering as a firefly.
She who is Gayā, whose mace is praised for its qualities, whose movement is dear, the mistress of the Gaṇas,
the one worshipped by the Gaṇas, the one adored by the Gaṇas, and the bestower of the Gaṇas.
She is the perfection of both virtues and non-virtues, the bestower of virtues, and whose very nature is virtue;
she is the mother, the most venerable, the fair-complexioned Gaurī, and the granter of the fruits of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
She who grasps the Dharma well, she whose nature is the Dharma, she who dwells within both Dharma and non-Dharma;
she with a throaty and formidable face, the destroyer of the terrible Daityas.
Ghorā, Ghoravatī, Ghūrṇā, Ghoraputrī, Ghanālayā, Carcarī, Cārunayanā, and Cāruraktacaturguṇā. || 12-168 ||
She consists of the four Vedas; she is the moon, yet has four faces like the moon;
her eyes are like those of the cakora bird, O you with restless collyrium-smeared eyes. (12.169)
She whose eyes are like trembling lotuses, she who possesses trembling lotus-eyes;
she who holds a parasol, she who is fond of the parasol, she who is the parasol itself, and she who is adorned with the parasol and the chowrie.
Chinnachidra, Chinnaśiras, Chinnanāsā, Phalānvitā; Calādyā, Calamantrastā, Chalanāyā, Chalāchiyā. (12-171)
She whose abode is the syllable *cha*, she who is enriched by the syllable *cha*, she who is fond of guile;
she who is hidden, she who delights in deception, and she who dwells within the deceitful mind.
The beloved life of Jagannātha, the beloved old age of Jagannātha, like the wife of an aged cloud, adorned with the beauty of a withered form. || 12-173 ||
She who is called Amātṛ, the bestower of boons, Jṛmbhā, the bearer of the Jayā, Malā, and Arjuna;
she who is endowed with speed, the destroyer of speed-born obstacles, and the giver of the supreme boon to Jambharāmi.
Jitā, Jayatrī, Jayadā, Jayadātrī, and Jayapradā;
likewise Ṛllarālillatī, Lillī, Ṛri, and Ṛllarikā. (12.175)
She who produces the sound "ṭaṃ," she whose commentary is the sound "ṭaṃ," she who bears the sound "ṭaṃ" and the ṭaṅka weapon;
she who strikes with the syllable "ṭa," Tulasī, the devourer of palm trees. (12.176)
Tulā has crossed over the Taulinika shore; likewise, she is Tārā, Tārālikā, skilled in tantra, devoted to tantra, knowledgeable in tantra, and a bestower of tantra. (12.177)
Therein are the *Īkātantrayoga*, the *Tantrasārā*, and the *Tantrayā*;
the *Tantradhārī*, the *Tantrakārī*, the *Tantranārī*, and the *Tarāntarā*. (12.178)
Austerity is her dawn; the knowledge of austerity is she who bestows the fruit of the essence of the Tantras;
ascetic practice is Taulinī; she has crossed over the three worlds and is adorned by the gods.
She is filled with moonbeams, adorned by the rays of the moon;
she is like the cool season, possessing a cool and perfectly even posture, and having a cool and perfectly even radiance.
She whose speech is as sweet as the rays of the moon, who is as beautiful as the moon,
who is equal to the abode of frost, and whose radiance is perfectly like that of snow.
She who delights her sons beginning with Tuhina, whose limbs are like palm trees yet devoid of palms,
the Star (Tārā) accompanied by the celestial arrow, the Star adorned by the gods.
She whose abode is the six syllables beginning with *ṣa*, who is adorned by the letter *ṣa*;
she is compassionate, devoted to the wretched, and the destroyer of suffering and poverty. (12.183)
She who destroys the poverty of misfortune, she who brings about the destruction of misfortune, she who is the daughter of the Lord of the Dānavas, and the kinswoman of the distressed. || 12-184 ||
She who bestows gifts, who is devoted to giving, who is purified by the honor of charity, who cultivates grain and other provisions, the giver, and he who is solely intent upon Damodara. (12.185)
Dadhici, Pravadākhyā, Dānavendrivināśinī,
Dīrghanetrā, Dīrghakacā, Dīrghanāsā, and Dīrghikā.
She who pacifies the suffering of poverty; she who is the enemy of the demons of suffering;
she who is free from deceit, pride, and hypocrisy; she who destroys the lords of the Dānavas.

She is the bestower of wealth and grain, the auspicious one, the giver of the riches of the Lord of Wealth; she is the virtuous one, the source of righteousness, the embodiment of dharma, and the increaser of both dharma and its practice.
She is the mistress of wealth, the sustainer of dharma, the increaser of the bliss of dharma;
she is the presiding deity of riches, fond of wealth, enriched by wealth, and satisfied by wealth.
She is steadfast, yet possesses courage; she is bold, the giver of wealth, and resembles the Bhoja and Jasa tribes.
She is the earth, the sustainer, the nurse, the leader at the forefront, and the one who bestows white tears.
She is righteous, endowed with Dharma, and free from those who revile the Dharma;
she is ever-new, born from the lotus, the giver of what is lowly, and the sovereign of the mountains.
O beautiful one with eyes like fresh lotuses, you are the fresh food for the serpents;
you are the serpent-maiden worshipped in the realm of the Nāgas, and the divine abode of the Nāga kings.
Nāgarājagagatī is fierce, adorned with garlands of serpents;
she is Bhāgīśvarī, mounted upon a mountain, the sovereign mistress of the serpent kings.
She who delights in the singular digit of the moon, the beloved of Nandikeśvara,
the lotus-born, the lotus-eyed, and she whose eyes are like a pair of lotuses.
Born from the waters, originating from the waters, she who bestows the waters and is pure;
she is enriched by the serpent as her sacred thread, and she wears the serpent as her sacrificial cord.
She is satisfied by *nāgakesara* flowers, she wears a garland of *nāgakeśara*, and she is adorned with the nectar of fresh *tarkī* and *kunda* blossoms.
The heroine is the heroine; the heroine is pleased; the heroine is gratified by pleasure;
the heroine is accompanied by the deceased; the heroine is satisfied by love. || 12-197 ||
The heroine is the abode of bliss; she is not one who causes dancing, nor is she intent on worldly action, nor is she devoted to sleep, nor is she solely dedicated to ritual acts.
She was named Narmakapriyā, devoted to the dharma of play;
she delighted in play and took pleasure in play, yet remained devoted to the meditation on the Dharma. || 12-199 ||
She is accompanied solely by playful activity and is the sole protector of playful activity;
she delights in the virtues of men and women and bestows boons upon men and women.
She is devoted to Nārāyaṇa, supreme, free from all defects, and characterized by the letter *na*;
she is fond of flowers, delights in flowers, and is the ultimate refuge for those who possess flowers. || 12-201 ||
She who loves flowers, who is worshipped with flowers, and who is adorned with flower garlands;
she who bestows merit, who is the meritorious full moon, and who grants the fruit of ten million merits.
She is the ancient altar of the womb, concealed by the ancient Āgamas;
she is protected by the ancient Āgamas and gratified by the ancient Āgamas.
Ancient in her range of experience, she is the primordial destroyer of arrogance;
she is the joy of Prahlāda’s heart, playful, the mistress of the household, and one whose conduct is meritorious.
Phalgunī, she who is fond of Phālguna, she who sustains the deceased of Phālguna;
the bestower of fruit, she who is attached to the arts, adorned with ornaments of fruit. || 12-205 ||
She whose every limb is the peak-syllable *pha*, who increases the bliss of Phalguna,
who is devoted to Vasudeva, who is wise, and who brings about wisdom.
She is like Vīṇāvatī, the sovereign of the Valakas, or like Vīyūṣā;
she is a young girl, Sumati, worthy of praise, and adorned with a necklace of knowledge.
Vidyāvatī, Vaidyapadā, Pītā, Vaivasutī, Vali, Khānivilāsakāriṇī, Varāṅgasthā, and Varānanā. (12.208)
Viśrūḥ, Bahusthalā, Sthūlā, Pārvatī, Vindhyavāsinī, Vāṇī, Varuṣaṃsthā, and Vāṇīraṅgasamutsukā. || 12-209 ||
She who removes fear, she who destroys terror, she who is radiant with a splendor equal to a mass of rays;
she who is the object of worship for Bhārgava, she who is worthy of honor by Bhṛgu, and she who is saluted by Bharadvāja.
She who causes fear, she who is possessed of terror, she of terrifying form, and yet beautiful;
she who maintains illusions, and he who is intent upon honoring the mind.
She who bestows bliss upon Mādhava, whose eyes are intoxicated with wine, endowed with the quality of great enthusiasm, ever devoted, and arisen from passion. 12-212.
Madirāmodavanitā is devoted to bathing in wine;
Yaśodharī is glory, knowledge, and the increaser of the joy of Yaśodā. (12.213)
Her fame is as white as camphor; she is adorned by the river Yaśodā;
she is the path of union with Yama’s sister (Yamunā); and she is the one who causes the prosperity of Yoga-nanda.
She who brings joy, who increases the bliss of the Yādavas,
who is pleased by sacrifice, who consists of sacrifice, and who is adorned by ritual action in the sacrifice.
The beloved of Rāma, devoted to Rāma, intent on pleasing Rāma;
she who is worshipped in sacrifice and in the royal family, the sovereign lady of the kingdom of kings, is Ramā.
She is as delightful as a jewel to Rāma and Rāmī, she increases the bliss of Rāma, her face is like that of the son of the night-maker (the moon), and her eyes are like red lotuses.
Lāṅgalī, Premamaṇdā, Lāṅgalī, Praṇayapriyā, Lākṣārūṇā, Lalitā, Līlāvatī, and Layā.
She possesses the qualities of the Lord of Laṅkā, she bestows the boons of the Lord of Laṅkā;
she dwells in the wind, she resides in the house of the Sun, and she maintains love. (12.219)
Straight, yet not straight, she who is beyond counting, the one worthy of arrows, the beloved of Śrīśara;
she resides in the lotus at the center of the hexagon, adorned by the three forms of prosperity.
Kṣemyā, Vā, Tathājñā, Ddhadva, the one beloved by the letter Ī, Agrākhyā, Ceṇī, and the one originating from the gods beginning with the letter I. (12.221)
Established in the color of the syllable *ṛ*, adorned with the vowel *ṝ*, she is the one who is to come, as well as the one who is to be consumed;
she is the bearer of the syllable *oṃ*.
The letter *a* is uncaused and well-guarded within all the Āgamas. 1000.
Whoever recites this hymn every day, endowed with devotion, || 12-223 ||
Day and night, as well as at the time of twilight, he is the master of the occasion;
by the mere recitation of this hymn, the King shall come as a servant.
197a) A man who honors all the Āgamas and all the Tantras himself [is purified] in a place of Śiva, on a bed, in an empty house, or at a crossroads. 12-225.
Whoever recites or even hears this, he shall become a yogin here; of this there is no doubt.
These names, which were uttered by Vairiṇa in connection with the Truth, [have been proclaimed]. (12.226)

O Sadāśiva, one should always utter the names [of the deity] or other [mantras], while touching a *tulasī* leaf that has absorbed the essence of Hara. One should never entertain thoughts of anything else, nor ever censure anything else. (12.227)
Through the chanting of this auspicious hymn, one gains mastery over the wind, the water, and the mind, and indeed renders fire cool. || 12-228 ||
One should recite the *Śrīyakara* [mantra] until the river Marī is filled; by holding it thus, one shall delude Rādhā and bring the three gods under one's control. || 12-229 ||
Whoever should always read or even hear this with a single-minded focus will become long-lived and happy; this [mantra] is the subduer of the eighty [great diseases].
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing at all sacred fords (tīrthas) and by performing a śrāddha at Gayā,
that entire fruit belongs to him who recites this with one-pointed mind.
For those whose faith I satisfy, and who are ever-striving and diligent, their purpose is accomplished everywhere; their destination is the abode of the gods.
Standing amidst the assembly of the six families, one should strike with a staff;
having recited and praised Mahākālī, one shall go to the state beyond duality.
One should worship on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth lunar days; on Saturdays, at the time of the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), on Tuesdays, at night, and on the new moon day.
O Goddess of the gods, his intellect is struck by joy and sorrow;
he is afflicted with misfortune, like a woman whose son has died and who is tormented at every step.
Whether she be barren, or one whose children are like crows (a woman who bears only one child), or a woman whose sons have died;
or one destitute of wealth and grain, and one who is overwhelmed by disease and grief. (12.236)
That same [mantra], O Great Goddess, may also be written on birch bark;
one should fasten it upon the arm immediately, and she shall become possessed of all happiness. (12.237)
In this way, even a man who has encountered suffering and is oppressed by it—whether in a council, in a terrible calamity, in a dispute, or in the perils of an enemy—[remains steadfast]. (12.238)
In the great battle with the Asuras, when one is oppressed on all sides by foot-soldiers, O auspicious lady, it comes to destruction from afar merely by being remembered. || 12-239 ||
O Goddess, she should always be worshipped with effort in an empty house, in a temple of Śiva, at the foot of a bilva tree, or in a kula-maṇḍapa. (12.240)
And likewise, the food offering (naivedya) should be prepared with flour-cakes (apūpa) combined with those [ingredients] prescribed;
one should offer this food offering to the Goddess with devotion and great care.
If that great meal is not eaten by Śiva himself,
one should worship the Supreme Goddess by this very procedure.
O Goddess, on this earthly sphere there is no doubt regarding direct vision;
by means of the great conch, one performs the recitation of mantras and other rites for many eons.
The power of the very essence of the entire lineage has been manifested by you;
it cannot be fully measured even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Out of rashness, I have said something concerning the Supreme Goddess;
it could not be fully described even in a thousand future births.
It should be given to one of noble birth who is devoted to you;
O Goddess of the gods of gods, it must never be given away, for it is always to be kept secret in all the scriptures.
O Goddess, it should always be recited in all the Āgamas;
O Goddess, it should always be recited, for such a state is very difficult to attain. (12.247)
Thus ends the *Sahasranāma* of Tārā and Nīlasarasvatī in the glorious *Nīlatantra*.
Now follows the hymn to Tārā.
Oṃ! O you of terrible form, O you of great roar, O destroyer of all enemies! O granter of boons to your devotees, bestow [your grace] and protect me who has come to you for refuge. (12-248)
O Goddess worshipped by the gods and asuras, served by the siddhas and gandharvas;
O Goddess who removes dullness and sin, protect me who have come to you for refuge. (12.249)
O Goddess who possesses a mass of matted locks and who mimics a flickering tongue, grant me swift intelligence; protect me, who have come to you for refuge! (3) 12-250 ||
Salutations to you in your gentle form, in your cruel form, and in your fierce form;
salutations to you in your form as the Creator; protect me, who have come to you for refuge. (4) 12-251
O Goddess who is as fond of devotees as a cow is of her calf, you destroy the dullness of the dull-witted;
O Queen of Gods, remove my delusion and protect me, who have come to you for refuge. (12.252)
O Goddess whose nature consists of the syllables *hūṃ* and *hūṃ*, beloved of the *bali* offering, homage to you!
O Ugratārā, homage always; protect me who has come for refuge. (12.253)
Grant me growth, grant me fame, grant me the power of poetry, grant it to me!
O Goddess of Gods, remove my delusion; protect me, who have come to you for refuge. (7) 12-254 ||
O Tārā, embodiment of compassion, who is praised by the hosts of gods beginning with Indra;
O you whose face is like the lord of stars, protect me, who have come to you for refuge! (8) 12-255 ||
The person who recites this on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the ninth day shall attain accomplishment within six months; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. (12.256)
One who seeks liberation attains liberation; one who seeks wealth attains wealth;
and one who seeks knowledge attains knowledge, such as logic, meditation, and the arts.
The person who constantly recites this hymn attains the destruction of his enemies and becomes possessed of great wisdom. (10) || 12-258 ||
Whether in times of affliction, in battle, during a great portent, or likewise in fear, whatever auspicious hymn one recites, for that person there is no doubt [of its efficacy]. (12-259)
Thus ends the King of Hymns to Mahogratārā in the Tārākalpa; may there be auspiciousness!

I bow to Mother Nīlasarasvatī, who bestows the wealth of good fortune upon those who prostrate before her; she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon the heart of a corpse, with a smiling face and eyes like blooming lotuses;
three-eyed, holding a chopper, a skull-cup, a blue lotus, and a sword, she is beloved by both gods and demons.
Take refuge in you, the Sovereign Lady. (12-260)
O Mistress of Speech, O Kalpalatikā of devotion, Sovereign of the attainment of all goals, you whose words arise as both prose and verse, bestower of the perfection of omniscience;
O Goddess with three eyes dark and lustrous, O Ocean of Compassion, showerer of the nectar of good fortune upon those who act rightly!
Out of compassion, please sprinkle us who are like this. (12.261)
Dwarfish, filling the entire assembly, and radiant with all her limbs and ornaments; O fair-faced one, she is draped in a tiger skin,
her waist adorned with tinkling bells, and her hair bound with the skin of a black antelope and marked by the three seals.
O Goddess, who destroys fear with your garland made beautiful by a string of human heads! (3) || 12-262 ||
O Māyā, O you who possess the nature of the cow, the fire, the lotus, the drop (bindu), and the half-moon, you are indeed HŪM and PHAṬ;

O you whose essence is mantra, you alone are the refuge for one such as me. You are the subtle, supreme form, fashioned from the three worlds and the three abodes, which is not within the scope of the Vedas.
I take refuge in those who have somehow attained the state of being free from pride. (12.263)
O Mother, through service to no other do the virtuous attain such honor; for even the three-eyed Lord Śiva, Brahmā, and the other progenitors of the universe—
whose bodies are struck by the immersion in worldly existence— along with the foremost gods led by Indra and their celestial consorts, [attain this] only through service to Your feet.
Why does she serve me with her face turned away? (12.264)
O Mother, the dust from the imprint of your two lotus feet has entered the crowns of the gods without fear during their victory in the battle between the gods and asuras;
they carry it within themselves with great effort, as if it were their own abundant prosperity, thinking, "This is our wealth in this world."
The selfs go toward purity and imperishability. (6) || 12-265 ||
By the remembrance of your name, the hosts of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and rākṣasas,
as well as yakṣas, lords of the nāgas,
the foremost of daityas and dānavas, sky-dwellers, tigers, and other beasts, flee when seen by others and are rendered powerless.
And the ḍākinīs and the enraged Antakas will devour the person on the surface of the earth in an instant. (7) || 12-266 ||

O Mother, by the dust of Your feet, those very powers—prosperity, the hosts of *siddhis* beginning with the *pādukā*, the immobilization of waters, the paralyzing of elephant herds on the battlefield, and even the power of enchantment—truly become accomplished for men; O Radiant One, [grant] splendor! Splendor!
Even Vācaspati finds a vulnerability in the mind-born god. (12.267)
The man who, endowed with devotion, recites this Ugratāṣṭaka at dawn and at midday, being self-restrained and pure on festival days— ‖ 12-268 ‖
He attains divine poetic skill and becomes a knower of the meaning of all scriptures;
having obtained his heart's desire for prosperity, he enjoys the pleasures that lie along his path. (9) 12-269 ||
May there be fame, peace, and health for all, as well as their well-being;
may they attain renown throughout the worlds and, at the end, achieve liberation. || 12-270 ||

Thus ends the *Śrī-Ugratārāṣṭaka*. Regarding the constellations, one should not alter the knowledge [of the stars]. Having dismissed the mantra, it should be given even to the eldest son who is humble; how much more so to another of a different lineage? One’s own prowess [should be bestowed] upon him. (12.271)
Even for an eldest son, instruction must be given once his discipline has been recognized;
and thus it is said:
"The initiation of a father is one thing, and the initiation of one who dwells with wealth is another. (12.272)

"The initiation of those who do not practice asceticism—that initiation destroys one's wealth. Such is the saying. The Kaulika initiation is a "void" initiation; it is forbidden for anyone else, let alone for one of a different lineage (gotra).
The connection is that one should bestow one's own manly prowess and fame;
and so it is said:
One should always [place] the mantra and one's own guru within the footprint of the cow (gopada).
By that means, the vidyā becomes potent; otherwise, it would be devoid of power for the one who reveals it. (12.273)
Between the one who initiates [one into Vedic study] and the one who imparts the Veda, the giver of the Veda is more venerable;
therefore, one should always regard him as even greater than one's father. (12.274)
Likewise.
Through instruction, the limb-mantra and likewise the bali-mantra should be known by the wise; through the attainment of this mantra, there is success. || 12-275 ||
The limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) are the mantras for the empowerment of the water and so forth; likewise.
The *uyāṃśu* [japa] is a hundredfold [more effective], and the mental recitation (*mānasa*) is a thousandfold; success is attained without delay through the *mahāśaṅkha* rosary. (12.276)
Thus it is stated in the ritual manual for the worship with the *vali* mantra.
And that has been stated in the Matsyasūkta:
Because she bestows speech through her divine play, she is Nīlasarasvatī;
because she is high-pitched (tāra), she is remembered as Tārā, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Because she is the savior for the fierce, she is proclaimed as Ugratārā;
she is also known as Tārā and Ekajaṭā, and is considered the bestower of great liberation.
In the Kubjikātantra.
Whatever conduct is prescribed in a particular mantra, that is seen as the fatherly dharma therein;
by means of it, one becomes successful in attaining either heaven or even liberation. (12.279)
One should not feel fear in that regard, for the loss of accomplishment arises [from fear];
here, one should possess a pure mind, and accomplishment will grant liberation.
Having bowed to Tārā, the Great One of the Cīna tradition who delivers the three worlds, I shall now proclaim her sādhana; listen, for it is the cause of omniscience. (12.281)

Mahācīna is a particular region where Buddhists reside; they do not propitiate her through ordinary conduct, nor does one quickly attain the fruit by propitiating her through such conduct. And the procedure there is as follows:
Divine mental worship, including mental libations and so forth, is always auspicious; nowhere does an inauspicious time exist.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor during the twilights or the dead of night;
there is no restriction regarding clothing, posture, standing, mountains, houses, the body, touch, and so forth, or water. (12.283)
One should not perform purification there; rather, one should let the mind dwell in the non-conceptual state. Having bathed and finished eating, one should always worship the Goddess.
One who has not bathed is one devoid of bathing in water.
That has been stated in the Gautamī Tantras:
Likewise, one should first offer the earth-element oblation, and then those belonging to air, and the divine one as well.
The sevenfold bath is traditionally taught as the Varuṇa bath and the Mānasa bath;
[the latter begins with] the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and so forth.
Thus some [say]; that is to be considered.
At midnight, in a pure place, one should cause the offering to be given with the bali-mantra.
One must never harbor hatred toward women; rather, one should especially honor them.
Having offered a great conch shell at the place of victory, one should thereafter proclaim the victory.

Having offered with devotion betel-leaf, other edible substances such as meat, fish, curd, honey, milk, and sugarcane juice, as well as all remaining items, and having performed worship, one should perform the recitation of mantras (japa). (12.287)

In this [practice], there is no restriction regarding direction and so forth, nor any restriction regarding posture and so forth; there is no restriction of time for the recitation, nor for the worship and the offerings. (12.288)

In this practice of one's own great mantra for the sake of one's own accomplishment, there is no unrighteousness (adharma) produced by acting according to one's own will; rather, some form of merit (dharma) is generated. || 12-289 ||
Or else, one whose mind is purified may proceed here according to his own will,
considering himself to have achieved his purpose, satisfied within his own heart toward you.
In the Matsyasūkta: "Whether it be the censure of this practitioner or of this mantra, I shall take away the life-force of that person along with the hosts of great elements. (12.291)
In this regard, he states the location for the propitiation of the mantra:
"In a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads—staying there, the yogi should accomplish Tārā, the witness of the three worlds. (12.292)
Within five *krośas* of a single *liṅga*, there is no other *liṅga*; as it has been said:
Where one does not see another Liṅga within an interval of five krośas, that is declared to be an Eka-liṅga; there, the highest siddhi is attained.
But he who diligently worships Durgā on the Mahāṣṭamī shall destroy, at that very moment, the sin accumulated over three lifetimes. || 12-294 ||
In the Matsya Sūkta.
Wherever Tāriṇī resides in the form of a stone within a sacred seat (pīṭha), there one should practice with diligence; no limit in the number of repetitions is prescribed.
In the Kali age, the number is fourfold.
The meaning is that one should follow the prescribed number.
One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times at a place where Tāriṇī resides, remaining free from desire and having performed worship especially with rice grains. (12.296)
One should worship with fragrant white and red flowers and leaves;
and [offer] honey, milk-rice, milk, clarified butter, and sugar.
One should offer an oblation with lotus petals; indeed, the offering of a monitor lizard is especially distinguished.
In the *Nīlatantra*, it describes *āsava* (fermented liquor) as follows:
Wine should be given to the Brahmins, but molasses with the juice of the *īka* plant.
One should offer a crocodile made of sugar for the accomplishment of all desired aims;
one should pour coconut water or honey into a vessel of bell-metal or copper.
The best of those who know the mantras should offer oblations of plantain fruit and *sālamatsya*;
having attained all accomplishments in succession, he shall finally attain liberation.
In another tantra:
"In the practice of *vīrasādhana*, one should not use any [corpse] that is devoid of life or that has not been born from a womb;
having set aside the Brahmin and the cow-dung [corpse], one should accomplish the *vīrasādhana*. (12.301)
Having abandoned both a brahmin and a woman, one should accomplish the heroic practice (*vīrasādhana*);
for those who perform the rite of the base ones, this is recommended for the attainment of all perfections.
Whether it be an empty house or again a secluded dwelling;
as it has been said:
In a temple of the gods, in a place devoid of deities, or in a solitary, secluded dwelling. || 12-303 ||

Regarding what must be done upon obtaining the mantra, it is said: "Having received the mantra according to the rule and having likewise satisfied the guru," [one should practice] even in a desolate mountain or at a deserted crossroads. (12.304)
Seated upon a soft woolen rug, or on other woolen rugs,
or relying upon grass mats, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi.
And so it has been said:
"O daughter of that [Brahmā], previously Brahmā [taught] this mantra to us, and I have taught it to you;
O Nīlasarasvatī, it is the mantra that bestows poetic skill and removes obstacles. (12.306)
"But lack of attachment is the second [factor]; there is nothing else that causes an obstacle.
Regarding the statement "poetry is poetry," it means that lack of attachment is not an obstacle; thus says someone.
There is no such thing as a "non-existent entity"; this is the reading. Therefore, in the word *vāgbhava*— [Śrī Gaṇeśāya Namaḥ] ||
It destroys the darkness of ignorance and effects the deliverance from cyclic existence.
The great [destruction] of the three cities, performed by the self-restrained Damavat with his bow, is described in the Vārāhītantra. (200b)
She who was called Vālā in the Kṛta age is the primordial weapon.
In the Tretā age, Lalitā is praised; in the Dvāpara, Pañcakuṭā; and in the Kali age, Ṣaṭkuṭā is the teacher, hidden in all tantras. (12.309)
The beautiful Supreme Goddess is present at all times and in all ages;
she is endowed with the six peaks and the seed-syllable *māyā*, as established there in the *Vārāhitantra* within the *Jñānārṇava*.
O Goddess, Tripurā is threefold; first, hear about Bālā.
By the mere knowledge of which one becomes a direct teacher of the gods,
as follows:
Having uttered the solar sound (sūryasvara), which consists of the bindu, nāda, and kalā; || 12-311 ||
Ending with a vowel, situated on the earth, adorned with the fourth vowel, and pervaded by the bindu, nāda, and kalā; it possesses the visarga, and is the imperishable Bhṛgu. (12.312)
This three-syllable Vidyā is considered to be endowed with the sound of Śakra (the vowel *au*).
The sound of the Sun is the vowel *ai*; the letter *ka* at the end of the vowels is the letter *la* of the Earth;
the fourth vowel is *ī*; and the sound of Śakra is the vowel *au*.
By him [are uttered] the mantras: Ai Klī Sau;
the lower [syllable] is enriched with a garland of bindus, and Brahmā (A) joined with Indra (L) and the moon (I). || 12.313 ||
The second Manu, rich with the lineage of Bhṛgu, is declared to be Tāmasa;
their daughter, renowned as Vālā, was the subduer of the three worlds.
The lower [lip] is the bindu of the vowel *ai*, followed by the anusvāra.
The letter *a* is Brahmā, the letter *la* is Indra, and the moon is the bindu.

The mantra consists of *ī*, *yu*, *taḥ*, *bhṛgu* (the letter *b*), *sakāra* (the letter *s*), the first *sarga* (the letter *a*), enriched with *visarga* (*ḥ*), followed by *manu* (the letter *m*) and *aukāra* (*au*).
Thus, the mantra is: *ai klī sau*.
[She is] like the Ganges, bestowing auspicious feet with the shimmering, playful waves of her ripples.
She shall be the generator of great good fortune and the bestower of great happiness.
Possessing great beauty and auspiciousness, she is the destroyer of great death; the Goddess, who embodies all sacred fords, bestows gold, jewels, and other riches. (12.316)
She is the eternal bestower of great liberation and the giver of great enjoyments;
by means of the Vagbhava [syllable], she bestows the state of Lord of Speech through a thousandfold speech.
O virtuous one, she who deludes the three worlds with the seed-syllable of Kāmarāja, which has the luster of a glowing insect, and with the seed-syllable of Śakti.
The splendor of his abode is like that of one with a golden complexion;
thus it is stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtitantra.
The first with the beginning, the middle with the middle, and likewise the end with the end; that very [mantra] becomes one of swift fruition.
O Mistress of Tripura, the nine syllables [of the root mantra] joined with the *praṇava* constitute the ten-syllable [mantra].
The beginning is the syllable *aiṃ*; that very same one again: *aiḥ aiḥ*. The middle becomes the seed-syllable of desire, *klīṃ*; and again, that very same one twice more.
Thus.
Klīḥ klīḥ klīḥ; O God, the final syllable "sauḥ" again twice; sauḥ sauḥ sauḥ.
Thus it occurs. At that time, the seed-syllable *aiṃ* and the *maṇḍā* should be given.
Likewise, the mantra is: *aiṃ aiṃ klīṃ klīṃ sauḥ sauḥ sauḥ aiṃ*.
When the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) is placed at the beginning of this, it becomes ten syllables long.
For example: Oṃ aiṃ aiṃ klīṃ klīṃ sauḥ sauḥ sauḥ aiṃ. Thus is the mantra.
Regarding whatever is offered in his worship and so forth, it is like the worship itself.
Also in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"How is the auspicious Goddess Tripurā seated upon the lion-throne? (12.319).
Tell me, O Great Lord, how the lion-throne (siṃhāsana) is formed:
Śiva and Candra situated in Fire, followed by Vāgbhava and Nanda. (12.320)

Śiva is the letter *ha*, the Moon is *sa*, Fire is *ra*, Water is *va*, and Space is *i*; thus, it becomes *hasarai*. Likewise, O Goddess, the seed-syllable of Kāma is Śiva conjoined with the Moon (*hasara*).
Then follows the seed-syllable of Earth, preceded by Fire (*ra*), which is the third; listen to this, O Beloved. (12.321)
The seed-syllable of desire is the letter *ka*;
Śiva is the letter *ha*; the moon is the letter *sa*;
and the seed-syllable of earth is the letter *la*.

The fire (ra), the letter ṛ, the left eye (ī) joined with the bindu—by that [is formed] *hasakalarī*. Thus it becomes. O Supreme Goddess, O Great Goddess, having abandoned the *garbha* which consists of the *bindu*, one should join Śiva to the seed-syllable of Śakti.
The goddess Tripurā Bhairavī is the bestower of great prosperity.
One should remove the *visarga* situated in the third seed-syllable of the *kumāryas* and join it with the *bindu*; by that, *sau* is formed.
*Śiva* is the letter *ha*, and *vahni* is the letter *ra*; thus, *hasarau* results.
And so it is said:
The mantra is *hasarai hasakalarī hasarau*. Regarding this, he states a specific detail:
"Having made the seed-syllable of the Earth (*pṛthvī-bīja*) such by [adding] *hitva*, and having removed the *sarga* (the visarga), one should join the *bindu*";
this is the meaning.
Therefore, in another tantra:
"Bhairavī is the bestower of prosperity;

therein, having abandoned the third seed-syllable (the nasal *ṃ*) which is distinct [from the others], one should place Sundarī, who is bowed down, where the innate (*sahajika*) Viduḥ has been cast out."
Some say that in the third seed-syllable there is no *ha* because it has been released (*mukta*). [The mantra is:
Viyat (the letter *a*), Bhṛgu (the letter *b*), Hutāśa (the letter *ra*), situated in the *bhaitika* (the letter *i*), topped with a bindu;
then Viyat (the letter *a*) again, followed by Kendra (the letter *ka*), Agni (the letter *ra*), situated in Vāmākṣi (the letter *ī*), and possessing a bindu. (12.323)
The syllable *Ā* (Sky) situated in *Bhṛgu* (the letter *U*) and *Vahni* (the letter *R*), followed by the *Manu* (the letter *Ka*) possessing the crescent moon (*Indu-khaṇḍa*);
this is the first seed-syllable, *Vāgbhava*, and the second is *Kāmarāja*. (12.324)
The third is called the Seed of Power (śaktivīja); this Vidyā, consisting of five peaks (pañcakūṭātmikā), is proclaimed by means of three seed-syllables as Tripurabhairavī. (12.325)
"Consisting of five peaks" means being composed of the syllables of the mantra of five peaks.

Having received initiation from a guru who possesses distinguished characteristics and bestows true prosperity, one should recite the obtained mantra with great self-restraint until one million repetitions are reached, according to the reality of the principle.

When the fire has been properly kindled with palāśa flowers whose stalks are sweet-smelling, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations toward the thousand-rayed sun even with the flowers of the aśvāri;
"aśvārisūna" refers to karavīra flowers.

O Goddess of the gods, having purified one's body through either ten or twelve principles (*tattva*s), one should then perform the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*). O Great Mistress, the seer (*ṛṣi*) of this [mantra] is the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti. (12.326)
One should place [the syllable] *nyase* on the head because it is worthy of worship; the *pakti* metre is on the mouth, O beloved;
the deity is the Supreme Goddess Tripurā Bālā in the heart. (12.327)
The seed-syllable is said to be *vāgbhava*; one should cause that power (*śakti*) to delude.
Having performed the placement from the navel to the feet, and another from the throat to the navel. (12.328)
One should place the three syllables in sequence from the crown of the head down to the throat; thus it is said.
Or, O best of mantra-knowers, its accumulation is at the navel; it originates from the syllable Vāgbhava.

"One should place the seed-syllable of Kāma from the heart down to the navel," and so forth; for in the *Nibandhas*, there is a technical definition using the term "Vāgbhava" and the others. However, in the *Unmūla* [Tantra], even for Bhairavī and the rest, one should likewise invoke them in this manner.

Thus, regarding the phrase "with three seed-syllables," it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra*: "That which is supreme is indeed common for a year. Where one should place the seed-syllable that is supreme—the fivefold group beginning with Vāgbhava and so on—without distinction:
one on the left palm and likewise one on the right palm. (12.330)
One should place the Vidyā with the three seed-syllables within the cavity formed by both hands; thus it is said.
One should place the first [mudrā] on the two hands, and the second on both [feet].
Having placed the three seed-syllables again in sequence upon the crown-center and the heart—
this is to be extracted from the *Nibandha* itself by us alone,
on the strength of the consistency of the text.
Likewise, in the *Pramāṇakaumudī*:
"Then, O Śivā, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the knowledge [mantra] by means of the three seed-syllables in their proper sequence. (12.332)
First, one should place [the mudrās] on the hands—at the wrists, the palms, and the backs;
having placed them on the right and left, as well as at the armpits, the elbows, and the palms.
Furthermore, O Goddess, one should likewise place [the mantras] on the right and left feet;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should place them at the end of the Nāda, in the heart, and in the liṅga.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place these [mantras] among the limbs according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhāra);
know, O Supreme Goddess, that the Vidyā is according to the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭi). || 12.335 ||
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the three seed-syllables upon the nature of the nine wombs:
again on the two ears, the chin, the two cheeks, and once more on the mouth.
One should place [the mantras] on the two eyes, the nose, the pair of arms, and the heart-lotus;
then on the two shoulders, the two knees, and the crown of the head.
One should place the three seed-syllables in sequence upon your feet, the secret place, the two sides, the two breasts, the throat, and that which is called the womb.
Regarding the phrase "vāhuyugā," the reading in the *Nivedha* section is "aṃsayor jaṭhare punar" (on the two shoulders and again on the belly).
In the case of the ear and other [limbs], the placement (*nyāsa*) follows the sequence from left to right,
as was previously shown in the case of the hand-placement (*hasta-nyāsa*).

One should place the three seed-syllables on the surface of the *vasta* (the sacrificial ground): the first on the left, the second on the right, and the third on both; this is stated in the *Prapañcasāra-tantra* according to the maxim that "what is determined in one instance [applies] everywhere."

Furthermore, regarding this placement (nyāsa), it is stated in the *Tripurāsārābhidhāna*: "The wise one should place [the syllables] 'kṣa' and 'ṇa' on the left [eye], then on the forehead, and then on the pair of ears.
This is because the term *savya* is used even for the right side when performing the placement.
The ancients maintain that the sequence here begins with Dakṣa and others. Now, the extraction of the yantra:
having performed the internal worship, one should then perform the external worship.
There, sitting facing the east, one should perform the extraction of the yantra.
The preceptor should draw straight lines from Īśāna to Agni;
then, having drawn two lines from the tips of those [lines] at Īśāna and Agni.
Having unified [these] within the western [direction], there is the line of power (śaktirekhā) in the supreme Śiva;
this pair of powers, O Śivā, has the form of a triangle and is the seat of the phukapa. || 12-341 ||
But if the foremost of the previously possible [lines] is absent, O Supreme Goddess, one should draw a line like a jeweled staff from the northwest corner to the southwest corner. (12.342)
Following the very sequence of breaking the joints, one is then able to draw the two lines from the two sheaths; having drawn them, place those that go forward from the rising point.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, O Auspicious One, one should draw this square fire-maṇḍala, which is fierce in its eastern direction and enriched with the beauty of nine triangles. (12.344)
Having drawn the yantra, which is enriched with the beauty of four gates and always brings joy to all, one should worship it on a surface made of gold, silver, or whatever else is available.
On the ground, upon sandalwood pedestals, with saffron, agallochum,
and sandalwood paste, or even with vermilion powder, musk, saffron, and the like.
O Goddess of Gods, having drawn the yantra— either fashioned with lines of gold and jewels or else made of clay— one should prepare the articles for worship.
Now I shall explain the procedure for worship, which is concealed in all tantras:
having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, one should meditate upon the Guru on the crown of one's head. (12.348)

At dawn, one should first recite his name and then meditate upon the Guru as Śukra, seated upon a lotus, possessing two eyes and two arms, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and peaceful in appearance. (12.349)

Having propitiated the Root-Vidyā with mental offerings and having recited it as much as possible, one should perform the twilight rites (saṃdhyā-karma) as before, [placing] the *krāmit* syllable within the *kuśa*-mudrā;
[one should then contemplate] the holy waters created from within the belly of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
"By that truth, O God, grant me a ford, O Maker of Day! (12.350)

Having invoked the sacred bathing sites (tīrtha) along with their respective maṇḍalas by reciting "Oṃ Gaṅge ca Yamune ca," and so forth, one should immerse oneself three times, rise, and while reciting the root mantra, place the water upon the crown of the head three times with the *kumbha-mudrā*, saying, "I consecrate Śrī Tripurabhairavī; obeisance. Then one should sip water for purification (*ācamana*).
Having uttered the first peak-syllable: *ātmatattvāya svāhā*. Having uttered the second peak-syllable: *vidyātattvāya svāhā*.
Having uttered the third peak-syllable: *śivatattvāya svāhā*.

Having thus sipped water, touched the respective parts of the body, immersed oneself, emerged, and performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), one should perform the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*), reciting the root mantra:
"I offer libation to Śrī Tripurabhairavī, svāhā."
Having thus satisfied [the deity] three times, rising from the water, putting on two garments, sitting down, and sipping water (ācamana), while reciting the root-mantra (mūlavidyā),
one should offer water upon the head three times with the tip of a *kuśa* blade and then recite the *gāyatrī*.
Having completed the recitation (*japa*), one should fill a copper vessel with red sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, water, and flowers;
holding it with both hands and touching the forehead while reciting "Hrīḥ Hrīḥ Śaḥ, obeisance and *svāhā* to Kula-Mārtāṇḍa-Bhairava together with Prakāśa-Śakti," one should pay homage to the Sun.
Having meditated upon the circle of Bhairavī within that water and taking it with both hands while touching the forehead, [one recites]:
*Ai/ Tripurāyai vidmahe, bhairavyai dhīmahi, tanno devī pracodayāt* (3).
Thus reciting.
As before, one should offer the *argha* to the Goddess.
He states the extraction of the mantra:
"Tripurā," and likewise, one should extract the word "ṅentaṃ vidmahe."
Then it was said by the Bhairavīs, and thereafter one should say "dhīmahi."
Then, having uttered the word "Devī," one should pronounce "pracodayāt.
This is known as the Gāyatrī-purī; one should extract it beginning with "vāk" and so forth.

Then, remaining silent and turning away from conversation due to his lack of yoga, he should go to the northern side. Having placed the ordinary *arghya* offering in a copper vessel and having sprinkled the door with the *arghya* water;
To Gaṇeśa, salutation on the right of the door;
to Kṣetrapāla, salutation on the left;
to Gaṅgā, salutation at the pair of their sides.
"Salutation to Yamunā; salutation to Śrī, the door-keeper;
salutation to the Goddess below. Then, having recited this, one should enter the house and sprinkle the interior with the *arghya* water.
Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā.
Oṃ, obeisance to Vāstupuruṣa. Having thus worshipped and drawn a triangle on the ground, one should purify the earth with "Hrīḥ" and [place] the woolen rug.
Having spread the seat and sprinkled it with arghya water, one should meditate and recite:

"The seer is Merupṛṣṭha," and so forth; then, [reciting] "O Earth, you... and "Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Lotus-Seated Support-Power" (Mādhāraśakti-kamalāsanāya namaḥ), one should worship the seat and sit facing either east or north.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *parā* and then the *ādhāra-pūraka*,
one should write the word *śakti* and then write the *kamalāsana*. O Dear One, having spoken the word *oṃ taṃ namaḥ*, this is the mantra of the seat (*āsana*).

Taking unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), reciting "apasarpa tu" (depart), and scattering the grains, one should strike the ground with the left foot while reciting "astrāya phaṭ. Then, clapping three times, one should expel the obstacles moving through the sky with the mantra ending in *ṇa* (*praṇava-ṇa*), those in the intermediate space with the *layā* [mantra], and those in the ten directions with the nine-faced [mantra]. Having thus cast out the threefold obstacles, one should offer [the grains] to the Gurus on the left.
Salutation! To Gaṇeśa, salutation on the right;
to Tripurabhairavī, salutation in the center.
Thus, three *tāla* gestures are performed upward as previously described.
Having purified both hands with perfume and flowers, one joins the palms in *añjali*.
For this *Bhairavī* mantra, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the *ṛṣi*, *paṅkti* is the meter (*chandas*), and Tripurabhairavī is the deity (*devatā*).

The first seed-syllable is the seed; the letter *ra* is the power (*śakti*); the letter *repha* is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of all desired goals through the Vidyā. One should offer salutation to the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the head, and to the Pakti metre on the mouth.
"To Tripurabhairavī in the heart, salutation. With palms joined, "This is my application (*viniyoga*) for the sake of attaining the desired goal, beginning with knowledge.
Then, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
The purification of the elements that constitute the form of the body,
through union with non-dual Brahman— this is considered *bhūtaśuddhi* (purification of the elements).
Having placed both hands palm-upward upon your own limbs, [visualize] by means of the mantra "So 'ham" that which resides in the heart, shaped like the flame of a lamp.

Having meditated upon the individual soul (jīvātman), together with Kuṇḍalinī, as residing in the Mūlādhāra and then dissolved into the Supreme Self within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus situated in the head; and having likewise dissolved earth into water, fire into water, air into fire, and space into air, [one should then dissolve] space into primordial nature (prakṛti).

Furthermore, having dissolved that Māyā-śakti, who is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, along with the entire aggregate of bodies— the phenomenal world— into the Supreme Self, [one should contemplate] the beginningless accumulation of existence in the form of a person, as previously described, beginning with "headed by the murder of a Brahmin" and so forth.

Then, either in the mouth or in the mind, one should fill the body with air through the left nostril sixteen times using the wind-seed syllable *yaṃ*, which is smoke-colored; then, performing retention (*kumbhaka*) sixty-four times with the syllable *vyaṃ*, one should thoroughly purify the body; and then [perform it] thirty-two times with the syllable *yaṃ*.
One should exhale the air through the right nostril.

Then, having increased the fire-like air, one should fill the body through the right nostril while reciting the fire seed-syllable *Raṃ* sixteen times; then, performing the retention (*kuṃbhaka*), one should recite it sixty-four times.
204b) Having reflected that "it has been brought under control," one should recite the syllable *ra* thirty-two times and exhale the breath through the left nostril along with the ashes.
Then, one should [place] the lunar seed-syllable *ṭha*, which is of the nature of *prakṛti*, into the forehead, which is of the nature of *puruṣa*, by means of the left nostril.
Chanting "Candra" sixteen times, one should not [proceed] further; then, as previously stated,
by means of the syllables from *ca* to *kṣa* originating from the moon on the forehead, having caused a rain of these syllables to fall, one worships with that Goddess.
Making his entire body fit by reciting "laṃ" thirty-two times, and contemplating his whole body as having become firm,
he should exhale the breath through the right nostril.
"Once again, may I generate a body"—beginning with this, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is here proclaimed.
Thus, according to the previously mentioned sequence, holding the nostrils and retaining the breath: *ahaṃ saḥ*, *so 'ham avatara 2 prajvala 2 haṃsaṃ sohaṃ svāhā*.
Then, as for the principles beginning with earth, it is as follows:
"Āṃ so'haṃ mama prāṇāḥ" (Āṃ, I am he; my vital breaths), and as follows: "So'haṃ mama prāṇā iha prāṇāḥ" (I am he; my vital breaths are here).
"O, may I [be] my life-force;
thus may all my sense-faculties, speech, and mind abide in happiness—svāhā. Thus one should place the seed-syllable.
The mantra for the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) is as follows:
Having first uttered the circular syllable (*mukhavṛtta*), one should then utter the *haṃsa* reversed; O Īśānī, this vidyā shall consist of these syllables. (12.353)
The mantra for the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) accomplishes all rites;
its mode of application is through the mouth.
The ancients say it is "with the bindu"; therefore, the reverse of "Āṃ" is "So'haṃ.
Thus, the mantra is "Ā So'haṃ.
By this instrument of the Śakras, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) occurs merely by the recitation of this.
Thus, one should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform it either with the root mantra or with the dissolution [mantra],
as follows:
The root mantra [should be recited] sixteen times or sixty-four times according to the previously mentioned sequence.
Now follows the internal placement of the Mātṛkās (antarmātṛkānyāsa): One should place the sixteen vowels upon the sixteen-petaled lotus at the throat. (12.354)
One should place the twelve letters beginning with *ka* upon the twelve-petalled heart-lotus;
on the ten-petalled lotus at the navel, one should place the ten letters beginning with *u*.
One should place six [syllables] beginning with *va* in the six petals situated in the center of the *liṅga*;
and one should place four syllables beginning with *u* on the four petals of the *ādhāra*.
O Śivā, one should place the two *bhakṣas* upon the two petals of the earth-lotus in the center of the *bhū*;
having thus performed the internal *mātṛkā*-nyāsa, one should perform the *sarvāṅga-nyāsa*.
Now follows the Mātṛkānyāsa:
O Pārvatī, one should duly place [the letters] on the head, the face-circle, the eyes, the throat, the nose, the cheeks, the lips, the teeth, and the head and mouth. (12.358)
O Śivā, one should place [the syllables] in sequence upon the inner joints of the pair of hands and feet, as well as on the two sides, the back, the navel, and the abdomen.
One should indeed place the *yā* and other [syllables] along with the *dhā*; those are *prāṇa*, *jīva*, and *brahman*.
[One should place them] in the heart, at the base of the arms, and likewise on the back of the neck, O Śivā.
O Goddess, one should likewise install the pervasive wheel (vyāpakacakra) in the armpits, at the edge of the heart, on the pair of hands and feet, and on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet.
"Spreading" means starting from the heart and pervading the head;
"at the edge of the heart" refers to the specific attributes such as the *yāṇī* (the tongue).
This is for the sake of attaining abundance; thus, starting from the heart, it extends to the pair of hands and feet.
Thus, this is precisely that meaning; as follows:
Aṃ, homage to the forehead; Iṃ to the right eye; Ī to the left eye; U to the right ear; Ū to the left; Ṛ to the right nostril; Ṝ to the left nostril; Ḷ to the right cheek;
Ḹ to the left cheek; Ai to the upper lip; Ai to the lower lip; O to the upper teeth; Au to the lower teeth.

Aṃ on the crown of the head; A on the face; Kaṃ on the base of the right arm; Kha at the elbow; Ga at the wrist; Gha at the base of the fingers; Ṅa at the tips of the fingers; Ca at the base of the left arm; Cha at the elbow; Ja at the wrist; Jha at the base of the fingers; Ña at the tips of the fingers.

Ṭa at the base of the right thigh; 205b) Ṭhaṃ at the knee; Ḍaṃ at the ankle; Ḍha at the base of the toes; Ṇa at the tips of the toes; Ta at the base of the left thigh; Tha at the knee; Da at the ankle; Dha at the base of the toes; Na at the tips of the toes.
*Pa*: on the right side; *pha*: *namo* on the left side; *va*: on the back; *bha*: on the belly; *ya*:

in the heart, which consists of the skin; *ra*: at the root of the right arm, which consists of the blood; *la*: at the nape of the neck, which consists of the flesh; *va*: at the root of the left arm, which consists of the fat.
ŚA: to the Ātman of bone, from the heart and so forth, on the right hand; ṢA: [to the Ātman of] marrow and so forth, on the left hand; SA:
to the Ātman of semen, from the heart and so forth, on the right foot; HA: NAMAH to the Ātman of breath, from the heart and so forth, on the left foot.

*La*: to the individual self (*jīvātman*), from the heart to the stomach. *Kṣa*: obeisance to the supreme self (*paramātman*), from the heart to the mouth. Now follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Śrīkaṇṭha and others.
Śrī Vāsudeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *paṅkti* meter (*chandas*), and Īśāna is the deity (*devatā*); this is the application (*viniyoga*) for the rite of ritual placement.

One should especially place the three born of the heart (*hrdaya*) in their respective locations: *aiṃ* to Rati at the *mūlādhāra*; *klīṃ* to Prīti in the heart; and *sauḥ* to Manobhavā between the eyebrows. Amṛteśī, Yogeśī, Viśvayoni, and Kramā are the first [of these].
Having performed the placement with the reverse seed-syllables (*vilomabīja*), one should carry out the placement of the forms (*mūrttinyāsa*).
"With the reverse seed-syllables" means with the seed-syllables beginning with *sauḥ* and ending with *vāsā*.
At the *mūlādhāra*: *sauḥ*, *amṛteśyai namaḥ*. At the heart: [same].
*Klī*, salutation to Yogeśī; at the center of the eyebrows.
*Ai*, salutation to Viśvayonī.
Then one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the forms (*mūrti*).

At the head: *Saharaḥ*, obeisance to Īśāna together with Manobhava; obeisance. At the heart: *Saharuḥ*, *huṃ-huṃ* to Aghora together with Kumāra and Kandarpa. At the throat: *Sahariṃ*, obeisance to Vāmadeva together with Manobhava.
One should place the *saharu* mantra on the two feet for Sadyojāta, accompanied by Kāmadeva;
then, one should assign it as before to the faces facing upward, east, south, north, and west, conjoined with the syllables of Bhṛgu (S), Vyoman (H), and Agni (R). 206a)
The seed-syllables of these are said to begin with the five short vowels, starting with *a*.
Bhṛgu is the letter *sa*, Vyoman is the letter *ha*, Agni is *ṛpha*, and Satya is the letter *o*; beginning with that is *caṃkam*.
The nature of the vowels *u*, *e*, *ū*, *ī*, and *aṃ* is their respective seed-syllables (*vīja*): *saharau*, *sahare*, *saharūṃ*, *sahariṃ*, *saharam*.

To the upward-facing [face], *maharaṃ*—salutation to Īśāna together with Manobhava; to the eastern-facing [face], *saharaṃ*—as before, salutation to Tatpuruṣa, the dolphin-bannered one (*makaradhvaja*).
To the southern-facing [face], *saharuṃ*; to the northern-facing [face], *sahariṃ*; to the western-facing [face], *saharam*.
Thus ends the placement (*nyāsa*) of the four-faced one upon the four cardinal directions.
Now follows the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*).
It is taught that the ritual of the limbs (*aṅgakriyā*) is performed with the seed-syllable *Nā* (Na) joined with its long vowel.
*Hsro*: *Namaḥ* to both thumbs, beginning from there;

*hsrau*, *hsrū*, *hsrai*, *hsraṃ*(ḥ): *namaḥ* to both palms and backs of the hands. Thus far is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). In this manner is the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
"Hsro! Hṛdayāya namaḥ," and so forth, up to "Astrāya phaṭ.
Having performed the three *tālas* as before, one should bind the ten directions.
This is the fivefold placement (*pañcāṅganyāsa*).
One should place the five arrows sequentially upon the fingers of the hand, [reciting] "Oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth, up to "Astrāya phaṭ.
Having performed the three *tāla* gestures as before, one should bind the ten directions.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the five arrows.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the five arrows in due order upon the fingers of the hands, proceeding sequentially from the thumb to the little finger. (12.363)
"Drā, Drī, Klī, Plū"—by pronouncing these, O Moon-faced One, one becomes possessed of the natural flow [of power].
O Goddess Pārvatī, hear these names of the five arrows:
Kṣobhana (the Agitator), Drāvaṇa (the Melter), and likewise the one known as Karṣaṇa (the Attractor). || 12-364 ||
O fair-faced one, the methods for subjugation and intoxication have been explained in due order;
know that Kāma is present therein—now hear their seed-syllables (bījas).
O Parameśvarī, [the seed-syllable] Vāgbhava consists of the supreme [letter], the middle arrow, and then the fourth arrow;
thereafter, O Dear One, is the feminine seed-syllable (strīvīja) in that sequence. (12.366)
O Goddess, O beloved, hear these names of the five Kāmas: he who is known as Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja. || 12-367 ||
O Maheśānī, the fifth is proclaimed as Mīnaketu;
the four following *sa*—namely *drāḥ*, *drīḥ*, *klīḥ*, and *plūḥ*—along with *saḥ*, constitute the five arrows.

One should place [the mantras] on the thumb and the other fingers in sequence: *hrīḥ*, *klīḥ*, *aiḥ*, *vlūḥ*, *strīḥ*—these are the five desires (*pañcakāma*)—and *drāḥ*, *kṣobhanāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
One should place [the mantras] on the thumb and the other fingers in sequence: *krīḥ*, *kāmāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
Immediately thereafter, the practitioner should likewise assign the five arrows to the head and other parts from the Trailokyamohana [mantra]. (12.368)

The syllable *drāṃ* for driving away, *drīṃ* on the head for crushing, *klīṃ* at the feet for agitation, and *vlūṃ* preceded by the seed-syllable for subjugation at the mouth and the secret place. (12.369)

The syllable for attraction is *hrīṃ*; again, the end of creation (*kṣaṃ*) conjoined with Bhṛgu (*u*) is the goddess Saṃhohinī; this is declared to be the placement of the arrows (*vāṇanyāsa*) in the sequence of withdrawal (*yamikrama*).
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is as follows: *drāṃ* to Drāviṇī on the head; *drīṃ* to Kṣobhiṇī on the feet; [and *klīṃ*] on the face.
VLU / To Vaśīkariṇī, at the secret place (guhya).
VLU / Salutation to Ākarṣaṇī, at the heart (hṛd). SAḤ, [the letter] Sa with the Bindu and Trikoṇa (triangle), joined with Bhṛgu (the letter Bha) at the end of creation (Sarga). Thus.
The creation [arising] from the syllable *bhṛgu* (ma) is the emission (*visarga*); thus it becomes "ma.
Next is the placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with Śubhagā and so forth.
Having performed the placement starting with "to the heart, namaḥ" using [the seed-syllables] beginning with *vālabrumaya*, one should meditate.
Oṃ! [I salute the deity] who is the color of a bandhūka flower and gold, holding a beautiful rosary, a noose, and a goad, with hands, face, and belly bestowing boons;
who wears ornaments of crescent moons and possesses three eyes.
May I constantly take refuge in the body that possesses half of Viṣṇu’s matted locks.
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkās* in their respective locations.
Now: "Obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha and Pūrṇodarī" on the forehead;
"Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta and Virajā" on the face.
Iṃ to the subtle one for the sake of discernment; ī to Trimūrti Lolākṣī;
oṃ to Amareśvara Vatulākṣī; ū to Arghyeśa Dīrghaghoṇā.
Ṛ: To Bhārabhūta, to Dīrghamukhī; Ṝ: To Atithīśa, to Yogamukhī; Ḷ: To Sthāṇuka, to Dīrghajihvā.
Ḷ / To Harā, with Kuṇḍodaryā.
Ai / To Ṛṃ-Ṭheṃśa, with Ūrdhvakeśī.
Ai / To Bhautika, with Vikṛtamukhī.
Oṃ / To Sadyojāta and Jvālāmukhī; Auṃ / To Anugraha and Ulkāmukha; A / To Akrūra and Śrīmukhī.
Homage to Mahāsenā Vidyā.
Ka: Homage to Krodheśa Mahākālī. Kha: Homage to Caṇḍīśa Sarasvatī.
ga/ Homage to Gaurī, the embodiment of the five ends (Pañcāntaka).
gha/ [Homage] to Śivottama, the Vidyā of the three worlds. ṅa/ [Homage] to Ekāmātra, the power of mantra (Mantraśakti).
And: *ca* to Kūrma and Ātmaśakti; *cha* to Ekanetra and Bhūtamātṛ; *ja* to Caturānana and Laṃbodarī.
Jha: to Ajeśa and Drāviṇī; Ña: to Sarveśa and Nāgarī;
Ṭa: to Someśa and Khecarī.
Ṭha: to Galina Mañjarī; Ḍa: to Dāruka Rūpiṇī;
Ḍha: to Ardhanārīśvara Vīriṇī.
Ṇa: to Umākāntā and Kākodaryā;
Ta: to Āṣāḍhinī and Pūtanā; Tha: to Daṇḍitā and Bhadrakālī.
Da: to Adreśa, to Yoginī; Dha: to Dharmīśa, to Vikhinī; Na: to Meṣa, to Garjinī.
Pa, to Lohitā Kālarātri; Pha, to Śikheśa Kubjinī; Va, to Chagalatuṇḍa Kapardinī.
Bha: to Durudeśa and Kapālinī; Ma: to Mahākāleśa and Jayā;
Ya: to Tvagātman and Vāliśa, and to Sumukhīśvarī.
And: to Bhujaṅgeśa, whose self is Amṛga, [and] to Revatī;
la/ to Pinākīśa, whose self is Māṃsa, [and] to Mādhavī;
va/ to Khaḍgīśa, whose self is Medas, [and] to Vāruṇī.
Śa: To the Ātman Śa, to Keśa, with the Vāyavyas;
Ṣaṃ: To the Ātman Ma, to Śveteśa, with the Rakṣovidāriṇīs;
Sa: To the Ātman Śu, to Bhṛgvīśa, with the Sahajās.
Ha! Salutation to Nakulīśa, the self of vital breath (prāṇa), and to Mahālakṣmī.
La! Salutation to Śiveśa, the self of power (śakti), and to Vyāpinī.
Kṣa! Salutation to Saṃvarteśa, the supreme self (paramātman), and to Mahāmāyā.

Now, the ritual placement of the mantras (mantra-nyāsa): Having placed [the first mantra] from the navel down to the feet, and the other [mantra] from the throat up to the navel, one should place the three-syllabled [mantra] in sequence from the head down to the throat.
Thus is the placement (nyāsa) of the Vālā-mantra;
it is the same even for the Bhairavī-mantra.
Having placed [the mantra] from the navel down to the feet, the best of mantra-knowers should apply the Vāgbhava-mantra.
One should install the Kāmarāja mantra from the heart down to the navel.
One should install the seed-syllable of Śakti from the crown of the head down to the heart; for example: *hsrai namaḥ* from the navel up to the feet, and *hsrai namaḥ* from the heart up to the navel.
*Hasakalaṃrī*—salutation from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) down to the heart.
*Hsrauḥ*—salutation. Now, the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*).
One [mudrā] on the palm of the left hand, and likewise one on the palm of the right hand.
O Śivā, in the case of the Bhairavī mantra, one should place the seed-syllable of the woman (strīvīja) as the *sapuṭī* between both [syllables].
One should place the first [syllable] on the two hands and the second on the two [feet], and the third on both. (12.375)
In the order of the right:
*hsrai* / *namo* to the right hand;
*hasakalarīṃ* to the left hand.
Hsrau! Homage to the palms and backs of the hands.
Having placed [the seed-syllables] in sequence upon the root-support (mūlādhāra), the heart, and the head—hsrai! Homage to the head; hasarī! Homage to the heart; hsrau! Homage to the root-support.
Hsrau! Homage! Now, the placement of the nine syllables:
Hsrai on the right ear; Hasakalarīṃ namaḥ on the left ear.
Civuka: *hsrau* / *namaḥ*. On the two cheeks, on the face, on the two eyes, on the nose, on the two ears, on the belly, on the two elbows, and on the flanks.
In the knees, the genitals, the feet, the secret parts, the sides, the heart, the breasts, and the throat—thus for all [the limbs].
In the root, Rati; in the heart, Prīti; and in the middle of the eyebrows, Manobhavā.
The needle for piercing hair, the face, and the neck; the needle for the neck and the heart. (12.376)
The goddesses beginning with Pañcatārā and Śubhagā, who are auspicious and powerful, should be installed by the practitioner according to the ritual procedure upon the navel and the foundation.
Then Bhagasarpiṇī, followed by Parābhagamālinī; then Anaṅgā, Raṅgakusumā, and Anaṅgamekhalā. (12.378)

All these women, whose limbs were stirred by passion, languid with the intoxication of amorous agitation, and whose speech was full of desire, were again prepared as couches for the five gods. (12.379)
Then the best of practitioners should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) known as *bhūṣaṣā*. As for the placement:
*ai* / *klī* / *vlū* / *strī* / *saḥ* to Śubhagā on the forehead; [and] at the center of the brows.
Ai Klī Vlu Strī Saḥ; salutation to Bhagā on the face.
To Bhagasarpiṇī in the middle of the throat (five times). To Bhagamālinī on the throat (five times). To Anaṅgā in the heart.
To Anaṅgakusumā at the navel. To Anaṅgamekhalā at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
On the *liṅga*: "Salutation to Anaṅgamadanā. Thus is the *bhūṣaṇanyāsa*. One should perform the placement [of mantras] on the head, forehead, eyebrows, ears, pair of eyes, and nose. (12.380)
One should place the vowels upon the cheeks, the lips, the two rows of teeth, and the mouth;
then upon the chin, the throat, the neck, the two sides, and the pair of breasts. (12.381)

[One should worship] on the base of the thighs, the two elbows, the two hands, the regions of the backs, the navel, the private parts, and again on the two shanks, the two knees, and the two calves. || 12-382 ||
With a concentrated mind, one should install the letters beginning with *ka* in these locations: on the buttocks, the soles of the feet, the anus, and likewise on the elephant-like big toes. (12.383)
In Kāñcī and Graiveyaka, then in Kaṭaka, Hṛd, and Guhyaka; Karṇa, Kuṇḍala, Mūla, Vadana, Anuśakha, and Sārṣaha. (12.384)
Having thus laid out these eight [lines], O Goddess, the best of instructors should place there the term "kāñcī" and so forth, which serves as an indicator of those locations. (12.385)
Regarding the placement of two syllables each on the eyebrows, ears, and so forth,
the placement is as follows:
on the head, *aṃ* *namaḥ*.
ĀM on the forehead; IṂ and ĪM on the pair of eyebrows; UṂ and ŪM on the pair of ears; ṚṂ and ṜM on the pair of eyes;
ŚṚ on the nose; Ḷ on the two cheeks; AI and AU on the two lips.
*Auṃ* on the two rows of teeth; *Aṃ* on the mouth; *Kaṃ* on the chin;
*Khaṃ* on the throat; *Gaṃ* on the neck; *Ghaṃ* and *Ṅaṃ* on the two sides; *Caṃ* and *Chaṃ* on the two breasts;
*Jaṃ* and *Jhaṃ* with *Namaḥ* at the root of the arms; *Ñaṃ* and *Ṭhaṃ* on the two forearms.

*Ṭha* and *ḍa* on the two hands; *ta* on the two backs; *tam* on the navel; *tha* on the private parts; *da* and *dha* on the two thighs; *na* and *ya* on the two knees; *pha* and *va* on the two shanks; *bha* and *ma* on the roots of the thighs after having touched them; *pa* and *ra* on the soles of those [feet]; and *la* and *va* on the two big toes of the feet.

*Śa* on the hips; *ṣa* on the neck; *sa* on the bracelets (in the place of the armlets); *ha* on the heart—*namaḥ*; *la* on the private parts; *kṣa* on the ears and the crown—*namaḥ*. In the *Jñānārṇava*: "Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon his body, he, with a concentrated mind,"
The mass of supreme bliss, through bliss, should contemplate the Supreme.
Then, having meditated upon the goddess in the sky within the center of the heart-lotus:
"Oṃ! She whose splendor is like a thousand rising suns, who wears a red silk garment and a garland upon her head..."

I bow to the Goddess who is red in hue, whose breasts are smeared with sandalwood paste, who holds a rosary, a book, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā in her hands; she possesses the splendor of a three-eyed, radiant lotus-face, wears a crown of jewels and the cool-rayed moon, and is graced with a gentle smile.

Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, one should form the *yonimudrā* and pay homage to the lotus-face, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the *brahmarandhra*. It is as follows:
"The one known as the Yoni is celebrated in the heart; she is the protectress of the three worlds."
O Great Goddess, when the Supreme Sovereign named Trailokyadrāvaṇā is situated in the mouth,
she becomes the Attractor of the Three Worlds when stationed between the eyebrows.
O Great Goddess, she who resides in the forehead is the subduer of the three worlds;
residing in the aperture of Brahmā, she alone is the supreme one who brings delight to all.
"O Goddess who consists of the five mudrās, one should display the *yonimudrā*.
Having thus paid homage, one should place the *argha* vessel. As follows:
(209a) on one's left, having drawn a triangle containing the syllable *ī*, upon that [draw] a hexagon and a square."
Having placed [the vessel] upon that and set it on a three-legged stand, one should worship the three-legged stand with the mantra:
*oṃ vahnimaṇḍalāya dhūmrārcirādi-daśakalātmane namaḥ*.
Then, having washed the conch with *phaṭ* and placed it upon that [stand], [one worships] with *aṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya*.

Having worshipped the conch with the mantra "Obeisance to the one whose self consists of the twelve digits beginning with Tapinī," and having filled it with pure water, he worships that circle of nectar with the mantra "Obeisance to the one whose self consists of the sixteen digits beginning with Amṛta. Then, having performed the worship of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon that water, [he offers] *hasakṣamalavarayū* to Ānandabhairava.
*vauṣaṭ namaḥ*.
Likewise, *vauṣaṭ namaḥ* to Ānandabhairavī. Having thus worshipped the water, while touching the water, one should recite the root mantra eight times and [offer] perfume and unbroken rice grains.
Having protected it with the Astra-mantra, veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra, rendered it nectarine by means of the Dhenu-mudrā,
and displayed the Yoni-mudrā, one should draw a triangle within that water and worship the five jewels in the cardinal directions as well.
And after the *ga*, *ma*, *ya*, and *la*, the *indra-sthā* [position] follows in sequence, O Śivā. (12.390)
Joined with the left ear [the letter *v*] and adorned with the resonance (*nāda*) and the point (*bindu*),
O beautiful one, these are the five jewels in the midst of the five seed-syllables.
Glū / Homage to Gagaratna. Slū / Homage to Martyaratna. Plū / Homage to Svargaratna.
*vlū*: salutation to the Jewel of the Netherworld (*pātālaratna*). *mlū*: salutation to the Jewel of the Nagas (*nāgaratna*).
"And *gamu*" means the letters *ta*, *ma*, *ya*, *va*, and *la*.
The letter *la* is Indra; the left ear is the letter *ū*.
Having thus worshipped these five jewels, one should invoke the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) from the solar orb with the mantra beginning "O Gaṅgā and Yamunā," and [place them] to its south.
Having poured a small amount of water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should sprinkle oneself and the ritual implements with that water and worship the pedestals upon the yantras.
[In the center] of the pericarp:
Homage to Maḍūka!
Homage to Kālāgnirudra!
Oṃ, homage to Kacchapa!
Oṃ, homage to the Earth. Oṃ, homage to the Ocean of Milk.
Oṃ, homage to the Jewel Island.
Oṃ, salutation to the Kadamba forest. Oṃ, salutation to the wish-fulfilling tree composed of colors. Oṃ, salutation to the jeweled pavilion.
Oṃ, homage to the Jewel Lion Throne.
In the corners starting from the southeast:
Oṃ, homage to Dharma.
Oṃ, homage to knowledge. Oṃ, homage to dispassion.
Aiṃ, homage to sovereignty.
In the directions beginning with the east:
homage to Adharma;
homage to Ignorance.
Salutation to Advairāgya. Salutation to Anaiśvarya.
Again, in the pericarp (karṇikā), in an upward sequence.
Aṃ, obeisance to the solar disc consisting of twelve kalās; Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc consisting of sixteen kalās.
Then, one should worship the nine Śaktis in the filaments.
Oṃ, homage to Icchā. Homage to Jñānā. Homage to Kriyā. Homage to Kāminī. Homage to Kāmadāyinī. Homage to Rati. Homage to Priyā.
Homage to Nandā. In the center: Homage to Manonmanī. Ai/ Homage to Parā.
Homage to Aparā. Homage to Parāparā. In the intermediate space between the east and the north, homage to the venerable Gurus.
*Hsau*. Homage to the seat of the great corpse Sadāśiva.
Then, [the practitioner], carrying a handful of flowers as red as the rays of the sun, [visualizes] the Goddess within his own heart via the nostril.
Having brought [the deity] together with five *praṇavas*, one should invoke the form (*mūrti*) into that [image] and worship it.
Then, the specific distinction at the beginning of the mantra is as follows: *vākśakti-kamalā* is *hasakhaphreḥ* and *hasrau*. Again, the mantra begins with these:
*oṃ aiḥ hrīḥ śrīḥ hasakhaphreḥ sauḥ*. Thus is the mantra.

Having recited the root mantra and performed the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the form with the words: "I fashion the form of the glorious Mahātripurabhairavī as the embodiment of immortal consciousness; obeisance," one should place the deity upon the pedestal, touch it with the hand, and perform the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).
As follows:
Śrā / Hrī / Kro / Ha / Saḥ | 210a) The vital breaths of the illustrious Tripurabhairavī are here the vital breaths.
Thus is the seed-syllable (5).
Thus, the life-force of Śrī Tripurabhairavī remains established here.
May all the sense faculties, speech, mind, and so forth, come here and remain happily for a long time; svāhā!

Having thus performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath), having displayed the *āvāhana* (invocation) and other mudrās, and having performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa*), one should worship again with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) after meditating [upon the deity]. As follows:
the seat, welcome, water for the feet, arghya—[these are] according to the sequence of the sixteen services; this is the worship.
"Welcome" is the inquiry after one's welfare. Here is the *arghya* (water for honor). Here is the *pādya* (water for the feet).
This is the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). This is the *madhuparka* (honey-mixture). Here is the water for sipping. This is the water for bathing (*snānīya*). These are the silk garments.
This is the golden ornament; this is incense; this is the flower; this is the incense-lamp. Then, having brought the food offering (naivedya) before [the deity], [recite] *astrāya phaṭ*.
