Having sprinkled [the offering] with water while reciting "Hūṃ," and having veiled it with the left index finger while reciting "Vaṃ," and so forth; then, having offered this food (*naivedya*) with the words "Obeisance to the venerable Tripurabhairavī," and having discarded it, one takes up water and offers it with the mantra beginning "Thou art the spreading of nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*) and ending with "To the arrow, Svāhā! (*vāṇāya svāhā*).

Having offered the five *prāṇāhuti* oblations and contemplated the internal acceptance with the mantra "Amṛtapidhānam asi svāhā," and having again offered the bliss with "Ayośānandatvā," one should offer these handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) while worshipping the inner deity Śrī Tripurabhairavī at the mouth of the Goddess.
Having satisfied [the deity] three times, one should worship with the six limbs as follows:
*hastrāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*;
*hasrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*.
Hasrūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
hsrai, huṃ to the armor;
hasrau, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.
Having worshipped with "Sahaḥ astrāya phaṭ" in the directions starting from the east, and having paid obeisance to Tripurabhairavī,
one should worship the Śrāvaṇas.
As in the center, in the triangle:
in the eastern corner, *ai*—*namo ratyai*.
In the southern corner.
Ai! Salutation to Prīti in the left corner. Ai! Salutation to Manobhavā. Then, in the eight yonis:
One should worship the eight powers:
ai/ klī/ klu/ strī/ maśubhagāyai namaḥ (5).
Homage to Bhagasarpiṇī. (5)
Salutation to Bhagamālinī. (5)
Salutation to Anaṅgā.
Salutation to Anaṅgakusumā (5).
Salutation to Anaṅgamekhalā.
Salutation to Anaṅgamadanā.
Then, on the filaments.
One should worship the powers of Brahmā and the others in the sequence beginning from the east.
Beginning with "To Brahmi" and so forth, up to "To Mahalakshmi."
Homage to Asitāṅga at the five tips; to Rukha.
To Caṇḍa, to Krodha, to Unmatta, and to Kapālī.
For the terrifying [deity] of withdrawal, that is on the exterior.
One should worship Indra and the other deities.
Outside of that, one should worship those who are not women.
Then, having worshipped the Goddess with a handful of flowers, performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), and paid homage to the gurus, one should perform the recitation (japa).
Having completed the *japa* and performed *prāṇāyāma* once more with the water of the *argha* offering, [one should say]:
"O you who guard the most secret of secrets, accept this victory achieved by us.
O Goddess Maheśvarī, may success be mine through your grace. (12.392)

Having thus offered the *japa* consisting of light into the left hand of the Goddess, and having visualized it as accepted by the Supreme Sovereign (*Parameśvarī*), one should offer betel-leaf with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), worship her again with perfumes and other offerings,
display the *yonimudrā*, and then sit upon a staff-seat (*daṇḍapavi*). Thereafter, as before...

Whatever has been done by me through the authority of the vital breath, the intellect, the body, and the sense-objects—whether in the waking state, the dreaming state, and so forth; whatever was performed with the mind, speech, and other faculties; whatever was thought, spoken, and so on—all that becomes an offering to Brahman, [accompanied by] "Svāhā.
Having thus offered oneself, including all that is mine and myself, and having paid obeisance...
"Once again, water for sipping.

Having uttered the root mantra thus: "O Blessed Tripurabhairavī, you have been worshipped; please forgive me," one should withdraw [the deity] into one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. Then, having performed *prāṇāyāma* and contemplated oneself as being of that same form, [one should offer] the *nirmālya*.
Taking the flower, one should cast it toward the northeast, saying: "Obeisance to Nirmālyavāsinī.
Then, having drunk the water from the feet and accepted the food offering (*naivedya*), one may enjoy oneself as is pleasant.
Thus ends the *Śrītripurabhairavī-pūjā-paddhati*.
Now follows the armor (kavaca) of Tripurabhairavī.
Oṃ, salutations to Tripurabhairavī!
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are proficient in all the scriptures!
Have mercy for the sake of the world, O Knower of Dharma, O Great-minded One!
Sundarī is called the "City of Others" (*parapurā*), the knowledge (*vidyā*) that fulfills the three cities (*tripurapūrikā*).
Tell me truly her divine armor (*kavaca*). (12.393)
Having heard those words of hers, the Lord of the World spoke:
"The wonderful armor of the goddess has been rendered beautiful and then disfigured. (12.394)
The illustrious Lord said: I shall tell you the armor (*kavaca*) of the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*), which is difficult for all to obtain.
Listen to it according to the prescribed rite; having heard it, you too must keep it secret. (12-395)
By whose grace I sustain the entirety of the three worlds;
from whom everything has arisen, and in whom it still remains even now. (12.396)
Mother and father, honored by the world, the very form of the universe;
the bestower of perfection, the perfected one, [who is] among wicked beings... (6) || 12-397 ||
May the Goddess who brings benefit to all beings, who embodies the nature of all beings, the passionate one who grants desires, protect me in the syllable *ka*. (7) 12-398
May the Goddess Ai, whose nature is the Mūlādhāra, protect me;
may the supreme Goddess Ikāra, who bestows delight and all prosperity, [protect me]. (8) 12-399.
May the goddess Lakārī, the beloved of Indra, protect me;
may the goddess Hrīṃkārī, the beauty of Śambhu, protect me everywhere. (12.400)
May Śāmbhavī, the Great Māyā consisting of these syllables, protect my head.
May the Goddess Śarvāṇī, the consort of Hara, protect me in the syllable *ka*. (12.401)
May the Goddess, the destroyer of all sins, protect me in the syllable *ma*;
may the Goddess, who always assumes forms at will, protect me in the syllable *ka*.
May the Goddess, the beloved of Śavarāri, always protect me at the syllable *ka*;
may the Goddess, who assumes the form of the earth-supporting mountain, protect me at the syllable *la*. (12.403)
May the goddess Hrīḥ, who shares half the body of Śaṅkara, protect me;
by these syllables, Mahāmāyā, the beloved of Kāmarāja, indeed [protects]. (12.404)
May the goddess Makārī protect me, the progenitor, whose nature is the lotus everywhere;
may the goddess Lakārī protect me, Lakṣmī, who possesses all auspicious marks. (12.405)
May she who utters *hrīṃ* protect everywhere, O Goddess, Sovereign of the Three Worlds;
by these syllables, Mahāmāyā is indeed the very embodiment of the power of speech (*vāk-śakti*). (12.406)
May Vāgbhava protect the head; may Kāmarājikā protect the face;
may she whose nature is Śakti, the bestower of success upon me, protect the heart. (12.407)
May Sundarī always protect; may Sundarī embrace [us]. May the red-colored one always protect; may Sundarī, the giver of all, [protect us] forever. 12-408.
Adorned with various ornaments, may Sundī protect [me] at all times;
may she who is beautiful in every limb and the bestower of auspiciousness protect me everywhere. (12.409)
May she who generates joy for the world, who is the very form of Śambhu, and who bestows all good fortune, protect me always as the essence of all mantras. (12.410)
Adorned with various ornaments, may the beautiful goddess, who bestows supreme bliss, protect me at all times; she is the goddess who consists of all prosperity. (20) 12-411
May the auspicious Goddess, who possesses various treasures such as conch-shells, protect me at all times;
thereafter, may the Goddess Śarvāṇī, the bestower of everything, who possesses the lotus-treasure, [protect me] always. (12.412)
The Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra is the seer (ṛṣi) located everywhere upon the head;
the Pakti meter is its form, which effects the attraction of all things. || 12-413 ||
May she who brings delight to all protect me; may she who always agitates all protect me;
may the Blessed One who bestows all accomplishments protect me at all times. (12.414)
May Māheśvarī protect me always, and Kaumārī likewise at all times;
may she who causes all joy and brings all under her control protect me everywhere. (27) || 12-415 ||
May she who brings security always protect [me]; may she who is beautiful in all her limbs always protect [me];
may she who is youthful in every limb protect [me], she who bestows all good fortune. (28) || 12-416 ||
May Vāgdevī protect me always; may Vāṇinī protect me always;
may Vaśinī protect me always, she who forever bestows great siddhis. (29) || 12-417 ||
May Sarvavidrāviṇī protect you; may Gaṇanātha always protect you.
May Goddess Durgā always protect you; may Vaṭuka always protect you. (30) || 12-418 ||
May Kṣetrapāla protect me always; may Ādhāraśakti protect me; may Ananta protect me forever; and may Varāha protect me at all times. (12.419)
May the Earth protect me at all times, as well as the Lion Throne of Varṇa; and may the Red Nectar, along with Samantata, protect me for all eternity. (32) || 12-420 ||
May the ocean of nectar always protect you; may the wish-fulfilling tree always protect you.
May the white parasol always protect you; may the jewel-lamp always protect you. (33) || 12-421 ||
May the guardians of the directions, Indra and all the others, likewise protect this [place] constantly for the sake of all accomplishment, as if it were their own pleasure garden. (34) || 12-422 ||
May the mounts always protect; may the missiles protect at all times;
may the weapons protect at all times; may the Yoginīs protect at all times. (35) || 12-423 ||
May the goddess Siddhā, the bestower of all accomplishments, protect you always;
may the goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī protect you everywhere and at all times. (12.424)
O Goddess, whose form is bliss, whose nature is consciousness, and who consists of consciousness; O Sundarī, beautiful in every limb, may you protect me—be present as Sundarī! (37) 12-425
O beautiful one, may Śiva protect me in a terrible temple of a separate deity, in a perilous place, on an inaccessible mountain, or even in the middle of a vast forest. (12-426)
O Pārvatī, this is called the Indrakavaca, and the extraction of its mantra has been taught;
he who, having become restrained, disciplined, and pure, recites it at the three junctions of the day, (39) 12-427.
Whatever is intended in his mind shall have its every purpose accomplished, using either gorocanā, saffron, or red sandalwood. (40) 12-428

The Self-Existent One [should be worshipped] with white flowers by the Son of the Earth (Mars) or Saturn, either in a cremation ground, a wilderness, an empty house, or a temple of Śiva. (41) // 12-429 //
Having worshipped the yantra with the Guru and his Śakti, the young maiden should worship that mantra and especially the lineage of Gurus. (42) 12-430 ||

Having worshipped according to her ability and having praised the sage according to the prescribed rite, the young maiden, after worshipping it herself, should have the *yantra* worn by the Guru. (43)
Having worshipped that [liṅga] in its source, as well as the lineage of gurus, one should then offer the oblation to the Goddess with men, cats, and pigs. (44) 12-432
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with mongooses, buffaloes, and rams, one should place [the image] within gold and wear it on the neck, the head, or the arm. (45) 12-433.
On an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation, as well as at the rising of the sun,
a man who wears this armor shall obtain all perfections.
O Great Goddess, even in hundreds of years I am not able to describe the majesty of this armor, nor its fruit that it yields. (47) 12-435
For him there is no fear of thieves, nor is he there afflicted by disease; there is no famine there, nor is there ever any oppression. (48) 12-436
It pacifies all obstacles, destroys all diseases, provides protection for every living being, and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. (49) 12-437
One should never speak of it or give it away here or there;
having obtained the mantra according to the ritual injunctions, the wise person should worship it constantly. (50) 12-438
Even there, O goddess of divine form, I consider this armor to be difficult to obtain;
for only after receiving the grace of the Guru and attaining the well-guarded Vidyā can it be acquired. (51) 12-439
Even there, one who is restrained and pure should recite this verse concerning the divine armor, difficult to obtain in the three worlds, which is established in reality. (52) 12-440 ||
The accomplishment of all his aims shall come to pass, as proclaimed by Śaṅkara:
"Hara is the Guru and the God manifest, and Pārvatī is his consort.
For him who worships them without distinction, success is not far off. (53) 12-441.
Thus ends the armor (kavaca) of Tripurabhairavī in the Viśvasāra Tantra. Now follows the thousand names (sahasranāma) of Tripurabhairavī.
Oṃ, salutations to Tripurabhairavī.
For the eight-syllable mantra beginning with "Ahaṃ Rudra," Vākstaṃbhanarṣi is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, Vākstaṃbhanadevatā is the deity, and the application is for the propitiation of Durgā.
Oṃ! In the center of the ocean of nectar, within a pavilion of jewels, upon the central altar,
she who is seated upon a lion-throne— she who is completely surrounded, whose complexion is entirely yellow,
adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, jewelry, and garlands.
I worship the Goddess who has held the tongue of her enemy with a mallet.
O Maheśānī, I shall now declare the thousand names of the Goddess, by the grace of which, O Maheśānī, one may obtain the fruit of all the [four] goals of human existence. (12-443)
This hymn, which pacifies all diseases, destroys all death, and brings about all peace, was spoken by Śakra. (12-444)
There is no praise higher than this, no austerity higher than this,
no knowledge higher than this, and no supreme sacred ford higher than this.
O Maheśvarī, in her everything is completely purified; in her it remains even today, and all that shall go to dissolution at the time of dissolution. (4) 12-446

Of this hymn of a thousand names of the illustrious Tripurabhairavī, the Venerable Śiva is the seer (ṛṣi), the Pakti meter is the metre (chandas), the Primordial Power (Ādyāśakti) is the lineage, the Blessed Goddess Tripurabhairavī is the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Oṃ! O Tripurā, Supreme Goddess, dweller in the perfection of yoga;
O Goddess who consists of all mantras, endowed with all powers. (5) 12-447
The goddess Sarvadhāriṇī, the auspicious bestower of all prosperity, the Yoginī, the Mother of Yoga, and the one who sets in motion the ocean of yoga. (6) || 12-448 ||
The Yoginī is the object of meditation, the mother of yogis, and she who delights in the enjoyment of yoga;
she is play, sport, and pastime, existing in the form of Time. (7) || 12-449 ||
She is the form of Time, the Night of Time, Kālī, and the dweller in the lotus;
she is Kamalā, the embodiment of splendor, the sovereign of Kāmarāja, and Kriyā. (8) 12-450 ||
Kuhuḥ, Kapaṭaveśā, Kapaṭā, Kupaṭā, Kupaṭākṛti, Kumudā, Carcitā, Kāntā, Kālarātri, and Kriyāspada— (9) || 12-451 ||
Ghorarāvā, Ghorarūpā, Ghorarāvā, Ghṛṇāpahā, Ghargharā, Ghariṇī, Cūrṇā, and Ghoranādā are always her beloveds. (10) || 12-452 ||
Ghorākārā, Ghoratarā, Gharmā, Gharmapradā, Rati, Ghaṇṭā, Ghargharanādā, and Ghaṇṭānādapriyā—she is always beloved of sound. (11) || 12-453 ||
Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmatarā, Sthūlā, Atisthūlā, Mahāmati, Kṣamā, Bhāmā, as well as Bhīmā and Bhīmanādapravartinī. (12-454)
She is of unconventional form, the remover of fear, the giver of fear, and the destroyer of fear;
she is the Goddess who dwells in the cremation ground and resides in the abode of the cremation ground. (12-455)
She whose seat is a corpse, who carries a corpse, who moves with a corpse, who is herself a corpse, she who takes away corpses;
she who dwells in the region of the throat and wears a garland of skulls. (12-456)
Ranturā, Sudatī, Satyā, Satyā, Sukeśavāśinī, Satyadehā, Satyahaṃrā, and Satyavādavilāśinī. (12-457)
She whose body is truth, who seizes by means of truth, and who sports with truthful speech;
she whose abode is truth, who is united with truth, who is truth itself, and who dwells in truth. (12.458)
She is the unattached and the well-attached, the company of the virtuous, and the deluder through union;
she is the mistress of illusion, the Great Vidyā, and the one who revels in the great intoxicant. (12.459)
She who takes up liquor, she who drinks intoxicants, the destroyer of those who revile liquor;
she who wears a garland of dripping blood and dwells upon the two corners of the mouth. (12.460)
She is attached to great intoxicants and madness; she dwells in the snare of flesh and in blood and meat.
She takes away flesh, she sustains the month, and she consumes the eaters of flesh. (12-461)
She drinks blood, delights in blood, has a red mouth and red eyes;
she feeds on blood, loves blood, and destroys those who revile her with blood. (12.462)
Red-handed, delighting in red, with a red body, and intensely red;
the self-arisen one, the sacrificial pit, svāhā, the self-arisen one, eager for the sacrificial pit.
She who has the self-existent as her lake, she who has the self-existent as her garment;
(21) she who is delighted by the flowers of the self-existent, she who is herself delighted, she who is born from the birth of the self-existent.
(12-464) She whose food consists of the flowers of the self-existent, she who has the self-existent as her garment and her covering; (22)
She is the delight of the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, and she is eternally devoted to the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*.
Kuṇḍagolā, Priyakarī, and she who is born from Kuṇḍagola;
Śukrāsikā, Śukrakarā, Suśukrā, and Śukriṇī. (12.466)
She is the worshipper of Śukra and the one worshipped by him; she is the reviler of those who revile Śukra.
She wears red garlands, possesses red flowers, and has blossoms of red Puṣpaka.
Her limbs are sprinkled with red sandalwood; she is a worshiper of red sandalwood.
She is a fish, beloved of the fish, belonging to the fish, the food of the fish, and of great prosperity. (12.468)
You who desire fish, you who seize fish, you who destroy those who revile fish;
you with squinting eyes, likewise cruel, you who dwell among cruel beings. (12.469)
Terrible at the end, with a body like a thunderbolt, born from the vajra of Indra and the vajra;
possessing a vajra-body, a vajra-body, she who carries away the vajra-skeleton. (12-470)
O remover of the fear of *nirvāṇa*, O giver of fear, O remover of fear, O bestower of fear, O you who are not terrifying, O you of terrible roar! (28) 12-471.
She was beautiful, radiant, truthful, patient, and likewise one who acts with propriety;
her parting was adorned with vermilion, and her form resembled that very vermilion. (29) || 12-472 ||
With a nose adorned with pearls, she has a beautiful nose and a glossy nose;
she may be short, or have a protruding belly, or be tall, or long-legged, or have large lips. (12.473)
Kuṭilā, Carcikā, Caṇḍī, Caṇḍanādā, and Caṇḍikā; (31) Acicaṇḍā, Mahācaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, and Caṇḍaveginī. || 12-474 ||
Caṇḍālī, Caṇḍikā, she whose form is the fierce sound, Mahācalā (32); Caṃpā, Caṃpāvatī, Ukṣā, Tikṣṇā, Atikṣṇā, Priyā, and Kṛti. (12.475)
When she is the giver of water through her union, she brings joy to the world;
she is the sustainer of the world, the mother of the world, the earth, and the forbearance of the world. (12.476)
Jayā, Jayā, Jayitrī, Jayadā, and likewise Jayinī; Jananī, Jagaddhātrī, she who is named Jayā, Jayamātā, Jayā, Vijayā, and Janā. (12.477)
She possesses the sixfold army and has the form of the sixfold [senses]; she holds a pleasant sword and the sixfold [objects].
She has the form of space, her hands are marked with the syllable *ṣaṃ*, she sings the syllable *ṣaṃ*, and she is beloved by the syllable *ṣaṃ*. (36) 12-478 ||
Ṣaṅgadā, Khaṅgamāyā, Ṣaginī, and Ṣaṅgamaṇḍalī;
Śaṅkhinī, Vāpinī, the goddess Vajriṇī, and Musulīmatī. (37) 12-479.
Vāṇinī, Bhiṇḍipālī, Pāśā, and Aṅkuśeśvarī; Ṭaṅkinī and Muṇḍinī with Dhanuṣī, Karṇā, and Nāsikā. (38) 12-480.
She who originates from the weapon in the form of a mallet and a plough;
she who is to be perceived and who takes away what is perceived; she who is red lac, easily obtained, and whose very nature is gain. (41) || 12-481 ||
The possessor of wealth, the giver of wealth, the auspicious one, the bearer of an auspicious form, the bow;
she who dwells in the desert, she who is called by the word "bow," the one who possesses the measure of a bow, and the supporter of the earth. (42) || 12-482 ||

She whose sound is profound, who is worthy of honor, whose limbs are wealth, who dwells in wealth, the giver of wealth, the attainment of wealth, she who is obtainable through wealth, and the great bow-bearer. (43) 12-483 ||
She is unpeaceful yet has the form of peace; she dwells upon the path of the breath;
she is served by the multitude of the sky; she is the host of hosts, beloved of the hosts. (44) || 12-484 ||

She is the giver of the assembly, the destroyer of the assembly, she who is to be counted, she who is reached through the path, she who delights in going; she who is to be attained, she who is without coming, she who is peace, the destroyer of disease, and the increaser of health. (45)

She who delights in what is dear, she who is destined for what is dear, she who is beloved, she who is love itself, she who is the body of the beloved, she who bestows what is dear, and she who is to be cherished by the beloved—she dwells in the abode of the Beloved. (46) 12-486.
Firm, of stable form, bestowing stability, and increasing steadfastness;
restless, fickle, moving, O dweller in the hearts of the fickle! (47) || 12-487 ||
Gaurī, Kārī, as well as Chinnā; Māyā, Prabhā, Sundarī, Tripurā, Bhavyā, and you who dwell in Tripureśvara. (48) 12-488 ||
The goddess Tripurā is the terrifier; Tripurā is the destroyer of life.
She is Bhairavī and she is Bhairava; she is the beloved body of Bhairava. (49) 12-489
Bhairavāṅgī, Bhayakarī, Bhairavī, Priyā, Vallabhā, Kāladā, Kalarātri, Bhadrakātyāyanī, and Kriyā. (50) 12-490
Krayadā, Krayahā, Krevyā, Krayaprāṇakriyā, as well as Klīṃ, Kālī, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Śakti, Svāhā, Vibhu, and Prabhu. (51) || 12-491 ||
Both Prakṛti and Puruṣa bear male names and possess a masculine form;
likewise, Puruṣī and Prakṛti assume feminine forms. (52) 12-492
The Supreme Person and Māyā-Nārāyaṇī, as well as the intellect—namely Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī. (53) || 12-493 ||
Vārāhī, Cāmuṇḍā, Rudrāṇī, Haravallabhā, Kauverī, Śāmbhavī, Kṛṣṇā, and Kātyāyanī are also to be worshipped. (54) [12.494]
Rākṣasī, Ḍākinī, Citrā, Vicitrā, and likewise Citkramā;
Haṃsinī, Rākinī, Tīkṣṇā, Gāndhā, and Vigandhavāhanā. (55) || 12-495 ||
Kekarī, Koṭarākṣī, Nirmo, Kṣamāṃsikā, Lalajihvā, Sujihvā, and Vadana-vanadāyinī. (56) || 12-496 ||
Candrā, Candraprabhā, Cāṇḍī, and she who is intent upon the splendor of the moon; Amṛtā, Pādanā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti. (57) || 12-497 ||
In the moon are Caṇḍikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, Kalpalatikā, and Kalpadānahā. (58) || 12-498 ||
She holds in her hands both the conceptual construction and its absence; she is the one who brings about the end of the aeon (*kalpa*).
She is known as the aeon, she is worthy of the aeon, and she is the one who is worshipped by those who worship the aeon. (59) || 12-499 ||
Śucimukhī, Pretamukhī, Ulkāmukhī, Mahāmukhī, Sumukhī, Ulūkavadanā, Kākāsyā, and Vikaṭānanā. (60) || 12-500 ||
Kṛkīlā, Sāpāsyā, Ārtkuṭalī, Śarabhānanā,
Nānāmukhī, Nānarūpadhāriṇī, and Dharaṇīdharā— (61) || 12-501 ||
Worthy of universal veneration, Mother of the Universe, named the Universe, existing as the essence of the universe;
she is the Sun, possessing the radiance of the sun, the very splendor, residing within the solar orb. (62) || 12-502 ||
Sūryakānti, Sūryakalā, Sūryākhyā, Sūryabhāvanā, Naṣinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, and Ruci. (63) [12.503]
Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Vodhinī, Dhāriṇī, Kṣamā;
Yugadā, Yugahā, Yogyā, Yogṛthādā, and Yogyavardhinī. 504.
She resides within the circle of fire, her abode is the circle of fire;
she is beloved by fire, she plunges into fire, and she performs the rites of the gods with fire as her food. (65) 12-505
She is the splendor of fire, the passion of fire, the giver of fire, and the destroyer of fire;
she is beloved by fire, the maker of fire, and is eternally established within the fire of the digits. (66) 12-506
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Svaḥstrī, Kapilā, and likewise Havyakavyavahā—these are her forms. (67) 12-507.
The Goddess is manifoldly radiant, the consort of the Supreme Brahman;
the Goddess consists of the light of Brahman, having the very nature of the Supreme Brahman. (68) 12-508

She is the Supreme Self, supremely meritorious, the giver of merit, the increaser of merit, the destroyer of [worldly] merit, she whose name is Merit, the beloved body of the friend of merit. (69) || 12-509 ||

She whose name is merit, who is honored for her merit, who increases the limbs of men, whose body is merit, who performs meritorious deeds, and who is the destroyer of those who revile merit. (70) 12-510 ||
She who takes away the time for merit, the meritorious one, the supremely meritorious, the garland of merit;
she whose character is merit, whose play is merit, whose name is merit, and who is equal to the Supreme (71). || 12-511 ||
She is the service of merit, subtle merit, and the beloved of the ancient city; she is the person, the life-force of persons, and the one whose nature is manifest through grace. (12.512)
She who possesses the limbs of a man, she who is a man, and the body dear to the man;
she who is the Suṣumṇā, whose life-breath is the Puṣpaka, the destroyer of flowers, and the beloved of flowers. (73) || 12-513 ||
She who loves flowers, who wears flower garlands, who delights in the joy of flowers;
she who abounds in flowers, who wears flower wreaths, and who destroys those who revile flowers. (74) || 12-514 ||
Gāndhārī, Gandhapūjyā, Sugandhā, Premagandhikā, Durgandhā, Pūtigandhā, Sugandhā, and Sugandhikā. (85) || 12-515 ||
She of great fragrance, worthy of sweet scent, the destroyer of those who destroy fragrance;
Padmā, Padmāvatī, Premā, and she who is sweetly scented with the fragrance of a lotus. (86) || 12-516 ||

She whose abode is the lotus, who holds a lotus in her hand, whose vehicle has a lotus as its mount, who stands upon a lotus, whose face is like a lotus, who sports with the lotus, and who possesses a beautiful fire. (87) || 12-517 ||
Padmāntakā, Padmavahā, Padmaprāsādaśaṅkiṇī, Padmanindakanindā, and Padmasantoṣavāhanā. (88) || 12-518 ||
The goddess holds a red lotus; she is always fond of the red lotus.
She possesses the fragrance of the red lotus and dwells within the red lotus. (89) || 12-519 ||
The beautiful woman has a dwelling of red lotuses, is enchanting with red lotuses, has eyes like intensely red lotuses, and assumes the form of a deeply red lotus. (90) 12-520 ||
She is the woman, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa’s abode;
she dwells within the body of Nārāyaṇa and is the one who captivates the mind of Nārāyaṇa. (91) || 12-521 ||
Residing within the body of Nārāyaṇa, saluted by Nārāyaṇa, born from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, she is the beloved form of Nārāyaṇa. (92) 12-522 ||
She belongs to Viṣṇu, she is worthy of worship by Viṣṇu, and she dwells within the bodies of the Vaiṣṇavas;
she is worshipped by those who worship Viṣṇu, and she is established as the Vaiṣṇava form. (12.523)
She is to be worshipped by Hara, the most excellent of Hara, the beloved of Hara, the destroyer;
she resides within the body of Hara during the dissolution and is intent upon the worship of Hara. (94) 12-524.
Born from the body of Hara, dwelling upon the limbs of Hara, she burned [all impurities];
she is worthy of worship by the worshippers of Hara, and is devoted to the delight of Hara. (95) 12-525.
Mounted upon the body of Hara, she is the sport of Hara and eternal delight;
free from attachment even to good company, she is the destroyer of all attachment. (96) || 12-526 ||
She is solitary, victorious, and difficult to attain; she increases the body that is hard to master.
She is the ender of the body that is difficult to overcome, she possesses an invincible form, and she is the water that is hard to cross. (12.527)
She is beloved by the pretas, the maker of pretas, and born from the bodies of pretas;
she dwells within the limbs of those who are pleased, and she is delighted as she crushes the bodies of pretas.
The ḍākinī, the yoginī, the goddess, Kālarātri, who is always beloved; she who removes Kālarātri, the dark one, whose body is black, and who possesses great ascetic heat. (99) 12-529
She of slender limbs, she whose body is like a thunderbolt, she who possesses a vajra-body and assumes a vajra-form;
she who bears various bodies, the blessed one, who dwells in the sequence of the six cakras. (12.530)
Residing in the *mūlādhāra*, she is always established in the *mūlādhāra*;
Mahāmāyā, whose form is wind, dwells upon the path of the wind. (12.531)
Joined with wind, creating wind, filling and purifying with wind, the goddess who assumes the form of wind moves along the path of the Suṣumṇā. (12.532)
Abiding in the body, having the form of the body, that which is to be supported by the body, possessing a beautiful body;
(103) having the form of the channels, abiding in the channels, the subtle [sound] within the lotus of the flute. (12-533)
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, and Sarasvatī—she who brings delight to Sadāśiva and assumes the form of the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti). (12.534)
O Amṛteśī, O Maheśānī, you who dwell in the abode of the erotic sentiment; you who are the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction, and who reside in the state of dissolution. (12.535)
She is associated with the great dissolution, and she is the cause of creation and destruction;
she is Svadhā, Svāhā, the bearer of oblations, the oblation itself, and she who is ever fond of oblations.

She is the state of the oblation, the consumer of the oblation, and she is born from the body of the oblation; she is the play of the oblation, the embodiment of the wish-fulfilling cow, and the source of all forms. (12.537)
Surabhinandinī, Puṇyā, Yajñāṅgī, Yajñavallabhā; (108) Yajñasthā, Yajñadehā, Yoginī, and Yonivāhinī. || 12-538 ||
Born not from a womb, truthful yet untruthful, unchaste and slender;
Ahalyā, Gomatī, accessible to all, and the destroyer of Videha. (12-539)
Gandhārī, Draupadī, Dūtī, Śivādūtī, and Śivapriyā; (110) Tripureśī, Pañcadaśī, Paurṇamāsī, and Caturdaśī. || 12-540 ||
The fifth, as well as the sixth, the ninth, and likewise the eighth, (111) the eleventh and the twelfth, are of the nature of wind and bestow fear. 12-541.
She is the transition (*saṃkrānti*), the form of flesh, the form of the seasons, and she who is dear to the seasons;
she is the form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and so forth, and she who assumes the form of the *ghaṭikā* and the *daṇḍa*. (12.542)
Yāmarūpā, Mahākālī, Sandhyā, Susaṃganāśinī, Triyāmā, Sāmarūpā, Yamakanyā, Yamī, and Yamā. (113–12-543)

Mātaṅgī is of beautiful form, of noble lineage, yet the destroyer of her own family; she is the beloved of the clan, with slender breasts, increasing the size of the frontal globes of elephants. (114, 12-544)
Tvaritā, Kulavṛddhā, Satvarā, Aruṇaprabhā; (115) Nadī, Sāgaragā, Śānti, Śāntirūpā, Suśāntikā. || 12-545 ||
She is hope, thirst, hunger, and agitation; she dwells in the form of agitation.
She is the mistress of the rivers and the peace of the household, yet she is not the bearer of the Vedas and the Smṛtis. (12.546)
She is day and night, the body composed of the five elements, and indeed the one with a beautiful form;
she is Kuru-kulyā, Chinnamastā, and she who wears the sacrificial thread made of a serpent. (12.547)
Varṇinī, Ḍāginī, Śakti, Kuru, Kuṣṇyā, Sukṛllikā, Aparājitā, Pratyagī, Rajitā, and Jayanāśanī. (12-548)
Jayā and Vijayā are likewise proclaimed as the Kauravyas. This recitation of the names of the Goddess consists of one thousand and eight names;
even one burdened with great sins is liberated by this—of this there is no doubt. (122–123)
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the wife of one's guru—these constitute ten million great sins (mahāpātaka), as well as minor sins (upapātaka). (124) [12.550]
When it is held at the throat, everything perishes in that very instant, whether one recites the entire hymn, a single verse, or even merely remembers it while reciting. (125) 12-551 ||

Whether one recites it oneself or causes it to be recited, one is immediately released from bondage—at the royal gate, in fear, in a fortress, in a crisis, or in a mountain pass difficult to traverse. (12-552)

Whether on a mountain in the morning, or on a boat, or when confronted by the danger of fire, or overwhelmed by the fear of lions and tigers—(127) [in these cases], Maheśvarī [is the protector]. (12-553)
O mortal, by reciting and remembering this, which destroys all calamities, a sonless man obtains a son, and a poor man shall acquire wealth. (128) 12-554 ||
A Brahmin devoted to all the scriptures shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices; a debater becomes mute, and kings along with their servants become excellent ascetics. (129) 12-555.
One who, with single-minded devotion, writes this hymn with saffron using a *golo* brush—even if instructed by a Vaiṣṇava guru—shall obtain the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments. (12.556) [217a]
Having worn it set in gold, one then obtains all desires;
it should be worn on the left arm by women, and likewise on the left hand by men. (131) 12-557.
O Maheśvarī, on a Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, or even a Saturday, there shall be the fruit of all accomplishments. (132) 12-558.
In the morning, or in a cremation ground, at night, or at midnight, or even in an empty dwelling or a house, the preceptor should paint [the mandala] with great care. (133) 12-559.

Having seen one who is menstruating or being afraid, or having touched her, one should always draw [the deity] with flowers of the self-born tree (*svayambhū*), with *śukra*, and with fragrant sandalwood. (12.560)
Having carefully inscribed [the mantra] with musk and red arsenic, and having thus written it down, one who is single-minded attains wealth and sovereignty. (12.561)
Having worshipped the maidens, and especially the women, having honored them with beautiful flowers, perfumes, sandalwood, and garments. (136) 12-562.
One should worship with vermilion and red flowers through the yoga of devotion;
one should worship the eight goddesses, or the maiden, or the tenth [deity]. (12-563)
He too obtains the fruit of all his desires at that very moment;
herein there is no dependence on success or the like, nor any defect caused by friends or enemies. (12-564)
One should not, day or night, offer the sacrifice of physical exhaustion through excessive exertion. (140) [12.565]
One should worship the goddess Pārvatī, who is Bhairavī accompanied by Tripurā;
one should daily feed ten or twelve Brahmins. (141) 12-566.
Whoever recites this with this ritual at the three junctions of the day for one month, the childless shall obtain a son, and the poor shall become wealthy. (12.567)
One does not attain the fruit of the rite by following the procedure for two months, nor for three months, nor likewise for four months. (12.568)
One long afflicted by disease is liberated; in the fifth [month], one becomes a sovereign ruler (*ekavirāj*).
Likewise, even a wretched person shall obtain all-encompassing sovereignty in the sixth month. (144) 12-569
In the seventh [house], there is wealth; in the eighth, one becomes a lord of speech.
In the ninth, there is the attainment of all perfections; in the tenth, one is honored by the world. (12.570)
In the eleventh [repetition] he becomes subject to kings; in the twelfth, he becomes a lord of cities.
He who recites this single boon shall obtain the world of Śakra after being honored. (146) 12-571 || 12-571 ||
Whoever, being restrained and pure, recites even a single verse with correct pronunciation, obtains the fruit of worship; so it was spoken by Bhairava. (147) 12-572.
O Maheśvarī, the Āyuṣmān [yoga] is for union with joy, especially with Brahmins; the Saubhāgyasiddhi [yoga] is for good fortune and auspiciousness. (148) 12-573.

Whether on the fifth or the sixth lunar day, wherever one may stay, there shall be no doubt and no fault regarding one's mother or others. What more need be said, O Goddess? One shall obtain the fruit of all desires. (12.574)
Thus ends the complete hymn of the Thousand Names of Śrī Tripurabhairavī in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Now follows the hymn to Tripurabhairavī.
Oṃ! Even Brahmā and the other gods do not truly know your subtle form—the beginningless embodiment that is the source of the universe;
therefore, I bow to your heart with two streaks of saffron.
We praise the gross [forms], which consist of the totality of all speech. (12-575)
Instantly possessing the splendor of a thousand rising suns, her hands bear the marks of the knowledge-gesture, the rosary, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness;
she is adorned with three lotus-eyes and wears garments and a lotus.
O Tripura, we worship you, who are radiant with the weight of your necklace.
Resplendent with streams of vermilion, bowed by the weight of her breasts, attainable only through the singular fruit of merits accumulated in previous births—
[may she protect you] from the mutual strife and discord caused by the divisions of pride.
Those whose intellects are dull from the beginning do not know your form and this [other]. || 12-577 ||
The sages declare you to be gross,
while the Vedas proclaim you to be subtle; some say you are the dwelling place of the entire universe, and others call you the root of all worlds— thus do they speak of you, O Bhava.
May another show great compassion toward me, O cruel one. (4) || 12-578 ||
One meditates upon you in the heart— adorned with a crescent moon and a skull, white as the autumnal moon, holding within your five-fingered hand the book, the rosary, and the jar filled with nectar.
And she who, with her lotus-like hands, bestows exposition, possesses three eyes. (5) || 12-579 ||
You are Śambhu, having taken half the body of the Daughter of the Mountain; you alone are Viṣṇu, whose body is embraced by Kamalā;
you are the sacrificial thread, and you are the dwelling place of the mace.
And their activities in the world, O Tripura, are you alone. (6) || 12-580 ||
Having resorted to the four states beginning with the "supreme" (para), which are established within these [levels] starting from the "vāgbhava," you,
the Supreme Deity, are drawn forth by the ears and other sense organs.
Consisting of pure consciousness, I never forget [it] within my heart. (7) || 12-581 ||
Having restrained the vital breath and conquered the enemy, and gazing with an unwavering mind at the tip of their own nose,
they meditate upon Him who is adorned with the crescent moon upon His head, situated within the crown of the head.
Your form is like that of the young sun, O eloquent one. (8) || 12-582 ||
"Having obtained you as the half-body of the enemy of Manmatha,
he creates the worlds"— this is the Vedic proclamation,
O Daughter of the Mountain, O Sole Mother of the World; it is indeed true.
If [the world] were to cease, the very stability of the remaining world would not exist. (9) || 12-583 ||
Having performed worship with flowers of the celestial trees upon your throne within the caves of the golden mountain,
the Siddhas sing together with the wives of the Kinnaras.
Their lotus-like eyes, reddened by the essence of the nectar they had tasted, [were gazing]. (10) || 12-584 ||
Bearing the splendor of a body that flashes like lightning, she brings a sense of renunciation from her own dwelling to the royal capital of her garment,
causing the lotuses on the path of beauty to blossom.
The goddess should worship her whose limbs are sprinkled with the supreme nectar. (11) || 12-585 ||
I praise her whose abode is birth after birth, who is the source of the Vedas, whose body consists of pure consciousness,
and whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.
Just as [she was] the abode of the birth of good fortune in Tripura. (12) || 12-586 ||
She who, in the form of the Moon, creates the world that consists of word and meaning;
she who, as the bodiless one, sustains it again by her own power;
and she who, as the nature of Fire, withdraws all of that at the end of the age.
Having placed that Śāradā in my mind, I do not forget her. (13) || 12-587 ||
O Nārāyaṇī, who carries one across the ocean of hell; O Gaurī, who allays suffering; O Sarasvatī, who bestows knowledge—O you adorned with three eyes!
Having led her away, she cried out, "She is the daughter of the King of Madra! (14) || 12-588 ||
O Mother of the World, those who praise you in succession with these twelve verses shall attain perfection of speech and reach supreme glory. (15) [12.589]
Thus ends the Śrī Tripurabhairavī Stotra in its entirety.
After the worship, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*). Having sprinkled [the area], one should then perform the daily fire-oblation for the Goddess;
O Mistress of the Gods, one should offer five oblations in sequence with the root mantra.
One should know that the five oblations have as their essential nature prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna. (12.591)
The six oblations offered to the six limbs are declared to be the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma).
Having performed the rite of the daily fire-sacrifice, one should carry out the rite of offering the sacrificial food (bali).
O Goddess, one should draw a set of four mandalas in the corners starting from Īśāna,
and around the Śrīcakra, one should draw a triangle and the void (vyoma).
Alternatively, one should draw a single mandala on the left side;

the meaning is that it is the "sky-pervading" (vyomavyāpaka) mandala. The word "alternatively" (athavā) implies a conjunction (*samuccaya*), because the offering of the *bali* is prescribed there as well; thus, it is indeed an option (*vikalpa*).
If one is unable [to perform the ritual in full], some say that the entire offering (bali) should be made right there;
O Daughter of the Mountain, having worshipped Vaṭuka and the others with the previous mantras.
"Come, come, O Goddess! O you whose sons are the Vaṭukas! O Nātha! O you who possess a mass of matted hair as bright as Kapila! O Three-eyed One! (12.595)
In Jvālāmukha, however, all of them destroy obstacles;
accept this offering (*bali*) together with all the side-dishes, O you who have two feet! (12.596)
The mantra of Vaṭuka is said to be accompanied by the wife of Vahni (the fire-god).
O Goddess, one should offer the bali-oblation to Vaṭuka according to this procedure:
"Oṃ, come, come, O Son of the Goddess, Lord Vaṭuka, radiant with the mass of tawny matted locks, three-eyed, flame-faced!"
Destroy, destroy all obstacles! Accept, accept this offering together with all ritual services, svāhā!
Thus is the mantra.

Whether she resides above the Brahmāṇḍa, in the expanse of the celestial sphere, in the netherworld (pātāla), in the forest, in water, in wind, or wherever else; whether she has taken her station in sacred fields (kṣetra), seats (pīṭha), and secondary seats (upapīṭha); may that Goddess—who is worshipped by the Lord of Devas and is ever pleased by incense, lamps, and the performance of auspicious bali offerings—protect us.
At the end of this, O Maheśānī, [one should utter] "yāṃ vīyogini," and then "bhyaḥ svāhā"; at the end of all mantras, one should write the word "yoginī."
Having written the armor (kavaca) and then written the wife of fire (svāhā), one should again write:
"By this mantra, O Goddess Yoginī, one should offer the oblation. (12-598)
O Lord of Gods, immediately following that: "Yo yoginībhyaḥ svāhā | Yoginī huṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this is the mantra.
One should then write the letter *kṣa* conjoined with the six long vowels.
In the *Mūrtisaṃhitā*, it is stated that at the letter *kṣa* there is the *bindu*, the practice (*ācāra*), and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Furthermore, the station of the field-guardian (*kṣetrapadapāla*) and the incense, lamps, and so forth of the *yoginīs* are to be drawn. (12.599)
O beautiful one, this is the mantra of Kṣetrapāla, joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-syllable *svāhā*).
O Goddess, with this mantra, one should offer the bali-oblation to Kṣetrapāla.
Kṣā Kṣī Kṣū Kṣai Kṣau Kṣaḥ! Accept, accept this bali offering accompanied by incense, lamps, and other articles for the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla), svāhā!
Thus is the mantra.
Having written the three syllables *gā*, *gī*, and *gū*, one should utter the word "Gaṇapati. One should then write "varānta," "varadā," "te," "ca," "sarvān," "te," and "janam. (12.601)

One should likewise bring about well-being; the mantra, joined with the word for "oblation" (*vali*) and ending in two parts, accompanied by the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*), should offer the oblation to Gaṇapati.
*gā gī gū gaṇapataye e varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa svāhā* — thus is the mantra.
The offering for Vaṭuka should be made with the left thumb and ring finger;
one should join the thumb, middle finger, and ring finger in the shape of a vulva.
For the rite of increasing prosperity on the left, make the two feet [resting] and the index finger straight;
by this mudrā, O Goddess, the offering to the Kṣetrapālas shall be accomplished. (12.604)
Likewise, make the finger situated in the middle of the fist straight;
this is the Gajadanta Mahāmudrā, which becomes an offering to Gaṇapati.

O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, one should worship according to this rite. For the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), there should be one hundred thousand recitations of the mantra for each syllable; then, O Auspicious One, one should offer oblations (*homa*) amounting to a tenth part of that.
Thereafter, one should perform the act of dedication (*arpaṇa*); thus, one shall become a possessor of all good fortune.
In the treatises,
it is stated by implication that one should recite the target of reality (*tattva-lakṣya*). From the recitation of Bhairavī, [one attains] mastery over the regions.

In that regard, the principles (*tattvas*) are ten, having reached an intermediate state, because the *śakti*-principles are ten in number; thus, in reality there are twelve principles, as stated in the *Prapañcasāra*: "I shall explain the principles."
There is no contradiction;
for this refers to the different ages (yugas), since it is stated that "the number [of years] in the Kali age is fourfold. This is the meaning.
Now follow the rites for specific desires: "The man who performs this rite for the Goddess with a bilva leaf shall obtain everything, whatever object of desire he longs for. (12.607)
One should offer the meat of a buffalo or a ram, including the hair,
or a white lotus together with milk-rice, combined with honey.
Having performed a million oblations with jackfruit (*panasa*), one becomes illustrious and free from disease;
through *dūrvā* grass, men obtain wealth, grain, and the birth of sons. (12.609)
The *lulāva* is the buffalo.
On the eighth day, one should worship two [deities], and likewise on the fourteenth and ninth days;
for one should worship them at night with an extensive display of great wealth.

One should avoid using *palāśa*, *kuśa*, and *kāśa* grasses, as well as *tulasī*, for worship; by doing so, one becomes a sinner, and even if [the plant] has withered, it would take away one's prosperity.
Likewise, in the Nibandha:
In this way, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall accomplish his own desired goal.
When this is done, the world becomes auspicious, and illusion (māyā) becomes truth.
By performing a fire sacrifice with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets, or with red pārijāta flowers, using vessels containing ghee, one shall bring the entire world under one's control.

The practitioner of mantra obtains mastery over speech by offering oblations of *karavīra* flowers along with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and *palāśa* flowers. One should offer oblations of forest-grown, unblemished, and sweetened foods. (12.614)
Every day, one should feed twice-born men numbering one hundred thousand or half that amount;
one should gratify beautiful young women with the thought that they are deities.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), one should satisfy one's own preceptor with wealth, grain, and other gifts;
the wise person should offer guggulu resin mixed with camphor and agallochum.
He attains divine knowledge; he becomes a seer (kavi) indeed through these Sāman chants. By means of oblations of *amṛtā* pieces soaked in milk, one conquers all untimely death.
One should perform a fire sacrifice for three days with *durvā* grass blades smeared with milk;
by means of flowers from the *girikarṇī* plant, one shall bring brahmins under one's control.
Girikarṇī is Aparājitā.
By offering oblations of Kalhāra flowers, Pārthiva flowers, Karṇikāra flowers, and Mallikā blossoms, one brings princes under one's control. (12.619)
One attains subjugation through *koraṇṭaka* flowers, and from a low-caste person (*vṛṣala*) through those born of the *pāṭalā* tree.
*Koraṇṭaka* is well known as *kiṃṭhiti*. It is endowed with the name of the target (*sādhya*) situated between the forward and reverse [mantra syllables]. (12.620)
Having recited the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with honeyed substances mixed with ghee; thus, he shall bring even a king under his control in an instant. (12.621)
By this very same procedure, his wife and his sons [should also worship] with bilva-born flowers combined with the three sweets (madhuratra). || 12-622 ||
One may bring men and women under one's control by performing oblations with flowers of jasmine and *vakula* mixed with sandalwood paste. (12.623)
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with fruits produced from the *vilva* tree combined with the three sweets; within a year, he shall obtain poetic talent.
One who desires to bring the world under control should perform oblations with *ṣāṭhala* flowers, *kuṇḍa* flowers, *utpalas*, and *nāgacaṇḍūpaka* flowers; thus he attains accumulated prosperity.
He who offers oblations with blossoming *naṃdyāvarta* flowers arranged in garlands becomes,
for a year, one whose prosperity surpasses that of the king.
One should offer oblations of *naṃdyāvarta* and *tagara* with clarified butter while reciting mantras; by this one will become prosperous.
One who desires to bring others under control should offer oblations of musk, saffron, and camphor.
One attains immediate and superior beauty surpassing that of Kandarpa by offering parched grain (lāja) soaked in curd, milk, and honey while reciting the mantra. (12.628)
Having conquered all the worlds while still alive for a hundred autumns,
[he offered] two parts of sandalwood paste and one part of saffron and camphor.
Having ground together one part of *gorocana* and three parts of *piṣṭa* with water, one should apply a tilaka on the forehead; whoever sees it, or by whom it is seen, [is protected]. (12.630)
Those which are seen when looking at [the reflection] will appear as such to him after a long time.
One should prepare equal parts of camphor, *kapīca*, and *urāṇa*. (12.631)
Four parts each of jaṭāmāṃsī, māṃsī, rocanā, and amarā; saffron (kuṅkuma) should be seven parts, and sandalwood (candana) is considered to be one part.
Aguru should consist of nine parts; thus the portions are established.
All of this, having been finely ground with snow-water, is well-prepared. (12.633)
One should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) on the forehead to subdue kings, men intoxicated by pride, women arrogant with vanity, and elephants maddened by rut. (12.634)
A man wearing this tilaka may lie down even upon seeing lions, tigers, great serpents, bhūtas, vetālas, or rākṣasas. (12.635)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the procedure for the offering to Śrī Tripurabhairavī, in the Āgamakalpalatā.
I shall now declare the Vidyā of Chinnamastā, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals;
by knowing which, the sages attained supreme perfection. (13.1)
I shall now explain, in brief, the extraction of mantras as taught in the Phetkārī Tantra, which brings happiness to practitioners through diligent effort. (13.2)
Namely: Lakṣmī, Lajjā, as well as Māyā, Mātrā, and Dvādaśikā; then Vajravairocanīye, and after that the pair of Māyās. (13.3)

Combined with the syllable *phaṭ*, followed by *svāhā*; then *lakṣmīḥ* (śrī), *lajjā* (hrīḥ), *māyā* (hūṃ), and the twelve-syllabled *mātrā*: *ai vajravairocanīye*. Then the essential form (*svarūpa*) which is *māyā* doubled: *hūṃ hūṃ*.
The nature of *phatkāra* is the form of *svāhā*. By that [mantra]:
*śrī hrī hū ai vajravairocanīye hū hū phaṭ svāhā*. This is the sixteen-syllable mantra.
That which begins with the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī is then Śrī Sarvatomukhī.
Because of the seed-syllable of modesty (*lajjā*), yogins attain subjugation; and by the first seed-syllable of illusion (*māyā*), there is the destruction of great sins. (13.5)
The seed-syllable consisting of twelve measures (mātrās) is the primary cause of liberation.
And so it is stated in another tantra:
"The left eye [the letter *i*] conjoined with fire [the letter *r*], adorned with the bindu and nāda. (13-6)
O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of Śiva is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of Lañjā (Lajjā).
Having extracted Īśāna and the seed-syllable of Purāri (Rudra), adorned with the Bindu and embellished by Nāda,
and having placed the left ear (the letter U) all around it, the wise call that Māyā— thus it is stated therein.
"Māyā is the twelvefold" means it consists of the twelve vowels; "adorned with Nāda and Bindu" is stated in that very same place.
He states another mantra:
"One should proclaim the seed-syllable of the mantra as Nādi-vija, O Mantra-kinnara. (13.7)
Following that, for Vajravairocanī, there should be the seed-syllable *māyā*;
joined with *phaṭ* and *svāhā*, this is the mantra for the great serpent-mantra practitioner. (13.8)
It bestows all accomplishments, is meritorious, and brings about the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It has the nature of the syllable *oṃ*, the beginningless seed-syllable; it has the nature of *vajravairocanīya* and the seed-syllable of illusion, *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. By that [mantra]:
Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the thirteen-syllable mantra. And so it is said in that *Bhairava* tantra:
In the syllable Om (praṇava), however, reside the three gods: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
In the syllable *va* is Varuṇa himself; in the syllable *ja* is the Lord of the Gods;
in the syllable *ai* is the Goddess Tripurā; and in the syllable *re* is Tripurasundarī. (13.10)
The goddess Trailokyavijayā is eternally born of Time;
the moon-god made [the syllable] 'ca', and the leader [made] 'na' as well. (13.11)
In the letter *ī* is Kamalā herself, and in the letter *yo* is Sarasvatī;
likewise, in the pair of *māyās*, the Goddess is united with Prakṛti.
In *phat* resides Prakṛti herself; in *svā* resides the Flower-Armed One (Kāmadeva); and in *hā* resides Rati. These are the deities who abide in the conjunction [of the syllables]. 13-13.

"Thus [it is] by means of the mantra" refers to the mention of the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ), because it is the designation specifically for the second mantra; there is no connection with the *praṇava* in the first mantra, as it does not exist there.
This is because such an extraction occurs even in the *Tattvabodha* and other texts. Furthermore,

if the reading in the *Mantra* [section] is "a mantra joined with the *praṇava* accomplishes all aims," then the meaning is that by virtue of its conjunction with the *praṇava*, it constitutes a different mantra altogether.

Thus it is said in the Prācīna; in another tantra: "One should extract the seed-syllable of speech consisting of the three principles (*tritattva*), the *tārā* mantra, and at the end [the words] 'Vajravairocanī'; the Blessed One shall then become Māruta. (13–14)
The *kūrca* is *hūṃ*, the weapon (*astra*) is *phaṭ*, and these end with *svāhā* (*dviṭh*). This is declared to be the mantra of the Three Powers (*triśakti*).

The Power (*śakti*) is *hrīṃ*; the three principles (*tritattva*) are *hūṃ*; the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*) is *aiṃ*. The *tāra* is *oṃ*; the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) is *ekāra* (the letter *e*); the wind (*māruto*) is the letter *ya*; the *kūrca* is *hūṃ*; the weapon (*astra*) is *phaṭ*; and it ends with *dviṭha* (*svāhā*).
Svāhā! By that: Hrīḥ Hūṃ Aiḥ Oṃ Vajravairocanīye Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā.
This is the fifteen-syllable mantra of the three powers.
Bhairava is declared to be its sage, O fair-faced one, and the Anuṣṭubh is its meter.
The deity of this [mantra] is Chinnamastā; its seed-syllable is the pair of Māyās (Hrīṃ Hrīṃ). The pair of Māyās constitutes the two Kūrca seeds, namely Hūṃ Hūṃ.
He states another mantra in the *Tattvabodha*:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall also proclaim the sixteen-fold sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The Ramā-kūrca, likewise the Lajjā, the Vag-bhava, the Vajra, and indeed the Pada;
the Rocanī, the Parā, the Dvandva, the Astra-mantra, and the Agni-vallabhā. (13–17)
Ramā (the seed-syllable of Śrī): HŪṂ. Lajjā (the seed-syllable of Modesty): HRĪḤ.
Vāgbhava (the seed-syllable of Speech): AIṂ. O Vajravairocanīye! [Your] own form is Parā, the pair: HRĪḤ HRĪḤ. The Weapon: PHAṬ.
To Agnivallabhā (the Beloved of Fire), SVĀHĀ. And likewise:
Śrī hūṃ hrīṃ aiṃ vajravairocanīye hrīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This is the sixteen-syllable mantra.
The mantra of the three powers (triśakti) is as follows:
And so he speaks another mantra:
"One should utter the word 'Veda' at the beginning for Vajravairocanī; one should say 'Sarva-pada'; likewise for Buddhiḍakī, one should proclaim 'Vajra-mukta'. (13–18)
In the description [of the mantra], there is the sixth letter of Śiva (Ś) conjoined with two vowels and the moon (bindu).
Phaṭ is twofold, followed by Vahni (Ra), Vanitā (Ī), and the syllable Bha; this is the great mantra. (13–19)
222a) The beginning of the Veda is *oṃ*. The essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Vajravairocanī is "sarvabuddha. The essential nature of Vajravarṇanī is "ḍākinīye.
*Śiva* is the letter *ha*; the desired vowel is *ū*; the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*. One should make the moon and the half-moon twofold.
The two seed-syllables are *phaṭ* and the nature of sound (*svarūpa*). *Svāhā* is the consort of fire (*vahnivanitā*). By that [mantra]:

*oṃ vajravairocanīye sarvabuddhi ḍākinīye vajravarṇinīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the twenty-seven-syllable mantra. Now, I shall describe the ritual of worship (*pūjāvidhi*) which bestows all prosperity (*sarvasaubhāgyadāyinī*).
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and so forth, and having meditated upon the Guru at dawn with his head bowed and so forth,
one should worship him with mental offerings. Having paid homage with the words "Salutation to the Gurus," one should meditate upon the Goddess.

Having led the Kulakuṇḍalinī through the Suṣumṇā by means of the armor-mantra (varman) and the piercing of the six cakras, one should contemplate the identity [of the self] with the Supreme Śiva (paraśiva).

One should contemplate one's own body as being pervaded by a mass of light that is the very essence of the bliss of nectar, extending from the base to the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), subtler than a fiber of lotus-stalk.
Having meditated upon oneself as having that form, one should perform external worship.
Having completed the morning rites and having recited [the mantra] according to one's capacity, one should go home. As for the Gāyatrī:
*Oṃ vajravairocanīye vidmahe chinnamastāyai dhīmahi tanno devī pracodayāt* (3).
Having gone home and washed one's hands and feet, one should enter the place of worship and, according to the previously mentioned sequence,

beginning with "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti Kamalāsana," and so forth, draw the *yantra* upon a pedestal made of gold or other materials using red sandalwood, saffron, and the like; then, one should place it in front upon that pedestal as follows:
Having drawn a square with four gates, a circle, and an eight-petaled lotus,
one should draw within its center a radiant mandala consisting of a triangle joined with three lines representing the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; and within that very triangle,
having drawn a lunar mandala (soma-maṇḍala) joined with three lines and two openings, one should place "hūḥ hūḥ" in the middle of the triangle.
And one should write the syllable *phaṭ*.
Having written these three, and having placed them upon the seat as described, [one should say]:
"Homage to the Gurus on the left."
To the right: "Obeisance to Gaṇeśa.
"Obeisance to Chinnamastā, who has severed many [heads].
Having thus paid homage, O beautiful one, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) according to the method stated for the seed-syllable.

Placing his two hands palms-upward on his own lap, with the mantra "So'ham," he should unite the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the *kuṇḍalinī* from the heart through the sequence of piercing the six chakras up to the thousand-petaled lotus according to the previously mentioned method; then,
having dissolved the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth, he should become the beginningless portion that has the form of the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*).

Having meditated upon [the deity] whose head is the slaying of Brahmā, and having joined the *iḍā* at the mouth with the left [nostril], one should place the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth in their respective locations; then, having brought the Goddess into the heart-lotus and placed the hand upon the heart.
Ā HRĪḤ KRĀ HAṂSA MA MA PRĀṆA, and so forth; thus are the five seed-syllables (5).
"O Jīva, remain here thus! Having come here, may all my senses [attain] happiness; may you dwell long; svāhā!"—with this, one should install the Jīva. As follows:
One should perform [the recitation] sixteen times with "Iḍā vakre vā mane sī hūm" and so forth; thus one should do this three times.
Now, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and others: for this mantra, Bhairava is the seer, *samrāṭ* is the meter, Chinnamastā is the deity, and "hūṃ" is the seed-syllable.
The seed-syllable is *svāhā*; the power (*śakti*) is for the attainment of the desired goal; the application (*viniyoga*) is as follows:
salutation to the sage Bhairava on the head;
salutation to the metre *samrāj* and to Chinnamastā.
With palms joined in reverence, [one prays]: "May my desired goal be accomplished. Now follows the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
One should perform the placement on the hands and limbs in the sequence beginning with the little finger, as follows:
Āṃ, svāhā to the sword and the heart, on the two little fingers; ī, to the sword and the ring fingers;
Ūṃ, vauṣaṭ to the vajra and the crest-lock, on the two middle fingers.

Ai! To the noose, for the armor: hūm. To the middle fingers. Oṃ! To the hook, for the three eyes: vauṣaṭ. To the thumbs. For the protection against evil, for the weapon: phaṭ. To the palms and backs of the hands.
Thus, having performed the *maṅganyāsa* and struck the three *tāla* sounds upward and upward, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*).
Then, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

Furthermore, having again assumed the form of the Goddess, one should contemplate her who is like the radiance of the moving moon, the most excellent of lamp-wicks, appearing as a maiden of sixteen years, seated within the mandala. (13-20)
Furthermore, even within the human body, the mantra-form of the Self is the Goddess; I shall now describe her meditation for the sake of accomplishing all desired aims. (13-21)
Iṅgalā, Piṅgalā, and especially Suṣumṇā—the goddess is the union of these three channels, and likewise the threefold qualities (guṇas). || 13-22 ||
White and red, yet with a black body, she is the embodiment of Brahmā, Īśvara, and Viṣṇu;
one should meditate on a pure, white, fully blossomed lotus at one's own navel.
And in the center of that lotus bud is the mandala of Caṇḍaroṣiṇī, resembling the Japā flower and shining like fresh vermilion. (13.24)
And in the center, the Goddess herself is always present, with a radiance equal to ten million suns;
she holds that Goddess upon her own head with her left hand.
With its mouth wide open, terrifying, and licking with its fierce tongue,
it emitted a thick stream of blood flowing from its own throat.
With her mass of hair disheveled, adorned with various ornaments, naked,
most terrible, she stands in the pratyālīḍha posture.
Some yogins meditate upon her as seated for sexual pleasure, while others meditate on her as being in the reverse posture, charming and full of youthful vigor. (13.28)
The goddess, joined by Varṇinī and Ḍākinī on her left and right respectively, is drinking from the stream of blood flowing from her throat. (13.29)
The goddess wears a garland of bones and has the *nārāyaṇa* thread as her sacred cord;
on her left side is the Ḍākinī, who resembles a blazing skull. (13.30)
She whose row of teeth appeared like flashes of lightning,
whose face was formidable with fangs, and who possessed full, swelling breasts.
The Great Goddess, most terrible, with disheveled hair and naked,
licking with her great tongue and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
O best of practitioners, one should meditate upon the Goddess, who, though holding a terrifying skull-cup in her hand, is not at all terrifying herself, and who has been served by the Primordial One.
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall explain in due order:
within one's own navel is a beautiful white lotus, adorned with a circle of solar radiance.
The womb-wheel (yonicakra), properly joined and endowed with the three qualities (guṇa), is there; in its center, one should meditate upon that Great Goddess as the presiding deity. 13-35.
Having assumed the form of a lamp-flame, exceedingly terrifying,
she stands with her hands bound in the *karkaṭikā* gesture, seated in the *baddhapadma* posture.
With the *yonimudrā* joined together, one should visualize Locanā situated in the heart;
this is the meditation on the partless (*niṣkala*), as well as that which abides as the beyond-part (*atikala*). (13.37)
Having meditated thus and worshipped with mental offerings, and having paid obeisance, one should place the *argha* vessel.
It is as follows:
having prepared a triangular mandala and placed a three-legged stand upon it, [one should worship] "Maṃ" for the fire-mandala.

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the one whose self consists of the ten digits," and having washed the argha vessel with "Phaṭ, to the weapon," [he worships] "Oṃ, obeisance to the solar orb" as previously described;
having covered it with the armor-mantra and so forth, and having cast in perfume, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, he [purifies] himself with that water.
One should also prepare the articles of worship; then, having placed [the deity] upon the pedestal atop the yantra, one should worship as follows: "Obeisance to Ādhāraśakti! Obeisance to Kuvera!
Obeisance to Pṛthivī! Obeisance to Surāsamudra!"
Homage to Ratnadvīpa. Homage to Kalpatarudyāna. Homage to Suvarṇavedikā. Homage to the Kalpavṛkṣas.
Homage to the Ratnamaṇḍapa. Homage to the Ratnasiṃhāsana.
Salutation to the bulb of bliss. Salutation to the severed stalk.

Salutation to the lotus whose essence is all principles (*tattva*). Salutation to the petals composed of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Salutation to the filaments consisting of transformation (*vikāra*). Salutation to the pericarp enriched with the fifty seed-syllables.
Aṃ, obeisance to the solar disc consisting of twelve kalās; and so forth. Saṃ, obeisance to sattva. Raṃ, obeisance to rajas. Naṃ, obeisance to tamas.
Āṃ, obeisance to the self (ātman). Aṃ, obeisance to the inner self (antarātman). Paṃ, obeisance to the supreme self (paramātman).
Ṛ / Homage to the Self of Knowledge. Oṃ / Homage to Rati. Klīṃ / Homage to Kāma.
With the root mantra: Homage to the seat of the Goddess Śrī Chinnamastā.
(224a) Thus one should worship.
Then, having led the Kundalini— residing in the Mūlādhāra, in the form of a flame, consisting of light, subtler than a lotus fiber—

through the sequence of piercing the six wheels (cakras) into the Supreme Śiva; and having brought her, who had attained a gross state through the yoga of Śiva, out through the right nostril and drawn her back with a handful of flowers.
Having placed [the object] upon the machine, one should drive it with this:
"Oṃ, O Goddess who bestows all accomplishments, O Varṇanīyā, O bestower of all accomplishments, O Ḍākinī, O Chinnamastā, come, come!
Grant all accomplishment! Stay, stay! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Thus one should recite.
Then, having touched the yantra, one should perform the *prāṇa* [consecration]:
*āḥ hrīḥ kroḥ svāhā*, "O Chinnamastā, [this is] your life-force," and so forth, as previously stated; likewise for all the senses, the limbs, the mind, the eyes, and so on.

Oṃ, O Blessed One Chinnamastā, come here! Stay here! Be present! Be firmly established! Bestow your empowerment here! Accept my worship! Having invoked the Goddess with the mudrās of invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), bringing near (sannidhāpana), firm fixation (sannirodhana), nectarization (amṛtīkaraṇa), total integration (sakalīkaraṇa), and concealment (avaṃguṭhana): oṃ bhagavati chinnamaste ihāgacha iha tiṣṭha saṃnihitā bhava saṃniruddhā bhava atrādhiṣṭātaṃ kuru mama pūjā gṛhāṇa.

Having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon the body of the Goddess, and having again meditated upon the Goddess while holding a flower, one should worship her with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). As follows:
one should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
While reciting the root mantra: "This is the water for the feet (pādya); likewise, [this is] the arghya, svāhā," according to some;

having offered the water for sipping (ācamanīya), the bath-water (snānīya), clothing, ornaments, fragrance, flowers, incense, and lamps, and having brought the food offering (naivedya) before him, one proceeds with the water for the arghya and so forth.

"Naivedyaṃ chinnamastāyai kalpayāmi namaḥ" (I offer this food-oblation to Chinnamastā; salutations). Having thus relinquished [the offering], and having offered the five oblations beginning with "Amṛtopastaraṇam asi svāhā" (Thou art the spreading of nectar, svāhā) and "Prāṇāya svāhā" (To Prāṇa, svāhā) as previously stated, one should contemplate her acceptance [of the offering] and then [offer] "Amṛtāpidhānam asi svāhā" (Thou art the covering of nectar, svāhā).

Having again given water for rinsing the mouth (*apośāna*), one should worship these betel leaves with three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) while reciting: "To Chinnamastā, this flower, *vauṣaṭ*. Then, reciting the root mantra, one should satisfy the Goddess in her mouth three times, [offering] four [times] by way of the right and left [nostrils].
Having worshipped the six limbs in the four directions, one should worship the enclosures as follows:
*Namaḥ* to Gaṇeśa in the northwest (*vāyavyā*); *namaḥ* to the Gurus in the northeast (*aiśānī*);
*namaḥ* to the Paramagurus in the southeast (*āgneyī*); *namaḥ* to Kṣetrapāla in the southwest (*nairṛtī*).

Salutation to Pūrvokta-kara in the east. Salutation to Atikarāla in the south. Salutation to Vikarāla in the west. Salutation to Mahākāla in the north. Salutation to Ādhāra-śakti in the center. Oṃ, salutation to Kūrma. Oṃ, salutation to Ananta.
Oṃ, salutation to the Earth. Oṃ, salutation to the Root of Bliss (Ānandakanda). Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa. Oṃ, salutation to the Lotus. Oṃ, salutation to the Pericarp (Karṇikā).
Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to the Solar Orb (Arkamaṇḍala), whose self consists of twelve digits (kalās).
Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to the lunar maṇḍala, whose nature consists of sixteen digits.
Maṃ, obeisance to the fiery maṇḍala, whose nature consists of ten digits.
Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to sattva. Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to rajas. Oṃ taṃ, obeisance to tamas.
Oṃ, obeisance to Rati. Oṃ, obeisance to Kāma.
Having thus worshipped, one should worship on the petals in the leftward order of the Goddess:
Oṃ Hrīḥ, obeisance to Ekaliṅgā. Oṃ Hrīḥ, obeisance to Yoginī.
Oṃ hrīḥ! Homage to the Ḍākinī! Oṃ hrīḥ! Homage to Bhairavī! Likewise to Indrāṇī. To Asitāṅga! Likewise to Saṃhāriṇī. In the center:
Homage to the Goddess on the Lion Throne! The Goddess to the south.

Oṃ krīṃ! Homage to Prakṛti Valinī on the left. Likewise, having worshipped with "Homage to Prakṛti Ḍākinī," one should again worship the Goddess with perfumes and other offerings, and honor her with three handfuls of flowers.
One should offer an oblation (*bali*) consisting of meat and other items. The mantra for the oblation is as follows:
*oṃ sarvabuddhiprade vi varṇanīya sava siddhiprade ḍākiniye chinnamaste ehyehi imaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa 2 hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having thus offered the bali-oblation, having visualized oneself in that form, and having paid homage to the Guru, one should first recite the Gāyatrī of the Goddess; then one should recite the root mantra one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times.
As for the Gāyatrī, it is as previously stated; once that has been recited, one should recite the root mantra.

Then, having completed the recitation (*japa*) and performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should take a flower and, with the mantra beginning "The secret of secrets" (*guhyātiguhyam*), offer the essence of the recitation into the left hand of the Goddess.
Having presented *sāmāmbūla* with the root mantra, offered praise, and performed a prostration like a staff, one should sit down and then [proceed] with the water for the guest-offering (*argha*).

Whatever was previously performed within the jurisdiction of the vital breath, intellect, body, and duties—namely, the states of waking, dreaming, and so forth; that which was done by means of mind and speech, through the six [senses], through the belly, and so on; and whatever other actions were performed—all that shall be an offering to Brahman, Svāhā! To Śrī Chinnamastā, who is both "I" and "mine," I offer this.

Having thus offered himself along with his retinue to the Goddess, and having again performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he says, "O Blessed One Chinnamastā, you have been worshipped; may there be well-being," and taking a flower from the worship-mandala with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, he smells it while holding it.
Through the nostril, one should pray with the *namas-mantra* for the Goddess to come into one’s own heart:
“Oṃ! Born on the northern peak, dwelling upon the mountain of the earth, arisen from the womb of Brahmā—come, O Goddess, into my interior! (13.38)

Reciting thus, having led the Goddess within, established her in one's heart, and meditated upon oneself as being of that same form, one should place the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering) upon the head, drink the nectar of her feet, and dwell in happiness as one pleases.
Thus ends the *Śrīcinnamastā-pūjā-paddhati*. Now follows the *Chinnamastā-sahasranāma*.
Salutations to Chinnamastā.
The Great Goddess had a hundred faces and many hundreds of heads;
at the mere sight of her, Bhairava was struck with wonder. (13.39)
Bhairava said:
O Lord of Gods, O Bull-bannered One, the Goddess assumes various forms; she is of terrible appearance and fearsome. I wish to hear [of her]; please tell me. (3) 13-40.
Listen, my child, I shall proclaim out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
even one who merely knows this shall become the Lord of the Universe himself, as manifest by the Goddess. (13.41)
The secret more secret than the secret, the elixir of mantra-yoga, is the great distinction of various mantras; there are various meditations, yet no vehicle. (4) 13-42
"O child, I have understood this supreme thousand names;
formerly, Saṃhārabhairavī was recited before me in the past. (13.43)
O Great Hero, though unmanifest, even the noble heroes have been made manifest.

Of this mantra of the Thousand Names of the Glorious Hṛllekhā, Ānandabhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda), and Chinnamastā is the deity (devatā). Its application (viniyoga) is in recitation for the sake of attaining the fourfold aims of human life (caturvarga-puruṣārtha).
Oṃ! The goddess Triguṇā is of the nature of tamas; she is Karālī, the destroyer of time, Mṛtyumāri, the great intellect, and the liberator from the noose of time. (7) || 13-44 ||
The Goddess consists of the three qualities, yet she transcends the qualities; she is the supreme Śakti.
She is Yoganidrā, Mahāmāyā, beyond yoga, and the supreme Self. (8) || 13-45 ||
Vindu, Nāda, Kalā, Vālīśā, Khinī, Nādagarjinī, Kriyākāṇḍajanī, Kūrā, Padmagarbhā, and Prabodhinī. (9) 13-46 ||
The moving self, the restless one, the wheel-bearer, the one who obstructs the sequence of the six wheels;
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Piṅgā, Suṣumnā, and Sarasvatī. (10) 13-47.
Paśyantī, Pādyamāvāṇī, Vaiśvarī, Jāghanāśinī, Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, and the supreme [Śākinī]. (11) || 13-48 ||
Śākinī, Hākinī, and Yākinī, who brings about speed; she who is the state of equanimity, the lover of aesthetic flavor, and the increaser of semen and blood. (12) || 13-49 ||
Tapaśvinī, Tapaśighrā, Aparṇī, Pāpanāśinī, Aruṇā, Vaktrā, Candravaktrā, and Padminī. (13-50)
With eyes like those of a deer, she was as graceful as a doe with the gaze of a gazelle;
she was deeply bent by the weight of her breasts, possessed slender limbs, and wore a girdle around her waist. (14) || 13-51 ||
The Vidyā residing in the triangle, whose mark is the syllable *ḍi*, whose form is the *bindu*, red in color, the great womb, her body covered with matted hair. (13-52)
She has a deep waist, is mature, possesses throbbing auspicious hips, delights in bowing, is beloved, and wields the flower-arrowed god’s bow of radiant beauty. (16) || 13-53 ||

Pañcālī, she who possesses five arrows, she who dwells in five places; she of three forms, she of three steps, the wholesome one, she of the triple city, and she whose nature consists of three steps. (13.54)

She who possesses three fires and three notes, she who is swift, she who illuminates the three worlds, she who sings from her mouth, she of restless eyes, and she who is fond of the tilaka mark of vermilion. (13-55)
She was like a female elephant, intoxicated and yet not wild, her limbs heavy with rut, afflicted by passion, endowed with fresh youth, and her eyes rolling with intoxication. (19) 13-56.
O Kālī, marked by the Lord of Desire, O passionate one, you who are the limit of desire;
O you whose form is twelve years of age, you who long for the play of love. (13-57)
In her sixteenth year, the young woman Mālatī, with full and elevated breasts, was both naked and yet wearing a garland of jasmine flowers. (21) 13.58
Fierce and having the form of a skeleton, she who destroys at the terrible time; she who is the skeletal one, whose face is Time, and who conforms to the faces of the various mouths. (22) || 13-59 ||
With a flickering tongue, she blows forth [her breath] from her mouth, which is dear to her;
