her hair is disheveled, her eyes are red, and she is adorned with black earrings. (13-60)
She who wears a garland of skulls and skull-ornaments, she whose garland is wine, she who licks the hālāhala poison;
she who has a dark-blue banner, she who is blue-limbed, and she who dwells in the sky. (24) || 13-61 ||
Tārā, who delights in the sequence of the Caine [mantra] and carries one across the waters of existence;
Siddhakālī, Mahākālī, Bhadrakālī, O wielder of the Pināka bow! (26) || 13-62 ||
Kulukā, Siddharātri, Padmāvatī, the beloved of Hari;
Lakṣmī, Kāmāturā, Kāntā, Dhuti, and Śrīharivallabhā. (26) || 13-63 ||
Haridrā, Śīharāharā, Nṛsiṃhanāśinī, Khaḍginī, Khaḍgahastā, Vajreśī, and Vajravallabhā. (27) || 13-64 ||
She is the one who bestows color, whose form is color, whose essence is color, and who dwells within the forest of colors;
she is Pūtamī, Pūtanā, the purified one, the Ḍākinī, and she whose nature is the Ḍāmara. (28) || 13-65 ||
She who wields the trident, she whose hand holds the trident, she who dwells upon the peak of Trikūṭa;
she who is supreme, she whose limbs are supreme, and she who dwells within the supreme body. (29) || 13-66 ||
She who has serpents for her head-ornament, serpents for her girdle, and serpents for her purification;
she whose stream flows upwards, who supports the earth, who is red, whose limbs are red, and whose eyes are red. (30) || 13-67 ||
Always delighting in drinking blood, she is intoxicated by the passion of the channels;
she is Muṇḍinī and Muṇḍalā, Ruḍinī and Ruḍakallabhā. (31) || 13-68 ||
Holding a skull-bowl in her hand, adorned with eight serpents, she is the creeper, the great vine, shining with vajra-flowers. (32) || 13-69 ||
Indravallī, Somavallī, Muravallī, Śaṅkhinī, Mādhavī, Madapūrṇā, Vāruṇī, and Varuṇāpriyā. (33) 13-70.
The Gauḍī liquor is the favorite of the Gauḍas; the Mādhūkī intoxicates one into a state of exhilaration;
the Drākṣajā bestows sovereignty; and the Kharjūrī destroys enemies. (34) || 13-71 ||
She is proclaimed as the giver of grain and the giver of wealth, the beloved of the mountain, Mātaṅgī, intoxicated by her mace, the lady of Kāśmīra, and rosy with saffron. (35) || 13-72 ||
She holds a skull-topped staff, moves through the sky, is short of stature, possesses beautiful hair, and has eyes like those of a fish;
she is adorned with a braid of flowers and creepers, and is decorated with a crown of matted locks. (36) || 13-73 ||
Kinnarī, Kinnarā-kanyā, Yakṣaṇī, Dakṣajātmikā, Cācarī, Caturāṅgī, Caturāṅgī, and Vāturīreśvarī. (37) || 13-74 ||
Mārdhavī, Gandharūpā, Nāgakanyā, Sureśvarī, Ekavīrā, Vīrasthā, and [the goddess] who dwells in * * *. (38) || 13-75 ||
Vīreśī, Vīramātā, Vīrapatnī, Vasundharā;
Rājeśī, Rajanī, Rājñī, Rājapatnī, Rajeśvarī. (39) || 13-76 ||
Kuraṅgī, Malinī, Śyāmā, Pītā, Kṛṣṇā, Karburā, Puṣpiṇī, Puṣpahastā, and Supuṣpākīrṇakomalā. (40) 13-77.
A woman who delights in another man, though she be a woman of noble family, well-vowed, chaste, devoted to her husband, virtuous, beautiful in form, and a universal yoginī— (41) || 13-78 ||
A mother, a sister, a woman of one's own womb, a daughter, or a woman of noble family; one with hanging lips, protruding teeth, red limbs, or who is entirely red—(42) 13-79.
Tripurā is the three-syllabled seed-mantra that destroys the fear of Bhairavī;
she is the Self, Māyā, the Great Mantrī, Hallekhā, and the beloved of Hara. (43) 13-80
Lajjā, Rasavatī, Devī, Pārvatī, Bhuvaneśvarī,
Bhautikī, Śukravarṇā, Raktāṅgī, and Madanākṣarā— (44) || 13-81 ||
Śivā, Abhyāsā, Sarasvatī, Śakra-sthā, Vālikā, Kulasundarī, Gaganā, Candravarṇā, Anālambinī, and Kṛteśvarā. (45) 13-82 ||
Vindu, Nāda, Kalā, Padmā, together with Śiva and Śakti;
Avarṇā, Revatī, Lolākṣī, and Vinduvallabhā. (46) 13-83.
Vipat, Priyā, Sahajā, Vahni, Colkamukhī, Madā, Cakriṇī, Triguṇā, and Māyā, endowed with the digits of Nāda and Bindu. (47) || 13-84 ||
The glorious Mantripurabhairavī is joined with the half-moon; likewise, there are the two *kūrca*s, *māyā*, and Dakṣiṇakālikā. (48) 13-85
The seed-syllables ending in *jā* with the fire (*ra*) are the supreme leaders of mantras;
the woman who delights in the reverse [position] during sexual union is the bestower of boons. (49) 13-86
She who possesses the three genders and the three forms, dwelling within the intermediate corners;
Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Siddhā, Kāverī, and Śatarudrikā. (50) 13.87
Sarayu, Candrabhaga, Varmanvati, Vedika, Girija, Gahvara, Vasi, Totila, and Tilakapriya— (51) || 13-88 ||
Kaulinī, Nīlarūpā, Dīpinī, Asthimālinī, Puṣpāvatī, Mahānīlā, and likewise Sarvasaṃpatpradā. (52) || 13-89 ||
Your form consists of the seven elements, you are composed of the five [elements], and the five-fold five;
you dwell in the cremation grounds, possess a terrifying form, and reside under a solitary tree. (53) || 13-90 ||
Bhasmāṅgī, Bhayarūpā, Bhāvīnī, Bhasmavanditā, Unmattā, Mātaṅgī, Cāṇḍālī, Cañcalā, and Nalā (54). || 13-91 ||
Śavarī, Śāṃvarī, Māyā, Sumakhī, Mukharañjanī, Nṛgalā, Vallavī, Śakti, Pītavarṇā, and Viśāradā. (55) || 13-92 ||
The Trailokyavijayā Vidyā, Jayantī, Jaṅghākariṇī, the goddess Pratyaṅgirā, Aṅgirā, Toyadā, and Adrpaṭṭikā— (56) || 13.93 ||
She is both salty and saltless in form, and she is fond of sea salt;
she laughs with loud, boisterous laughter, for she is the beloved of Hāṭṭa Ḍivāha. (57) 13-94
From Tārāvajra come Kiravīrā and Svarūpā, as well as Aṭṭahāsā;
likewise, the pair of Māyās and Svavidyā grant success when born from the fire-syllable. (58) 13-95.
Lakṣmī, endowed with the fulfillment of desires, and Chinnamastā, the bestower of victory; she is white and dark-hued, and always wears white garments. (59) 13-96
The teeth are bright white like the month of Śukra, marked with white lines, and polished;
they are neither too red nor pale, not discolored or crooked, and the lips are red. (60) 13.97.
With her limbs smeared with red sandalwood, the beautiful one has a corpse as her leader;
she is the black-colored Mahākālī, the skeleton who deceives Death. (61) || 13-98 ||
Ghoradṛṣṭrā, Karālī, Bhīmanādā, and Bhayānakī;
Hā hā, Hu hu, Kahā, Kāra, Kahakahā, Ha dahā. (62) || 13-99 ||
She whose nature consists of laughter, terror, sport, and play;
she who is both the striker and the one being struck—by her, the remover of sins, [I am protected]. (63) 13-100
Trotinī, Sphoṭinī, Sphoṭā, Śṛṅkhalāvaddhavardhinī, Sarvabhakṣakārī, Bhadrā, and Śatrupakṣavimardinī. (64) || 13-101 ||
The upward-streaming [river] grants satisfaction to ten million;
she who rains blood, the great red one of Varuṇa, is intensely red and fond of sinners. (65) || 13-102 ||
Kaṭākṣīkā, Vedā, Kāmālī, Kaṭicañcalā, Sphuradyoti, Mahoyoni, Dṛḍhayoni, and Sulomajā. (66) || 13-103 ||
The line of body hair is the great sky; she is wavy and playful on the stage of the limbs;
she is the sister, the garland of the vulva, and the one who increases the joy of the Lord of Orgasm. (67) || 13-104 ||
She who possesses fortune and she who bestows fortune; she who is the beloved of the Blessed One;
she who arises from the *liṅga* and whose form is the *liṅga*; she who is the auspicious *liṅga* and the nourisher of the *liṅga*. (68) || 13-105 ||

She is poisonless yet has the form of poison; she is the Great Destroyer and the Divider; she has the form of the *mādivī* plant and the *iṅgada*; she is the Delighting One, blazing with intoxication. (69) || 13-106 ||
Śoṣiṇī, Dāhanī, Dīrghā, Sukośavallabhā, Trikaṭā, Triśarā, Bhillā, Tripuṭā, and Putranāśinī. (70) || 13-107 ||
She who possesses afflictions and holds afflictions in her hand, she who moves upon the earth and is beloved by the Lord of the Earth;
she who causes the setting [of the sun] and is greatly wrathful, she who is fleshless and yet fond of meat. (71) || 13-108 ||
Slightly reddish and with red eyes, adorned with matted hair and ashes, wearing an elephant hide, naked, and decorated with human skin and bones. (72) || 13-109 ||
Pretinī, Pretavṛndā, and she who dwells in the abode of the pretas;
the illusion of the pretas, the great preta, the bestower of liberation from the state of a preta. (73) || 13-110 ||
And there was a cat, worn out by old age, born of a paramour, yet increasing affection;
she was modesty, sleep, and the bliss of compassion, belonging to that lineage and character of the Yuga. (74) 13-111.
Vedavidyā, Gāndhārī, Gaṇikā, Naṭatāriṇī, Yajñadīkṣā, Mahādīkṣā, and Yogadīkṣā, O Yoginī. (75) 13-112
She possesses manifold artistic designs, is like a serpent, a garland of flames, and is free from blemish;
she is the mistress of the city of Nāgas, ever humble toward the lords of men, and always fond of verses and songs. (13-113)
She is the youthful, radiant playfulness, mature in her grace, and the beloved of the fifth note;
she is the defining characteristic, the giver of a hundred thousand boons, the embodiment of a hundred thousand forms, and whose essence is consciousness. (77) 13-114
She is the form of the bindu, the Great Coarse One, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Rātrikā;
she is like lightning, the form of the clouds, having the bindu as her face, and the Destroyer. (78) 13-115
Dāruṇī, Dānadātrī, Bhāminī, Bhagavīhvalā, Kauverī, Kuraṅgākṣī, Kuṭilā, and Kūṭavallabhā. (79) || 13-116 ||
Puṣpāvatī is the great Puṣpā; she is clothed in blue flowers and is most excellent.
Her body is smeared with musk and camphor, and her crest is marked with gorocanā. (80) 13-117.
Nupurā, Kaṅkaṇā, Kāñcī, Dāminī, Meghamālikā, Kṛṣṇadantā, Vimbauṣṭhī, Hemāṅgī, and Mṛduhāsinī. (81) || 13-118 ||
She who devours the blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen of the goat;
she who is in the elephant, the horse, and the lion; the Yakṣī who destroys the Yakṣas. (82) || 13-119 ||
Māhiṣī, Mahiṣāmāri, Sūkarī, Jantughātakī, Śākambharī, Śivā, Durgā, and the beloved Naranārāyaṇī. (83) || 13-120 ||
She is short-statured yet has rounded eyes, and she is fond of the sword and the blue lotus;
she is the agitator of the unagitated, the agitation itself, appearing in the form of a serpent, and possessing three forms. (84) 13-121.
The funeral pyre is indeed dispassionate, and the funeral pyre is eternally perishable;
it has the form of a bound cloth and banner, adorned with the five mudrās.
She is the embodiment of all mantras, manifest as the very nature of the syllable *Dha*; she is the will for creation and maintenance, the great cause of the cycle of existence. (86) 13-123
She consists of drops and half-drops, she is made of crystal, she possesses a hooded serpent;
she is seated upon the throne of Śiva, mounted upon a bull, and her nature is the pratyālīḍha stance. (87) || 13-124 ||
She has the appearance of a sword-belt and a banner, adorned with the five mudrās;
she possesses a goad and acts with the skill of a goad, raining down nectar upon nectar. (88) || 13-125 ||
Idrāṇī, Indramāyā, Īśvarī, Indravigrahā, Umā, Ūrdhagatī, Gaṅgā, Urdhānnā, and Mantranāyakā. (89) || 13-126 ||
In Māgha, she is Ruṣṭiṛkāriṇī, the one who effects the sounds *lī* and *ḷ*;
she is Ekadantā, the single-toothed one, established upon the support of the vowel *ai*. (13.127)
Oṣadhī is the sustainer of vision, Auṣadhā is the healer, Aṃvikā is the giver of food, Visargā is established in creation and preservation. (91) 13-128
Kapilā, Piṅgalā, Piṅgākṣī, Tisvarā, Ṛddhidhāriṇī, Gālinī, Gomati, Godhā, Ghargharā, Ghūrṇā, and Nāyakā. (92) || 13-129 ||

She whose nature is the syllable *ṅa*, the knowledge (*vidyā*) consisting of the syllable *ṅā*, the Mistress of the Multicolored One (*Citreśī*), the Beloved of the Multicolored One (*Citravallabhā*), she who has severed the eye of the goddess Lāchilā, the Bestower of Victory (*Jayadā*), and the Increaser of Victory (*Jayavardhinī*). (93) || 13-130 ||
Jhaṃkārī, Jhaṇṭaṇākārā, Jhāṇinī, Jamavallabhā; Ṭīpaṇi, Ṭopadāruṣṭā, Ṭaṃkāri, Dviṭhavallabhā. (94) || 13-131 ||
Ḍāmarī, holding a hand-drum, she who performs fierce and playful gestures, ṇīṇāpīrūṇā, the destroyer, Tānasī, and the piercer of mantras. (95) || 13-132 ||
Sthānī, Nisthānamānyā, Nalinī, Nālavallabhā, Dāminī, Dīrghakeśī, Dīrghajihvā, and Dayāvatī. (96) || 13-133 ||
Dhāriṇī, Dharā, Dhārā, Sūndharā, and Dharadhāriṇī;
born of men, having the form of a man, the mother of men, the great ocean. (97) || 13-134 ||
She who possesses arrows, she who wears a garland of leaves, she who rests upon a lotus petal;
she who utters "phaṭ," she who is the science of weapons, she is Bhavānī, the savior from worldly existence. (98) || 13-135 ||
The one who brings awakening, the knowledge of awakening, the bestower of boons, the one who utters the supreme sound;
she who grants devotion, she who is endowed with devotion, and she who increases the state of devotion. (99) || 13-136 ||
Mātari, Mātareśā, and Mātulī are the eight Mothers;
Yaśasvinī, Yaśaḥśīghrā, and Yaśodānandanandajā. (13.137)
Rohiṇī, the remover of disease, Rodanī, Rocanā, Priyā, Lakṣmī, she who is full of auspicious marks, Latā, Līlā, and Sulakṣaṇā. (13.138)
Vallivāṇī, Vāgīśī, the bestower of the bliss of Vāgbhava, Śoṣiṇī, the mother of Śoṣa, Viśokā, and the destroyer of sorrow. (2) || 13-139 ||
She is the Sixteenth, consisting of sixteen syllables, and the beloved of the sixteen vowels;
she is the Innate, the Sāvitrī, the Hāṭṭakī, and the Hāṭakīśvarī. (13–140)
She is the one who utters the syllable *kṣe*, the bringer of security, the mistress of the field (*kṣetra*), and the one who increases the destruction [of defilements].
She is of the mind, possessing the form of the mind, and is entirely devoted to meditation. (4) || 13-141 ||
She is the purifier, the purifier, the digestive process, the dramatic performance, and she who possesses nine leaders.
She bears the peak of fire, she is the supporter, the gastric fire, and she who dwells in the Vindhya mountains. (5) || 13-142 ||
Ameghā, Meghamālā, Sāttvikī, Śailavāsinī, Rājasī, Ratnamālā, and the highly exalted Ratnamālā. (6) 13-143.
The *Tāmasī-tantramālā* and the *Mālinī-dīpamālikā*, O Maheśānī, dweller in the Akula and Kula, are the givers of liberation. (7) 13-144.
The mantra Vardhinī increases prosperity, Vyādhihartī removes disease, Kākini restores the dead to life, Parāparāyaṇī is the supreme refuge, and Pūrvāmnā is the increaser of joy. (8) 13-145.
Dakṣiṇā, Paścimā, Śrā, and Uttarāmnā are the leaders;
Hūti, Hūti, Priyā, Kānti, Garbhiṇī, and Bhargavāsinī. (13–146)
Vandhyā, Vandhyanivāsinī, Śūlinī, Mahiṣamardinī, Dvārikā, Madhurā, Māyā, Ayodhyā, and Yuddhavallabhā. (10) || 13-147 ||
Niśā, Niśācarī, Rātri, Mahārātri, Tapodhanā;
Gāyatrī, Gāruḍī, Māyā, Gambhīrā, Abhī, Bhīmavallabhā. (13–148)
She who possesses the splendor of the half-woman, the half-man; Gaurī, who rides upon the bull;
Caṇḍamuṇḍapracaṇḍā; Maheśvarī, who wears a garland of skulls. (12) 13-149.
O impeller, O agitator, O you who are hungry, O dweller in the abode of the lowly;
O you whose dwelling is Śrīnivāsa, O virtuous consort of Śrī, O bestower of treasures upon the Lord of Śrī. (13–150)
Mālinī, Mālatī, Mālā, Bhavānī, Bhavatāriṇī, Kavargā, Vargasaṃsthā, Nityaklinnā, and Sureśvarī. (14) || 13-151 ||
Vārtyālī, Vārāhī, Viśvavandyā, Vināyakā, Maṅgalā, Bhīruṇḍā, Tvaritā, and Śīghraphaladā. (15) || 13-152 ||
She is the accomplishment, the delight of the *ḍākinīs*, adorned with the crest-jewel of Alakā;
she is the knowledge, the sovereign of knowledge, the universal one, praised by Meru and Amaru. (16) 13-153.
Nandinī, Merupṛṣṭhā, Merupṛṣṭhanivāsinī, Candramaulinī, and Candrāṅgī—these four [names] correspond respectively to the three [mantras]. (13-154)
Sarpā, Sarpavirūḍhā, Sarpinī, Bhagasarpinī, Nigrahā, Graharūpā, Grahamālā, and Vivardhinī. (18) || 13-155 ||
Slow-moving, she who surpasses fire in her movement, she who possesses motion;
she who is stationary, she who is stable, she who is firm, she whose limbs are firm, and she who moves with steadiness. (19) || 13-156 ||
The moving one, the knowledge that moves, the female form of yoga, the beloved of yoga;
the knife, she who has the shape of a knife, the small knife, she who performs cutting. (20) || 13-157 ||
Śṛṅkhalā, Kuśahastā, Pāśadharī, Cāpadharī, Dhanurdharī, Aśvadā, Gajadā, Ratnadā, and Laliteśvarī. (21) 13-158.
The great vidyā Hṛllocanā bestows success upon practitioners;
one should recite it daily at the three junctions of the day, whether pure or impure. (22) 13-159.
Even though born into a noble family, he alone became a protector of the earth; at that time, there was neither sorrow for the householder nor separation from loved ones. (23) 13-160 ||
Free from disease, she gives birth; enemies have met their destruction.
This [mantra] constantly bestows knowledge, long life, glory, fame, and auspiciousness. (24) 13-161.
Whoever recites this supreme thousand names ten times, having brought about both worldly enjoyment and liberation, shall attain proximity to Śiva. (25) 13-162.
Thus ends the complete *Chinnamastā Sahasranāmastotra* within the *Rudrayāmala Tantra*, in the dialogue between Śiva and Bhairava.
Now follows the hymn to Chinnamastā.
Oṃ! At the navel, in the center of a radiant white lotus, is a brilliant solar disc as red as a *bandhūka* flower; within its interior is the great wheel of yogis (*yogicakra*).
In its center is Pradyumna, intent on inverted sexual union, who sustains that [disc].
She stands upon his back, possessing a nature of splendor that shines like ten million rising suns. || 13-163 ||
In her left hand she holds a severed head, and in her other hand a large knife; she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, naked, with her mass of hair disheveled upward,
and intent on drinking the streams of blood spurting from her own severed head.
Shining with a radiance equal to the rising sun, resplendent with three eyes. || 13-164 ||
Other than from Rāma, the Nāḍī flows intensely with streams of blood falling profusely;
she who is adorned with bones, possessing the form of a fair-browed maiden, holding a shining lotus and a knife, red in hue with reddened hair, her garment submerged in water— this is his own Śakti.
The Yoginī Pratyālīḍhārūpā holds a damaru and a skull-cup in her left hands, and displays the yoga-mudrā in her right hands. (3) || 13-165 ||
[He beheld] his own form as one naked, with disheveled hair, possessing a terrible appearance like a mass of clouds at the end of an aeon,
fierce and difficult to behold, with the tips of her flickering tongues flashing from the cavities of her mouths;
with a pair of eyes darting like lightning and a female serpent gliding upon the slope of her heart.
The *Ḍākinī* Dharmayati [is present] at the freshly severed neck where blood is flowing. (13.166)

I take refuge in Chinnamastā, the praised Mother of the three worlds, who is the essence within saṃsāra; whose bliss-bestowing feet are placed upon the heads of Brahmā, Indra, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others; who is contemplated incessantly at every step by those self-knowing ones, the foremost of yogis, as the very form of the thinkable. 230b)
I contemplate with my mind that beloved goddess, the bestower of desired boons, who removes the impurities of the Kali age. (5) || 13-167 ||
If Brahmā, Acyuta, and Śūlapāṇi are merely transformations of the world due to the three guṇas, assuming bodies of three forms to effect its creation, maintenance, and destruction,
then I meditate in my mind upon the primordial, manifold Prakṛti for the perfect attainment of my goal.
Those who possess longing for the pair of lotus-feet of the Lord of the Mind are like swans [in their devotion]. (6) || 13-168 ||
I am one for whom the city of women is [adorned with] wine and flesh; I am worship through the enjoyment of sensory delights;
I am honored by the undertaking of various kula-rites;
I am averse to the state of the fettered (paśu); I am established as Bhairavī.
I am the one whose feet are the Guru; I am Bhairava; I am Śiva. (7) || 13-169 ||
This hymn of great merit was spoken by Brahmā in the past;
whoever, having risen in the morning, recites it—whether a god, a human, or even a pitṛ—[attains the highest reward]. (13.170)
Upon its accomplishment, O Goddess, there shall arise the attainment of desired objects;
one will certainly obtain wealth, grain, sons, a wife, horses, elephants, the earth, and the Great Vidyā—these eight siddhis. (13–171)
Thus ends the hymn to Chinnamastā in the Brahmayāmala.

Now follow the rites for the fulfillment of specific desires.
One should cast white flowers for the purposes of enjoyment, liberation, and pacification; for attraction and subjugation, one should specifically prescribe red flowers.
For the mantras of paralyzing and bewildering, one should cast yellow flowers;
for driving away and killing, one should cast only black [flowers]. (13.178)
In all rites performed for specific desires (kāmyakarman), there should be meditation on the deity according to the color of the flower.
"According to the color of the flower" means that one should meditate upon the deity as having the same color as the flower with which the worship is performed.
At night, an offering of oblations (bali) should be presented with fish, meat, and other such delicacies.
Alternatively, through the abundance of wealth such as the drinking of honey-wine and other luxuries, that glorious one, devoted to service toward his guru, spoke thus. (13.180)

One should recite the mantra, for by doing so one is indeed liberated from all sins; yet this cannot be accomplished without those two [fish and meat], as well as all other [forbidden foods]. (13.181)
The Goddess does not grant the accomplishment of mantras if the offering consists of meat and cooked rice;
therefore, with every effort, an offering should always be given using substitutes.
Without material offerings (*āmiṣa*), the Goddess does not grant satisfaction there.
And "Sure" refers to the *ramā* class. For this very reason, he states a distinction regarding other powers (*vāmaśakti*) even among the twice-born (*dvija*).
Alternatively, some maintain that in the compound *madhupāna*, it is a *dvandva* (meaning drinking together), whereas *kṣīra* and so forth are indeed *karmadhārayas*.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of connection (*ananvaya*) in the *validāna* (offering). The *validāna* mantra is written in the *Pūjāpaddhati*:
"Lack of resolve, internal obstacles, and lack of faith in the act of recitation [constitute hindrances]. (13.183)
Laziness, cowardice, lack of power, loss of the mantra, lack of firm resolve, the fault of women, hatred, impurity, and even Yama—none of these [obstruct the practitioner]. (13.184)
Because the mantra has been perfected, there is no need here for the exertion of practicing through the [four] ages; whether awake or asleep, do not rise, nor eat, nor engage in sexual intercourse.
One should always recite the mantra that bestows the desired accomplishment;
having written the mantra on one's own hand, a person should touch the patient.
One is liberated from disease by means of Hara, and long life is attained;
by the mere meditation on Śukla, one may even raise a dead man back to life.
One who has been bitten by hundreds of mahoragas can certainly be raised from death;
by means of blood, all beings come under one's control and the entire world is drawn in. (13-188)
By means of yellow [meditation], one may paralyze the entire world or the likes of the gods;
by means of black meditation, a person may drive away an enemy.
O Kṛṣṇa, one should honor [the deity] effortlessly through meditation; of this there is no doubt.
One should also perform a libation with milk or with milk-rice (pāyasa).
The practitioner of mantras [should offer oblations] with clarified butter, honey, or wine, according to the sequence for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. (13.191)
Through the performance of the *tarpaṇa* rite, accomplishment arises by force. Likewise:
"The Brahmins should be satiated with milk, and those born of the royal lineage with clarified butter. (13.192)
With honey from those of the Vaiśya caste and with fermented liquors from those of the Śūdra class,
one should then perform the rite of victory (jaya), by which success (siddhi) arises.
Having recited one hundred thousand times his own mantra, one shall obtain the desired accomplishment;
O Goddess, everything is accomplished through recitation and fire-offerings, without a doubt. (13.194)
Now I shall describe the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa), which bestows all accomplishments;
having first prepared the mandala according to the rules, facing the east.
One should perform the installation of the fire within a six-cornered mandala;
thereafter, one should carry out the fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial wood, flowers, and grains.
A fire sacrifice (homa) performed here with great effort using *śrīphala*, *palāśa*, and likewise *udumbara* wood, bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
Having performed one hundred and eight [repetitions], one should then perform the recitation;
thereafter, a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with *mālatī* flowers mixed with honey.
Or even when combined with ghee, it bestows the status of Lord of Speech;
an offering should always be made with cooked rice mixed with clarified butter and meat.
For one who practices diligently for six months, his prosperity shall become stable.
Likewise, goat meat soaked in bright red ghee [should be offered]. (13.200)
The king shall come under the control of that person who offers ten million oblations with white *karavīra* flowers and performs the fire sacrifice correctly.

By performing the rite with just one hundred thousand [offerings], one who is bitten by a venomous snake while still alive may offer thousands of *karṇikāra* flowers together with clarified butter. (13.203)
O beautiful goddess, by offering ten thousand *bandhūka* flowers into the fire, he attains the supreme perfection he desires. (13.204)

The goddess of that [mantra] becomes pleased, bestowing the fruit of all accomplishments (siddhi), for whoever performs the oblation (homa) of sesame seeds and rice grains with clarified butter. (13.205)
O beautiful goddess, the worlds become his friends;
by practicing for just one month at the three junctions of the day, he shall attain the state of Vāgīśvara.
Thus, O Goddess, the sequence of the fire-offering (homa) rite has been described by me;
furthermore, I shall explain another [procedure] specifically for the fulfillment of desires.
One should offer the flesh of a lizard with honey using the left hand;
even the gods will come under one's control, let alone insignificant mortals.
O fair-faced one, by performing a fire-oblation with the meat of a Ruru deer and clarified butter,
one attains every accomplishment, even those difficult for the gods to obtain.
O beautiful one, having offered buffalo marrow together with honey, one may paralyze the army of enemies even when it is situated at a great distance. (13.210)
O Daughter of the Best of Mountains, O Auspicious One, by offering oblations of *caṇupaka* mixed with clarified butter for a long time,
you paralyze even a most terrible enemy army.
In the Sadyoga rite, one should offer meat with blood accompanied by liquor;
indeed, the accomplishment of all success shall then come into his hand. (13.212)
If one performs the homa with jackal fat at night while reciting the mantra, he would become equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), yet he would cause the ruin of the kingdom. (13.213)
He who performs one hundred thousand oblations with *śrīphala* fruits, *palāśa* fruits, and *udumbara* fruits,
shall become equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
O Goddess, the best of practitioners should offer one hundred and eight oblations of human flesh mixed with honey at the three junctions of the day. (13.215)
If one recites it while touching the entire earth, there is no doubt that within six months the ḍākinīs, filled with affection, will bestow sovereignty upon him. (13.216)
He who offers a hundred thousand oblations of *kokilā* flowers into the funeral fire brings about the destruction of his enemies, even those situated far away. (13.217)
If an oblation is performed with crow feathers in a fire of *patrūga* wood,
mixed with the oil of *ālotryaka* and pungent substances, it effects immediate bewitchment and killing.
One should likewise perform a square for pacification and attraction;
for subjugation, a triangle; and likewise for killing and expulsion. (13.219)

The wise one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is circular and shaped like a mandala for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; likewise, O Goddess, one should perform a long pit for the same purposes.
Now, the domestic offering (*gṛhabali*): "Hrīḥ! To all the yoginīs, accept, accept, svāhā! With this, one should offer the domestic offering.
"Kṣāṃ kṣaḥ! Kṣetrapāla, accept this offering, accept, svāhā! One should offer this in the corner of the house.
Hrīḥ Hrīḥ! O Vaṭukanātha, son of the Goddess, accept this bali offering as previously described; one should offer it in the center of the house.
Hrīḥ! To the Yoginīs, those dwelling in all sacred fields (kṣetra), in all seats (pīṭha) and sub-seats (upapīṭha), and to all the Saṃvartas, [I offer] the body...
"O Catu, O Caturo, dwell here eternally; accept this offering (bali) in the house, svāhā!
One should offer the monthly food-offering (māsabhaktabali).
Furthermore, I shall explain that which reveals the materials for the vidyā.
Then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, when the night is pitch black, the practitioner [should proceed].

Having become one who has entered the interior of the house, liberated ten days after performing the rite, the best of practitioners, recollecting the form of the Goddess with devotion, should meditate upon her. (13.222)
Having first drawn the primary mandala, one should draw a hexagon therein;
O Dear One, one should worship the limbs and the goddesses as described for the mandala.
There, the best of practitioners, having visualized the Goddess in her form, should worship her with various kinds of flowers—white, yellow, and red. (13.224)

One should recite [the mantra] a thousand or even ten thousand times, concentrated with devotion; and there, from the time of bathing until the end, one should offer the bali-oblation with the mantra. (13.225)
Having adorned those women with garments, ornaments, and decorations while reciting mantras,
he should feed the Brahmins and likewise give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
By this method, one shall obtain the entire Vidyā of Lakṣmī;
in a single night, O Lakṣmī, one acquires the Vidyā—of this there is no doubt. (13.227)
By a two-night fast one obtains a mass of glory, by a three-night fast one becomes a guru oneself;
"liberated" means being devoid of attachment for ten nights.
O Śivā, in a previous kalpa, the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) was always to be observed.

Having risen every day at dawn and having taken his place upon the bed... (13.229)
Having meditated upon and mastered Chinnamastā, one should recite her mantra one hundred and eight times;
or one should recite it three hundred times daily, or one thousand and eight times.
Within six months, one shall become a great poet capable of composing both prose and verse; after one year, one will certainly attain mastery over the Vedas and the Śāstras.
After three years have passed, he becomes like another Lord of Speech;
by the mere sight of him, the debaters are rendered lusterless. (13-232)
They flee upon the ground just as a woman does out of fear of a lion;
[this occurs] by a tenth part of the protective mantras, in accordance with the root mantra.
O Śivā, one should constantly recite this [mantra] once, or sometimes for a fortnight.

She is considered first as the creator of emanation (*sarga*), then as the nourisher (*poṣikā*), and finally as the bringer of dissolution (*saṃhārakāriṇī*); thus she alone is called the triple-formed (*trimūrti*).
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled the Section on the Worship of Chinnamastā, in the Āgamakalpalatā.
Now, the miscellaneous [rites]:
now the Sārasvata mantras: "Speak, speak, O you who are bound by speech! Svāhā! One should recite this ten hundred thousand times.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One! Speak, speak, O Goddess! Svāhā! One should recite this eight hundred thousand times.

Oṃ aiḥ hrīḥ, homage to Sarasvatī! One should recite this one million two hundred thousand times. Aiḥ, O Lord of Speech, O Immortal One, float, float! One should recite this eleven hundred thousand times.
Now, the mantras of Lakṣmī: [The mantra for] twelve hundred thousand recitations of Śrī is:
*aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namo kamalavāsinyai svāhā*. [The mantra for] one million recitations is: *namaḥ kamalavāsinyai svāhā*.
Oṃ aiḥ hrīḥ klīḥ hsauḥ, obeisance to the Mother of the World. One should recite this twelve hundred thousand times.
Oṃ śrīḥ hrīḥ śrīḥ, O Kamalā, whose abode is the lotus, be gracious; śrīḥ hrīḥ śrīḥ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī. [Recite this] one hundred thousand times.
Now, the mantras of Bhūniśvarī: one should recite *hrīḥ* thirty-two hundred thousand times;
*aiṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ* twelve hundred thousand times; *aiṃ hrīḥ aiṃ* one hundred thousand times; *āḥ hrīḥ klauḥ* one hundred thousand times. Now, the mantras of Tvaritā:
Oṃ hrīḥ hūḥ khe ca che traḥ strīḥ hūḥ kṣaḥ hrīḥ phaṭ | hūḥ kṣe kṣatrikaṇṭhakīyam | kṣastrīḥ kṣavaṇya trikaṇṭhakegram | One should recite this three million times.
Oṃ hrīḥ aiḥ nityaklinne madadravye aiḥ hrīḥ svāhā (3). Aiḥ klīḥ nityaklinne made drave svāhā (4).
Aiḥ hrīḥ nityaklinne madadravye svāhā. This is the Vajraprastāriṇī mantra (1).
Śrī / Hrī / Klī—this is the Tripuṭā.
Oṃ Āṃ Hrīḥ Klo Ehi Parameśvari Svāhā—this is the Aśvarūḍhā. Hrīḥ Namo Bhagavati Māheśvari Annapūrṇe Svāhā—one should recite this sixteen thousand times.
*Hrīḥ padmāvati svāhā*. These are the ten mantras of Tvaritā.
Now, the garland-mantras (*mālāmantra*): *Oṃ hrīḥ duḥ durgāyai namaḥ mahiṣamardini svāhā*.
Oṃ durge durge-si svāhā | jvala jvala śūlini duṣṭagraha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | This is the mantra of Vanadurgā: Arise, O lady! Why do you sleep? A danger has approached me.
Whether it be possible or impossible, O Blessed One, pacify that for me, svāhā! Whatever has arisen for me— whether it be possible or impossible— O Blessed One, pacify that for me, svāhā!
Thus are the five mantras of Durgā: Vālā: Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Hsaiḥ Hasakari Hsrāuḥ. Now, the mantras of Mātaṅgī.

Ai Hrī Śrī Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, O Śrīmātaṅgeśvarī, who captivates the minds of all beings, who is the queen of all happiness, who brings joy to all mouths, who subjugates all kings, who subjugates all women and men, who subjugates all wicked beasts, who subjugates all sentient beings— grant success to [Name] in all worlds!
Svāhā!
The eighty-eight syllable mantra: one should recite it ten thousand times. The Gaṇapati mantra: *gaṃ*. (4) The Mahāgaṇapati mantra.
Oṃ śrī hrī klī glo gaṃ! To Gaṇapati, the bestower of excellent boons, bring all people under my control, svāhā!
Ga! For swift propitiation, svāhā!
The Haraṃbha mantra:
Oṃ Gūṃ, Namaḥ.
Now, the Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati mantra.
Oṃ hasti piśāci likhe svāhā (16,000 times). Oṃ to the elephant-faced one, to the long-bellied one, to the great one who eats leftovers, kroḥ prāḥ hrīḥ, to the one who eats leftovers, svāhā!
To the elephant-faced one, the long-bellied one, the great-souled one who eats leftovers: ĀḤ KROṂ HRĪḤ ŚRĪḤ KHAIḤ KHAIḤ KHAIḤ.
To the one who eats leftovers, SVĀHĀ!
This is the twenty-nine-syllable mantra. Now follows the Vakratuṇḍa mantra.
HŪṂ to Vakratuṇḍa! HRĪṂ to Vakratuṇḍa! NAMAḤ! [52,000 recitations]. Now follows the Haridrā Gaṇapati mantra.
Oṃ hūṃ ga glauṃ! O Gaṇapati, bestower of boons, paralyzer of the hearts of all people, paralyze, paralyze!
Svāhā!
One should recite this one thousand and eight times every day.
Now, the Kārttikeya mantra:
Oṃ vaṃ caḍbhuve namaḥ. Now, the Candra mantra: Sau momāya namaḥ. Now, the Vidyā mantra:
*Vidye vidyā mālini candriṇi candramukhi svāhā*. Now, the Sūrya mantra:
*Oṃ ghṛṇi sūrya āditya hrāḥ hrīḥ sa 12 haḥ sa 12*. These two mantras are for the fire.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Agni Jātavedas, come here; accomplish all rites, svāhā! (12)
"Arise, O man, tawny like a monkey, with blood-red eyes! Give to me! Cause [them] to give! Svāhā!
This is the mantra for Agni and Indra:
"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Agni Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here; accomplish all rites! Svāhā!"
Arise, O man, tawny as a lion, with blood-red eyes! Give to me, cause [them] to give; svāhā!

If the two seed-syllables *hrīḥ* and *śrīḥ* are placed at the beginning of the vidyā, the three-peaked [vidyā] becomes one that appears as five-peaked;
the four-peaked Śāṅkarī becomes six-peaked.
Vasukūtā belongs to Viṣṇu;

Pañcakūtā belongs to Śambhu. Having placed the Praṇava at the beginning of those two groups of mantras—namely, "Oṃ Hrīḥ" and "Oṃ Śrīḥ"—if it is given at the beginning of the Vidyā, then the Trikuṭā becomes a Ṣaṭkūtā.

Likewise: the Śāṅkarī [mantra] consists of seven *kūṭas*, and the Vaiṣṇavī of nine *kūṭas*; such is the threefold division. First, the three preceding seed-syllables (*bīja*) should be given in reverse order; thereafter, the three seed-syllables *klīṃ*, *aiṃ*, and *sauḥ* should be given. Following that, the six *kūṭas* should be given.
Then, the five previously given seed-syllables (*bīja*) should be bestowed in the manner of encapsulation (*puṭita*).
Thus is the fourfold division.
If one seed-syllable is placed in the midst of the seed-syllables *hrīḥ*, *śrīḥ*, *klīṃ*, *oṃ ai*, and *ī*, then—

All the *trikūṭas* consist of sixteen syllables; for the Vaiṣṇavī, there are nineteen syllables. Thus, first the five seed-syllables (*bījas*) should be given, and thereafter the nine-peaked Vaiṣṇavī should be given.

One should see that, according to the sequence of reversal, the nineteen syllables of the first *vija* (seed-syllable) are to be given: *vaiṣṇavī* is *hrīṃ*, *gaurī* is *ha ka ya la hrīṃ*, and *hāṭakeśvarī* is *ha ka ya la sa hrīṃ*. The second and fifth [groups] are:
*ka e ī la hrīṃ*, *ha sa ka la hrīṃ*, *ha ka ha ya la hrīṃ*, and *ha sa la hrīṃ*.

Now, [I praise] her who consists of bliss, who is directly the very nature of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
I praise the consciousness that is the cause of the universe for the sake of attaining all prosperity.
I bow to the pure and auspicious goddess Umā, who is the vehicle of the lotus,
who manifests the forms of Viṣṇu and Śiva,
and who effects the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the three worlds.
Having praised you, O Ambikā, with words that are vast and free from desire—15.2.
The great power of the Lord, who bears the form of the Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Hotr, Moon,
and Sun, is likewise that of the slayer of Mura.
O Daughter of the King of Mountains, you alone are indeed the cause. (2) || 15-3 ||
O Mother of the Gods, those three types of darkness accumulated by all the world are indeed the specific cause for [the attainment of] the measured divinity;
yet, they are purified by the pollen of your lotus feet.
That which is the constant rolling about [of the moon] within the matted locks of Śambhu. (3) || 15-4 ||
The lord of the stars (the moon) may delight the night-lily, or the sun (the enemy of the lotus) may greatly distress the day-lily; yet,
who else but the Lord of the World possesses the power to bring joy to both simultaneously?
But you, by your own vision, take delight in phenomenal proliferation. (4) || 15-5 ||
You are the primordial source of all worlds, yet you possess fresh youth;
though you are the daughter of the Mountain King, you are exceedingly delicate; and you have not been beheld by the three Vedas, which are white with the foam of the gods.
O Gaurī, you are established upon the head of my mind even as I seek success. (5) || 15-6 ||
Having attained after a long time a birth among humans— which is so difficult to obtain— and having further acquired proficiency in their own senses,
those who worship you, O Mother of the worlds, are truly blessed.
Having ascended the ladder, they fall down once again. (6) || 15-7 ||
O Bhavānī, those who, with great eagerness, worship you with camphor powder that produces coolness, mixed with sandalwood paste and well-arranged clusters of flowers— [for them...]
Indeed, they traverse all the worlds of the earth without exception. (15.8)
Entering the state of Maya within the first lotus,
you shall wander through the universe like a sleeping queen;
bearing the graceful play of a circle of lightning-vines.
The lotuses consist of five kinds of medicinal herbs. || 15-9 ||
Having emerged from that [state], they bathe their bodies with the waters of immortality;
yet, having attained dissolution once more on the path through passion,
those in whose hearts the unborn [Reality] does not throb shall not exist.
O Mother, O Consort of Maheśvara, you who bear the embryo of the universe! (9) || 15-10 ||
With her hair adorned by curls hanging down to her cheeks, her face beautiful, her breasts full and firm, and her waist slender and rounded;
holding in her hands the rosary for meditation, the water-pot, and the lotus that destroys all sins.
I revolve in my mind the form of the ninefold Gaurī. (10) || 15-11 ||
Having established herself in yoga and conquered the six enemies, she resides within the group of senses and the tranquil mind;
her faces display hands holding a noose, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.
O Sovereign of the World, yogis behold you. (11) || 15-12 ||
Resembling molten gold, being sprinkled by four elephants with jars of nectar,
she carries a beautiful lotus in her hand.
Padmā also bestows fearlessness, boons, and spiritual accomplishment. || 15-13 ||
O Rudra, having mounted the king of beasts with your eight creeper-like arms bearing various weapons,
you [overcame] those who are the enemies of the immortals, possessing the luster of durva grass.
O Bhavānī, you are Durgā, the Mother who acts [for our protection]. (13) || 15-14 ||
Her face is beautified by the spray of long, flowing water;
she wears a necklace fashioned from the fruit of the *bhuñjā* tree;
her body possesses the dark luster of a red parrot, yet she is devoted to the god of love.
I shall repeatedly intoxicate myself and remember the body of Pulinda. (14) || 15-15 ||
Followed by swans whose gait was like that of dancers and whose anklets produced a sweet sound, as if they were embodied speech;
with their lotus-like faces upturned and their beautiful noses prominent.
Śrīkaṇṭhapalli placed its head at your feet. (15–16)
The eighth mind-born daughter of Brahmā was created by the bull-bannered god from his two eyes so that he might behold her;
she, filled with the weight of intense passion, gazed at him.
O Bhavānī, I am yours; I shall leap over and break even the three worlds. (16) || 15-17 ||

I remember her thighs, which surpassed the plantain trees in both their stoutness and softness; they were as smooth as the trunks of conquered elephants and were fashioned with a curvature capable of supporting the weight of her hips.
O best of those without pride, by means of your slender waist, [you surpass] the middle of a pillar. (15-18) || 15-18 ||
Her two breasts and her thighs are simultaneously expanding; her physical essence is drawn out by a youth that has passed beyond childhood,
and her form is made manifest by the play of the line of hair.
Let it flash forth in the center of my heart. (18) || 15-19 ||
The water of beauty, filled by fresh youth, belonging to Smara— who fears the fire from the eye of Śiva—
was like an unassailable lotus stalk offered as a refuge.
O Goddess, I shall never forget your navel. (19) || 15-20 ||
To the Lord, who wears ash as a secret mass and whose body is anointed with saffron paste,
there belong two hands that appear like foam from the moment he rises after bathing.
The two frontal globes, smeared with vermilion, call to mind the temples of a rutting elephant. (20) || 15-21 ||
Her two arms, radiant with the glow of auspicious and lustrous beauty, shone as they were raised to grasp his neck; her hands,
long and slender, were pressed against his throat by the touch of his own enemy’s hand.
May my mother not pass beyond the path of my memory. (21) || 15-22 ||

The neck of the Daughter of the Mountain King, which steals the grace of a gracefully turned conch shell that is not too elongated, and which shines with various ornaments and decorations, possesses a most enchanting quality.
Having reflected, I shall never again experience such satisfaction. (23) || 15-23 ||
Her face, with its long eyes, a well-born forehead, and the lines of her cheeks slightly blossoming with a gentle smile,
possesses full lips and a high, long nose.
He who remembers this even once is truly born [again]. (23) || 15-24 ||
That swarm of bees, possessing abundant fragrance and flowers, which, as it moves, cannot be distinguished from a traveler,
has entered your mass of hair, mistaking it for a letter written in saffron ink.
O Goddess, his own ancient bond falls away from his body. (24) || 15-25 ||
This hymn, composed by Śrutisucaritā, is for the wise; he who, with an eternally moist inner self, recites it here in this mortal world,
becomes one who attains the highest state, bowing at her feet.
For the sake of the glory of the crest-jewels of the lords of the earth, [he was] the ornament of auspicious marks. || 15-26 ||
Thus ends the Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī Stotra; may it be auspicious!
241a) Now, the Armor of Annapūrṇā.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"The various Vidyās of Annapūrṇā that have been told are very difficult to obtain."
Out of compassion, everything was told; it was heard by me and has been understood. || 15-27 ||
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen, O Pārvatī, I shall speak; attend with careful attention. I will describe the true nature of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), which brings about great sovereignty. (15-28)

By reciting and retaining [this], a mortal shall become a possessor of sovereignty over the three worlds. [Now follows] the procedure regarding the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor (kavaca), which possesses the characteristics of the three worlds. || 15-29 ||
The metre is Virāj, the deity is Annapūrṇā, the bestower of all accomplishments;
it is proclaimed as having application for the sake of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. (15.30)
Hrīṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, Māheśvarī; then the word "Annapūrṇe," and likewise "Svāhā"—this is the seventeen-syllable [mantra]. (15.31)
May she who is known as Sādā, filled with food, protect me—she who is celebrated throughout the three worlds;
and again, this Vimāyā is to be sounded through the apertures of the directions and likewise through the mouth. (15.32)
May she who begins with the Praṇava protect the space between the eyebrows; may she preceded by Vāgbhava and Agni protect the throat;
and may this Īśvarī, beginning with the Kāma-bīja, protect the heart. (15.33)
*Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), *Śrī*, *Hrīṃ*, *Namaste*, and then the word *Bhagavati*;
then the word *Māheśvari*, and *Annapūrṇe Svāhā*—may this protect me. (15.34)
May Māheśvarī, who consists of nineteen syllables, protect me always at the navel;
thereafter follows the sixteen-syllable mantra beginning with Tāra (Om), Māyā (Hrīm), Ramā (Śrīm), and Kāma (Klīm). (15.35)
May the Great Vidyā Annapūrṇā, whose nature consists of twenty leaves, always protect his head; may Bhuvaneśvarī, [seated on] Hrīḥ, protect him. 15-36.
May Hrīḥ, Śrīḥ, and likewise Krīḥ, along with the Liṅga and Tripuṭā, protect my anus;
may she purify my six limbs with the seed-syllables endowed with the six long vowels. || 15.37 ||
May Indra protect me in the east, and Mayobhū in the southeast;
may Brahmā and Ananta protect me from above and below respectively. (15.38)
May the weapons, beginning with the vajra, protect [the practitioner] in the ten directions in their proper order.
Thus has been described this supreme merit, the auspiciousness of the three worlds. (15.39)
By holding and reciting which, all the gods attained sovereign power;
for it is through recitation and retention that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra [attained their status]. (15.40)
In every kalpa, he separately creates, sustains, and destroys;
thereafter, one should recite the "Eight Handfuls of Flowers" (Puṣpāñjalī-aṣṭaka) at the root-mantra for the Goddess.
Whatever fruit one may obtain from performing worship for millions of ages, speech shall dwell in his mouth; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
The preliminary ritual (puraścaryā) for this is said to consist of one hundred and eight recitations.
If one wears a pill inscribed with it on birch bark and placed within gold, [one attains success]. (15.43)
O Pārvatī, at that time, Maya, having entreated him, [received] the Brahmā-astra and other weapons from his throat and right arm, which were then entirely filled with them.
Garlands are indeed nothing but flowers; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Śrī-Annāpūrṇā Devī Kavaca.
Now follows the Thousand Names of Annapūrṇā.
The Goddess said: [She spoke] to Mahādeva Maheśvara, who was seated upon the peak of Kailāsa.
Pārvatī, with supreme affection, questioned the moon-crested Lord.
Śrī Pārvatī said: "How [is it that] Īśāna is the all, the omniscient, the lord of the world, and the highest bliss? (15.46)
Men always obtain [these things] and are not oppressed by suffering;
for the intellect of those whose thoughts are destroyed by poverty does not shine forth. (15.47)
And since the destruction of the earth by laziness does not arise from non-affliction, how, O Lord, do you obtain the stable happiness of sovereignty? (15.48)
Tell me that, O Lord of Gods, if you have affection for me;
for you are omniscient, O Mahādeva, the one who bestows grace upon the worlds.
"Tell me the means for destroying poverty, which bestows imperial sovereignty.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"The primordial Goddess Śivā is the great lore (mahāvidyā) Annapūrṇā."
When propitiated in this world, she bestows abundant prosperity;
she is the eternal giver of enjoyment and liberation, and the bestower of the happiness of imperial sovereignty. (15.51)
By her this universe was created, and by her alone it is protected;
she is the supreme power who bestows happiness, renowned as the Sovereign known as Māyā.
Her hymn known as the Thousand Names is the sole means to liberation;
it destroys poverty in this world and bestows great sovereignty. (15.53)
By the recitation of this, Viṣṇu certainly protects the worlds.
Having risen in the morning, a human being should remember her names. (15.54)
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and having praised the Blessed Śivā,
being purified, one should worship the auspicious Goddess who is clothed in variegated garments.
Red in complexion, she holds a golden vessel in her right hand,
while in her left she carries a bowl made of māśika, filled with sweet food, which is highly honored.
Having fully worshipped that Goddess of the gods, who is always delighted in the gift of food and possesses a gracious countenance, one obtains abundant prosperity. (15.57)
Or else, if one merely [recites] the thousand names upon her cloth, he shall obtain happiness and the supreme bliss of sovereignty. (15.58)
In that very same way, food is offered and consumed by me along with my attendants;
this thousand-name hymn is the supreme praise of Bhavānī. (15.59)
Out of affection for you, I shall proclaim [this] for the sake of the happiness of the worlds.

Oṃ. For this hymn of the thousand names of Annapūrṇā, Mahādeva is the seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrī Annapūrṇā is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for my attainment of prosperity and wealth.
Oṃ, Annapūrṇā, the great vidyā, Mahālakṣmī, the enchanting one. || 15-60 ||
She is Vidyā, Nārāyaṇī, Śāntā, the Mother of the World, Sarasvatī;
she is Viṣṇu’s Māyā, Mahāmāyā, Śivā, Śāntā, and the Beloved of Śiva. (15.61)
Padmā, Padmāvatī, Padmamukhī, Padmavibhūṣaṇā, Sunandā, Nandinī, Nandā, and the auspicious Nandagopasutā. || 15-62 ||
O Supreme Goddess Tripurā, you are Bālā, the bestower of boons through your syllables; you are Bhavānī, the consort of Bhava, and the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence. 15.63b–64a.
Siddhavidyā, Mahāśakti, Svadhā, Svāhā, Ramā, Rati, Māheśvarī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Suprītā, and Prītivardhanī. || 15-64 ||
She is the wholesome one, renowned for her love, and the embodiment of supreme bliss;
she is dear to Indra, the earth, and the bestower of supreme sovereignty. (15.65)
Durgā is the thunderbolt, Durgā is the bestower of victory, the lotus-eyed one; she is patience, the maker of endurance, splendor, the passionate one, or the giver of life.
Apūrṇā, Śāṃkarī, Gaurī, Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, as well as Yoganidrā, Mahānidrā, Tantrā, and Tantraprakāśinī. (15.67)
Muditā, Madanollāsā, the beloved of Madanāntaka, Prabhāvatī, Mandahāsā, Tārā, and she who dwells in the Void. || 15-68 ||
Prajñā, Madhumatī, Dhyātrī, Śailarājasutā, Jayā, Mātaṅgī, Vasudhā, Vālā, Vālikā, and Vasundharā. (15.69)
The daughter of the Ocean of Milk, red in hue, wearing a red lower garment and upper robe, the divine daughter of Himavat, worshipped by all the gods. (15.70)
Oṃ-kārā is the supreme light, the bringer of supreme bliss;
she is Kṣiti, who bestows security, Kṣemā, and the destroyer of hunger and agitation. (15.71)
Abiding as the half-measure, she is eternal, adorned with the crescent moon;
she is the bestower of desires, the luminous one, the desirable, known as Kāmā, and the protectress of the Kula. || 15-72 ||
Kāśī, Kāñcī, and Avatī; Durgā, the destroyer of miserable states; Kamalā, Kāruṇā, and Kīrti; she who goes to the Lord of Kuñjalin.
Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Raudrī, who manifests the three qualities (guṇas), Māheśvarī, Subhadrā, Vārāhī, and Nārasiṃhikā. (15.74)
Kaumārī, Kumudā, Kālī, Mālinī, Siṃhagāminī, Viśvamātā, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Padmā, Rājalakṣmī, and Prabhāvatī. || 15-75 ||
She has beautiful eyes, is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), possesses three eyes, and has lotus-like eyes;
her face is like a full-blown lotus, and she wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
"O King, she is remembered as Vaktrā; she is worshipped by the Kālindī family. She is Mandākinī, Jāhnavī, the daughter of Jahnu, and the Mother of the World. (15.77)
The Kāverī, the Vipāśā, the Śatadru, the Sarasvatī, the Kiratoyā, the Sarayū, the Revā, the Phalgu, and the Kauśikī. (15.78)
The Candrabhā, the Gāṇḍakī, the Narmadā, and likewise the Devikā—the abode of merit, the embodiment of merit, pure, supreme, and transcendent. (15.79)
In the morning she is Savyā, Puṇyanāmī, Puruṣārthapravartinī,
Triśakti, Mokṣadā, Raṃbhā, Viṣañcī, and Pinākinī.
Icchā, Māyā, Mahāśakti, Bhairavī, the destroyer of fear;
Girirājasutā, Gaurī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahodayā. (15.81)
The Blessed One is Bhogavatī, she who reclines upon her coils;
she has a beautiful smile, a lovely countenance, a charming laugh, and speaks with affection. (15.82)
Satyāvatī, Sītā, the virtuous Satyā, the refuge of holy people;
her limbs were reddish-gold in hue, and she was adorned with various excellent ornaments. || 15.83 ||
Kātyāyanī, the Mother of the World, who dwells in the ocean of nectar;
she is the immortal one, the giver of honor, Pūṣā, whose face resembles the full moon.
O Supreme Goddess Tripurā, you are Sundarī, the Beauty of the Cities; you are the Śruti, the Smṛti, and the Great Vidyā, the abode of all virtues.
Kātyāyanī, the Mother of the World; Hemavatī, born of the Himālaya mountain;
she of the beautiful smile, the fair-faced one, the gentle, the beautiful, and she who is worshipped by the gods. (15.86)
Beautiful in all her limbs, red and possessing a radiance like the rising sun,
she is the sixteen-year-old, the fifth Vidyā, and likewise the great seventeenth.
Ugrakālī, Mahākālī, Bhadrakālī, Parājitā, Śivadūtī, Mahānidrā, Yoganidrā, and Purātanī. (15.88)
She is the young woman, the aged one, the one with eyes like collyrium, the digit, the minute fraction, and the hour; she rains down the nectar of compassion. (15.89)
She who loves fragrance, she who is sweetly scented, she who bears the aroma of camphor;
she who delights in the arts of Kāmadeva, the maiden who is fond of worship. (15.90)
Madhuśrī, Mādhavī, Mādhvī, she who moves like an elephant in rut, Madahāsā, Mātaṅgī, and she adorned with pearl necklaces. || 15.91 ||
Śākaṃbharī, Suśīlā, Śītalā, Śobhaneśvarī, Madhumatī, Mahāsiddhi, Siddhavandyā, and Śubhānanā. || 15-92 ||

She consists of the life-force of the world, she is the sacrifice, she delights in the performance of sacrifice and the Yajus formulas; she is the abode of the essence of the Jha-kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, she is the beautiful woman, and her delight is in Rāma, who is dear to Rāma.
Resembling the rising sun and possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons,
she stood in the midst of a jeweled pavilion, seated upon a pedestal of precious gems.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, radiant with a crown and earrings, her nose adorned with pearls, she has cheeks like the frontal globes of a lordly elephant in rut.
Adorned with sun-gems, moon-stones, and the like, and resplendent with the brilliance of diamonds, she was fashioned from precious jewels and equipped with armlets and bracelets.
Her limbs were variegated with finger-rings, she was pure in meditation, possessed a beautiful girdle,
had the sound of anklets and other ornaments, and her nose was adorned with a fine crest-jewel.
She whose teeth are like pomegranate seeds and jewels, whose lips are like the bimba fruit, who is stainless and incomparable;
O compassionate one, remover of suffering, destroyer of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa! 15.98
Mṛgākṣī, Mṛganetrā, and Mṛgī; Madhurabhāṣiṇī; Hrī; she who is called Kāmarūpamāyā; Kaṃbugrīvā; and Ādyasastanī. (15.99)
Bestowing growth and bestowing perfection, she is the supreme one who delights in the path of speech and wisdom;
eternally situated in the *mūlādhāra*, she moves along the path of the *kuṇḍalinī* lineage.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, Hastijihvikā, Citriṇī, Śaṅkhinī, Pūṣā, Piṅgalā, and Yaśasvinī. (15.101)
Alambuṣā and Kuhū likewise are granters of desires and able to assume any form at will;
they are the color of vermilion-red and resplendent with a tilaka mark of vermilion.
O Senā, Sītā, Satī, Bālā, bestower of true good fortune, sister of Maināka, worthy of honor, she who is to be revered, and O high-minded one! || 15.103 ||

Endowed with qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and so forth, you who dwell in the sequence of the six wheels (ṣaṭcakra), you are the Ḍākinī, the Śākinī, the Kākinī, and likewise the Hākinī. (15.104)
Rākiṇī, Lākini, Līlā, Lāvanyā, Vuddhi, Caṇḍikā, Dhaniṣṭā, Dhanadā, Dhānyā, Dhīrā, and Dharmavivardhinī. (15.105)
Saudāminī, Mukkeśī, Śarvāṇī, Halavallabhā, Haripriyā, Sarvahetu, Sarvādyā, and Sarvadāyinī. || 15-106 ||
Maṇḍahā, she of the smiling face, the supreme daughter of the ocean, the Yoginī endowed with yoga, and the promoter of sacrificial rites. || 15.107 ||
Kaumārī, Vṛttikā, Kīrti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Kṣamā, Kṣiti, Vicitrā, Citriṇī, Citrā, Caturā, and Annapūjitā. (15.108)
Totalā, Tulasī, Tuṣṭā, Turiyā, Vimalā, Tulā, Kātyāyaṇī, Krītu, Svasthā, Suśabdā, and Sanātanī. (15.109)
She who subdues poverty, who is self-controlled, who is devoted to Dāmodara,
who is compassionate, whose mind is full, and who is affectionate toward the Moon-faced One.
Without beginning or end, she is skillful, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s elder brother;
she is honored with perfumes, the possessor of fragrance, and served by the hosts of Gandharvas.
Padmagandhā and Patākā, who bestow supreme bliss;
Amṛtā, Prāṇadā, Prāṇā, Pragatmā, and Pārameśvarī. (15.112)
Lopāmudrā, the queen of the gods, her lotus-like face blooming with joy at Śiva’s dance, cast glances as radiant as the moon.
Arundhatī, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Rāvaṇanāśinī, Svapnāvatī, Citrarekhā, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā. (15.114)
Resembling the flower of the hibiscus, she is the one who has crossed over, whose power is to cross over;
she whose resolve is blissful truth, and who fulfills every intention.
She is radiant, adorned with playful ornaments, the beloved of the Lord of Beings who is himself the ornament;
she is dear to Śiva, auspicious, beauty itself, and the increaser of all good fortune. (15.116)
She is the art of desire (*kāmakalā*), action (*kriyā*), play (*krīḍā*), the Kaula goddess, born of the *Kula*, and stainless (*amala*).
She is the wish-granting creeper (*kalpalatā*), the woman of the *Kula* (*kulastrī*), the night (*nakuhuḥ*), and the destroyer of Kaiṭabha (*kaiṭabhanāśinī*). (15.117)
O destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, O dispeller of great fear!
O Caṇḍihā, O you of fierce form, O destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa! || 15-118 ||
Ākri-Ānandabhairavī, Bālābhairavī, the beloved of Bhairava, Caitanyabhairavī, Nityābhairavī, and Rudrabhairavī. (15.119)
Kāmeśvarī Bhairavī, and likewise Tripurabhairavī;
Bhuvaneśī Bhairavī, and likewise Tripurabhairavī. (15.120)
Bhuvaneśī, Bhairavī, and likewise Mahāsaptadaśī;
Pañcadaśī, Ṣoḍaśī, and Śrī Tripurasundarī. (15–121)
Kauśāṃvī, Kauśakī, Kṛṣṇā, Kuśajñā, Kumudasmitā, the renowned Kāmāntakapriyā, Sugatā, and Khagavāhinī. (15.122)
The river Guṇā is composed of the three qualities;
Guṇā is Gaurī, who is exceedingly heavy. 15.123.
Ghamā, Asutṛhiṇī, Ghoṣā, Śāṃ, and Ghanālayā;
the fifth is Vāgmaya, and Candrā bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. (15.124)
The supporter of the earth, the beloved life-force, the destroyer of old age and death;
the resonance Jhaṃkāra, the sudden Jhaṃjhā, and the Jhaṃkāra that is dense and pervasive. (15.125)
Caṇḍī is the very nature of the sound of the wind; Ḍimī has the ḍamaru drum as her beloved;
Ṭakkā possesses musical instruments; and Dṛkkā is the destroyer of the shame of suffering. (15.126)

She whose form is the letter *tha*, the ocean of compassion, the bearer of the burden, the destroyer of the wicked, the bringer of joy, the boat [of salvation], and the beloved of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (15.127)
She who is fond of the lotus, who holds a lotus in her hand, who is dear to Phalguna, who dwells upon the chest of Vishnu, who is Bharati, and who is honored by Bharata. 15.128
She who delights in drinking honey, she who is honey itself, she who is dear to Mādhava, she who is born from the lineage of Yadu—she is the Goddess who is worshipped by the gods. (15.129)
Ramā, beloved of Rāma, the delightful one, Lakṣaṇā, the beloved of Lakṣmaṇa, devoted to Vāsudeva, eloquent, and as red as the Bandhūka flower.
Śeṣikā, Sukhirā, and Ṣaṣṭi are situated in the six-cornered wheel;
they are Sadgati, Sumati, and Haṃsī, born of the Kṣatriya caste, and are to be served. (15.131)
The destroyer of ignorance, the command, the sovereign sense-faculty, the beloved of the Lord;
Umā, the heat, the letter Jha, and the letter Jhṛ, O you whose form is the Asura! (15.132)
Ketakī, Cakrakārā, Kṛntikī, Kṛtikā, and Surā;
Eka is the bestower of sovereignty, as are Auṣadhī and Auṣadha. (15.133)
She is the form of the *bindu* and the *visarga*, the goddess Śāṅkarī who is all deities;
she belongs to the great lineage (*mahākulinā*), she is free from desire, yet she possesses desire and is the life-force of desire.
She is a wish-fulfilling gem, she who is to be meditated upon, the clever one with four faces;
she holds a vessel of food, she is full, and she is compassionate, with a sacrificial ladle in her hand.
She who intoxicates with camphor, who dwells in Kāmarūpa,
who possesses a beautiful smile, a lovely face, and a gentle nature— she is Śakuntalā, the embodiment of the Sāman chants.
Madhumatī, Jayantī, Jayadākṣābhanaśinī, Puṣpariyā, Puṣparatā, and she who is adorned with various flowers. (15.137)
Seated upon a lotus, holding a lotus in her hand, with a lotus-like face and lotus eyes;
bearing the flower-arrows, she is the flowering one, full and moon-eyed. || 15-138 ||
The deer-eyed one, seated upon the king of beasts, the fawn-eyed maiden;
she who holds the *bhusuṇḍī* weapon, the bow, the noose in her hand, and the iron club. || 15.139 ||
O Śaṅkhinī, you who hold a discus in your hand; O Padmahastā, whose gait is like a mace; O Varjinī, you who hold a bow; O Khadgadhāriṇī, you who ride upon a lion! || 15.140 ||
Vasudhā, Vasudhārā, Jayā, Śākambharī, as well as Vijayā, Jayantī, and Sarvaśatrūvināśinī. || 15-141 ||
Śītalā and Suśīlā, who bestows the beauty of the Śāla tree;
Ajitā, Mohinī, and Mānyā, who is resplendent with the glory of victory.
Aparājitā, Amitā, Daurghrī, and likewise Vilāsinī;
Triśūladhāriṇī, Dhūmrā, Dhūmrārcis, and Dhūrjaṭipriyā. (15.143)
O wielder of the trident, O goddess with spear in hand, O bearer of the excellent sword;
O Pinākī, O compassionate one, O destroyer of Dambha and the younger brother of Indra through your power! || 15-144 ||
She is the beloved of the supreme and subordinate powers, the destroyer of Tripura through her three energies;
she is Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Aindrī, Vaiṣṇavī, and the beloved of Viṣṇu. (15.145)
The power of desire (*īcchā-śakti*), Viṣṇu’s Māyā, the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*)—O you who possess all arts!—is four-armed, two-armed, six-armed, and likewise eight-armed. (15.146)
She who has a hundred arms and a thousand eyes, the eye of Indra, worshipped by Indra;
she who is worshipped by Kuvera, the auspicious one, the daughter of Kuvera, with a smile like the kumuda lily. || 15-147 ||
She is Mahālakṣmī, served by the Siddhas; she is Mṛḍānī, the gentle beloved of Śiva; she is Pṛthvī, the favorite of Indra; she is Pārvatī, the supreme deity. (15.148)
Prabhā, Jyotsnā, Kṣamā, Kṣemā, she who brings about all auspiciousness;
Dātā, Padmāvatī, Nandā, Sunandā, and Surananditā.
She who acts with beloved fortitude, the knowledge of sacrifice belonging to Śaṅkara, Aparṇā, and she of noble lineage—she who is renowned and served by the Siddhas. (15.150)
She is the Great Conflagration, the Joyful One, the Light, and she who smiles like a white water-lily;
she is Wisdom, the Wisdom fully perfected, whose essential nature is the supreme light. (15.151)
Candracūḍā, Caṇḍāsyā, Candramalavartinī, Sāmrājyadāyinī, Dheyā, Tārā, Madhumatī, and Madhu—[these are the names]. 15.152.
Endowed with fresh youth, walking like an elephant in rut,
Śāradā, who delights in her practitioners, stands at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree.
Adorned with the crescent moon, auspicious, Bhāratī is borne by a swan;
she is Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭkāra; she is the giver of funeral offerings, O compassionate one.
She is the Mother of the Vedas, the triple Veda, the science of livelihood, the company of the virtuous,
the supreme refuge, faith, intellect, memory, wisdom, Lakṣmī, and the beloved of Keśava.
Devashakti and Suparva are devoted to truth and righteousness;
they are the sustainers of the world, mounted upon bulls, and resemble blazing gold.
She is one whose mantra is perfected, the knowledge of the Vedas, the promoter of the Vedic path;
she has a neck like a conch, is of excellent intellect, the messenger of Śiva, pure, and possessed of a gentle smile.
Kuṇḍalinī, who contains the universe within her womb, dwells in the mūlādhāra;
she is the movement of inhalation and exhalation, the life-force that destroys old age and death.
Abiding in the center of the lunar disc, raining down the supreme nectar;
performing penance, the perfection of penance, the bestower of the perfection of penance. || 15-159 ||
Three are perfected through asceticism; Tāpasī is dear to the five; Ambikā, Vālikā, and Vandhyā are the bestowers of boons from the king of the gods.
O Goddess whose form consists of the fifty letters, you are even the Supreme Brahman;
O Śivā, you who perform the dance, you are differentiated, joyful, and sweet-voiced.
Saudāminī, Sumadhyā, Śarvarī, Tāmasī, Dayā, Cārvāṅgī, Triṇābhāntā, Aditi, and Satyavādinī. (15–162)
She is gross, subtle, and subtler than the subtlest; she is the performer of all auspiciousness, identical in nature to the Supreme Self, and her very form is consciousness and bliss.
She is the sweet-voiced one, the one with a conch-like neck, she who possesses passionate and beautiful tones;
she is the Mistress of Speech, the self-controlled one, and she who bestows distinguished blessings upon both the disciplined and the undisciplined.

Established in her own state, endowed with splendor, she is Splendor itself; she is Subhadrā, compassionate toward her devotees, the bringer of bliss to her devotees, devotion itself, and the fulfiller of the prosperity of her devotees. || 15-165 ||
She is beautifully smiling, radiant with the joy of passion, and embodies the seed-syllable of Kāma; she is possessed of goodness, devoted to righteousness, the mistress of speech, and full of power.
She who grants mastery over the world, she who is herself under control yet possesses power, she who is worshipped by Vyāsa;
the mother of the three worlds, she who is pleased and who increases the satisfaction of all. || 15-167 ||

She who brings satisfaction to Śiva, she who is peaceful, adorned with the crescent moon as her emblem, the wise one, the wish-fulfilling creeper, and she who is affectionate toward those who seek auspiciousness. || 15-168 ||

She consists of all the gods, she is auspicious, the bestower of wealth, and the dancer of Śiva; she is the wish-fulfilling gem, the one to be meditated upon, ever-awake, and a mother to the wretched. (15.169)
She whose manifold forms are both manifest and unmanifest, the sovereign purifier of the three worlds, the enchantress of all enemies, and the bestower of all auspiciousness. (15.170)

She who possesses all modes of conduct, the presiding deity of all celestial maidens, she who is to be beheld, she who is worthy of worship, the radiant one, prosperity itself, she who is to be saluted, and the expounder of Brahman.
Moon-faced, with eyes like those of the cakora bird, she possessed beautiful eyes and lovely vision;
her eyes were like the petals of the three-eyed one’s lotus, and she had the radiance of the interior of a lotus.
O source of splendor, O gazelle-eyed one, O enchanting one;
O Vārāhī, O lady of virtuous conduct, O you who contain the universe within, O eternal one! (15.173)
Hiraṇyagarbhā, who liberates from the suffering of the womb;
she is gentle, southern, western, eastern, and likewise belonging to the south-west.
Śatākṣī, Sahasrākṣī, Śuddhā, Śośī, Dhṛti, Dharā, Rukmiṇī, Jānakī, Sītā, and you who dwell in Satyaloka. (15–175)
She whose domain is the Purāṇas, she who is ancient, she who bestows great devotion, she who possesses the majesty of Viṣṇu, she who is Ahalyā, and she who fills the universe. 15-176.
Manoharā, Manujñā, Māheśī, Varavarṇinī, Mahāsmṛti, Kāmarūpā, Viśvarūpā, and Mahomati. (15–177)
Bhāgīrathī, Kāśapī, the lovely daughter of the Mountain, the beloved of Hari, the daughter of the Mountain, and she who is born from the Ocean of Milk. (15–178)
O you who dwell in the Vindhya, whose abode is the Vindhya, you who reside in the divine place;
O Padmāvatī, O Candrakalā, O Kamalī, O Kalāvatī! 15–179.
Jñāneśvarī, the giver of knowledge, the bestower of the command of knowledge; Bhadrakālī, Viśālākṣī, Vahulā, Trikuṭā, and Tithi. || 15-180 ||

The one who seized the Pārijāta tree, the eloquent, the fourth [state], whose locks are disheveled; she who holds the noose and the goad, the praiseworthy, the one who brings all under control. 15-181.
She who steals the heart of Śiva’s body, she who dwells within the lotus of the heart,
she who is the refuge, she who is the protection, she who is dark-complexioned, and she whose luster is equal to the autumnal moon.

The glorious one, the stainless one, the delighted one, the cool one, the daughter of the mountain; she who is honored by the gods, the most excellent of goddesses, the destroyer of the fear of those who bow before her.
The wife of Hara, the daughter of the mountain, Śarvāṇī, the beloved of Hara;
she is the creator, the destroyer, and the protectress, bestowing the fruits of all desires. (15.184)
She is fond of praise and is praised; she is fond of oblations and is the oblation itself.
O beautiful one in every limb, she is devoted to the city of Kauśāmbī and is fond of the *kausumbha* flower. (15-185)
In former times, Lopāmudrā, Arundhatī, Nandinī, Vasumālikā, Gṛhiṇī, Pūrṇā, and the beloved of the lotus-eyed one [Viṣṇu] were likewise [liberated]. (15.186)
O you who possess a multitude of virtues, O virtuous one, O beautiful one through the weight of your qualities;
O refuge of all, O you who possess all virtues, O you who cause joy to all! || 15-187 ||
She consists of all mantras, she is the Delighter, the Red One, the Illuminator of the Limbs;
she is Kumārī, pleased with her worshiper, and she who observes the vow of a maiden.
Kuśāvatī, Kauśalyā, Jagadambā, Vuje-kṣaṇā, Supremā, Suprabhā, Sādhyā—the bestower of the desires of practitioners. || 15-189 ||
She who creates the eons, she who is like all eons, she who bestows all eons;
she who is auspicious, beautiful, pure, and the giver of all auspiciousness.
Whoever, being self-restrained and with a mind full of devotion, should daily recite this hymn called the Thousand Names, which was spoken by Śivā to Śiva; || 15-191 ||
Fortune remains steady for him, and speech becomes a dancer upon his face;
may his good fortune, as well as his wealth, grain, and other possessions, increase eternally. (15.192)
Poverty shall never arise in his family; there shall be a festival of joy, and for him, famine is always pacified wherever he dwells. (15.193)
Sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, cattle, buffaloes, and the like, as well as elephants and human sovereignty, shall increase day by day through him. (15–194)
Whether she be barren, or one whose children die like crows, or a woman who has lost her offspring, upon hearing this hymn, she obtains a long-lived son. (15.195)
If one writes [the mantra] with gorocanā and saffron on a birch-bark leaf and, having worshipped it, wears it on the arm, the head, or the neck; || 15.196 ||
Those who are devoted to worthy objects according to their desires shall, in the end, become a divine host;
therefore, O King, they indeed proceed to the eastern quarter, to Kavaścaṃ. (15-197)
When enemies are absent, the happiness of friends increases;
and whatever desires men long for, they shall obtain them by force.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, rākṣasas,
and dānavas are not capable of seeing even that which is not seen, if they have not held this great hymn.
Fortune that is ever-shifting becomes steady in his house;
the Goddess of Speech dwells in his mouth—this is the truth, there is no doubt. (15-200)
Having recited this hymn, wherever one goes, there one shall always obtain victory and the highest enjoyment. (15.201)
Thus ends the Thousand-Name Hymn of Annapūrṇā, from the Śrī Rudrayāmala, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
Now, the hymn to Annapūrṇā:
Oṃ, salutations to the auspicious goddess, the beloved of Śaṅkara;
salutations to the goddess who is fond of devotion, O Annapūrṇā, let there be salutations unto you. (15–202)
Oṃ, salutations to you who assume forms through illusion; salutations to you, the beloved of Śrīkaṇṭha!
O Māheśvarī, salutations to you; O Annapūrṇā, let there be salutations to you! (15.203)
O Mahāmāyī, wife of Śiva; O beloved of Hara in the form of a consort; O bestower of desires, O Sovereign of the Gods; O Annapūrṇā, salutations be to you! (15.204)
O Great Goddess Annapūrṇā, who possess the splendor of a thousand rising suns, who are adorned with three eyes, and who have the moon as your crest— salutations be to you!
O Goddess who wears variegated garments, O sinless one who delights in the gift of food, O Annapūrṇā, who take joy in the dance of Śiva—salutations be to you! (15.206)
O Goddess, grant the desires of the practitioner; O destroyer of the suffering of existence! O Goddess, you who possess the weight of breasts, O Annapūrṇā, salutations be to you! (15-207)
O Goddess who began with Indra, whose lotus feet bear the form of Rudrāṇī, O Bestower of all prosperity, O Annapūrṇā, salutations be to you! (15.208)
Whoever recites this hymn with a concentrated mind at the time of worship, in his home prosperity becomes stable; of this there is no doubt. (8) [15.209]
Whoever recites this at the time of dawn, preceded by the muttering of mantras, for him there shall be an abundance of food, increasing day by day. (15.210)
That which must never be given to anyone nor revealed at any time—since from such revelation there would be a loss of accomplishment—one should therefore guard it with great effort. (15.211)
Thus ends the *Annapūrṇāstotra*.
Now follows the *Annapūrṇāstotra*. The Goddess said:
"O Śaṅkara, tell me truly: by bowing to which deity will poverty cease to exist quickly, as if it were equal to a mere drop of water? (15.212)
Śaṅkara said:
I shall proclaim the [mantra of] Annapūrṇā, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
by the mere remembrance of whom a Kaulika may live having accomplished his purpose.
The Mistress of the wheels beginning with the Mūlādhāra, who has reached the further shore of the lineage of the six paths, she is the manifest Ānandalaḷikā, the Great Goddess Annapūrṇā. (15.214)
Situated in the midst of the peak of the gods, she rests upon the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*;
she is eternal, soundless, without support, pervasive, and radiant with splendor. (15.215)
Piṣṭayeśī, Parā Lakṣmī, Kāmastārā, and likewise Tārā; "Bhagavatī Annapūrṇā"—thus it has been inscribed for me. (15.216)
"O giver of food, Svāhā!"—thus she is renowned as Mantrasārā;
she consists of twenty-seven syllables and is served by hosts of Yoginīs. (15.217)
O you who have crossed over all states, whose nature is the bliss of discernment;
the universe is your radiant form, and the state of the *prājña* is your vast essential nature. (15.218)

She who consists of the nature of the four states is called by the name Vimarśā; she is designated by the names of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, which are the names for her manifold form. (15.219)
Renowned among the masters in the three worlds, she was revealed in the fourfold [tradition] as Śrīvidyā, the secret convention of the Cakra, or as the one whose form is composed of the elements.
In the four corners beginning with the world (bhuvana), there are the deities of the four Āgamas;
in the Eastern Tradition (pūrvāmnāya), the power of Rudra is directly the refuge of the three worlds. (15.221)
She who is known by the name Kamalā is Rudrāṇī Dakṣiṇāmbikā; she who is among the Subhagās is Kubjeśī Paścimāmbikā.
By the designation of supreme knowledge (parā-vidyā), she is remembered as the one beyond the three;
Oṃ-dyatraya is the supreme atom of the three, and Oṃ-dyatraya is the eternal refuge. (15.223)

Established in the threads prescribed by tradition, born from the assembly of skulls, she is the one who deludes the three worlds, whose form is unmanifest, yet who is revealed as the refuge of Tripura. (15.224)
O Tripureśvarī, that entire wheel of the Pūraka is secret;
it resides in the agitation of all things and is endowed with the most profound secrecy.
She who always dwells in the city resides in the center of the circle of Sundarī;
she who dwells in the Kukola family abides in the state of the accomplisher of all aims.
The illustrious Goddess is of bound form, followed by the protectors of all;
she is known as Nigabhā and Mālinī, the supreme remover of all diseases. (15.227)
From the secret [teaching], she is fully perfected, the bestower of all accomplishments;
she abides in the supreme and non-supreme secret, the sovereign of all wheels.
The source of the universe, she who knows the signs and conventions of the three-part mudrā;
in her right hand she holds a golden ladle, and she bestows all desired objects upon those who serve her.
In her left hand she holds a vessel of nectar that grants the desires of her servants;
she is easily accessible through the blissful consciousness of the path of the left, the mistress of that way. (15.230)
