Dark-complexioned, endowed with excellent luster, she is a woman of supreme beauty;
her girdle is a network of tinkling bells, and she is a noble lady of increasing prosperity.
Her moon-like smile filled all the quarters of space;
the crescent moon upon her forehead shone brightly, and her curved eyebrow was like a sprout of foliage.
Sundarī, however, possessed the luster of a creeper; she was the daughter of the fisherman Pūrṇaka, with eyes like water and the corners of her eyes like waves, and a lovely lotus-face. (15.233)
The great moonlight of the luster of her nails filled [the world] on all sides;
she possessed a pair of full, elevated breasts and a waist marked by the three folds.
Her excellent [breasts] are very pure and well-rounded, and she has a slender waist;
her line of body hair is endowed with radiance, and her girdle rests upon her hips.

Her thighs were lovely like the trunk of a plantain tree, her hips graced with a beautiful region, her shanks were rounded, her ankles were well-concealed, and she was endowed with a pair of lotus-like feet.
Her sprout-like lower lip was colored with betel-leaf moistened with camphor,
and her body was anointed with a paste of musk-scented camphor.
Complete in all her limbs, she captivates the mind of Śiva;
she possesses great zeal for the gift of food and bestows the fruit of the desires of her devotees. (15.238)
Lakṣmī bestows the fruits of both earth and heaven; she is uniquely protected by the gift of jewels;
she is free from ailment, has destroyed all afflictions, and grants the singular fruit of happiness.
The bestower of enjoyments, the blessed one, the dwelling place, she who has attained fortune, whose womb is fortune;
the bestower of prosperity, endowed with splendor, gentle, compassionate, beautiful, and unconquered.

Gaurī, the bestower of supreme longevity, has brought the three worlds under her control; by her grace, poverty was seen no more even when the sacrificial ladle was full at the tip of the *ḍama* drum.
Thinking "Alas, I am struck by sudden fear," she trembled;
yet anyone who, having touched a leaf fallen from a mountain slope, remembers that Śivā— (15.242)

The supreme teacher of the lineage is like a mountain of wealth that bestows immeasurable riches upon those who approach it; he is like a full vessel of food for the bee-like body of the mountain of poverty. (15.243)
Having remembered her, one who has accomplished his purpose should wander among those possessed of food and wealth;
she is the sinless goddess Rudrā, of great disposition, who resides within the eightfold group of the Yamalas.
She is the family and the non-family, the support of the vital essence, the bestower of the fruit of the elements;
she is the glory of the lotus of eternal bliss, whose form is consciousness and bliss.
The pair of hands of the one who has destroyed the poverty of his devotees through pride holds a lute;
she is the nectar of consciousness, surrounded by joyful female devotees who are like excellent maidens. (15.246)
The four-petalled lotus at the root-support (mūlādhāra), situated in the center of its pericarp,
is joined with the Udyāna-mudrā and the garland of Mātṛkā letters.
The Maṇipūraka is the cessation at twenty, the perfection of the ten teeth;
it is situated in the middle of the central channel, accessible through yoga, and eternal. (15.248)
Delighted by the unstruck lotus (*anāhatābja*), she resides within the twelve-spoked [lotus];
situated in the center of the Viśuddha-cakra, her intellect is serene within the sixteen spokes. (15.249)

Cāṇḍī resides in the wheel of command (ājñācakra); she bestows nectar upon the tips of the two petals, is the abode of the life-force of the ultimate reality, and increases the host of the five arrows.
The state of the plane is without support, dwelling within the center of space;
it resides in the middle of the thousand-petaled lotus, having attained the unimpeded divine siddhis.
Residing in the lotus at the center of the earth, she is intent upon her own continuity;
she is certainly designated as Dhruvā, Śaṅkhinī, and Vadhubhāvanā. (15.252)
The nectar-moonlight of the thundering collision of the moon, sun, and fire;
she whose body is the installation (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* [phonemes] beginning with the head and face and ending with the hair and feet. (15.253)
In the foundation, the navel, the heart, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā;
in the center of the moon, the throat, the heart, the root foundation, and so forth, up to the feet. (15–254)
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the letters of the Bhavānī-mūla-vidyā in their proper sequence;
at the end of the twelfth [petal], there is a lotus with sixteen petals and a single pericarp.
The intellect, which is the fit ground for the state of Nirvāṇa, is ablaze with the brilliance of a thousand suns;
it is endowed with the luster of ten million flashes of lightning and consists of the nectar of the knowledge of Brahman. || 15-256 ||
The deity, whose mind is unified with the mantra and the yantra, is the supreme teacher;
she is the Goddess residing within the food, her abode being that which is called the Haṃsa.
The triangular Mātṛkā-lotus, the square, the urāsanā, the world and so forth, the Mother of the World, and the fourfold enclosure of Śakti’s limbs. (15.258)
Established in the reality of the Great Vidyās and so forth, she is the presiding deity of consciousness,
as well as of mantras and those who recite them, and likewise of yantras and those who employ them.
The deity presiding over Annapūrṇā herself directly bestows food; this very [deity] is Annapūrṇā, having been composed by me in fifty verses. 15-260.
Renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Kalpavallī, she quickly bestows great sovereignty upon those who bow before her. (15.261)
She removes poverty for ten million lifetimes and bestows prosperity upon whoever recites this hymn of praise, which destroys sins and grants all desires. (15.262)
His sins perish like various kinds of evil spirits;
this is that supreme longevity, prosperity, fame, and so forth. (15.263)
It bestows supreme joy and sons who excel in the qualities of learning; what need is there for much speaking here? Whatever the practitioner desires, [it grants]. (15.264)
Aṇṇapūrṇeśvarī herself bestows that [attainment], and not otherwise;
provided it is properly bestowed upon one who is devoted to the guru and possessed of wisdom. (15.265)
Through the complete mastery of self-knowledge and by practicing this in the midst [of the breath], one should meditate upon this again and again, repeatedly desiring what one desires. (15.266)
The wish-fulfilling tree bestows vast enjoyments upon those who worship it, for the glorious deity of food and other such things dwells within his heart. (15.267)
The abundance of Kuvera is seen,
which has arisen through her grace; and the sovereignty of Varuṇa is seen, which is the means for subjugation, [all belonging] to Annapūrṇā.
In former times, Lakṣmī gave her heart to the playful Lord, and Jayā gave hers to Viṣṇu.
By bestowing her upon him, Śrī attained the status of Viṣṇu’s consort;
and by Śambhu, Caṇḍikā became his wife—this is the fruit of the law of beauty. (15.269)
Through supreme devotion, the worship consisting of recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites has been accomplished for the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and likewise for the Guhyakas. (15.270)
And the miraculous power of the Siddhas, which is free from old age and death,
as well as that of the Ṛṣis, the Munis, the Vīras, and likewise the Yogins.
O sages, omniscience and preeminence are bestowed with reverence upon him who, being ever-vigilant, recites this [mantra] daily at dawn in truth. (15.272)
Whosoever [practices this], for that very person there will be great accomplishment;
may the deities of the mantra and the deities of the name remain well-established through the offering of food.
"Residing within that very house, yet remaining motionless within the inner self"—having thus constantly recited this with minds free from worldly attachment, [they attain liberation]. (15.274)
"O Annapūrṇeśvarī, when bound [by this mantra], she recites everything as if it were her own.
Thus ends the complete hymn, the *Annapūrṇā-kalpalatā*, from the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*.
Now begins the Tripurā Stotra:
Oṃ! [I salute] Śiva, who has two arms with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who is gracious, supremely serene, and seated upon his excellent Śakti.
I worship the Guru, whose bimba-like lips are serene and whose smile is beautiful, seated in the center of a lotus upon his head. (1) || 15-275 ||
Those men who worship the syllable *vaka*, situated in fire (*va*), graced by the three forms (*ka*), joined with the moon (*u*), the first among the Blessed Ones, its own seed-syllable,
radiant with the luster of its own color— the beloved of the Triple Power— attain good fortune. (2)
Having joined the sky, the friend of the wind, then the left eye, the abode of *svadhā*, and the wave, with the single-faced one;
having meditated upon your own secondless seed-syllable, which is praised by the gods and worthy of contemplation, they attain the glory of Śrī.

Then, having visualized this mantra—beginning with *viriñci* (*oṃ*), followed by *kṣiti* (*laṃ*), then *vāma* (*e*), and *ravidhu* (*sa*) joined with *nāda* (*ī*), forming the seed-syllable of the Sun-god (*saiṃ*)—kings who recite it attain lordship over the three worlds while deluding all beings. (4)
O beloved, I remember those who, having concentrated on the triad and meditated upon your limbs, chant [this] at the three junctions of the day;
for them, no enemy causes even the slightest fear, and the goddess Śrī dwells in their homes. (5)
In the presence of Sukha, the goddess Sarasvatī manifests as compositions in prose and verse; the gods do not harm him, but bow down to him.
The pair of her feet is the ornament upon the heads of kings, and the difficult-to-attain supernatural powers (*siddhis*) come into his hand; they abandon those who are hard to reach. (6) 15-280.
In the forest of *pārijāta* trees upon the earth, one should contemplate that golden radiance within a house formed by a mass of ink;
indeed, one should visualize two bodies in the sky, an eight-spoked lotus with a shimmering jewel lion-throne at its center.
(7) One should expand the supreme pair of *yoni*s within the pericarp, situated inside that golden radiance.
Shining with earrings, moon-faced, three-eyed, with a throbbing conch-like neck, and bowed by her breasts. (8) || 15-282 ||

With her multitude of arms resplendent like great jewels, she holds her two lotuses, a book, a bow, a golden goad, and flower-arrows; she is adorned with vast jewel ornaments, possesses a beautiful voice, and has lovely hips. (15.283)

With her feet beautiful with the tips of her anklets, adorned with crowns and other ornaments, and gracious; holding white chowries and a hand bearing the gesture of granting boons, she sustains the golden triple world.
(10) She is the creator of the three worlds, the dispeller of the world’s suffering, eternally full of joy, and whose syllable is the half-sound *ha*.
I worship her who agitates the world, who protects the world, who is the nature of the three dots, and who possesses the three powers. (15.285)
Having meditated upon this very form of the Hero as being right before me, I worship it with devotion;
even an immortal, having worshipped the Self-Existent One with flowers and other offerings, attains the accomplishment of the four aims of life. (12)

Having worshipped Śrī and Śrīpati, Pārvatī and Īśvara, Rati and Kāmadeva together with Ṣaṇḍa, and likewise Bhavānī joined with her own vehicle, each in their proper order, that king shall become [prosperous]. Furthermore,
having visualized them on both sides and worshipped the queens, he should then worship the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Having worshipped the weapons there at the tip of the spear, even a human being may obtain the eightfold supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*) of Bhava.
(14) You are the Earth, the Ordainer; you possess the agency of creating the world. You are also the Waters, Viṣṇu, and the protector of the world.
You are Fire, Rudra, and the bringer of death to the world; endowed with your own sovereignty, you are the illuminator of the universe. (15)
O Śivā, you are the primordial mistress; O beloved refuge of the world, you eternally move within the *brahmarandhra*.
You are the supportless goal, the singular merit of Bhava, and you who are like the single tongue of flame—O Bhavānī, be gracious! (16) 15-b)
O Lord, you who, in the midst of existence, render all pride of the sages utterly small with bliss;
therefore, I do not know you, O embodiment of consciousness and bliss, O embodiment of praise—be gracious, O Bhavānī! (15-291)
Having chanted one hundred thousand times with a mind delighted by your presence, one attains poetic genius through chanting alone.

Contemplating your own form, one obtains the three worlds; O Mother, be gracious to me, for you are the supporting power (*ādhāra-śakti*) and you are the form of that which is supported (*ādheya-rūpā*), pervading the universe as the pervasive form of the world.

You are non-existence, you alone are the form that transcends the qualities; you alone are existence, O Bhavānī, be gracious! (19) You are the cosmic egg, you are the all-pervading Lord, you alone are the universe; what praise could there be for you who shine throughout the world?
Nevertheless, they offer praise to the very direction of your qualities—O Bhavānī, be gracious! (20)
Thus ends the hymn to Tripurā.
Now, the armor of Tripurā.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the armor (*kavaca*) that grants all perfections (*siddhi*).
By reciting and wearing it, a man is liberated from distress.
O Goddess, he who recites the mantra of Durgā’s limbs without knowing her armor (kavaca) shall not obtain its fruit; in the end, he shall go to hell. (15.296)
Oṃ! May Umādevī protect the head; may Śūladhāriṇī protect the forehead; may Sugandhā protect the nose; may Sarvasādhanī protect the mouth. (15.297)
On the tongue you are the goddess Caṇḍikā, and on the two thighs you are Vindhyavāsinī;
thus you abide, O Goddess of gods, as the very essence of the protection of the three worlds.
"Protect me in all my limbs, O Goddess Durgā; salutations to you! Thus ends the *Tripurākavaca*.
Now follows the *Durgāśatanāmastotra* (The Hymn of One Hundred Names of Durgā).
The illustrious Lord said:
"I shall proclaim the hundred names; listen, O Kamalānana!"
By the mere grace of whom the virtuous Durgā becomes pleased:
Oṃ, Satī, Sādhvī, Bhavā, Prītā, Bhavānī, the liberator from worldly existence! || 15-300 ||
The noble Durgā, Jayā and the others, the three-eyed one who wields the trident, the bearer of the Pināka bow, Citrā, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, and Mahātapā.
Salutations to her who is growth and ego, whose form is consciousness, who is both conscious and unconscious;
she who consists of all mantras, who is eternal, and whose essential nature is truth and bliss. (15.302)
She is the one who has subdued the horse, she is the capable one, she is the auspicious one, and she is the eternal future;
she is Śākambharī, the mother of the Vedas, the wise one, and she is always fond of jewels.
She is the knowledge of all, the daughter of Dakṣa, and the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice;
she is Aparṇā, the one of many colors, Pāṭalā, and Pāṭalāvatī.
Clad in fine silken garments, resplendent with golden ornaments,
immeasurable in her prowess, cruel yet beautiful, she was the most excellent woman in the city.
Vanadurgā and Mātaṅgī, who is worshipped with ritual baths performed by Matanga;
likewise Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Aindrī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī. || 15-306 ||
Cāmuṇḍā, Vārāhī, Lakṣmī who has the form of the auspicious Puruṣa, Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Satyā, and Vahnidā. (15.307)
The slayer of Nisumbha and Sumbha, the crusher of the demon Mahisa.
She is the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the destroyer of Candra-muṇḍa, the annihilator of all asuras, and the slayer of all dānavas. || 15-309 ||
She consists of all the scriptures and is the truth; likewise, she possesses the wisdom of all weapons.
She holds many scriptures in her hands and rends asunder with many missiles.
The maiden, the girl, the adolescent, the young woman, the ascetic, the immature, and the mother of an old man—[these] bestow strength. (15.311)
O Goddess Parvati, for one who constantly recites these one hundred and eight names of Durga, no misfortune whatsoever exists in the three worlds.
Wealth, grain, a son, a wife, horses, and likewise elephants—
one shall obtain these four aims of life, and finally, eternal liberation.
Having worshipped the maiden and meditated upon the Goddess, the sovereign of the gods,
one should worship her with supreme devotion while reciting the "Eightfold Hundred Names."
O Goddess, his success shall come to pass even through the boons of the Lord of All;
he attains the splendor of royal joy and shall obtain the glory of sovereignty. (15.315)
Having drawn the yantra according to the prescribed rite with gorocanā, lac, saffron, vermilion, camphor, and the three sweets,
one who knows the ritual should always wear it; for Murāri dwells therein on the Bhauma-Avasyā days when the moon enters those [asterisms].
Having inscribed this mantra of dissolution here, one may become the abode of all prosperities.
Thus ends the "Eighty-Verse Hymn to the Names of Durgā" as spoken in the Viśvasāra.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the armor (*kavaca*) that grants all desires;
by obtaining the grace of which one becomes Sadāśiva himself. (15-317)

Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, the practitioner of mantra should daily recite the armor (*kavaca*) for the sake of attaining the mantra and for the successful realization of the mantra's phonemes.
For the armor (kavaca) of Mahiṣamardinī, the venerable Mahākāla is the seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas),
the primordial Śakti Mahiṣamardinī is the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of human life.
Klī! May the goddess Kāminī, the bestower of desires, protect my head;
may the goddess Makārī, the Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī), protect me with her pair of eyes. (15.319)
May Hiṅgulā, the leader of the gods, protect me with the syllable *hikāra* in my mouth;
may Śvetā protect me with the syllable *ṣaṃkāra*, and Aparājitā on my tongue. (15.320)
May the goddess Makārī protect me, the subduer, the leader of the gods;
may the goddess Dikārī protect me, the bestower of the fruit of liberation. || 15-321 ||
May Nīkāri, the eternal one, protect me in the heart, the two arms, the two sides, the navel, the penis, the anus, the throat, and likewise in the two untouched ears. (15.322)
May she protect my crest and my armor; likewise, may she protect my arms and shanks. May she who is endowed with all powers protect me in every limb, Svāhā! (15.323)
May Kāmājyā protect me, Svāhā! May Mardinī protect my head; may the great ten-syllable Vidyā, Mardinī, protect all my limbs. (15.324)
May Mardinī protect [me] constantly; may she always destroy the wicked. May Maheśānī protect [me]; may Kanakā protect [me] at all times. (15.325)
May Nandinī protect me constantly; may Mudrā always protect me. May Jayā always protect me; may Lakṣmī Viśuddhā protect me at all times. (15-326)
May the Ḍākinī protect me constantly; may the Siddhas always protect me;
may the Goddess Mahiṣamardinī protect me everywhere and at all times. (15.327)
Thus has this divine armor, which grants all desires, been told to you.
It must not be spoken of here or there; it is concealed in all tantras but revealed in the Viśvasāra.
Having given it to them, O Great Goddess, they attain the two stages in succession.
The mantras become averse and bring about a most terrible calamity after having granted a boon. || 15-328 ||
It would become impure for him; therefore, one should not conceal it with effort.
O Maheśvarī, [one should write] gorocanā and saffron on a birch leaf. (15.329)
Having written it with an auspicious conjunction (*śubhayoga*), O Lord of Brahmins, likewise during the *vaidhṛti* yoga;
one becomes long-lived through the *siddhiyoga*, whether it be *vāla*, *vāla*, *va*, *kaula*, or *vā*. (15.330)
For a merchant, [it is auspicious] under Śravaṇā and likewise under Revatī;
also under the three Uttaras, under the Yogas, and under the three Pūrvās.
Under the asterism Aśvinī or Rohiṇī, on the third or ninth lunar day, or on the eighth, the fourteenth, the sixth, or the fifth lunar day. || 15-332 ||
And on the new moon and the full moon, likewise at night in the wilderness, in solitary linga-shrines, in cremation grounds, in empty houses, and in places of dissolution. (15.333)
With offerings to the gurus, or to the Vaiṣṇavas, or likewise with the Svayaṃbhū rites, using white or red flowers mixed with honey. (15.334)
Furthermore, having written [the mantra] on cloth with thread-dyed ink, one should wear it;
for him, all goals will be accomplished—so it was spoken by Śaṅkara. (15.335)
Having worshipped a young maiden and offered the Devīsūkta,
and having recited it, a wealthy man should feed the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas.
The hunt was recounted to the princess for three days;
then there arose the great protection, the armor that grants all desires. (15.337)
For him there are no mental anxieties or physical ailments, nor is there ever any suffering, grief, or fear;
even upon seeing him, the king and his servants become as mute as if they were dumb. (15.338)
He who, being self-restrained and pure, recites this for one month every day, should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) by day and devote himself to strength (śakti) at night. || 15-339 ||
One should always feed six thousand [beings] every day;
within six months or three months, one will certainly attain the state of a Khecarī.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth becomes wealthy; one who is diseased becomes strong; and even a king may fall into servitude. (15.341)
A woman in her menses should constantly recite this Vidyā over her private parts according to the prescribed rule;
the wise man who does so is indeed Śrī Sadāśiva himself. (15.342)
Thus ends the armor of Mahiṣamardinī in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Now follows the hymn to Mahiṣamardinī.
The illustrious Bhairava said: O Goddess Pracaṇḍā, who has pulverized great delusion within my mind with your fierce roar,
grant me, at your own will, this wave of the wind from the formidable fortress of Pracaṇḍa.
Therefore, having turned away from this world, may he who has entered the forest of the glorious lotus-feet [of the Lord] rejoice for a long time in my presence. 15.343.

O fierce goddess, having abandoned their pride—which was as vast as Mount Meru and expanded with fingers raised in defiance—the gods, skilled in seeking refuge, always serve the Lord Nṛsiṃha, the giver of gold, who is expert in destroying his enemies;
tell me, what enemy could remain there? For they serve His glorious feet, which are ever-ready for the fierce task of devouring foes.
What could be the fear for one who serves? (2) || 15-344 ||

O Caṇḍī, if that syllable which is the essence of the objects of the senses has entered within the range of your hearing, then that reality is proclaimed by Brahmā and the other gods as being followed by the *puruṣa* and *prakṛti*.
Therefore, O Goddess, [worship] your radiant and glorious lotus-feet, the sole abode of the nectar-essence of all the deities.
Honor me today by being intent upon our embrace. (3) || 15-345 ||
O Mother, whether it be a cause for reproach according to the customs of my family, or whether it brings no fame,
let my practice be such that it performs worship to ten million Śivas;
O Mother, you who are the abode of service to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Agni, and the gods— [I offer] this recitation at your glorious feet.
The mind is always intent upon the practice of forest-dwelling. || 15-346 ||
If I am instructed in the two stages of meditation joined with Your feet, then let such instruction be granted to me; what need is there for other forms of discipline?
Therefore, O Goddess, may Your compassion descend upon this body of mine, so that my mind may behold the wealth of Your two glorious lotus feet.
May you grant security and peace; may this be forgiven. (5) || 15-347 ||
Having attained his own self, the Lord of Beings, who had reached a state of vast exhilaration, would not have been capable of protecting his life had it not been for fate;
for he has become filled with the honey dripping from the interior of the *prāgastya* forest, which is like sandalwood and the moonlight of lightning.
The *Aikakamālā* was compiled by Modena. (6) || 15-348 ||

Alas, alas! O Mother, for one such as I— whose heart is rendered tasteless within by the entire ocean of beginningless delusion, despite the sprinkling of the nectar of Brahman-bliss through the knowledge of Your speech—
the rainy season of the nectar of Your glorious devotion has become a dark storm, while the intense heat of worldly suffering remains unextinguished even for a moment.
But for a noble person, O Ārya, there is always an overflow. || 15-349 ||

O Lord, Your divine triad— consisting of the stainless consciousness and bliss that radiates to the end of reality— is the source from which the host of gods, beginning with Brahmā (Aṇḍaja), emerge from the throbbing lotus of Your feet;
it expands the maintenance of the world, stretches out creation, and then again dissolves it.
May there be for us, through my very self, a great heart like a cloud as dark as freshly split collyrium. (8) || 15-350 ||

That Durgā is worshipped, whose head is the supreme among the most excellent, having attained a steady and formidable splendor as she strides forth, trampling the great buffalo-demon; she who removes misfortune when recited, who dwells upon the boat [of the world], and who satiates Bhairava while rending the enemies.
[It is] delightful to people, [and] it conquers [the enemy]. (9) || 15-351 ||

When the army dances with shields and whisks, its horses neighing loudly as their hooves circle the ground, and its vanguard is struck down by the enemy’s fierce onset like a peacock’s plumage being torn apart,
then the wise man should abandon the field at once—
before the host, spreading like a gale, with its heads severed, is destroyed by the arrogant and wicked foe.
Resplendent with a noose of jasmine-like eyes shining like a cluster of blossoms. (10) || 15-352 ||
In this *cañcatkāmu-virāma-kāmalakalanā* [meter], which is intensely languid and intoxicating, situated within the space between the eyes of a buffalo-like beast,
there is a beautiful, excellent red hue bound by three left [lines] in the middle of the eight sons of Vasu (eight syllables) in a golden-colored field.
(11) "ṇamudā ghūrṇāya māṃ nasmaraṇam" (15-353).
I bow to Śivā, who holds in her upper and lower hands— arranged right and left— a discus, an arrow, a flaying knife, a shield, a bow, an arrow, a trident, and the gesture that dispels fear;
she is dark-complexioned like a blue rain-cloud, adorned with earrings, and has her topknot tied up so tightly that [her hair] slips down.
Her mouth is terrifying with its lolling tongue and bared fangs, and she is formidable with her loud, raucous laughter. (12) || 15-354 ||
Thus, O Goddess, those who meditate upon your form in the Anadyā river— which is worshipped by Śakra and others such as Durga— perform the subjugation of enemies, the agitation of adversaries,
and so forth; they attain sovereignty, victory over Indra, wisdom like that of Bṛhaspati, the nectar-like eloquence of Kāvya (Śukra), and the powers of immobilization and expulsion.
For those who perform acts such as killing, [the result] arises for them spontaneously. || 15-355 ||

O Goddess, if those who desire wealth, liberation, and other goals listen to or recite with devotion this hymn— which I have composed through the focused meditation on the pair of Your lotus feet, and which contains the extraction of mantras and the secret instructions on the family rites— then these [attainments] shall come into their hands.
They worship me, the Lord of the worlds; salutations to you, O Victorious One! (14) || 15-356 ||
Thus ends the hymn to Mahiṣamardinī; may there be auspiciousness.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the armor (*kavaca*) of Lakṣmī, which grants all desires;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes Sadāśiva himself. (15-357)
A person who performs her worship and recites her mantra shall become a son of Pārvatī, honored by all the scriptures. (15.358)
This [mantra], which is especially dear to Viṣṇu, should be served by one seeking the entrance to knowledge.

Of this Śrī-Caturakṣarī, the consort of Viṣṇu, the Lord Śiva is the Ṛṣi, Anuṣṭubh is the metre, Vāgīśvarī is the deity, Vāgbhava is the seed-syllable (bīja), Lajjā is the power (śakti), and Ramā is the bolt (kīlaka).

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining all perfections and prosperity: [the seed-syllable] consisting of desire (*kāma*), the sense of "mine" (*mamatva*), poetic skill (*kavitva*), and constant nourishment (*pāntritya*).
May Vāgbhavī, the bestower of all accomplishments, protect [me] with a single hair-tip on the crown of the head. || 15-359 ||
Hrī! May Śāṅkarī protect the space between the eyes and the pair of eyes;
[may she protect] the tongue, the circumference of the mouth, the two ears, the teeth, and the nose. (15.360)

May Lakṣmī, the consort of Viṣṇu, who embodies the syllables of the word "Śrī," protect me—she who resides in the upper and lower lips, the two rows of teeth, the root of the palate, and the jaw. (15.361)
Pārvatī [is to be worshipped] on the pair of ears, the pair of arms, and the pair of breasts;
again, on the heart, the wrists, the neck, and the two sides. (15.362)
Likewise on the back, in the secret place, on the left and the right, in the genitals, on the hips, at the navel, and again on the two shanks. (15.363)
One should place *jānu* on the two feet, *guṭikā* at the base of the fingers, *svadhā* in the vital power (*prāṇaśakti*), *mesī* in the other [place], and again *punar* on the head. (15.364)
May the Great Goddess Kāmeśī, who is highly exalted, protect all my limbs;
may Mahāmāyā, the Auspicious One, protect me, and may Utkṛṣṭi always protect me. (15.365)
May the goddess Varadvipā, who is beloved by Śambhu everywhere and is the embodiment of speech (Vāgbhavī), protect me always; may she, the consort of Hara, protect me.
May the goddess Ramā protect me always; may the consort of Hara protect me—may the goddess Ramā protect me always, she who is herself the self-sovereign (Svarāṭ).
May Lakṣmī, the illusory power of Viṣṇu and queen of the gods, protect me in all my limbs;
may Vijayā protect my home, and Jayā always protect me.
May Śivadūtī always protect you, O beautiful one; may she protect you at all times. May Bhairavī protect you everywhere; may Bhīruṇḍā protect you always. (15.369)
May Tvaritā protect me always; may Ugratārā protect me always. May Kālikā protect me always; may Kālarātri protect me always. (15.370)
May Vanadurgā protect me always; may Kāmākhyā protect me at all times; may Yoginī protect me always; may the Mudrās protect me always. (15.371)
May the hosts of Yoginīs stationed upon the wheel of the Goddess protect [us] always—in all places, in all undertakings, in all actions, and at all times. (15.372)
"May Lakṣmī, the goddess of gods and the source of all prosperity, protect me.
Thus has this divine armor been told to you for the sake of attaining all perfections.
O Maheśvarī, one should not speak of that [teaching] anywhere to a deceitful person, one devoid of devotion, or a slanderer, even if one perceives it to be for one's own benefit. (15.374)
One should never show [the deity] with missing limbs or with extra limbs;
nor should one show the divine form as "not yours," for by showing it thus, one becomes a destroyer of Śiva.
One should bestow this supreme armor upon one who is of noble birth, possessed of great aspiration, devoted to Durgā, a pure Vaiṣṇava, and thoroughly purified.
To one's own disciple who is peaceful, virtuous, and likewise wise;
on Saturdays and Tuesdays, and with red-colored lamps.
On a Saturday coinciding with a Tuesday, one should write the mantra, complete with all its constituent parts, using red sandalwood and barley-gruel paste.
The Self-Existent One himself should draw the divine armor with auspicious flowers, both his own and those of others, combined with various fragrances. (15.379)
With *gorocanā*, saffron, or red sandalwood, on an auspicious lunar day, in a favorable astrological conjunction (*yoga*), or under the asterism Śravaṇā on a Sunday. (15.380)
Under Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, or Phalgunī, under Maghā, in conjunction with Pūrvabhādrapadā, or under Svāti on a Tuesday. (15.381)
One should write and recite this hymn during an auspicious conjunction in one's own home, especially during the *āyuṣmat*, *prīti*, and *brahma* yogas. (15.382)
In the Indrāgra, Śubha-yoga, and likewise in the Śukra-yoga; in Kaulava, Yālava, and Vaśija as well, O most excellent one. (15.383)
In an empty house or a cremation ground, and especially with Vijayā,
having worshipped a young maiden, one should sacrifice to the eternal Goddess.
One should worship the Supreme Deity with fish, meat, vegetables, and roots, as well as with clarified butter and other offerings, and especially with incense and lamps. (15.385)
Having fed the Brahmins, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
there, one should perform the narrative of Ākheṭaka for three days.
Then there shall be great protection as spoken by Śaṅkara;
they obtain [the powers of] killing, causing hatred, and so forth—of this there is no doubt. (15.387)
Pārvatī might give birth to a son who has been excluded from all the scriptures;
the teacher is the god Hara himself, and his wife is the beloved of Hara.
For one who strives with an unbreakable resolve, success comes in a mere moment;
that mortal who recites this here, with a heart full of inner devotion, [attains it]. (15.389)
By this inference regarding the fruit of his merit, he shall obtain the status of a chamberlain;
he shall long occupy a high station among those whose feet are bowed by the earth—the very mark of the Fortune of the crowns of kings.
Thus ends the Śrī Viśvasāra Tantra, with the Lakṣmī-kavaca complete and finished.
Now, the *Lakṣmīsahasranāma* is being written.
Oṃ! I shall make you fortunate, the goddess Lakṣmī, worshipped by the three worlds. Come, come, O Goddess, lotus-eyed one, whose abode is made in the lotus lake! 15-390.
Come, go, O Giver of Boons; behold me with your own eye!
Come indeed, O auspicious one, who consists of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Thus, with words of praise according to the rule, the younger sister, the highly fortunate one, was truly praised for her truthful nature by Candra, the Supreme Soul.
And those two, O Goddess, the Moon and the Sun, were rescued from the ocean by Raudra;
as soon as they were born, they took refuge with Śiva and Keśava. (15.393)
Sanatkumāra, having addressed that ancient ṛṣi,
spoke this unsurpassed hymn of praise to Lakṣmī as an itihāsa.
O best of sages, how can there be liberation in this world for those who are wicked from such a most terrible hell of poverty? (15.395)
Oṃ. Sanatkumāra said:
Oṃ. Once, in the Kṛtayuga, Brahmā, the creator of all worlds, having performed the creation according to the prescribed rules, subsequently fell into reflection. (15.396)
What shall be the sustenance for the subjects born upon the earth through you?
What destroys poverty, and how does liberation arise from that? (15.397)
Reflecting in his mind that death is better than poverty,
the Lotus-born One went to Uttarakuru, which is situated beyond the Ocean of Milk.
Having performed intense penance there, he once beheld the Supreme Lord,
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the universe, who has Rīkākṣa as his son.
To the omniscient one, the abode of all powers, the eternal, the Lord of all,
Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu, the Lord and husband of Lakṣmī.
Resembling ten million moons, resting upon the bed of the serpent Ananta within the beautiful expanse of the ocean of milk, he is the abode of Śrī.
Resembling the vast sun, the Lord of the great sovereigns of yoginīs,
devoted to the yoga-sleep, the illustrious Lord, the sovereign of all the gods.
The cause of the causes of the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the world;
the orb of the solar disc filled with the rays of millions of powers.
Surrounded by weapons and embodied beings such as the discus and others,
it was difficult to behold even for the gods, the Siddhas, and hundreds of great yogis.
Having beheld the lotus— the support of all powers, the supreme splendor, difficult to perceive, and the Lord of many manifestations— there arose the Source (Sambhava).
Placing his head [upon the ground] and taking up a handful of water, he spoke preceded by a hymn of praise:
"O Maheśvara, fulfill my heart's desire by granting its accomplishment. (15.406)
Oṃ! Be victorious, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, the creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the Great Being. || 15.407 ||
O Supreme Being, who is beyond all others, the joy of the people, and the supreme Lord—
be gracious to me, your devotee, and dispel the darkness born of my doubt.
Thus praised by Brahmā, whose birth is manifest, the Blessed One,
his eyes resting in sleep, turned toward him with favor and spoke.
"I am pleased with you, O Hiraṇyagarbha; speak whatever you desire.
I shall tell it to you without doubt, for you are my devotee, O observer of noble vows."
Having heard these words from Keśava, his heart overcome with compassion,
the highly intelligent one replied to the Blessed Janārdana.
O Keśava, tell me the most wonderful secret for the protection of this fourteenfold creation of beings.
It pacifies poverty, brings fortune, is pleasing to the mind, and is supremely purifying;
it is the great majesty and the true form of all the lords and great Buddhas. (15.413)
257b) Likewise, [he taught] the glories that surpass all others, as well as eternal knowledge, and both the primary and secondary names of Acyuta. 15-414.
"I wish to hear from you, in accordance with reality, those words spoken from your lotus-like mouth.
Having heard his speech, he spoke this reply.
The splendor of the Lord Vāmadeva, whose body is composed of the six qualities and is filled with great majesty, is indeed eternally inseparable from him. 15-416.
Though appearing as distinct in each individual manifestation, like the moonlight of the sun's rays, she alone exists pervading the universe, consisting of all powers. (15.417)
Endowed with all the qualities of the Lord, eternal, and pure by nature,
she is the supreme vital power (prāṇaśakti), the eldest, who pervades everything on earth in every way.
And she is the supreme power (parākalā), the source of all the Śaktis;
indeed, this is the most excellent thousand names of her. (15.419)
Listen with an attentive mind to that which bestows supreme sovereignty:
*Namaḥ*.
Oṃ, she whose form is the glorious lotus is the Truth; she is known by the name of the power of the *ciñcā* fruit. || 15-420 ||
She is absolute, partless, pure, all-pervading, and has the void as her form;
she is the stream shaped like a lotus in the void, born from the nectar of the supreme void.
Dwelling in the imperishable firmament, she is the embodiment of supreme bliss;
eternally pure, eternally satisfied, and the destroyer of eternal poverty.
The power of knowledge, the power of agency, and the power of enjoyment bring about Śiva;
she is the Great Light, the Great Bliss, the Pure and Unshakable Sovereignty.
The manifestation of the power of Anavā is clearly manifest as the expansion of eternal bliss;
once pierced, it pervades all powers and surrounds the ocean [of consciousness]. (15.424)
The eternal form is seated within the heart, waveless and free from affliction;
it is accessible through knowledge, consisting of both the knower and the known, and it causes the expansion of both knowledge and its object.
The power of the word is profound, unwavering, and brilliantly pure;
it is the foundation for all ornaments, free from conceptual construction, and without support. (15.426)
Unmixed, perfectly peaceful, eternal, radiant, and stable; incomparable, free from conceptual construction, and flowing without being driven by external constraints.

Indivisible, yet the divider of the divided; the speech of Vaikharī, moving like a bird; ungraspable, yet mounted upon the foremost vowel 'a'; dwelling within the womb, she is the one whose form is the universe.
Inexpressible, unimpeded, seedless, Pārvatī, supreme, inconceivable, immeasurable, she is the destroyer of the delusion of worldly existence. 15-429.
The sovereign of the gods is threefold—consisting of one, two, and many—as well as beyond number;
she is the well-established, the great sustainer, the increase of consciousness, and the eternal course.
Īśānī, Mahimā, Ṛddhi, Pramodā, Ujjatā, Umā, Akṣarārdhā, Vasānā, Suprakāśī, and Vibhaṅgamā. (15.431)
She who is stainless and resplendent, eternal, victorious, the source, the auspicious reality;
she who dispels darkness, possesses many flames, is intensely radiant, and wears a garland of the earth.
Immeasurable, threefold, subtle, and bestowing supreme nirvāṇa; it is pure, perfectly cleansed, and known as the supreme-non-supreme beyond sorrow. (15.433)
She is the Sustainer, Pure Knowledge, the Great Sovereign of all beings;
she is the Goddess Lakṣmī, Nourishment, and the Great Deity, or Peace through fulfillment.
She who is the sovereign of all favors, the eldest in the world, the treasure-house of the universe;
she who is truth, who is to be invoked in ignorance, and who is auspicious in drawing forth [the soul]. 15-435.
She is the perfectly full, blissful, pure, luminous, immortal, and flowing one; she is like pollen, the bestower of grace, the devourer, the showerer, and the essence.

The goddess Parāvittamati bestows [blessings]; she is the digit (kalā) of Bhāsvatī and Śāntimatī; she is free from the conflict of parts and portions (kalā-kalaṅka-kalaha); she is Viśālā, the delight that illuminates. || 15-437 ||
She is the awakener and the captivator; by her power, she bestows existence and prosperity.
She is the flowing nectar, the giver of life, the mother of living beings, and she resides in the uvula. (15.438)
Dhūmrā, Kalāvatī, Prāṇā, Bhāsurā, Śubhā, Śubhā, Śuddhā, Dhvanisati, and Kṛṣṭi. || 15-439 ||
She is the one who leads forward, the giver of life, the humble, the one with variegated and pale garments, the wielder of the sword,
the bestower of wealth, the diamond-tipped tube, and she whose vehicle is the entire universe.
She whose form is infinite for the infinite ones, because that infinity has no origin;
she is the Great Power, the power of life, the giver of life, the most excellent beloved of the Heart. (15.441)
The entire great thousandfold world-system is the support of desire, bringing happiness; it is manifest Lakṣmī herself, appearing clearly as a sprout within the range of the intellect. (15.442)
She who assumes various bodies and expands through many forms; she whose nature is auspicious, whose desires are fulfilled, who possesses all colors, and who speaks in every tongue. || 15-443 ||

The primordial consciousness, possessing manifold forms, preceded by sound, and most ancient; manifesting as the space for both the unmanifest and living beings, she is the fulfillment of all desires. (15.444)

She is the fulfillment of all intentions, the epitome of reality, the essence of truth, existence and non-existence; she is the refuge of all beings, the nature of consciousness, possessed of the three qualities, and proud of her own attributes. (15.445)
The sovereign lady of progeny, the fierce one, the sustainer of all, the bringer of happiness;
she who brings about auspicious growth and the destruction of the [world-]ages.
Indeed, she is formless, with an uninterrupted continuity, infinite, possessing the eight qualities, free from fear, composed of *māyā*, the *yogamāyā*, the beloved Mahāmāheśvarī. (15.447)
The Great Woman, Vimalā, Kīrtti, Jayā, Lakṣmī, Nirañjanī, the beloved of Pradyumna, the virtuous one, who bestows happiness, good fortune, and spiritual accomplishment. (15.448)
She is the ultimate goal, the desired state, the foundation, the eldest, the most excellent, the bringer of victory;
she is the alleviator of all suffering, joy, the power of the universe, and possesses great strength.
The most excellent Victors, the heroes, are victorious, bestowing victory;
they are the secret of the heart, the secret to be guarded, and the progenitor of the elephant-throne.
The Mistress of Yoga, attainable through yoga, the beloved of the Lord of Yoga;
she who is bowed to by Brahmā and Rudra, the Sovereign of the Vowels who bestows boons.
She who abides in the three cycles, she who dwells in the three worlds, she who arose from the step of Trivikrama;
she is Sutārā, the Savior Tārā, the one difficult to attain, the Deliverer, and the Supreme.
She who has already crossed over and enables others to cross, whose splendor is like that of the Lord of the Stars (the Moon),
she is the knowledge of the planets, the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the sacrifice, and the most beautiful among all branches of learning.
The inner science (adhyātmavidyā) is indeed Padmā, the Supreme Goddess residing in the lotus;
the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), the triple Veda (trayī), commerce (vārtā), and the science of government (daṇḍanīti) are Nipāminī.
Gaurī, Vāgīśvarī, Gostrī, Gāyatrī, Kamalodbhavā, Viśvaṃbharā, Viśvarūpā, Viśvamātā, and Vasupradā. (15.455)
Siddhi, Svāhā, Svadhā, Svasti, Svadhā, the accomplisher of all aims; Ichā, Sṛṣṭi, Dyuti, Bhūti, Kīrti, Śuddhā, and Dayāmati. (15.456)
It bestows learning, intelligence, and fortitude; it is a science revered by the wise.
It is the mother of food, the source of the sun’s course, and the destroyer of cough and asthma. (15.457)
The manifestation of her vow is the sky; her radiance is that which illumines the universe.
She is memory, the mother of all speech, and she is the Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī [Samā] forms of speech.
Sandhyā, Medhā, Prabhā, Bhīmā, Bhīmāsarvakārasvatī, Kāñcī, Māyā, Mahāmāyā, Mohinī, and Mādhavapriyā. (15.459)
She is the enjoyment of the gentle, the enjoyer, the bestower of enjoyment;
she is golden-hued, possessed of beautiful hips, the delight of the deer-like [sage], and the goddess Ramā;
she is the moon, the golden one, the moonlight, the lovely, the splendor, and the bringer of auspiciousness. (15.461)
The beautiful woman who is the most beautiful in the three worlds, the bearer of the splendor of Rāma,
seated upon a lotus, dwelling in a lotus, and adorned with a garland of lotuses.
The beloved one holds a pair of lotuses, adorned with divine ornaments,
rich with various garlands and perfumes, and possesses diverse vehicles for battle.
The goddess Mahānārāyaṇī, the Vaiṣṇavī praised by heroes, Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī, Dhārā, Tattvasaṃkarṣaṇī, and Harā. (15.464)
The all-pervading one who fills the world, adorned with Mahābhairava, Varuṇī, she who is called the Giver of Boons, whose ears are adorned with a staff, the unconquered one. || 15.465 ||
Nṛsiṃhī, Bhairavī, Brāhmī, Bhāskarī, Vyomacāriṇī, Aindrī, the emanation of the bow of desire, the womb of desire, and Mahāprabhā. (15.466)

She who possesses the power of entering trees, the Great Power, whose self-vision consists of the power of the seed-syllable, whose heart is mounted upon Garuḍa, the fierce one with a sweet face. || 15-467 ||
Vārāhī of most fierce form and Nārasiṃhī have destroyed the enemy;
she is like the fire at the end of an eon, with hands as tawny as the sun's rays.
Terrifying to the three worlds, formidable, dark-hued, and enchanting the three worlds;
possessing great fangs, wearing a great garland, most fierce, and a great devourer.
Śaṅkhinī, Lekhinī, Svasthā, Kikhinī, Khecareśvarī,
Bhadrakālī, Citrarūpā, Kaumārī, and Bhagamālinī.
Kalyāṇī, Kāmadhṛk, Jālāmukhī, Colapalamālikā, Vālakā, Dhanadī, Sūryahṛdayā, and Utpalamālikā. || 15-471 ||
Vālakā, Dhanadī, Sūryahṛdayotpalahastikā, Ajitā, Karṣiṇī, Rīti, Bhūsuṇḍā, and Garuḍāsanā. || 15-472 ||
Vaiśvānarī, Mahāmārī, the adorned Mahākālī, she whose power is like that of Mahāmāyūrī, the bliss of Śiva, the bestower of delight. || 15-473 ||
Udgati, Padmamālā, Vandhūvegā, Vibhāvinī, Bhāvinī, Satkriyā, Devasenā, Hiraṇyā, and Rajatā. (15.474)
The mother of sacrifice, who awakens with the trumpeting of elephants, possessing the color of golden lotuses—the auspicious and irresistible Bhadrā—has been slain. (15.475)
Sūryā, Hiraṇyā, Prāvārā, Sadṛṣṭi, Hemamālinī, Padmānanā, Nityapuṣṭā, Devamātā, and Mṛtodbhavā. (15.476)
Possessing great wealth, newly attained, with a neck like that of a crow;
having the color of the sun, the luster of the moon, and always fragrant for seven leagues.

She who is worshipped with choice offerings, whose growth is like that of forest trees, who is worthy of praise, the beloved of Viplu, the auspicious one, the giver of boons, the beautiful one, and the Śrī dwelling on the Vindhya mountains in the left [direction]. 15.478.
Yoganidrā, she who delights in yoga, Devakī, she who has the form of a celestial being (kīma), the one who puts Kaṃsa to flight, Durgā, Kumārī, Kauśikī, and Kṣamā.
Kātyāyanī, Kālarātri, Niśātṛpti, and Durjayā;
Virūpākṣī, Viśālākṣī, the supreme protector of her devotees. (15.480)
She possesses many forms, her own true form, and diverse forms, yet she is devoid of form;
she abounds in the resonance of bells and has a sound like the thundering of clouds.
The crusher of the great Indra, with a frowning brow and a tawny face; she who is truth, the consumer of sins, the Kaurī, and the observer of celibacy.
This lineage bestows sons, wives, virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation;
it pacifies poverty and suffering, and destroys the miserable states of existence. (15.483)

She who removes the distress of her devotees, she who is auspicious, she who destroys the cycle of worldly existence; she who is nourished by milk, the daughter of Nanda, the lotus-born, the one who dwells in the lotus, and the Earth.
Rukmiṇī, Rohiṇī, Śītā, Satyabhāmā, Yaśaśvinī, Prajñā, Dhārā, Amitā, Buddhi, Vedamātā, and Yaśovatī. || 15-485 ||
Concentration, meditation, loving-kindness, compassion, devotion, tenderness, the inner altar, sacrificial fees, and the supreme goal of the celibate life. 15-486.
Dīkṣā, Vikṣīparokṣā, Samīkṣā, Vīravallabhā, Vichinnā, Virujārājñī, Tāpinī, and Vindumālinī. (15.487)
Kṣīradhārā, Sujaladā, Suprabhā, Camurārcitā, Havyagarbhā, Anyagarbhā, Juhvatī, and Yajñasaṃbhavā. (15.488)
O auspicious one, you are the bestower of all desires, possessing beautiful radiance and all auspiciousness;
you are dressed in pure white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents.
The female swan who brings benefit to the swan, whose abode is the heart-lotus;
she who possesses a white parasol, who has beautiful hips, whose eyes are like lotus petals, and whose gaze is steady. (15.490)
Sāvitrī is of true resolve, the giver of desires, and she who fulfills every wish;
she is beautiful to behold, visible, worthy of being seen, touchable, worthy of being touched, serviceable, and the most excellent woman.
Bhogapriyā, Bhogavatī, Bhogendraśayanāsanā,
Ādrā, Puṣkaraṇī, Puṇyā, Ṣaṣārṇā, and Yamūdanī.
The glorious Caṇḍabhāskarā bestows supreme sovereignty and prosperity;
she possesses inconceivable and infinite majesty, and she is the dispeller of the state of existence and non-existence for the Lord of beings.
The goddess Niḥśreṇī, who resides within all bodies and is saluted by all beings,
is the youthful Valāvalāyikā, praised in song by Gokulayā.
Toṣaṇī, Cūrṇacandrābhā, Ekānandā, Śatānadā, Saṭgrāmanagadvāra, Hamyā, and Pavanavāsinī. (15.495)
Kuśyā, Tridāruṇī, Caṇḍā, Kirātī, Mandarālayā, Kālāyanī, Kalagamā, Bhayadā, and Bhayanāśanā. (15.496)

Saudāminī, whose roar is like the thunderclouds, the crusher of Daityas and Dānavas, the Mother of the World, the creator of existence, the sustainer of all beings, and exceedingly difficult to attain. || 15-497 ||
Kāśyapī, Śubhadantā, Vanamālā, Vasundharā, Dhanyā, Dhanyeśvarī, Bhavyā, Ratnadāmā, and Suvardhinī. || 15-498 ||
Gāndharvī, Revatī, Gaṅgā, Śakunī, Vimalānanā, Iḍā, Sātikarī, Tāpasī, and Malayālayā. (15.499)
She who is of the nature of clarified butter, the Vajra-Kaumārī, the drinker of Soma, she who rests upon flowers;
she who is beloved by the world, whose chariot is the moon, the unconquerable one, whose vehicle is a bird.
Born of the mind, moving through desire, frequented by the Siddhas;
she is the Fortune of the Sky, the Great Fortune, the Fortune of Splendor, blazing with majesty. (15.501)
She is the beauty of taste, the source of the world, the beauty of fragrance, and the splendor of the forest;
she is the one to be heard, the glory of the ear, the eye, the tongue, and the one who moves through the breath.
The mother of Viriñca, the source of prosperity, the bestower of boons, she whose vehicle is straight;
the heroic one, the sovereign of heroes, the barren one, the sorrowless one, and the increaser of wealth.
The unstruck sound, residing in the *kuṇḍalinī* and dwelling in the *dhana*, she is saluted by elephants and *gandharvas*, and is the virtuous one saluted by the lord of the gods. 15-504.

The most auspicious of all that is auspicious, the bestower of the supernatural power for all desires, the embodiment of all bliss, eternally blissful, possessing true fame, and served by the perfected ones (siddhas). || 15.505 ||
Senāvalī, Kuhūrā, Kāmā, Utpalanivāsinī, Arundhatī, Vasumatī, Bhārgavī, and Vāstu-devatā. (15.506)
The peacock-feathered one, the Vajra-Vetālī, with vajras in her hands and a beautiful face;
she is the primordial dhāraṇī, steadfast, adorned with jewels and gems. (15.507)
She is the glory of kings accompanied by beauty, the glory of Brahman honored by the Brahmins;
she is to be known as the glory of victory that bestows victory, and the glory of heaven for the virtuous who attain heaven. (15.508)

She is Supuṣpā (well-flowered), Puṣpanilayā (the abode of flowers), Phalaśrī (the glory of fruit), and Niphala-priyā (fond of being fruitless). She delights in the bow-vine and dwells within the anger of others.
Kadrū, Dhanañjaya, Kapilā, Surasā, Sarasā, Dhanu, Mahāśvetā, Mahānīlā, and Mahāmūrtti are the destroyers of poison. (15.510)
Suprabhā, Jvālinī, Vyāpti, Tṛpti, Prāpti, Prabhākarī, Tejovatī, Padmabodhā, Madalā, and Aruṇāvatī. || 15-511 ||
She is the jewel among jewels, the source of existence, the dispeller of darkness through her hundredfold radiance;
she is the triple-syllabled proclamation, the protection, the one who brings joy, and yet she is devoid of sound.
The goddess Sādhyādinirditi is seated upon a deer;
she holds a bilva fruit and a blue lotus, and her hands rest upon a bull and a jewel.
She is adorned with gold and silver, auspicious with conch shells, and seated upon a lotus; she is fond of cow dung and milk, and has curd, ghee, and water as her abode.
Marīcī, Cīravasanā, Pūrṇacandrā, Arkaviṣṭarā, Susūkṣmī, Mivṛti, Sthūlā, Nivṛtā, and Vati. (15.515)
Cāmarī, Jvalinī, Dhūmrā, Havyavāhā, Hiraṇyadā, Dīpinī, Kalavṛddhi, Śoṣaṇī, and Saṃprabodhinī. || 15-516 ||
Bhāsvarā, Asaṃhati, Tīkṣṇā, Pracaṇḍajvalanojjvalā, Saṃjñā, Pradīptā, Caṇḍā, Vaidyutī, and Sumahādyuti. (15.517)
Kapilā, Nīlaraktā, Suṣumnā, Visphuliṅginī, Arviṣmatī, Suharaṇī, Dīrghā, Dhūmāvali, and Jalā. (15.518)
She is Pūṣā with her full orb, she who sheds light and is most enchanting;
she is Yaśas, the bringer of contentment, the Shadow, the mental one arisen from the heart. (15.519)
The supreme gold-maker in the battle for reviving the dead,
the auspicious one who creates vastness, the excellent medicinal herb that effects union.
She is most devoted to Brahman, united with Brahman, born of the *bindu*, resembling a jewel;
she possesses the luster of lightning, is endowed with the *bindu*, and is Ambikā, whose qualities consist of the three natures.
She is eternally radiant, eternally joyful, and ever seeking the fulfillment of desires;
she is marked by the lotus and the thunderbolt, possesses a vajra-staff, and is full of grace.
Vaidehī, Pūjitā, Kanyā, Māyā, Vijayā, Vāhinī, Mālinī, Saṃgamā, Mālyā, Mālinī, and Mālabhāriṇī. || 15-523 ||
The Sovereign of All, she whose intellect is composed of the qualities, the Mistress who adorns the mandala;
beloved by Hari, daughter of the Earth, she who bestows a pleasing mind. (15.524)
Yaśodhanī, Ratnamālā, Tṛṣṇā, Trailokyabandhanī, Amṛtā, Tāraṇī, Harṣā, Vinatā, Vallabhī, and Śaśī. (15.525)
She is the illusory manifestation of conceptual thought, the beloved who is a mixture of the Kadamba and the nectar;
she has not come, yet she has departed; she is firm like a diamond, yet endowed with the moments of existence.
She accomplishes all aims, destroys all poverty,
is born from the source of compassion, has lotus-like eyes, and possesses the luster of the moon.
Śobhā, Dīpti, Mahādīpti, Mahājvālā, Vikāśinī, Mālā, Kāñcanamālā, and Sadvajrakanakaprabhā. (15.528)
The supreme process is said to be the agitator that brings about the arising of bliss;
expanding forth, it is called Vajra, with eyes like the golden *śṛṅgāla* flower. (15.529)
She who brings victory, the honeyed one, Hāritī, Śaśinī, and Śivā;
she is the primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti), the body of the Lord (Īśārī), the Mother of Yoga, and she who is as swift as thought (Manojavā).
Dharmodayā is radiant; Dharmamodā has likewise gone [to that state].
Facing the earth of *kusuma*, she is the supreme one who perfectly awakens to complete enlightenment. (15.531)
Possessing bodies as vast as a *vyāma* and capable of great power, they move through the sky and are composed of the Blessed One:
the Gaṅgā, Vitastā, Yamunā, Candrabhāgā, and Sarasvatī.
Tilottamā, Vaśī, Bhadrā, Svāminī, Svarasundarī, Vāṇapraharaṇā, Bālā, Vivoṣṭī, and Cāruhāsinī. (15.533)
She who possesses a beautiful palate, who is beheld by those with longing glances, and who bestows visible fruits;
she who is the mistress of desire and desires, who is desirable, and who moves gracefully at will.
Resembling the king of snowy mountains, with a preeminent lordly elephant as her vehicle,
she is the source of all happiness and good fortune, the most excellent womb.
She is the most excellent, consisting of all things, beloved by the Lord of all and non-all;
she is the manifest source of all speed, the sovereign of the lords of the primary principles.
"She is the goddess who removes sin; may she grant me the threefold [aim].
Thus was the thousand names of Lakṣmī, which bring auspiciousness, proclaimed. (15.537)

A person free from pride should constantly recite or listen to this [text], which is distinguished by the higher and lower divisions and the distinction between the secondary and the primary. (15.538)
Having become pure and composed, and endowed with devotion and faith,
one should worship Śrīnivāsa with flowers, incense, and unguents.
And with enjoyments such as honey-cakes and other foods, perform the Jaya rite according to your ability;
having fully worshipped the Goddess Śrī, the beloved of Śrīdhara, who stands by His side for the sake of prosperity. (15.540)
Then one should satisfy the Supreme Goddess with the Thousand Names;
whoever recites this entire hymn, the Garland of Jewels of Names, [attains the goal]. (15.541)
Prosperity, with her face turned toward him in favor, bestows everything upon him;
for him, there arises the splendor born of Lakṣmī, whose beloved is Acyuta.
Those who recite this constantly obtain their desired success;
there is but one Lord of the world, the powerful, infallible Master. (15.543)
And just as the empowered [practices] such as the ritual depositions (nyāsa) belong to her,
so too does the one supreme Śakti, the venerable one, who is the locus of her cause.

That which is called the supreme Prakṛti, consisting of the qualities (guṇas) such as the intellect (jñāna) and so forth, is indeed one; His Śrī-Śakti is not a second [entity]. She is eternal, existing in all forms through her nature as both the transcendent (parā) and the immanent (aparā). (15.545)
And she who possesses infinite names is the leader of the wheel of powers;
pervading all this world of moving and non-moving beings, she remains established therein. (15.546)
From that, one supreme Śrī alone is to be known as having a universal form; she is gentle, established in a gentle human form, acting for the sake of the seed of humanity. (15.547)
Whosoever attains the state of manhood, he is certainly Viṣṇu;
whosoever, however, is in the state of womanhood, in him Lakṣmī is established. (15.548)
Prakṛti and Puruṣa are distinct, and a third does not exist at all;
what more need be said? Hari consists of both man and woman.
The Supreme Goddess, who is divided into many different forms in her play and is beloved by great majesty, [is attained] by one whose refuge has fallen away from the state of *vaṃti*. 15-550.
Those whose consciousness is perfectly pure attain supreme fortune;
having obtained this, the Lotus-born One then recited this hymn in due order.
That which is divine by virtue of its eight qualities, he indeed approached out of devotion;
it bestows the fruits of desires upon those with desires, and liberation upon those free from desire.
We praise Lakṣmī, who holds a book, an eye, a lotus, and other attributes; she is clad in white garments, possesses three eyes, and is seated upon a great lotus. || 15.553 ||
In one place, she holds a full pitcher marked with the syllable *oṃ*; in another, she stands upon a pure elephant, her hands bearing a conch and a lotus;
in yet another, her hand is occupied with a fly-whisk on the lap of her beloved; and in another, she shines with the luster of gold, wielding a triple-pointed spear.
Thus ends the complete *Lakṣmī-nāma-sahasra-stotra* as proclaimed by Puruṣottama.
Now follows the *Lakṣmī-stotra*.
Agastya said:
O Mother, I bow to you, O Kamalā, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals; you who dwell in the heart-lotus of Śrī Viṣṇu, the Mother of the Universe!
O Lakṣmī, fair as the tender interior of a lotus on the shore of the Milk Ocean, you who are the eternal refuge for those who bow to you—be ever victorious! (1)

O Śrī, O Rūpendra, sole mother of Madana, you shine like moonlight upon the moon, and you shine with abundant splendor in the world, O you whose face is as beautiful as the moon; O Lakṣmī, refuge of those who always bow to you, be gracious! (2) 15-555.

O Jātavedas, you always possess the power of burning; by your creative impulse, you would fashion this entire world. O Viśvambharā, you too would sustain everything through your nature. O Lakṣmī, you who are the refuge for those who constantly bow to you, be gracious! (3) 15-556.
O stainless one, even Hara takes away this [sin] through devotion to you; you protect, you grant liberation, and you are both the supreme and the non-supreme.
O stainless one, even Hari became such through your grace; O Lakṣmī, be ever gracious! Salutations to you, O refuge! (15.557)
He alone is a hero, he alone is wise, he alone is virtuous, he alone is fortunate, and he alone is worthy of honor by virtue of his mastery of all the arts of the preceptor;
he alone is pure in this entire world of delusion, upon whom your auspicious glance of compassion has fallen.
And in that moment, O Lord, in which great man—whether in an elephant, a lord of serpents, a leader, a lake, a divine lineage, a home, or a lotus—you have cast your gaze, [he becomes the foremost].

In the jewel, in the bird, in the animal, in the bed, on the earth, and in the lotus—there is only that which possesses *śrī* (prosperity/gloriousness), and nothing else here. Everything created by you alone attains purity when it is associated with you; otherwise, all this is impure, O Lakṣmī. Your names alone are auspicious among all words: "O Consort of Viṣṇu," "O Kamalā," and "O Dweller in the Lotus. (15–7)
May they always recite the names: Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kamalā, Kamalālayā, Padmā, Ramā, and me, Nalinayugmayugmakarā; and Kṣīrodajā, Amṛtakumbhakarendirā, and Viṣṇupriyā.
Where is suffering? (8) || 15-561 ||
Having thus praised the Blessed Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, the sage, together with his wife, prostrated himself like a staff, performing the *aṣṭāṅga* salutation.
Śrī said:
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you, O you who are born of Mitra and Varuṇa!
Having fallen, arise, O Lopāmudrā, O lady of auspicious vows! (15.563)
"Having been praised by this method, I am pleased; let that which is desired be chosen.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this, the sage then replied to Śrī.
Having prostrated, the illustrious Agastya spoke these words filled with devotion:
"If a boon is to be granted to me, and if I am worthy of a boon— " (15.565)
And those who shall always recite this hymn with devotion to you and with reverence—for them, may there never be suffering, and may there never be poverty. (15.566)
May there be no separation from beloved ones, may there be no interruption of the lineage;
may there be victory everywhere and no depletion of prosperity.
Śrī said: "So be it, O Sage; everything that has been spoken by you is thus.
The recitation of this hymn is the cause for my presence. (15.568)
Alakṣmī and Kālakarṇī may enter [the child] through that seizure;
this is the supreme means for pacifying children who are overcome by seizures of the hair (vālagraha). 15-569.
Having written it on birch bark, one should bind it around the neck;
this secret of the seed-syllable must be guarded with great effort.
One should give with faith, and one should never give to an impure person at any time.
Thus ends the complete Śrī Lakṣmī Stotra.
Now, the Gaṇeśa Stotra.

I worship the elephant-faced God, who is saluted by the hosts of deities, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon, whom they declare to be the primordial syllable *Oṃ*, and whom the Vedas and mantras recite. (15.571)

I bow to that Vighneśvara, who has the luster of a mountain peak, whose lotus feet are skilled in bestowing the rare fortune of liberation upon those devoted to them, and from whom the waters of charity flow incessantly. (15.572)
Who could forget this son of the enemy of Smara, who, anointed with fresh saffron and causing intoxication to the swarms of bees, wards them off with the rhythmic flapping of his own ears? (15.573)

Having brought with their lotus-like hands the water of the Gaṅgā dwelling in the matted locks of Śambhu, they worship Śiva with playful ease from nearby; having approached, they bow down and serve him with devotion. (4) 15-574.

Furthermore, for my sake during my childhood, while washing the trunk of the elephant-faced one with the spray from the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain King, I worship that charming face. (5) Those droplets released from the tip of the trunk by you as you lifted up the elephant's trunk— [I worship them].
The stars move within your immeasurable sky, possessing a luster equal to pearls on the neck of Time. (6) || 15-576 ||
Even while sporting in his own lake, he forcibly strides across the waters within the city;
contemplating the end of the eon, the gods praise the Lord of Kailāsa with sacred hymns. (7) 15-577.

O you whose face is like that of a serpent, when you were in the fourth stage, engaged in play with those resembling divine youths, you abandoned even the thundering of clouds for a moment and attained the splendor of the moon upon the bow. (15.578)

I take refuge in Heramba, who is as dark as a rain cloud, the sole friend of the gods, sages, and his devoted followers, whose five faces, radiant with intoxication, incessantly drink the honey of all the scriptures. (15.579)

And he does not abandon the elephant-faced one, who makes the earth and its waters fulfilled by his two lotus feet through his intense latent impressions, who is the causeless cause, and who has attained passion [for the world]. (10) || 15-580 ||
I worship that son of the Moon-crested Lord, who was propitiated by austerities, and by whose tip of his horn the ancient [Veda] was formerly offered to the son of Satyavatī;
he who is the goal of the Vedas, the object of praises, and the playful incarnation of the Supreme Self. (15)
Worship the Lord of Obstacles, who consists of sound or consists of the Puruṣa, and whose beginning is divided. (12)

I worship this beloved [form] of Śiva and Śivā, who holds a noose and a goad in his hands, whose tusk is broken, and who, with streams of spray brought to life by pearls released from the hollows of his trunk, sprinkles them both; he whose lotus-like face has eyes that stir the world. (15) She who dwells upon his own body, his own beloved, whose lotus-face has eyes that stir the world...
O Madhu, I worship Rudra, who, with his own lotus-face, deludes the entire universe. (14) || 15-584 ||

For those who have previously honored you, the elephant among speakers, and study all the treatises, there exists nothing other than what is established by you; if there were anything else, it would be as unreal as a falsehood, even if it appeared to be true. (15-585)

I take refuge in that virtuous one who is the golden-hued Lord of the universe, the ancient seer situated within the solar orb, the elephant-faced one, whom those who enter attain according to their own time. (16) 15-586 ||
I worship that Puruṣa who has sung the Vedas, the Self residing in the heart who is a mass of bliss;
by whom, as Gajānana, the darkness of obstacles for people is instantly dissolved. (17) 15-587
O Śambhu, with his mass of matted locks unified and his own lotus-face adorned by a crescent moon,
Kāma— having his teeth utterly shattered and crying out in pain from the wound on his foot— attained a state of supreme beauty.
(15) For the purpose of striking down those overwhelmed by obstacles, [he who is worshipped] with coconuts, plantains, fruits, and the like...
May I always worship the Lord whose face is like that of an intoxicated elephant, who grants all desires.

(19) Those who praise with hymns and according to the prescribed rite that primordial one with the face of a lordly elephant—who is to be propitiated through numerous sacrifices and manifold austerities—they all, O Goddess of the Elephants, become disciplined observers of vows. (20)
Thus ends the hymn to Gaṇeśa.
Now follows the Śrī Viṣṇu Stotra.
Oṃ! Having lifted the entire Veda from the ocean, you destroyed the most formidable enemy, the Śaṅkha;

I worship that primordial Viṣṇu in the form of the Fish, to whom great offerings were formerly given by those who bowed down. (15) When the great ocean was churned by the gods and demons for the sake of divine nectar, [the mountain] Mandara and others served as the churning rod.
I remember that tortoise situated upon his support, by whom the earth was shaken by a great force.

(2) I take refuge in the Lord of Arrows, the Primordial Being, by the water from whose tip of the tusk the earth—adorned with the mudraka-beads of its girdle, clothed in the river as its upper garment, and bearing the weight of Meru as its crown—was not uprooted. (3)

O Nṛsiṃha, I do not forget you, who today, out of a mind intent on destroying the suffering of your devotees, tore asunder the pillar with the tips of your sharpened claws, rending the enemy of the gods. (4) 15-594
I bow to the foot of that Trivikrama, who traversed all things, the sole one and no other among the gods, whose stride supported the four oceans and served as a vessel for their placement. (15.595)

I bow to that primordial hero Viṣṇu, who, by the strength of his staff-like arms, properly performed the libation for his ancestors with the blood-water of twenty-one kings he had slain. (6) 15-596 ||

I bow with devotion to that Lord of Sītā, who, having taken birth in the lineage of the Raghus, established a bridge across the ocean whose waters were half-submerged, and brought the Lord of Laṅkā under his sway. (7)
Having dragged all the Asuras by their hair, Haladhara reduced them to powder with blows from his mace;
I worship that Balarāma, the possessor of strength, who, having encountered Kṛṣṇa, became even more powerful through devotion. (8)

I bow down to that Buddha, the source of all, who in ancient times, having conquered the Asuras along with the Suras, honored the attire of excellent skins and established the scripture whose efficacy is unfailing. (9)

We worship that horse, the soul of the universe, who, by his splendor, utterly consumes the earthly [Rāhu], and who, in the mere twinkling of an eye, struck him with all his hooves after a long period of time.
[We worship Him] who holds the conch, the beautiful discus, the mace, and the lotus in His arms, and who is mounted upon Garuḍa.
I praise Viṣṇu, whose heart bears the Śrīvatsa mark, who is the primordial source of the universe, and who is absorbed in tamāla paste. (11) || 15-601 ||

I repeatedly remember the primordial one, who resembles a lotus, who is like a cloud, who reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa as his couch in the midst of the milk ocean, whose face is beautified by a smile, and whose lotus-eyes are fully blossomed; he is the source of the Vedas. (12) 266a)

One should gratify the Lord of the World, the Teacher of the World, the Supreme Person, with the two [offerings] consisting of food and drink, for the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (15.603)
Thus ends the fifth chapter (pallava) of the Āgamakalpalatā composed by Śrī Yadunātha.
Now I shall explain the mudrās, which are kept secret in all tantras; by performing these, the mantra-deities rejoice. (16.1)
And during the time of secret recitation (japa), in meditation, in rites for specific desires, in the rite of invocation, in the consecration of the conch, and in protection; || 16-2 ||
In the offering of food (naivedya) and likewise elsewhere, its essential nature is revealed;
in the proper place, the mudrās should be displayed, characterized by their respective defining marks.
The mudrās beginning with invocation (āvāhana) are considered common to all nine [deities];
likewise, the six-limbed mudrās (ṣaḍaṅgamudrā) are to be employed in all tantras. (16.4)
The wise have declared that Viṣṇu possesses nineteen marks:
the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the flute, the Śrīvatsa, and the Kaustubha. (16.5)
The Vanamālā, the Ājñā, the one called Mudrā-vilvā, and the supreme mudrā named Garuḍa—these bring satisfaction to Viṣṇu. (16.6)
The reading is *vardhinī* and *cāpinī*.
Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Hayagrīvā, and likewise Dhanuḥ;
Bāṇamudrā and Paraśu are considered to be Jaganmohanikā. (16–7)

The ten insignia (*mudrās*) of Śiva are: the Liṅga, the Yoni, the one called the Trident (*triśūla*), the Conch, the Discus, the Bell, the Skull, the Khatvāṅga, the one called the Kapāla, the *Ḍamaru*, and that which pleases Śiva. (16–8)
The Sun has only one [mudrā], the lotus-seat; Gaṇeśa has seven mudrās, known as the tusk, the noose, the goad, the obstacle-remover, the axe, the trident, and the mace. (16.9)
The three seed-mudrās are to be understood as the mudrās for the worship of Śiva:
she holds the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, the sword, the shield, and the bow. (16.10)
The Mausulikā, the Daurgī, and the Mudrāśakti are dear to me; likewise, the Lakṣmīmudrā is my mark for the worship of Vāgīśvarī and the others. (16.11)
The rosary, the lute, the gesture of exposition, the book, and the seal; these are to be known as the gestures called "Seven-Tongued," employed in the worship of Fire. (16.12)
The tenth mudrā should be known for the worship of Tripurā: Saṃkṣobhaṇī, Drāvaṇī, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśīkaraṇī, Āveśanī, Unmādinī, and Kṣobhiṇī. (16.13)
The Khecarī, Vīja, and Yoni are proclaimed as the three sections;
there should be the consecration with the Kumbha-mudrā, and likewise the Padma-mudrā on the seat.
Kāmakālī should be employed for the rite of pacifying obstacles;
and Gālinī should be employed for the rite of purifying water.
The lord of those who worship Śrī Gopāla is Nṛhari; for the worship of Nṛsiṃha, he is Nārasiṃhikā; and in the worship of Varāha, one should display the one named Varāha.
In the worship of Rāma, the gestures of the bow and arrow are used;
in the worship of Paraśurāma, they are to be known as those named "Deluder of the World" (jaganmohana).
When invoking Vāsudeva, one should use the Kumbha-mudrā for protection; and in all instances of prayer, one should employ the mudrā known as Prārthanā.
According to the sequence of their positions, those characteristics are released;
for those with hands joined in *añjali*, [the mudrā is formed] from the root joint of the ring fingers. (16–19)
Placing the two thumbs together is known as the *āvāhanī* mudrā;
likewise, both [thumbs] turned face down is known as the *sthāpanī* mudrā. (16–20)
The joining of the two fists with the thumbs extended is the *saṃnidhāpanī* (3);
that same gesture, with the thumbs inserted within, is considered the *saṃbodhinī* (4). || 16-21 ||
The two hands with palms turned upward and joined at the tips of the fingers are considered the *sammukhīkaraṇī* (gesture of facing).
(5) The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the body of the deity constitutes the *sakalīkṛti* (the act of making complete). || 16–22 ||
The fist formed with the right hand, with the index finger extended and pointing downward—this is the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā; when it is rotated, it is honored [as the *mahita* mudrā]. (16-23)
With the little fingers and ring fingers joined together facing one another,
and likewise the index and middle fingers, this is proclaimed as the Dhenu-mudrā.
O best of practitioners, by that [mudrā] the act of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) should be performed. With the thumbs interlaced and the other fingers extended, [this is the mudrā]. (16-25)
The wise should employ this Great Seal (mahāmudrā), which is supreme in bringing about joy, for the purpose of the deity’s act of purification. (16.26)
The characteristics of the mudrās for the assignment of limbs (aṅganyāsa) are now stated:
when the fingers of the hands are straight, that mudrā is for the heart and the head. (10)
The clenched fist with the thumbs tucked underneath is for the topknot. (2)
The lines on both hands are those of a Brāhmaṇa. (3)
The sound produced by the two hands joined at the fingers, the fists, the joints, the pair of arms, the thumbs, and the index fingers, when applied to the anus, is declared to be the mudrā. (4)
Wherein the two eyes are located between the index finger and the middle finger.
Where there are two eyes, it is the ring finger; thus the six-limbed mudrās have been described exactly as they are. (5)
Now, the characteristics of the Vaiṣṇava mudrās are being described as follows.
Having grasped the left thumb with the right fist, one should then stretch it out;
subsequently, one should extend the thumb of that fist.
The left thumb joined and extended together with the [other fingers], and touched by the right thumb—this is the mudrā known as the Conch (śaṅkha). (16-29)
Having brought the two hands together in front, well-warmed and well-stretched out, with the little fingers joined—this is the mudrā known as the Cakra. (2) 16-30.
Having placed the two hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced, and having joined the thumbs at the ends of the palms, this is the *padma-mudrā*. (16.31)
