Furthermore, when the middle fingers are joined together and then fully extended,
this is declared to be the *gadā-mudrā*, which brings satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
Having brought the two hands face-to-face and bent them, with the fingers raised and the thumbs joined at the base of the palms— this is the Padma-mudrā (4).
When the little finger of the left hand is joined to the thumb of the right hand, and the little finger [of the right hand] is extended, [this is the *uṣṭra* mudrā]. (16.34)
When the index, middle, and ring fingers are slightly contracted and moved, this becomes the flute mudrā; it is well known as the beloved of Hari. (5) 16-35.
One should bind the middle and ring fingers of each other's hands with the thumbs, positioned at the base of the little fingers. (16.36)
One should form the two index fingers; this mudrā is named Śrīvatsa. The ring finger of the right hand is joined to the back [of the left]. (16.37)
The little finger of the left hand is bound with the other two [fingers], and likewise the right index finger;
one should bind the left nostril at the base of the right thumb.
Placing the supreme straight [finger] upon my left middle finger and joining it with the thumb, and likewise touching the tips together—this is the mudrā known as the Kaustubha. (7) 16-39.
One should touch [the body] from the throat down to the feet with the index finger and thumb;
this mudrā, performed with both hands like a garland, is the Vanamālikā (8). 16-40.
Having released the index finger and thumb, one should place them at the heart;
then one should place the lotus-like left hand upon the crown of the left knee.
This Jñānamudrā is the beloved of Rāmacandra. (9)
Having bound the left thumb within the fist of the other hand like a lord, and having pressed its tip with the fingers of that [right] hand as well as with the fingers of the left hand,
the one of pure intellect should place it firmly upon the heart and utter for me the seed-syllable *raṃ*.
This ring, known as the *vilvā*, has been clearly described here; it must be kept secret by those who know the ritual procedure. (10) || 16-42 ||
Having turned the two hands away from each other and joined the little fingers,
the two index fingers should likewise be joined together with the thumbs.
One should move the two middle and ring fingers like two eyes;
this is called the Garuḍa-mudrā, which increases the satisfaction of Viṣṇu. (16.44)
Placing his knees together in the Kali age, with his chin and lips covered,
his hands held apart and trembling again and again.
One should open the mouth wide and repeatedly lick the tongue;
this is the Nārasiṃhī mudrā, which increases his delight. (16-46)
Then, having placed the thumbs and so forth of both hands upon the little fingers in sequence, this mudrā with all fingers facing downwards is considered that of Nṛhari. (16.47)
The wise one should place the left hand as a support or a barrier below;
thus it is declared that the mudrā known as Vārāhī destroys [all obstacles]. (14) || 16-48 ||
With the right hand facing upwards and the left hand facing downwards,
with the tips of the fingers joined together, this is the mudrā known as Vārāhī.
Having placed those fingers of the right hand with their tips downward upon the palm of the left hand, one should position the middle finger below and bend it inward.
The Hayagrīva-priyā-mudrā imitates that mudrā; one should join the tip of the left middle finger with the tip of the index finger. (16–51)
One should press the ring finger and the little finger with its thumb; this is declared to be the *dhenumudrā* when displayed at the left shoulder. (16-52)
One should form the right fist with the index finger extended as the arrow mudrā;
then, joining the palms of the two hands together obliquely, one should arrange the fingers. (16–53)
One should form the mudrā known as the axe by joining the hands together and extending them;
with two fists, the thumbs pointing upward, it is the mudrā that fascinates the three worlds. (16.54)

Having joined the two hands together with the fingers extended, the two index fingers should rest on the backs of the middle fingers, and the two thumbs should remain positioned upon the middle fingers. (16.55)
This Kāmamudrā is joyful and brings delight to all the gods. Now, the characteristics of the beloveds of Mahādeva shall be described. (19) 16-56.
One should join the raised right thumb with the left thumb;
one should join the left fingers with the fingers of the right hand. (16.57)
One should join the fingers of the left hand with those of the right;
this is declared to be the Liṅga-mudrā, which brings about the presence of Śiva.
The two index fingers are joined together like a pair of tongs; the two ring fingers are pressed upward against each other, while the two middle fingers are extended downward below them. (16.59)
Placing the two [thumbs] at the tips of the thumbs, this is declared to be the *yonimudrā*. Having bound the little finger with the thumb, the three middle fingers are held closely together. (16.60)
This mudrā, known as the Trident (triśūla), is proclaimed for the purpose of bestowing splendor;
it is formed by spreading the three fingers—the thumb, the index finger, and the middle finger—with their tips extended. (16.61)
One should extend the rosary; this is proclaimed as the *akṣamālā* mudrā. When the right hand is positioned below and extended, it is the *vara* mudrā. (16.62)
The left hand is raised and extended, forming the mudrā of fear;
one should join the ring finger and thumb together and place them at the tip of the middle finger. (16.63)
One should form the remaining fingers as prescribed; this is declared to be the *mṛgamudrā*.
The five fingers of the right hand are known to be raised upward. (16.64)
The Khaṭvāṅguṣṭha-mudrā is renowned; it is considered very dear when placed upon the head.
Likewise, having formed the left arm like a vessel, [one should hold] the garment in the hand. (16.65)

One should first perform the false speech according to the tradition of the Mudrākāpālinī; then, having bound the *mithilā* [mudrā] for nourishment, one should slightly bend the middle finger as desired. (16.66)
Having raised the right [hand], one should move it toward the region of the ear;
this is the ḍamaruka mudrā, which destroys all obstacles. (9) 16-67.
Then, the characteristics of the Gaṅgā and the oceans are described:
the *uttārā*, the *ūrdhvamukhī*, the *madhyā*, the *saralā*, and the *baddhamuṣṭikā*. (16.68)
The Danta-mudrā has been fully described by those proficient in all the Āgamas:
it consists of the index finger of the left fist and the index finger of the right fist.
Having joined the tips of the two thumbs, one casts them onto the tips of the index fingers;
this is the mudrā marked with a noose, as proclaimed by the learned. (16.70)
Having made the middle fingers straight and joining the index fingers at the middle joint, one should bend them slightly; this mudrā is known as Kuśa. (16.71)
The *madhyamā*, *anāmā*, *kaniṣṭhā*, and the thumb form a fist;
with the index finger pointing downward and elongated in form, this is the *madhyamāvighna-mudrā*. (16.72)
The well-known *paśumudrā* is called *ladumuṇḍikā*;
the *mudrā* named *bījapūra* has been omitted because it is already well known. (16.73)

Now the characteristics of the Śākya women’s mudrās are being described: the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, the bow, and the arrow are proclaimed [as their attributes]. (16.74)
The little finger and the ring finger joined at their respective thumbs on the right side,
while the other fingers are extended and closely pressed together— this is the position of the sword mudrā (khaḍgamudrikā).

Having placed the left hand across [the chest] and having placed the right hand over the left with both hands, joining them at the head—this is declared to be the Durgā mudrā. Likewise, having formed the Cakra mudrā and extending the two middle fingers, [this is the Cakra mudrā]. (16–76)
Likewise, having brought the two little fingers together, one should place the thumbs at their tips;
this supreme Lakṣmī-mudrā is the bestower of all prosperity. || 16.77 ||
Having bound those two with the lute-playing gesture, move them together, O Śivā;
this is declared to be the Vīṇā-mudrā, which brings pleasure to Sarasvatī. (16.78)
Forming the left fist facing oneself constitutes the book mudrā;
it is considered extremely dear to the two eyes of Śrī Rāma. (16.79)
Having placed the two hands with fingers extended at the wrist,
one should join the little fingers and thumbs together and then extend them fully apart.
This mudrā, known as Saptajihvā, is indeed beloved by Vaiśvānara;
in it, the little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined to one another.
The ring finger, middle finger, and middle finger joined together, with the index finger raised, is declared the *mudrā* of the *āgālinī*, which is praised as belonging to the conch. (16.82)
Having placed the right thumb upon the left thumb with both hands, one should form a single fist with space between the fingers; that is the *kuṃbha-mudrā*.
One should place the thumb within a clenched fist and set it at the tip of the index finger;
this is proclaimed as the Kula-mudrā, the supreme one that provides all protection. (16.84)
With the fingers extended and the two hands joined together, one should place them at one's own heart; this is the mudrā known as *prārthanā*. (16.85)
The *añjali-añjali-mudrā* is that which is called Vāsudeva;
it is formed by joining two fists together with their thumbs and little fingers touching. (16.86)
One should bring those two [thumbs] face-to-face; this mudrā is Kālakarṇikā.
It is a tight fist with the right hand, with the index finger placed upon the ring finger. (16.87)
The *mudrā* known as *vismaya* (amazement) is the *mudrā* that causes wonder. The right fist with the thumb pointing upward is the *nāda-mudrā*. (16.88)
By joining the index finger and the thumb here, this is the *bindu-mudrā*.
With the left hand facing downward, the right hand is placed with its face upward. (16.89)
One should join the extended fingers together and then release them;
this is known as the *saṃhāramudrā* (withdrawal mudrā), prescribed for the rite of dismissal (*visarjana*).
The *tramudrikā* taught in the *Vāmakeśvaratantra* has been revealed to you;
listen, O Goddess, for I shall explain the mudrās that grant the accomplishment of all aims. (16.91)
By worshipping with these [mantras] for a long time, the presence of the Triple City (Tripura) shall be attained.
Having rotated the hands, one should bring the two thumbs into contact and make them even.
Having placed the ring fingers within [the palms] and made the index fingers curved, one should gather the little fingers at their own place, O Maheśvarī. (16.93)
This is declared to be the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā for the practice of meditation on Tripurā:
having placed the middle fingers together in the center, the little fingers and thumbs are held against them.
Having formed the two index fingers like staffs, with the ring fingers above the middle fingers—this is the first mudrā, which causes universal agitation. (16.95)
O Supreme Goddess, when the middle fingers of this very same mudrā are made straight, it then becomes the one that induces sleep in all beings. (16.96)
With the middle and index fingers, and the little and ring fingers made equal, the Supreme Goddess [is formed] by the two middle fingers having the form of a hook. (16.97)
Placing the thumb upon the little finger and the ring finger, this is the mudrā of attraction; it is considered the attractor of the three worlds.
Having formed the hands into the shape of a casket and made the two index fingers like hooks, one should place the two middle fingers beneath them in a reversed order.
Gradually, those fingers beginning with the little finger and the ring finger should all be joined closely together at the tips of the thumbs.
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is considered the bestower of total subjugation;
having brought the two hands face-to-face, one should release the middle fingers into the middle [of the palms]. (16.101)

The two ring fingers (anāmikā) should be straight, with the two index fingers (tarjanī) outside them; then the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭha), positioned at the nail-base of the middle fingers, should be shaped like staffs.
The mudrā named Ullāsinī belongs to the female serpents;
it is formed by placing the two ring fingers below in the shape of *kuśa* grass. (16.103)
One should also apply the index finger in that same sequence;
thus is the Mahākuśā mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
O Great Goddess, having crossed the left hand over to the right side and the right hand over to the left side, and having turned both hands completely around; 16.105.
O Goddess, the little finger and the ring finger are joined according to that sequence;
both index fingers press down upon the middle fingers, which represent all the paths.
O Great Goddess, one should also make the two thumbs straight;
this is that mudrā known by the name Khecarī, the most excellent and beloved of all. (16.107)
And this khecarīmudrā, when applied to the earthly station (pārthivasthāna), is dear [to me]: the two hands are clearly turned and shaped like a crescent moon. (16.108)
Then one should join the pair of the index finger and the thumb together; having bent the little fingers downward, one should place them in the middle of me.
In the same way, when applied with both hands curved and the ring fingers placed at the very bottom,
this is the Seed Mudrā, which swiftly brings about the attainment of all accomplishments.
Having made the two middle fingers curved and positioned above the index fingers,
with the ring fingers likewise placed between them, as indeed are the little fingers.
Joining all [the fingers] together and pressing them with the thumbs—this is the supreme mudrā, known as the *yoni-mudrā*. (16.112)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Section on Mudrās," in the Āgamakalpalatā. (21)
Now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall briefly explain the common mantras according to various tantras. (17.1)

Now, the single-syllable mantras for Bhuvaneśvarī are as follows: *hrīḥ*. One should visualize the syllable *hrīṃ* situated within the abode of the rite to be accomplished, surrounded by the powers (*śaktis*) and brought forth; it is joined with the letters of Hari and Hara placed upon its cheeks, located in the corners.
This yantra, which bestows desired objects when not obscured by other letters, grants good fortune and prosperity when multiplied by nine (gaṇḍi) in the center of the city.
Regarding the phrase "with the syllables of Hari and Hara," some say it refers to the forms *hari-hara* or *hrīḥ hrīḥ*.

Having written the name of the practitioner situated within the seed-syllables, surrounded by Māyā (Hrīṃ), Ramā (Śrīṃ), and Manmatha (Klīṃ), enclosed by two fire-purifiers (the letter Ra), and having placed the three seed-syllables within the six cavities; then, outside, one should bind it with the six seed-syllables: Sā (Sa), Tā (Ta), Mā (Ma), Nā (Na), Ātma (Ā), and Īśikha (Ha). Furthermore, the syllable Hari (Ra) and Hariri (Ra) should be joined to the cheeks. Finally, it is bound on the outside by the six seed-syllables.

One should draw this divine yantra, which is sixfold and bestows the great siddhis of the heart, with its corners shining with Cintāmaṇi and Nṛsiṃha, and its interior filled with the lines of the *sandhi* (intermediate) script within the two houses of the earth. (17–2)
One should write the seed-syllable encircled by the *vyāhṛtis* within each of the two pairs of squares;
then, in the corners, one should write the seed-syllables of Gaṇeśa and Durgā, followed by the groups of letters arranged in pairs.

Within the *Gāyatrī*, one should place the nine openings as in the *Ravi-śakti* [diagram], surrounded by the eight deities, and the ground [square] should be encircled by the *mātṛkā* letters according to the principles of reality.
In the first age, the *siṃhacintāmaṇi* was present;
this diagram (*yantra*), multiplied by the Lord of Gods, is said to grant protection and bestow spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). || 17-3 ||
It generates all good fortune and wards off all enemies.

Now, for the sake of one's kinsmen and for obtaining a son, one should draw [the diagram] joined with eight lotus petals; in the center and on the petals, one should inscribe the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīḥ*).
This yantra, surrounded by vowels and situated within an underground chamber, bestows sons upon women. (17-4)

One should write "Tāre Huṃ" within the hollow of a lotus, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth; having written eight mantra-syllables upon the eight petals, that [lotus] is encircled three times with power (*śakti*). This is the Yantra, placed in a jar, situated upon a lotus, and facing downward.
It is proclaimed to bring subjugation, to protect against the fear of malevolent planets and the like, and to bestow prosperity and fame. || 17-5 ||

271b) Now, the Yantra of Navadurgā: One should draw a lotus provided with twelve petals; in its pericarp, one should write the *yūṣa*-tāra (the syllable *hūṃ*) together with the seed-syllable of Śakti and the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*); and in its filaments, [one should place the syllables] in sequence.
Having again arranged the letters of the *mardinī* mantra according to pairs from the human-originated class (*manu-saṃbhava*), one should write them upon the leaf of the *atyanta-danta* tree;
[the mantra] should be enveloped by the letters of the *mātṛkā* and placed between two *bhūpura*s (circles).
The Yantra of the Goddess dwelling in the Vindhyas has been declared, which bestows all prosperity.

It is especially a protector, a destroyer of malevolent spirits, a bestower of sovereignty upon those who have lost their kingdom, and a grantor of subjugation to those who desire to bring others under their control. (17.7)
It grants sons to those seeking sons and brings peace from disease to the sick; what more need be said here? That Yantra is a wish-fulfilling jewel.

The mantra of Mahiṣāmardinī is *mahiṣamardinī svāhā*. Having divided it according to its syllables, one should write three syllables on each petal. Next is the protective chart (dhāraṇapatra) of Bhairavī.

One should inscribe the seed-syllables of the nine *yonis* starting from the center; then the letters of the three *gāyatrīs* within the eight petals; and again, the syllables surrounding the voids. With the two [syllables] *bhū* and *viṃ* joined with the God of Love (*manmatha*) in the corners, the diagram is encircled. This is declared to be the *traiṣura* yantra, which agitates the three worlds and bestows prosperity.
The Gāyatrī is as follows:
*klīṃ*, "We know Tripura, we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī; may that *klīṃ* inspire us.
Now, the dhāraṇā-yantra of Gaṇeśa.

One should draw the seed-syllable situated in the center of a hexagon within a thick city of fire, with the *tāra* (oṃ) at its tip; in the directions, one should write the syllables of Lakṣmī (*śrīṃ*), Māyā (*hrīṃ*), and Kandarpa (*klīṃ*).

Then, in the cavities of the petals, one should inscribe the six seed-syllables. At the junctions of those [petals], one should place the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) in an eight-petaled lotus, and the letters of the root-mantra, three on each petal.
Let the learned man inscribe it on leaves according to their qualities, ending with the Palāśa leaf.

The Lord of the Gaṇas has described this yantra, which is not contained within the three houses [of the diagram] even when viewed through the *āvīta* letters in their successive order by means of the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
Having written it upon the surface of birch bark— or on gold— with lac, saffron, gorocana, and musk, one should carry it with devotion.
One shall obtain that prosperity which is sought after by all. || 17-10 ||
Thus has been declared the ritual of Mahāgaṇapati, which is honored by the gods;
it bestows all accomplishments upon men and grants all human goals.
Now follows the dhāraṇayantra of Śrī Raghunātha.
One should write the *tāra* (OM) in the center and the mantra within the six corners; at the joints, one should inscribe the *māyā* (Hrīṃ) syllable, and at the tips of the corners,
the letter *ḍa*, followed by *ṣupa*.

In the *kijalkas* (filaments), one should place the groups of gods; in the center, the *mumālā-mantra* is considered to be the eightfold *guha*. It is encircled by the ten-syllable mantra, and the letters beginning with *ka* are placed in the *bhūpura* (the outer square).
One should write the seed-syllables of Narasiṃha and Varāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) is as follows:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate raghunandanāya madhuraprasannavadanāyāmitatejase balābalāmāya viṣṇave namaḥ*.
The seed-syllable (bīja) of Nṛsiṃha is *kṣau*. The seed-syllable of Varāha is *hū*.
Now follows the dhāraṇā-yantra of Śrīnṛsiṃha.

Having drawn two fire-palaces (triangles), one should meditate upon and draw the Śakti within their interior; then, in the six corners, one should place the letters of the petals of the mantra, and in the filaments, the vowels.
In the eight petals, one should sequentially place the letters prescribed for the King of Mantras, four by four, starting with the consonants beginning with 'ka'.
Furthermore, O supreme one, one should contemplate the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) in the corners of the earth that is being returned.
This Narasiṃha yantra, when written on a birch-bark leaf and bound upon the head, quickly removes diseases, malevolent spirits, and fevers. (17.14)
Now, the Sudarśana Yantra.

One should draw a six-cornered [figure] with the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ) together with the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) in its center; then, one should place the remaining letters in the corners.
Having placed the *aṅga-mantras* at its junctions, that yantra, when employed according to the ritual procedure, provides protection. (17.15)
Now, [the ritual] of Śrī Puruṣottama.
The five endings, the earth, the support, and adorned by Manu and Indu—
this is said to be the supreme seed-syllable of the Piṇḍa, which bestows all accomplishments.

One should draw the *piṇḍa* mantra surrounded by the root-mantra within a pair of fire-purifiers (triangles) at the king of corners; then, one should fashion a lotus with ten radiating petals in the directions, surrounded by the *kāmavīja*.
The lotus stands upon the filaments, its petals shining with the modifications of the vowels, while the filaments possess the ten syllables.
In the eight petals of the eight-spoked wheel, one should place the syllables of the *anuṣṭubh* verse, enriched with fans and arranged in a transformed manner.
The eight-syllable yantra, adorned with nooses and goads, surrounded by a garland of skulls, and resting upon the earth supported by four pairs of arms, has Govinda as its presiding deity. (17–18)
It bestows the fruits of dharma, artha, and kāma, and is remembered as providing all protection; now, [the mantra] of Śiva.
Having drawn this [diagram] with two squares for the earth and atoms, one should then draw a plough at the tips of the lines; thereafter, one should place a pair of vowels at the junctions.
Encircled by the Pole Star (Dhruva) and situated within the house of the earth, it becomes the bestower of the fruits of one's desires wherever it is applied.
This is for men. || 17–19 ||

One should write "halo likhet," then "raṃ kaṃ śaṃ saṃ raṃ yaṃ. One should write this mantra, enriched with the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), within the triangle inside that hexagon;
the six limb-mantras (aṅgamantras) in the hexagon, and the eight mantra-syllables in the spaces of the eight-petaled lotus.
Outside [the central figure] is a lute (*vīṇā*) surrounded by the *kalās* beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*; that earth-circle is joined with the *nṛhari* mantra.
This is the "house-destroying" (*gṛhaghna*) Yantra, which destroys the enemy's dwelling.
First, having drawn a hexagonal mandala, one should write the *prāsāda* seed-syllable (*Hrīm*) in its center, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
In the six corners, one should place the seed-syllable *praṇava* (oṃ); in the petals of the five-syllable letter-treasury, one should arrange the syllables of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
There, one should fashion five petals. On the petals: *Iśānāya namaḥ*, *Tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*, *Aghorāya namaḥ*, *Sadyojātāya namaḥ*.
"Salutation to Vāmadeva"—
thus one should write these five mantras in the order starting from the east.
Having fashioned eight petals outside of that, one should write the eight groups of the Mātṛkā letters upon those petals.
One should encircle that with a triple line.
Encircled by recitation, fire-oblation, and so forth, this [yantra] accomplishes the four aims of human life.
Now, one should draw the dhāraṇa-yantra for rites of pacification and the like.
Thus it is said in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra:
"O you of excellent vows, [one should write] on gold-leaf, or on birch-bark, or even on cloth. (17–20)
One should draw [the design] with a bamboo pen, provided with the eight fragrances;
and having drawn it again with a stalk of dūrvā grass and the root of kuśa grass.
Also in the Ekavīrā-kalpa.
One should wrap the creature with a yellow cloth.
One should tie it with a yellow cloth as an ornament for the necks of children;
for women, on the left arm, and for others, on the right arm. (17–22)
A barren woman obtains a son, and one who is poor becomes wealthy;
this protection was formerly bound [upon themselves] by Gautama and others for the sake of knowledge. (17–23)
For the sake of fame, by the Pāṇḍavas and others desiring victory in battle—

the meaning of this is as follows: having prepared a mixture of saffron, gorocana, sandalwood, and jaṭāmāṃsī on a birch-bark leaf with a golden stylus in the center of a hexagon, one should write the root mantra in sequence around its perimeter.
Hṛllekhā, in the middle of the letter *ra*: "Protect [the name] of so-and-so" (2).
"May there be auspiciousness for such-and-such persons," or: "Accomplish, accomplish the attainment of knowledge for this person."
Having written [the mantra] beginning with these words, together with the *sādhya*, within a hexagon, one should write the long vowels associated with the *klī* syllable: *ā, ī, ū, e, ai, o, au, aḥ*.
On the eight petals, one should write the eight syllables as follows:
Ai Hrīḥ Oṃ Ai Hrīḥ Phaṭ Svāhā.
[One should utter] Vāgbhava, Kuladevī, Tāraka, and likewise Vāgbhava again. (17–24)
Hṛllekhā and the Astra-mantra, followed by the wife of Vahni (Svāhā)—this is declared to be the eight-syllabled mantra, said to be the essence of all mantras. (17–25)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter (22) of the Āgamakalpalatā, titled "The Explanation of the Dhāraṇā-yanttras."
Now, the mantra of Mātaṅgī:
Listen, O Great Goddess, as I tell you the mantra exactly as it is:
one should utter the word *ucchiṣṭa* and likewise *cāṇḍālinī*. (18.1)
Immediately after that, one should recite the goddess as "Sumukhī";
thereafter, [the mantra] "Mahāpiśācinī," followed by the seed-syllable of Māyā.
Then, O Great Goddess, there is the triad of the letter *ṭha* joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, followed by the *visarga*; this bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). (18.3)

And here, by the very force of the context, one should recite "Caṇḍālinī" as a word ending in the nominative singular; therefore, it is understood from the hearing [of the text] that the status of object belongs only to the word "Devī. However, some desire the vocative case everywhere.
*Hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable of Māyā: *hrīḥ*. The letter *ṭha* with the vowel *u*, the bindu, and the nāda is *ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*.
This is its essential form (*svarūpa*).
[The mantra is: *Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī sumukhī devī mahāpiśācinī hrīḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. (22)
Thus he spoke within the mantra: *aiḥ soḥ aiḥ hrīḥ āḥ klīṃ aṣṭamātangi namāmi ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālini trailokyavaśakari svāhā* (30).
Thus is one mantra.
Alternatively, one should utter the words *ucchiṣṭacaṇḍāli mātaṅgi*, and then at the end [add] *sarvavaśaṃ kuru* with the heart [syllable] and the fire-flame woman (*vahnivallabhā*). (18.4)
With nineteen syllables, it shall accomplish all desired aims.
Thus: *ucchiṣṭacaṇḍā mātaṅgi sarvaśaṅkari namaḥ svāhā*.
Whoever indeed recites this mantra, this Vidyā that rests upon the Aparāṅga;
This is the knowledge, the great knowledge, which destroys all sins.
This knowledge bestows heaven, bestows liberation, and likewise bestows prosperity and good fortune;
having kept one's mouth always free from remnants of food, one should remember the Goddess who grants victory. (18.6)
Then, O Goddess, even without performing a rite of exorcism, the unfortunate woman shall become fortunate, and the sorrowful woman shall become happy. (18.7)
Even a barren woman obtains a son who lives for a hundred years;
the weak gains strength, and the fool may acquire knowledge.
I shall now describe the ritual procedure here; listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance.
There is no fault regarding enemies, nor obstacles, nor impurity, nor restriction, nor can it be attained by impediments.
O Sovereign of the Universe, I shall correctly explain her meditation. (18–9)
Seated upon a corpse, she is the destroyer of all sins;
she is endowed with red ornaments and adorned with a necklace of *guñjā* seeds. (18.10)
And she was a young woman of sixteen years, with full and swelling breasts,
holding a skull and a chisel in her hands, and possessing the nature of the supreme light.
The knower of mantras, meditating by means of the union of the left and the right, should offer the bali-offering with the remnants and recite the mantra with his mind fixed upon that. 18-12.
One must certainly not perform recitation while impure from food remnants; for one who is certain of accomplishment, all perfections arise for one who recites while in that state. (18.13)
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall proclaim that which yields fruit:
the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa), for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. (18–14)
Having drawn a square mandala upon the sacrificial ground with a concentrated mind, O Goddess, the knower of mantras should worship the mandala with the root mantra. (18.15)
Then, having taken up the goddess who is established in the form of fire and having meditated upon her,
one should perform the homa with curd and rice grains for the sake of attaining perfection.
By performing one thousand oblations, one may bring a king under one's control;
with the flesh of a cat, one should perform an oblation for the Goddess.
One attains the supreme knowledge that brings all scriptures under one's control;
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with goat meat combined with honey.
By performing the rite one thousand times, the success of the fruits is attained;
one should perform the homa with milk-rice mixed with sugar, while reciting the Vidyā-mantra.
For one who [offers] with honey and milk-rice (pāyasa) from the garment of a woman in her menses, fourteen [years] certainly come to pass immediately. (18–20)
Having performed the *homa*, the Great Goddess brings the three worlds under her control.
One should perform the *homa* with *nāgavallī* leaves and milk-rice mixed with sugar. (18–21)
By performing ten thousand repetitions of this single method, the desired accomplishment will certainly be attained in this world;
[this occurs] immediately when [the rite is performed] with cat-flesh together with ghee and honey.
With [an offering] joined by the hair of a Caṇḍāla, attraction will certainly occur;
likewise with the flesh of a hare mixed with honey. (18–23)
Having performed the *homa*, one obtains wealth, property, and excellent women;
one should perform the *homa* in the fire of the mind combined with the wood of the *datura*.
An oblation with the feathers of a cuckoo and a crow brings about the destruction of enemies;
and the knower of mantras should perform an oblation for the eradication of enemies. (18–25)
275a) According to the previously described procedure, one should offer the fuel of the wood of the *cittā* tree;
having prepared the oblation with the feathers of an owl and a crow, one should perform the fire sacrifice continuously. (18.26)
One should cause enmity among enemies through mutual strife and family discord; by means of an oblation of owl feathers, the miscarriage of the fetus of an excellent woman occurs. (18–27)
With a focused mind, one should construct the abode according to the single method of the thousand-fold rite,
offering bilva leaves along with ghee continuously for one month.
Even a barren woman obtains an excellent son who lives long, whether she performs this at a mountain cave, a cremation ground, an empty house, or a crossroads. (18–29)
By the offering of the oblation, the Goddess certainly becomes manifest.
This Goddess was recited by me while desiring the form of Bhairava. (18–30)
Thus has this goddess, the pacifier of all sins, been described;
by the mere utterance of her mantra, there is the destruction of all sins. (18-31)
Having abandoned the impurity of remnants, one will certainly become possessed of the *pavitra*.

Although the *puraścaraṇa* is mentioned here, it should be understood that the recitation (*japa*) consists of eight thousand [verses], and the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites should be performed with a tenth part of that.
For those [mantras] for which no specific number has been stated by the wise regarding recitation (japa) and burnt offering (homa), [the following applies].
Their number is eight thousand, according to the statement that this count applies to both recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*).
As it is said in the *Vārāhītantra*:
"One should perform eight thousand oblations; the recitation is proclaimed to be one hundred thousand."
Thus is the reading on the northern petal; or likewise, that which is stated in the mantra of Dakṣiṇakālī,
because of the context of the tantra.
In reality, however, because these are perfected vidyās, there is no need for preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth; this is the meaning.
Thus ends the section on the Mātaṅgī mantra.
The Goddess said: O Lord, you are the most excellent Bhairava, and I am your beloved.
O Great Lord, tell me quickly about Mātaṅgī. (18-33)
Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, O Goddess, my beloved, I shall fully declare that which is most secret;
by the mere knowledge of which the three worlds shall become exceedingly happy. (18.34)
That goddess Mātaṅgī always precedes the remnants [of offerings];
she is the goddess who bestows all accomplishments and destroys all sins. (18.35)
By the mere knowledge of which the practitioner himself attains success—this supreme goddess of knowledge, the destroyer of all sins. (18.36)
This goddess, when previously perfected and free from defects, bestows heaven and liberation, as well as royal power and enjoyments for men. (18.37)
Recited but once, this Vidyā removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
she is the Goddess who bestows all happiness and grants prosperity to the world. (18.38)

O Goddess, if one should remember the goddess Piśācinī while having a mouth soiled by food remnants, then that food becomes [as if consumed] even without having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana). (18.39)
Surely the unfortunate shall become fortunate, and the suffering shall become happy;
even the barren woman shall obtain a son and attain a hundred years of excellent life. (18.40)
The poor shall obtain wealth, and one shall attain the possession of knowledge;
whatever success one prays for, that very thing one shall obtain by force.
Through this goddess, men shall attain perfection free from old age and death;
O beautiful goddess, listen as I now describe the ritual procedure.

In the midst of a meal, even if the ritual rinsing (ācamana) has not been performed, the knower of mantras should offer the oblation (bali) according to the prescribed rule at the beginning of the meal. 18.43.
Then the wise one, having meditated upon the mantra that grants the accomplishment of desired goals, should recite it;
having first recited the root mantra, he should thereafter recite the mantra again. (18.44)
O Great Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, the extraction of the mantra is as follows:
the first syllable is Vāgbhava, O Goddess, and the second is Kāmarāja. (18.45)
Nevertheless, she should then utter the word "ucchiṣṭa," and likewise "caṇḍālinī";
thereafter, the goddess Sumukhī should be proclaimed. (18.46)
Then [comes] Mahāpiśācinī, followed by *la* and the seed-syllable (*vīja*), likewise joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), and then three instances of the syllable *ṭha*. (18.47)

O Great Goddess, that which includes the *visarga* and ends with *svāhā* bestows success; it requires neither a specific lunar day nor a particular constellation, nor does it depend on the placement of limbs or the recitation of mantras. (18.48)
For him in whom this mantra resides, there is no fault regarding the lunar day, no obstacle, and he is not consumed by fire; for such a person, accomplishment is not far off.
O Supreme Goddess, I shall describe his meditation exactly as it is: [he is] seated upon a corpse, red in color, and clad in garments of raw flesh. (18.50)
Adorned with red ornaments and decorated with a necklace of guñjā berries,
she is a sixteen-year-old young woman with full and lofty breasts.
She had ears shaped like skull-cups, was intoxicated with wine, held a broom in her hand, possessed a beautiful face, generated supreme bliss, and was the embodiment of all auspiciousness.
They play [the instruments] which pierce the vital points with a swooning resonance;
one should meditate upon the supreme consort of Māttaṅginī through the union of the left and the right. 18-53.
One who desires future success must never perform [the practice] while impure;
for one who recites the mantra while impure and meditates, it bestows all accomplishments. (54)
I shall explain that path; listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance!
It consists of the triad, the pentad, the octad, the sixteenfold, and likewise the fourfold.
For malevolent rites (abhicāra), one should use a corner [of a cloth] on a stone or a slab of dead skin;
for the purpose of subjugation (vaśya), one should employ a triangle upon a bell-metal vessel.
For the sake of wealth, one should write it on the ground; likewise, for the sake of a maiden, on gold;
and for the sake of protection, on birch bark—therein one should employ a triangle.
Having written the supreme mantra mixed with camphor and vermilion, combined with saffron, hair-syrup, and other fragrances, [one should apply it] to one another. (18.58)
The Mohana Yantra is always auspicious during the period of withdrawal;
I shall now describe another [yantra] which fulfills many kinds of desires.
The propitiation of the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed for the sake of accomplishing all desires;
having drawn a well-proportioned square mandala on the ground, one should remain composed. (18.60)
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus in its center, provided with a lunar disc and filaments,
the knower of mantras should then recite the root mantra, O Goddess, while subsequently consuming food.
Then, having invoked the Goddess who is established in the form of fire and having performed the ritual preparation, one should perform the homa with curd, white mustard seeds, and rice grains.
By performing this rite one thousand times according to the single method, the king becomes submissive;
in brief, he is not harmed by a cat nor by honey.
For the certain attainment of wealth, one should perform a thousand-fold sacrifice according to the single method;
and for the sake of desire for knowledge, one should perform the oblation with sugar, clarified butter, and milk-rice.
Or, having performed a fire-oblation with a cloth from a menstruating woman mixed with honey, the Great Goddess shall bring the three worlds under one's control. (18.65)
By performing the rite with *nāgavalī* leaves, honey, and ghee, according to the single method of ten thousand repetitions, one's desired goals are indeed accomplished. (18.66)
If [the offering] contains liquor, cat meat, honey, meat, or ghee;
or if it is mixed with the hair of a caṇḍāla, the summoning will certainly not succeed. (18.67)
One should perform a thousand-fold oblation with goat meat mixed with ghee and honey; having performed this, one may bring the three worlds under one's control.
With the flesh of a śara deer, honey, and ghee, combined with the hair of a caṇḍāla, the rite of attraction will certainly succeed. (18.69)
One should perform a fire sacrifice with goat meat combined with ghee and honey;
having performed the homa, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.
And by performing the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule with the flesh of a hare,
having completed the oblation, one obtains the Vindhyādhara-vārā, which bestows boons.
The knower of mantras, using a combination of gold and wood at the seat of the mind, should perform a fire-oblation with the feathers of a cuckoo and a crow to destroy enemies. (18.72)
The fire for the funeral pyre has been described according to ten types;
by means of the feathers of an owl or a crow, even the fetus of an enemy's wife may be caused to fall. (18.73)
If one consumes bilva and parched grain (lāja) here continuously for one month, O daughter, she shall never be barren and shall attain supreme longevity. (18.74)
Having prepared a *vandhūka* flower combined with ghee and grapes, one will certainly attain the happiness of good fortune and the power of attraction. (18.75)
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with the fragrance of jasmine flowers;
within six months one attains success, and the power of attraction will certainly be achieved. (18.76)
A celestial maiden, a Gandharva maiden, and likewise a Gaṇa maiden—anyone who, having arrived by force out of desire, lies down overwhelmed; || 18-77 ||
O Goddess, this great vidyā, which bestows the fruits of the left-hand practice (vāmācāra), [should be recited] in a forest, a cremation ground, an empty house, or at a crossroads. (18.78)
Having performed the *homa*, the procedure as it was taught for the Great Goddess [is complete].
Thus ends the chapter on Mātaṅgī Sumukhī in the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra, within the Guhyakālī Tantra.
Now, another method [follows].
Salutations to Sumukhī.
Now, therefore, O beloved, I shall fully proclaim the secret body of the Goddess.
By means of which mere consciousness the three worlds are agitated—she is the goddess Mātaṅgī, preceded by the *ucchiṣṭa* [rite], the bestower of all accomplishments. (18.80)
O Goddess, you who destroy all calamities and are free from all diseases;
by that Goddess, who is ever-present at the end of decay, she is fully known.
The Goddess, taking refuge in the bodies of her own devotees, destroys obstacles—whether stationary or moving, artificial or natural. (18.82)
Thus, by mere knowledge [of this], she removes all sins, bestows heaven, grants liberation, and yields the fruit of royal happiness. (18.83)
"O Goddess, although this vidyā was previously recited by me during my silent chanting, once it is uttered, it purifies even the sin of killing a Brahmin. (18.84)
The Goddess is the remover of all sins and the bestower of worldly prosperity;
one should never ever utter the name of the Goddess while having the remnants of food on one's face.
Likewise, O Goddess, even one who has not performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) should recite [this mantra];
may the unfortunate woman become fortunate, and may the suffering woman obtain happiness. (18.86)
Whatever accomplishment one seeks through Haṭha, that very thing one shall obtain.
O Goddess, listen as I describe the procedure according to the prescribed rite. (18.87)
O Goddess, while moving among foods, even without having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), the practitioner should first offer the oblation (bali) with the root mantra. (18.88)
Then, having meditated upon that goddess for the sake of attaining his desired success, he should mutter the mantra;
he should utter the word "ucchiṣṭa" and then "caṇḍālinī. (18.89)
Then one should recite the goddess Sumukhī immediately after that;
from her follows Mahāpiśācinī, and after that the seed-syllable of Lajjā.
O Goddess, the practitioner should employ this mantra, which consists of three *ṭha* letters joined with *nāda* and *bindu*, ending with *svāhā*. (18.91)
And this Vidyā, having been recited once, bestows all accomplishments.
Now, the extraction [of the mantra]: *ucchiṣṭacaṇḍalinī sumukhī devī mahāpiśācinī hrīḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*.
Thus, having accomplished the pure mantra;
this is the extraction of the mantra consisting of twenty-four syllables. || 18-92 ||
One need not observe the lunar day, nor the asterism, nor the day of the week; nor should one perform the ritual of limb-assignment (nyāsa) before the three men undertake the task. || 18.93 ||
Neither defects nor obstacles shall cause destruction here for one in whom this mantra abides; he is never overcome by obstacles. (18.94)
I shall describe her meditation just as [that of] Vajragadeśvarī: she is seated upon a corpse, clothed in red garments. (18.95)
Adorned with red ornaments and resplendent with a necklace of *guñjā* berries, she has full and elevated breasts and is sixteen years of age, her body drenched in milk. (18.96)
One who desires liberation should meditate upon her whose hands hold a skull as a vessel, whose nature is the supreme light, and who is situated on the left and right sides. (18.97)
Meditative concentration.
O Goddess, reciting [the mantra] while remaining in the state of impurity (ucchiṣṭa) leads to the attainment of all perfections (siddhi).
Furthermore, O Goddess, bestower of fruits, listen as I shall explain another [method]. (18.98)

Having prepared a mandala on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), he, being composed, should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa) for her, for the accomplishment of all desires. || 18-99 ||
The knower of mantras should worship the mandala with the root mantra of the Goddess;
then, having taken up the Goddess who is established in the form of fire.

Having meditated upon the Goddess, one should perform a fire-oblation with curd, white mustard seeds, and rice according to the procedure of one thousand repetitions; thus the king becomes subject to one's will.
And with the flesh of a cat, the goddess should perform a fire-oblation;
she shall obtain supreme knowledge that brings mastery over both weapons and scriptures. (18.102)
One should perform a fire-oblation with goat meat combined with honey, according to the procedure of one thousand [recitations]; thereby, the attainment of wealth occurs. (18.103)
One desiring knowledge should perform oblations with pebbles and milk-rice;
when the oblation is thus performed, the fourteen branches of knowledge become perfected.

Having performed a *homa* with honey or milk-rice (*pāyasa*) using a garment belonging to a menstruating woman, one may bring the three worlds under one's control by means of the *mādevyā* [mantra]. (18.105)

One should perform the oblation with honey and ghee using the *nāgavalī* plant according to the single method for ten thousand recitations; indeed, the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) will then be attained. (18.106)
With the flesh of a dog and a cat, together with ghee and honey, and combined with the hair of a Caṇḍālī woman, the great summoning [of the desired object] is certain. (18.107)
By performing a *kṛtyā* oblation with the flesh of a hare and blood mixed with honey, one obtains the women of the best of the Vidyādharas. (18.108)
By means of the application of *datura* wood and the feathers of a cuckoo and a crow, the knower of mantras shall destroy his enemies in the fire of the funeral pyre. (18.109)
The knower of mantras should perform a fire sacrifice for the eradication of enemies according to the previously mentioned procedure, using a fire fueled by *citrā* wood.
Having performed the fire-oblation continuously for one month with the feathers of an owl and a crow, [one conquers] all the limbs and parts of the body of one's enemies and adversaries.

By means of an owl's wing-feather, a great mantra-practitioner, concentrated in the performance of the fire-oblation (homa), may cause the miscarriage of the fetus of an enemy woman, even up to a thousand times. (18.112)
By offering bilva leaves along with clarified butter continuously for one month, even a barren woman shall obtain an excellent son who is long-lived. (18.113)
One should offer an oblation of red *vandhūka* flowers mixed with honey and white sugar;
one should offer an oblation of red *vandhūka* flowers mixed with honey and white sugar. (18.114)
For a goddess who may be unfortunate, one should perform one hundred and eight recitations with *japā* flowers and clarified butter to bestow good fortune and happiness. (18.115)
Through practice for six months, the summoning will certainly succeed:
the daughters of the nāgas, the daughters of the yakṣas, the daughters of the gods, and even the kinnarīs. (18.116)
Having arrived by force, she forcibly embraces the man until the end of desire; thus the Goddess Mahāvidyā bestows the fruit of the left-hand path (vāmācāra). 18.117.
Through the practice of right conduct, she becomes the bestower of dissolution;
one should properly offer the *bali* offering every single day after eating.

O Dear One, one should worship the mantra with the remnants [of the offering] one hundred and eight times, whether in a secluded place, a cremation ground, an empty house, or at a crossroads. (18.119)
"O Goddess, the offering of the skin-curls is certainly manifest;
this, O Goddess, was recited by me while desiring the form of Bhairava. (18.120)
Thus has this goddess, the destroyer of all sins, been described;
by the utterance of her mantra, one becomes free from all sins. (18.121)
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for Sumukhī in the Rudrayāmala Tantra. Now, the liturgical manual (paddhati) for the worship of Sumukhī is being written.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the manual in prose form for the daily worship of Sumukhī, which is the most excellent essence among all essences.

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and assuming the firm *padmāsana*, one should meditate upon one’s own Guru seated within the pericarp of a thousand-petaled lotus facing downward located at the crown of one’s head— the Guru adorned with white ornaments, embraced on the left by his own Śakti, who is clad in red garments.
Having fully worshipped with mental offerings (*mānasopacāra*), prostrating like a staff and receiving his command,
one should come outside, cast away the *ajña-sūtra* and other items, and perform the ritual of anointing the limbs with the letters of the alphabet (*akṣaravarṇa*).
Then, having gone to a river or similar place, one should take a tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*) twelve finger-breadths long and consecrate it with the *Kāmarāja-mantra*.
Having prepared the ritual enclosure with the seed-syllable *vāgbhava* (AIM), having performed three mouthfuls of rinsing (*gaṇḍūṣa*), and having washed the base of the penis and the mouth,
[one should recite]: *Oṃ hrīḥ maṇidharivajriṇi śikhāparisare rakṣa rakṣa ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having thus tied the topknot (*śikhā*) with the root mantra (*mūla*), having sipped water three times (*ācamana*) with the root mantra, and having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *Kāmarāja* mantra, one should perform the ritual bath for the removal of impurities by drawing [the water] up with the *Sāṃsya* mantra; then one should perform the mantra-bath (*mantrasnāna*).
Then, having brought earth with the root mantra, one should sprinkle the water. Then, having formed a handful of water with the root mantra—
Having thoroughly inspected it, one should purify the clay; then, having purified one portion of the clay with a *śūla* [ritual implement], one should [use] another portion of clay [with the mantra]:
*Oṃ ga gū ga ge ge ca Yamune caiva Godāvari Sarasvati*.
O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in this water!
Having thus invoked the sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), [he recites] with the second [mantra]:
Oṃ klīṃ! O Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālī, O Great Piśācinī, O remembered one! O Goddess, together with your retinue, come respectfully to this water. (18.124)

Thus, having invoked the goddess Śivā with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, having visualized the *yantra* in the water, and having smeared his own limbs with [the substance] by means of the third [mantra], he should descend into the water himself and, reciting the root-vidyā three times, perform the *nyāsa* from the head down to the feet. There, having performed the six-limbed *nyāsa* of the root-mantra and meditated upon the deity, [he should proceed].

Having recited the root mantra ten times and performed the cleansing of the head with the root mantra, one should offer three *arghya* oblations to the Sun, saying: "Oṃ Hrīḥ Haṃ Saḥ, this *arghya* is for the venerable Sūrya; obeisance. Then, having caused [the deity] to descend from the water and having clothed him in other garments, [one should proceed].

One should begin the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*). Therein, having performed the sprinkling of water three times on one's own head with the root mantra as before, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) three times:
*oṃ klīṃ ātmatattvaṃ śodhayāmi svāhā*.

Oṃ klīṃ, I purify the principle of Śiva-Śakti, svāhā! Aiṃ klīṃ, I purify the principle of Vidyā, svāhā! Having sipped water in this manner and performed three rounds of breath control—namely, inhalation for twelve [counts], retention for sixteen [counts], and exhalation for thirty-two [counts]— [End of segment]
Having performed [the visualization] in this manner, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*):
*Klīṃ Hrīṃ*, salutation to the heart (*hṛdayāya namaḥ*). *Klīṃ Hrīṃ*, *svāhā* to the head (*śirase svāhā*). *Klūṃ Hūṃ*, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*).
*Kleṃ Hreṃ*, *hum* to the armor (*kavacāya hum*). *Klauṃ Hroṃ*, *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes (*netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*). *Klaḥ Hraḥ*, *phaṭ* to the weapon (*astrāya phaṭ*).
Having thus performed the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*), having recited the root mantra (*mūla*) and taken water in the hollow of the palms, covering it with the right hand,

and having consecrated it three times with *ha ya va ra la*, one should recite the root mantra while sprinkling that water seven times with drops from the *tadṛtva-mudrā*. Then, taking the remaining water in the right hand, [one should contemplate] the fire.
Having meditated on the form, one should recite the root mantra. Then, one should recite the Gāyatrī:
*ai klī uchiṣṭaṃ candrālini vidmahe sumukhī devī dhīmahe hrīḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ tanno mātaṅgī pracodayāt*. (3)
Having thus recited the Gāyatrī as much as possible and offered three *arghya* oblations to the Goddess together with Śiva, [one should say]:
"May the venerable Amṛteśvarānandanātha Bhairava be satisfied;
may he be satiated with honey-water together with his Śakti. [This is for] the southeast.

One should offer libations to the venerable supreme guru, Svarēśvarānandanātha, in the southwest. One should offer libations to the intermediate guru, Ānandanātha. One should offer libations to the supreme-teacher guru, Siddhēśānandanātha.
Thus, having once satisfied the gurus belonging to the *divyaugha*, *siddhaugha*, and *mānavaugha*, one should satisfy the Goddess.
Having visualized the water as the *yantra* with the root mantra: "I satisfy Uchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī together with Śiva; obeisance.
Thus, one should perform the satisfaction seven times with the root mantra. (1)
I satisfy Mataṅga; obeisance! [Recite] the root mantra.
I offer Mātaṅgī, together with her weapons, retinue, and vehicle, accompanied by Amṛteśvara; obeisance! Having thus offered libations at the crest [of the head], again—
Oṃ hrīḥ haḥ saḥ, obeisance to the glorious Mārtaṇḍabhairava;
with this, having offered the threefold *arghya*, one should satisfy the *piṇḍas* with the root mantra. Then, one should again recite the Gāyatrī according to one's ability.
Then, one should again recite the Gāyatrī according to one's ability. Having recited the Gāyatrī ten times, one is liberated.
"Even one joined with all sins, even if possessed of great transgressions (mahāpātaka), goes to the supreme city of the Goddess.

Having thus offered the recitation of the Gāyatrī of the God and Goddess, the victory-recitation, and the root-mantra (mūla) by means of the root-mantra and the *saṃhāramudrā*, and having dismissed the God and Goddess from his heart by means of the Vidyā-mantra, he should return to the sacrificial hall.
Thus concludes the ritual for the twilight (sandhyā).
Then, having arrived at the door of the house and washed one's feet, one should worship the deities of the threshold:
*Oṃ Śrī Gaṇeśāya namaḥ* in the east.
Oṃ kṣāḥ! Homage to Kṣetrapāla; in the south. Saṃ! Homage to Sarasvatī; in the west. Oṃ vāṃ! Homage to Vaṭuka; in the north.
Oṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā—[at the] bottom. Salutation to the Root Deity—[at the] middle.
Having thus performed worship and entered within the house, one should purify the seat according to one's own tradition.
Oṃ. Of this Śrī Āsanaśuddhi-mantra, Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Kūrma is the deity (devatā), Sutala is the meter (chandaḥ), and its application (viniyoga) is in the mantra for the seat.
Prīṃ! Salutation to Pṛthivī (the Earth).
Oṃ Pṛthivī! By you the worlds are supported; you, O Goddess, are supported by Viṣṇu.
May you always support me and make this seat pure.
Oṃ Hrīḥ Āḥ, obeisance to Ananta (3 times). Obeisance to Kūrma (3 times). [Recite] the root mantra.
Salutation to the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*), which is colored by its nectar.
(3) Salutation to her whose girdle is the ocean. (3) Salutation to Sarasvatī.
(3) Having thus worshipped, [one recites] the root mantra once. (1)
"May those spirits depart who reside upon the earth;
may those spirits who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
Having thus uttered this and performed the three *tāla* gestures, one should expel the obstructing spirits from that place by striking with the left heel.
One should display the *nārāca-mudrā*. Having thus purified the seat, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) as before,
performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and performed the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) through the application of breath control.

Saying "Oṃ Hūḥ," by means of the Suṣumṇā path, one leads the individual soul (jīva)— shaped like the flame of a lamp— to the end of the Brahma-path; having brought that light into Sadāśiva, one first [places] the syllable *Yaṃ*, the seed-syllable of wind, sixteen times, which is smoke-colored and four-cornered, upon the sinner located in the left side of the abdomen.

Dry it. Then, with the fire-seed *raṃ* recited ten times, which is red in color, one should burn it. With the Indra-seed *laṃ*, recited ten times, which is yellow in color, one should flood it with a falling rain of nectar from within a hexagon.

Having purified one's own body of all impurities by means of that rain of nectar through the *vandharuṇa* seed-syllable (*vam*) recited sixteen times, and having visualized it as a divine body, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*. Thus ends the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
*Oṃ sohaṃ haṃsaḥ; my vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are here, my vital breaths; my life-force (*jīva*) is established here, my...*
"May all the senses—speech, mind, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and breath—come here and remain happily for a long time; svāhā!
Having thus performed the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) preceded by the ritual assignments (*nyāsa*).

Oṃ. Of this mantra for the daily worship of the illustrious Sumukhī, Mataṅga is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda), the illustrious Uchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī-Sumukhī is the deity (devatā), Ai is the seed-syllable (bīja), Hrī is the power (śakti), and Klī is the pin (kīlaka).
Its application (viniyoga) is in worship for the sake of attaining the fruit of the four aims of life.
Now, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*):
Salutation to the sage Mataṅga on the head. Salutation to the *anuṣṭubh* meter on the mouth.
Salutation to the deity, the auspicious Uchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī Sumukhī, on the heart. Salutation to the seed-syllable *aiṃ* on the navel.
*Hrīṃ*, salutation to Śakti at the secret place; *Klīṃ*, salutation to Kīlaka at the feet; *Viniyogāya namaḥ*, salutation to Viniyoga at all limbs. Thus is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

Ai Klōṃ, salutation to the two thumbs. Ai Klīṃ, salutation to the two index fingers. Ai Klūṃ, salutation to the two middle fingers. Ai Kleṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers. Ai Klīṃ, salutation to the two little fingers. Ai Klaḥ.
*Namaḥ* to both the palms and the backs of the hands. Thus is the *karanyāsa*. Now follows the *ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*:
*Aiṃ klīṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*. *Aiṃ klīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*. *Oṃ klūṃ* to the tuft (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*. *Aiṃ klūṃ*... [to the armor (*kavaca*)].
*Śavacāya hūṃ*. *Oṃ klīṃ*, to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*. *Oṃ klaḥ*, to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*.
Thus is the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). *Aiṃ klīṃ*, to the heart, *namaḥ*. *Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī*, to the head, *svāhā*. *Sukhadevī*, to the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
*Vaṣaṭ*. *Mahāpiśācinī*, *hūṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*). *Hrīṃ*, *ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*, *vauṣaṭ* for the two eyes. *Svāhā*, *phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*).
Thus is the placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra.

Now, the *triśakti-nyāsa*: *Aiṃ*, salutation to Rati-Mātaṅgī at the *mūlādhāra*; *Klīṃ*, salutation to Dhṛti-Mātaṅgī at the heart; *Hrīṃ*, salutation to Prīti-Mātaṅgī between the eyebrows. Having performed this placement (*vinyāsa*), one should perform the *śakti-nyāsa*.

Ai Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, obeisance to Hṛllekhāmātaṅginī on the head (3). Obeisance to Gaganamātaṅginī on the face (3). Obeisance to Raktamātaṅginī on the heart (3). Obeisance to Karālinīmātaṅginī on the private parts (3). Obeisance to Mahocchuṣmāmātaṅginī on the feet.
Having thus performed the placement [of the syllables], one should perform the placement of the arrows (*vāṇanyāsa*):

Now, the armor-mantra of Sumukhī:
For this armor-mantra of Sumukhī, Mātaṅga is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, Sumukhī is the deity;
its application is in the recitation of the mantra.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the auspicious armor (kavaca) of Mātaṅgī.
It must be kept secret, O Great Goddess; one should perform its recitation. (18–126)
The Goddess said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Mahādeva! Tell me, O Maheśvara, by what correct procedure the recitation (japa) of practitioners may be performed. (18.127)
Without meditation, without mantra, without fire-offering, and without a sacrificial victim—by the mere recollection of whom the practitioner becomes a lord of the earth. (18.128)
Śrī Bhairava said:
This divine armor of Mātaṅgī bestows complete protection upon men,
as well as poetic talent, wealth, and the faces of elephants and horses.
She bestows the auspiciousness of the staff of Sumu, the power of atomization (*aṇimā*), and other such qualities;
she is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, yet the Great Sovereign (*Maheśvarī*) is the primordial source of them all. (18.130)
Whatever man recites even a single verse or half-verse correctly, royal fortune is always in his hand; of this there is no doubt. (18.131)
Having left the remnants of food on his face and seated upon a lotus throne,
he should form the *yonimudrā* with his hands and remain intent on the meditation of Śakti.
Having brought [the breath] through the aperture of Aḍmara and established it in the name of Ucchiṣṭā, one should always protect the forehead with the mantra "Mahācāṇḍālinī. (18.133)
May Sumukhī protect them at the navel; may the goddess Rakṣā protect the nose;
and may Mahāpiśācinī and Campā always protect the mouth. (18.134)

May the letter *la* protect my sense of shame; may the two letters *da* and *na* perform the cleansing with the teeth; may the letter *ka* perform the wiping with the hand on the chin and the region of the hips; and thereafter, the triad of the letter *ṭha*. (18.135)
May Mahādevī, together with the Visarga, protect my heart at all times;
may Kālikā, whose eyes are red as lac, grant me constant protection at the navel.
May Cāmuṇḍā protect the belly, and likewise may Kātyāyanī protect the linga;
may Ugracaṇḍā protect the anus, and may Avikā protect the feet.
May Sarvāṇī protect [me] in battle; may Candrabhīṣaṇā protect the heart;
may Mātṛkā protect the tongue; and may Pūṣṭikā protect [me] in the east.
May Uttarā protect Kṛttikā; may Vidyā protect [her] in the west.
May Vijayā protect [her] in the south; may Medhā protect [her] in the southeast. (18.139)
May Prajñā protect in the southwest; may Lakṣmaṇā protect in the northwest;
and may the goddess Mātaṅgī, the performer of auspicious deeds, protect in the northeast.
May the Great Goddess, who acts for the benefit of the gods, protect me above;
may Vāmukī, whose form is the universe, protect me eternally in the netherworld. (18.141)
May Vāmukī, who possesses a universal form, protect me eternally in Pātāla;
and may she, having sounded her drum upon the six-petaled lotus of Vaṭuvarmatī, always protect you.
The Goddess always protects the city within the four-petalled lotus at the end of the speech-path.
Having recited this mantra—Oṃ kṣā śrī prī prī chrī chrī ṭhaḥ hrī ṭhaḥ ai ṭhaḥ svāhā—one should wear it on the left arm. (18.143)
Whoever wears this on their neck becomes Maheśvara himself along with all the gods;
upon seeing him, all the deities bow down from afar. (18.144)
By the power of his splendor, even Indra and others would be unable to approach him;
the king would treat such a being like a servant. (18.145)
His desires shall be fulfilled, as well as the powers beginning with *aṇimā*; likewise, he shall attain fame, splendor, and whatever [powers] such as *māraṇa* there may be. (18.146)
That man who, without knowing the armor-mantra (kavaca), recites [it] while the Goddess is well-disposed toward him, sometimes attains royal favor through his devotion and worship. (18.147)
O Goddess of gods, he perishes; the Yoginīs devour him. He shall become one who experiences the sufferings of this world, utterly abandoned. (18.148)
For ten million lifetimes, one who is always mute does not attain the accomplishment of mantra;
however, when the wise person receives the mantra while honoring the feet of the guru, [they attain it]. (18.149)
But then, O Goddess, by wearing the armor with all its parts and through the grace of the Guru, one becomes a conqueror in this world and shall attain liberation in the hereafter. || 18-150 ||
O Sovereign of the Gods, one should not awaken [this knowledge] for another's disciple, for a wicked person, for a slanderer, for one of evil conduct, nor for one intent on harming Śakti. (18.51)
If one gives the auspicious armor of Mātaṅgī to someone who is not very pure, the Yoginīs drink his blood and devour him. (18.152)
Those who behold that supreme object attain all accomplishments;
it is to be guarded, more to be guarded than the unguarded, a great secret more secret than the secret. (18.153)
O auspicious one, this must not be disclosed even at the cost of one's life, even when that life is at the throat;
ten millionfold worship is equal to a single hymn of praise, and ten millionfold recitation of hymns is equal to a single mantra-recitation.
Meditation is equal to ten million recitations; absorption is equal to ten million meditations;
this science is equal to ten million absorptions—it must never be disclosed.
Thus ends the *Sumukhī-kavaca* in the *Guhyakāla-tantra*. Now follows the *Sahasranāma* of Sumukhī:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall now proclaim it before you.
The thousand names are supreme for the successful accomplishment of the mantra.
One who recites the Thousand Names shall be victorious everywhere;
he shall suffer no defeat, whether in an assembly, in the forest, or on the battlefield.
O Goddess, Mistress of the Gods, by reciting this, the goddess Sumukhī becomes so pleased with him that the practitioner becomes Śiva himself. (18.158)
By reciting this once, thousands of horse-sacrifices and tens of millions of Vājapeya sacrifices are produced; she becomes well-pleased and her countenance turns gracious. (18.159)
The deity is Mātaṅga, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the goddess is proclaimed to be Sumukhī;
her application is for the sake of attaining all prosperity. (18.160)
Having meditated thus, one should recite this if one desires one's own welfare;
it shall bestow success in all undertakings. || 18-161 ||
Now, as for the visualization:
the Goddess is sixteen years of age, seated upon a corpse, reeling from the intoxication of honey-wine;
she has a dark-blue body, is most excellent with a reddish glow, and is adorned with broad breasts and rows of beautiful arms.
One should meditate in the mind-lotus upon the Blessed Lady Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī, who holds in her two hands a stainless skull-cup as well as a sharp razor.

Salutations to Śrīsumukhī. Oṃ Sumukhī! She is the intellect to be served; she is Sarasvatī; she is the one who bears the moon upon her crest; she is Samānā; she is Sāmidhenī; she is the one whose face is turned toward all that is to be praised. 18-163.

She who brings about the attainment of all things, who is equal toward all, who dwells in the dust [of the earth], who is the source of splendor, who is the crest-jewel of the world, and who is the essence of the nectar of immortality— worship her for a month.
O essence of the nectar of the Vedas, O excellent one, O wearer of the forest garland;
O lotus-eyed one, O you of excellent conduct, O delighter in the forest. || 18-165 ||
Veginī, Vegadā, Velā, Vagalāsyā, Valādhikā, Kalā, Kālapriyā, Kolī, Komalā, and Kālakāminī. (18.166)
Kamalā, Kamalāsyā, Kamalasyā, Valāvatī, Kulīnī, Kuṭilā, Kāntā, Kaukilā, and Kalabhāvinī. || 18-167 ||
Kīlakerī, Kalā, Kālī, Kapālinī, Kāvikā, Keśinī, Kuśāvantā, Kauśāmbī, and Keśavapriyā. (18-168)
She is Kāśī, the purifier of Kāśī, the radiant one, the one who resembles all, and the bestower of the kosa;
she is Kuṇḍalī, she who dwells in earrings, and she who is adorned with a mace and earrings.

She who causes the night-lotus to bloom, who increases the joy of the white water-lily, who is dear to the sacrificial vessel, who possesses the luster of the *kunda* flower, and who delights the deer with her scent. (18.170)
Her eyes are like those of a deer, her breasts resemble jasmine buds, and her hips are as delightful as rubies; she is slightly slender, with a waist adorned by a girdle of tinkling bells.
Kaṇṭhedā, Karuṇā, Kāṣṭā, Kaumudī, Kaṃvukandapi, Kapardinī, Kapaṭinī, Kaṭhinī, and Kālakaṇṭikā. (18-172)
With parrots in her hands, the maiden is fond of *kuruṇḍaka* flowers;
she stands upon an elephant, possesses the gait of an elephant, and her two breasts are like the frontal lobes of a female elephant.
Kuṃbhigā, Karabhauru, Kadalīdalaśālinī, Kupitā, Koṭarasthā, Kaṅkālī, and Kandaraudarā. (18.174)
Dwelling in the forest of Kaupila, her hair trembling slightly,
Kādambarī stood amidst a cluster of Kadamba trees, bearing the fragrance of saffron.
Kuṭuṃvinī, Kṛpāyuktā, Kratuḥ, Kutukarī, Kriyā, Kātyāyanī, and Kṛbhikā—[these are the names] in the month of Kārttika. (18.176)
She whose voice is the sound of sacrifice, she who has a harsh mouth, she who dwells in sport;
she is the consort of Kāma, the giver of desires, whose nature is desire, and who is saluted by Kāma.
She who takes forms at will, whose course is desire, who desires and is deluded by desire;
she who bears a sword, who moves through the sky, who is lame, who is the shatterer, who is sharp, and whose nature is space.
She who has a harsh gait, a harsh sound, and a harsh face; she who is fond of play;
she whose rays are harsh; she who holds a chalk-stick, a bedstead, and a staff with a skull at its end.
Khalakhaḍa is also known as Khaṇḍitā, Khāṇḍavī, Sthirā, Khaṇḍapriyā, Khaṇḍakādyā, Indukhaṇḍā, and Janī. (18.180)
The Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Gauḍī, and also the Gomatī and Gautamī; Gayā, Guñjā, Gaganagā, Gorūḍī, and Garuḍadhvajā. (18.181)
She is the Song, fond of song, and the singer; she delights in molasses and speaks words of weight.
She is the Cow, Gaurī, whose abode is on the cheek, and who possesses the multitude of cows and cowherds of Gokula.
Godā, she who is established in Govinda, the Unconcealed, she whose form is hidden,
Guñjanī, Gañjagā, Gopī, the Destroyer of Lineages, and Gaḍā.
The daughter of the mountain king, the increaser of the cow-pen of the cows,
the savior from destruction, the one without passion, the one with beautiful forest-thighs, and the one without sound.
She who brings about union, she who moves with a jingling sound, surrounded by ghughukas; she who is fond of the ringing of bells, the bell itself, and she who carries clouds of thundering rain.
Ghorabhūyā, Ghorā, Ghṛtaprīti, Ghanāñjanī, Ghanākṣī, Ghanamuṣṭi, Ghaṭighāṭī, and Ghaṭimṛtā. (18–186)
She who holds a jar in her hand, the fashioner of the jar, the remover of suffering;
she is cleverness, the flickering one, the beautiful, the moving, the clothed, the ever-moving, the ever-moving.
She is the female bee, the female chakora bird, Cāmuṇḍā, and the bearer of the spies;
she is the ancient one with four heads, possessing the brilliance of gold.
She is the wielder of the bow, the fickle one, the prose-poem, the knower, the wish-fulfilling jewel, and the funeral pyre;
she consists of the four social orders, the beak, the thief, the act of stealing, and the cause of wonder. (18.189)
She is the bride of the universal monarch, she who possesses the wheel, she whose limbs are like wheels, she who delights in the wheel;
she who moves within the mind, she who is the activity of thought, and she who bestows the fruit of one's intentions.
Cāmpī, Caṃpakaprīti, Dīnā, Ḍālavāsinī, Virañjī, and Ciñcā, who dwells at the foot of a tree—[these were the goddesses] at that time. (18–191)
The knife (churikā) stands in the midst of the semen (chukra); she is consciousness (cit), the cutter (āchedakā), and the incision (chidā).
She is the hedgehog (chuñchundarī), fond of flesh (palaprīti), the hedgehog (chuchundarī), and she whose sound is "namas. (18–192)
Chalinī, chaladā, chinnā, chiṇṭikā, chuṭaka, as well as chucminī, chābdasī, chīyā, and kṛchardi—thus [they are known]. (18–193)
She is victory (Jayā) and the giver of victory (Jayadā), the lineage (Jāti), the victorious one (Jayinī), and she whose palms are joined in reverence (Jāmalāñjali).
She is fond of the hibiscus flower (Japāpuṣpapriyā), she who is to be meditated upon (Japyā), the life-force of the world (Jagajjīvā), and the progenitor of the world (Jagajjanī). || 18-194 ||
She who is dear to the *jaṃbu* tree, she who is devoted to recitation (*japa*), she who is beloved by both the moving and the unmoving;
she who is the living being (*jantu*), the foremost among beings, and who flows like the waters of the ocean at the end of time.
"Know her to be dear, established in life, and possessing a complexion like a cloud," so sang the female attendants to their mistress, she who wears a garland that crushes living beings.
O Brahman, as long as you are swift, increase your speed; O blazing one, be radiant!
Worship that which consists of wind; do not be one who causes harm through harshness.

She who utters the sound "jiṭī," she who utters the sound "kṛ," she who utters the sound "jaṃ," she who wards off the seatless, she who bears the seal of the letter "ṭa," and she who is the playful dance of the letter "ṭa. (18-198)
From the root *ṭakṛ*, there is indeed *kṛti*; she is born naked and aged.
She is Ḍākinī and Ḍāmarī, O you who rejoice in the midst of the foam of the ocean.
Ukkāpriyā, Svanā, Ukkā, Tapanī, Tāpinī, as well as Taruṇī, Tuṇḍilā, Luṃdā, Tāmasī, and Tamapriyā. (18-200)
Tāmrā, Tāmrāvaśā, Rātālī, Tālī, Tālīdalavibhūṣaṇā, Turaṃgī, Tvaritā, Annetā, Notalā, Todilī, and Tulā. (18.201)
O Tāpannayaharātāla, O Keśītamālinī; O Tamāladalacchāmā, O Tālasthānapanātamī. || 18-202 ||

O Tāriṇī, O you whose splendor is like the scorching sun, those who stand on the banks of this river of heat— whether they be as small as sesame seeds or as vast as mountains— are brought across by you, who possess fierce and even fiercer prowess through both heat and darkness.
Tilontamātī; Tilāntamālilakavuntārakādhīśekharā; Tilapuṣpapriyā; Tārā; Tālakeśī; Kuṭumbinī. (18–204)
The wife of Sthāṇu, the stabilizer, the giver of vessels, the increaser of vessels,
she who is established, she who dwells in what is established, the establisher, and she of massive form.
She who possesses tusks, she who holds a staff, the distressed one, she who is difficult to know, she who is compassionate toward the wretched;
the goddess, the consort of the gods, the pitiable one, she whose restraint is "dam," and she who is adorned with ivory ornaments.
O compassionate one, O self-controlled one, O giver of self-restraint, you whose breasts are like pomegranates; O goddess who resembles a venomous serpent, O destroyer of demons, we bow before you.
The couple, who are embodiments of divinity, are intent on the sport of the swing;
they abide as the wick and the lamp, both destroying defects and causing the cessation of defects. (18–208)

She who pacifies the suffering of difficult paths, she who dwells in the inaccessible fortress, she who destroys the distress of hardships, she who is established in the unassailable, and she who brings an end to evil dreams. || 18-209 ||
Difficult to overcome, she is sounded by the drum; she dwells afar, O you who live in the distance!
She is the giver, the consumer, the one who cries out "Alas!", the compassionate one, the giver, the daughter, and the one who subdues the senses.
She is the bearer of the burden, the leader, the steadfast one, and the bestower of wealth;
she is the wise, the firm, the earth, the giver of righteousness, and the one whose mind is tranquil.
Dhanurdharā, Dadhvanī, Dhūrnā, Dhūrntaparigrahā, Dhūmavarmā, Dhūmapānā, Dhūmalā, and Dhūmamodinī. (18.212)
Nalinī, Nandinī, Nandā, Nādinī, and Nandavālikā;
she who is new in name, in giving, in pride, and in her firm resolve regarding discipline.
The Vedic traditions are stainless through the fires of the rivers;
blue gems are like lotuses; and greed is a succession of qualities devoid of merit.
Blue-necked, licking [the sacrificial offerings], and stainless, she is yours;
she is the beloved woman who has transcended the nine [states] and who causes one to descend from the state of being a child in hell.
O Nārāyaṇī, you are formless, skillful, and the beloved of the skillful; you are the night that destroys the darkness, immeasurable, and yet measured.
She is without pill (nirguḍikā) and free from the defects of the guḍī plant; she is the nose (nāsikā) that destroys the slumber of ignorance.
