She is the essence of the learned (sārāpaṇḍi), formless (nirākārā), and skillful (nipuṇā). She delights in the cooking of the ripened state (pākapāka-kṛtvarata-parāparakatva-priyā).
Abiding in the wind (pavanasthā), she is a beautiful grove (supavanā) that increases the joy of the wind (pavana-sa-prīti-vardhinī).

She who causes the increase of cattle, nourishment, and prosperity; she who increases flowers, the possessor of flowers, she whose hair is like a book, and she who dwells at the foot of the Punnāga tree.
The beloved of Purandara, delight, dwelling on the city path; the fetus, the noose, the one with noose and goad, the destroyer of bonds, the one with fetters, and the beast. 18–219.
She possesses a formidable host, wields the battle-axe, and likewise holds the noose;
she is the destroyer of sin, the wife of her husband, and she subsists upon the consumption of flesh.
She who holds a drinking vessel and a wine-cup, intent on the service of providing drink;
she who is beloved and renowned for her eyes, whose desires are fulfilled and overflowing. (18–221)
She who is both moving and not moving, or repeatedly departing;
she who is muddy and submerged in mud, and she who is beyond the cage of enemies. (18-222)
Pañcamī, Pañcayajñā, Pañcanāpañcamapriyā, Picumandā, Puṇḍarīkā, and Kīpiṅgalalocanā. (18–223)
Priyaṅgu, jarī, piṅgu, jarīpiṇḍī, paṇḍinā, duraprabhā, pretāsana, priyālu, pāṇḍurā, and pīnasā. (18-224)
Phalinī, Phaladāntī, Phanā, Śrīphaṇibhūṣaṇā, Sphutkārakāriṇī, Sphāṭā, Kullā, Kullambujānanī. (18–225)
Phiraṅgaphāsphitamatiḥ, Sphītikīrttikarī, Tathā, Valamāyā, Valārāṇi, Valinī, and Valavardhinī. (18-226)
Vīṇāvādya is she who brings forth the forest-dweller; Vidya is knowledge, the bestower of knowledge, the awakener, and the giver of awakening. (18.227)
Vuhimālā, Vuhā, Vanamālā, Valīvarā, Varadā, Bhaṇī, Vīṇā, and she who is intent upon playing the lute. (18–228)
She who dispels that which is opposed, she who abides in delight, she who belongs to Viṣṇu, she who is dear to Viśva;
she who is the physician, she whose nature is the science of medicine, she who is helpless, and she who pervades the universe.
She is the two sciences (*vidyā*), the shore of the *ṣitkula*, the one who has transcended signs (*vitajñāṣi*), and she whose radiance has subsided (*gatajvalā*).
She is the one without passion (*virā*), the one of manifold forms (*vividhākārā*), she whose lips are like the *bimba* fruit (*bimboṣṭī*), and she who is devoted to the *bimba* (*bimbavatsalā*).
She who possesses the knowledge of the sciences, who is worshipped by heroes, and who is devoted to the drinking of the hero’s draught;
she who is the knower of the Vedas, who is to be known, who is the object of knowledge, and who is devoted to the drinking of the hero’s draught. (18.231)
She is to be known through the Vedānta, she is the object of knowledge, she is devoted to the drinking of heroes, she is the wise one, she is Vijayā, and she bestows victory. || 18-232 ||
O increaser of opposition, O venerable one, O barren one who wards off bondage;
O sister, O garlanded with the *bhaga*, O Bhavānī, O you who exist within the state of worldly existence! 18-233.
Terrible, with a terrifying face, I am crooked and of fearsome appearance;
I am the bearer of smeared food offerings, O Bhīma, the river that overcomes with its fierce roar. (18.234)
She who possesses the vulva, whose forms are the vulva, whose abode is the vulva, whose seat is the vulva, who takes pleasure in the vulva, and who is delighted by the sounds "bharī" and "bhaṃkāra."
The Goddess is indeed terrifying, with a terrifying roar;
she is the ornament [of all], born of Bharadvāja, the giver of enjoyments, and whose ornaments are the serpents that have become her very being.
She is the giver of prosperity, the foremost among givers of land, and the bestower of the status of a sovereign;
she is the female bee, the one who moves like a bee, the formidable one, and she resides upon the crowns of kings.
She is considered the measure of wisdom, the one who takes away pride, the intoxicating one, and the earth;
she is Mahālakṣmī, the one with intoxicating eyes, wine, and the abode of wine. 18-238.
Intoxicated with pride, she dwells on Mount Matanga; she is Mādhavī, the crusher of Madhu;
she is wisdom, the maker of purity, the pure one, the slender one, and she who abides in the middle age.
Madhyayāmā, Malā, Matsyā, Mādinī, Maithunodvatā, Mahāmudrāvatī, Mātrādhvī, and Mahiṣamardinī. (18-240)
Mahāmāyā, Mahāvidyā, Mahāmārī, Maheśvarī;
she who is honored as the consort of Mahādeva, the six-faced one with the orb of Meru.
The fat-bodied one, the abode of splendor, the slayer of Mahiṣāsura;
she who dwells in the maṇḍala, she who dwells in the monastery, and she who is intoxicated with wine.
The giver of liberation, she who wears a garland of severed heads, she who sports with the garland of skulls;
O Mātaṅginī, O Mātaṅgī, I go to that which is the conviction of the Mātaṅgas.
Yamaghni, Yame, and Kanya, who possesses the very form of the sacrificer;
she is the sacrifice, the act of sacrificing, and the sacrificial spirit, as well as the one who brings about fame and the fulfillment of desires.
Yakṣiṇī, mother of the yakṣas, Yaśodā, bearer of glory, giver of the sacrificial thread, the eldest, and likewise the performer of sacrificial rites. || 18-245 ||
The illustrious one, residing in the letter Pa, dwelling in Pūṣan-nambha, she who is colored red, the wife of the king, Ramā-rekhā, and Parī-vaṇā. (18-246)
She is the dust and free from dust; she is thought, the one who colors, and the mistress of the night.
She is the giver of gifts, the radiant one, the queen, the bestower of sovereignty, and the increaser of sovereignty.
O King, she is the forest-dweller, the policy of kings, and likewise the inhabitant of the people;
she is the delightful woman, the most beautiful one, the giver, and the delight beyond Rāma.
She who is satisfied by the essence of joy, who bestows the essence of joy, who performs the yoga of the heart;
she who is the stage, who possesses the stage, who is the stage itself, who knows passion, and who creates passion. (18.249)
Rantika, Rañjikā, Rañjā, Rañjinī, Raktalocanā;
she who wears red skin, Raṃbhī, Raṅgasthā, and Raktavāhinī. || 18-250 ||
Rambhā is fond of the rambha fruit; Rambhorū is your beloved; Raṅga is charming with its movement; Rodasī is the home of the two worlds. 18-251.
She who causes obstruction, she who seizes the warriors, she who possesses the knowledge of forms, she who counts the hosts;
she who is praised by bards, she who is the praise itself, she who is the sixfold, she whose garments are the *dhūr* and *dhūṃka* flowers.

She who is praised like a wreath, she whose names are beautiful, she who is the arrangement of the Vedhas, she who is the speech of the wise, she who is the fruit of speech, she who abides in speech, and she who is affectionate toward speech. || 18-253 ||
Vedi, Vignā, Vilagnā, Vidhi, Vidhikarī, Vidhā, Śaṅkhinī, Śaṅkhavalayā, Śaṅkhamālā, and Vaniśamī. (18–254)

She who destroys Śaṅkhapāda, whose sound is like a conch, who has a conch upon her neck, and who is as white as the moon; she who is the inferior, the consort of Śaṅkara, the female conch, the female Śaṅkuka, and the destroyer of the mass of corpses.
Śaṃvī, Śarāvati, Śyāmā, Śyāmāṅgī, Śyāmalocanā, Śmaśānasthā, Śmaśānā, and Śmaśānasthalabhūṣaṇī. || 18-256 ||
She is the destroyer of both tranquility and pride, the bearer of the conch, and she whose crest is the moon;
she is peace itself, the bestower of peace, the remainder, and the one who withers away all that is parched.
Śṛgiṇī, Śṛṅgīpala, Kuśāṅkurākarī, Śam, Śaṅkāśaṅkāpahā, Saṃsthā, Śāśvatitalā, and Śivā. (18-258)
O you who dwell in corpses, you who are skilled regarding corpses, you whose belly is the corpse of ritual action;
O you who cast curses, you whose crest is the corpse, you who hold the noose of the corpse, you who remove the sin of the curse! (18-259)
She is the Kuṇḍalinī of Śiva, devoted to Śiva, with veins as cool as a spray of water;
she has a girdle of corpses, possesses the splendor of the rainy season, wears a garland of skulls, and has the form of Śivā.
Śavatā, Śaṅkuvasani, Śrīladā, [and] Yini; Sidhu, Sārasvatī, Sidhu, Sundari, and Sundarānanā. (18-261)
Excellent! O Siddhi, giver of success, Siddhāsiddha Sarasvatī; you who bestow progeny as well as prosperity and the granting of boons.

She who possesses the essence of the wives of the gods, she whose essence is Sarasvatī, she who is Svadhā, she who is like a lake, she who is incomparable, she who is to be propitiated, and she who bestows all things.
Samidā, Saṃmadā, Saumyā, Sarmohā, Samadarśanā, Sīmati, Samadā, Sīmā, Sāvitrī, and Savidhāsani. (18-264)
She whose stream is the dwelling place of the *savana* [pressings], who is accompanied by the *sāman* chants,
who is ever-moving, who is to be attained, and who carries away those with long lutes.
Haṃsī, haṃsagati, haṃsaujvalanī, caula, puk, halinī, haladā, hālā, halaśrī, and halavallabha. (18-266)

O playful one, O you who possess playfulness! O neighing, O neighing, O you who increase the standing of the neighing! O slayer, O destruction, O horses! Alas, alas! O you who cause the destruction of those who utter "Hā"! || 18.267 ||
She is the maker of the syllable *haṃ*, the state of being *haṃ*, the one who possesses *haṃ*; she is indeed the one who strikes, the one who destroys, the destroyer;
she is the weapon, the giver of gold, the wearer of necklaces, and she is esteemed by Hārīta.
She is the hour (horā), the Hotṛ priestess, the Holikā, that which is to be offered in the fire (homyā), the oblation (homā), the sacrificial offering (havirhari);
she is the golden-hued one (hariṇī), she whose eyes are like those of a deer (hariṇīnetrā), and she who dwells upon the Himālaya mountains.
Laṃbodarī, Laṃvakarmā, Laṃvikā, Laṃvavigrahā, Līlā, Līlāvati, Lolā, Lalanā, and Lālitārasā.
Lalāmatomala, Nālocyā, Lālākṣī, Lakṣaṇā, Lalā, Laṃpanī, Laṃpatī, Laṃpā, Lopāmudrā, and Lalaṃvinī.
O you who hang from the creeper-like [limbs], you who are suspended; O you who possess lightness, you who are of moderate build;
O you who are most capable, you who have subdued the pride of the small; O you who ward off the spider’s web! || 18.272 ||

The mother of the world, whose every hair is like a blade of grass, she who tosses about, she who shatters with a *lululuṃ* sound, she who stands as the destroyer, the great wave, and she who is the refuge of Indra.
She who destroys the night, she who is the maker of the moon, she who is pungent, she who bestows milk, she who is the ocean of milk;
she who brings security, she who causes decay, she who takes away the breath, and she who grants the moment.
Kṣīraṇī, Kṣudrikā, Kṣudrā, Kṣut, Kṣarā, and Kṣīṇapātakā—(1000)—Umā, Tuḥ; this thousand names of the most excellent one bestows success. 18-275.
Whoever recites this upon rising in the morning shall indeed become Maheśvara;
one who recites it daily after sipping water shall become a giver of wealth, even if he be poor. (18.276)

O Goddess, one who is speechless becomes a lord of speech; one afflicted by disease among those with passion shall attain freedom from disease; and one without a son obtains a son, as declared in the Vedas throughout the three worlds.
Thus, the son born of her shall possess two qualities that are difficult to restrain;
his grain shall multiply manifold, and the cows shall yield milk as hard as adamant.
Kings will clearly bow at his feet like servants; even his enemies, though full of longing, shall go to their destruction. (18.279)
Merely by seeing him, even a base man becomes a hero;
he himself becomes the doer and the taker—of this there is no doubt. (18.280)
Whatever desire she may wish for, she certainly attains it;
there is no misfortune for her, nor is there ever any sorrow. (18.281)
The supreme practitioner who recites this at a crossroads or at night—being solitary, renowned, fearless, and heroic—will reach the end of ten recitations. (18.282)
Whatever task is mentally intended by her will undoubtedly be accomplished; provided that one never recites the mantra without the Thousand Names. (18-283)
Success does not arise for him even through hundreds of mantra rituals;
he should always recite it at midnight, in a cremation ground, or at midday. (18.284)
He becomes a performer of a hundred sacrifices, a doer and a taker of men in this world, if he recites this while seated upon ashes during the night of the affliction of disease. (18.285)
If one should always be fearless, one should recite the mantra at midnight in a cremation ground or on a Saturday. (18.286)
If one recites this Thousand Names ten times during the interval of eight [breaths], then Śivā herself indeed comes there.
If there were no fear at that time when she roars with a terrible jackal-like sound in the form of Mahāmāyā, then the word "dehi" (give) would have been uttered. || 18-288 ||
Then one should offer an animal sacrifice, and Caṇḍikā herself shall accept it;
having granted the desired boon, the auspicious and benevolent Śrī Sumukhī protects [the devotee]. (18.289)
Having first applied *rocanā*, *aguru*, *kaśyūrī*, camphor, *mada*, and sandalwood, one should write [the mantra] upon a birch-bark leaf with saffron. (18.290)
Having performed the propitiatory rites for the wind at an auspicious conjunction of stars,
and having completed the procedure for recitation, hold [it] in your right hand.

One who has conquered the senses, having placed the *Sahasranāma* in a golden vessel as well as the *Kavaca*, should bow to whomever that practitioner intends; that person, even if angry, becomes submissive along with his wife. (18.292)
To whomever one gives this blessing, that person shall become like the Giver of Wealth (Kubera); among all beings, no fear whatsoever shall arise for them in any place. (18-293)
This protection, which brings about the fulfillment of desires, should be heard even by a pregnant woman;
it effects delusion, paralysis, attraction, killing, and expulsion.
Indeed, for the practitioner, a vessel will surely arise from this practice, provided that what is drawn with blue garments remains upon a banner. (18.295)
Then even a fierce enemy army will be destroyed;
if one should wear this great consecrated ash upon the forehead. (18.296)
When even the servants of that living being become subject to his very sight, as if they were the wives of a king, what need is there to mention other women of the city? (18.297)
By reciting this hymn for one month, one becomes a great poet, a scholar, and a great debater; of this there is no doubt. (18-298)
One should recite the hymn ten thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa);
one should offer oblations with ten thousand lotuses soaked in honey.
Then Lakṣmī herself comes to his abode along with Sarasvatī;
the fair-faced woman attains mastery over mantras and becomes [one who is] well-disposed.
Infinite merit shall arise and demerit shall go to destruction;
whatever fruit may come from bathing at sacred fords such as Puṣkara, [that shall be attained]. (18.301)
A living being obtains that fruit by reciting the hymn to Sumukha.
O fair-faced one, this, my very essence, has been told to you as a secret. (18.302)
O Goddess, this must not be revealed by you if you wish to attain perfection;
through its disclosure, perfection would be lost, and O fair-faced one, she would become enraged.
There is no other hymn in this world that bestows spiritual accomplishment upon living beings as this one;
therefore, with every effort, this supreme hymn must be kept secret.

Oṃ, I pay homage to the illustrious Sumukhī, whose mind is serene, whose face is like the orb of the full moon, whose head is marked with vermilion, who is swaying with intoxication, who wears a string of pearls, and who,
with her lotus-like hands darkened by *śyāmāka* grain and collyrium, is teaching [the scriptures].

Adorned with clusters of parrots and guñjā berries; her braided hair is like a creeper releasing parrot-like fruits. Thus ends the *Sahasranāma* of Sumukhī, the bestower of swift results, within the *Umāmaheśvara-saṃvāda* of the *Śrī-Nandikeśvara-Uttara-khaṇḍa*.
Now, the hymn to Sumukhī.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess; I shall proclaim this hymn, O Mātaṅginī, which is dear [to you].
Having recited this, the practitioner who then recites it upon the ground becomes like Bhairava.
Of this *Śrīsumukhī-pañcāṅga-stotra*, Mataṅga is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*),

Śrīsumukhī is the deity (*devatā*), Ai is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Klī is the power (*śakti*), and Klī is the pin (*kīlaka*). It is employed (*viniyoga*) for recitation and chanting for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation (*dharma-artha-kāma-mokṣa*).
Now, as for meditation:

[one should visualize] a beautiful sixteen-year-old girl lying upon a corpse, intoxicated by honey-wine, her limbs rolling and trembling, ruddy in complexion, and adorned with the beauty of distinct rows of fingers and toes.
I meditate upon you, Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī, who holds in her two hands a stainless skull-cup, a seed-syllable, and a small knife, and who rests upon the lotus of the Mother.

He who recites this seed-mantra, the crest-jewel of all mantras, which is beloved by Vāgbhava-taśiva and meditated upon as the sole ocean of nectar, at the time of twilight or at midnight, shall himself possess the eight supernatural powers of Śiva. (2) 18-307
And one should recite the mantra of Kāmarāja ten million times in a temple;
by that, Urvaśī, who is subject to desire and possesses a face like the moon, shall become submissive to him. (18.308)
O Śivā, he who is tormented by a host of enemies should recite the Uchiṣṭacaṇḍālī Mantra-king;
he shall conquer all his adversaries and attain nourishment, sovereignty, and the splendor of a kingdom, as proclaimed by the circle of kings. (4) 18-309.

O Śivā, O Sovereign of Poets, that name which has entered the midst of the mind during recitation—though the fool calls it "itkāmalā," it is the supreme nectar, the night of the moon in the sky of consciousness; recite it quickly!
O Mahāpiśācinī, recite this name within your heart.
Brahmā and the other gods are subject to his command and remain under his control. (6) || 18-311 ||

One should mutter the seed-syllable of Māyā (*cāṃ*) while meditating on the mantra; for one who is afflicted by desire, Rambhā, adorned with flowers, will eternally appear before him in a form like that of the celestial nymphs of heaven. O Goddess, he who mutters this lotus-born seed-syllable, which is dear to the Blessed One, [attains such a state].

Having crushed [the enemy] on the battlefield, he protects the earth and becomes a king; and at midnight, one who is diligent should mutter the mantra ending with *mantrāntayā*—which is like fire—at the center of the Meru-wheel, O Mother, progenitor of all beings, and he goes to heaven. (18) || 18-8 ||
With the sprouts of their side-glances, they looked upon those to be converted; they were gazed upon by the Lord of the Thirty-three as he ascended to heaven, and honored by Smara. (9) || 18-314 ||

One should meditate upon Piśācinī in the heart, seated upon a corpse, resembling the rising sun, possessing three eyes and two arms, intent on drinking wine, supreme and most transcendent, and situated within the Śrīcakra. (10) 18-315 ||
If a practitioner recites this meritorious hymn to Manu on earth,
he shall obtain jewels and be freed from all sins; having long enjoyed pleasures here on earth together with his sons and grandsons, he subsequently goes to heaven and attains liberation.
Sasarvamure svāra. (11) || 18-316 ||

Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, this hymn consisting of the *manus*, which is the primary, supreme essence, and which has become five-limbed, should be protected as a secret by those who guard the limbs of liberation. (18-317)

Thus, in the case of the goddess Śrī Sumukhī, this [teaching], which is difficult for even the five-limbed deities to obtain, must not be disclosed; it is to be given [only to the worthy] and kept secret like one's own womb. (18-318)
Thus ends the hymn to Sumukhī, which constitutes one of the five ancillaries, in the *Śrī-Bhadrayāmala*, the *Guhyakālī-tantra*.
The Goddess said:
"O Goddess, I shall proclaim the hymn to Sumukhī, which bestows an auspicious face immediately."
For those men to whom he gives, all forms of prosperity arise. (2) || 18-319 ||
Śrī Śiva said:
The goddess Sumukhī is nectar, free from the fear of being left over; she is ever smiling-faced, and by her grace, she brings about the inexhaustible birth of devotion. (3) 18-320.
She who is dear to Śiva, whose form is auspicious, who bestows love upon Śiva;
she who wears a necklace of *guñjā* berries, and whose radiance is equal to ten million suns. (4) 18-321.
Her beautiful left hand is adorned with a blue lotus; she wears a necklace of *guñjā* berries and embodies the form of supreme bliss. (5) 18-322
The Goddess, whose very nature is constant laughter, possesses a form of exquisite beauty;
she is eternally known by the name of her devotees, and her teeth are most delightful to contemplate. (18.323)
Always remaining in a state of not eating, always intent on the *manthāra* [practice], with eyes constantly speaking, and always uttering words of intoxication. (18.324)

She whose dwelling is fashioned by the syllables *krī*, *kāra*, and *kṛt*, who has made her abode within the fire and the *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), I praise that fair-faced Goddess, the three-eyed one, who is the embodiment of the Vedas and is worshipped by the gods. (8) 18-325.
O Pārvatī, it is the truth, the absolute truth: for those who, being self-restrained, recite this *Iṣṭakam*, their supreme calamities shall certainly perish.
Whether they recite it once or twice a day, for them there is accomplishment at every step. (9) 18-326.
Thus ends the *Sumukhy-aṣṭaka* in the *Bhadrīyamala*.
The Śrī Devī said:
"I bow to the twenty [verses]; speak, O Sumukhī, you who bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*)."
By which, in a short time, all prosperity is produced, O Kāleya.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, I bow to the twenty-syllable [mantra], the king of hymns that is captivating to the mind.
Out of affection for you, I shall now proclaim it, which has not been revealed by me before. (18-328)

She is fair-faced, beautiful, delightful, and she destroys the pride of the enemies of the gods; she who leads one’s own recitation is the best among those devoted to liberation in the southern quarter. (18.329)
She bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; she is playful in playing the lute;
she possesses beautiful limbs; she is short; she is the left-handed goddess; she is expert in discerning the paths of the Vedas.
If one who possesses the discipline of discernment studies this king of hymns frequented by the complete [assembly], for that woman with playful eyes, accomplishment is never-failing. (5) 18-331
Prosperity increases, worshipful and bestowing supreme bliss; this *Hāra* should be recited at midnight by one who has consumed the remnants of food (*ucchiṣṭa*). (6) 18-332.
O lady of excellent limbs, by your command alone, one shall very soon become the lord of the wealth of Śrī and the Jina through the service of Śaṅkara. (18.333)
May there be another hymn equal to this, so that for one who chants it, no evil arises that resembles sin. (8) 18-334 ||
Thus ends the *Sumukhī-stavarāja* from the glorious *Bhadrayāmala*.
Now, the mantra of Mañjughoṣa:
[I praise] the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, who is seated comfortably upon the summit of Mount Meru.
Pārvatī questioned Śaṅkara, the Supreme Goddess.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, regarding Mañjughoṣa—who bestows desired objects in this world according to all the scriptures, Agamas, and so forth—you speak of him to me. (18.336)
Śrī Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the great mantra that brings happiness to practitioners;
by knowing it, one of dull intellect generally becomes equal to Vācaspati.

The mantra bestows success through recitation when accompanied by the placement of limbs (aṅganyāsa), the placement of the hands (karanyāsa), and the external placement (vahirnyāsa); it is not accomplished merely by worship and other such rites. (18.338)

Whether one recites it oneself or causes another to recite it according to the prescribed ritual for the practitioner, one attains omniscience; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Pārvatī. (18.339)
One should mutter that mantra as far as the face of Kārttikeya;
by this, one becomes equal to Vācaspati in all the śāstras.
The seer is named Vṛhadāraṇyaka; the meter is known as Virāṭ; the deity is called Mañjughoṣā, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (18-341)

One should mutter that which bestows immediate success, pertaining to Viṣṇu and characterized by the quality of goodness (sāttvika); that which bestows immediate success and is declared to be characterized by the quality of darkness (tāmasa) is likewise [to be muttered]. (18.342)
He states the mantra for its retention: "The six-syllable mantra, *viṣṇugni-pāsi-śaśi-yuk-kudhī*, is proclaimed for the worlds;
it bestows omniscience upon one devoted to the knowledge of Vedānta, and, being ever-auspicious, it grants wealth. (18.343)
The letter *a* is Viṣṇu, the letter *r* is Agni, the letter *va* is Pāśī, and the letter *śa* is Śāśīśa.
"Dhī" is your essential form (*svarūpa*), while "aravaśvadhi" is the mantra.
If the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is a master of mantras, he should recite this first mantra.
Having partaken of the *naivedya* of Vali, like another Bṛhaspati in person, a man should perform the *puraścaryā* for three months;
from his mouth, O woman of excellent complexion, eloquent speech shall flow forth. (18.344)
Within three months, one becomes a poet of a hundred [verses], of this there is no doubt;
[this applies when using] cow-dung, the back of a cow, a leaf, or even cow-mash.
Having first written the mantra upon the yantra, one should write the mantra again afterwards;
having first performed the meditation alone, the wise person should contemplate it for a long time.
Having reached a deserted place, one should mutter the mantra while facing downwards;
having reached the full moon day, [one should offer] flowers and thorns into the sacrificial pit.
Having worshipped with eight offerings, one should recite the mantra at a crossroads;
having performed the mounting of three skulls, one should remain at night with hair disheveled.
If a practitioner of mantra who knows the ritual procedure recites [this] for just six months, he becomes a speaker equal to Bṛhaspati; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (18.349)
The single-headed [form] of the dog, the single-headed of the jackal, and the three-headed of the bull—this is renowned as that which brings happiness to practitioners. (18.350)
One should perform the worship after placing the seat upon a cow’s skull, a *kukku* skull on the left, and a jackal’s skull on the right. || 18-351 ||
Behind it, one should clearly draw a half-moon shape on the left;
there, one should write the mantra and perform worship with *kuda* flowers.
With his left lotus-hand performing worship to Jayā and the others, and with his right hand adorned with the practice of erotic grace (śṛṅgāra),
one should meditate upon him who is white like the moonbeams of autumn,
standing atop a bull on the bank of a crossroads; having visualized him seated upon the head of a dog, the most excellent practitioner [should worship] with jasmine.
He recites aloud:
"The maṇḍala, fashioned to the size of a cow-hide and consisting of a single liquid-corner, is not even [drawn] with saffron or yellow pigment."

Having fashioned [the image] according to the ritual procedure by means of a *vīra*, and having worshipped it in the cremation ground— [him] whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals and red as blood— 18.353.

Having carefully taken only refined oil with his sprout-like hands in the house of the Arishta plant, and having offered that which was prepared with it as a golden flower to him, he recites the mantra aloud. (18.354)
Having smeared one's feet with the root of the *aśoka* plant at its base, and having moistened the face with nectar,
one should remain standing for only the duration of three *muḍas* during the night on the full moon day and recite [the mantra] according to one's ability. Furthermore,
in the middle of a *lakuca* tree, having meditated upon [the deity] as white as the rays of the moon while standing for the duration of a single *muḍa* at midnight.
If one recites it one hundred thousand times, then within three fortnights, the Self becomes manifest in this world; there is no doubt about this. (18-355)

Seated upon a seat fashioned from three skulls beneath a cluster of flowers from the *āmra*, *kadalī*, and *taru* trees, he performs worship to the Lord, just as the Moon at its fullness pays homage to the Lord of Mountains. His own head acts as the sacrificial vessel for the offering.
Having extended his tongue and worshipped it with hundreds of flower-arrows from the lotuses of his own hands,
Goyī should mutter the *rasa-lakṣa* mantra daily; if he mutters this for the Lord (*Īśa*), how much more so for the Lord of Speech (*Akupati*) who possesses but a single face?
The speech was recited: "He who, standing at the time of nightfall upon the bank of the Rajani river, equipped with a sword, conquers the full moon of the Kanyā month—
or even the entire month— by force, that minister shall emerge from his mouth like a lotus freed from its stain."
Even for one who has performed the practice of holding a tooth-stick made of *karañja* wood, the word of Gīṣpati (Bṛhaspati) is certainly obtainable from that [practice].
(297b) With sesame oil, *maṇiśā*, and the flowers of the white water-lily (*kudakairava*), the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with effort; he shall attain all accomplishments. (18-358)

Having applied a *tilaka* on the surface of the forehead with *mañjiṣṭhā*, *nāga*, *suvarcalā*, *sitabhānu*, *puṣpa*, *siṃhāṅga*, blood, and *kuṇṭhaka*, one who stands engaged in recitation (*japa*) shall become like Bṛhaspati through the mastery of the science of debate.
[Furthermore,] that which is known as *māraṇāla* is white; *vādha* is *citraka*; and *kuṣṭha* is well-known as *kudu*.
He speaks of the subsequent mantra:
"Listen, O Goddess, to the great mantra consisting of seven syllables and six syllables; by reciting it even once, O Goddess, one becomes a wise man who is liberated. (18.360)
Joined with the sun-bindu (ra-vindu), it becomes the fire of night conjoined with peace (śānti).
The letter kṣa is earth and fire; the bindu is extracted as peace (śānti). || 18-361 ||
This seven-syllable mantra is declared to be the deliverer of practitioners;
by its recitation, a practitioner becomes like another Vācaspati.
I bow to the one who possesses the most excellent luster of a very young child, who resembles a dark blue cloud, who holds a skull-cup joined with two full-blown lotuses,
whose face is brightened by a smile, who wears five topknots, who has three eyes, who is capable of burning away evil intellect, and who possesses a beautiful voice.
I pay homage. || 18-363 ||
The practitioner should form the limbs (aṅgas) with the seed-syllables possessing long vowels:

*ma* is the sun (*ravi*), *ru* is the end of the *ja*-group (*jānta*), *la* is the end of the *ra*-group (*rānta*), *ī* is peace (*śānti*), and *la* is the earth (*pṛthivī*). [The mantras are: *maṃ*, *ru*, *laṃ*, *rī*, *kṣa*, *la*, *rīm*.

Thus, the mantra consists of seven syllables: *maṃḍularīkṣalarī*. According to another source, there is a mantra consisting of six syllables. Likewise: "O Goddess, having meditated in this manner, one should recite [the mantra] with concentration for one hundred thousand times."
And one should offer as a fire-oblation a tenth part of that [number] with mustard seeds mixed with salt.
The seer is Kaṇva, the sovereign rishi; the meter and the deity are known as Vaṭuka.
O Lord, one should worship the goddess Vāgīśā daily according to the instructions of the Mothers. (18.365)
298a) Having first worshipped the limbs, one should afterwards worship these Śaktis:
Yoga, Satyā, Vimalā, Jñānā, Buddhi, and again Smṛti. (18.366)
Meditation and wisdom are within the efforts; the mudrā holds a book.
The world-protectors are worshipped outside, and their weapons are outside of them. (18.367)
Having drunk that consecrated water, one should recite the mantra a thousand times every day;
within a month, the practitioner will undoubtedly become a great poet. (18.368)
One should practice despicable conduct, eat with the left arm, and every day smear one's limbs with the oil remaining from a lamp. (18.369)
One should perform the ritual of offering at night with only a garment; every night,
one should present him with an oblation of food that has been eaten, while meditating upon the heart-mantra, the throat-mantra,
and the *japa*.
He becomes a king worthy of honor, an object of love for women, a leader among poets, and a scholar. || 18-370 ||
One should always perform that worship and recitation in the proper place at once;
one who seeks poetry shall produce poetry, and one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth. (18.371)
O Mārdaṇa, he shall bring forth a poetic composition that expands for men, and after a long time, he becomes an expounder of all the Vedas, Āgamas, and other scriptures. (18.372)

The presence of the Lord of the Mind, who bestows the sovereignty of knowledge along with all his bones, arises through faith in the realization of reality; thus, perfection is attained both in this world and in the next. (18.373)
O Goddess of gods, for one devoid of faith, there is no success even in hundreds of lifetimes,
whether in the recitation, the fire-oblation, or the libation of these very vidyās.
Whatever has been composed according to one's own will should be understood through awakening;
whatever is realized within the heart of the knowledge of reality [should be taught]. (18.375)
One should understand this very reality as it was proclaimed by the venerable Kīrti.
Thus ends the Mañjughoṣa-prakaraṇa in the Śrī-Bhairava-tantra.
Now, the Varadagaṇapati-pañcāra is being written.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. To Mahādeva, seated comfortably on the peak of Mount Meru, the three-eyed one... [18.376]
It was joined by hosts of gods and asuras, and honored by Brahmā and Acyuta,
as well as by Siddhas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Bhūtas, and Piśācas.
He saw Śiva, who was pleased by prostrations and hymns along with Pārvatī,
smiling as he conversed with Brahmā and Hari.
Pārvatī, having bowed down, spoke these words:
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all truths, illuminator of all dharmas! (18.379)
"O Lord, by what means do obstacles arise for the work of the gods and likewise for human beings? O Śaṅkara, please dispel my doubt. (18.380)
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, this great answer to your question is a secret;
it must not be spoken to those who are not devotees, for it is the means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Great Goddess, he who is the Lord known as Vināyaka and Gaṇeśa is renowned as the creator of obstacles for the world, yet as its protector and the remover of obstacles. (18.382)
O Goddess of gods, O Maheśvarī, no obstacle ever afflicts that mortal devotee who always worships him. (18.383)
O Goddess, one should apply that mantra and wear its armor;
one should recite the Thousand Names, for the hymn is the sole means of accomplishment. (18.384)
"Neither obstacles shall afflict him, nor shall there be any failure in his undertakings.
The Goddess said: "O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Lord of the world, [tell me] concerning Gaṇeśa! (18.385)
O Supreme Lord, because of your greatness, I desire from you the mantra, the yantra, the hymn, the armor, and the supreme thousand names, as well as the means for worship. (18.386)
Bhairava said:
He who is the God of gods, the bestower of boons, Gaṇeśa, the leader of obstacles, elephant-faced, the presiding lord of the Gaṇas, is known as Vināyaka. (18.387)
I shall describe its entire five-limbed ritual for your pleasure;
therein, O Maheśvarī, I shall first explain to you the extraction of the mantra.
In this [tantra], Mahāgaṇapati Śiva is the source of extraction and the limb of dissolution.
Now follows the extraction of the mantra:
Tāra (Oṃ), Māsa (Ma), Kalā (La), Smara (Ra), Maṭha (Ma), Śiva (Śa), and the two words "Vare" (Vare) and "Saryaḥ" (Saryaḥ).
From this, the syllable *jīmutaśarma* is like a layer of rice;
*bhekī*, *kham*, *lavaṇam*, and *samīrahasitam* are the mantra. With two *ṭha*s at the end, this Vaināyaka mantra is declared to consist of twenty-eight syllables. (18-389)
Thus, the root mantra consisting of one hundred thousand recitations is proclaimed as the preliminary rite (puraścaryā);
one should perform the recitation at a banyan tree, a crossroads, a deserted house, or a cemetery.
For him there is no obstacle, nor grief, nor the failure of mantras; there is no affliction, nor evil intellect, nor delusion, nor sorrow. (18.391)
O Śivā, this mantra of Mahāgaṇapati is established as all-pervading; I shall now describe the extraction of its yantra, which fulfills all desires. (18.392)
O Maheśī, this Śrīcakra of Gaṇeśa, the Lord of the World, which deludes all, is proclaimed as follows:
it consists of a triangle joined with the letter Kha (the void), a ten-spoked wheel, and likewise a well-rounded eight-petaled lotus;
it is perfectly circular and endowed with four gates—this is the celebrated Śrīcakra of Gaṇeśa previously described.
Now I shall proclaim the meditation that bestows all accomplishments, by the mere remembrance of which all obstacles flee away. (18.394)
Holding in his arms the rising sun, a vessel resembling the moon, a water-pot adorned with a crown of jewels, a bowl filled with sweetmeats, a golden jar, a lotus, and a rosary of lotus seeds;
possessing a radiant body born from a pure serpent and shining with serpents.
One should meditate upon Gaṇapati, the wish-fulfilling gem of the three worlds, seated in the lion-yoke posture (siṃhayugāsana).

Thus ends the section on meditation. O Parameśvarī, I shall now describe the limb of absorption (layāṅga), which is the worship of the Yantra; it has been concealed in all the Tantras, O Śarajanman (Kārttikeya). (18.396)
Indra, Dharmeśa, Varuṇa, and likewise Kuvera,
are to be worshipped in the east and west, as well as in the south and north.
Nandivīreśa, Saubhāgya, Bhrṅgirīṭi, Virāṭakā, Puṣpadanta, Vikārttāntapa, Cittalohita, and Sundara. (18.398)
O beautiful one, the sixteen Gaṇas— fierce in their deliberation regarding the sound of anklets and dancers to the sleeping kings— are to be worshipped in the sixteen spokes.
Karāla, Vikarāla, Saṃhāra, Ruru, Bhairava, Mahākāla, Kālāgni, Sitāsya, and Asitānana. (18.400)
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the eight Bhairavas upon the eight petals:
Vināyaka, Vighnarāja, Gaṇādhyakṣa, and Gajānana.
One should worship Heramba, whose food is sweetmeats, who has two mothers, who tames the river,
who has a single tusk, and whose face is like a trunk, amidst the Śāras.
O beautiful goddess, one should worship Kumāra, Jayanta, and Pradyumna within the triangle, and the Lord Mahāgaṇapati at the bindu.
And likewise Gaṇeśa, O son of Gaṅgā; thereafter, the lion-throne, a vessel marked with sweetmeats (modaka), and similarly the axe and the spear.
One should worship the conch at the *bindu*; by this, the forehead-mark (*tilaka*) is perfected.
The seer (*ṛṣi*) of this mantra of Gaṇeśa is proclaimed to be Brahmā. (18.405)
The Gāyatrī metre is said to be its meter, and the deity is remembered as Gaṇapati;
the seed-syllable (bīja) is that of Śiva, while Māyā is declared to be its power (śakti). (18.406)
The two *kurus* should be black; all this is the sole means for the mantra.
O Goddess, its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed as being for the conquest of the three worlds. (18.407)
And having offered oblations into the fire of a funeral pyre at the root of a banyan tree, one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times;
thus one may paralyze all the worlds, as well as the forces of disputants and thieves.
One should recite the root mantra ten thousand times and offer oblations of ghee from a young sprout;
thus one may delude the Supreme Lord and destroy the circle of enemies.
By means of the river, the practitioner shall quickly conquer by performing ten thousand oblations;
if he offers the flesh of an elephant, he will certainly cause the enemy to be eradicated. (18.410)
At home, one should recite this according to this rite ten thousand times;
O Girijā, there is no doubt that even Brahmā can be incited to enmity thereby.
Having offered oblations in a forest with *vidura* and having recited the root mantra ten thousand times,
one can bring even a king under control and attract women.
Thus, this secret chapter belongs to the Great Lord of the Gaṇas, Śiva; therein lies the entirety of everything, which must be guarded with special care. (18.413)
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Method for Extracting Mantras" from the Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra.
Now, O Śivā, I shall describe the ritual manual (paddhati) of the Great Gaṇapati,
which is the singular essence of all prose and a single wave of bliss.

The practitioner, having risen at the end of the night, assuming the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*), and having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) three times with the root mantra, should meditate upon his own guru— adorned in white ornaments— seated within the pericarp of a great thousand-petaled lotus in his own head. Having taken leave of him and come outside, he should perform a bath for the removal of impurities.
Having drawn a triangle there with the root mantra and the goad mudrā, [one should say]:
"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in this water! (18.415)

Thus, having invoked the sacred ford (tīrtha) and having invoked the Lord together with Śiva at the root [of the mantra], one should not invoke [them] again at the root. One should sprinkle [the water] three times for the sake of happiness.

Having recited the mantra over the water three times—*hrīḥ haṃsaḥ śrīsūryāya eṣa te'rghyo namaḥ*—and having offered these three *arghya* offerings, one should descend from the water and perform the twilight worship (*sandhyā*).
Or, having taken the *nalā* [stalk] in the hand, or having covered it with the armor (*varman*),

one should consecrate it seven times with the root mantra. Then, having sprinkled it with drops of water from that movement, or having led it inside, one should expel it through the left nostril, hold it in the right hand via the *suṣumnā*, and [place it] on the left with the mantra "phaṭ."
Having sat upon the serpent, one should expand [the breath] while reciting the *aghamaṛṣaṇa* mantra. Then, one should perform three *prāṇāyāmas*:
inhalation (*pūraka*) for sixteen [counts], retention (*kuṃbhaka*) for thirty-two, and exhalation (*recaka*) for sixty-four. Having performed this, one should mutter the *gāyatrī*.
"Oṃ hrīḥ, we meditate upon the one with the elephant face; śrīḥ klīḥ, we meditate upon the one with the single tusk; glauḥ gaḥ, may that Gaṇapati inspire us.
Having thus recited this as much as possible, and having offered three *arghya* oblations to the two deities with the *goyatrī*, [one should offer] the whole [oblation] with the root mantra.

I offer libations and salutations to Mahāgaṇapati, the leader of the Gaṇas, who removes obstacles from the worlds, the son of Hara, who is praised by the Gaṇas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and bards, whose face is manifest and formidable, and who possesses both supreme and inferior forms; to the elephant-faced one, I bow.

Having thus satisfied [the deities] three times and dismissed the two deities there with the *sahara-mudrā*, one should return to the sacrificial pavilion; such is the ritual for the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vidhi*). This concludes the section on the sacrificial pavilion.
Hrāḥ Śrī Klī Ga Gaṅgāyai namaḥ in the east (3); Yaṃ Yamunāyai namaḥ in the north (3); Saṃ Sarasvatyai namaḥ in the south (3).
"Obeisance to the Yoginīs in the west" (3). "Obeisance to Kṣetrapāla. Having thus worshipped the deities of the door in the center, one should enter inside the house and purify the seat.

For the mantra of the purification of the seat (*āsana-śuddhi*): Meruṣṭa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sutala is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Kurma is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is with the seat-mantra. *Aiṃ*, obeisance to Earth; *Eṃ*, obeisance to Ananta.
Vaṃ, obeisance to Vasudharā.
O Earth, by you the worlds are supported; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
Therefore, support me as well, O Goddess, and make this seat pure. (18.416)
Oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ klīḥ, homage to the Lotus Seat (3). Homage to the Lion Throne. Homage to the Auspicious Seat. Thus: May those spirits depart who are spirits dwelling upon the earth.
May those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva. || 18-417 ||
Having thus performed three claps of the hands (*tāla*) and displayed the *nārāca* mudrā, one should meditate upon the Guru:
"Salutation to that illustrious Guru by whom this [universe] was shown, which is of the nature of an unbroken circle and by whom the moving and the unmoving are pervaded. (18.418)
Having thus meditated upon the Guru, one should sip water:
*gauḥ*. "I purify the principle of the Self, svāhā! I purify the principle of knowledge, svāhā!
I purify the principle of Śiva, svāhā! I purify the principle of Śiva’s power, svāhā!"

Having thus performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should sprinkle the aforementioned vital breaths (prāṇas) with "Oṃ Klīṃ. Having brought the presiding deity there and contemplated one's own body as having been reduced to ashes, one should contemplate the *brahma* syllables Yaṃ, Raṃ, Laṃ, Vaṃ, and then the inner individual soul (jīvātman). There, by means of the mantra "Haṃsa," one should bring down the nectar and flood [the body] with it.
Having visualized the body as free from impurity, one should bring forth the life-force (*jīva*) residing therein and establish the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). This is *bhūtaśuddhi*.
ĀḤ HRĪḤ KROḤ YA RA LA VA ŚA ṢA SA HA SO HA SAḤ: [My] vital breaths (16).

"O my life-force, stay here! O all my senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and breath—come here indeed and remain happily for a long time, Svāhā! Thus is the ritual for the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
Then, having sipped water (ācamana) once more and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) preceded by the preliminary rites:
"Of this Śrī Varada Gaṇeśa mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda),
the illustrious Gaṇapati is the deity (devatā), *gaṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *hrīṃ* is the power (śakti), *kuru kuru* is the pin (kīlaka), [and] the illustrious Mahāgaṇa..."
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of [attaining] joy. 301b) *Namaḥ* to the Brahman-seer (*brahmarṣi*) on the head; *namaḥ* to the Gāyatrī metre (*chandas*) on the mouth;
*namaḥ* to the deity Mahāgaṇapati on the heart; *namaḥ* to the seed-syllable *gaṃ* at the navel.
*Hrīṃ*, salutation to Śakti at the secret place (*guhya*). *Kuru kuru*, salutation to Kīla at the feet.
Salutation to the application (*viniyoga*) for the purpose of attaining the three goals (*trivargasiddhi*) during recitation (*japa*), at all limbs.
*Gā*, salutation to the heart (*hṛdaya*). *Gī*, *svāhā* to the head (*śiras*). *Gu*, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

*Gai* kavacāya *huṃ*. *Gau* netrebhyo *vauṣaṭ*. *Gaḥ* astrāya *phaṭ*. Thus is the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart and other limbs. Now, the hand placements (*karanyāsa*): *Gā* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; *gī* to the two index fingers, *namaḥ*.
*Grū* to the two middle fingers, *namaḥ*; *gai* to the two ring fingers, *namaḥ*;
*gau* to the two little fingers, *namaḥ*; *ga* to the palms and backs of the hands, *namaḥ*. Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*).
The principle of the Self (ātmatattva) is for the heart: *namaḥ*. The principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) is for the head: *svāhā*.

The principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is for the crest-lock: *vaṣaṭ*. The principle of the Guru (gurutattva) is for the armor: *hum*. The principle of Yoga (yogatattva) is for the eyes: *vauṣaṭ*. The principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is for the weapon: *phaṭ*.
Thus is the *aṅganyāsa*. Thus is the *karanyāsa*. Thus is the *tattvanyāsa*:
*aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ ā* (and *a*)—*namaḥ* to both thumbs;
*iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ*—*namaḥ* to both index fingers.
uṃ ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ū—salutation to the two middle fingers (madhyamā).
e ta tha da dha na ai—salutation to the two ring fingers (anāmikā). o pa pha ba bha ma o—salutation to the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhā).
Aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ (ḥ). Aḥ, homage to both palms and backs of the hands. Thus is the heart-assignment (*hṛdayanyāsa*).
Gaṃ, obeisance to the seat of Kāśī; at the heart. Gaṃ, obeisance to the seat of Kāñcīpurī; on the head.
Gaṃ, obeisance to the seat of Madhupurī; on the crest-lock.
Gaṃ, obeisance to the Uḍḍiyāna-pīṭha; [assign] to the armor (kavaca).
Gaṃ, obeisance to the Ayodhyā-pīṭha; [assign] to the eyes (netra). Gaṃ, obeisance to the Jālandhara-pīṭha; [assign] to the weapon (astra).
Thus ends the Pīṭhanyāsa.
Oṃ, salutation to the heart. Śrī Mahāgati, svāhā to the head.
Kāṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock that grants the best of boons. Klīṃ, huṃ to the armor for all people.
*Glau*, I bring [them] under my control from the eyes—six times. *Gaṃ svāhā*, *phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*).
Thus is the ritual placement of the hands (*kara-nyāsa*).
Having performed the ritual placement in this manner and having visualized the Śrīcakra, [one visualizes] the square and the sixteen-petaled [lotus].

Having visualized an eight-petaled lotus, a ten-spoked wheel, a triangle, and a bindu, and having established [the deity] upon the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) with the root mantra, one should perform the worship of the yoga-seat (yogapīṭha):
"Hrīṃ, salutation to Maṇḍūka; salutation to Kālāgnirudra."
Salutation to the Primordial Nature (Mūlaprakṛti). Salutation to the Supportive Power (Ādhāraśakti).
Salutation to the Tortoise (Kūrma). Salutation to Ananta. Salutation to Varāha.
Salutation to the Earth (Pṛthivī). Having worshipped [these] one above the other, [one should worship] in their midst the Ocean of Nectar (Sudhārṇava).
Salutation to the island consisting of nine sections, adorned with jewels and made of gold.
Therein, to the eight sections beginning with the northeast, salutation to the nine jewel-sections in clockwise order. In the center of this, salutation to the ruby section.
In the center, obeisance to Suvarṇaparvata; in the center, obeisance to Nandanodyāna; in the center, obeisance to Valāvalāvana; in the center, obeisance to Nandanodghāna;
in the center, obeisance to Sarovara; in the center, obeisance to Padmavana.
Homage to the center, whose ground is inlaid with various jewels.
Homage to the pavilion of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*) inlaid with various jewels, measuring fifty-four *yojanas* in extent, possessing a thousand pillars but lacking a central pillar.
In the center, [one should offer] salutation to the jeweled altar-platform (*vedikā*) inlaid with nine gems;
salutation to the jeweled lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) above; salutation to the lofty white parasol (*chatra*) above;
and, according to the recitation, salutation to Dharma and the others in the southeast corner and the other directions.
Salutation to Adharma and the others in the previously conceived directions [East, etc.]. In the center:
Salutation to the Root of Bliss (Ānandakanda), the trunk of consciousness. Salutation to the one whose seat is the thousand-petaled lotus.
Salutation to the stamens consisting of Prakṛti. Salutation to the petals consisting of Vikṛti.
Salutation to the pericarp (karṇikā), which is enriched with the fifty seed-syllables of the letters and is the embodiment of all principles (tattvas).
Above: Aṃ, salutation to the solar disc (arkamaṇḍala); Saṃ, salutation to the lunar disc (somamaṇḍala);
Raṃ, salutation to the fiery disc (agnimaṇḍala); Taṃ, salutation to darkness (tamas); Raṃ, salutation to passion (rajas).
Saṃ satvāya namaḥ hrīḥ gaḥ hrīḥ | Homage to the seat of all mantras!
Having uttered "Oṃ am ityādi kṣātaṃ," [one says]: Homage to Śiva-Śakti, Sadāśiva, Mahāgaṇapati, and the Self of All; homage to Saṃ satvāya!
Having thus performed the worship of the Yoga-pīṭha, one should establish the vessels.
Having drawn a yantra consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square on one's left side,
and having displayed the conch-mudrā while worshipping with the six-limbed mantras beginning with "Oṃ Gāṃ" and ending with "Astrāya Phaṭ," [one should proceed].
Having washed the pedestal with the root mantra and established it, [one says]: "Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala consisting of ten kalās.
Then: "Obeisance to the seat for the vessel of Mahāgaṇapati."
Having thus worshipped with perfumes and unbroken rice grains (akṣata),
and having placed a vessel upon that, [one says]:
"Salutation to the solar disc, whose self consists of twelve kalās."
"Salutation to Mahāgaṇapati, the vessel for the destruction of sins.
Having thus honored him with perfumes and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should then invoke the Ganges from the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) using the *kuśa* mudrā.
Having worshipped it with the root mantra and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) eight times, one should cover it with the *matsya* mudrā, saying "phaṭ."
Having struck with finger-snaps (*choṭikā*) and being stirred up, having veiled [the deity] and consecrated [the offering] as nectar,
having displayed the mudrās of the Yoni, Conch, Discus, and Mace, and having remembered the sacrificial vessel,
one should sprinkle [it] with that root supreme nectar in the form of Mahāgaṇapati, Caṇḍala, and Nivāsa, and with the nectar of the moon at evening.
"Fill, fill the vessel; fill, fill! Make me immortal, kuru kuru au hau ju saḥ svāhā!
With this, one should sprinkle everything.
Then, having placed the vessels for the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) to the north of that, and having worshipped oneself—
Having meditated upon [the deity] as being composed of that [essence], one should worship with:
"Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One; homage to the infinite Self, who is endowed with the power of all qualities and is the essence of the Yoga-seat.
Having thus worshipped, one should invoke the Lord together with His Śakti by means of the root mantra, and display the nine mudrās using the root mantra.

Having performed the six root-limbs (*mūla-ṣaḍaṅga*), having established the vital breaths (*prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā*) and uttered "Welcome," one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and the guest-offering (*arghya*) with the root mantra.
Having thus performed the rites of water for the feet, the guest-offering, the respectful reception (*ācamanīya*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the bath, and so forth,
one should worship with the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet and present incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so on, followed by three handfuls of flowers.
Having given [the offering]:
*oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ indrāya namaḥ* in the east;
*vahaṇāya namaḥ* in the west.
"Salutation to Dharmarāja" in the south;
"Salutation to Kuvera" in the north.
Having thus worshipped with scents, unbroken rice grains, and *dūrvā* grass.
The first enclosure:
Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra, one should worship sixteen times in a clockwise direction:
Oṃ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, obeisance to Mandin; obeisance to Vīreśa (three times); obeisance to Saubhāgya.
Salutation to Bhṛṅgirīṭa (3). Salutation to Viṇṭhaka (3). Salutation to Puṣpadanta.
Salutation to Vikartana (3). Salutation to Ambhya Gaṇeśa. Salutation to Cintaraṇa (3).
Salutation to Lohita (3). Salutation to Sundara (3). Salutation to Nūpurāḍhya (3).
Salutation to Vicāra; salutation to Ugrahaya (3); salutation to Supta (3);
salutation to Vinartaka (3).
Having thus worshipped with perfumes and unbroken rice grains, [this is] the second section (3).
Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra:
*oṃ śrī hrī karālāya namaḥ* (3), *vikarālāya namaḥ*, *saṃhārāya namaḥ*, *ru ru bhairavāya namaḥ* (3), *mahākālāya namaḥ* (3), *kālāgnaye namaḥ* (3).
Salutation to Sitātman. Salutation to Ahitātman.
Thus is the third enclosure (3). Oṃ Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, salutation to Vināyaka (2). Salutation to Vighnarāja.
Salutation to the Lord of the Gaṇas. Salutation to the Elephant-faced One.
(3) Salutation to Heraṃbha. Salutation to the devourer of delusion. (3) Salutation to the son of two mothers. (3) Salutation to the subduer of enemies.
"Salutation to Ekadanta" (3). "Salutation to Vakratuṇḍa.

Having thus worshipped with perfumes, unbroken rice, and dūrvā grass, the fourth enclosure is completed by circling clockwise to the right. Then, having offered a handful of flowers at the ten spokes with the root mantra—
Oṃ śrī hrīḥ, obeisance to Kumāra (3). Obeisance to Jayanta at the front (3).
Obeisance to Pradyumna on the right. Having thus worshipped the triangle with scents, unbroken rice, and dūrvā grass, this is the fifth enclosure (5).
304a) Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra and having recited the root vidyā:
"Hrīḥ! Obeisance to Gaṇapati accompanied by Svarākrisa.
Thus, having worshipped him seven times, this is the sixth enclosure (ṣaṣṭhāvaraṇa).
Having offered a handful of flowers with the root mantra:
*Gāṅgeyāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the Son of Gaṅgā). *Mūlasihāsanāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the Root Lion-Throne).
*Mūlaṃ vighnāntakāya namaḥ* (Root: Salutation to the Destroyer of Obstacles). *Mūlaḥ ākhuvāhanāya namaḥ* (Root: Salutation to Him whose vehicle is the rat). *Mūla*.

*Tripuratnakāya namaḥ*. Thus, having worshipped the seventh enclosure with incense, unbroken rice, and *dūrvā* grass above, and having offered a handful of flowers, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times above, ending with *namaḥ*.
Salutations to the garland of teeth. Salutations to the jar of nectar. Salutations to the axe. (1) Salutations to the conch. Salutations to Pañcajanya.
By the mere sight of the conch, what need is there to mention its touch? All sins go to their dissolution.

"Himavān, Āditya, Udaya"— having thus worshipped in seven ways, this is the eighth enclosure (8). Then, having recited the root mantra, [one should offer] perfumes, unbroken rice, dūrvā grass, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and water for rinsing the mouth.
Having set aside the betel-leaf, the umbrella, and the fly-whisks before the deity, having performed the six-limbed preliminary placement (*ṣaḍaṅga-pūrva-nyāsa*),
and having meditated upon the deity to be worshipped, one should worship the rosary with the root mantra according to one's capacity; then,
having performed the preliminary placement (*pūrva-nyāsa*) and meditated upon the deity, one should worship the rosary with the root mantra.
Reciting the root mantra according to one's ability,

then having uttered the root mantra and offered the *yajanīya* (the sacrificial portion), one should perform the recitation of the armor (*kavaca*) and the hymn of a thousand names (*sahasranāmastava*) before the deity.
From morning onwards, whatever I do—whether it be going out or returning in the morning—let that, O Lord of the World, be an act of worship unto you. (18.419)

Thus, with the *saṃhāramudrā*, one should dismiss the Lord together with His Śakti. Thus, O Goddess, one should by all means guard this divine manual of the daily worship of Mahāgaṇapati, which is composed in prose form.
Thus ends the Śrī Gaṇapati Paddhati in the Rudrayāmala Tantra.
The venerable Bhairava said: O Great Goddess, [I shall now describe] the procedure for the high-souled Gaṇeśa, the bestower of boons.
I shall now proclaim for you the armor known as the Vajrapañjara.
Of this *Śrī Mahāgaṇapati Vajrapañjara Kavaca*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śrī Bhairava, the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Gāyatrī,

the deity (*devatā*) is Śrī Mahāgaṇapati, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *gaṃ*, the power (*śakti*) is *hrīṃ*, and the peg (*kīlaka*) is *kuru*. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining the perfection of the Vajra-vidyā and other goals in the recitation of the *Mahāgaṇapati Vajrapañjara Kavaca*.
Oṃ Śrī Hrīṃ Gaṃ! May the Lord Mahāgaṇapati protect my head;
may Vināyaka, the King of Obstacles, protect my forehead and my cheeks. (18.421)
When the leader of the Gaṇas was about to depart, he did not perceive the nose of the cloud-born one;
however, Heraṃba [perceived] only the praise, while Gaṇeśa ate the modakas.
May the subduer of enemies protect my two motherly faces; may he guard my lower lip;
may he protect my teeth, O one with a single tusk; and may he protect my tongue, O one with a curved trunk. 18.423
May Gāṅgeya protect the feet; may Siṃhāsana protect the shoulders;
may Vighnāntaka protect the thighs; and may Mūṣakavāhana protect the hands.
May the God who scorched the three cities protect my chest forever;
may Kumāra be my heart, and may he be at both my sides as I recite [his name].
May Pradyumna protect my back; may the son of Śaṅkara protect my navel; may the host of Kaṭinandin protect my hips; and may Vīreśvara protect my penis.
May Saubhāgya protect my penis; Tṛṅgirīṭī, my private parts;
Vināyaka, my thighs; and Puṣpadantaka, my knees. (18.427)
May Vikartana protect my calves; may the other Gaṇas protect my ankles. May the Cittagaṇa protect my feet, and may Lohita protect the soles of my feet.
May Sundara protect my feet; may Anupūrva protect my ankles;
and may Gaṇeśa always protect that place which has been forgotten. (18.429)
May Hrīṃkarā protect me in the east; may Vikarālaka protect me in the southeast;
may Skanda protect my shoulders in the south; and may Ruru Bhairava protect me in the southwest. (18.430)
In the north, [the wheel] has six spokes; in the northeast, it consists of blackness;
at dawn, it should have a hundred spokes, while in the center, it has a thousand spokes. (18.431)
May the tooth-garland and the others protect you; may the vessel protect you always at night;
may the jar protect me at midnight, and likewise the axe at the end of the night.

May the pair of conchs protect my life everywhere and at all times! Oṃ / Auḥ / In the royal court, when there is fear from the friction of weapons, Hrīḥ / Hrīḥ / may they protect those engaged in gambling!
Śrīḥ / Śrīḥ / In the house of Indra (the palace), Śaśau / when there is danger from water, Klīḥ / Klīḥ / may they attend to the forest!
Glau! Gaṃ glai! In times of fear for one's life, in great diseases and afflictions, glau! Ga gāṃ! Constantly [recite this] against yakṣas, piśācas, bhūtas, and phaṇis! Glau! Ga Gaṇeśo va tu!
This secret armor (kavaca), hidden in all tantras, [is thus concluded]. || 18-433 ||
This [tantra] named Vajrapañjara is a constituent part of that great-souled Gaṇeśa; it is composed by Maya and is the sole means for accomplishing all conduct. (18.434)
Without this, there can be no accomplishment of worship or victory;
therefore, one should always recite or wear this meritorious armor (kavaca).
O Great Goddess, its accomplishment is worldly and within one's grasp;
whatever desire one longs for, that very thing one obtains through recitation. (18.436)
One who recites this daily at midnight shall obtain all desired fruits.
Thus, O Supreme Goddess, even for the Lord of Great Gaṇas, this *Mūrdhaṃsu-kavaca*, which consists of all perfections and is worthy of worship, must be kept secret. (18.437)
Thus ends the *Gaṇeśakavaca* within the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, concerning the Great Gaṇapati.
Now follows the *Sahasranāma* of Gaṇeśa.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to my secret which has been proclaimed by me;
out of devotion to you, I shall declare this thousand names of Gaṇeśa.
The illustrious Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, my heart yearns to hear the thousand names of the great-souled Gaṇanātha, the bestower of boons. (18.439)
Bhairava said:
O Śivā, at the time of the destruction of Tripura, hosts of obstacles arose;
deluded by ignorance, they all became arrogant with power. (18-440)
Having then praised the Lord, the Chief of the Gaṇas, with thousands of names, today, through devotion to you and for the benefit of practitioners, [I shall do so]. (18.441)
For this hymn of a thousand names (*sahasranāmastotra*) of the illustrious Varadagaṇeśa, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śrī Bhairava, the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī,
the deity (*devatā*) is the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati, *gaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *kuru kuru* is the pin (*kīlaka*).
Its application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation for the sake of attaining the three aims of human life (*trivarga*).
Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau gaṃ: Gaṇādhyakṣa, Gaṇapati, Guṇa, Guṇāḍhya, Guṇin, Goptṛ, Gajavaktra, Vibhāvasu. || 18-442 ||
Viśveśvarī, Vibhā, Dīptā, Dīpanī, Ūrdhvā, Vā, Rodhanī, Sadīśāntā, Jagattrātā, Viśvaksena, and Vibhākara. (18.443)
He is trust, victory, the physician, the unsurpassed ocean of waters;
he is more subtle than the subtle, the most excellent of riches, the eldest, the song, the beloved, and the teacher. (18.444)
The womb of creation, the sustainer of the world, the supporter of the universe, the lord of the world;
the husband, the yellow-clad one, whose limbs are adorned, with red eyes and a crimson sacrificial thread.
Virūpākṣa, dwelling in his celestial palace, is disciplined, well-guided, and happy;
he is true to his own nature, virtuous, truthful, pure, and the delight of Śaṅkara.
Lord of rivers, great joy, praised by bards, wise,
crusher of the Daityas, ever-intoxicated, with eyes red as wine.
The self of Māra, the sustainer of the universe, the creator of the universe, the ointment;
the supreme Brahman, the supreme light, the witness, the three-eyed one, the divider. (18.448)
Vīreśvara, slayer of heroes, increaser of good fortune and enjoyment;
Bhṛṅgirīṭī, wearer of the garland of bees, resounded by the humming of bees.
The transformer, the disciplined one, the joy of Vinatā, he is upon that funeral pyre; the son of Vinatā, whose limbs are free from clothing, the leader of the leaders of the universe. (18.450)
Virāṭaka, Virāṭa, Vipādha, Vidhi, Ātmabhū, Puṣpadanta, Puṣpahārin, and Puṣpamālyavibhūṣaṇa.
Among flowers he is the churner; he is asked about the cutter, the hand that wields the knife;
he is the approaching destroyer, the one who steals away wealth, the multitude of virtues, the mind, and possessions.
Inconceivable and yet having a conceivable form, he is the circle agitated by pain;
he is red, he is smeared, he is effaced, he has red eyes, and he is the one who entices.
Lubdhaśaya was devoted to greed; his body was overcome by greed.
Sundara had a son named Sundarīputra, who was a destroyer of all the gods. || 18-454 ||
Nūpurādya bestows prosperity; Naranārāyaṇa is the Sun; Vicāra is the fire that vomits forth speech; and Vijayeśvara is the one who moves with discernment. || 18-455 ||
He is asleep, he is awakened, he possesses the form of a woman, he is the giver of happiness, and he is served by those who seek bliss;
he is the cutter away, he moves through the sky, he is the sound, and he is the dancer and the leader of dancers.
The actor, the lover of drama, the sound, the joy, the infinite, the essence of qualities, the creator of the universe, the destroyer of the universe, the one whose mouth is Vinatā, and the dancer.
Karāla, Kāmada, Kāmada, Kānta, Kamanīya, Kalādhara, Kāruṇyarūpa, Kuṭila, Kulacārī, and Kuleśvara. (18.458)
The destroyer of transformations, the foremost in battle, the annihilator whose ornament is a necklace;
he who is the fire of time in his intoxicated form, with fire, sun, and moon as his eyes.

White-faced, wearing white garlands, with white teeth and possessing the radiance of the white moon; he whose soul is seated in tranquility, the Bhairava, the possessor of good fortune, the Blessed One, Bhaga.

The son of Bharga, the one whose abode is fortune, the giver of enjoyments, the increaser of worldly existence, the maker of auspiciousness, the pure, the peaceful, the most excellent, the one worthy of being heard, and the lord of Śacī. 18-461.
He is the beginning of the Vedas and the author of the Vedas; he is the eternal physician of the Vedas.
He is the bestower of knowledge, the essence of the Vedas, the follower of the Vedas, and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
The hero is devoted to the sound of the Vedas and has mastered the meaning of the Vedas and Agamas;
he is the knower of reality, all-pervading, virtuous, the embodiment of both the existent and the non-existent, and the manifest form.
He is the source free from disease, formless, fearless, and yet assuming various forms;
he is without enmity, the destroyer of all enemies, and resembles a rutting elephant.
The bringer of auspiciousness, the son of Śiva, the increaser of the bliss of Śivā;
he who is cool, whose face rests upon Śvetā, the charming one, whose food is sweetmeats.
The god of gods, the maker of day, the possessor of fortitude, the radiant Mādhava;
he whose self is pure, whose intellect is pure, and whose splendor is pure, observing the vow of purity. || 18.466 ||
Śaraṇyaśaunaka, Śūla, Śarada, Bhojadāraka, Dāraka, Śiśu, Atyugra, and Śitaśaṅkarapūjita. || 18-467 ||

Śaṅkara is fearless, yet he is subject to control; he is the creator of fear and intent upon the dance (lāsya). He is the one who revels in the play of the Lūtolī, delighting in aesthetic flavor (rasa), and he is the delusion that is the playful grace of Śiva.
Bhramaṇa, Śaśibhū, Sūrya, Śani, Dharasmin, Ānandana, Vadha, Vivudhasevya, Budharāja, and Dhara. (18-469)

The living soul, the giver of life, the victorious, the one worthy of praise, the one worthy of hymns, the beloved of prostrations, the progenitor, the one whose fame is unsurpassed, the knower of the path, and the establisher of the Jaina path. || 18-470 ||
The son of Gaurī, the teacher, the voiceless one, the fair-limbed, the one worshipped by elephants;
the supreme, the beyond-supreme, the destroyer of the supreme, the Supreme Self, the poet, the son of the Earth. (18.471)

Rāhu, the seizer of the head of the Daitya; Ketu, adorned with golden earrings; the lord of the planets; the one who causes others to be seized; the possessor of qualities; and the one resounding with a gurgling roar. (18.472)

Parjanya is the nourisher, Potrin is the one with a full chest, and Parājita is the unconquered; Vanecara is the lord of the forest, while I am a dweller in the woods, and Smara is the supreme. (18.473)
Meritorious, pure, the god who pierces, the supreme self, the one whose form is complete;
he whose appearance is like the full moon, the conqueror of Māra, whose desires are fulfilled. || 18-474 ||
The worthy soul, the bearer of yoga, the sacrificer, the performer of sacrifices,
the lover of sacrifice, the illustrious one, the beloved of those who offer oblations, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the cage of the thunderbolt.
Maṇibhadra is composed of jewels and is to be honored; he rests upon the fish-bannered one.
The fish-bannered one is captivating, a knower of yoga, and an increaser of yoga.
The Seer, the Creator, the Ascetic, the Embodied One, the Lover of Ascetics;
composed of those two, the Form of Penance, the Sun, and He whose Wealth is Austerity.
Rūcaka, Mocaka, Bhrasta, Tuṣṭa, Tomaraghātaka, Daṇḍijaṅgha, Suravyakta, Kamaṇḍaludhara, and Nagha. || 18-478 ||
Delighting in the acts of desire, he causes the quarters to cry out with his play of time;
he is the one who causes wandering, honored by the people, the destroyer of dullness, and the slayer of the inert.
Jāladhara, Jagadhrāsī, Hāsya, Kṛt, Dhavala, Hari, Haviṣmān, he who is called Havyavāha, Hāṭaka, and Hāṭakāṅgada.
Sumeru, Himavān, Hotṛ, Haraputra, Halaṃkaṣa, Hālāpriya, Hṛdistha, Kāntā, and Hṛdayapoṣaṇa. || 18-481 ||

The one who withers, the destroyer of afflictions, the fierce one, whose actions are harsh and rigid; the sovereign, the embodiment of wisdom, the one to be meditated upon, the meditator, the wise one, and the ordainer of compassion. (18.482)
The most distant one, practiced in passion, the giver, the protector, equal to Śiva;
he has emerged from the conduct of the merchants, a person without people, with matted hair. (18.483)
Like a mother, he has conquered his enemies; he pervades the world and consists of the world itself;
he is the primordial one, surpassing even refined gold, with eyes like lotuses. (18.484)
He is the illuminator, the liberator, the mantra, and the one who rests upon ten million mantras;
he consists of the five elements, possesses five arrows, and has five faces.
The fifth has disheveled hair at the back and front, is a cripple with a crooked arm, has a heart devoid of hair, a decorated neck, and a graceful disposition.
Fickle-minded, with a large nose, possessing months, fortnights, seasons, and the earth;
he is stable, of stable gait, righteous, a follower of dharma, a lover of sound, yet he is not [truly] beloved. (18.487)
He who swallowed the world with Agastya, the sole remover of the world's impurity,
the ocean, the one with beautiful eyes, the blissful, and the one praised by the virtuous.
The husband of Satī, he who is of equal flavor (samarasa), Sanaka, the straightforward one,
the divine being, the beloved of the gods, the lord of wealth, Vāsava, and the one honored by the Vasus.
The extensive one, the lord of wealth, the bestower of riches upon the wealthy;
he whose eyes are like rows of lotuses, the giver of memory, and the speaker of the Kṛttikās.
The horse-headed one belongs to the Aśvins; Śubhra is dear to Bharaṇī;
Kola has Kṛttikā as his seat; Rohiṇa is the one who ascends by means of Rohiṇī. || 18-491 ||
Vibhaveṣṭa, Īrimardī, Rohiṇī, Mohana, Amṛta, Mṛgarāja, Mṛgaśirā, Mādhava, and Madhuradhvani. (18.492)

He whose hands are moist, who possesses great wisdom, who is of vast intellect, and who is adorned by great serpents; he whose power consists of the casting down of the earth and the fangs, and who is the formidable Punarvasu of the earth. || 18-493 ||
Tittiri, Stimiketu, Timitārakaghātaka,
Tiṣya, Tulādhara, and Jeya— these sixteen are the kings of the gods in the Vaikuṇṭha realm.
Mānada, Mādhava, Māgha, Vācāla, Macava, and Mata; Māgha, Maghāpriya, Mogha, Mahāmuṇḍa, and Mahābhuja. || 18-495 ||
Pūrvaphalgunika, Sphīta, Phalgu, Uttaraphalguṇa, Pheṇila, Brahmada, Brahmā, and Saptantanusamāśraya. (18.496)
Ghoṇahasta has four hands, the face of an elephant, and a plow as his weapon; he wears variegated garments, his feet are honored, and he bestows auspiciousness—such is the form of Svāti. (18.497)
Śikhākhaśikhise is the brother of Dhvaja;
Aṇureṇu is the son of Kaṇasphāra, and Rurureṇu is the son of Anara. (18.498)
Anurādhā, Priya, Rādha, the illustrious Śrīmān, Uśukra, Śucismita, Śucipūrva, Ṣāḍha, and likewise Uttarāṣāḍha. (18-499)
Śravaṇa, Śrotādhana, Dhanya, Dhaniṣṭhaka, Śātātapa, Śātakaumbha, Śatijyotis, and Śatabhiṣaj. (18–500)
Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Revatī have been assigned; Rāma’s son Reṇuka [is under] Revatī, and Ramano-raka [is under] Revatī. (18-501)
The king’s own physician, Tāraka by name and star-like in appearance, was renowned, exalted, pervasive, transcendent, and supremely beneficial. (18.502)
The supreme one is the five elements and the fivefold wind; he is the highest, worthy of worship.
He is the knower of the Purāṇas and Āgamas, the buffalo-headed, the donkey-faced, and the fierce one. (18.503)
Graha is Aries; Vṛṣa is Maṇḍa; Manmatha is honored as Gemini;
Kalkabhū is Cancer; Dīna is Monkey; and Karkaṭāghṛṇī is [Cancer]. (18.504)
He is the jungle-born cock, the swan, the supreme swan, and the jackal;
he is the lion, the lion-throned, the ornament, and the one whose vehicle is the mouse that steals away delusion.
The son is the savior from hell; the daughter is the one who brings joy and upholds the lineage.
The bearer of the scales (Dharma) is the bestower of incomparable boons, having the scales themselves as his witness.
Wearing a garland of lotuses, with knees covered in hair like that of a crocodile, a maker of water-pots, a beggar, hunchbacked, and well-satiated with the flesh of fish. (18.507)
The Lord of the World, consisting of the zodiacal signs, stars, and planets, and abounding in lunar days, is majestic, ever-active, beloved, second [to none], and certain in his non-duality. (18.508)
He who possesses the three forms, the third eye, the triple body, the beloved of the fourth [state], the god who has reached the further shore, the fifth [element] free from fear;
the one who tastes the six flavors, the wise one, the lover of the sixty-six [deities];
the essence of the movement through the seven oceans, the lord of the seventh [note], the Sovereign Lord. (18.509)
The eighth is Nandanānanta; the ninth is worshipped with devotion;
the tenth is honored by the lords of the ten directions and is considered the slayer of enemies.
The eleventh is that of the Gaṇas, and the twelfth is thus described;
it is equal to the thirteenth mantra, O beloved of the fourteenth vowel.
The fourth is equal to Indra, his body complete on the full moon;
he is the new moon, the vision, the forest-dweller, and the lord of sages.
He is the silent one, the sweet-spoken, the root, the embodied one, the one whose vehicle is the cloud,
the great elephant, the conqueror of anger, and the refuge for those who have conquered Indra through recitation.
The Fierce One, beloved by Rudra, who causes distress to the great sons of Rukma;
he who is dear to Bhava, desired by Bhavānī, the bearer of the burden, whose vehicle is the spirits (bhūta). || 18.514 ||
Skilled in the arts of the Gandharvas, Vaikuṇṭha, served by Vṛtuhā, the destroyer of obstacles, the one whose chest laughs at impediments,
the remover of all misfortunes,
Mañjara, intoxicated by cats, the son of Durgā, and Durālasa.
He is of infinite knowledge, the essence of nectar, and the sole bestower of the heroic power of heroes. || 18-515 ||
His crown-jewels resounded continuously, his network of small bells tinkled,
he possessed a trunk, was restless, wore earrings, and bore a garland of severed heads.
He has lotus seeds and a lotus in his hand, and is worshipped by those named Padma;
he is celebrated as being rich with human teeth and adorned with garlands as ornaments. (18.517)
Nārada has ears that dangle down to his shoulders, while Śūnyakarṇaka has empty ears;
Vṛhadullāsana has ears that extend beyond and pervade the entire circle of the three worlds.
Delighting in the essence of the joy of fierce battle, they were bewildered within the circle of the *iḍā*;
with their massive hands they held the serpent Śeṣa, and they had conquered the Dānavas in combat. (18.519)

His face was like shimmering vermilion; his eyes were like flickering flames of fire. He resounded with the fierce roar of flashing jewels, and he scattered a multitude of water droplets from the flowing river waters.
His lotus-like feet were worshipped by throngs of wandering elephants. || 18-521 ||
Brahmā, Acyuta, and Mahārudra preceded him as he was worshipped by the gods;
he was attended by a multitude of serpents, beginning with Ananta and Śeṣa. || 18.522 ||
