Roaring with the sound of its mouth, it reached the sky, the earth, and the fire;
with cries of "Hā hā! Hū hū! it caused the minds of all to be bewildered by its most terrible voice.
His body was consecrated by mantras enriched with the seed-syllables of the fifty letters,
and he drenched the surface of the earth with streams of the nectar of the Vedānta scriptures.
He has pervaded the entire expanse of the sky down to the netherworld with his roar;
he is the great wrestler Cintāmaṇi, holding a spear in his hand, and is beloved by Bali.

He who causes the three worlds to shine, manifesting the Kṛta and Tretā ages; he who is the Dvāpara age, acting as the moon for the nectar that dispels the darkness of the sole duty regarding the world beyond.
His body is smeared with nectar, pervading the shell of the universe and all that it contains;
he blazes with the rows of letters from the syllable 'A' to the syllable 'Kṣa'.
The mine of mines resounds with loud, resonant cries;
at the syllable *ī*, he is intent on the rotation of the garland of mantras beginning with *kara*. (18.528)
He whose form consists of the syllables *u* and *o*, who has a fierce serpent as his sacred thread,
and who is radiant with two lotuses marked by the syllable *jhṛ* and adorned with the vowel *ṛ*.
He whose two lips are like conch shells, filling the quarters of space;
he who is expert in drinking from the breasts of Girijā, which resemble the syllables *e* and *ai*.
Exhausted by the process of creation beginning with the universal *oṃ* and *oṃkāra*,
he pervaded the entire circle from the feet to the head with the series of vowels starting with *aṃ*.
His body was cleansed by the extremely fierce wind blowing from the shape of his ear-tubes;
his feet were reddened by the crest-jewels on the heads of the lords of the demons who had been struck down by his sword. (18.532)
His ears are intent upon the songs of all the proud gandharvas; he is worshipped by the gods who move before Ghanavāhana and Vāgīśa. || 18-533 ||
Adorned with a single tusk shining with a stream of nectar flowing from his tusk, his divine body is smeared with moonlight, saffron, and flames. (18.534)
Adorned with a parasol, chowries, and jewels, his face was embellished by a crown;
he shone with a bound mass of matted hair, resplendent with a row of highly precious gems.
Resounding with the humming songs and music of swarms of bees,
he brandished a mallet filled with the blood of the Daityas, which had been fashioned from the letter *ña* and brought about their destruction.

She who is shaken by the fruit of the ṭaṃkāruka tree, she who destroys the remainder of all suffering, she whose beginning is the letter ṭha and whose end is the letter ṅa, and she who is satisfied by the bliss of the letter ḍha. (18.537)
O Lord who bears the stream of nectar marked by the nine syllables, whose splendor upon the surface of Your forehead is enriched by the worship of vermilion and copper-red pigment. 18.538
Even though he was born from the lineage of Thakāra Dhanapākya, that twice-born one was devoted to his vows;
with a heart-lotus full of compassion, he had shaken off the circle of worldly existence.
His lotus feet are served by great yakṣas such as Dhanada;
he is adorned by the jewels in the crowns of all the gods who bow before him.
He is supremely skilled at piercing the vital points of the worldly realms and liberation;
his throat-region is adorned by the encircling coil of a serpent.
O you who are most profound and fierce with your ever-increasing majesty, you who have terrified both gods and asuras;
O sole moon that increases the joy of Bhavānī’s heart! 18-542.
His single, formidable lotus-hand was filled with a jar of wine,
and likewise, he had prepared his weapons against the multitude of obstacles to knowledge.
O beloved of the daughter of the ocean-treasure, O increaser of splendor and fame!
O Laṃbodara, you who have made the bodies of the gods appear small, you are most formidable.
He whose worship is performed by Varuṇa and the other lords of the directions, who is beloved solely by Śakra, O Bhauma, and who increases the joy of the eyes. 18-545.
Skilled in singing songs to the rhythm of the sixteen *śvarita* beats,
he is the fierce fire that dries up the rivers of all miserable rebirths.
He is the reciter of the *Harivaṃśa*, the *Brahmavaikuṇṭha*, the *Brahmagītā*, and other such texts;
he is filled with forgiveness like a lotus, and he protects all things moving and unmoving.
Your body is marked by the seed-syllable mantra *tārāṭ*, and your form blazes with light;
you are adorned with ornaments consisting of the knowledge-mantras from the letter *a* to the end of *kṣa*.
Oṃ Śrī Vināyaka Au Hrī! Vighnādhyakṣa, Gaṇādhipa, Heraṃba, Modakāhāra, Vakratuṇḍa, and Vidhi are remembered [as his names]. (18.549)
The six-syllabled mantra is sung in the Vedānta for the seeker of knowledge;
it is the perfected mantra of Gaṇeśa, the boon-bestowing god, for the practitioner of the twelve-syllabled mantra.
The one consecrated by seven crores of great mantras, the remainder of whose body is adorned with ornaments;
he who is the lord of the Gaṇas, the one honored by the assembly, the auspicious one born of two mothers. || 18-551 ||
Oṃ śrī hrī klī glau gaṃ—the Lord Mahāgaṇapati. This thousand-fold recitation is known as the Mahāgaṇapati-sahasranāma. || 18-552 ||
It is secret, most secret, and worthy of being guarded, concealed within all tantras;
it is the divine treasury of all mantras, the destroyer of all obstacles. (18.553)

This Brahman, consisting of planets and stars, the collection of zodiac signs and the succession of phonemes, is free from all obstacles; it is the means of accomplishment (sādhana) beloved by the practitioner.
And this entire secret of Gaṇeśa, which belongs to the dwellers of heaven, bestows desired fruits in the world and fulfills the chariot of one's wishes. (18.555)

Consisting of the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*), it bestows the desired goal upon practitioners, even without worship, without fire-offerings (*homa*), without ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and without sacrificial oblations (*bali*). (18.556)

The practitioner of mantras should recite at a crossroads at midnight during the fourth watch for the attainment of the eight siddhis, beginning with *aṇiman*, through the mere power of mindfulness. (18.557)
O Great Goddess, one should write this meritorious *Nāsāhasraka* on birch bark;
on the fourteenth day, at midday, one should wear it upon the head or on the arm.
One may even paralyze Brahmā, delude Śaṅkara, bring the three worlds under one's control, and slay even a powerful enemy. (18.559)
By reciting [this mantra], one may uproot the necks of enemies, pacify [calamities], and increase wealth;
a barren woman shall quickly obtain a son, and a poor man shall attain riches. (18.560)
O Śivā, he who recites this three times at night before Gaṇeśa, accompanied by a naked Śakti, O Goddess, shall enjoy all desired pleasures. (18.561)
One should behold Gaṇeśa, the bestower of boons, as if he were visibly present, O supreme bestower of boons;
he who recites this daily a thousand times, preceded by the enjoyment [of food], [attains his desires]. (18.562)
Likewise, for one who desires wealth, high status, prosperity, and so forth,
or who faces danger from battle, kings, or gambling, one should recite the *Sahasranāma* (Thousand Names) of Mahāgaṇapati; it is to be kept secret and hidden like one's own private parts.
Thus ends the *Mahāgaṇapati-nāmasahasra*, complete with the *Tvarāja* [mantra], from the glorious *Bhadrayāmala-tantra*.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, O All-pervading Mahāgaṇapati!"
Speak, O Lord of Great Kings, according to the reality of the root mantra.
Bhairava said:
O Mahāgaṇapati, I shall proclaim before the Lord this hymn which defines the ultimate reality and swiftly bestows liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
Of this hymn to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati, Śrī Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas),

the illustrious Gaṇapati is the deity (devatā), *gaṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *hrīṃ* is the power (śakti), and *kuru kuru* is the peg (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of attaining liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) through the recitation of this hymn.

One should meditate upon Gaṇeśa in one's heart—the Lord of the Gods, whose limbs are adorned with two, four, and fourteen colors; who has eyes like the full moon, the sun, and fire; whose neck is adorned with serpents; and who is rotating a rosary at his heart. (18.566)
O Lord, for that supreme practitioner who constantly sings the *tāra* (*oṃ*) at the beginning of the night, at dawn, at the mouth of night,
or in an empty temple during the festival of Śiva, may the lotus-face of Your memory appear daily, radiant with the ladle of beauty.
And all the lords of the quarters, as well as all the kings on earth and in heaven, become submissive;
when one recites the entire mantra of Gaṇanātha, which is dear to him, in its complete form. (18.568)
Who on earth shines with feet shimmering upon the heads of all sovereigns—he who, free from desire for wealth, meditates in his heart upon the Goddess Kamalā situated between her breasts? (18.569)
Then, by the power of your mantra, Kamalā shall remain steadfast in his abode;
for he who, afflicted with love, recites this collection of a hundred verses day and night, Kamalā shall be ever present.

He who, out of devotion to Gaṇanātha, recites the Maṭha-mantra at night in a deserted house with disheveled hair, becomes like a bee at the lotus-face of Urvaśī, longing for the pollen of the earth. (18.571)

Just as one who conquers his enemies in battle becomes a sovereign emperor (cakravartin), so too, if a practitioner recites the mantra of Śiva in the forest near a corpse according to the ritual injunctions, he attains sovereignty. (18.572)
Moving through the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, he is the universal sovereign of all the gods;
thus one recites, worships, and chants the root mantra "Gaṇapataye. (18-573)

He who, even at night, constantly recites this "O Bestower of Boons" (*varavarada*) hymn, praised by hosts of Gaṇas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, Suras, and Asuras, attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (*gāṇapatya*). || 18-574 ||
In the hundredfold assembly of your mouth, speech, lotus, and even devotion to you reside;
those who recite the king of mantras, "ma iti sarvajanaṃ," at the conclusion of their meal [attain this]. (18.575)

O Blessed One, if one recites "Smara, smara taṃ hṛdaya," [the deity] brings them under control; they then enjoy playful dalliances with celestial beauties among the trees of the Nandana grove, such as sandalwood and others. (18.576)

Vaśamati, the daughter of the Kinnaras, and Urvaśī, who are ever skilled in bowing to the gods—this pair of syllables from the mantra "svāhā" brings victory even at the end of the day and at the time of eating and other such occasions. (18.577)

All diseases without exception go to their dissolution, just as darkness does when the sun has risen. Those who remember Him— who holds a lotus in His hand, who resembles nectar and fire, and who bears another pair of conchs, who is three-eyed and like unto fire— they go to the third heaven traveling in celestial chariots.

Those who meditate upon you— the adorable one whose form is the supreme protector of the three worlds— residing within the lotus of the heart, which has a point, a triangle, and ten spokes, situated in the midst of the Vedas and stages of life;
having conquered the earth through the power of their subtle contemplations, they attain the state of being free from fear and endowed with great splendor.
O Gaṇeśa, your state is difficult to attain even for the gods and the asuras.
Thus, one who constantly recites, reads, or listens with devotion to this supreme hymn of Gaṇapati, which consists of mantras and contains all secrets,
shall here obtain wealth, prosperity, and auspicious virtue; and in the end, being liberated while living, he goes to the third heaven.
In another [life], he is accompanied by his spiritual practice. || 18-580 ||
Thus, O Goddess, this supreme hymn of the Great Gaṇapati is most secret; it must always be kept hidden, O beautiful one who possesses the five limbs. (18.581)
O Pārvatī, this five-limbed secret of Gaṇeśa must not be given by me to one who is not a disciple, nor likewise to one who is not a practitioner (sādhaka).
At that time, one should act without stinginess; one should not cause stinginess to be grasped.
Otherwise, there would be a loss of accomplishment; therefore, one should practice generosity in every way. (18.583)
The chapter, the manual, the phonemes, the thousand names of the mantra,
and the hymn— this entire five-limbed cycle must be kept secret like one's own birthplace.
Thus ends the *Mahāgaṇapatistotra* in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra*, the great secret. Now follows the *Jvālāmukhimantra* from the *Phetkāriṇī Tantra*:
"Obeisance to the Blessed One; [the mantra] begins with *pratkā* and thereafter follows *jvālāmālini*."
Surrounded by a multitude of jackals, he was addressed with cries of "Hai! Hai! from both sides.
By him:
"Homage to the Blessed One, Jvālāmālinī, surrounded by a multitude of vultures, svāhā!"—
this is the mantra.
Oṃ, *namaḥ* is declared for the heart; *śiraḥ* is remembered [for the head].

*Jvālāmālini* and *ni* are for the crest (*śikhā*). *Gṛddhagapavṛte*, *varma*, and *svāhā* are for the armor (*varman*). One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) joined with these seed-syllables (*jāti*), ending with *namaḥ* for the weapon (*astra*).
This mantra for victory must certainly be recited by a victor before the battle:
*hrīḥ jvālāmukhi svāhā*.
It is also known as "Rudra-jvālāmukhī" because it was born from the fire that is the consort of Rudra.
Immediately following [the mantra] of Jvālāmukhī, another mantra has been fully explained. (18.586)
During a lamp festival, on a full moon day, at night, on a day sacred to the Guru, or on a Sunday, one should recite eight thousand [mantras], or even three times that number, O Brahmin.
"He gives six palas every day; of this there is no doubt.
Thus it was told by Nārada to Agastya, and it was told again.
Those who desire complete success should not even utter the name of the Gopīs, especially that of the son of the righteous King. (18.589)

Due to the gravity of the task at hand, even a king who is of correct conduct and knowledgeable in mantras should perform the rite of the Nine Durgās according to the prescribed injunctions, using various kinds of wealth.
Having offered [the oblation] according to the rule, one should thereafter burn it with the syllables of the mantra;
by mere recollection, indeed, the syllables destroy all enemies.
One should give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of one thousand or even a hundred cows, gold niṣkas, land, and clothing rich with rice;
he shall obtain all peace and become a performer of all protection. || 18-592 ||
The Ornament Without Desire.
Thus ends the section on Jvālāmukhī. Now follows the invocation of the Piśācas.
*Kahakāhe kālike gṛhṇa gṛhṇa piśāci svāhā*.
Two *kaha*s, then *kālike*, likewise two *gṛhṇa*s, followed by *piṇḍaṃ piśāci svāhā*—this is the mantra declared for kings. (18–593)
One should meditate upon the Piśācī: dark-complexioned, very tall, and youthful; possessing three eyes, she holds a moving trident in her hand;
she has disheveled hair, a pale complexion, and a slender, rounded waist, with a necklace fashioned from Guñjā berries adorning her neck.
Until the setting of the sun on the twenty-first day,
he should daily cast his own food, as a single morsel, upon the image of Hari at sunset.
Having three middles and four ends, that Piśācinī goes to the bed and also tells the story of twenty-five regions.
O Goddess of the Gods, in thirty days one should bring forth the narrative of Jambūdvīpa;
in thirty-two [days], one should reveal that mountain in Ayukarṇa.
Likewise, O Gaurī, by thirty-two [repetitions], one certainly causes the three worlds to hear;
by the offering of the three sweets as a bali-oblation, everything is spoken at that very moment.

If she speaks favorably in an assembly, in a crowd, or during a game of dice, then that Piśācinī is certainly pleased and will quickly reveal everything. Even if no one offers her an oblation, the practitioner shall behold her. (18.599)
Thus ends the section on Karṇapiśācinī.
Now follows the mantra of Bhūtinī.
Furthermore, in the Phetkāriṇītantra:
Oṃ hrīḥ hrīḥ phaṭ! Vibhīṣikā hūḥ hūḥ!
Today [is the day of] the goddess Adyā, who wears supreme earrings;
likewise Hāriṇī, Siṃhinī, Haṃsinī, and then Nadī.
The goddess Kāmeśvarī is indeed proclaimed, as well as the goddess Ratipriyā;
at the end of the two [mantras] of Krodha and Astra is Māyā, and Bhūtinī is from Trikūrca. (18.601)
The *tārā* (om), *lajjā* (hrīḥ), and the two weapons (*phaṭ*); at the end of these is the terrifying one (*vibhīṣikā*).
This mantra, ending with the two *krodha*s (*huṃ*), is proclaimed by Vibhūṣi-rāja. (18.602)

Krodha is "huḥ huḥ," and that very same one is "krom," so says someone; moreover, she holds a scimitar in her hand and a human head of lofty form as an ornament, and by her fangs she has consumed flesh, blood, and fat,
observing the vow of the spirits (bhūta).

May she protect us—she whose hair-tufts are the entire earth and its mountains, while her back is the broad earth and her locks are as fierce as the serpents of Time and the formidable beasts of the Satvata lineage. 18.603.

Having gone to the foot of a single tree, one should recite eight thousand [times] during the first watch of the night while traveling; likewise, wherever one's mind is distracted, there too [one should recite]. (18.604)
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform worship by name and offer molasses incense;
at midnight, Vibhūṣaṇī becomes enraged and arrives.
If she is offered water mixed with sandalwood, the Lord of the Waters will certainly grant his blessing;
likewise, one’s mother, sister, wife, or even a beloved goddess will be delighted. (18.606)
Having made [the world] into molasses and become its mother,
she always provides ointment and ornaments for the assembly of one hundred and eight.
O sister, if a great yogi brings a woman from even a thousand yojanas away and gives her [to you], along with divine elixirs and alchemical preparations; || 18-608 ||
If one places his wife upon his back, she leads him to heaven at that very moment;
furthermore, there is a thousand dīnāras, as well as mercury and an elixir of life.
The goddess Vibhūṣaṇī always fulfills all desires;
she is said to possess the pair of the Dhruva and Māyā weapons and to wear earrings. (18.610)
O you who wear earrings upon your ears, O you who wear moon-like earrings!
Today the Creator himself says that even life, along with blood, shall be given away as a gift. || 18-611 ||
O practitioner, what must be done until [the goal] is attained?
Even within fifty days, it will grant you the three worlds.
The mantra for the one who steals the sindūra from the pair of angry ones joined in union is proclaimed as "sindūrariṇī" with three *kūṭas* and weapons;
she is the excellent one who steals golden ornaments and whose branches sway with trembling, moving leaves.
With a smile like the moon, her radiance surpassing the luster of the stars, she caused his body to tremble with longing.
May that trident-tipped spear, which bestows continuous splendor, which is the eternal beauty of the three worlds, and which captivates with its vermilion hue, protect us. 18.614
Having gone to an empty temple, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
she who has departed will quickly return and become his wife, O passionate one. (18.615)
O Goddess, for twenty-five days it protects one from [the loss of] clothing, ornaments, and finery; for twelve days, the sidūrahāriṇī [protects].

The pair of the two *lajjā* [syllables] and the pair of weapons, together with the three seed-syllables of *krodha*, is proclaimed as the *siṃhinī* mantra; thus is the *siṃhinī* mantra described. (18.617)

O you whose fangs are like the heavens amidst the suffering of the mountain peaks, O destroyer of the Daityas in their miserable state; O you who consume those whose mantras have fallen from every bone of Viṣṇu’s feet!
You who, with a tinkling sound, hold fast that which was offered—O Siddha-woman, protect us!
May this garland, which causes all the Kula lineages to tremble, protect you.
Having gone to Ekaliṅga, one should mutter this mantra with devotion;
then, being worshipped, the boon-granting Siṃhinī becomes exceedingly joyful and departs. (18.619)
Whatever one desires, she indeed becomes a wife who fulfills those wishes;
she bestows dinars, pairs of garments, and elixirs of alchemy.
Then one should perform the three *tāras* (oṃs) from the pair of *yugas*; thereafter is *sītījūtinī*.
That which is taught as being within the three *kūcas* is *haṃsinī*, [followed by] the winds (*marutaḥ*). 18-621.
Her eyes resembling white and dark lotuses, she was adorned with milk and wine; having respectfully partaken of the food prepared for her,
she slightly turned her body with a trembling gait, her face charmingly downcast.
May the illustrious Haṃsinī, graceful with necklaces swinging from strings of pearls, protect us. 18.622
Having gone to the house of Vajrapāṇi, one should draw a beautiful image;
having worshipped it with Hayamāra, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
O Goddess, as long as the night remains until midnight, the Haṃsinī moves through the mind;
by offering an oblation of sandalwood, she becomes joyful toward the practitioner.
"What should I do for you, O fulfiller of desires? Shall I provide clothing, ornaments, food, and so forth for your expenditure? (18.625)
Then, when one does not grant all the requested objects and becomes enraged, one should utter the word "nadī" (river) while joined with the weapon-mantra of Tārākrodha. 18-626.
This *pakṣiṇī* meter is said to end with the syllables *kur-ca-rva-yānta* and *ṅe-kt-o-yaṃ*.
[It describes her] whose face is as beautiful as a full-blown blue lotus, who possesses high pitcher-like breasts,
who sports with a pair of charming eyes like collyrium, and whose smile brings an inexhaustible joy.
Having brought the playful lute from the shore of the ocean of milk— which is resplendent with its sound and possesses the eloquence of the humming of swarms of bees— she played it.
Having formed an association with those of low status, I have arrived here for the sake of recitation and worship;
at sunset, one should perform the recitation with sandalwood paste, even if it be a form [of the deity]. (18-628)
That Goddess Śrī, who grants fearlessness from desire, becomes his dancing wife;
she departs after leaving behind a single *pala* of gold for his expenses. (18.629)
Day by day, the goddess Naṭī certainly becomes established;
then follow Tārā, Kūrca, the pair of weapons, and the pair of attendants (Ceṭī). (18.630)
Having spoken thus, the best of men described the pair of wrathful deities and the pair of female servants:
"She goes along, speaking in measured tones, moon-faced, with her upper garment fallen away. (18.631)
Carrying a jar of stainless lotuses, she was like a woman from the interior of the Śrīkhaṇḍa mountains;
her pure body was honored by the fragrance resulting from the application of sandalwood paste. (18.632)
Whatever has been acquired through righteous means is offered by the five female servants, beginning with Karapāyā;
merely by the utterance of [the Lord's] name in any terrifying place, [all dangers are dispelled]. (18.633)
Certainly, once the female servant has arrived, she performs the service;
or else, I shall perform my recitation at home during the night.
Having arrived, the goddess will surely perform the service as a female servant. (18-634)

The mantra of Kāmeśvarī is declared to be the syllable TĀR (tāra), the *kūrca* (huṃ), the weapon (*astra*) (phaṭ), the syllable ME, the word ĪŚVARĪ, and then BHŪTI, followed by the two syllables DVI and the three *krodha* syllables (huṃ phaṭ). 18-635.
The embodiment of desire, endowed with sweetness, possessed of vāsantī flowers,
singing with a face of sweet lips and smiles, holding a lute, and fickle;
she who has eyes like those of a Bhoja woman, filled with the intoxication of honey, shines with equanimity.
From Pādyā comes Pravyadhanurdharā, Madhumatī, Kāmeśvarī, and Bhūtinī. || 18-636 ||
Having approached the place of the Mothers and having partaken of meat, one should offer an oblation of meat-eaters for seven days, a thousand times each day. (18.637)
Through recitation, she certainly arrives; she drenches him in blood and causes him to experience [ecstasy].
Kāmeśvarī becomes pleased, and the wife becomes a desired wife. She fulfills all hopes and certainly bestows a kingdom. (18.638)
The Tāra, along with Lajjā, joined with the two [syllables] of the beard and the weapon, is Rati-priyā;
she is joined with the three Krodhas, and for Meśvarī, the ritual action is as stated in the mantra.
In the midst of a golden rampart, upon the slope of a divine tree, stands a Yakṣī made of snow; her mass of hair is radiant with scattered flowers,
and she is of a slightly reddish hue, her broad and high breasts swelling, as she holds a blue lotus with both hands.
Shining with the luster of a swaying red lotus, she is joined by celestial musicians and adorned with divine ornaments and unguents.

One should utter the word *devi* joined with the pair of weapons and the two wrathful deities (*krodha*); having worshipped the pair of wrathful deities ending in the suffix *-ṅ*, the consort becomes accomplished. (18.641)
At night, having gone to the temple of the deity, one should prepare a bed there;
one should cause white cloth, sandalwood, and *jāti* flowers to be offered. (18.642)

Having offered incense of guggulu resin, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, she always arrives through kissing, embracing, and other such acts. (18.643)
The maiden goddess Satyā becomes his beloved wife;
she shall then give him eight dināras and a pair of divine garments.
He will provide divine and desirable food for his retinue;
furthermore, he bestows household goods and wealth upon others.
If one recites these a thousand times at the conclusion of the practice, success is certain.
One should constantly recite the mantra again and again, having subdued the lord of the heart, anger, and the earth. (18.646)
Having bowed to the Lord of Wrath with a sky-like face, Vajrapāṇi, the Destroyer of Gods—Kali, Kali, Kalpatābhū—the goddess Bhūtinī bestows accomplishment (siddhi). 18-647.
"Elsewhere there are only clouds; here, something has been adorned.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, named the Bhūtinī-prakaraṇa, in the Āgamakalpalatā.
[From the Rudrayāmala (29)]
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mantra consisting of the Supreme Self, by the mere knowledge of which the three worlds are not difficult to attain. (19.1)
One should utter the wife of Rudra, the great yoginī; then one should say the word "Gaurī," followed by "who causes fear to the world," and finally extract the weapon-mantra "Vam. (19–2)
*Rudrajāyā* is *hrīḥ*; therefore, [the mantra begins] with *hrīḥ*. O Mahāyoginī Gaurī, who causes fear to the world, *hūṃ phaṭ*!
Likewise, O Yoginī, the half-mantra here is joined with the seed-syllable (*vīja*) endowed with the six long vowels.
The Heart-mantra is formed with the upper half of that, and the Armor-mantra (*varma*) is formed with its lower half; from that, the Head-mantra follows in sequence. (19-3)
Then follow the crest, armor, eye, and weapon, according to this sequence of binding.
Thus, by the sequence of half-measures;
likewise, the seer is said to be Aṅgiras, and the goddess Gāyatrī is the meter. (19.4)
Then, having uttered "Siṃhavaktrā, the terrifier of spirits,
and the deity Mahākṛtyā," one should perform the meditation.
She has the face of a lion, a dark complexion, and hanging breasts;
her mouth is formidable with fangs, she has three eyes, and she blazes on all sides.
Clad in a black garment, possessing a luster like fire with smoke,
she holds a trident, a discus, a cup, and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) in her hands.
Having meditated upon her great tongue as flickering and her gaze as terrifying as lightning,
the best of mantra-knowers should worship with his two hands according to the ritual procedure.
Having meditated, one should worship Kṛtyā with wild red flowers;
likewise, for rites of killing, one should worship the black [Kṛtyā] with meat, blood, and liquor.
And Kṛtyā, Madanā, and likewise all the Uchchāḍani-kanyās;
then Bhīṣaṇā, Srīmatī, and after that Pratiṣṭhā. || 19-10 ||
The wise one should worship the Vidyā in sequence upon the eight petals; all [the deities] are followers of Śaṅkara, white in color, and holding a noose in their hands. (19–11)
She has two arms and a gentle countenance, holding a noose and a goad; she is auspicious.
On her right side is another four-armed goddess, who utters the lion’s roar and holds a blazing trident and a skull-cup.
In the west is the one named Vāruṇī, golden-hued with a smiling face, her hands holding a trident, a sword, and a chisel, and adorned with all ornaments. (19.13)
[She gave] a bright golden garland and a beautiful, fearless fang;
in the north, she gave [the goddess] named Bhīṣikā, who causes fear to the four castes.
Having performed worship, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Then, the practitioner should always perform its ritual application (viniyoga). 19-15.
Having determined the proper time, one should have an image made of beeswax,
twelve finger-breadths in size, including the nails and hair of the enemy.
The heart-mantra, the name, and the syllable *phaṭ* are for all rites;
then, having established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), one should smear [the image] with black pepper. (19.17)
With the hair of a deceased Brāhmaṇa and a Caṇḍāla tied separately to her two feet,
she should stand facing the opening of a water tank beneath an archway made of Āraskara wood.
To its south, one should prepare a triangular fire-pit (vahnikuṇḍa) provided with a girdle;
having placed the corpse there, one should strew it with reeds and grass around the fire.

One who intends the killing of another should prepare an oblation of *vibhītaka* fruits and offer them into the fire with the palms joined (*nivāta*), using the wings of a raven, an owl, and a crow smeared with lac.
Having said, "Hold him! Dry him up!
Kill him!", the wise one should perform the oblation with this [mantra] exactly one hundred and eight times.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, having performed the rites according to the rules and worshipped the Fire-god in his presence, [he recited]:
"The pain caused by the seizing of my throat, whether it be far away or even in Vartika... (19–22).
Having offered it with longing, one should present the blood of that [victim] to the fire;
having protected the fire according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the practice for nine nights.
By offering oblations with the mantra "mṛta tiṣṭha" (die, stay), the death of that enemy occurs in this world.
"Śāraṃśarākāṣṭhabhavam" means made from the wood of the Śara and Śara trees; "śāvāgni" refers to the fire of the cremation ground.
Having fashioned an image of the enemy and having prepared its head, [one should place it] in a pit. (19–24)

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having recited the mantra a thousand times, one should immediately perform a ritual immersion and thereby effect self-protection for whomever [one intends]. (19–25)
Having recited the mantra according to the ritual procedure, one should offer it with the lion-mudrā;
after six months, even an enraged person will die at both twilights.
Then, having taken a long, upturned leaf or a flower bud from a *bhītaka* tree, the minister should scratch [the target] with it in the dust of a black cobra. (19–27)
One should repeatedly mutter the seed-syllable of Vāyu at the end of the name of the enemy;
then, in that person's very home, he will surely wander about like a crow. (19.28)
By means of wood raised by the wind with well-heard leaves, or wood struck down by lightning, or by the charcoal of camel dung, the eradication of Śakra occurs. (19.29)
Thus ends the section on Dhūmāvatī.
Thus, in the Rudrayāmala, the Vagalāmukhī mantra was spoken there by Bhairavī:
having first uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should then employ the steady *māyā* (Hrīṃ).
Having uttered the word of address, one then says "Śrī Vagalāmukhī. (19-30)
Then, having uttered the words "of all the wicked ones," followed by "the speech, the mouth,
and the feet," and then the word "paralyze" (staṃbhaya), and the word "pin down" (kīlaya).
Having bestowed stable illusion, one destroys the increase; then one should write again.
One should write the syllable Oṃ once more and utter the word Svāhā. (19-32)
This thirty-six-syllable vidyā is difficult to obtain even for the gods. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ vagalāmukhi, paralyze the speech and mouths of all the wicked!
"Kīlaya vuddhināśaya klī hrīḥ oṃ svāhā. This means that the mantra "sthirā" is joined with the fourth vowel (ī) and the letter *ha* situated after the letter *la*;
thus, it becomes "hrīḥ."
The Vidyā known as Stambhinī, Vagalāmukhī, is to be understood as that which paralyzes the three worlds.
The seer is Nārāyaṇa, the metre is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is Balāmukhī;
one should assign Hrīḥ as the seed-syllable, Dviṭha as the power, and the Mudrā to the letters beginning with Ra. (19-34)
In the even-numbered *rasas*, there are those born from the seven seasons and the ten vowels;
they are Bhrāmaṇī, Mandagamanā, Bhogasyā, and Bhoginī. (19–35)
One should worship the enjoyments upon the sixteen petals with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata);
they are conjoined with the sixteen heroes according to the tradition of the Kula lineage.
In the midst of these, one should arrange an eight-petaled lotus upon the desired seats;
on the eastern petal and the others, [one should place] the Mothers beginning with Brahmāṇī, conjoined with the eight Bhairavas.
All [the goddesses] beginning with Sthiramāyā are to be fully worshipped according to one's lineage;
if they reside in the heart, they are placed within the six limbs, as are the sevenfold dhātumātṛkās.

317a) One should worship the Root-Vidyā in the midst of the fire with three handfuls [of offerings], using flowers, incense, and other food offerings (naivedya), as well as perfumes, betel, and lamps. (19–39)
Afterwards, according to the rite of *nīrāja*, one should announce the number of recitations (*japa*).
Then, O Goddess, [one should perform] the three circumambulations, worship, and so forth with great festivities. (19–40)
Thus it has been told, O Goddess; one should observe the command of the Guru.
O Mistress of the Gods, the *jayamālā* consists of knots made from turmeric thread. (19–41)
Seated upon a yellow seat, intent on the meditation of the Yellow [deity],
and constantly worshipping with yellow flowers, one should perform the recitation ten million times.
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with one-tenth of that [number] using very beautiful yellow substances;
one should utter the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and [the result] will come to pass.
By reciting this vidyā that causes the obstruction of movement, one becomes motionless;
by means of another [mantra] consisting of sweet syllables, one should accomplish the names of men.
Likewise, by performing rites with *lodhra*, the three sweets (*trimadhu*), neem leaves, and oil-anointed [substances], one achieves supreme success in causing enmity. (19.45)
O Goddess of Gods, know that *hṛditāla* and *haridrā* combined with salt are *tavana*; likewise, *prajñā*, *gati*, and *mati*. (19-46)
For the pacification of all diseases, one who is firm in his vows and observes celibacy should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while offering parched grain mixed with the three sweets.
On a mountain peak, in a great forest, at the abode of a Siddha,
or likewise at the confluence of a great river, those who follow the way of prostitutes (vaiśikās) should accomplish [their goal] by themselves.
One should dye the sandals at the root of the white Brahma-tree with the red dye of lac, marked with the new seal.

The vidyā consists of thirty-six syllables; when the target is not a lakṣika, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times together with that [vidyā], and an ointment should be applied to all the limbs. (19.50)
O Goddess, I beheld a great and wondrous phenomenon with an invisible cause:
mercury, cinnabar, yellow orpiment, and honey-like beeswax. (19.51)
O beloved, one should collect the warm milk of a single-colored cow during the evening and morning milking times, mix it with sugar and honey, and consecrate it thirty times with the mantra.
And having drunk it, O Goddess, it removes poison from both stationary and moving beings.
Likewise, O Goddess, a man should recite the *māridyamocana* mantra one hundred thousand times. (19.53)
O Goddess, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with these substances ten times [the number of recitations],
one indeed becomes endowed with Lakṣmī and destroys the host of enemies.
In another tantra:
"Know that she who is devoid of piercing, joined with the pair, and united with all—Vagalāmukhī—should be proclaimed as one who paralyzes the speech of those who behold her. (19.55)
"Jijvāṃ kīlaya buddhiṃ ca vināśaya"—thus one should say the word *pada*.
Then follows the *pūrṇabīja* (the full seed-syllable), then the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), ending with *vahnijāyā* (the fire-born woman, *svāhā*).
This thirty-four-syllable mantra of Vagalāmukhī is superior to the *Tārā* [mantra]. (19–56)
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ klīṃ vagalāmukhi, paralyze the speech and mouths of all evil ones; pin the tongue; bind the intellect! Klīṃ oṃ svāhā.
Thus is the mantra.

For this Vagalāmukhī mantra, Śrī Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), the Paṅkti meter (chandas), the venerable Vagalāmukhī is the deity (devatā), *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), and *svāhā* is the power (śakti). Its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of paralyzing the mouths of all enemies.

Here, having performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) using the seed-syllable *tvaṃ* for the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) known as *sthiramāyā*, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Then, one should meditate.
Āṃ! [I meditate upon her] seated upon a lion-throne at the center of a jeweled pavilion with a gem-studded altar, situated within a pure abode;
she is of a deep yellow hue, clad in yellow garments, and adorned with golden ornaments and garlands.
O Goddess, I worship her whose tongue holds the enemy of the mallet (the serpent Śeṣa).

I bow to the goddess who, with her left hand, holds the tip of her tongue and thereby torments her enemies, and with her right hand, which strikes down others, wears yellow garments; she has two arms. (19.58)
Thus ends the chapter on Śrī Pītāmbarā in the Rudrayāmala Tantra. Now begins the ritual manual (paddhati) for Pītāmbarā. Homage to Śrī Pītāmbarā!

In the morning, one should first recite the Guru’s name and then meditate upon him as being white in color, with two eyes and two arms, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and peaceful in appearance. (59)
"I worship the Śrīpādukā, which is the primordial Lalitā of the Guru, endowed with Śakti; obeisance.
Having thus meditated upon the venerable Guru at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one should offer salutation.
Having performed the rules of purification, having used the tooth-stick and so forth, and having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), [one should wash] the feet.

Having washed and sipped water, [recite] with the root mantra: "I purify the principle of the self (ātmatattva), obeisance. With the root mantra: "I purify the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), obeisance. With the root mantra: [I purify the principle of the teacher (śivatattva), obeisance].

"I purify the Śiva-principle; obeisance. With the root mantra: "I purify all principles; obeisance. Having performed these four sips of water (ācamana), one should enter into the midst of the water reaching up to the navel.

Having formed a triangle and a square in the midst of the water, and having meditated upon the seed-syllable of Earth (Laṃ) in its center, one should invoke the holy waters from the solar orb using the *aṅkuśa* (hook) mudrā:
"O Gaṅgā, O Yamunā, O Godāvarī, O Sarasvatī!"
"O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, be present in this water!
Having thus remembered [the deities], the practitioner, having become *mayo* (the creative power), should perform the bath.
Having performed the fourfold *ācamana* as previously described, having chanted the *Gāyatrī*, and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he should proceed.
Having offered the *arghya* to the Sun,
and having recited the root mantra "Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ" as many times as possible, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*),
place the solar orb (*mārttaṇḍa*) within the mandala of the sacred site (*tīrtha-maṇḍala*), and meditate upon the Goddess in one's heart.
"I know that my engagement is with Dharma, and I know that my engagement is not with non-Dharma;
O Hṛṣīkeśa, I act exactly as I am directed by You who abide in my heart.
Having thus recollected this and perceived that everything is merely his own vision, he entered the cave.
Having washed one's feet and sipped water (ācamana), one should enter the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa).
*Gaṃgāyai namaḥ*—to Gaṅgā, on the upper lintel of the door. *Viṃ vidhātre namaḥ*—to Vidhātṛ, below the door.
*Daṃ dvāraśrīyai namaḥ*—to Dvāraśrī, in the middle of the door. *De dehalyai namaḥ*—to Dehalī, at the threshold.
"Vaṃ, obeisance to the Vāstupuruṣa.
Having thus worshipped with flowers, sandalwood paste, and unbroken rice grains, one should approach the altar of worship and establish one's own seat according to one's desire.

Having sat upon one's own seat with the mantra "Salutation to Ādhāraśakti Kamalāsanā," [one should perform the purification of the elements] with the mantra "Sphoṭe astrāya phaṭ" for the removal of obstacles.
With this mantra, one should perform the terrifying of the spirits; having remembered the Guru upon the head, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

Following the sequence of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should contemplate the wind-seed syllable *Yam*, which has come from the six-cornered [cakra] called Svādhiṣṭhāna; being black in color, it should dry up those [elements].

Sitting correctly on a seat, having performed inhalation (*pūraka*) through the right nostril, and having performed three-fold retention (*kumbhaka*) in the form of holding both nostrils, one should exhale through the right [nostril].
Holding the nostrils with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb constitutes *prāṇāyāma*.
For the emaciation of the body, one should meditate upon the Person of Sin (pāpapuruṣa) in the left side of the abdomen:

having a head consisting of the murder of a Brahmin, two arms consisting of the theft of gold and the theft of caste-colors, a heart consisting of the drinking of liquor, limbs consisting of minor sins such as the eating of forbidden food, and [the organ] for violating the Guru’s bed.

Having visualized him as standing there, enraged, bearing a sword and shield at his waist, one should— with the fierce wind together with the "Man of Sin" (pāpapuruṣa), having dried up the body, exhale through the left nostril with a single rotation.
Then, having performed the immersion in nectar with the mantra "vaṃ" while that [deity] is being brought forth,
one should immerse one's own body in that nectar with the mantra "ut".
This is the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Now, the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths): Ā Hrīḥ Kroḥ Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Ha Sa Ha Saḥ | O Moha Vagalāmukhi, may you be established here!
Ā Hrīḥ Kroḥ [22 times] Vagalāmukhi, [may you establish] all the sense faculties!
Ā HRĪḤ KRAUḤ 22 Vagalāmukhi! Speech, mind, hearing, smell, and breath—having come here itself, remain for a long time in my mouth, svāhā!
Then, one should contemplate one's own body as stable and firm.
Thus it is said according to the previously stated method.
This concludes the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā. Now follows the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
Of this venerable Mātṛkā mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) on the head;
the goddess Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas) in the mouth;
and Mātṛkā is the deity (devatā) in the heart.
The consonants are the seeds; the vowels are the powers located in the secret place and the feet.
Now follows the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā*:
A Ka Kha Ga Gha Ṅa Ā—*hṛdayāya namaḥ*.
i ca cha ja jha ña ī: svāhā to the head; u ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ū: vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock;
ai ta tha da dha na ai: hūṃ to the armor.
O / PA / PHA / BA / BHA / MA / AU / Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.
A / YA / RA / LA / VA / ŚA / ṢA / SA / HA / LA / KṢA / AḤ / Phaṭ to the weapon.
Thus is the Mātṛkā-ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa, which removes all sins.

One should place the sixteen vowels— *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*— and the [consonants] *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, within the boat, the ocean, the spring, and the lotus.
One should place ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa,
and pha in the liṅga, the six-spoked [wheel], and the lotus; one should place va, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, and va [in those same locations].
On the four-petaled support,
one should place *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*;
in the center of the earth, on a two-petaled lotus flower.
Ha Kṣa—thus one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Mother-letters (mātṛkā). Now, the meditation on the Mother-letters:
She whose form consists of the fifty letters, whose matted locks are adorned by the moon, and who is the color of crystal.

In her heart, which is radiant with full sesame seeds, the Mother carries a rosary for recitation, a vessel, and a bowl of milk-rice; she possesses the exquisite beauty of pure silk garments and ornaments of various clusters of jewels, even surpassing collyrium; and in her right, left, and joined lotus-like hands, she bears the foremost of rosaries, a conch, and a vessel. (19–60)
Having meditated thus, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*):

*aṃ* on the head; *āṃ* on the perimeter of the mouth; *i* and *ī* on the two eyes; *u* and *ū* on the two ears; *ṛ* and *ṝ* on the two nostrils; *ḷ* and *ḹ* on the two cheeks; *e* and *ai* on the two lips.
Oṃ and auṃ are on the two teeth; aṃ is on the crown of the head; a is at the end of the mouth.
Kaṃ, khaṃ, gaṃ, ghaṃ, ṅaṃ, caṃ, chaṃ, jaṃ, jhaṃ, and ñaṃ are on the roots, joints, and tips of the right and left hands.
Ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ, taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ at the roots and tips of the joints of the right and left feet; paṃ phaṃ vaṃ bhaṃ ma on the two sides, the back, the navel, and the abdomen.
Yaṃ is on the skin at the heart; raṃ is on the blood at the base of the right arm; laṃ is on the flesh at the base of the left arm; vaṃ is on the fat at the lower part of the throat;
śaṃ is on the marrow at the right armpit; ṣaṃ is on the marrow at the left armpit.
*Saṃ* in the *śukra* (semen), from the heart to the two hands; *haṃ* in the *ātman*, from the heart to the two hands;
*haṃ* in the *ātman*, from the heart to the two feet and the mouth;
*laṃ* in the *jīvātman*, pervading the stomach; *kṣaṃ* in the *paramātman*, pervading the seat.
Thus indeed is the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkā-nyāsa). Homage to the venerable Vaglamukhī.
I shall now explain, in brief, the procedure for the worship of the Brahmāstra.
For the benefit of practitioners and for the immobilization of enemies.
Having performed the daily obligatory rites (nityakriyā),

and having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), purification of the site (sthalaśuddhi), purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and the ritual placement of the letters (mātṛkānyāsa)— preceded by breath control— one should worship the lotus feet of the Guru upon one's head.
Of this Śrī Vagalāmukhī-vidyā: Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), [to be placed] on the head; the Gāyatrī meter is the goddess, [to be placed] in the mouth;
Śrī Vagalāmukhī is the deity, [to be placed] at the heart.

*Klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) on the right breast; *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*) on the left breast; *oṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*) at the navel. For the sake of accomplishing the fourfold aims of human life (*caturvidhapuruṣārtha*), there is application (*viniyoga*) in this recitation (*japa*). Having thus formed the mudrās with the fingers, one should pay obeisance.
Alternatively, one may sprinkle water on the ground with the hollowed palms. Now follows the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*):
*oṃ aiṃ hlā vagalāmukhi* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*.
auṃ aiṃ hāḥ vāgīśvarīmukhi tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ | auṃ aiṃ hlāḥ vāgīśvarīmukhi madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ | oṃ aiṃ hlāḥ vāgīśvarīmukhi anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ |
Oṃ Ai Hlā Vagalāmukhi, salutation to the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhā). Kṣo Ai Hlā Vagalāmukhi, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands (karatalapṛṣṭa).
Ā Hlā, salutation to the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭha). Oṃ Hlī, salutation to the two index fingers (tarjanī).
Oṃ hlū, salutation to the two middle fingers. Auṃ hlai, salutation to the two ring fingers. Oṃ hlau, salutation to the two little fingers. Oṃ hlaḥ, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands.
Vagalāmukhi, salutation to the two index fingers. To all the wicked ones, salutation to the two middle fingers.
Salutation to the ring fingers for paralyzing speech, the mouth, and the steps; salutation to the little fingers for pinning the tongue and removing the intellect;
*hlīḥ auḥ svāhā*, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands.
Now, the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*):
OṂ AI HLĀ VAGALĀMUKHI HṚDAYĀYA NAMAḤ | OṂ AI HLĀ VAGALĀMUKHI ŚIRASE SVĀHĀ | OṂ AI HLĀ VAGALĀMUKHI ŚIKHĀYAI VAṢAṬ | OṂ AI HLĀ VAGALĀMUKHI KAVACĀYA...
HŪṂ | O | AI | HLĀ | Vagalāmukhi, VAUṢAṬ for the three eyes. O | AI | HLA | ṢAṬ for the weapon.
HLĀ, NAMAH for the heart. As before.

Oṃ hlā hṛdayāya namaḥ. Vagalāmukhi on the head as before. Thus is the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Then, having uttered the root mantra: "I worship Vagalāmukhī, who pervades the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*), in the heart."
Reciting the root mantra, I worship the venerable sandals of Vagalāmukhī, who pervades all principles (*tattva*), upon the head.
Having recited the root vidyā, I worship the venerable sandals of Sarvatattvavyāpinī Vagalāmukhī in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Now, for the meditation:
In the center, within a jeweled pavilion [situated] upon an ocean of nectar, is the Goddess of Knowledge (Vidyā), seated upon a lion-throne, possessing a deep yellow complexion.
I meditate upon the Goddess whose limbs are adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and garlands, who holds a mallet and has seized the tongue of her enemy.

I bow to the two-armed Goddess, who holds the tip of her tongue with her left hand while crushing her enemies, and who strikes them with a mace held in her right; she is richly adorned with yellow garments. (19.63)
Having meditated upon the Goddess who bears the trident, the bestower of all accomplishments, and who is enriched with every kind of graceful ornament and attire, one should worship her. || 19-64 ||
Profound and intoxicated with passion, resembling molten gold,
she has four arms and three eyes, and is seated upon a lotus throne.
Holding a mallet in her right hand and a conch in her left, as well as a tongue and a vajra, she whose every limb is beautiful—I meditate upon Vagalāmukhī. (19.66)
Wearing yellow garments, she has full, firm, and swelling breasts;
she is adorned with golden earrings and bears a crescent moon as her yellow head-ornament.
Her limbs adorned with yellow ornaments, seated upon a golden lion-throne, she has three eyes and two arms; she is beautiful and decorated with yellow jewelry. (19.68)
One should meditate upon Vagalā held in the heart—she who is joined with a yellow mallet, who dwells within the hearts of the wicked and the afflicted;
she who is yellow in color, anointed with yellow perfumes and unguents, and possesses the luster of molten gold. (19–69)
Having meditated thus, one should perform worship.
Then, having uttered the root mantra and worshipped the thirty-six syllables of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one begins the external sacrifice.

Having drawn a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-petalled lotus, a sixteen-petalled lotus, and a square— the yantra for daily worship— using a stylus made of *paṃcaka* wood and with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and musk, one should offer obeisance in the center of the triangle with:
*aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ādhāraśaktaye kamalāsanāya namaḥ*.
Having thus worshipped the seat of the Goddess, one should then, by means of the previously described yoga of meditation,
draw her forth from the heart-lotus in the form of light through the left channel (vāmanāḍī) while she resides in the ādhāra-cakra.
Again, within the triangle in the center of the imagined pedestal:
"Come, come, O Śrī Vagalāmukhī! Descend into the middle of the pavilion; perform, perform your presence!
I invoke the Supreme Goddess; obeisance!"
Thus one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*). [The rites are:

invocation (*āvāhana*), stabilization (*saṃsthāpana*), confinement (*saṃnirodhana*), bringing near (*saṃnidhāyana*), facing toward (*sammukhīkaraṇa*), veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), the rites of the mandalas (*maṇḍalaiḥ*), the rite of making the deity whole (*sakalīkaraṇa*), the rite of nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), the rite of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*), and the rite of self-identification (*nisvasva*).

Having performed [the ritual] with mudrās and so forth, one should offer the water for the feet (pādya) and the other offerings. Then, having recited the root mantra: "O Śrī Vagalāmukhī, accept this water for the feet, accept it; accomplish my purpose, accomplish it."
I offer water for the feet (pādya) to the Goddess Śrī Vagalāmukhī; obeisance! [Recite] the root mantra.
O Śrī Vagalāmukhī, accept this water of honor (arghya); perform my task, perform it! I offer the water of honor to the Goddess Śrī Vagalāmukhī; obeisance! [Recite] the root mantra.
321a) O Śrī Vagalāmukhī, I offer this madhuparka, together with the beginning and end [mantras] and a seat; *namaḥ*.
Then, in front of her, one should draw an eight-finger square mandala with sandalwood paste and other substances, and in its center—
Having drawn a hexagon and placed upon it a tripod (tridanda) washed with protective substances, one should place a supporting vessel (ādhārapātra) upon that. It is as follows:
"Oṃ vaṃ, obeisance to the smoke-colored flame (dhūmrārciḥ); laṃ, obeisance to the tawny one (kapilā)."
Vaṃ, salutation to Visphuliṅginī; śaṃ, salutation to Jvālāmālinī;
ṣaṃ, salutation to Arciṣmatī; saṃ, salutation to Havyavāhā;
haṃ, salutation to Rauḍrī; laṃ kṣaṃ, salutation to Sāriṇī.

Having thus worshipped the fire-element (agnikalā), one should then worship the solar orb (arkamaṇḍala) with its twelve digits (kalā) in that vessel containing water scented with camphor and other substances, while reciting the reverse Mātṛkā and the root-vidyā. It is as follows:
Kaṃ vaṃ, salutation to Tapinī. Khaṃ bhaṃ, salutation to Tāpinī.
Gaṃ kaṃ, salutation to Śodhinī. Ghaṃ paṃ, salutation to Śoṣiṇī. Ṅaṃ naṃ, salutation to Bhrāmiṇī. Caṃ dhaṃ, salutation to Kledinī.
Chaṃ thaṃ, obeisance to Vareṇyadā; jaṃ thaṃ, obeisance to Susumnā; jhaṃ taṃ, obeisance to Ākarṣiṇī; ñaṃ ṇaṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣṭivāhā;
ḍhaṃ jyeṣṭāyai, obeisance to Jyeṣṭā; ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ, obeisance to Hiraṇyadā.
Thus one should worship the digits of the Sun.
In the water, one should worship the lunar disc and its digits as follows:
*Oṃ* *aṃ* *namas* to Amṛtā; *oṃ* *namas* to Manasī.
Iṃ, obeisance to Tuṣṭi; īṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi; uṃ, obeisance to Pīti; ūṃ, obeisance to Rati;
ṛṃ, obeisance to Dhṛti; ṝṃ, obeisance to Śaśinī.
Oṃ, salutation to Kālā; auṃ, salutation to Sapūrṇamaṇḍalā;
aṃ, salutation to Pūrṇāmṛtā; aḥ, salutation to Vāmanā.
Thus one should worship the sixteen digits of the moon. One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) within the water.
322a) One should offer the root-mantra, unhusked grains, sandalwood, and flowers.
Then, one should display the *dhenumudrā* and the *yonimudrā*.
*Śa śīṃ śuṃ śe śau śa śukraśāya vimocinyai svāhā*.
Thinking thus and recollecting the nectar (*amṛta*), one should recite: *aiṃ klīṃ śau amṛte amṛtodaye amṛteśvari amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya sāṃ juṃ saḥ | amṛteśvaryai svāhā*.
Having thus recited the Nectar-mantra, one should display the Dhenu-mudrā and the Yoni-mudrā.
"O Ānandabhairava, O Surādevī, I worship your venerable sandals; I offer libations; obeisance!
Having thus cast sandalwood paste, incense, flowers, and unbroken rice grains into the second vessel on the right or left, one should fill the vessels:
first the *kuṃbha*, then the *śaṅkha*, the *śrīpātra*, and the *śaktipātra*.
The vessel for the *vali* offering and the vessel for enjoyment;
the vessel for the *vali*, the vessel for enjoyment, and the seven vessels for the heroes—
having thus worshipped these seven vessels with the *ātmatattva*, *vidyātattva*, *śivatattva*, and all the *tattvas*.
Taking four drops from the vessel of nectar-water within the *argha* offering with another vessel, one should place them in the mouth and perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having offered seven times with the root mantra using the combination of the index finger and the thumb, one should offer three handfuls of flowers (*tripuṣpāñjali*).
Having performed [the preliminary rites]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa" at the eastern [door]; "Vaṃ, obeisance to Vaṭuka" at the southern door;
"Daṃ, obeisance to Durgā" at the western door; "Kṣaṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla" at the northern door.
Having worshipped the lineage of gurus beginning from Īśāna up to Vāsinyā,
[one says]: "I worship, satisfy, and bow to the venerable sandals of Śrī Pūrṇanātha Ānandanātha, who is joined with Lalitā and his Śakti."
"To the illustrious Gaganānandanātha, together with the Mother, the Power of Consciousness (Cicchakti), I worship the venerable sandals; I offer libations; obeisance!
Having thus fully worshipped the Guru, [one proceeds].
One should worship with these three alone, which are indeed free from passion and darkness.
"I worship and I satisfy [the deities] in clockwise order, beginning from the east; salutations.
Thus, one should perform the secret placement (nyāsa) with "Salutations."

Iṃ, salutation to Kṛmbhiṇī. Īṃ, salutation to Māhinī. U, salutation to Vaśvā. Ū, salutation to Acalā. Ṛ, salutation to Calā. Ṝ, salutation to Bhūdharā. Ḷ, salutation to Kalmaṣā. Ḹ, salutation to Dhātrī. E, salutation to Kalanā.
Ai, salutation to Kalakaṣiṇī; O, salutation to Bhrāmikā; Au, salutation to Mandagamanā;
Aṃ, salutation to Bhogadā; Aḥ, salutation to Bhāvikā.
Thus, with flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings, [one worships] in the sixteen joints (*sandhi*).
She who is joined with the sixteen vowels is well-known in the Kula tradition.
One should write [the mantra] on the middle and desired petals, as stated in the Kalpa, and then on the eight petals:
*aiṃ hrīṃ brahmāṇyai vapa cha mama kāryaṃ kuru 2 | aiṃ hrīṃ śrībrahmāṇi ava śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi tarpayāmi namaḥ*.

O Maheśvarī Ambā, come, come! Accomplish my task. I worship the sandals of Maheśvarī; salutations (twice). O Kaumārī Ambā, come, come! Accomplish my task (twice). O Vaiṣṇavī Ambā, [I worship] the venerable sandals...
I worship; salutations!
O Mother Vārāhī, come, come! O Mother Vārāhī, I worship the Śrī-pādukā that accomplishes my purpose;
salutations!

O Indrāṇī Ambā, come, come; accomplish my task, accomplish my task. I worship the venerable Śrīpādukā of Indrāṇī Ambā; obeisance! O Cāmuṇḍā Ambā, come, come; accomplish my task, accomplish my task. [I worship] the venerable Śrīpādukā of Cāmuṇḍā Ambā.
I worship; obeisance!
O Mother Mahālakṣmī, come, accomplish my purpose, accomplish it! I worship the venerable sandals of Mother Mahālakṣmī; obeisance!
Having thus worshipped the eight petals, one should worship the six petals:
*hlīṃ*, "I worship the auspicious Śrī-pādukā, obeisance," in the east;
*hlīṃ*, "O Bhagasarpiṇī," [in the southeast]; *hlīṃ*, "O Bhagavahā Śrī," [in the southwest].
Oṃ / Hlī / Bhagasiddhāyāḥ Śrī (4). Hlī / Bhagapatityañcāyāḥ Śrī (5).
Hlī / Bhagamālinyāyāḥ Śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ.
Having thus worshipped all these in the sequence of the hexagon, then follows the worship of the triangle.

I worship and satiate the venerable *śrīpādukā* of the Kāmarūpa-pīṭha; obeisance! [I worship] the venerable [pādukā] of the Jālandhara-pīṭha, the venerable [pādukā] of the Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha. [In the] triangle, one should worship the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) within the womb with three handfuls of water. Having uttered the root-mantra:
Or [one may worship] Aparā Vagalāmukhī or Śrīpādukā with the root mantra. Or [one may worship] Parā Vagalāmukhī or Śrīpādukā with the root mantra:
"I worship and satiate Parā Vagalāmukhī or Śrīpādukā; obeisance."

One should worship in the center of the *yoni*. One should offer three handfuls of flowers. Reciting the root mantra: "I offer this handful of flowers to Śrī Vagalāmukhī, obeisance. With the root mantra: "I offer flowers, obeisance. With the root mantra: [offer] incense (*dhūpa*). With the root mantra: [offer] the lamp (*dīpa*).
The food offering with the root mantra: "To Śrī Vagalāmukhī, for the vital breath (prāṇa), svāhā! With the root mantra:
"To Śrī Vagalāmukhī, for the out-breath (apāna), svāhā! Thus I present the food offering; obeisance! With the root mantra.
"I offer water scented with camphor and other perfumes; obeisance! [Recite] with the root mantra.
"I offer betel leaf; obeisance! [Recite] with the root mantra. The woman should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony and announce the number of recitations (*japa*).
O You who protect the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us;
O Supreme Goddess, may success be mine through Your grace. (19.71)

Having performed one hundred and eight or one thousand recitations of the mantra of Śrī Vagalamukhī, one should offer it for the attainment of all goals, saying: "I offer salutations. Thus, having announced the number of recitations, one should offer three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra.
"O supreme Vagalāmukhī, I offer this handful of flowers; salutations.
Thus, one should offer three handfuls of flowers. One should recite hymns and so forth.
"O Goddess, by the mere recitation [of this], the method for subduing Madana is accomplished according to rule."
Then one should offer three folds [of cloth], accompanied by divine medicinal herbs.
With the root mantra, one should offer the three-fold *vargala* as follows: "O supreme Vagalāmukhī, accept, accept this offering together with the substances and herbs, svāhā!
In the same manner, one should offer the three *vargalas* beginning with "O supreme-non-supreme," and so forth.
Then, at the beginning of the rite, having worshipped Bhairava, who holds a club and a skull-bowl:
*aiḥ hrīḥ śrīḥ a* Caṇḍabhairava Kṣetrapāla, come, come! Destroy my obstacle!
Destroy such-and-such a wicked one! Eat, eat! *hrīḥ*, paralyze the mouth of such-and-such a person, paralyze it twice!
"Accomplish, accomplish what is desired by me; accept this offering, twice, svāhā!
With this mantra, the worship of the offering should be performed. One should satisfy the venerable Guru upon one's head with the vessel, saying: "Obeisance to the Guru;
[this is] the vessel."
One should give a vessel to Śakti and a vessel along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the practitioners.
Thus, he who worships with devotion attains success;
he shall obtain the state of Agni, Śakti, and Śambhu. (19.73)
Thus it has been told, O blessed one: he who should transgress the command of the Guru, even having attained supernatural success (*siddhi*), will indeed act for his own detriment. (19.74)

Thus concludes the *Pitāṃbarā-pūjā-vidhi*, according to the teachings of the *Rudrayāmala*, composed by the venerable Śrī Nandatha, the bee at the lotus feet of the illustrious Maheśvarānandanātha. May there be auspiciousness!
Salutations to the illustrious Pitāṃbarā!
The illustrious Mahāpītavāsas said:
This manual for the worship of Pītavāsas, which follows the instructions given for the circle of kings, is complete. May there be auspiciousness.
Salutations to the illustrious Pītavāsas.
The illustrious Mahāgratārā said:
O Mahādeva, [this applies] to kings, to those crawling with impurities such as circles of power (*maṇḍala*), and to all the *gaṇas* whose minds are transformed by wealth. (19.75)
Śaṅkara said: "Tell me of the immobilization of elephants, serpents, and other creatures.
Śrī Bhava said:
"O Goddess, formerly in the Kṛtayuga, when a disturbance of the winds had arisen..."
The gods, including Indra, Agni, and Viṣṇu, all approached me in fear, having reached the seven oceans which were free from agitation.
The gods said:
"O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, O Lord of Bhūdra, protect us who have come to you for refuge from this great ocean, which is agitated by great winds and other disturbances. (19.78)
O Goddess of the gods, having done so, I gave this armor, fashioned of old and capable of cutting through all great fears, to all the Vedas.
O Śiva, [I have received] the great armor known as Vagalā, which bestows life;
formerly, I myself was overwhelmed by fear due to the terror of Bhasmāsura. (19-80)
Therefore, O Supreme Goddess, protect my vital breaths;
for Śiva is the bestower of life, and thus he is renowned as the supreme protector. (19.81)

Of this *Śrī-Vagalāmukhī-kavaca*, Śrī-Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *uṣṇih* meter (*chandas*), the non-dual form, the great paralyzer, Śrī-Pitāmbharā is the deity (*devatā*), the syllable *sthira-māyā* is the seed (*bīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), and the *praṇava* is the pin (*kīlaka*). [It is for the purpose of] the speech of all wicked beings, whether they be far away or standing nearby.

The application (*viniyoga*) for this recitation is for the purpose of paralyzing the movements [of enemies], for the purpose of paralyzing the mantras, yantras, and medicinal herbs of hostile armies, for the purpose of deluding all royal families, and for the sake of pleasing the supreme Śrī Vagalāmukhī. Now follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

Oṃ hrāḥ, homage to the heart. Oṃ hlīḥ, svāhā to the head. Oṃ hluḥ, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock. Oṃ hlaiḥ, huṃ to the armor. Oṃ hlauḥ, vauṣaṭ to the eyes. Oṃ hliḥ, phaṭ to the palms for the weapon-mantra.
In this manner, one should perform the placement from the thumbs to the palms of the hands.

oṃ / hlīṃ / *namas* to the heart. *Vagalāmukhi*, *svāhā* to the head. *Vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*) of all the wicked. *Hūṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*): paralyze the speech and the face; *kīlaya* (pin) the tongue, destroy the intellect, *hlīṃ*! *Vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes.
Oṃ Svarahā Astrāya Phaṭ. Meditation:
[I behold her] seated upon a lion-throne in the center of a jeweled altar within a pavilion of gems, situated in the midst of an ocean of nectar.

I bow to the Goddess, whose complexion is deep yellow, who is clad in yellow garments, whose limbs are adorned with ornaments and garlands, and who holds a mallet against the tongue of her enemy. 19-82.
May the supreme goddess Vagala, consisting of thirty-six syllables, protect [me];

may the Guru protect [me] with power in the thousand-spoked [cakra], O supreme one! May the supreme power in the form of lightning, residing in the forehead and the abode of Śiva, [grant] the pair of *bhū* (earth).
O Mahākālī, you are the supreme sovereign, the pair of my eyes. || 19-83 ||
Worshipped with yellow flowers, she has a radiance like that of the breast of Skanda upon her neck and shoulders;
she wears yellow garments, and with her right arm she holds [her consort], while her left hand embraces his waist.
May my heart, with its pair of breasts, bear the orb of the sun as its face;
may my back, bearing the arrow, assume the form of Kandarpa at the waist. (19.85)
The Śiva-power, pure and in the form of the individual soul (jīva), resides in the heart-lotus; she whose form is knowledge dwells in the Ājñā-cakra as the mistress of the Supreme Brahman.
May she who abides in her own essential nature within the thousand-petaled lotus at the aperture of Brahmā, the Supreme Power Camarī with her curling locks of hair, protect me. 19-87.
The Vidyā consists of thirty-six syllables; she bears a body that is yellowish-golden in hue.
She is worshipped with yellow flowers, and she is fond of yellow food offerings and other oblations.
May she who is auspicious in all her limbs protect me; she who causes the paralysis of enemies, who is supreme in the aperture of Brahmā, and who brings an end to the suffering of saṃsāra. (19.89)
The Great Goddess, who grants the desires of the mind, delivers [beings];
in the wheel of the unmanifest (ajñācakra), she takes the form of the Guru and is the destroyer of great fear.

May she who possesses the power of all sciences protect the tongue; may she who possesses the power of the age of the scriptures [protect] the palate; and in the sixteen-petaled lotus of purification, may she who possesses the power of the age of the Lord of Life [protect] the soul.
May she who is called the form of the thirty-six principles, residing in my throat, always protect me;
O Lord of Bhavānī, you whose supreme self consists of both form and formlessness, dwell in the lotus of my heart.
One should tear asunder and utterly destroy the great enemies, beginning with the senses;
in the ten-petaled Maṇipūra, Mahāviṣṇu assumes his own form.
Tearing asunder all delusions, she who is "Māmā" is indeed that Supreme One;
she who, in the form of Prajāpati, resides in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra] with six spokes. || 19-94 ||
May the one who possesses the form of the Gaṇas, whose knowledge is the cause of creation and maintenance, and who is the flesh-eater with a gaping mouth, protect me in the four-doored foundation.
May the supreme Kalā protect me within the person consisting of the sixteen vowels:
Ka, Kha, Ga, Gha, and likewise Ṅa; Ca, Cha, Ja, Jha, and likewise Ña, as well as Va and Tu. (19.96)
Ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, and tvaṃ; mā, kā, ga, ṇa, ta, tha, da, and likewise va, tu, dha, ta, pa, pha—may these, while intent on meditation, protect me from my enemies. (19.97)

Va, bha, ma, ya—having torn apart the meaning of the enemies, O you whose nature is speech, [protect] me! Ra, la, va, śa, as well as ṣa, sa—having likewise torn apart the tongues of the enemies! 19-98.
May Me, Va, Ca, Mu, and Ma protect my face and tongue;
may Ha, La, and Kṣa protect everything. May they protect my supreme glory. || 19-99 ||
The *praṇava* (oṃ), the first [syllable], the third, and likewise the pair of vowels;
the third [syllable] beginning with a vowel, and the fifth vowel at the beginning of the quarter-verse. (19–100)
The second [syllable] is the right eye, well-remembered for all malevolent beings;
it paralyzes the speech of the sixth day and likewise that of the tongue, leading to the state of bliss.
The second [syllable] which they fix as a stake likewise destroys growth;
likewise [is] *sthiramāyā*, and at the end [is] *tāra* followed by the consort of Fire (*vahnivadhū*). (19.102)
This is the lore, the great lore that causes the paralysis of enemies;
having recited the mantra three times, perform the pervasion of all the limbs.
One should indeed mutter [the mantra], there is no doubt; O Great Serpent, [one should take] the clay from a potter's [wheel] with the left hand as a lamp for the brave enemies. (19.104)
Having prepared and ignited [a fire] with oil, one should recite the mantra over a beautiful vessel on the left;
thus, for three nights, one may paralyze the enemy army in a great battle.
Having worshipped the young girl of fair complexion with yellow flowers with devotion,
and having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) upon his body, the yogi should worship her and recite the mantra.
Having satisfied that Śakti with yellow offerings and services, one shall surely bring even the Lord of the World under control; how much more so a lowly human? (19.107)
O Dear One, one who desires the paralysis of speech should worship a beautiful-faced Vīraśakti sixteen years of age, having adorned her with gold and other ornaments. (19.108)
Having recited the thousand-fold root mantra of even Acyutapati, one should utter "Paralyze! (staṃbhaya) for the sake of paralyzing even the most excellent or the lowliest of human beings.
One who desires to bring others under one's control should firmly gird the loins,
place the *śakti* upon the *liṅga*, and recite the mantra three thousand times.
He brings even Indrāṇī under his control, how much more so an ordinary human woman?
O Lord of the Maṇḍala, he who stands facing north becomes a subduer. (19.111)
Having placed his hands upon the breasts of the clever-faced one—who was sixteen years of age, possessed a beautiful smile, and had a laughing countenance—he drank from her first [breast]. (19.112)
Having installed [the image] upon the linga and kissing its mouth while reciting the Pītāmamantra three thousand times, O Great King, one certainly brings [her] under control; it is not otherwise.
By whatever means possible, one who is devoted to Vagalā and intent on her worship shall paralyze all the worlds and bring even Śaṅkara himself under his control. (19.114)
He slays the host of enemies and causes even mountains to crumble; he strikes down Candra, the architect of the gods—what common person could he not destroy? (19.115)
O Pārvatī, where has the majesty of this armor been described, when the great mountain was being consumed by fire and the dissolution of the world was at hand? (19.116)
And once, O Goddess, by a single utterance of *jaya*, the host of Cātakas was paralyzed;
this is that supreme Vidyā, the destroyer of great enemies. (19.117)
Knowledge should not be given to an atheist, a thief, a wicked person, a fool, or one who considers himself a scholar; by giving it, one incurs sin.
This supreme [mantra] should be given to one who is well-behaved, well-disciplined, devoted to the guru, pure, and a reciter of the great mantra. (19.119)
Having first donned the excellent armor and being composed in meditation, one should recite the mantra;
otherwise, there is no certainty that this paralyzing vidyā will be accomplished. (19–120)
Thus ends the Vagalāmukhī-kavaca in the *Śrī-Ekavīra-tantra*, within the dialogue with Mahogratārā, in the section on the Jewel of Knowledge consisting of thirty-six syllables.
Now follows the Thousand Names (*Sahasranāma*).
Oṃ! In the preeminent abode of the gods, the beloved of Vagalāmukhī recounted thousands upon thousands of [mantras] for Maheśvara, the God of gods. (19.121)
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the thousand names of the Goddess,
which is the supreme Brahma-weapon knowledge that bestows the fruit of the four aims of life.
O Goddess, you are secret and more secret than the secret, uniquely adored by all the Siddhas; you are the most secret Vidyā, nourished within all the Tantras. (19.123)
She is the adversary of hosts of obstacles, the deluder of the wives of others,
the paralyzer of royal armies, and the confuter of opposing disputants.
And in the past, during the terrible time of the single ocean, in that most fearsome epoch, the Lord Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, was accompanied by Sundarī.
Seated upon the serpent-throne, I entered into yogic sleep;
at the time of sleep, the eternal Citkeli was addressed by me.
"O Lord, please recite either the hymn that causes great paralysis or the supreme Thousand Names of some deity. (19.127)
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Gods, to this supreme secret:
by whose grace I am the unborn Viṣṇu, the Lord of all, O Goddess.
It must be guarded with effort; from its disclosure comes the loss of accomplishment.

For this hymn of the thousand names of the venerable Pītāmbarā, the seer (ṛṣi) is the blessed Lord Sadāśiva, the meter (chandaḥ) is Anuṣṭubh, the deity (devatā) is the venerable Jagadvaśīkaraṇī Pītāmbarā, and the application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of attaining all desired accomplishments through recitation.

Now, the meditation: [She is] clothed in yellow garments, with full and elevated breasts, enriched by the splendor of a crown of matted hair, and bringing happiness to the ancestors and the gods. (19.129)
Holding a sword, a tongue, and a mallet, she is supremely beautiful;
she is renowned throughout the three worlds in all the Āgamas and Purāṇas. (19.130)

I shall tell you that which is to be heard with every effort—that Great Goddess who is the primordial source of creation, maintenance, and destruction; she who is to be guarded with all diligence. (19.131)
I bow to that Goddess who destroys the world, who brings about freedom from old age and death,
the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) who bestows supreme sovereignty.
Having first uttered the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should then speak the firm Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by "Vagalāmukhi sarve" and "duṣṭānāṃ vācam. (19.133)
"O Siddhimat, paralyze the mouth, fix the feet, and nail down the tongue;
destroy!"—one should then utter the *tāra* (Om) and the stable *māyā* (Hrīṃ).
The mantra, accompanied by the beloved of Vahni, bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. Now, the names:
Brahmāstrā, Brahmavidyā, Brahmabhūtā, Sanātani. (19–135)
O Brahmeśrī, O Vimalā, O Vagalā, O Brahmacāriṇī!
O Nityānandā, O Nityasiddhā, O Nityarūpā, O Nirāmayā! (19.136)
She is the sustainer, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the one who casts sidelong glances;
she is Kamalā, Vikalā, Nīlā, Ratnatā, Bhṛguṇā, and Asitā.
Maṅgalā, Vijayā, Jāyā, the bringer of all auspiciousness; Yāminī, Kāminī, Kānyā, Kāmukā, and Kāmacāriṇī. (19.138)

O you who are fond of desire, who delight in desire, whose very nature consists of the longing for desire; O you who are named Kāmā, who abide in the seed-syllable of desire, and who dwell in the sacred seat of Kāma.
Bestower of desires, destroyer of desires, Kālī, she who possesses the splendor of a skull-bearing Rākṣasī;
the enemy of Kaṃsa, the lotus-like one, Kālī, beloved of the Lord of Kailāsa.
Kātyāyanī, Keśavā, she who is joined with Karuṇākāmakīla, Kriyā, Kīrttikartṛkā, Kāśī, and Kāmāturā Śivā. (19.141)
She is the destroyer of desire, she who has the form of Kālī, Tārā, and she who is pure as the moon;
she is Khecarī, whose body is space, and the supreme one who supports both the small and the great. (19.142)

She who holds a sword in her hand, she who is most fierce, she whose beloved is Khaḍginī and Khaṭvāṅga, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, she who moves gracefully, she who is sung of, and she who increases the lineage. || 19-143 ||
Godhārā, Gaukarā, Gopyā, Gandharvapuravāsini, Gāndharvi, Gandharvakalā, Gopalī, Garuḍāsanā. || 19-144 ||
O Govindābhā, O Govindā, O Gādhārī, O Gandhamādinī; O Gaurāṅgī, O you whose form is that of a cowherd girl, O dweller in the cow-pens of the cowherds!
