Gandhā, Gajendragamanī, Gaṅgādhara-priyā, Gada, Ghanāghorā, Ghorarūpa-naśreṇī, and Ghanaprabhā. (19.146)
O Lord of the Daityas, [you who possess] a loud bell-sound and a terrible resonance;
you are the Ḍākinī, Umā, Upendra, Urvaśī, and she whose seat is a serpent. (19.147)
Uttamā, Unnā, Unnā, dweller in the highest place;
Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍī, the remover of fierce pride. || 19-148 ||
Ugracaṇḍā, Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, Caṇḍadaityavināśinī, Caṇḍarūpā, Pracaṇḍā, Candrā, and Caṇḍaśarīriṇī. (19.149)
Four-armed and fierce, she dwells within the moving and the unmoving;
her head is like an umbrella, and her two arms are exceedingly restless and deceptive.
She who is of deceptive form, the bearer of deception, the Kṣatriya, the destroyer;
she who is Jaya, Jayadurgā, the victorious one, and the supreme bestower of victory. (19.151)

Jathinī, Jaṭinī, Jyotsnā, the beloved wearer of matted locks (Jaṭādhārapriyā), the Conquered (Jitā), she who has conquered the senses (Jitendriyā), she who has conquered anger (Jitakrodhā), the rosary for recitation (Japamālā), and the Mistress of the Waters (Jaleśvarī). || 19-152 ||

She who has conquered death, who is beyond old age, whose nature is the daughter of Jahnu (Gaṅgā) and the son of Janaka; she who resounds with the humming of bees, who possesses a deep, resonant sound, and who is beautiful with the whistling of the wind.
Jharjharajhamurājhāri, jharājharatarā parā; Ñaśābhrametā, Ñakārī, Ñaṇākalyāṇadāyiṇī. (19.154)

With this mind, she is eternally engaged; she is the beloved of Śaṅkara, the one who removes defects, the one who causes trembling, the one who bestows fearlessness, and the one who is dear to the tranquil. (19.155)
She who bears the syllable *ṭha*, she who is *ṭhīvā*, she who consists of the letter *ṭha*, she who is fond of the *ṭhīra* hand;
she who is the act of *ṭhekana*, she who possesses the *ṭhaka*, she who is the mistress (*ṭhāminī*), and she who is dear to *ṭhamana*. 19.156
Ḍarahā, Ḍākinī, Ḍārāmarā, the beloved of Ḍāmara;
Ḍaṃginī, joined with Ḍarāṅ, and she who is dear to the sound of the ḍamaru drum. (19.157)
She who awakens the word *hāṭola* through the syllables *ṭha*, *kā*, *ḍa*, *kā*, and *ṭo*;
she who is the *ḍhāminī*, who delights in the *ḍhamana*, and who is revealed by the *ḍhagata-tantra*. (19.158)

She who possesses manifold forms, the command (ānā), the bestower of the siddhi of atomization (aṇimā), the one who addresses (āmatriṇī), the one who acts (ākārī), and she who is praised by the sun as it bows down (ānamadbhānu). || 19-159 ||

O Tārā, O Tantrī, you who are both the Tantra and the one afflicted by fear; O ascetic lady, whose form is the Tantra itself; O Tarangiṇī, O supreme Tantra, whose very body is the essence of the Tantras! 19.160
She is the embodiment of reality, the sustainer of the threads [of existence], and the one who reveals the vow of the threads;
she is the noble chariot of the tantras, not merely a playful dancer in the lower realms.

The giver of seats, the giver of the wish-fulfilling tree, the desirable one, the steadfast, the most steadfast, the compassionate, [the one who bestows] form and so forth, [and] the lightning-like compassion. 19-162.
Durgā, the goddess who overcomes difficulties, the destroyer of wicked Daityas, the bestower of joy, the slayer of demons, and she whose ultimate refuge is compassion. (19.163)

She is the destroyer of miserable rebirths, the giver of joy, and free from attachment; she is dear to the sky-clad ascetics, the bestower of gifts, and the shatterer of the deceit of the Daityas. || 19-164 ||
Damanā, the ten sisters, the destroyer of the lords of the Dānavas;
she who possesses compassion, the proud one, and she who sports gracefully upon the sacrificial grass.
Dharaṇī, Dhīraṇī, Dhātrī, Dharādhara, Dharapriyā;
Dharmajñā, Dhavalā, Dhūlī, Dhanadā, Dhanavardhinī. || 19-166 ||
The goddess Dharā is the daughter of Dhara; she is Sudharmā, the one who wards off unrighteousness;
she is Dhīrā, the bestower of success upon the steadfast and the wise; she is Yaśī.
O Caṇḍī, you who support the earth, whose nature is the elements;
O Nārāyaṇī, O Nārasiṃhī, eternal bliss, O Anaromā! (19.168)
She who dwells at night, she who is ever-present in the night, she who is in the proximity of the blue jīmuṭa cloud;
she whose limbs are blue, she who wears blue garments, and she who resides on the Blue Mountain.
Munīlā is adorned with flowers, possessing a luster like that of a blue lotus;
she is the eternally renowned sixteenfold Vidyā, who bestows both eternal and transient happiness. (19.170)
Narmadā, the delighter of Nanda, she who is praised by Sunanda,
whose eyes are the joy of Yaśodā, and who dwells in the Nandana grove.
Nagāntakā, Nāgavṛddhā, Nāgapatnī, and Nāginī; Namitā, Śoṣajanitā, Namaskāravatī, and Namaḥ. (19.172)
Pārvatī was clad in yellow garments and adorned with yellow ornaments;
she wore yellow garlands and yellow clothing, and her hair was tawny-yellow.
She who is more radiant than yellow flowers, worshipped with yellow flowers,
possessing supreme splendor, the mistress of the ancestors, and the destroyer of enemy armies.

She is the supreme, she is dependent on the Supreme, she is the mantra of the Supreme, and she is higher than the highest; she is the supreme knowledge, the supreme accomplishment, and the bestower of the supreme abode. (19.175)
Puṣpā, Puṣpavatī, Puṣpā, adorned with garlands of flowers;
she is ancient, the bestower of the former, latter, and intermediate siddhis.
The father brought her; she has drunk deeply; she possesses full and elevated breasts;
she is the middlemost of women out of love; she remains, sporting like a lotus petal. (19.177)
Padmāvatī, lotus-eyed, Padmā, lotus-faced, supreme;
seated upon a lotus-throne, lover of the lotus, whose nature is like a ruby. || 19-178 ||

O you who hold the vessel of the purifying stalk, O auspicious one devoted to the wives of others, O you who abide among the spirits of the departed, O you who are supreme bliss, O you whose nature is the Supreme Brahman! || 19.179 ||
The goddess is beloved by Jīveśvara; she is fond of the pleasure of blood from the bound soul (paśu);
she loves the flesh of the bound soul; she is the supreme leaf (parṇā), devoted to the highest nectar.

O Goddess who holds the noose, who possesses the noose, who protects, who brings forth progeny, who bestows the sacrificial fee for cattle; O Goddess who grants supreme bliss, you who destroy the bonds of the bound souls (paśu). (19.181)
Her face is like a full-blown lotus, her body is like a blooming blue water-lily;
she utters the supreme sound "Phut," and her eyes have the luster of a full-blown night-lotus. (19.182)
Phaṇ-mantra, crystalline one, svāhā, the bursting and the burst, O you whose form is *pha*, the crystal, the pill, the wise one, O you whose nature is crystal and so forth! (19.183)
She is the excellent woman, the bearer of boons, the one who wards off [evil], and indeed the most excellent among the virtuous;
she is the abode of the *bindu*, the possessor of the *bindu*, the beautiful one, and the dweller in the wheel of the *bindu*. (19.184)
She is a Vidyādharī with wide eyes, beloved by the people dwelling [in her],
possessing the knowledge of the Vedas, having deformed eyes, and appearing like the earth at the end of a cosmic age.
She who possesses five powers and is free from the sixfold energies, she who has five faces and is beloved by Śiva;
O Goddess dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha, you who are the beloved of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha. (19.186)
The Goddess is the personified form of Vaikuṇṭha, the bestower of the supreme Vaikuṇṭha;
she is the embodiment of Brahman, the consort of Viṣṇu, the Great Sovereign of the Supreme Brahman.
She who loves existence, she who manifests existence, she whose forms are existence, she who arises from existence;
she who is beyond existence, she who is existence, she who is the stream—O fortunate one, you who do what is pleasing! 19-188.
Bhadrā, Subhadrā, Bhavadā, the destroyer of the Daityas;
Bhavānī, Bhairavā, Bhīmā, Bhadrakālī, and Śubhadrikā. (19-189)
The sister, she whose form is the *bhaga*, Bhagamālā, most excellent in *bhaga*; O Goddess, she who possesses the *bhaga*, she who is full of *bhaga*, she whose appearance is the *bhaga*. 19-190.
O Goddess, you who were created by Bhaga, O Bhagavatī, whose form is Bhaga, who consumes Bhaga; you who are fond of the Bhaga-linga, O Goddess, and who are devoted to the Bhaga-linga.
She whose nature is the vulva and the phallus, she who delights in the vulva;
O Goddess, she who has entered the vulva and the phallus, she who sports with the vulva and the phallus. (19.192)

She who is the garland of *bhaga*s, the digit of *bhaga*, whose form is *bhaga*, who is clothed in *bhaga*; she who is the impetus of *bhaga*, adorned by *bhaga*, the sovereign of *bhaga*, whose nature is auspicious fortune. (19.193)
She is the enjoyment of the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*; she brings about the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*.
She possesses the sweetness of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, and she is served by the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*.
Having thoroughly worshipped the bhaga and liṅga, she is endowed with the bliss of the bhaga and liṅga;
she is detached from the bhaga and liṅga, yet completely enveloped by the bhaga and liṅga.
Mādhavī, Mādhavā, the venerable one, Madhurā, O you who wear a garland of honey;
the slow-smiling one, Mahāmāyā, the enchantress, the most exalted.
She is great delusion, great knowledge, most terrible, and great mindfulness; she is the wise one, delighting in honor, the enchantress, and the sweet-faced one. (19.197)
Mallikā is proud, adorned with the jewel of a sun-stone, wearing a garland on her head;
she is the bearer of garlands, most auspicious and supreme.
Māttasiṃhā, Samollāsā, Mattasiṃhamahāsanā, Madanā, Sundarī, Medhā, Madhumattā, and Madhupriyā. (19–199)
Mahendravallabhā, Śailā, the daughter of the Couple (Mithunātmajā), Mahāmālyā, Mahākālī, Manobuddhi, and Mahotkaṭā. || 19-200 ||
Maheśvarī, Mahāmāyā, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura; Madhurā, Kīrttikā, Mattā, she who moves with the gait of an elephant in rut.
She who is fond of intoxication, who delights in meat, who is endowed with passion, and who possesses the letter *ma*;
she who is beloved by couples, the Goddess, the Great Bliss, and the Great Festival. (19–202)
Mārici, Marīci, Mānā, the bestower of mind and intellect;
Mahāmokṣā, Mahālakṣmī, the bestower of the great state. || 19-203 ||
Yamarūpā, Yamunā, Jayantī, Yaśaḥpradā, Yāmyā, Yāmavatī, Yuddhā, and Pādoḥkulavivardhinī. (19–204)
She is Ramā, Rāmā, the wife of Rāma, the one adorned with a garland of jewels, the beloved of Rati,
seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, and decorated with ornaments of precious gems.
Delightful and most charming, devoted to the highest delight,
she rejoices in bliss, full of joy, and increases the lineage of the Raghus.

She is delight, the one who delights, beyond the limit, the stream of joy, born from the most excellent jewels; she is the very nature of the essence of the mantra, the night that brings about the bliss of the nectar of immortality. || 19-207 ||
Born of the seasons, she bestows prosperity and removes poverty; she is the form of the seasons and is fond of the seasons.
She loves the color red, delights in red, and her teeth are stained with red pigment.
O Lakṣmī, Lajjā moves; O Kālī, you whose eyes are like playful creepers!
O Lilāvati, with hair standing on end, the goddess Lalāṭapadikā stands [there]. (19–209)
She is of the nature of Brahman, the knower of Brahman, the mother of the Vedas, and the Vedic goddess;
she is born from Brahman, a portion of Brahman, and is devoted to the discourse on Brahman.
She is the embodiment of the Vedas and the form of the Vedas; she is a woman and she is ever-steadfast.
She is a girl, a young maiden, and an aged woman, devoted solely to the rites of Brahman.
She who dwells in the Vindhyas, she whose lover is the Vindhya, she who is adorned with the silver of the Vindhyas;
she who possesses knowledge, the bearer of the Vedas, the pervasive one, the embodied digit;
she who is fond of the left-hand path (vāmācāra), she who is fire, and she who is devoted to the left-hand path.
The Goddess is the practice of the left (vāmācāra), the beloved of Vāmadeva, and the auspicious one; she is pure consciousness and the senses, and she is adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
She is the liberator from bondage, the daughter of Varuṇa, and the one whose abode is Varuṇa; she is auspicious, dear to Śiva, both pure and impure, and white in color.

She who loves white flowers, she who is white, she who is devoted to the dharma of Śiva, she who dwells in semen, she who emits semen, she who is pure, she whose form is pure, and she who is the essence of purity.
Wearing white garlands and garments, she is white in form;
she is the embodiment of the six seasons, moves through the six seasons, and dwells within the six cakras.
Possessing the six knots, she is sixteenfold, the supreme measure, and consists of six;
she is the goddess who is the youth of the six limbs, and she is the primordial nature of the six limbs.

O six-faced one, O you who possess the six tastes, O beloved of the sixty-sixth Lord, O you whose conversation is sixfold, O sixteen-year-old, O you whose nature is the sixteen-fold ritual placement! 19–218.
She who pierces the six cakras, whose own nature is the six cakras;
she who is the form of the sixteen vowels, possessing six faces and endowed with six arms.
She is the very embodiment of Sanaka and the others, devoted to the dharma of Viṣṇu;
she is pure, possessing the seven white notes, beautiful of form, and the most excellent among women.
Siddhividyā, Siddhimātā, Siddhidā, Siddhirūpiṇī;
Harā, Haripriyā, Hārā, Hariṇī, and likewise Hāriyuk. (19–221)

O you who are the color of Hari, the supporter of Hari, whose eyes are like those of a deer, and who possess the splendor of Hara; O you who are the cause, who delight in the Cause, who shine for the benefit [of others], and who possess a form dear to your devotees.

She who removes [suffering], she who takes away [passion], she whose beloved is Hara, she who wears a necklace, she who captivates the deer, she who is endowed with grace, she who has the form of Hari, she who bears the color of Hari, she who has eyes like a deer's, and she who possesses the splendor of Hara. (19–223)
She whose cause is love, who delights in her cause, who is beneficial and of a helpful form;
she who possesses patience and forbearance, who is the embodiment of forgiveness, and who is adorned with tiny bells.
O destroyer of [defilements], O witness of the earth, O most beautiful one in the center of the *su* syllable;
O unborn, O colorless, O beyond purchase, O you who recline upon Śeṣa! (19–225)
She is peaceful and virtuous, yet she does not possess a limited form; she is formless, stainless, noble, and endowed with infinite qualities. (19.226)
Savidyā, Vidakā, Vidyā, Aradhinvavirocanā, Aparājitā, Atijārā, Ajeyā, and Amalāvati. || 19-227 ||
Whether few or many, she is the wealthy one who bestows primordial accomplishment;
she is the primordial knowledge, the primordial being, and the bestower of primordial accomplishment. || 19-228 ||
The goddess Satkārarūpiṇī is adorned with every seat;
she is Indriyapriyā, Indrāṇī, and Candrayatnatavāsinī. (19-229)
Indrākṣī, Indravajrā, and likewise Indramukhyakṣiṇī;
she who dwells at the tip of Ilā, Ra, the Sovereign, the beloved of the Lord. || 19-230 ||
She who is the mother of the gods and others, the cloud that performs the work of the Lord, Umā, Kātyāyanī, Ūrdhvamenā, and Uttaravāsinī. (19.231)
Umā is the beloved goddess, auspicious and embodied as the syllable Oṃ;
she is the daughter of the Ṛṣis, the meter of the Ṛṣis, and the bestower of perfection upon those seeking perfection. (19.232)
Utsavotsavasīmantā, Kālī, Kālī endowed with virtues;
she is the Vidyā of the letter *i*, as well as the Vidyādharā of the gazelle (*eṇī*). || 19-233 ||
Those who are the dissolution of the syllable *ai* are the supreme digit (*paramā-kalā*) of the syllable *aiṃ*;
she is the speech that speaks, *ai*, adorned with the syllable *iaṃ*. (19.234)
Aindrī, holding a thunderbolt in her hand, dwelling beyond the world of *aiṃ*;
she whose seed-syllable is in the midst of the syllable *oṃ*, and who bears the form of *oṃ namas*. (19–235)
She is the nature of the Supreme Brahman, the beloved of Aṃśuka and Aṃśuka;
she consists of the syllable *Aṃ*, ends with *Aḥ* and *Phaṭ*, and is adorned with the letters of the alphabet.
She has the form of both mantra and non-mantra, and is endowed with the recitation of speech;
she has the form of the *praṇava* and the *oṃkāra*, and furthermore, she partakes in the utterance of the *praṇava*.

She whose form is the syllable *hrīḥ*, who acts with modesty (*hrī*), whose ornaments are the seed-syllables of speech, who is the "scraper of the heart" (*hṛllekhā*), the union of accomplishment (*siddhiyoga*), and who is seated upon the lotus-heart. (19–238)
The seed-syllable known as Netrahṛdayā is Hrīḥ; the seed-syllable Bhuvaneśvarī is Klīṃ;
and Klinnā, the King of Desire (Kāmarāja), bestows the fruits of the four aims of life. || 19–239 ||
Klīḥ Klīḥ Klīḥ! The goddess Rūpikā, Krīḥ Krīḥ Krīḥ! She who bears that name, whose seed-syllable is the power of Kamalā, and who is adorned with the noose and the goad. || 19-240 ||
The Great Vidyā Śrīśrīkāra is then endowed with faith and lack of faith; Oṃ Ai Hrī Hrī is Śrīparā, and Hrī is Kālī Paramālā. (19–241)
She whose nature is the syllable Śrīṃ, the bestower of the fruits of all actions,
she is the Goddess who is the first of all, as well as the Sovereign of all accomplishments (sarvasiddhi).
The Goddess is omniscient and omnipotent, the bestower of the manifestation of speech;
she is the giver of all liberation and the bestower of all enjoyments.
O Goddess, you are most beloved by the Guṇas, the bestower of all powers,
the sovereign of all cakras, and likewise the sovereign of all siddhis.
She is the one who makes everything dear, the giver of happiness everywhere,
the goddess who bestows all praise, and she who is intent upon the supreme bliss of Brahman.
She who grants the heart's desires, worshipped by the intellect of the mind;
she whose form begins with the letter 'a' and ends with 'kṣa'; Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune.
Padmā, Hastā, and Sunetrā; Svadhā and Svahā, who bestows the *ṣṭ* sound; endowed with the *ka*-group, the *ṭa*-group, and the *pa*-group. (19–247)
Antasthā, Uṣmārūpā, Navadurgā, Narottamā, Navasiddhipradā, Nīlā, and likewise Nīlapatākinī. (19–248)
Nityarūpā, Niśikarī, Stambhanī, Mehinī, Vaśīkarī, Uccāṭī, and Umādinikarṣiṇī. (19–249)
Mātaṅgī, Madhumattā, Aṇimā, Laghimā, as well as Mokṣapradā, Nityā, and Nityānandapradāyinī. || 19-250 ||
With red limbs, red eyes, and adorned with red sandalwood, she possesses minor accomplishments; she is like a thorn [to the wicked] in the lineage of the divine heroes and the Śukras. (19-251)
The Transmigration and All-Knowledge, adorned by the seven days:
the first, the second, the third, and the fourth. (19–252)
The fifth and the sixth are indeed pure, as is the seventh;
likewise the eighth, the ninth, the tenth, and the eleventh.
The twelfth day, the fourteenth, the full moon, the new moon, as well as the prior and the subsequent full-moon days. (19-254)

She who holds the six [weapons], the wielder of the discus, the terrible one, the wielder of the mace and the trident, likewise the wielder of the bow, adorned with monkeys, and adorned with all weapons. (19.255)
She is the Mistress of the Kula, devoted to the Kula tradition,
deeply attached to the rites of the Kula, and the awakener of the Kula conduct.
Fame, Fortune, the Sovereign Goddess, the Garden of Delights—constant salutation to the Noble Dharma!
O you who consume the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree, you are Forgiveness, Fortitude, Memory, and Intelligence! 19-257.
The fierce Ugrā, O God, becomes manifest as the awakening Vidyā; she is likewise Sādhī, Siddhā, Susiddhā, and Ripurūpā. (19–258)
Kālī, Karālī, Kātyā, the destroyer of the Kāla-demon,
Kaulinī, Kulinī, and she who delights in the group of phlegm (kapha).
Victorious is Jayapuṣpā, and likewise Jayadā and Jṛmbhiṇī;
the goddess Śrīvinidrāvinī, Bhemaṇḍā, and Vahnivāsinī.
She is the form of light, the bestower of victory, and filled with garlands of flames;
she is both differentiated and non-differentiated radiance, the one who removes obstacles, and possesses diverse forms.
Aśvinī and Bharaṇī were born from the Vasu-nakṣatra;
Kaḍū was known as Vinatā, as well as Diti and Aditi. (19–262)
The goddess Kīrtivāmā is beloved; she is Kīrti, the increaser of fame.
She is instantly greedy for raw flesh, with hands that sever heads in the very house.
The southern, northern, eastern, and likewise the western direction; the south-eastern, south-western, southern, and the north-western direction are thus remembered. (19–264)
The upward-moving [power] is known as Dhoratā; she is black, red, and yellow.
She belongs to the four ages, possesses four colors, has four faces, and is manifested in four ways.
She is four-faced, possesses the four Vedas, is fourfold, and has four faces; she possesses the four qualities, the four measures, and bestows the fruits of the four castes. (19.266)
The woman who dwells in the abode of the Hero is of three types, consisting of the triad of the three pairs; she is the goddess, the giver of joy, the mistress of water, born from Meda and Nimeḍaka.
Ardhakālī, Siddhikālī, Dakṣiṇākālikā, Śivā, Nīlasarasvatī, Tārā, Vagalā, and Chinnamastakā. (19–268)
She is the sovereign of all, the accomplished science of knowledge, the supreme and non-supreme deity;
she is Hiṃgulā, whose limbs are vermilion, and who dwells upon the lower lip of Hiṃgula.
She has the excellent hue of vermilion, she is fond of the fire-drill of vermilion;
she is the earth, the mother of the world, and the beloved of the Lord of the World.
The goddess beloved by Janārdana, endowed with victory, fond of victory, the one who brings joy to the world, and the one who causes delight to the world. (19-271)
May she who bestows knowledge, the lore beloved by Jānaki and Janaka, who grants the fruit of recitation, and whose splendor is like a blazing fire, be ever victorious! (19-272)
Vimvodharā, Vimvoṣṭhī, Kailāsā, Calavāsinī, Vibhāvā, Vaibhavamaṭā, and Agnihotraphalapradā. (19-273)
O Goddess, you are the supreme form of mantra, and likewise the embodiment of the Guru;
you are Gayā, Gaṅgā, Gomatī, Prabhā, and Puṣkara as well. (19.274)
O Goddess, you who delight on the Vindhya mountain, you who dwell in the forests of the Vindhyas; O beautiful one with many arms, you who are the destroyer of the demon Kaṃsa.
Śulinī, holding a trident in her hand, and Vajrā, who also holds a thunderbolt;
Durgā, Śivā, the bringer of peace, Brāhmaṇī, the beloved of Brahmā. || 19-276 ||
She is the leader of all worlds and the destroyer of all worlds;
she is auspicious, beautiful, pure, partless, and the supreme source of all.
Viśvarī, Viśvamātā, Lalitā, Valitā, Valitāvalā, Sadāśivā, Umā, Kṣemā, Caṇḍikā, and Caṇḍivikramā. (19.278)
O Goddess, you who consist of all the gods, you who remove fear from every limb, you who are saluted by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and you who bring about every auspiciousness. (19.279)
Yoginī and Yogamāyā abide in the heart of the Lord of Yogins;
she who is born of Yoga, possessed of Yoga, O Lord of Yogins, is the Yoginī.
The Goddess who is bowed to by Indra and the other gods, the Sovereign beloved of Īśvara;
she bestows purity, removes fear, and strikes terror into those who hate her devotees.

She who assumes the guise of worldly existence, she who is full of desire, she who possesses a terrifying splendor, and she who performs wondrous deeds; she who consists of the five elements, she who is the sovereign power over all beings, and she who sustains the earth.
She who has a lion as her vehicle, she who is indeed to be honored, she who destroys the noose of delusion;
she who is full, the temple, the seal, and the bearer of the seal and the mallet.
And the great goddess Sāvitrī, who is beloved by others and brings about discipline;
likewise Piṅgākṣī, the messenger of Yama, as well as Vaiṣṇavī and Śāṅkarī.
Candrapriyā, Candranā, and Candanārarāpavāsinī;
she who is joined with the moon and the moon, and the destroyer of the fierce Daityas. (19-285)
She is the sovereign of all, the Yakṣiṇī, and likewise the Kirākṣasī;
she is the goddess who removes great sins and likewise removes great fears.
The Goddess who bestows great enjoyment, the giver of great liberation;
she who withdraws the universe, whose form is the universe, and who effects the dissolution of the universe.
She is the nurse of all the worlds, the benefactress of the gods;
she is the passionate one, the lotus-born, the subtle, the goddess to be pierced, and the one of great power.
She is worshipped by the Lord of the Gods, she is known as Sandhyā and Amatejavatī; she is the supreme goddess Bhūpavatī, whose form is the essence of the three worlds.
One thousand [verses].
Thus, O Goddess, this *Sahasranāma* (Thousand Names) of Pītā has been told to you.
Whether one recites it oneself or causes others to recite it, all perfections (*siddhi*) shall become dear. (19–291)
O Pārvatī, this supreme [mantra] for the sole purpose of great immobilization (*mahāstambha*), spoken by Viṣṇu to the two [sages] Iti and Ibhi,
should be recited at dawn, at midday, and during the evening twilight.
One should recite this once; all success will be attained.
For whoever recites it even once, there shall be the destruction of all sins. (19-292)
Whoever recites it on even days shall become like Gaṇeśa;
by reciting it three times, O Goddess, all perfections are attained—there is no other way. (19–293)
O you of excellent vows, through the power of this hymn, liberation is attained;
one who seeks liberation obtains liberation, and one who seeks wealth obtains wealth. (19.294)
A seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge along with the science of logic and its practical application;
like the lord of serpents [Garuda], he becomes a destroyer of enemies. (19-295)
O beloved, the king of the Vaśas was like Smara himself;
he who always recites this with devotion becomes endowed with prosperity. (19-296)
The representative of the head of the community, like another poet in his verse,
must always be concealed with great effort, just as a mother conceals her paramour.
He shall always be endowed with reason and always possessed of power;
he who recites this constantly shall become entirely one with Śiva. (19-298)
While living, she shall enjoy life, dharma, and wealth; upon death, she shall become a mistress of liberation.
This is the truth, the truth, O Great Goddess; this is the truth, the truth, O Maheśvarī. (19-299)
By the power of this hymn, he rejoices together with the god;
and all the asuras are paralyzed by the recitation of this king of hymns.

Thus ends the *Pitāmbarasahasranāmastotra* (The Thousand-Name Hymn of the Yellow-Robed One) within the *Nāgendraprayāṇatantra*, a work of sixteen thousand verses concerning the departure of the Lord of Nagas, spoken in the dialogue between Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara, composed in the year of the illustrious Utkaṇṭha.
[Salutation] to him who is clothed in yellow garments and anointed with yellow perfumes.
Through recitation, Surasundarī shall become the bestower of supreme bliss. || 19-301 ||
Now, the hymn to Pītāmbarā. 334a) Salutation to Śrī Pītāmbarā.
The cloth of the *oṃ* syllable, enclosed within two [syllables], is bound by the two veins of *māyā*.
In the center of that, one should write the pure invocation "galāmukhi" (O face of the throat) on all sides;
then "tuṣṭā" (the pleased one), or alternatively "mā śuca mukhaṃ saṃstambhaya" (do not grieve, O face, paralyze);
and "jihvāṃ kīlaya" (nail down the tongue) and "kalaya" (control it). Likewise, one should destroy the intellect. || 19-302 ||
The Brahmāstra, which generates the accomplishment of all goals and consists of thirty-six syllables,
was proclaimed of old by the Lotus-born One for the conquest of the worlds;
it shines in the mouths of those whose threefold intellects illuminate the state of liberation.
May you be the rays of the moon in the nectar-ocean that dispels the pairs of opposites, and may you be the cakora birds for whom those rays are a necklace. (2) || 19-303 ||
Victory to You, O Śivā, whose essential nature is the primordial sound (*drōṇi*), from whom speech— containing within it the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*)—
is manifested in the form of clear syllables for the sake of others by Brahmā and the other gods;
who, though sought even by the five elements, is sinless, accessible through the awakening of consciousness, and difficult to know except through the practice of yoga.
It is somehow grasped by the mind of yogins. (3) || 19-304 ||
He in whose heart the seed-syllable *hrīḥ* shines with purity possesses stable fortune in his home; his fortitude remains even in the midst of adversity, and his lifespan on this earth is long.
Furthermore, the stainless creeper of his lineage flourishes even until the end of the kalpa.
He attains valor and steadfastness before him, and his adversaries flee from him. (4) || 19-305 ||
The Lord of Janaka’s daughter, intent on rescuing his bride, meditated upon you, O wearer of yellow robes,
and thus constructed a bridge during the recent drying up [of the ocean];
having conquered the fierce enemy Rāvaṇa, the King of the Gods released the captive women.
O Ambikā, he composed this [work] which brings about fame, worldly happiness, and prosperity, and which shall endure for an eon. (19.306)
When Śrī Nityāva melts, the earth shrivels its head and becomes a beggar, speech becomes mute, fire becomes cold, the wicked man acts like a saint, and Vāsuki turns into a flower;
thus has she been made into a mechanical puppet by your syllables and words.
If the crown, though as radiant as the sun, falls while being restrained by the cooing of peacocks, [the king will perish]. (6) || 19-307 ||
O Lāvaṇyā, your compassion, which is filled with nectar, has entered the body of this man;
even though he is the very embodiment of Brahmā, Indra, and the other lords of the quarters, they perceive him as being like a blade of grass.
Yet those in whose hearts resides that power capable of protecting the universe, which rests upon the throat of Śiva, [perceive him differently].
They cause beings who have been initiated to become even more firm, making them free from obstacles by means of obstacles. (7) || 19-308 ||
It is no wonder that a man attains preeminence in your assembly through a mere sidelong glance;
rather, it is a marvel that he himself becomes capable of destroying the path of creation!
For by his mere thought, the world appears as "mine," and at the mere breath of him, your very vision [of the world] vanishes.
Indeed, all [the siddhis], beginning with *aṇimā*, will certainly and exceedingly propitiate him. (8) || 19-309 ||
O Ocean, you who stand there bestowing boons upon the weary mariners;
O Moon-faced One, you who wear yellow garments, the Supreme Śivā, who take refuge even in those terrified by lions, tigers, and the like amidst dense thickets and mountain caves.
I worship her who holds a double-headed mace in her hand and, with her left hand, uproots a sword. (9) || 19-310 ||
O Vagala, those who prostrate at will before your two feet clad in yellow garments obtain all perfections exceeding their desires; furthermore, O protectress,
the seeker of your grace now performs that which is most difficult to accomplish.
That gaze of yours, with its sidelong glance from the corner of your eye, appears as if it were conscious. (10) || 19-311 ||

That speech of yours, consisting of the liquid essence of the nectar of liberation, adorned upon your mouth, and bringing about the fulfillment of [your] curses— speech that is the sole kinsman of the delight of poets— only one of vast intellect would be capable of explaining it; yet this servant of yours attempts to do so with his voice.
If even a small portion of that [reality] were to manifest within the abode of ten million cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa), (11) || 19-312 ||

O Goddess, because they have beheld your devotion, the mountains, headed by Himavat, become like mere dust; time and its cycles become like garlands of flowers; the Nagas attain the state of being like the rays of the nectar-moon;
Indra and the lords of speech resort to silence; and the oceans attain a state of incomparable stillness.
King Samudra does not possess a state of insignificance; his enemies flee, scattered and routed in battle. (16) || 19-313 ||
Having beheld the stainless seed-mantra of the mantra-king, which has the power to paralyze, subjugate, attract, slay, pierce, agitate, and expel the flood of evil beings,
the foot of this Foremost One— clear as a vajra— is manifest and awake within his heart and mouth.
Those enemies who wander about as lords of the seven continents have been struck down at his feet. (13) || 19-314 ||

She is the supreme Goddess of Jewels, adorned with stainless gems of various kinds, residing on an island in an ocean of nectar; she dwells within the forest of Kṛṣṇa’s face during the eon-fire, seated upon a lion-throne consisting of a lotus formed by five corpses fashioned from thread.
I meditate upon her who creates compassion, who surpasses Hari and Hara, and who grants all desired objects. (14) || 19-315 ||

O Goddess of Speech, you reside in the mouth; O Lakṣmī, you grant prosperity through the *Satyavrata-tantra*; O Anandā, you are ever compassionate toward the heart; and O Vīrā, you always bestow heroism in battle.
For your devotee, the dawning of reality occurs to cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
Those who do not perceive this world as having the appearance of a lotus leaf floating upon water—(15) || 19-316 ||

I meditate upon you, who possess four arms and three eyes, with a fierce countenance and a protruding tongue, whose garments are yellow like refined gold, who is radiant with a crescent moon as an ornament, and who wears armlets, bracelets, necklaces, and earrings— manifested for the arising of devotion.
You alone draw out the wicked from the depths of hell, and you alone are my protection in the throat of danger. (19-317)

O Mother, the greatness of Your formidable power has been proclaimed by humans through their own words, according to their capacity and with great effort; yet, O Goddess whose abode is the lotus, even the Lord of the gods [Viṣṇu] is unable to describe it fully due to his own limitations.
You alone are omnipresent, eternally praised as being both existent and non-existent, yet always having the form of existence. (17) || 19-318 ||
The wind causes the lame-legged Tārkṣya to exert himself with great effort, yet the lame-legged one exceeds Tārkṣya; O Śivā, that manifest power which lies within the water and fire in the bed,
that seed is "vagalati," and it is always joined with basil (tulasī) and remains pure.
That which is difficult even for Brahmā and others to attain is obtained by those endowed with their former vital merits. (18) || 19-319 ||
Even the wind becomes motionless before him who wears yellow robes; were the ocean but a mere water-lily stalk to him, and Mount Meru but a single bean,
while the celestial palaces of Kalpavṛkṣa, Kāmadhenu, and others stand as his jeweled porticos.
One who quickly gives musical instruments, water for honor, and abundant gifts, even when distressed, brings prosperity to oneself and to others as well. (19) || 19-320 ||
By whose grace pure knowledge, beginning with the *Diśoṣā* and others, shines forth from the mouth—
knowledge consisting of thirty-six syllables, proclaimed with many virtues and seed-mantras (*bījas*) that grant all goals—
to all those lords of sages, gods, and brahmins, I bow down.
His own creative power has pervaded the remaining great manifestation and has traversed the abode of the three worlds. (20) || 19-321 ||
Whatever pure jewel shines in the world that bestows great bliss, whatever noble conduct gives birth to that which is supremely beautiful,
or whatever exists that is not cast down by the sound of "bhūta"— [all these belong to her].
All that, O Vagālā, who bestows liberation from saṃsāra, is indeed your very form. (19-322)

Those men who, while awake, are filled with the nectar of His abundant compassion and, for a moment, possess minds fixed on the vow that bestows all goals within His glorious sidelong glance— even though they have fallen into the ocean of worldly existence—
their fortune is beyond the senses, such that even Brahmā and the other gods are unable to describe it.
O you who are incapable of protecting others from the constructions of mere conceptualization and discursive thought—this is the cause for your [suffering]. (22) || 19-323 ||

Having grasped his bow in hand, which was heavy with a multitude of arrows, whatever he bestowed upon the enemy in the great battle— whether it be the mastery of the Brahma-weapon or the skill acquired through arduous penance in duels—
all that was witnessed by the hosts of gods and the Siddhas who fanned the chariot of his foe; such was his valor, worthy of praise.
O you who wear yellow garments, all that night shines as your own splendor. (23) || 19-324 ||
Those men who meditate upon the Goddess— who wears a pair of swaying earrings hanging from her ears,
who holds in her hand the crescent moon, bracelets, armlets, nooses, mallets, clubs, and the vajra,
and who is adorned with yellow ornaments— quickly attain auspiciousness through the destruction of the hosts of Māras.
From the intense [practice], there is incomparable perfection and the state of a Kevalin. (24) || 19-325 ||
The compassionate glance of the Lord, which possesses a splendor that leaves no room for any other source of attainment, is capable of uprooting even the most deluded multitude of women;
yet, O Lord of Wealth, how many times has this world of three realms been bitten by the fangs of the Sun, who bears such ill-formed breasts?
In an instant, he surpassed even the pride of Kandarpa. (25) || 19-326 ||

Those for whom there is that [yantra]— the victorious, the pacifier of manifold sufferings, situated within the supreme *tītha*, established upon the two syllables *Tāva* and *Kāra*, encompassing all desired objects, triple-encircled,
with its outer circle consisting of eight petals, and surrounded by the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
By the power of their destiny, they dwell there, capable of creating the universe. (26) || 19-327 ||
Those men who daily worship the feet of Vagale with camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, musk, gorocana, and saffron,
attain wonderful prosperity and enjoyments for a long time on this earth; having attained that [state], they enter the supreme union.
One should not look at anything that is excessive; this is the supreme [rule]. (27) || 19-328 ||
O Śivā, having found delight in the pair of your feet, even a lowly person attains the status of the Lord of the Gods and sports in heaven with the stainless enjoyments of celestial beauties;
whereas those men who, devoid of speech, abandon devotion to you and remain indifferent for a long time, fall from their high state.
But those who have turned their backs on the Dharma carry this burden here in this world. (28) || 19-329 ||

By worshipping whom Śiva attained the state of being Hara, and Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, attained the state of being Hari; and by whom even the entire ocean of speech was purified and rendered sweet;
even the sun, though he too wears yellow robes, swiftly removes all darkness merely by meditating upon him—[to that Lord] [Śukra], at the end of his curse, spoke.
Even the Lord, with his crest-jewel resting [upon him], was made to blush by the act of desiring her. (29) || 19-330 ||
"O Vagalāmukhi, grant us prosperity, destroy the wicked, paralyze the movement of those who utter evil names against us,
crush the treacherous, slay the malicious, and protect the virtuous for a long time— those who, having thus obtained the power of your words, shall recite [this prayer]."
Those who, once mounted upon it, are always capable of making the entire mass of water vanish. (30) || 19-331 ||
O Vagala, having meditated upon you in the past, Śiveśvara offered the fallen sacrificial oblation (*bali*) into the fire of his resolve;
at that moment, the daughter of the Mountain, her power melting away, joyfully entered that fire. Therefore, you are known as Kāgalī.
She is called Vagalāmukhī, the eternal, supreme Yoginī. (31) || 19-332 ||

O Goddess, you are eternally unassailable by the lords of the nāgas, the gods, the hosts of the best of sages, the dānavas, the lords of the rākṣasas, the guardians of the quarters, the lords of the elephants of the directions, the sun and other luminaries,
the tāla-demons and their like, and by Brahmā and others, whether gross or subtle; you are the supreme, the state beyond the mind.
Clad in yellow garments, she who pacifies the fear of enemies resides upon the hearts of her devotees. (32) || 19-333 ||

At this festival of the Tandava dance, Śambhu, whose mind is intent on singing the praises of the six qualities [of the Lord], has placed the *nīrājana* offering at his feet under the guise of causing the moonbeams to tremble.
This worship is performed by the golden lotus petals of the mountain peaks, which are filled with water and made joyful by the silent sages. It is an offering that increases day by day.
[He was honored] with thousands of salutations and other [gestures of reverence]. (33) || 19-334 ||

O you whose form consists of the syllables of the six chakras! She whom even the four-faced Brahmā holds in his mouth seated upon a lotus; she whom Hari embraces on his chest, seated upon Śeṣa and clad in yellow garments; she whom the conqueror of cities (Śiva) took as half of his own body, his sister and wife—[salutations to her].
The goddess who protects the world was on Bhajamukha’s face. (34) || 19-335 ||
In his hand, the mace always shines, subduing all suffering; on his jewel-adorned arm is a bracelet, and his feet are illuminated by the gems of his excellent anklets.
On his neck is a necklace, and upon his ear is a mark of musk paste applied forever.
To you who possess the auspiciousness of the left-hand path and who contemplate the yellow umbrella, [I offer salutations]. (35) || 19-336 ||

Those who know, worship, constantly meditate upon, or sing the praise of her— who resides within the enclosure of two *Śrī*-syllables, who is established in the *Vidyā-āgama*, who consists of thirty-six syllables formed from the essence of the seed-syllables of the six cakras— they move about, venerable to the awakened ones.
In this world, they are perfected for the sake of attaining perfection. (36) || 19-337 ||
Svāhā is the form, Śivāsana is the seat, the seer is the illustrious Nārada, and the deity is declared to be the auspicious Vagalāmukhī; the meter is Triṣṭubh, composed of the fourfold Māyā,
and it is said to consist of various types of stambhana (paralysis/immobilization), bearing the splendor of a lotus.
The subsequent application is also a factor [of action]. (37) || 19.338 ||
This heart-pleasing and wonderful hymn, which is difficult even for the lords of all the gods and the sages to obtain, should therefore be kept secret.
Those who, by virtue of their own good fortune, obtain it, shall live for six months after having conquered the god with eloquent speech and the giver of wealth with riches. (337b)
Through battles with Śiva, she will sport with you, becoming equal to Śiva himself. (38) || 19-339 ||
The Goddess, appearing in a dream, gave me a marvelous painting of her own name; before me, a divine weapon fell, spotless and with lines the color of vermilion.
With my hair disheveled by the thrill of joy and my body bristling with horripilation, I attained supreme bliss as I beheld it.
This supreme knowledge was [revealed] by Kavindra and others. (39) || 19-340 ||
I have obtained from the mouth of the venerable Vagalāmukhī this *Sad-bīja-ratnāvalī*, consisting of thirty-six verses, which is my own composition preeminent for its singular excellence;
when it rests upon the necks of those who possess it, it shines forth, capable of providing sustenance to the world.
In the rites of subjugation, attraction, delusion, and killing, as well as in paralyzing and opening [the gates], (40) || 19-341 ||
Thus ends the Śrī Pitāmbara Ratnāvalī Stotra in its entirety:
[I bow to her] whose beautiful cheeks are made to shine by the swaying golden earrings,
who possesses the radiant luster of a blooming golden campaka flower, and whose face is like the moon.

I remember Vagalamukhi, who has struck down her adversaries with her mace, whose tongue is curled and lolling, who is ever-active, and who paralyzes the flow of speech from those who turn their faces away [from her].
Salutations to the venerable Pitāmbara.

Oṃ. Of this mantra of the Śrī Vagalāmukhī Stotra, the venerable Lord Nārāyaṇa is the Seer (Ṛṣi), the venerable Vagalāmukhī is the Deity (Devatā), and the Bṛhatī is the Metre (Chanda). [It is employed] against those wicked persons who are in close proximity.

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of paralyzing those who are distant and hostile by means of the tongue of their mouths and feet, for the sake of my own success, for the destruction of adversaries, and for the pleasure of the venerable Vagalamukhi during the recitation of the hymn and mantra. (1)

One should meditate upon that Vagalāmukhī, who is clad in yellow garments, possesses beautiful eyes, has two arms, blazes with the syllables *dā* and *hṛṃ*, and holds a rock and a mountain in her hands. (2) 19-343.
In the center, upon a jeweled pedestal within a pavilion of gems, seated on a lion-throne,
I salute the Goddess whose body is of a deep yellow hue, adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and garlands, who holds a sword and has seized the tongues of her enemies.
Having meditated upon the Goddess who holds a trident, who bestows all good fortune, and who is adorned with every elegant ornament and attire, one should worship her. (4) 19-345.
I meditate upon Vagalāmukhī, whose beautiful cheeks shine with trembling golden earrings, who possesses the radiant luster of a blooming golden campaka flower,
whose face is like the full moon, who has struck down her adversaries with her mace, and whose tongue flickers playfully from her hand.
Turning away, facing toward, and paralyzing. (5) || 19-346 ||
O Goddess, seated upon a throne of skulls that rests on the crest of a lion-throne within a radiant orb of shimmering nectar-like curd,
you possess a golden luster; with your hand you crush the tongues of your enemies, and you possess the splendor of a whirling mace.
For whomever it will go, all obstacles immediately dissolve away. (19.347)
O Goddess, the practitioner who places an offering of yellow flowers or a mudrā upon your lotus feet, and then, with a beautiful mantra,
meditates upon you while mastering the supreme *kuṃbhaka* breath, should contemplate the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of that [deity] whose face is like that of a friend.
The voice will become paralyzed in the heart in an instant. (7) || 19-348 ||

O Mother Śrī Vagalāmukhī, your mantra is sufficient for crushing adversaries; your hymn is pure, and your yantra is the instrument for those who debate, the instrument for the three worlds, and it is pure. For one by whom your name is praised with its charming syllables, "Śrī Vagalāmukhī," through the utterance of that name—
At that moment, the mouth of the disputant becomes paralyzed. (8) || 19-349 ||

O eternal Vagalāmukhī, when restrained by your sound, the eloquent become mute, the king becomes a pauper, the lord of the universe becomes destitute, the extremely wrathful becomes peaceful, the wicked man becomes a virtuous one, the foul-mouthed becomes lame, the arrogant is humbled, and everyone becomes dull-witted day after day.
Homage to you for eons! (9) || 19-350 ||
O Death, [grant me] that which subdues the wicked, pacifies fierce obstacles, destroys poverty,
brings about union with the earth, and attracts deer-eyed women; that which is the sole abode of good fortune for my eyes and is filled with compassion.
O Mother, may this form of yours appear before me for my destruction. (10) || 19-351 ||

You are the supreme knowledge, O Mother of the three worlds, the destroyer of the flood of obstacles, the female elephant-driver for the ears of men, and the sole eradicator of the pairs of deluded opposites. You are the performer of wicked enchantments, the creator of infatuation in the minds of people, and the paralyzer of the tongue.
The supreme science of the Brahmāstra weapon was mastered by Vairbhava. (11) || 19-352 ||

O Mother, paralyze the faces of my enemies; nail down their flickering tongues with the Brahmī Mudrā; arrest the movement of the fire of their intellects! O fair-limbed one clad in yellow garments, quickly pulverize, pulverize my foes with your wrathful gaze! O Destroyer of the multitude of sins!
O Hara, you whose eyes are daily filled with compassion! (12) || 19-353 ||
O Mātā Bhairavī, O Bhadrakālī, O Vijayā, O Vārāhī, O refuge of the universe, O Śrī Nityā, O Samayā, O Maheśī,
O Vagalā, O Kāmā, O Śivā, O Ramā; O Mātaṅgī, O Tripurā, O you who are higher than the highest, O bestower of heaven and liberation— may my sin, which has arrived like a hunter’s arrow, be destroyed.
O Sovereign of the Universe, protect me out of compassion! (13) || 19-354 ||
In a battle with Sakti weapons, amidst a multitude of thieves, at the time of striking a blow, during an execution, in the midst of water, in fire, in a formal debate, in a dispute,

during the time of an enraged king or the like, at night; when subject to censure, in the act of paralyzing, at the time of slaying an enemy, in the removal of poison, or in battle— whether moving or standing still— one should [employ this].
This [practice] for reciting the hymn at the time of night bestows the accomplishment of one's purpose. (14) || 19-355 ||
If a man always recites this hymn of the Goddess with devotion, while wearing this yantra on his arm, hand, or neck at the proper time,
kings, beautiful women, thieves, serpents, lions, and the wicked will all become paralyzed before him.
Fortune that has gone to an enemy is as difficult to recover as it is for a gambler to regain what he has lost. (15) || 19-356 ||
The practitioner who recites this daily, which is delightful at the three times of day, becomes pure among the hosts of gods;
all his undertakings succeed, and being seen in the world, he becomes honored by the world as one who has attained supreme siddhi.
Those [verses] are likewise (16). || 19-357 ||
Thus ends the *Pītāmbarā-stotra* composed by the venerable Nārada.
This concludes the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vagalāmukhī Mantras," in the *Āgamakalpalatā*.
As it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
On the Kulāṣṭamī day according to family custom, and especially on the fourteenth day, the worship of the Yoginīs is performed there; therein, the Kula-worship is paramount. (20.1)
Just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on the lunar day sacred to Viṣṇu, bestows prosperity, so too Durgā, when worshipped on the lunar day sacred to the Kula, grants boons.
The sequence of the days of the week and so forth is as follows;
it is stated in the Rudrayāmala: "O Umā, the Sun, the Moon, Jupiter, and Saturn—these four are the Ālās."
Mars and Venus are called *kula*, while Wednesday is *kulākula*. (20.3)
The third, tenth, and sixth are declared to be *kulākula*; the first, fifth, ninth, eleventh, and full moon are the *kula* lunar days (*tithi*). (20.4)
The second, fourth, eighth, twelfth, and fourteenth lunar days are the *kula* dates; all odd-numbered dates are *akula*, and all remaining lunar days are *kula*. (20.5)
From Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) to Ābhijit, ending with Mūla, the Kulas are said to be the odd-numbered asterisms;
the remaining even-numbered ones are the Akulas. (20.6)

On any lunar day, weekday, or asterism, victory belongs to one who abides in the non-family (akula). One who abides in the so-called family (kula) is always victorious; likewise, there is equality for one who abides in both the family and the non-family (kulākula). (20.7)
Having understood the lineage and so forth, one should not perform the rite of the practitioner;
on the day before the commencement of the ritual, one should offer bali-oblations to the Śivās.
Śiva describes the manner of offering the *bali*:
as it is stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*,
"At the root of a *vilva* tree or in a secluded spot," and so forth, ending with "Salutations again and again to Śivā."
Thus, in the section on the offering (*bali*) to Śivā within the *Nīlasarasvatī-prakaraṇa*, it is written: "Now, herein is the complete definition of the six rites (*ṣatkarma*),
which, according to all tantras, grants the accomplishment of the fruits of practice."
Then follow pacification, subjugation, immobilization, and so forth, as well as causing enmity and schism. (20.9)
The wise ones constantly perform the six rites known as "slaying" (māraṇa), which bring about the destruction of diseases, malevolent spells, planetary influences, and the like. (20.10)

The subjugation of all people is declared to be "bringing under control" (vaśya); the awakening of activity is "arousing" (pravṛtti), and all [other effects] are described as "paralyzing" (stambhana). || 20-11 ||
It is considered to produce mutual enmity and generate aversion among those who are already hostile;
it is proclaimed to cause one's expulsion from one's own country. (20-12)
The taking of life from living beings is declared [to be the first]; causing distress to those who are affectionate and inciting mutual hatred is considered [the second]. (20.13)
Having known one's own deity, the directions, time, and so forth, one should accomplish the ritual action. The deities are, in sequence: Gati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī. (20.14)
The deities of the six rites have been declared; one should worship those presiding over the rites.
The directions are considered to belong to Īśa, Candra, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Agni. (20.15)

One should perform the rite for peace in the directions beginning with the north (the direction of Śānti), either according to this sequence, or starting from sunrise and proceeding in order through each one-hour period (ghaṭikā). (20–16)
The seasons, beginning with spring, occur day after day;
in each [season], there are ten *ghaṭikās*, and thus the ritual actions are performed ten times. (20.17)
In a single day and night there are six seasons, divided ten by ten: spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season. (20.18)
Hemanta is declared for the purpose of subduing enemies; Vasanta is for necessary rites;
Śiśira is to be known for immobilizing; and Grīṣma is said to be for causing dissension. (20.19)
The rainy season is to be known for the act of subduing, and autumn for the rite of killing.
By means of the skins of a ram, a tiger, an elephant, a camel, a wolf, and a snake, the practitioner should always perform various seats for each of the six rites for the sake of success.
Again the lotus-eyed, the svastika, then the formidable, and again the cock.
The wise call the Vajra "Auspicious" (Bhadraka);
it is used for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, causing hatred, expulsion, and killing. (20–21)
Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭ, Huṃ, Vauṣaṭ, and Phaṭ—these are to be known as the mudrās of the [six] objects in their respective order: the lotus, the noose, the mace, and the sword. (20–22)

In rites such as the peaceful (śāntika) and others—namely the pestle, thunderbolt, and sword—the six maṇḍalas should be prepared for the six types of ritual acts. For the rite of pacification, fire is declared to be auspicious;
for subjugation, it is said to be fire.
For the purpose of immobilization, the Earth is praised; for causing enmity, the Sky is proclaimed.
In the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the wind is considered dead; in the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), fire is considered dead.
That [element] should be present during the rising of its respective element, conjoined with its corresponding *maṇḍala*. (20–24)
Then that rite should be performed by the minister with a resolute mind:
cold, excellent water, earth, space, wind, and fire. (20–25)
Dārvī, tuṣa, eka,
grathana, virbhā, saṃyuta, rodhana, yoga, and lava— these are the six types of placement (vinyāsa) for the six rites.

One should perform the crossing over of the *mātṛkā*s according to the rules, syllable by syllable; one should know that this stringing together is highly praised for the ritual of pacifying (*śānti*). (20–27)
One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished situated between two pairs of mother-vowels; this is known as *vidarbha* by practitioners for rites of subjugation. (20–28)
When the mantra begins and ends with the name, it is known as a "sandwiched" (saṃpuṭa) mantra;
this is prescribed by those who know mantras for the purpose of paralyzing. (20–29)
The mental recitation of the mantra by means of its name at the beginning, middle, and end is declared to be highly praised in the ritual procedures for causing enmity. (20-30)
The application of the mantra at its end is for subjugation; the mind is directed toward expulsion.
A mantra with the name [of the target] at the beginning is for attraction; it is held that [a mantra] with sprouts [at the end] is for killing. (20–31)
White, red, yellow, and blackish-grey are proclaimed as the colors of the mantras for the six deities in the six types of ritual acts.
The substances for writing mantras are sandalwood, blue lotus, turmeric, soot from a house, charcoal, and poisons for rites of killing. (20.33)
White arsenic, salt, bile, the juice of *dattūra*, ghee, house-soot, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), and the eight poisons (*viṣāṣṭaka*)—these constitute the mudrā. (20.34)

Niśā, haridrā, gṛhadhūma, and hāyā are well-known; these are not [the same as] those well-known [substances]. Agni, citraka, loṇapitta, atilavaṇa, mūla, and trikaṭuka—namely śuṇṭhī, pippalī, and marica—the wise one, having understood the deities, kālamudga, and so forth, along with the grains.
One should employ the sixfold ritual for the sake of attaining the results as described. || 20-35 ||

Now, the rites for prosperity and so forth, which are to be performed according to the conjunctions of specific days and lunar dates, shall be explained here in accordance with the prescribed ritual. (20-36)
The fifth, second, third, and likewise the seventh lunar days,
when conjoined with Wednesday, are victorious for rites of pacification (śāntika).
The ninth day is praised for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), as are the eighth and tenth;
likewise, the tenth and eleventh days, when conjoined with the sun's transit (saṃkrānti).
For the rite of attraction, the new moon, the ninth day, the first day of the lunar fortnight,
and likewise the full moon joined with Sunday are prescribed for the rite of causing enmity.
Likewise, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and the eighth day of the month of Mādhava are auspicious lunar days for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana),
especially at the time of dusk.
The fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnight, especially the new moon,
as well as Saturdays and Tuesdays, are praised when yellow is used for rites of killing.
The fifth and tenth lunar days occurring on Wednesday or Monday,
as well as the full moon day, should be known as the appropriate dates for the rite of immobilization (staṃbhana).
A benefic planet at the rising of the day (lagna) brings about auspicious results, as does a benefic at the rising of the sun;
whereas a malefic planet, on the Riktā tithi, or when the sun is present, or during the Mṛtyu yoga, effects killing.
Now I shall explain the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) according to various tantras;
this is stated in the *Śāradātilaka*,
where it describes the application of the *Tvaritā* mantra:
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ hrīḥ hūṃ khecaradeva hrīḥ phaṭ.
Ten thousand recitations and baths are proclaimed as the required count.

One should perform the oblation here with blunt [materials]; having performed the *nijeṣkṛyā*, one should perform the oblation for the pacification of burning and other afflictions, but not with *palāśa* flowers. (20.44)
A small amount of water consecrated with that mantra, when placed in the mouth, removes poison;
one should give it to the afflicted person, having been empowered by the recitation of the mantra by the practitioner.
One is liberated from all diseases by the power of this mantra. Now follows the application of the Durgā-maṇḍala:
Oṃ hrīḥ duṃ, obeisance to Durgā.
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should then begin the Prayāga rite.
Having constructed the maṇḍala adorned with yantras,
one should perform the consecration according to the ritual rules for the sake of attaining all siddhis.
Having established these auspiciously marked footprints upon pure ground,
he should smear all their limbs with sandalwood paste and provide them with *durvā* grass and unbroken rice grains.
With eyes covered by a golden bandage, they filled them with water from the sacred sites;
[the bandages] were set with the nine gems and fashioned from refined gold.
The most excellent of teachers should place a lotus, together with the mantra and other ingredients, into the central jar:
sandalwood, ushira, camphor, nutmeg, kakkola, and saffron. (20.50)
Having ground kuṣṭha, aguru, tamāla, and elā together,
one should stir it into all the jars and also cast gems into them.
Lakṣī, dūrvā, sadābhadrā, mahādevī, madhuvratā, mumulī, śakuvallā, krāntā, apāmārga, and padmaka. (20.52)
Having washed priyaṅgu, mudga, wheat, vrihi, masha, tila, barley, śāli, taṇḍula, and mārṣa grains, one should place them therein.
Having also cast away the fruits of the dhātrī, vitvat, kadalī, and nārikela trees, one should cast down these flowers.
One should know the *padma*, the *saugandhika*, the *jāni*, and likewise the *mallikā* and *kula*; as well as the *caṇḍā*, *pāṭalā*, *aśoka*, *putrā*, *tulasī*, *ketakī*, and *bhava*. (20.55)
Having placed the sprouts of the banyan, the holy fig, the Plakṣa, and the Dūṃvara trees, as well as the Brahmakūrca, into cups accompanied by fruits and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Then, covering the jar-mouths with silken cloths, he filled them;
having diligently worshipped the Goddess in the primary *aṭṭā* water-pot on the path, [he proceeded]. (20.57)
And having worshipped the others with effort, the recitation (japa) is superior;
Jayā, Vijayā, Kīrti, Prīti, and again Pañcaprabhā. (20.58)
Śraddhā is declared to be Saurā, beginning with the first letter of her own name;
[the mantra] begins with "Obeisance to Vijayā" and so forth.
Having worshipped [her] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should consecrate the lord of men.
The king who conquers through dharma conquers his enemies;
he attains prosperity, long life free from disease, and is liberated from all ailments. (20.60)
Whatever boon one obtains through the rite of the twilight ablution (saṃdhyābhiṣeka),
that same result is attained by ghee consecrated with another mantra, which destroys minor planetary afflictions.
This practice of Mahiṣamardinī is especially protective for the fetus of pregnant women. The mantras are as follows:
"Mahiṣamardini svāhā.
Having recited the mantra eight hundred thousand times, one should then perform the ritual application.
If the mantra-practitioner performs a fire-oblation with *siddhārtha* seeds, he is instantly liberated from passions;
by offering lotuses, he conquers his enemies, and with *dūrvā* grass, he shall attain peace. (20.63)
Now follows the application of the mantra of Śūlinī.
The mantra is as follows: *jvala jvala śūlini dṛṣṭagrahaṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having recited the mantra of the Pañcarakṣā, the wise one should perform the ritual application.
Therefore, when one has meditated upon that goddess who bestows the thick clouds of death with weapons in her hands,
and having seen her, recites the mantra while identifying oneself with her, the seizing spirit is released from him.
The poison of all [creatures], such as scorpions and others, shall be swiftly destroyed.
Now follows the application of the Navadurgā mantra. The mantra is as follows:
HŪṂ! Arise, O Puruṣī! Whatever fear has arisen for me—whether it be possible or impossible—may it be pacified, svāhā!
Having recited the mantra thirty-seven times for four hundred thousand repetitions, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual applications.
Having offered ten thousand oblations on a fire kindled with excellent fuel-sticks from a banyan tree that possesses thorns, he shall destroy all calamities and distress. (20.67)
For long-distance sorcery, one should employ messengers and the like according to this ritual procedure at the proper time,
using either apāmārga plants with their roots, or sesame seeds grown in the forest.
Or, a *mālāmantra* made with mustard seeds destroys minor diseases;
one should recite it while touching the door-post, the house, or a serpent. (20.69)
Having touched it, the goddess Śūlakarī would instantly carry off the deity;
therefore, one should have a weapon fashioned from the Brahmavṛkṣa tree by a skilled artisan.
Having placed the conch, the discus, the chariot-wheel, the Śārṅga bow, and the Kaumodakī mace into the five products of the cow, and having touched them, one should mutter the mantra.
Having again prepared five thousand [offerings] among them correctly,
one should offer them with their respective mantras while worshipping in due order.
The mantra for the conch is as follows: *jaladharāya svāhā*. The mantra for the sword is as follows:
Cut, cut the paths! Shatter, shatter into pieces! As for the mantra of the wheel: *Sudarśana mahācakrarājāya svāhā*.
O terrifier of all the wicked, cut! rend! rend! supreme protector, devourer, destroy! destroy! cause to tremble! cause to tremble! *hūṃ* *hūṃ* *phaṭ*. Homage to the Discus (*cakrāya namaḥ*).
The mantra of the Śārṅga bow is as follows:
"Omnisvāhā! To the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, together with his arrow, svāhā! O Kaumodakī of great power, destroyer of all asuras, be gracious, be gracious, phaṭ svāhā!
Having extracted [the mantra], one should worship this [deity] in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as before.
One should perform the initiation in the five groves, beginning with the center and so forth, according to the rule.

Then, in his own pit, the practitioner should place the full vessel with flowers upon a mat, preceded by the fivefold sounds over the consecrated weapons; having arranged them in those [pits] starting from the center, he should perform the worship as before. (20.74)
It should be filled with sand as it was before;
having filled it with sand, one should make it level and easy to traverse with earth. (20.75)
And one should scatter an offering there with their respective mantras in due order;
having given the offering to the guardians of the directions, one should then feed the Brahmins.
One should satisfy the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others with food and other necessities;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to the extent of one's own wealth.
In whatever place—whether in a country, a district, a city, a village, or a house—this knowledge is established by means of the yantra, there all prosperities increase. (20.78)
Defects such as fires and portents, associations with spirits and ghosts, sorcery, malevolent spells, and calamities arising from the hostility of enemies and the like; (20.79)
When the asterism is *todi*, the deity should be known as one threatened by fear.
Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) for Mātaṅgī.
The mantra is as follows:

Ai Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, Mātaṅgeśvarī, who captivates the minds of all people, who delights the faces of all, who brings all kings under control, who subjugates all women and men, and who brings all wild beasts under control; may she bring [the person named] so-and-so under control, Svāhā!
The mantra consists of eighty-eight syllables; having recited the mantra ten thousand times, one should then perform the ritual application.
The fire kindled with *vañjula* wood does not spread its flame for a long time;

however, when oblations of sugar-candy soaked in milk are offered, it blazes up. By offering oblations of the root of *amṛtā* and *nirguṇḍī*, a man is released from poison that has entered his body. (20.81)
*Nirguṇḍī* is commonly known as *saṃbhālū*.
Now follows the application of the fire-mantra:
"O tawny-colored man, give me red; svāhā!"
Having gone for the morning bath, one should employ the mantra a thousand times.
Having conquered diseases and lived happily for a hundred years, a man, standing in water reaching up to his heart and gazing at the sun while remaining composed, [attains liberation]. || 20-83 ||
A person should constantly recite it four thousand times until the end of their life; [thereby] the fear of untimely death, disease, sorcery, and the occurrence of poverty [are removed]. (20.84)
Having destroyed the afflictions, the radiant one shall live happily for a hundred years;
O King, he should perform sacrifice before the two fires while the lamp is filled with oil.

"Jyotiṣmatī, mālā, and kaṅgunī—O woman, one should offer fuel-sticks of the aśvattha tree smeared with sheep's ghee on the new moon day; [the man] obtains a maiden, and she too shall obtain a husband. (20.86)
By means of which, when performed with purity, the fire-oblation becomes a supreme destroyer of fever.
Now follows the application of the Śrī-Nṛsiṃha mantra,
beginning with the mantra "ugravīram" and so forth.

Having worshipped the deity of the waters with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should daily offer oblations there with *dūrvā* grass one hundred and eight times; thus, calamities caused by minor spirits, demons, and the like will perish.
The rest is easy to understand. When a bad dream occurs at night, one should bathe and recite the mantra;
by reciting the mantra vigilantly throughout the night, a good dream will arise. (20.88)
O great savor, when one is agitated by fear of tigers, thieves, wild beasts, and the like,
the practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during other times of fear.
And consecrated with this mantra, the ashes will destroy the great terrors of poison and planetary afflictions very quickly, through the power of this mantra. (20.90)
O God, during a terrible malevolent rite, a great portent, or a time of great fear, one should recite the mantra and remember the God; thus a person shall be liberated from sufferings. (20.91)
Having fashioned a ninefold mandala endowed with mantras, the mantra-practitioner should place nine beautiful jars within it. (20.92)
Let it be filled with decoction water and endowed with gems and other such items;
in the center, one should worship the god Nṛsiṃha, whose form is radiant.
The practitioner of mantra should worship Tārkṣya and the others in due order, starting from the east;
then, with the waters thus consecrated, he should perform the most beloved consecration. 20–94.
Sorcery, possession by spirits, and insanity perish along with one's enemies;
then, being consecrated and at ease, one should worship the deity with devotion. (20.95)
Afterwards, one should worship the supreme guru with devotion as he truly is;
by this method, a king attains victory in battles. (20.96)
The śālmali, badarī, jambu, āmra, and likewise the vakula—these five are declared by the learned preceptors there to be astringent (kaṣāya). || 20.97 ||
Āṃ hrīḥ kṣauṃ krauḥ phaṭ!
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times during the appropriate season, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual applications.
The wise one should offer one hundred and ten oblations of dūrvā grass, milk, and ghee.
One should offer oblations every day; thus one shall attain a full and long life.
By means of the *roha* and other rites, his magical spells (*kṛtyā*) together with the *roha* and so forth shall perish.

Restraining his senses, he should daily offer the *mañjarī* of the *apāmārga* plant along with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for seven days, using the measure of one thousand recitations.
This oblation, performed in every way and at all times, shall destroy the afflictions caused by malevolent spirits and diseases;
[this is achieved] by offering three thousand pieces of *amṛtā* for four days as prescribed.
By this, the fire-oblation (homa) that destroys delusion and fever is ordained.
Now follows the application of the Sudarśana mantra:
having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times during the month of Arkalākṣa, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual applications.
He who offers oblations for three days, made of sugar and flour,
one thousand and eight times, shall conquer the state of being powerless.
O Udumbara, may you be a bestower of sons upon men;
[may you be] like the autumn moon, possessing the letter *sā*, raining down streams of nectar. 20-104.
One who meditates upon this [mantra] on the head shall live free from disease.
Musta, śuṇṭhī, niśā, brahmī, elā, yaṣṭi, vacā, and vṛṣā—[these are the ingredients]. (20.105)
One should [use] pāṭhā, viṭsa, mañjiṣṭhā, and drākṣādi-vicarohiṇī; with the three fruits (phalatraya) and taikta, along with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and ghee.
One should cook one *prastha* according to the rule, prepared with this mantra—either thirty-two *akṣas* [of seeds], as stated by oneself or indeed by one's own [teacher]. (20.107)

The wise know that pure *pañcagavya-ghṛta* (ghee prepared from the five products of the cow) bestows beauty, is auspicious for those with fangs, destroys the power of spirits, and protects the fetus. (20.108)

Now, regarding the five products of the cow (pañcagavya): one pala of milk is prescribed as the portion, and the cow urine is desired to be of the same measure; likewise, one pala of ghee and two tolakas of cow dung. (20.109)
A mere handful of curd is known as this *pañcagavya*.
Now follows the application of the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra:
having recited the mantra three hundred thousand times, one performs the ritual applications as previously stated. (20.110)
Having propitiated the fire according to the rules, the mantra-practitioner, with his senses subdued, should offer a thousand oblations of milk-rice and black gram.
Śaṅkara, his body moistened by that nectar, was satisfied;
he shall increase one's lifespan, health, prosperity, cattle, and sons. (20.112)
"Self-sustaining power, the vaṭa tree, sesame, dūrvā grass, milk, clarified butter, and milk-offering"—
thus it is said;
one should offer oblations with these seven substances on the seventh day.
One should constantly and without sloth recite one hundred and eight [times] in sequence.
One should always feed seven Brahmins together with virtuous people; O Minister, one should choose food characterized by its various preparations from the day after tomorrow.

One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the *hotṛ* priests—a cow that is not barren and is rich in milk—and afterwards, one should honor the teacher with forest produce and other offerings, regarding him as a deity. (20.115)
By this method, O noble one, having performed [the rite], one is freed from fever and other ailments; one shall live for a very long time and easily attain auspiciousness and happiness. (20.116)

In cases of malevolent magic, against Brahmā, the Guru, the Ātman, and diseases of the head; in incurable diseases, afflictions caused by *kṣetrapālas*, delusion, burning sensations, and great terrors—[one should employ this]. (20.117)
This oblation is declared to be bestowing peace and the granter of all prosperity;
one should offer these substances according to the rule throughout one's own births.
One should feed Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas with sweet foods;
thus one attains long life and obtains desired prosperity. (20.119)
Then, one should daily offer eleven oblations with dūrvā grass;
this increases longevity and health and removes the defects of untimely death.
A *homa* performed with jasmine flowers from Kāśmīra and other blossoms, along with honey, during three births, removes all death and disease. (20.121)
An oblation of cooked rice is prescribed for the destruction of great afflictions;
an oblation with fuel-sticks of *apāmārga* is the destroyer of all diseases.
Then, for the pacification of disease, Mahiṣa [recited] ten thousand times the Cintāmaṇi mantra:
"This seed-syllable, surrounded by *surā*, is the supreme nectar of the *vilalpa*. (20.122)
This lunar disc at the crown of the head removes the obstacles of meditation;
the seed-syllable *svarā* (the vowels) is for each hair-pore, and the fire-seed (*ra*) is situated in the house.

The syllable *ra* and so forth, shining with the *jatā* (braided hair) ornament, surrounded by a hexagon and encircled by fire; "and so forth" refers to *i*, *la*, *ka*, *ṣa*, *ma*, *ra*, and *ya*; this is the meaning, [arranged] in reverse order according to the vowels. (20.124)
From *aḥ*, *a*, *au*, *o*, *ai*, *e*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *ṝ*, *ṛ*, *ū*, *u*, *ī*, *i*, and *ā* down to *a*—this is the extent [of the vowels].
That which is known as the food of the elements, when placed upon the head, shall swiftly destroy the element. (20.125)

The seed-syllable of Smara (Kāma) situated upon the moon of the seed-syllable, with sixteen [digits] dripping a flood of *parasvadhā* (nectar), when meditated upon in the eyes, removes disease. (20.126)

In the very same way, the seed-syllable of mindfulness (smṛti-bīja) removes diseases such as colic in the womb, as well as boils, inflammation, poison, burning sensations, delusion, headaches, and vertigo. (20.127)
This seed-syllable, when meditated upon in that manner, destroys the afflictions; it should be placed upon a betel leaf and consecrated with this mantra.
When consumed, it properly destroys diseases of the head; of this there is no doubt.
This application of the Bhairavī mantra bestows prosperity. (20-129)
Having recited the mantra "Laṃ" [one hundred and] eight times, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual applications;
by offering oblations of milk, *akṣaka* seeds, *amṛtā*, and sugar-candy, one conquers all death. (20.130)
For three days, one should perform a fire-oblation with *dūrvā* grass that has put forth flowers and is smeared with milk;
the practitioner should offer parched grain (*lāja*) mixed with curds, milk, and honey. (20.131)
Having conquered all the worlds while still alive, he attained a portion of the state of Śiva.
Now follows the application of the Śrīvidyā mantra: having recited it one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule, the wise man is liberated from all obstacles. (20.132)

One who is oppressed by the fear of poverty shall obtain a kingdom through a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma). Through the oblation of a hundred thousand offerings, there is the pacification of calamities affecting the city and the subduing of enemies. (20.133)
Having performed a fire sacrifice at a crossroads at night, one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*).
O fair-faced one, having separated milk, curd, honey, and ghee individually, [one should offer them] with the mantra "Onion is life" (*palāṇḍu prāṇa*). (20.134)
