Having consumed cow's urine, meat, honey, and food while recollecting the mantra of Maheśvarī, longevity, strength, health, and prosperity arise for men. (20.135)
O Goddess, honored by heroes, having gone at night to a crossroads, one becomes a sky-walker (khecara) by performing a fire-oblation with curd, honey, milk, and parched grain. (20.136)
It is undoubtedly the destroyer of disease, the remover of time, and the slayer of death;
a homa performed with red lotuses correctly bestows prosperity. (20.137)
By means of a homa of guggulu resin, one shall destroy all suffering;
by means of a homa of sesame seeds and rice, peace shall prevail in the home. (20.138)
Accompanied by attendants (*vaṭukas*), one should destroy the obstacles;

likewise, for rites of pacification (*śānti*) as well as for agriculture, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be square. O Goddess, for the sake of both enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), one should employ a long pit.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the *Śrī-Āgamakalpalatā*.
Now I shall explain the practice of subjugation (*vaśya*) according to various tantras.
Next is the application of the mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī.
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the reality, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual applications.
Having taken camphor and agallochum combined with well-prepared saffron, the king should apply an excellent forehead mark (tilaka) that brings about tranquility. (21.2)
Having prepared a dish made of *śāli* rice mixed with honey and sugar,
and having consecrated it through the recitation of mantras (*japa*), one should consume it on a Sunday.
Having drawn a well-executed magical figure with ashes upon a wooden board or similar surface, one causes a king, a woman, or even a man to become submissive. (21.4)
At that time, while reciting the Darśana-mantra, one should comfortably offer oblations at night into the fire of the sun-god with mustard seeds mixed with salt and black gram.
The practitioner should not worship the king immediately, nor even his queen.
Now follows the application of the mantra for those in haste: having recited the mantra ten thousand times, one may perform the ritual applications... || 21-6 ||
The number of oblations (homa) is ten thousand, and the recitation (japa) is proclaimed to be of the same extent;
having prepared a yoni-shaped sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the oblation at the triple junction (trisaṃdhyā).
By offering oblations of jasmine flowers (*mallikākusuma*), one may subjugate the entire world;
by offering blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*), the practitioner of mantra may bring even the wife of a king under his control.
Having offered blossomed lotuses, the Goddess who subdues the lords of demons comes under one's control.
Now follows the ritual application for Mahiṣamardinī:
having recited the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
One may bring men under control, or even their images, by means of an oblation of sesame seeds.
Now follows the application of the mantra for Śūlinī:
with *akṣata* grains, sesame seeds, or those mixed with sweet substances. (21.9)
Through the fire sacrifice (homa), the practitioners quickly bring their desired objects under control.
Now follows the application of the mantra of Vanadurgā.
The mantra is as follows:
Having risen and recited the mantra four hundred thousand times, and so forth... || 21-10 ||
One should honor the Brahmins with flowers; [one wins over] a king by means of a lotus-homa;
his wife [is won over] by blooming blue lotuses through a homa of white water-lilies.
A wise man should [subjugate] Śūdras with the *lakkuṇa*-oblation and the assembly with *jātipuṣpa* flowers.
Now follows the application of the *Satpadā Bhairavī* mantra:
having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the reality (*tattva*), the intelligent practitioner should perform the ritual application. (21–12)
Having recited the mantra in reverse order, one should perform the rite for the accomplishment;
having uttered the mantra, the practitioner should offer oblations with [substances] mixed with honey.
With mustard seeds mixed with *paṭu* (salt), one brings kings under control in an instant;
by this very procedure, one likewise subdues their wife and even their daughter. (21.14)
Having ground together two parts of *layaja* (fragrant resin), one part of saffron filaments (*kuṅkumakesara*), and one part of yellow pigment (*rocanā*) from the feet with snow-water,
one should apply a tilaka on the forehead; by doing so, two travelers are made to vanish.
Those by whom one is touched while hunting, or those who are touched by him, shall come under his control after a long time. || 21-15 ||
One should prepare equal parts of camphor and *kapicūra*;
*jaṭāmāṃsī* should be four parts, and *rocanā* is considered to be the same amount.
Saffron should consist of seven parts, sandalwood is considered to be two parts, and agarwood should be nine parts; such is the sequence of the proportions.
Having received this entire well-composed answer from the daughter of the Himavat, the lord of the earth should take it and apply it as a tilaka upon his forehead. (21.18)
Having described those who are free from pride and arrogance, [he described] the lions, tigers, great serpents, spirits, vetālas, and rākṣasas born from the limbs of the dying Madonmatta.
A man who wears the *tilaka* becomes subject [to her] merely by seeing it.
Now follows the practice for the Mātaṅginī: having recited the mantra ten million times (*prayuta*), one should then perform the ritual application (*prayoga*). (21–20)

For the purpose of subjugation, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, gorocana, saffron, and other substances; thus he shall bring the entire world under his control.
Having recited these, one should perform the *nīlaka* rite; one will become beloved by the world.
With fruits produced at the root of a *vilva* tree, his three-fold oblation (*traivāhuta*) is accomplished.
For a prince, [the rite performed] with lotuses brings about the fire of sovereignty and he shall attain auspiciousness.

Now follows the ritual application (*prayoga*) of the mantra of Śrī Gaṇapati: Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the Vedas, the wise practitioner, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śukra,
should daily [offer oblations] ending with the dative case, using respectively coconut, parched grain flour, jaggery, and sesame seeds.
One should offer four hundred oblations, and all living beings will become submissive.
By offering parched grain that is sweet and free from husks into the fire, one bestows a daughter [in marriage].
By this rite, a maiden obtains her desired husband. (21–24)
By performing oblations at night for four days with curd and salt stirred together, one brings about great satisfaction;
likewise, it always effects subjugation.
O Śvetaketu, it was not made by Bhava using the root of a tree, nor by Raktacandana wood, nor by an image carved from an elephant tusk, nor by Dantidatta.
Having worshipped Vighneśvara during a lunar eclipse, one should conquer [the obstacles];
having touched it, O practitioner, while remaining without food, one should bear it upon the crest-lock.
In battles, in legal proceedings, and so forth, one shall obtain prosperity through recitation (*japa*).
When *rocanā* (yellow pigment) is consecrated with this meter and mixed with honey, [it grants success]. (21.28)
By means of the *tilakanniyā* [mudrā], one brings all human beings under control;
with the power residing in the *anuloma*, one should draw the *rasa*.
Having performed the worship and touched [the object], one should mutter the *prāṇa-mantra* ninety times;
thereafter, one should further mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Adopting the Mūta posture, one should consume [the substance] for seven days according to the prescribed measure;
there is no doubt that prosperity will swiftly come to the practitioner. (21–31)
Now follows the application of the Mahāgaṇapati mantra:
*Oṃ hrīḥ śrīḥ klīḥ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. Having recited the mantra four hundred thousand times.

By means of the lotus-homa, kings [are won]; by the three auspicious [flowers], ministers; by blooming water-lilies (kumuda), [one wins] Brahmins; and by those produced from the Pippala tree, [one wins] the same.
Through *plakṣa* trees grown from branches, one attains subjugation (*vaśyatva*); if the practitioner lacks faith, he does not come under control.
With honey, there shall be the acquisition of gold; with cow’s milk, one obtains cattle.
By means of an oblation of clarified butter, a person attains great glory.
By burning [the offerings], all prosperity shall be attained; by means of food, one becomes a lord of men.
Herein follows the application of another mantra:
having recited the mantra three hundred thousand times, the wise one should perform the ritual applications. (21–34)
Having offered cakes smeared with the three sweets, one shall bring earthly rulers under control;
with salt mixed with honey, one shall bring women under control.

The application of other mantras: Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, the wise one may perform the ritual applications; by means of an oblation of clarified butter, he shall bring all living beings under his control. (21–36)
O Mantrin, by daily reciting the *hūṃ* mantra over a ripe coconut fruit wrapped in a piece of hide from a *lāṣṭra* animal, one shall attain accomplishment (*siddhi*) from the mandala. (21.37)
One should perform oblations with eight substances combined with the three sweets;
by this rite, one shall bring all the wives of kings under one's control.
He spoke of the offering consisting of eight substances:
"With sweetmeats, flattened rice, parched grain with husks, along with *ikṣu* stalks, coconut, pure sesame seeds, cooked plantains, and fruits. (21.39)
The eight substances of the obstacle have been declared by the wise sages.
Now follows the application of the Śrīnarasiṃha mantra:
having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the season, [one attains] the yogas.
Having bathed and being endowed with the three sweets, they offered oblations at the proper times.
Thereafter, the maiden shall attain perfection, and she shall become the excellent consort of Kaṭyāyana.
Now follows the application of the Cintāmaṇi mantra of Maheśvara. (21–41)
"One hundred thousand times"—as previously stated.
This bright triad of seed-mantras, possessing the luster of saffron, situated upon the forehead:
by whose head it is meditated upon, that person becomes submissive after some time. (21.42)
The seed-syllable named Sādhya, with the letter *ra* above it, is situated within the abode of fire; it is established in the name joined by two abodes of fire and the short vowel *u*. (21.43)
Anointed with *pratiloma* liquor and placed in the location of the hearth (*culle-sthāna*), she will, from that very moment until death, become submissive like a slave. (21.44)
Having fashioned an effigy out of rice flour mixed with the three sweets,
and having consecrated it by bestowing life-breath upon it, the one seeking subjugation should consume it and then offer it as an oblation.
By reciting [the mantra] for three days, she will become subject to his control; this is achievable by a beginner.
Now follows the application of the Vaṭukabhairava mantra: having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one may perform these applications.
For the purpose of subjugation, one should offer oblations in the cardinal directions with *śalaka* wood to bring people under control.
One should perform oblations with beautiful, blossoming white water-lilies for the sake of obtaining a son;
by offering salt mixed with honey, one may bring women under one's control.

A woman who has not conceived and desires a son should take one *pala* of powdered *vacā*, consecrated with mantras and mixed with cow’s clarified butter; having divided it, she should consume it while performing the *maṇḍala* rite. (21.48)
One obtains a disciplined son endowed with intelligence, health, and strength;
at the beginning and end of the ritual application, one should offer a row of *vaṭuka* oblations.
Mudga-pulse mixed with meat, stirred with the three sweets (honey, sugar, and ghee), along with uśīra, sandalwood, kuṣṭha, deodar wood, and saffron. (21.50)
O Vārāhī, one should dry and powder the root of white Arka, Lakṣmī, Kṣīra, Mahi, and Nṛha, along with the root of Urvilva and Naroma. (21.51)
Having made balls [of clay] from powder mixed with cow dung in the courtyard,
and having purified them, [he should offer them] into the consecrated sacrificial fire.
Burned with the root mantra, one should place that ash in a pure vessel;
having prepared the ash, one should perfume it with *kaṭekī* or *mālatī* flowers.
Having seen the well-worshipped ashes, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
then, taking this [ashes] daily, he who applies the sectarian mark (puṇḍra) becomes possessed of life-force (prāṇa).
His diseases perish—sorcery, possession by spirits, and afflictions—and no fear arises for him from enemies, thieves, wild beasts, or the like. (21.55)
All calamities increase, yet he is honored by all people;
even the king, along with his entire retinue, shall become subject to him. (21.56)
Now follows the application of the Bhairava mantra:
having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the reality (tattva), one performs the following applications.
With red stones, or with *ruru* deer, or with *vāha* and *pārija* flowers, smeared with honey...
Having offered Mallikā flowers as an oblation, he leads the prince to his own portion.
With flowers such as *evavilla* and *bhavai*, combined with the three sweets, one should bring men and women under control by offering them to the Lord of Men. (21.58)
Having ground together one part of *pādahṛya*, one part of *malapaja* from the filaments of saffron, and one part of *gorocana*, [one should] apply this to the forehead.

One should apply vermilion on the forehead; by means of that, whatever one sees, whatever one looks upon, whatever one touches, or whatever touches one—all those shall belong to him for a long time. (21.60)
One should prepare equal parts of camphor and *kapicūra*;
one-fourth part of *jaṭāmāṃsī*, and the same amount of *rocanā* and *manā*.
Saffron shall consist of seven parts, sandalwood three parts, and agarwood nine parts; such is the sequence of the proportions.

Having taken this, which has been prepared with snow-water and ground with a maiden, and which contains all medicinal herbs, one should apply it as a tilaka on the forehead; O King, it will subdue men.
Women, those intoxicated by pride and the like, elephants in rut, lions, tigers, great serpents, bhūtas, vetālas, and rākṣasas—[he subdues them all]. (21.64)
Merely by seeing [this], a man who wears the *tilaka* comes under his control.
Now follows the application of the *Śrīvidyā* mantra:
having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one performs the ritual applications (*prayoga*).
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, this is the meditation on the Great Kāmakalā and its yoga.
One should agitate the women of the heavenly realm, the world of mortals, and the depths of the netherworld;
[using] one part each of *rocanā* and saffron.
Then, O Goddess, one should grind two equal parts of sandalwood together; by making them into a single essence, it becomes the cause of subduing the three worlds.
Having consecrated [the object] one hundred and eight times with the mantra, one shall bring it under control. Thus ends the section on subjugation (*vaśya*).
I shall now fully explain the rites of immobilization (*stambhana*) according to their various types.
Now, for the swift mantra:
ten thousand (ayuta) recitations are proclaimed as its measure;
having prepared a vulva-shaped sacrificial pit (yonikuṇḍa), one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to one's own desire. (21.69)
Through a monthly *homa*, one becomes a destroyer of enemies by means of the *unmattī* [mantra].

Now follows the application of the *śūlinī* mantra: having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables, the wise practitioner should accomplish the ritual application. (21–70)
Having taken cow dung, one should then recite the mantra three thousand times in the open air;
having gone to the gateway and buried it there, immobilization (staṃbhanam) will occur.
Now, regarding Vanadurgā:
having recited the mantra four hundred thousand times, one may perform these applications;
for the paralyzing of an army, O practitioner, [one should use] substances produced from the Kāraskara tree.
One should offer a thousand flowers as an oblation; that [result] one should bestow upon one's wife.
It is well known as *kāraskara-kucila*. Now, regarding the *mātaṅgī*:
having first recited the mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*), one should then perform the ritual application (*prayoga*).
One should paralyze the enemy with weapons smeared with powdered turmeric.
Now, regarding Nṛsiṃha:
"Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its color,
one should duly perform [the rite] for the warding off of an enemy army."
When the fire is kindled with Vibhītaka wood, it crushes the enemy.
Having meditated upon the Lord Nṛhari and worshipped Him with flowers and other offerings,
one should daily offer ten thousand oblations separately with *śala* wood, including the roots.

O King, having offered oblations for seven days while reciting the mantra "ṛpuṃ khādan nivajad vāhni," one should cast [the substance] into the fire; thus, O Lord of Ministers, the enemy army will become as sweet as nectar.
Having established it in an auspicious lagna for the sake of obtaining [victory], one should perform the recitation for the kingdom with diligence;
before that [recitation], one should strike down that circle of enemies belonging to Hari.
Having touched [the object], one should perform the ritual application until it returns;
then, having conquered all enemies, one will easily attain the glory of a hero along with happiness.

Having arrived, the victorious king should properly gratify the minister with villages, fields, wealth, and other riches, according to his heart's desire; for if the minister is satisfied, O lord of men, there shall be no misfortune.
Now, regarding Vaṭuka:
having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its color,
one should offer ten million oblations of pure salt for the purpose of paralyzing [an enemy] in the shade.
The application for the sake of liberation from the *nigraha* (subjugation) and other rites has been declared.
Now, he describes the application of the *Śrīvidyā*:
"Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, the wise practitioner should perform the applications. (21.80)
Having drawn [the diagram] with yellow pigments and offered yellow flowers,
one facing the eastern direction shall paralyze all disputants.
O Goddess, one who has a thousand faces becomes mute at that very moment,
when Yāmī, facing him, presents a black discus.
For whomsoever [the name] is inscribed, for that person a loss of the mantra occurs;
by offering *caṃpaka* leaves, one attains unsurpassed prosperity. (21.83)
One obtains great power over those who support this world through the *mātṛ* [mantras];
by means of white offerings and oblations, there is the paralyzing of enemies, O crow-like one. (21.84)
Now, regarding Chinnamastā:
O beautiful one, having offered buffalo meat with honey, one may quickly paralyze enemies, even those situated at a great distance. (21.85)
O daughter of a king, O auspicious one, by offering *caṃpaka* flowers mixed with clarified butter into the fire,
one shall swiftly paralyze even a most terrible enemy army.
Thus ends the section on immobilization (*staṃbhanaprakaraṇa*).
I shall now fully explain the rite of causing enmity (*vidveṣa*) according to the sequence of the *Nāgārjuna-tantra*.
He states the application of the *Tvaritā* mantra:
The number of oblations (homa) should be ten thousand; the recitation (japa) is proclaimed to be of that same amount.

Having fashioned a vulva-shaped sacrificial pit (yonikuṇḍa), one should then perform the fire oblation (homa) according to one's own desire. With whatever substances [are available], one should likewise cause those who are divided to be reconciled with one another. (21.88)
Now, with eighty thousand oblations of Mahiṣamardinī, the fire-sacrifice is performed; it spreads hatred among men. Now, with Śūlinī:
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed color, one should offer oblations of cow-dung cakes (*ūlikā*) produced from cow dung, numbering eight hundred. (21.89)
Within seven days, it causes enmity between two friends.
Now, as for Vanadurgā:
having recited the four-syllable mantra...
Having recited [the mantra] over the ash arising from the mind at Agakhara Kulika, || 21.90 ||
One who is hated by an enemy should cast [the substance] upon the head of that foe, and he shall depart from the country.
Now, regarding Śrīvidyā:
having recited it one hundred thousand times according to the rule, a man performs the ritual application. || 21-91 ||
Having extracted the juice from buffalo dung and horse dung onto a stone slab,
one should scratch [the name] with cow urine and append the name as before.
Having placed [the substance] in the midst of salt, it becomes a cause for inciting enmity;
having thrown [it] into salt, it is placed in the midst of *āraṇāla*—thus in the *Catuḥśatikā*. (21.93)

The *āraṇālaṃkācika* [is used]; the *cakrarāja* placed in oil will cause enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*). "Written with *rocanā*"—the word *yantrarāja* (king of diagrams) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
Thus ends the section on causing enmity.
Now I shall proclaim the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) according to various tantras.
Now follows the swift application of the mantra:
ten thousand is the number for the fire-oblation (homa), and the same amount is prescribed for the recitation (japa).
Having prepared a vulva-shaped sacrificial pit (yonikuṇḍa) here, one should perform the oblation according to one's own desire. (21.95)
Having become one of noble birth like a *patra* tree, one may swiftly cause an enemy to be driven away;
this refers to Vanadurgā.
Having recited the mantra four hundred thousand times—thus it is said.
Holding a bow and arrows, he was fearsome, seated upon a lion, and resembled a blazing fire.
One who stands in the midst of water should meditate upon me and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times; then volleys of arrows will be discharged, running toward the enemy.
One will certainly and swiftly expel both the enemy and the supreme [opponent].
Now, regarding the Śrī Narasiṃha mantra:
"Manujatva" (O you who have become human), [visualize] the form of a lion, most terrifying, with extremely fearsome claws and fangs.
Having remembered oneself as the enemy, one should afterwards [conquer] the enemy Mṛgaśiras by means of expenditure.
Having gone to the house, one should again look at that [target] at the throat;
then the enemy undergoes eradication by means of sons, friends, wife, and so forth. (21.99)
Previously, at Mṛtyupada, Hari himself, having performed the rite of naming the one to be subdued,
shattered the enemy Smara into pieces with his sharp claws, fangs, and other weapons.
One should constantly recite this mantra written by me one hundred and eight times;
before long, even an enemy becomes a lover of wealth.
Having recited the mantra of Śrīvidyā one hundred thousand times,
one should write the name situated in the middle of the syllable *kāka* using yellow pigment (*rocanā*).
Then, that which is being recited in the sky brings about the eradication of enemies. || 21-102 ||
Properly placed in the midst of cow urine, it becomes a destroyer of enemies.
Now, as for Chinnamastā:
a homa performed with crow feathers in a fire of datura, while remaining composed, [achieves this]. (21.103)
Having stirred it with pungent oil, there is immediate expulsion and killing;
for expulsion, the hearth (kuṇḍa) should be circular and well-proportioned.
Now, regarding Nīlasarasvatī:
having taken a skull from a cremation ground at night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, and having wrapped it in a black cloth, one should bind it with the aforementioned mantra. (21.105)
Having consecrated a dog with mantras, one should cast it into the enemy's house;
within seven days, this will bring about their eradication.
Thus ends the section on eradication (*uccāṭana*).
I shall now fully explain the rite of killing (*māraṇa*) according to the sequence of names and mantras.
Now, as for Tvaritā:
Having performed the recitation ten thousand times, it is proclaimed as "japa. || 21-107 ||

Having prepared a vulva-shaped sacrificial pit (*yoni-kuṇḍa*) here, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). By performing it with mustard seeds, one obtains the destruction of all enemies through the oblation.
Furthermore, O Goddess, by means of grains, one shall destroy spirits, thieves, ghosts, and the like.
Now, regarding Śūlinī; now, regarding Vanadurgā;
the mantra is four hundred thousand recitations.
Where the winds flow by means of those [channels] arising from the single flavor of attachment. || 21.108 ||
Having fashioned a very beautiful image out of *kāraskāra* wood, the dust from its feet shall utterly destroy the enemy. (21.109)

Having recited [the mantra] and established the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), one should pierce the limbs; thus, having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the syllables, one should perform the fire-oblation (*juhuyāt*) with sesame seeds, *siddhārtha* (white mustard), and so forth, one hundred thousand times according to the rule.
One should recite the mantra joined with the name of that person who is destined to meet their death.
Now, regarding Vanadurgā:
the mantra consists of four hundred thousand recitations.
It is formed with the letter *ka* produced from the essence (*rasa*) and fallen leaves from the desert (*marut*).
An enemy shall destroy his fire-oblation with dust from the feet of that [deity].
Having fashioned a beautiful image according to the prescribed proportions,
and having performed the recitation of mantras and the rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), one should then dissolve it limb by limb.
Combined with the fat of a crow and an owl, one thousand and eight [oblations] should be offered into the sacrificial fire in a cremation ground on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
One should offer oblations for three days; thus, by night, [the enemy] is destroyed.
From the oblation of *utpala* wood, one becomes intoxicated through a hundred [repetitions of the] recitation.
The eating of an owl and a crow.
Now, regarding Narasiṃha:
having first performed the meditation according to the instruction of Mṛtyu—that the mantra consists of one hundred thousand syllables—this Hari [is to be worshipped].
Recalling his enemy, one should constantly and fearlessly mutter the mantra one hundred and eight times while being torn apart by sharp claws, fangs, and the like.
Within the mandala, one is born as an enemy dear to Vaivasvata.
Now, regarding the Sudarśana weapon:
"Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times as many as the sun (one hundred and twenty-one thousand),
one should visualize its wheel, equal to a forest fire, upon the head of the [enemy]."
Fainting from that food, he meets his death from the mandala. || 21-116 ||
O Maheśānī, if [the victim] is burnt in the fire of the maṇḍala for forty-nine days, O Śiva, one shall kill the enemy.
The mantra "jvara-jvara" placed in the middle will bring about the destruction of the enemy;
by reciting it and performing oblations at night, one may cause the downfall of an entire kingdom.
One should offer oblations of *kokilā* wood into the fire of the funeral pyre;
thus one slays the army of enemies even when they are situated at a great distance.
For the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), the wise practitioner should construct a circular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). || 21-119 ||
Now, regarding Nīlasarasvatī:
one should write the mantra upon a human bone using turmeric mixed with alkali;
having recited it a thousand times, one should cast it into a cremation ground at the three junctions of time.
"Death shall befall him in whose house [the object] is deposited within three months. Thus ends the section on killing.
This is the twenty-seventh sprout in the *Āgamakalpalatā*.
Now, the family-bath (*kulasnāna*).
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
"With a *darbha* blade from the family-vessel (*ācāntakula*), [one performs the bath] together with a *darbha* and a family-mark (*kulapuṇḍra*) [21.121]."
Having taken a vessel of noble lineage, along with a cloth, a wooden ladle, and a wick,
one should perform the ritual bath for the pleasure of the family deity.
Having formed this resolve, he should place the *kulacakra* in the water.
The *kuladevī* is *nāda*;
she possesses the forms of the moon, sun, and fire, as well as the three strikes of the phonemes.
Silver is known as the moon, gold as the sun, and copper as fire;
these are declared to be the portions of metal according to the numerical value of their respective syllables. (21.124)
One should prepare a mudrā with these [ingredients] mixed together;
having recited [the mantra] more than a thousand times, one should then offer it as an oblation after asking permission.
Into that [liquid], the woman should pour mustard seeds according to the previously mentioned number;
having placed that mudrā into a jar, she should perform the consecration as described in the section on abhiṣeka.
Having invoked the Goddess, one should worship her with composed offerings;
having sprinkled [the disciple] and dispelled his distress, one should give the mudrā to the Guru.
This amulet is a protection that destroys chest diseases, poisons, and fevers;
it especially provides protection against wild beasts, thieves, predatory animals, and the like. (21.128)

A lord of men who wears [this] shall attain victory in battle. Regarding the "iron portion": sixteen parts are of copper, twenty-five parts are of silver, and ten parts are of gold; of this [alloy], sixteen [parts] are [of iron].
Twenty-five and ten;
uncombined, not made into many. Having brought together the family-bath (kula-snāna), the family-seal (kula-mudrā), and the kuśa grass. || 21-129 ||
Having summoned all the family *tīrthas* right there into that water which is of the nature of Śiva,
one should perform the sprinkling three times.
As it is said in another tantra:

"O Goddess, having poured water three times upon the crown of the head with the mudrā known as the 'water-pot' (kumbha), the foremost of practitioners should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana). (21.131)
One should perform the rites for the knowledge of the Self and other practices;
as it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"O best of practitioners, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) for the Kula-sun, the deity. (21.132)
One should perform the expansion of the knowledge of the Self and practice other [rites] as well.
As it is stated in the *Jñānārṇava*:
"One should offer the arghya three times to the divine Kulasūrya. (21.133)
353a) Obeisance to the gods and likewise to the ancestors; satisfy them, O deity, with water.
Now, regarding family custom (*kulācāra*):
it is stated thus in the *Bhadrakālītantra*:
And I shall proclaim the conduct which, when performed, causes one to hear [the truth] even after death.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, he observes the conduct of his commitments;
he abandons transient actions and is intent upon the performance of eternal duties.
Devoted solely to the state of Śiva through the mere propitiation of mantras, he offers all his actions to the Supreme Deity. || 21-136 ||

Devotion to the worship of other mantras, the propitiation of other mantras, the disparagement of noble women and heroes, and the recitation of that which is composed of the nature of poison; || 21-137 ||
One should always avoid striking women in anger, and furthermore, one should contemplate the entire world as being composed of *māyā* according to the prescribed method. (21.138)
One should contemplate with a restrained mind that everything—the drink, the chewed, the sucked, the licked, the house, and even pleasure—is the form of a young woman. (21.139)
Seeing a young woman of noble birth, one should bow with a concentrated mind;
one should perform that very mental worship toward her there.
O beautiful one, whether she is young, intoxicated by the forest, old, or likewise despicable, cruel, or wicked, one should meditate upon her after having paid homage. (21.141)
One should never, under any circumstances, engage in their laughter, derision, crookedness, or unkindness; otherwise,
it will cause an obstruction to success.
Women are the gods; women are the vital breaths; women are the ornament of the bedchamber. || 21-142 ||
One should not find fault with women; rather, women are to be honored.
As it is stated in the Vīratantra:
"In this [practice], there is no restriction of direction or time, nor is there any restriction regarding standing still and so forth. (21.143)

There is no restriction regarding time for the worship of the image and so forth, nor even for the offering of oblations; rather, it is said here that in the practice of the Great Mantra, one may follow one's own will as the rule.

One should not seek purity through clothing, seats, dwellings, houses, or the touch of the body and so forth by means of wind; rather, one should resort to the state free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) therein. (21.145)

One who acts according to their own will is here called a fool, wandering with a mind distracted by worldly pursuits; how could such a person pass the time? Only through the nectar of the practice of yoga and other such means can they do so. (21.146)
The sacrifice of heroes, which consists of the worship of deities through recitation, offerings, and other such rites, is praised at all times. (21.147)
It should be performed in every land and at every sacred seat; there is no doubt about this.
As it is stated in the Śivāgama:
"Śakti, Śiva, Śakti, Brahmā, Janārdana..."
Indra’s power is the sun’s power; the moon is the power of the planets, which is constant.
The entire world is of the nature of Śakti; he who does not know this is a denizen of hell.
In the Vīra-tantra it is said: "Bathing and other rites consist of mental purity; mental victory is supreme. (21.149)
Mental worship is divine; mental offerings and so forth are likewise.
Every moment is auspicious; no inauspicious time exists anywhere.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor at twilight or in the dead of night;
worship the Goddess always, whether you have bathed or not.
At midnight, in a pure place, one should cause offerings to be given with the bali-mantra; O Goddess praised by heroes, a great worship must be performed during the night.
O lady of excellent vows, the *nādī* must by all means be performed according to my instruction;
it occurs during the *mahāniśā*,
after midnight, and also during the two [periods] of the *mūrti*.
That is declared to be the great night; that [attainment] becomes an indestructible tooth.

As it is stated in the *Gandharvatantro*: "Having observed the earth to be of dull intellect, he who constantly recites the thousand-foot [mantra] will, due to that obstacle, be struck down from his own established doctrine and fall to the surface of the earth. (21.154)

Having placed his hand upon Parvata, being fearless and striving with a focused mind, he too shall go to the shade of the tree of poetry, and you as well shall attain the nectar of immortality. || 21-155 ||
354a) Regarding moderation, he says: Having seen the household as a house of death, a man who is firm-minded should apply himself with a single measure of non-attachment. (21.156)
Then, by means of this mantra, one should obtain the mouth of the minister:
"O you with terrible fangs, O you with a gaping mouth, kiṃ iti śabda praṇādi. (21.157)
O you of terrible and most terrible form, O you who dwell within consciousness, salutations to you!
Having beheld the red garment and likewise the flower, [she became] Tripurārvikā.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, a person should mutter this mantra:
"O Tripura, who resembles a *vadhūka* flower, who destroys fear! (21.159)
O lady of excellent complexion, you have appeared for our good fortune; salutations to you!
O prince, [accept] this black cloth as well as these flowers and royal ornaments.
An elephant, a horse, a chariot, garments, a board, an ancient man, a buffalo, and the family deity—having seen these, as well as Mahiṣamardinī. (21.161)
Having prostrated before Jayadurgā, one will not be afflicted by obstacles;
O Goddess, O Mother of the World, O Tripurā, O Goddess, O Deity! (21.162)
O Goddess, bestower of boons upon devotees, O slayer of Mahiṣa, salutations be unto you!
Having beheld a vessel of food, fish, meat, and a beautiful woman— || 21-163 ||
And having seen Bhairava, O Goddess, one should bow and contemplate the mantra for the destruction of terrible obstacles and for the prosperity of the Kula conduct. (21.164)
I bow to you, O most excellent goddess, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
I bow to you whose face is drenched with streams of blood. || 21-165 ||
O Goddess who removes all obstacles, salutations to you, the beloved of Hara!
If they do not perform the vision of these [deities] in this manner, [the rite is incomplete].
If one prioritizes the mantra of power (śakti-mantra), its accomplishment does not arise.
Therefore, I shall now explain that which arises from devotion and bestows the desired accomplishments upon the practitioner.
354b) This has been stated in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*:
Śrī Bhairava said:
"The convention of the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*) and the very convention of the state (*bhāva*)."
But it has been indicated by me, O Goddess; please speak out of compassion.
The Śrī Devī said: O Vīra, the state (bhāva) is indeed threefold, arising from the semen (śukra) of the Mother;
likewise, the gurus here are threefold, as are the mantra-deities.
This state is Mahādeva; it bestows all prosperity.
Between the two [states] is my own, and the third is censured by all. (21.170)
What is the use of hundreds of thousands of heroic practices (*vīrasādhana*), or what is the use of the *kula* and *akula* methods of attraction?
They say that Śiva is the *akula*, while the *yāmeśvarī* is the *kula*.
Of what use is the state of the senses, or the performance of family customs, if one whose self is pure in being does not have the family as his ultimate refuge? (21.172)
Through devotion one attains liberation; through devotion the lineage is increased.
Through devotion there shall be the growth of the clan; through devotion the family is purified. (21.173)

What is the use of elaborate ritual deposits (nyāsa), what is the use of extensive purifications (bhūtaśuddhi), and what is the use of worship with offerings such as food (naivedya) and the like? Is it not the case that the true state [of reality] is not found in these? 21-174.
O Lord, due to excessive recitation, burnt offerings, and extensive physical austerities, the mantra-vidyā will not bestow its fruit. (21.175)
Due to the absence of fruit, there is neither existence nor non-existence for mantras;
this secret, when told, should inspire a mind free from doubt. (21.176)
The three worlds are filled with envy; wherever he has gone, he has encountered it.
As I behold Arjuna alone, I shall relate this story to you.
The Śrī Devī said:
First, the divine state is described; listen with respect. [In this city] there is a mass of splendor (*tejaḥpuñja*) which is the deity and its respective color. (21.178)
Having visualized the entire world as consisting of light, one should conceive of it as having form;
having made oneself composed of that [light], one should likewise do so for all states of being.
Having meditated upon all that within the woman, one whose mind is intent on wealth should contemplate her;
she is endowed with an entire lineage, not born of a low caste.
Whether born in various lands and endowed with virtue and beauty, she may be a second [type] from after the age of eight up until her eighth year. (21.181)
To that extent, a young maiden is to be known as one who bestows the fruit of mantra and vidyā;
indeed, through the worship of a young maiden and even through feeding a young maiden [this result is attained]. (21.182)
He shall become a treasury of knowledge simply by remaining in a state of concealment;
or else, a man should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) with his hair disheveled.
One should recite it ten thousand times; for this is remembered as its substitute:
the pith of the Mahācīna tree-creeper and bilva leaves.
The best of practitioners, honored by a thousand goddesses, attains that kingdom in the cremation ground if he remains devoted to the practice. (21.185)
In the *Vākucūḍāmaṇi*:
"Alone, in a desolate region, in a cremation ground, in a lonely forest, in an empty house, or on a riverbank, one should always dwell free from attachment. (21.186)
O Goddess, having meditated upon the Great Cinadruma tree there, one should worship it;
one should worship with flowers born from its sap with a spirit of devotion. || 21-187 ||
And Kaladeva, pure and descended through the lineage of his clan, together with Sabhaya,
meditated upon the Goddess according to the ritual rules within the great lotus of the Brahma-tree.
Thus, one should satisfy [the deities] in the mouth of Mātṛkā according to the procedure taught in the Tantras;
if one recites the mantra at night, it becomes a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā).
If it is recited twice as much on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days,
then for them there shall be that very accomplishment which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "Listen, my son, to my secret concerning that which arises from the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*);
for by being devoid of this, [beings] do not attain accomplishment even after thousands of millions of births. (21.191)

A man who follows the family scriptures and the traditional practices of his lineage, whose mind is elevated, who is all-pervading, and who is devoted to the Vaiṣṇavas—[he attains the supreme state]. (21.192)
One should endure the censure of others and always delight in helping them; one should dwell constantly on a mountain peak or in an empty monastery. (21.193)
If at a crossroads, in water, or in a deserted place, one should be accompanied by three deities;
having meditated for a moment and recited the mantra, one should bow and depart as one came.
One should pay homage to Gṛdhra, Vikṣama, Mahākālī, Kṣemaṅkarī, Jaṃbukī, and Yamadūtī while remaining unobserved.
Kukhaśūla, Bhūṣakāka, Kṛṣṇa, Mājīla, and Keśivali—these are dear to Mahācaṇḍā, who has a slender waist. (21.196)
To her whose face was serene with noble conduct, who was dear to the Lord of Kṛttivāsas,
and who was pure even in the cremation ground— he, having seen her, followed her while circumambulating.
There is no doubt that it bestows the fruits of all mantras and vidyās without exception;
from them [one may obtain] flowers, fruit, as well as unguents and so forth. (21.198)
Having offered this food offering (naivedya) consisting of betel-nut and other items, filled with that [divine] sentiment,
he should offer the toys, the bull, the earth, and so forth, to the one who delights in very dear conversation.
Having performed that act which brings about what is dear [to the deity] in whatever manner possible, one becomes a lord of the Siddhas.
One must protect it with great effort; one should cause the Nakṣatra [rite] to be performed therein.

One should worship her with great effort, so that one may not touch her at all; for if there is contact, there will be a loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*) and certain flight [from the state]. (21.201)
There is no Viṣṇu, nor Hari, nor Śaṃtu, nor Devī, nor even Ṣoḍaśī;
nor is there Mṛtyuñjaya, nor likewise Nārāyaṇa himself.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Āgamakalpalatā*, composed by the illustrious Yadunāthacakravartin.
It was written on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha in the year 1955; it is complete. May there be auspiciousness!
